units.la: GORGIAS Leontinus palliatorum disertissimus tantâ dicendi acrimoniâ, tantaque invenien-di ἀγχινοία[?] polluisse fertur, ut quemcunq; ponere sibi liberè iuberet, de quo quid audire, disseriq; à se cuperet, effecturum se protinus citra ambitionem quasi stipulato spondens, ut contrarias in partes quo libitum esset cumque, animi auditorum differendo rapiantur, flectanturque. Eadem facultate praeditos fuisse in scriptis antiquorum legimus praeter alios Sophistas, quorum meminerunt Philostratus, Eunapius, Suidas, & Hesychius Illustris, Libanium, Lucianum, Maximum Tyrium, Aristidem, Theonem, Himerium, Dionem Prusaeum, & inter Romanos mare illud Eloquentiae Tullium, ac principem omnis eruditionis Senecam, nec non Fabium Quintilianum Patrem, seu ut doctis placet, Avum alterius Fabii, cuius Institutiones Oratorias terimus[?]. Unde vero Graecis Latinisque tam propria persuadendi δεινότης[?] ? Non aliunde profecto, quam ex crebra assiduaque juventutis suae institutione atque exercitatione, cuius cum ad bene sapienterque dicendum undiquaque magnam vim esse intelligerent, nihil antiquius habuerunt, quam ut ad eiusmodi differendi de omnibus rebus ἀσκήματα primam aetatem deducerent, ea potissimum fini, ut in judiciis caeterisque negotiis quasi ἐν ἀπεχθῶς ψόγῳ[?] haberent, quod salutariter dicerent. Sic enim Eumenius Rhetor: Neq; enim tantum me aut negligentia, aut confidentia tenet, ut nesciam, quanta sit inter hanc aciem fori, & nostra illa secreta studiorum exercitia diversitas. Ibi armantur ingenia, hic prœliantur; ibi prælusio, hic pugna committitur. Nimirum quemadmodum olim tyrones gladiaturæ rudibus prius batuebāt cum lanistā, quàm ad iustam pugnam admitterentur: ita arb[?]ra-tum est, Scholam quasi ludum, forum quasi arenam esse, inquit Seneca. Atque ista Exercitationum genera Declamationes nominarunt veteres magistri, quibus scilicet fictis controversiis non linguam modò & vocem adolescentium exercebant, sed iis potissimum artibus imbuere studebant, in quibus de bonis & malis, de honesto, de turpi disputatur. Laudabile sane institutum, quod non umbratici modò homines amplexi sunt, sed & principes perf[?]æ, sicut de Germanico, Ne-rone, Severo, Gordiano, Impp. historici Scriptores memoriæ prodiderunt. Eius exercitii imago quædam in Scholis Christianorum patrum memoria conservata sit,cùm videlicet non leguleiis modò, & vulturibus istis togatis talem gymnasti-cen utilem necessariamque esse, verùm etiam sanctioribus pietatis sacerdotibus plurimum prodesse posse animadvertis-sent.Certe quidè Germaniæ nostræ Var-ro PHILIPPUS MELANCHTHON Brettanus hanc rationem exercendi juvé-tutem studiis pietatis & Ecclesiæ com-modis olim imbuendam, magni semper fecit.Coluit eamdem, atq; in Scholis nō sine fructu ingenti ursit alter ille Thales IOACHIMUS CAMERARIUS. E quorum Gymnasio postmodùm prodiit Palatinatûs nostri Phœnix,& litterarum sanctiorù Ocellus ZACHARIAS UR-SINUS. Hic enim cùm in Scholis patriç χεψμαλισμῷ[?] τὴν ἀπὸ φαινομένης σοφίας[?] tam-quam ὑποσταθμάτα[?] quædam veteris, (ut veteri verbo utar) tolutiloquentiæ repe-risset,Declamandi illam consuetudinem revocavit, suosq; veræ sapientiæ Mystas in hac arena non sine palma fortiter ex-ercuit. In hac etiam velut auctoramento lectum lōgus usus instituit DAVIDEM PAREUM, Parentem meum veneran-dum, qui se tam fideli magistro dignum semper præbuit discipulum, tantumque in omni litteratura divina adspirante gratia profecit, ut qui Præceptoris sui benemerentissimi lampada aliis quoque præ-ferret, superiorum prudentiæ idoneus visus fuerit. Successit igitur in docendi exercendique munere Magno illi VR-SINO, & Illustris Musæi, quod SAPI-ENTIÆ nominarunt, alumnos ad Christianæ sapientiæ adyta, ad exemplum Præceptoris annis compluribus recte deduxit, & cum in aliis multiplicis doctrinæ partibus, tum vel maxime in hac Exercitationum palæstra strenuè discipulos suos erudiit, atque ad Scholarum Ecclesiarumq; gubernacula ceu fidus Elysæus præparavit. Nec vero de aliis Parentis mei monumentis, quorum bonam partem Ecclesia Christiana utiliter iam legit, & nonnullam Deo sic clementer faciente, adhuc lectura est, nunc dicam, latuerunt diu in lecythis ipsius scholastica quædam γυμνάσματα de variis & gravissimis rebus, quarum cognitione & linguam & animum Candidatorum suorum informare solebat. Illa cum ab amicis & discipulis suis iam pridem diu multumque efflagitata fuissent, victus tandem & aliorum, meis quoque supplicis publicæ luci condonare non recusavit.
units.tr: Gorgias of Leontini, the most eloquent of the sophists in dress, is said to have so excelled in sharpness of speech and in quickness of invention [agchinoia] that he would promise, without any fee, at once to do whatever anyone bade him: that is, to speak on any subject he wished to hear and discuss, so that the minds of the hearers were carried off and turned to whichever side of an argument they wished. We read in the writings of the ancients that others endowed with the same skill existed, besides the other sophists whom Philostratus, Eunapius, Suidas, Hesychius Illustrius, Libanius, Lucian, Maximus of Tyre, Aristides, Theon, Himerius, Dio of Prusa mention; and among the Romans that sea of eloquence Tully, and Seneca, the prince of all learning, and also Fabius Quintilian the elder, or, as some scholars prefer, the grandfather of the other Fabius, whose Institutes of Oratory are worn by many readers. But whence came such a proper power of persuasion to Greeks and Latins? Certainly from nowhere else than from the constant and diligent training and practice of their youth. Since they understood that this was of great importance for speaking well and wisely in every respect, they held nothing more important than to lead their early years into exercises of this kind of disputation on all subjects, chiefly with this end, that in courts and other business they might have a speech that did good, rather than one held in hateful reproach. For thus the rhetor Eumenius says: "Indeed, neither negligence nor self-confidence so holds me that I do not know how great is the difference between this battle of the forum and those secret exercises of our studies. There minds are armed, here they fight; there is a sham fight, here the real battle is joined." Indeed, just as in former times novices in gladiatorial combat first practised with blunted weapons under the trainer before they were admitted to a proper fight, "so it has been judged that the school is like a training-ground, the forum like the arena," says Seneca. These kinds of exercise the ancient teachers called "declamations," in which they exercised not only the tongue and voice of young men with invented controversies, but strove chiefly to imbue them with those arts in which good and evil, the honourable and the base, are debated. A praiseworthy custom indeed, which not only private men embraced, but also princes, as the historians who wrote of Germanicus, Nero, Severus and Gordian, emperors, have handed down to memory. A certain image of this exercise has been preserved in the memory of the schools of the Christian Fathers, since they had clearly observed that such gymnastics was useful and necessary not only for lawyers and those vulture-like men in togas, but could also greatly benefit the more holy priests of piety. Certainly our Germany's Varro, Philip Melanchthon of Brittany, always thought highly of training youth in this method, to be imbued with the studies of piety and the advantages of the Church. That other Thales, Joachim Camerarius, cultivated the same and did not fail to pursue it in the schools with great profit. From his gymnasium afterwards came forth the Phoenix of our Palatinate and the Ocellus of the more holy letters, Zacharias Ursinus. For when he found in the schools a certain kind of veteran, (to use an old word) babbling, a sort of counterfeit of apparent wisdom, he revived that custom of declaiming and bravely trained his own initiates into true wisdom in this arena, not without the palm of victory. In this same arena, as if it were an oath of enlistment, long practice trained DAVID PAREUS, my venerable father, who always showed himself a disciple worthy of so faithful a master, and who made such progress in all divine literature, the grace of God breathing upon him, that he, who bore the lamp of his most deserving teacher even before others, was judged fit for the prudence of his superiors. Therefore he succeeded to the office of teaching and training after that great Ursinus, and for many years rightly led the pupils of the illustrious Museum, which they called of Wisdom, to the sanctuaries of Christian wisdom, after the example of his teacher; and while he trained his students vigorously in other parts of manifold learning, most of all in this wrestling-ground of exercises, he prepared them to steer schools and churches as a faithful Elisha. Nor shall I now speak of the other monuments of my father, of which the Christian Church already reads a good part with profit, and some part, God graciously granting it, is still to be read; these lay hidden for a long time in the chests of his school, certain scholastic exercises on various and weighty subjects, by which he was wont to form the tongue and mind of his candidates. When these had long and earnestly been demanded by his friends and pupils, he at last, overcome by the entreaties of others and of mine, did not refuse to give them to the light of public view.

units.la: Tibi verò VIR MAGNIFICE cur alienum hunc fœtum tolledum ego proponerem, causas æquissimas me habere arbitratus sum. Nam præter illas quas domi novi, numquid publica tua Dignitas hunc cultum à me requirit? Num ego te virum antiquissimi moris, & priscam gravitatem semper humanitate temperatam juxtà cum aliis vel tenuissimi muneris obsequio honorare verecundarer? A me verò tanta impietas quàm longissimè abest! Humanitatis clementiæque tuæ monumenta non una expertus est pater & meus & huius libri. Ego quoque, quā-vis Magnificentiæ Tuæ, quod sciam, nū-quam visus, benignitatis & favoris singularis signa laudare possum non obscura: quando annis proximè præterlapsis Nepotem Tuum IOH. GEORGIUM à GRYN, adolescentem in omnium virtutum exempla genitum, nostræ institutioni & disciplinæ tradidisti, in quâ simi-lis γυμνασίας[?] documenta à nobis percepit, feliciterque expressit, ita ut non levibus argumentis de tanto germine olim quid Tibi polliceri queas, colligere facile possis. Proinde huic Nepoti & Filio tuo hæc ipsa scribendi dicendiq; Pericula ut quàm studiosissimè commendata esse velis, impensè rogamus. Te namq; maximorum onerum mole, quæ solius Reip. causâ in te suscepisti, distractissimum, hisce legendis minimè vacare posse, libenter agnoscimus, certò nihilominus persuasi, hanc observantiæ nostræ humilem tesse-ram[?] Magnificentiæ T. haud ingratam futuram. Quâ fiducia freti supremum Numen assiduò invocamus, ut Te diu servet Electori Serenissimo FRIDERICO IV. Nutritio nostro clementissimo, Reip. Ecclesiæ, nobis. Ad S. Cyriacum in Vangionibus. Anno Christi Mediatoris ∞ IↃ CIX[?]. à.d. IV. Kall.Iulij.
units.tr: But to you, MOST MAGNIFICENT SIR, I thought I had very fair reasons for putting forward this foreign offspring to be lifted up. For besides those which I know at home, does your public dignity require this worship from me? Would I, who am ashamed to honour you, a man of most ancient custom and old-fashioned gravity always tempered with courtesy, with some small service of duty as with others? Far indeed from me be such impiety! Not one, my father and I, and the author of this book, has experienced the monuments of your humanity and clemency. I too, although I have never, as far as I know, been seen by your Magnificence, can praise no small signs of your kindness and singular favour: since in the years just past you handed over your grandson, JOHANN GEORG VON GRYN, a young man born as an example of all virtues, to our teaching and discipline, in which he received similar exercises from us and expressed them happily, so that from no slight evidence you can easily gather what you may hope for from so great a shoot. Therefore we earnestly ask that you wish these same Exercises in writing and speaking to be commended as diligently as possible to this grandson and your son. For we gladly acknowledge that you, distracted by the great weight of the burdens you have undertaken solely for the sake of the Republic, can hardly have leisure for reading these, yet we are nonetheless persuaded that this humble token of our respect will not be unwelcome to your Magnificence. Relying on this confidence we constantly invoke the supreme Divinity, that he may preserve you for long for the most serene Elector Frederick IV, our most gracious nourisher, for the Republic, for the Church, and for us. At St Cyriacus in Vangiones. In the year of Christ the Mediator 1609, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

units.la: Exercitatio I. Dehortatio adolescentum ab affectatione Sermonis obsoleti.
units.tr: Exercise I. Dissuasion of young men from affecting an obsolete style of speech.

units.la: Exordium sit à thesi: Nihil facilius κακοζηλία[?] : sed & nihil vanius. Ratio: Quia vitia rerum, ob naturæ corruptionem, pluribus placent, & facilius adhærent, quàm res ipsæ. Verùm à prudentioribus semper improbantur, & per se evanescunt.
units.tr: Let the introduction be taken from the thesis: nothing is easier than a perverse love of novelty [κακοζηλία], but nothing is also more vain. The reason: because the faults of things, on account of the corruption of nature, please more people and cling more easily than the things themselves. Yet they are always disapproved by the wiser sort, and vanish of themselves.

units.la: Hypothesis: Ita κακοζηλία[?] Sermonis obsoleti hodie multis præsertim adolescentibus arridet admodum: Opinantibus apicem & omne, quod dicitur, punctum eruditionis esse sic scribere, ut nemo intelligat: ita loqui quasi cum Evandri matre[?] sint educati. Gell.lib.1.cap.10.
units.tr: Hypothesis: thus a perverse affectation [κακοζηλία] of obsolete speech today pleases many, especially young men, very much. They suppose that the summit and the whole point of learning is to write in such a way that no one understands, and to speak as if they had been brought up with Evander's mother. Gellius, book 1, chapter 10.

units.la: Propositio: κακοζηλία[?] est fugienda.
units.tr: Proposition: the perverse affectation [κακοζηλία] is to be avoided.

units.la: Ratio: quia est inepta & perniciosa.
units.tr: Reason: because it is foolish and pernicious.

units.la: Confirmatio rationis fit inductio effectorum seu incommodorum, quibus antiquarii se & alios exctuciant.
units.tr: The confirmation of the reason is made by an enumeration of the effects, or disadvantages, by which the antiquarians torment themselves and others.

units.la: I. Privatio boni hominis proprii, & ad omnem usum vitæ humanæ necessarii, quod est animi sensa sermone vel scriptione significante exprimere: Hoc bonum turpe est antiquarios sibi & aliis admere.
units.tr: I. The deprivation of a man's proper good, which is necessary for every use of human life: namely, to express the feelings of the mind by speech or writing that signifies them. It is a shameful thing for antiquarians to deprive themselves and others of this good.

units.la: Amplificetur comparatione cum mutis: & illo Phavorini: Nōne homo inepte, ut quod vis abū-de consequaris, tacere potius. Gell.lib.1.cap.10.
units.tr: Let this be amplified by comparison with dumb animals, and by that saying of Favorinus: "Are you not foolish, that, in order to achieve abundantly what you want, you would rather be silent?" Gellius, book 1, chapter 10.

units.la: I I. Morosa superbia & αὐθάδεια: quia sordidibus linguæ latinæ investigandis dici non potest quam anxiè se macerent: investigatas pro auro inepte venditent.
units.tr: II. Stubborn pride and self-will: because, in searching out the dregs of the Latin tongue, they cannot be told how anxiously they torment themselves, and foolishly sell for gold what they have dug up.

units.la: I I I. Neglectus vel contemtus studiorum magis utilium, philosophiæ & aliarum facultatum: quia vocabularii in istis longam, in suis apicibus brevem viam ad eruditionis & nominis famam stulte putant sitam:
units.tr: III. Neglect or contempt of the more useful studies, of philosophy and the other faculties: because they foolishly think that the way to the fame of learning and of a name is long in those studies, but short in their own trifles.

units.la: I V. Ineptitudo ad docendum alios: quia cum aliis loqui non didicerunt.
units.tr: IV. Ineptitude for teaching others: because, since they have not learned to speak with others, they cannot teach them.

units.la: V. Audacia novandi, confingendi, & obscurandi sententias, phrases, & terminos recte constitutos & receptos in doctrinis: quæ futura est exitialissima scholarum & posteritatis pestis.
units.tr: V. The audacity of making new terms, of inventing, and of obscuring the opinions, phrases and terms that have been rightly established and received in the doctrines: which will prove the most destructive plague of the schools and of posterity.

units.la: VI. Temeritas critica: quia vix ullum authorem relinquunt intactum suis conjecturis, verisimilibus, divinationibus, notis, &c.
units.tr: VI. Critical rashness: because they scarcely leave any author untouched by their conjectures, plausible readings, divinations, notes, and so on.

units.la: Amplificetur ab incommodis: quod censuras sibi sumant etiam adolescentes, quibus judicium est parum confirmatum: Item, quod posteritas pro authoribus corruptis habitura sit multo corruptissimos.
units.tr: Let this be amplified by the disadvantages: that even young men, whose judgment is not yet sufficiently firm, assume to themselves the right of censure. Likewise, that posterity will hold authors to be corrupt who are in fact far more corrupt than they.

units.la: VII. Profanitas, quia plerique nimio profanorum authorum studio, etiam lingua & animis toti profanescant. Declaretur exemplis: quod jam non paucis nefas videatur, Deum vel Christum vel angelos nominare: libentius Deos, lovem, Mercurium, genios crepent: Item[?]: quod plerique religionem metiantur gloria: & sic facile fiant apostatae à fide.
units.tr: VII. Profanity: because most people, through an excessive devotion to profane authors, become profane both in tongue and in mind through and through. Let it be made clear by examples: that already, in the view of not a few, it seems a sin to name God, or Christ, or the angels; they prefer to cry out more gladly the gods, Jove, Mercury, and the genii. Likewise: that most people measure religion by glory, and so easily become apostates from the faith.

units.la: VIII. Addantur judicia veterum de antiquariis: Caesaris Augusti, Phavorini, Quintiliani, &c.
units.tr: VIII. Let the judgments of the ancients about antiquarians be added: those of Caesar Augustus, Favorinus, Quintilian, and others.

units.la: Obiectio 1. Antiquitas est veneranda & imitanda.
units.tr: Objection 1. Antiquity is to be revered and imitated.

units.la: Resp. moribus non verbis. Ratio. quia vocabula valent non vetustate sed usu, sicut nummi. Amplif. simili: Ineptus foret antiquitatis jactator, qui vernaculo nostro sermoni cultissimo veterum Teutonum vel Franconum obsoletum idioma hodie misceret vel anteferret.
units.tr: Answer: in morals, not in words. Reason: because words have their value not from age but from use, like coins. Amplified by a similar case: it would be a foolish boaster of antiquity who, in our most refined vernacular speech, should mix in today, or prefer, the obsolete idiom of the ancient Teutons or Franks.

units.la: Obiect. II. Elegantia placet. Resp. Haec non est sermonis obsoleti: sed puri & usitati: juxta illud Ovidianum:
units.tr: Objection II. Elegance pleases. Answer: this is not of obsolete speech, but of pure and current speech, according to that line of Ovid:

units.la: Munda sed è medio consuetaq; verba puella Scribite: sermonis publica forma placet.
units.tr: "Write with clean words, and those that the girl uses in common; the public form of speech pleases."

units.la: Obiect. III. Non solus Cicero, Cæsar, &c. scripserunt latinè:
units.tr: Objection III. Not only Cicero, Caesar, and others have written in Latin.

units.la: Resp. Sed hi purissimè. Magis igitur imitan-di.
units.tr: Answer: but these wrote most purely. They are therefore more to be imitated.

units.la: Obiect. IV. Authores sunt corrupti.
units.tr: Objection IV. The authors are corrupt.

units.la: Resp. I. Multi videntur corrupti, qui non sunt. II. Corrupta corrigantur, judicio, ex probatis authoritatibus: ab iis, qui possunt: non adolescentum temeritate vel conjecturis, quibus magis depravantur & dubii redduntur boni authores.
units.tr: Answer I. Many appear corrupt who are not. Answer II. Corrupt passages should be corrected by judgment, on the basis of approved authorities, by those who are able to do so, not by the rashness or conjectures of young men, by which good authors are rather further depraved and rendered doubtful.

units.la: (Conclusio breviter commendet studium purae latinitatis ex florentissimo Ciceronis seculo petendae: neglandes frugibus praferantur.
units.tr: (The conclusion should briefly commend the study of pure Latin, to be sought from the most flourishing century of Cicero: the chaff should be preferred to the grain.)

units.la: Exercitatio II.
units.tr: Exercitatio II.

units.la: Progymnasma in genere DemonstrativoDe obedientia Scholastica.
units.tr: Progymnasma in genere demonstrativo: De obedientia scholastica.

units.la: EXordium a praecepto Rhetorum: Interesse ubi quis quid laudet: Hypothesis fit Chria Socratis, laudare Atheniensem Athenis facile esse.
units.tr: The exordium, following the precept of the Rhetoricians: that one should be present where someone praises something. The hypothesis is made into a chria of Socrates: that it is easy to praise an Athenian at Athens.

units.la: Transitio ad propositionem per applicatione: Sic te existimare, Scholasticae obedientiae laudes ad Scholas pertinere.
units.tr: The transition to the proposition is made by application: thus you should judge that the praises of scholastic obedience pertain to the schools.

units.la: Propositio figuretur anthypophora: Videri quidem juventuti gravem: sed esse praecipuum & necessarium Scholarum nervum ac decus: suis decorandum laudibus ut ametur, &c.
units.tr: The proposition is shaped by anthypophora: it seems indeed burdensome to youth, but it is the chief and necessary sinew and ornament of the schools, to be adorned with its praises so that it may be loved, etc.

units.la: Commendationis argumenta sumantur ex locis suasoriis:
units.tr: The arguments of commendation are to be drawn from persuasive topics:

units.la: 1. Locus honesti explicet praecipua definitionis membra.
units.tr: 1. The topic of the honourable explains the principal members of the definition.

units.la: 1. Obedientia est justitia particularis erga Leges, Praeceptores, & ipsos discipulos suum singulis tribuens. Cic. 1. de Legib: Justitia est obtemperare legibus.
units.tr: 1. Obedience is the particular justice towards the laws, the teachers, and the pupils themselves, rendering to each his due. Cicero, De legibus 1: Justice is obedience to the laws.

units.la: 2. Est pars honoris parentum a Deo sancti.
units.tr: 2. It is a part of the honour of parents, which is sanctioned by God.

units.la: 3. Est pars gratitudinis, patronis & praeceptoribus debitae.
units.tr: 3. It is a part of the gratitude owed to patrons and teachers.

units.la: II. A[?] necessario: Ut sint Scholae: & rursus, ut Respub. & Ecclesiae. Hic breviter inferantur. Encomia Scholarum ex fine, qui est, efformatio talium, qui aliquando praesint & obtemperent. Cic. 3. de legib. Qui bene imperat, paruerit aliquando necesse est.
units.tr: II. From the necessary: that there may be schools, and again, that there may be the commonwealth and the Church. Here these things are briefly inferred. The eulogies of the schools arise from their end, which is the formation of such persons as will at some time preside and obey. Cicero, De legibus 3: He who commands well must at some time necessarily have obeyed.

units.la: III. Ex loco utilitatis & effectorum:
units.tr: III. From the topic of utility and effects:

units.la: 1. Obedientia habet promissionem divinae benedictionis.
units.tr: 1. Obedience carries the promise of divine blessing.

units.la: O[?]stendatur in studiis, moribus, & eventibus.
units.tr: It should be shown in studies, morals, and outcomes.

units.la: 2. Conciliat favorem Patronorum & Praeceptorum: cujus effecta ad universum vitae peragendae cursum pertinent.
units.tr: 2. It wins the favour of patrons and teachers, whose effects pertain to the whole course of life to be run.

units.la: A[?]ddatur antithesis ab incommodis contrarii, h.e, contumaciae.
units.tr: An antithesis is to be added from the disadvantages of the contrary, that is, of contumacy.

units.la: Exercitatio III.
units.tr: Exercitatio III.

units.la: A[?]n recte faciant Principes Germani, mittentes militem adiuvandum alienos subditos contra suos magistratus, saevientes in eos propter veram religionem. Pars Negans.
units.tr: Whether German princes act rightly in sending soldiers to help foreign subjects against their own magistrates, who rage against them on account of the true religion. The negative part.

units.la: EXordium sit narratiuncula praesentis expeditionis in Galliam: & varietatis judiciorum de ea[?]-tam magnatum quam vulgi.
units.tr: The introduction is a short account of the present expedition into France, and of the varied judgments about it, both of the great men and of the common people.

units.la: Propositio: Tibi etiam parum justam videri.
units.tr: Proposition: It seems to you also rather unjust.

units.la: Argum. I. quia videatur seditiosum armare subditos contra suum Magistratum.
units.tr: Argument I: because it seems seditious to arm subjects against their own magistrate.

units.la: II. Quia sit praeter vocationem ipsorum, regere vel defendere velle subditos alienos. Probe-tur ex officio magistratus. Amplificetur ex loco Petri: Nemo patiatur ut ἀλλοτριεπισκοπον[?]: Item ex regula aequitatis: Quod tibi non vis fieri.
units.tr: II: Because it is beyond their calling to wish to rule or defend the subjects of others. This is proved from the office of the magistrate. It is amplified from the saying of Peter: "Let none suffer as a meddler in other men's matters" [ἀλλοτριεπίσκοπος]. Likewise from the rule of equity: "What you would not have done to you."

units.la: Accommodetur: Nollent ipsi suos subditos armari ab aliis contra se. Item a contrariis exemplis: Multos ideo abstinere ab hac militia.
units.tr: It is applied: They themselves would not wish their subjects to be armed by others against them. Likewise from contrary examples: many therefore abstain from this soldiering.

units.la: III. Quia sibi & suis periculum accersant.
units.tr: III: Because they bring danger upon themselves and their own.

units.la: Declaretur, & amplificetur a publicis periculis magis jam patriae ingruentibus a Turca & Pontificiis, absente milite domestico.
units.tr: This is set forth and amplified by the public dangers now more and more threatening the fatherland from the Turk and the Papists, while the domestic soldiery is absent.

units.la: IV. Quia bella hoc modo latius spargantur, & plus sanguinis effundatur, cum alioqui inter paucos potuissent componi.
units.tr: IV: Because wars are spread more widely in this way, and more blood is shed, whereas otherwise they could have been settled among a few.

units.la: Obiectio: Religionis causa oppressos esse juvandos.
units.tr: Objection: those oppressed for the sake of religion must be helped.

units.la: Respond. Precibus & consolatione. Exules etiam hospitio & honestis officiis. Ratio: quia Evangelium non propagetur armis, sed confessione & patientia.
units.tr: Reply: with prayers and consolation; and with hospitality and honourable services to exiles too. Reason: because the Gospel is not propagated by arms, but by confession and patience.

units.la: Conclusio petat amici judicium; quia res gra-vis sit injustum bellum juvare.
units.tr: Conclusion: let him seek the judgment of a friend, because it is a grave matter to support an unjust war.

units.la: Pars affirmans.
units.tr: The affirmative part.

units.la: Quid recte[?] faciant pii Principes, iuvantes pro virili, subditos in Gallia, ipsorum opem implorantes in defensione necessaria contra Tyrannidem, religionis causa.
units.tr: What devout princes rightly do when they help, as far as they can, the subjects in France who implore their aid in the necessary defence against tyranny, for the sake of religion.

units.la: EXordium sit approbatio modestiae amici, quod audire cupiat aliorum sententias in re gravi. Exornetur dicto Aristotelis lib. 3. capit. 3. Ethic. συμβάλλυς δὲ ὠφελαμβανομένοις εἰς τὰ μεγάλα, ἀπέσωσιν ἡμῖν αὐτῆς ὡς ἱκανοῖς ἀξιγνῶ[?]-ναι: vel simili.
units.tr: The exordium should be a commendation of the friend's modesty, in that he wishes to hear the opinions of others on a weighty matter. Let it be adorned with the saying of Aristotle, Ethics book 3, chapter 3: "Those who contribute to great matters, being helped, have saved for us the power of it, as sufficiently worthy to be known," or something similar.

units.la: Transitio ad propositionem, per ἀνυποφοράν[?]. Etsi malis prudentiores consuli: tamen te gratificaturum amico.
units.tr: Transition to the proposition, by a figure of ... Although you might wish to be advised by wiser men, nevertheless you will gratify your friend.

units.la: Propositio. Te 1. probaturum esse, recte hac expeditione juvari Gallos religionis verae causâ periclitantes.
units.tr: The proposition: first, that you will prove that the Frenchmen, who are in danger for the sake of the true religion, are rightly helped by this expedition.

units.la: 2. Ad rationes ipsius responsurum.
units.tr: Second, that you will answer their arguments.

units.la: Confirmatio.
units.tr: Confirmation.

units.la: Argumentum I. Defensio justa juste adjuvatur ab iis, qui possunt, & a quibus postulatur.
units.tr: First argument: a just defence is justly aided by those who are able to do so and by whom aid is requested.

units.la: Hæc maior illustretur exemplis: Defensio contra Turcas, conservatio legum & disciplinæ, doctrinæ propagatio cum sit justa, juste etiam adjuvatur.
units.tr: This major premise is illustrated by examples: defence against the Turks, the preservation of laws and discipline, and the propagation of doctrine; since these are just, they are also justly aided.

units.la: Minor subjiciatur: Defensionem Gallorum contra hostes verae religionis esse justam.
units.tr: The minor premise is added: that the defence of the French against the enemies of the true religion is just.

units.la: Probatio 1. quia defensio vitæ, facultatum & dignitatis necessaria, qualis hæc sit, jure naturæ sit licita.
units.tr: Proof first: because the defence of life, property and dignity, when necessary, is by the law of nature lawful, and of what kind this one is.

units.la: Ostendatur hanc talem esse: quia propter religionem 1. sunt proscripti: 2. vita & salus omnium oppugnatur. 3. Facultatibus omnibus sunt exuti. 4. Consanguinei Principes à successione regni arcentur.
units.tr: Let it be shown that this is such a defence: because on account of religion, first, they are proscribed; second, the life and safety of all are attacked; third, they have been stripped of all their goods; fourth, the princes who are relatives are barred from succession to the kingdom.

units.la: Probatio 2. Quia etiam inferiores Magistratus (quales plerique hi sunt, qui à nostris juvantur) ex officio, ideoque justè defendunt vitam & salutem subditorum & vicissim subditi rectè illos juvant, contra Tyrannos armatos sive domesticos sive externos.
units.tr: Proof second: because also the lower magistrates (of which kind most are those who are aided by our people) by their office, and therefore justly, defend the life and safety of their subjects; and in turn the subjects rightly aid them, against tyrants, whether domestic or foreign, who are armed.

units.la: Amplificetur à causis, ob quas additi sunt inferiores Magistratus superiori: Ex dicto Traiani dicentis Tribuno, cui gladium tradebat: Hoc pro me utere, si justa imperavero: contra me, si injusta. Item à persona hostium: Quod non sint superior magistratus: sed pares regni seditiosè[?] affectantes, & crudelitate in pios à Rege & Pontifice promereri volentes successionem in regno.
units.tr: Let it be amplified from the causes for which the lower magistrates were added to the superior: from the saying of Trajan to the tribune to whom he handed over the sword: "Use this for me if I command justly; against me if unjustly." Likewise from the person of the enemies: that they are not superior magistrates, but equals of the kingdom, seditiously aspiring, and wishing to earn succession to the kingdom by cruelty against the pious, from the king and the Pope.

units.la: Obiectio: Etiam regem oppugnari. Responsio, quasimul confirmetur, minor probationis secundæ. Non regem, sed Tyrannum. 1. quia impia præcipiat, & in non parentes atrociter sæviat[?]. 2. quia contra leges naturæ & regni consanguineos excludat & persequatur.
units.tr: Objection: that the king too is attacked. Answer, at the same time confirming the minor of the second proof: not the king, but a tyrant. First, because he commands impious things and rages savagely against non-subjects. Second, because he excludes and persecutes the relatives of the kingdom, contrary to the laws of nature and of the realm.

units.la: Conclusio primi argumenti hic nectatur, & inferatur circunstantia, quòd non temerè, sed de auxilio sollicitati nostri opem ferant justè se defendentibus.
units.tr: The conclusion of the first argument is attached here, and the circumstance is inferred, that our people bring aid not rashly but at the request of those who defend themselves justly.

units.la: Argumentum II. Ex regula æquitatis: quæ nobis volumus fieri, eadem etiam aliis præstemus.
units.tr: Second argument: from the rule of equity: whatever we wish to be done to us, we should also do to others.

units.la: Amplificetur minor expolitione à magnitudine desiderii nostri, & ab ejus æquitate, si in necessitate simili essemus constituti, & alii sine sua pernicie nos possent juvare. Conclusio inferatur in hypothesi.
units.tr: The minor is amplified by an elaboration of the greatness of our desire and of its equity, if we were placed in a similar necessity, and others could help us without their own ruin. The conclusion is inferred under a hypothesis.

units.la: Argumentum III. ex regula dilectionis, quę omnes quibus est facultas, obligat ad juvandum proximos. Probetur ex sexto præcepto: Non occides: cum quo ostendatur pugnare neglectum salutis proximi.
units.tr: Third argument: from the rule of love, which obliges all who have the ability to help their neighbours. It is proved from the sixth commandment, "Thou shalt not kill," by which it is shown that neglect of the safety of one's neighbour is contrary to it.

units.la: Argumentum IV. Quia etiam apud exteros, si fit possibile, propaganda est Ecclesia & gloria Christi. Ostendatur ex fine creationis & liberationis: Et ex petitione: Adveniat regnum tuum.
units.tr: Fourth argument: because the Church and the glory of Christ are to be propagated also among foreigners, if it is possible. It is shown from the end of creation and of redemption, and from the petition, "Thy kingdom come."

units.la: Argumentum V. Quia defendentes externos defendunt suos:
units.tr: Fifth argument: because those who defend foreigners defend their own:

units.la: Probetur: quia hostes oppressis illis etiam nos opprimere satagunt.
units.tr: It is proved: because the enemies, when they have crushed those others, strive also to crush us.

units.la: NAM tua res agitur paries cum proximus ardet.
units.tr: "For your own affair is at stake, when the wall of your neighbour burns."

units.la: Argumentum VI. Membra Ecclesiæ etiam aliarum gentium non sunt, quo ad dilectionis officia, pro externis habenda: quia sunt domestici fidei: membra Christi nobiscum. Ex symbolo: Credo communionem sanctorum.
units.tr: Sixth argument: the members of the Church, even of other nations, are not to be regarded as foreigners with respect to the duties of love, because they are household members of the faith and members of Christ with us. From the creed: "I believe in the communion of saints."

units.la: Amplificetur per collationem conjunctionis Politicæ & Christianæ Argumentum VII. quia liceret principibus nostris pacisci cum Gallis religionis sociis de ejusmodi auxilio. Ergo etiam licet auxilium ferre.
units.tr: Let it be amplified by comparing political and Christian fellowship. Seventh argument: because it would be lawful for our princes to make an agreement with the French, companions in religion, about such aid. Therefore it is also lawful to bring aid.

units.la: Antecedens probetur in thesi a minori: Fœdera cum exteris ejusdem Religionis de mutuis auxiliis contra Tyrannos aut latrones sunt licita: Ergo magis contra persecutores Religionis.
units.tr: The antecedent is proved in thesis from the lesser: alliances with foreigners of the same religion concerning mutual aid against tyrants or robbers are lawful; therefore much more against persecutors of the religion.

units.la: Argumentum VIII. ab exemplo Abrahami, defendentis nepotem Lothum oppressum, & utentis opera regum sociorum in eo bello.
units.tr: Eighth argument: from the example of Abraham, who defended his nephew Lot, when oppressed, and used the help of the allied kings in that war.

units.la: Confutatio.
units.tr: Refutation.

units.la: Responsio ad I. de seditione: per distinctionem majoris: Esse seditiosum, extra casum justæ defensionis, qualem hanc esse ostensum sit primo argumento: Addatur noëma: Antiquam esse calumniam, veritatis qualemcunque defensionem, seditionem esse.
units.tr: Answer to the first: concerning sedition, by distinction of the major: to be seditious is, apart from the case of just defence, which this has been shown to be in the first argument. Add the notion: that it is an ancient calumny that any defence of the truth whatsoever is sedition.

units.la: Responsio ad II. de vocatione. 1. Eos habere mandatum universale de tuenda salute proximorum, præsertim Ecclesiæ, si adsit facultas. 2. Iustâ petitionem eorum qui opprimuntur, esse vocationem specialem.
units.tr: Answer to the second: concerning the calling. First, that they have a general mandate to protect the safety of their neighbours, especially the Church, if the opportunity is present. Second, that the just petition of those who are oppressed is a special calling.

units.la: Ad locum Petri: eum prohibere πλυπεραγμο- συνίων abs-que vocatione, quam isti habeant.
units.tr: As to the passage of Peter: that he forbids meddling (πολυπραγμοσύνη) without a calling, which these men have.

units.la: Adregulam æquitatis: 1. per distinctionem eam non affectibus sed legibus æstimandam esse: At nolle juvari injustè à se oppressos, esse tyrannidem. 2. Ex antithesi: Quod tibi vis fieri, &c. per βίαιον. Juste vellemus similiter periclitantibus tibus nobis alios succurrere. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: As to the rule of equity: first, by distinction, that it is to be judged not by the passions but by the laws: but to be unwilling to be helped by others when one is unjustly oppressed is tyranny. Second, from the antithesis, "What you wish done to you," etc., by violence (βίαιον): we would justly wish, in similar danger to ourselves, that others succour us. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Ad exempla contraria: nihil ea probare contra regulam charitatis & æquitatis.
units.tr: As to the contrary examples: they prove nothing against the rule of charity and equity.

units.la: Ad III. de periculis. 1. per βλαβῶν[?]: majora pericula creari connivendo ad interitum vicinorum.
units.tr: As to the third, concerning dangers: first, by (βλάβων): greater dangers are created by connivance at the destruction of neighbours.

units.la: 2. Fortes contemnere pericula in causa ho-nesta.
units.tr: Second: brave men despise dangers in an honourable cause.

units.la: 3. Deum defendere justam causam.
units.tr: Third: God defends a just cause.

units.la: Instantia: Sæpe infelicem esse hujusmodi de-fensionem.
units.tr: Instance: such a defence is often unfortunate.

units.la: Respon. 1. ex dicto: careat successibus opto, &c. per negationem consequentiæ: quia possunt alia esse causæ infelicitatis præter culpam facti. Expoliatur hæc responsio enumeratione causarum: aliquando esse pœnam aliorum peccatorum, alias ἀδοκιμασίαν[?] infelicitatem in bona causa: Exemplo Benjamitici belli. Iud. 20.
units.tr: Answer: first, from the saying, "I wish they may lack success," etc., by denial of the consequence: because there can be other causes of misfortune besides fault in the deed. This answer is elaborated by an enumeration of causes: sometimes it is the punishment of other sins; at other times, a rejection (ἀδοκιμασία), misfortune in a good cause. Example: the war against the Benjaminites, Judges 20.

units.la: Prior causa amplificetur enumeratione peccatorum: fiducia armorum, non rectæ causæ finales & impulsive, temeritas, securitas, imprudentia consiliorum, impietas, neglectus precum. Hæc postrema pars amplificetur exemplo & ὑβριστῶν[?] flagitiosorum militum.
units.tr: The former cause is amplified by an enumeration of sins: confidence in arms, causes that are not right in their final and moving ends, rashness, complacency, imprudence of counsels, impiety, neglect of prayers. This last part is amplified by the example of wanton and shameful soldiers (ὑβριστῶν).

units.la: Ad IV. De belli propagatione ad plures. 1. per distinctionem: Si periculum sit aliis post alios, melius esse, illos conjunctim se defendere quam singulos aliis sublatis. 2. Si pauci non sint pares hostibus, melius esse multos periclitari, quam paucos deseri & perire.
units.tr: Answer to the fourth, concerning the spreading of war to more people: first, by distinction: if there is danger to some after others, it is better for them to defend themselves jointly than for each to be removed singly by others. Second, if the few are not equal to the enemies, it is better that many be endangered than that few be abandoned and perish.

units.la: Ad solutionem objectionis: per negationem consequensequentiæ: quia etsi non propagetur, tamen aliquando rectè defendatur armis religio.
units.tr: Answer to the solution of the objection: by denial of the consequence: because even if it is not propagated, nevertheless religion is sometimes rightly defended by arms.

units.la: Instantia 1. Non defendi armis. Zach. 4.6. Oseæ.1.7.
units.tr: Instance 1: that it should not be defended by arms. Zechariah 4:6; Hosea 1:7.

units.la: Respond. 1. eo tempore, quo Deus sine armis populum defendere voluit, 2. Principaliter: probatur, quia aliis temporibus arcu & gladio defendit, ut est in historia Josuæ, iudicum, Regum, &c. 2. quia etiam tunc Iudæi armati ædificabant, Neh.4.
units.tr: Answer: first, at the time when God wished to defend the people without arms; second, principally, it is proved, because at other times He defended them with bow and sword, as is in the history of Joshua, the Judges, the Kings, etc.; second, because even then the Jews, armed, were building, Nehemiah 4.

units.la: Instantia 2. Regnum Dei non est mundanum.
units.tr: Instance 2: the kingdom of God is not worldly.

units.la: Respond. Sed sæpe defenditur à mundano Ies. 49.23. Rom.13.4.
units.tr: Answer: but it is often defended by a worldly power, Isaiah 49:23; Romans 13:4.

units.la: Instantia 3. Arma nostra sunt spiritualia. Respond. arma nempe ministerii: sed carnalia arma sunt magistratus.
units.tr: Instance 3: our weapons are spiritual. Answer: indeed the weapons of the ministry; but the weapons of the magistrate are carnal.

units.la: Inst. 4. Armis carnalibus non convertuntur homines ad Christum. Respond. Sed tamen reprimuntur blasphemi, & contra impiorum tyrannidem atque latrocinia defenduntur pii: Exempla Macchabæorum: Constantini, &c.
units.tr: Instance 4: men are not converted to Christ by carnal weapons. Answer: yet the blasphemers are restrained, and the pious are defended against the tyranny and robberies of the impious: examples of the Maccabees, of Constantine, etc.

units.la: Conclusio: Iustam ergo esse expeditionem: sed orandum ut iuste geratur: & à Deo fortunetur.
units.tr: Conclusion: therefore the expedition is just; but it must be prayed for that it be justly conducted and be blessed with success by God.

units.la: Exercitatio IV. De usu scriarum[?] Scholasticarum Epistola ad amicum Scholasticum.
units.tr: Exercitatio IV. On the Use of the Scholastic Writings[?], a Letter to a Scholastic Friend.

units.la: Exordium sit [illegible, ~3 letters]: lucundam tibi esse recordationem præsentiæ amici & colloquii cum eo: cum superioribus feriis, præceptorum venia te inviteret[?].
units.tr: Let the opening be [illegible]: how pleasant it is for you to recall your friend's presence and conversation with him, when, during the recent holidays, the permission of his teachers invited you to it[?].

units.la: Ratio 1. quia eum amęs propter familiam & indolem.
units.tr: Reason 1. Because you love him on account of his family and his disposition.

units.la: 2. quia pręfectus mediocres in eo deprehĕderis.
units.tr: 2. Because you found in him moderate progress.

units.la: 3. quia expositio status & disciplinę Scholasticę tibi placuerit.
units.tr: 3. Because the account of the state and discipline of the Schools pleased you.

units.la: Anthypophora & Propositio: Etsi sub has etiam ferias reditus ejus tibi sit futurus gratus: tamen te potius cupere, ut eum differat, & nunc rectius utatur feriis.
units.tr: Objection and proposition: Although his return would be welcome to you even during these holidays, nevertheless you rather wish that he postpone it and now use the holidays more profitably.

units.la: Ratio 1. Quia itinera nunc sint passim infesta militib. ob authorationem exercitus Germanici in vicinia. Adspergatur aliquid de expeditione Gallicana ejusq; causa cum voto. (Lustrabatur tunc exercitus Germanorum Principū ad Hochhemum ditionis Moguntinæ, qui ductore CHRI-STIANO principe Anhaltino in Gallia suppetias ferret Heinrico Regi Galliarum & Navarræ contra Ligam Pontificiam.)
units.tr: Reason 1. Because journeys are now everywhere unsafe for soldiers, on account of the army of the Germans gathering in the neighbourhood. Something should be added about the Gallic expedition and its cause, with a prayer. (The army of the German princes was then being reviewed at Hochheim, in the territory of Mainz, which, under the leadership of Prince Christian of Anhalt, was to bring aid in Gaul to Henry, King of France and Navarre, against the Papist League.)

units.la: II. Quia tempus domi utilius locare possit lectionibus & exercitiis privatis.
units.tr: II. Because he could spend his time at home more usefully on private reading and exercises.

units.la: Ἐξήγησις: rationis, per occupat. à descriptione & usu feriarum, quod non sint ocium, sed vacatio ab auditione publica legibus concessa: 1. ut respirent docentes & discentes ab operis ordinariis: 2. ut excitetur in utrisque studiorum alacritas. 3. ut vacetur studiis privatis.
units.tr: Explanation of the reason, by occupation: concerning the description and use of the holidays, that they are not idleness, but a release from public instruction granted by law: (1) so that teachers and learners may get breath from their ordinary labours; (2) so that eagerness for study may be stirred up in both; (3) so that time may be given to private studies.

units.la: Amplificetur comparatione inducIarum, quarum finis non est ocium aut torpor militum, sed reparatio virium & armorum, tractatio consiliorum, &, nisi pax fiat, durior conflictus.
units.tr: Let it be amplified by comparison with a truce, whose purpose is not the idleness or sluggishness of soldiers, but the restoration of strength and arms, the handling of plans, and, unless peace is made, a harder conflict.

units.la: Applicatio : Etiam Musis[?] castra esse adversus hostes. Ignaviam, inscitiam, opinionem, arrogantiam, metum egestatis, turpitudinis, &c. cum quibus bellum tutius sit pace vel induciis multis.
units.tr: Application: The Muses too have a camp against enemies: against idleness, ignorance, opinion, arrogance, fear of poverty, disgrace, etc., against which a war is safer than peace or many truces.

units.la: Conclusio fit consilium. Vacet lectioni privatæ: antemeridianis horis sacri textus, & probati alicujus interpretis: pomeridianis historici primū[?] Latini, tum Græci alicujus.
units.tr: The conclusion is a counsel. Let him give himself to private reading: in the morning hours to the sacred text and to some approved interpreter; in the afternoon to a Latin historian first, then to some Greek.

units.la: Ratio 1. à tuo exemplo, quod tu olim hoc co-silium praeceptorum utiliter secutus sis.
units.tr: Reason 1. From your own example, since you once followed this counsel of the teachers to good effect.

units.la: 2. à temporis præstantia, cujus solius avaritiæ honesta: jactura irreparabilis.
units.tr: 2. From the excellence of time, whose loss through avarice alone is an irreparable and dishonourable one.

units.la: Exercitatio V.
units.tr: Exercitatio V.

units.la: Platonica communionis rerum omnium: ad amicum Defensio.
units.tr: Defence of Plato's communion of all things: to a friend.

units.la: EXordium breviter commendet jucunditatem & utilitatem lectionis librorum Platonicorum, maxime eorum qui sunt de Repub. Occu-patio, non ignorare te, multis absurdam videri il-lam Reipub. formam, in qua lib. 5. communione omnium rerum sancit. Amplif. multos cam[?] ap-pellare nevum[?] foedissimum in pulcro corpore. Propositio per advers. Sed videri tibi diversum.
units.tr: The introduction should briefly commend the pleasure and usefulness of reading the Platonic books, especially those on the Republic. The subject matter: you are not unaware that many think that form of commonwealth absurd, in which in the fifth book he sanctions the communion of all things. Amplification: many call it a most foul blemish on a beautiful body. Proposition, by way of contrary: but it seems to you otherwise.

units.la: Ratio 1. à forma: quia per talem rerum communionem civitas sit maxime unita seu una:cum omnes possint dicere: Hoc meum & non meum.
units.tr: Argument 1, from the form: because by such a communion of things the state is most united, or one, since all can say: This is mine, and not mine.

units.la: Addatur maior: Reipub. optimum esse, si sit quam maxime unita. Amplificetur simili: Sicut corpori humano optimum est: si omnia memut[?] inter sese voluptatem & dolorem communicent: ita civitas optime regitur, cum ad affectionem unius hominis, quam proxime accedit.
units.tr: Let the major premise be added: it is best for a commonwealth if it is as united as possible. Let it be amplified by a comparison: just as it is best for the human body if all its members share among themselves pleasure and pain, so a state is best governed when it comes as close as possible to the feeling of one man.

units.la: Ratio II. ab effectu: Quia sic optime consulatur publicæ paci & benevolentiæ civium. Osten-datur a remotione causarum, ex quibus lites nascuntur: Vt sunt: inæqualitas fortunarum, cum alius abundat, alius eget: & dissimilitudo conditionis, cum alius est nobilis, alius rusticus. Ampl. ex antithesi ab incommodis proprietatis, quæ parit φιλαυτίαν, avaritiam, injurias, lites, furta, &c.
units.tr: Argument 2, from the effect: because in this way the public peace and the goodwill of citizens are best provided for. It is shown by the removal of the causes from which quarrels arise, such as: inequality of fortunes, when one abounds and another lacks; and dissimilarity of condition, when one is noble and another a peasant. Amplification from the opposite: from the inconveniences of private property, which produces self-love, avarice, injuries, lawsuits, thefts, etc.

units.la: Ratio III. ab æquo & bono: Quia amicorum oporteat omnia esse communia. Cives autem bonos maxime amicos esse.
units.tr: Argument 3, from what is fair and good: because it is fitting that all things be common among friends, and good citizens are above all friends.

units.la: Objectio: Esse impossibilem. Resp. 1. per concessionem Platonis: addatur causa; id fieri ex accidente, propter φιλαυτίαν & avaritiam hominum. 2. per negationem Minoris. 1. quia Libyes, Cretenses & Lacedæmonii magna ex parte eam observarint. 2. Etiam apostoli olim in primitiva Ecclesia. 3. Etiam hodie Anabaptistæ alicubi.
units.tr: Objection: that it is impossible. Reply: first, by conceding Plato's point, adding the cause: that this happens by accident, on account of men's self-love and avarice. Second, by denying the minor premise. First, because the Libyans, the Cretans and the Lacedaemonians largely observed it. Second, the apostles too once did so in the primitive Church. Third, the Anabaptists even today in some places.

units.la: Conclusio: Petere te tamen de istis amici sententiam.
units.tr: Conclusion: nevertheless I ask you to give me your friend's opinion on these matters.

units.la: Exercitatio VI.
units.tr: Exercitatio VI.

units.la: Ad defensionem Platonicæ κοινωνίας omnium rerum, ex sententia Aristotelis Politic. lib. 2. cap. 1. 2. 3. Responsio.
units.tr: In defence of Plato's communion of all things, according to Aristotle's Politics, book 2, chapters 1, 2 and 3. A response.

units.la: EXordium à thesi: nec leviter probandâ: nec morosè damnanda esse omnia philosophorum placita.
units.tr: Opening, from the thesis: all the opinions of the philosophers are neither to be lightly approved nor peevishly condemned.

units.la: Ratio: quia multa ingeniosè & utiliter tradat: in multis vel ingenii abusu vel ignorantia aberrent à vero.
units.tr: Reason: because they set out many things ingeniously and usefully, and in many matters they go astray from the truth, either through an abuse of their talent or through ignorance.

units.la: Accommodetur ad hypothesin præsentem: Platonem quoque de repub. multa præclarè scribere: Recensentur nonnulla: Quod τὸ ὅσιον[?] hoc est, religio sit basis Politiæ: Quod τ' ὁμιλητικὸν[?] sit nervus societatis humanæ: Quod in repub. omnia ad communem utilitatem referre oporteat: Quod felix sit respub. quæ à Philosophis, h. e, piis & sapientibus gubernatur, &c.
units.tr: Applied to the present hypothesis: Plato too writes many things admirably in his Republic. Some are listed: that τὸ ὅσιον[?], that is, religion, is the foundation of the polity; that τ' ὁμιλητικὸν[?] is the sinew of human society; that in the commonwealth everything ought to be referred to the common advantage; that the commonwealth is happy which is governed by philosophers, that is, by the pious and the wise, etc.

units.la: Adversat. Sed portentosam insaniam esse, quam requirit in civitate, omnium rerum [illegible, ~11 letters]
units.tr: Objection. But the community of all things, which he requires in the state, is a monstrous madness, [illegible, ~11 letters]

units.la: Transitio ad propositionem: Cum amicus seu exercendi ingenii seu discendi causa ejus defensionem ad te miserit, te breviter responsurum: 1. de uxorum & liberorum 2 de facultatum [illegible, ~10 letters]
units.tr: Transition to the proposition: Since a friend, either for the sake of exercising his talent or of learning, has sent you his defence, I shall answer you briefly: (1) concerning the community of wives and children; (2) concerning the goods [illegible, ~10 letters]

units.la: Prima pars propositionis: Communionem uxorum & liberorum procul à civitate arcendam esse.
units.tr: First part of the proposition: that the community of wives and children must be kept far away from the state.

units.la: Ratio 1. quia sit impia repugnans ordinationi & verbo Dei. Homo adhærebit uxori suæ: Erunt duo in carne una: quisque vir suam habeat uxorem: viri diligite uxores vestras: Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam: Liberi obedite parentibus vestris, &c.
units.tr: Reason 1: because it is impious and contrary to God's ordinance and Word. A man shall cleave to his wife; they shall be two in one flesh; let every man have his own wife; husbands, love your wives; honour your father and your mother; children, obey your parents, etc.

units.la: Amplificetur à judicato, quod sit jam olim damnata hæresis Simonitarum, Nicolaitarum & Carpocratianorum: Augusl. [?] de hæresib. cap. 1. 5.7.
units.tr: Let it be amplified from the judgement that this heresy was long ago condemned: the heresy of the Simonians, the Nicolaitans and the Carpocratians. Augustine, On Heresies, chapters 1, 5 and 7.

units.la: Transeatur ad argumenta Aristotelis, quæ omnia revocentur ad unum.
units.tr: Let us pass to Aristotle's arguments, which can all be traced back to one.

units.la: Ratio I I. quia parceret horribiles confusiones in genere humano. Probetur enumeratione malorum, quæ Aristoteles vocat ἀνυχρείας [?] καὶ ἐλάττας [?].
units.tr: Reason II: because it would bring about horrible confusions in the human race. Let it be proved by an enumeration of the evils which Aristotle calls ἀνυχρείας [?] and ἐλάττας [?].

units.la: I. Sublatio graduum consanguinitatis & affinitatis. Ostendatur & amplificetur a consequenti: Extincta consanguinitate, exstingui amicitiam naturalem conjugum, parentum, liberorum, fratrum, patruelium, eoque tolli domum & civitatem. Inferatur simile Aristotelis de pauculo mellis in multam aquam infusi.
units.tr: I. The abolition of the degrees of kinship and affinity. Let it be shown and amplified from the consequence: with kinship extinguished, the natural friendship of spouses, parents, children, brothers and cousins would be extinguished too, and so home and state would be destroyed. Let there be added Aristotle's similitude of a little honey poured into much water.

units.la: I I. Interitus generis humani ex neglectu prolis, quæ nullius sit propria. Deducatur ex Thesi: quod nullius est proprium, id minus curari, & neglectum perire. Et hæc ostendatur ex causis curationis mutuæ inter homines, quæ juxta Aristotelem sunt duæ: τὸ ἴδιον καὶ τὸ ἀγαπητόν.
units.tr: II. The destruction of the human race through neglect of offspring, which belongs to no one in particular. Let it be deduced from the thesis: what belongs to no one is cared for the less, and perishes when neglected. And this is shown from the causes of mutual care among men, which according to Aristotle are two: τὸ ἴδιον and τὸ ἀγαπητόν.

units.la: I I I. Rixæ, injuriæ, læsiones, ac cædes parentum & propinquorum frequentiores. Ostendatur a causis, quia sublata reverentia & amicitia, nemo a propinquis lædendis magis abstinebit, quam ab extraneis.
units.tr: III. Quarrels, injuries, wounds and killings of parents and relatives would be more frequent. Let it be shown from the causes: since reverence and friendship would be removed, no one would refrain from harming his kinsmen more than he refrains from harming strangers.

units.la: I V. Incestæ nuptiæ & vagæ libidines parentum, liberorum, & propinquorum.
units.tr: IV. Incestuous marriages and promiscuous lusts of parents, children and relatives.

units.la: Transitio ad partem SECUNDAM per Ἐπιδιώξιν [?]: ad-dita ratione: Cum Platonem ipsum alibi sui pu-deat: non mereri confutationem prolixiorem.
units.tr: Transition to the SECOND part through Ἐπιδιώξιν [?], with the reason added: since Plato himself is ashamed of it elsewhere, it does not deserve a lengthier refutation.

units.la: Subjiciatur quæstionis de communione facultatum ex Aristotele triplex sensus: 1. an fundi proprii, fructus vero communes. 2. an fundi & cultus communis, fructuum portiones singulis proprię: 3. an fundi & fructus communes esse debeant.
units.tr: Let there be set under the question about the community of goods a threefold sense from Aristotle: (1) whether the land is private but the fruits common; (2) whether the land and the cultivation are common but the portions of the fruits private to each; (3) whether the land and the fruits ought to be common.

units.la: Propositio habeat ἀνθυποφέρειν[?]: Etsi Plato prioribus duobus modis rectè repudiatis, tertium tantum sanciat: tamen ne eum quidem probandum esse.
units.tr: The proposition should have ἀνθυποφέρειν[?]: Although Plato rightly rejects the first two ways and sanctions only the third, nevertheless not even this one is to be approved.

units.la: Ratio V.[?] à contrario: quia distinctio dominiorum sit juris divini. Proverb. 5. ver. 15. 16. 17. Fontes tui deriventur foras[?], &c. Et cap. 3. 9. Honora Deum de substantia tua, &c.
units.tr: Reason V[?], from the contrary: because the distinction of ownership is of divine law. Proverbs 5:15–17: Drink waters out of your own cistern, etc. And chapter 3:9: Honour the Lord with your substance, etc.

units.la: Ostendatur approbatio divina ex divisione terræ promissę in tribus, cognationes, & familias.
units.tr: Let there be shown the divine approval from the division of the promised land among the tribes, the kindreds and the families.

units.la: Amplificetur hæc ratio ex Aristotele à commodis proprietatis rerum: ut sunt. 1. Conservatio pacis & concordię: quia curę divise ἐγκλή-ματα incusationes non pariùt. 2. Possessionum diligentior cura & incrementum. 3. naturalis delectatio ex bonis propriis cum justitia particulari congruens. 4. Liberalitatis conservatio inter cives.
units.tr: Let this reason be amplified from Aristotle, from the advantages of the private ownership of things, which are: (1) the preservation of peace and concord, since divided cares do not produce ἐγκλήματα, accusations; (2) a more diligent care of possessions and their increase; (3) a natural delight in one's own goods, agreeing with particular justice; (4) the preservation of liberality among citizens.

units.la: Clausula. Hæc bona tolli è Repub. per κοινωνίαν omnium rerum.
units.tr: Conclusion. These goods would be removed from the commonwealth by the communion of all things.

units.la: Ratio II. ab effectis quia parereт continua dissidia & contentiones de inæqualitate sive laborum sive fructuum: Act. 6. murmur Græcorum contra Judæos.
units.tr: Reason II, from the effects: because it would produce continual dissensions and contentions over inequality, whether of labours or of fruits: Acts 6, the murmuring of the Greeks against the Jews.

units.la: Amplif. a thesi: quod omnis convictus & communitas rerum humanarum sit difficilis.
units.tr: Amplified from the thesis: that every association and communion of human affairs is difficult.

units.la: Ostendatur 1. exemplo pastorum Abrahami & Loti. 2. exemplo peregrinantium, qui facile obres leviculas dissident: ut Paulus & Barnabas. Actor.15.39. 3. à rixis domesticis etiam paucorum & conjunctissimorum.
units.tr: Let it be shown (1) by the example of the herdsmen of Abraham and Lot; (2) by the example of travellers, who easily disagree over trifling obstacles, as Paul and Barnabas did, Acts 15:39; (3) from domestic quarrels even among a few and the closest of kin.

units.la: Transitio ad confutationem rationum Platonis.
units.tr: Transition to the refutation of Plato's reasons.

units.la: Ad primam de unitate civitatis Responsio I. per distinctionem majoris: Optima est civitatis u-nitas, nempe possibilis, & non evertens ipsam ci-vitatem.
units.tr: To the first, concerning the unity of the state: Response I, by distinguishing the major premise: the best unity of the state is that which is possible and does not overturn the state itself.

units.la: Applicetur distinctionis pars utraque ad mi-norem, & ostendatur 1. quod unitas Platonica sit impossibilis: ex Platonis ipsius confessione: ex sententiæ mutatione in libris de Legibus: ex δυσχερείας[?] in secunda ratione primæ partis explicatis. 2. quod evertat civitatem ex definitione civitatis, quæ est multitudo hominum specie dif-ferentium, per se sibi ad vivendum sufficiens.
units.tr: Let each part of the distinction be applied to the minor premise, and let it be shown (1) that Plato's unity is impossible, from Plato's own admission, from the change of his opinion in the books On Laws, and from the difficulties explained in the second reason of the first part; (2) that it overturns the state, from the definition of the state, which is a multitude of men differing in kind, sufficient of themselves for living.

units.la: Responsio II. per negationem majoris, ex eadem definitione: quod non unitas, sed αὐτάρκεια[?] sufficientia rerum civitati sit optima. Hæc tutem[?] tanto fit major, quanto minor est unitas. Ostendatur ratione Aristotelis: quia domus magis suf-ficiens est, quam homo unus: civitas magis, quam domus una.
units.tr: Response II, by denying the major premise, from the same definition: that not unity but self-sufficiency, the sufficiency of things, is the best for a state. This sufficiency becomes greater the less the unity is. Let it be shown by Aristotle's reasoning: a household is more sufficient than one man, and a state more than one household.

units.la: Ad probationem Minoris: Quod in κοινωνίας[?] Socratica omnes dicere possint: Hoc meum & non meum. Responsio habeat [illegible, ~8 letters]: Etsi plus argutiæ habeat quam veritatis: & responsio Aristotelis videatur exilis: tetamen explicaturū, quantum possis.
units.tr: To the proof of the minor premise: that in the Socratic communion all can say: This is mine and not mine. Response, let it have [illegible, ~8 letters]: although it has more subtlety than truth, and Aristotle's response seems slight, nevertheless I shall explain it as far as you are able.

units.la: Ponatur totus prosyllogismus: cujus hæc sit sententia:
units.tr: Let the whole prosyllogism be set down, whose sense is this:

units.la: Vbi omnes dicere possunt: Hoc meum & nō meum : ibi civitas est maxime unita.In κοινωνίας[?] Socratica omnes id possunt dicere: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Where all can say: This is mine and not mine, there the state is most united. In the Socratic communion all can say this. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Deinde ostendatur fallacia compositionis & divisionis: in vocabulo OMNES: quod in Majore sensu diviso seu distributive: in minore sensu composito seu collective intelligitur: alioqui est falsa. (Sensus divisus est: cum omnes, h.e, singuli dicere possunt: Hoc meum & hoc non meum, i.e, ubi quis-que res proprias non alienas possidet: sic major vera est: quia unoquoque suum possidente ca-ventur lites: sed minor est falsa: quia in communione nihil est neque meum neque non meū. Compositus sensus est: quod omnes Platonici cives simul dicunt: Hoc meum & non meum: quia omnium. Sic minor vera, sed major falsa.)
units.tr: Then let the fallacy of composition and division be shown in the word ALL: which in the major premise is understood in the divided or distributive sense, in the minor in the composite or collective sense; otherwise it is false. (The divided sense is: when all, that is, each one, can say: This is mine and this is not mine, that is, where each one possesses his own things and not another's: thus the major is true, because when each possesses his own, lawsuits are avoided; but the minor is false, because in a communion nothing is either mine or not mine. The composite sense is: that all Platonic citizens together say: This is mine and not mine, because it belongs to all. Thus the minor is true, but the major is false.)

units.la: Adsimile συμπαθείας membrorum corporis:
units.tr: Adsimile of the sympathy [συμπάθεια] of the members of the body:

units.la: Respons. 1. negatione consequentiae à conjunctione animorum per virtutem: legibus praecepta: possibili & necessaria: ad communionem rerum externarum virtuti adversam impossibilem & noxiam.
units.tr: Answer. 1. By denying the consequence from the union of minds through virtue, prescribed by laws, possible and necessary, to a communion of external goods adverse to virtue, impossible and harmful.

units.la: 2. Per βίαιον[?]: membra omnia non fiunt unum: sed manent distincta partibus: situ & facultatib. Ergo nec civitas fit una confusis facultatibus & gradibus. Claudatur alio simili Aristotelis: Platonicam unitatem esse concentum unisonum, & versum unipedem.
units.tr: 2. By a violent [?] comparison: all the members do not become one; they remain distinct in their parts, position and faculties. Therefore neither does a state become one by confusing faculties and ranks. Let it be shut out by another likeness of Aristotle's: that Plato's unity is a unison concord and a one-footed verse.

units.la: Ad II. rationem: negatione minoris: Ad-datur ratio ex secunda ratione secundae partis.
units.tr: To the second argument: by denying the minor premise. The argument is added from the second argument of the second part.

units.la: Ad probationem 1. rursus per negationem minominoris, quòd in κοινωνίας rerum nullę sint rixarum causæ: ex eadem ratione.
units.tr: To the proof of the first point: again, by denying the minor premise, that in the communion of goods there are no causes of quarrels, on the same ground.

units.la: Addatur amplificatio à comparatis ex Aristotele: Teste experientia etiam paucos ex communi viventes magis diffidere, quam multos, proprium tenentes. 2. Per ostensionem non causa: non inæqualitatem fortunarum aut conditionis: sed improbitatem creare lites, quam κοινωνία non tollat, sed in malis augeat. 3. Per βίου: inæqualitatem fortunarum & conditionum moderatam maximè consulere paci civitatis 1. quia sit secundum naturam, & juris divini. 2. quia constituat civitatem: ex definitione: juxta di-ctum: non medicus & medicus sed medicus & agri-cola faciunt civitatem. 3. quia societ animos superiorum & inferiorum per communicationem officiorum & beneficiorum.
units.tr: Add the amplification from the comparisons drawn from Aristotle: experience bears witness that even a few who live in common distrust one another more than many who hold property of their own. 2. By showing that it is not the cause: not the inequality of fortunes or condition, but wickedness, creates quarrels, which communal living does not remove but increases in evils. 3. By the argument from the good: the moderate inequality of fortunes and conditions is especially conducive to the peace of the state: 1. because it is according to nature and divine law; 2. because it constitutes the state, by definition, according to the saying: "not doctor and doctor, but doctor and farmer make a state"; 3. because it joins the minds of superiors and inferiors through the sharing of duties and benefits.

units.la: Ad amplificationem ab incommodis proprietatis:
units.tr: To the amplification from the disadvantages of property:

units.la: 1. negatione consEq: quia per accidens hæc vitia comitentur proprietatem: cum etiam, & quidem magis sint in κοινωνία. 2. per βίου: magna esse proprietatis commoda: de quibus in prima ratione secundæ partis.
units.tr: 1. By denying the consequence: because these vices accompany property only by accident, when they are even more present in communal living. 2. By the argument from the good: property has great advantages, of which more in the first argument of the second part.

units.la: Ad III. rattionem: Per distinctionem: Omnia esse amicorum communia: non dominio & possessione: sed usu & delectatione secundum honestas leges.
units.tr: To the third argument: by distinction: all things are common among friends, not in dominion and possession, but in use and enjoyment according to honest laws.

units.la: Probetur 1. ex prima ratione secundæ partis. 2. à proprio amicorum, quod est gaudere mutua benevolentia & officiis beneficentiæ, quibi[?] demum fiunt, ubi res sunt propriæ, & quodammodo tamen communes.
units.tr: Let it be proved: 1. from the first argument of the second part. 2. from the very nature of friendship, which is to rejoice in mutual goodwill and in the offices of beneficence, which are done only where things are one's own, and yet in some measure common.

units.la: Adexempla: 1. in genere: non exemplis sed legibus ciuitatem constituendam esse. 2. in specie: per negationem conseq. quia sint partim vitiosa: Vt Anabaptistica confusio: partim dissimilia: Ostendatur dissimilitudo: 1. in Lacedemoniis Cretensibus & Libybus: quibus non dominio sed usu, servi, equi, canes, vehicula, &c. erant communia. 2. In apostolis, quib. κοινωνία bonorum fuerit. 1. utilis, facilis, & necessaria: 2. libera. 3. particularis. 4. temporaria.
units.tr: To the examples: 1. In general: a state must be founded not on examples but on laws. 2. In particular: by denying the consequence, because some are vicious, such as the Anabaptist confusion, and some are dissimilar. Let the dissimilarity be shown: 1. among the Lacedaemonians, Cretans and Libyans, among whom slaves, horses, dogs, carriages, etc. were held in common not by dominion but by use. 2. Among the apostles, whose communion of goods was: 1. useful, easy and necessary; 2. free; 3. particular; 4. temporary.

units.la: Addantur causa. 1. persecutio. 2. corum: anima una: Et μείων: non tamen fuisse immunem a querelis: Act. 6.1. Erat murmur Graecorum adversus Judaeos, &c.
units.tr: Add the causes. 1. persecution; 2. that they had one soul, and a "mine" and "thine" [?]: yet they were not free from complaints: Acts 6:1: "There was a murmuring of the Greeks against the Jews," etc.

units.la: Conclus. Tametsi prima fronte videatur speciosa & amabilis haec κοινωνία: esse tamen horribilem ἀπξία: Antithesis. Rectam vero esse Aristotelis reprehensionem: & sententiam: Distinctionem dominiorum, virtute civium, & moderatione legum rectarum cohonestatam, esse fontem beneficentiæ, pacis, & incolumitatis Reipublicæ.
units.tr: Conclusion. Although at first sight this communion seems splendid and lovable, it is nonetheless a horrible [ἀπξία] ... Antithesis. Rather, Aristotle's reproof and opinion is correct: that the distinction of dominions, adorned by the virtue of citizens and the moderation of right laws, is the source of beneficence, peace and the safety of the commonwealth.

units.la: Votum: Orandus Deus, ut a nostra Republica arceat barbariem & confusiones:
units.tr: Prayer: God is to be entreated that He may keep barbarism and confusions far from our commonwealth.

units.la: Exercitatio VII.
units.tr: Exercitatio VII.

units.la: Collatio Prodigalitatis & Illiberalitatis ex Ethic. lib.4. cap.1.
units.tr: Comparison of Prodigality and Illiberality, from Ethics book 4, chapter 1.

units.la: EXordium breviter exponat & improbet πα-ράδοξον[?] Stoicum de æqualitate peccatorum & vitiorum. ἀπολογία ab instantia fit Propositio.
units.tr: The introduction briefly sets out and refutes the Stoic paradox [?] on the equality of sins and vices. The defence is made from the opposing side. The proposition follows.

units.la: Quia illiberalitas multo gravius vitium fit Prodigalitate.
units.tr: Because illiberality is a much graver vice than prodigality.

units.la: Ratio I. quia magis repugnet virtuti, quam prodigalitas, quę tanquam simia quædam multa facit liberalitatis propria. 1. non accipiendo. 2. dando. 3. prolixe. 4. cum voluptate. Ostendatur hæc esse virtutis: & addatur discrimen rectę & vitiosę erogationis à circumstantiis modi, finis & objectorum.
units.tr: First reason. Because it is more opposed to virtue than prodigality is. Prodigality, like a kind of ape, imitates many things proper to liberality: (1) by not receiving; (2) by giving; (3) by giving lavishly; (4) with pleasure. Let it be shown that these belong to virtue, and let there be added the distinction between right and vicious giving, drawn from the circumstances of manner, end and objects.

units.la: Ἀντίθεσις. Illiberalitas deficiens dando: exsuperans accipiendo, dupliciter repugnat utrique.
units.tr: Antithesis. Illiberality, which falls short in giving, and excess, which goes too far in receiving, are opposed to each of these in two ways.

units.la: Ratio II. Superioris sit πλεονεξία: Prodigalitas est ἀσωτία[?]: facile curatur per ætatem vel egestatem.
units.tr: Second reason. Illiberality, the excess of getting, is the vice of the one who wants more [pleonexia]; prodigality is wastefulness [asōtia]; it is easily cured by age or by poverty.

units.la: Probetur ex thesi: quod in similia facilior fit mutatio: Antithesis: Illiberalitas est ἀνίατος[?]: incurabilis. 1. quia ætate & egestate augetur morbus. Aristot. Senectus & imbecillitas omnis avaros efficit. 2. quia πλεονεξία[?] magis est innata hominibus quam profusio.
units.tr: Let it be proved from the thesis that a change is easier in the lesser case. Antithesis: illiberality is incurable [anialon]: it cannot be cured. (1) Because the disease grows with age and with poverty. Aristotle: old age and feebleness make every man avaricious. (2) Because the desire to have more [pleonexia] is more innate in men than extravagance.

units.la: Ratio III. Prodigus multis prodest: Illiberalis nec sibi nec aliis.
units.tr: Third reason. The prodigal benefits many; the illiberal man benefits neither himself nor others.

units.la: Ratio IV. Prodigus stultitia: Illiberalis pravitate animi & αἰσχροκερδεία[?] peccat, utile præferens honesto.
units.tr: Fourth reason. The prodigal sins through folly; the illiberal sins through a perverse mind and shameful gain [aischrokerdeia], preferring what is useful to what is honourable.

units.la: Obiect. 1. Prodigus peccat in seipsum.
units.tr: Objection 1. The prodigal sins against himself.

units.la: Respond. Illiberalis magis: contrahens morbum animi incurabilem, perdens famam & salutem: cum ille tantum facultates & valetudinem profundat, quæ sunt recuperabilia: & sit ἀσωτία[?].
units.tr: Reply. The illiberal man sins more: he contracts an incurable disease of the mind, losing his reputation and his welfare, whereas the other squanders only his property and health, which can be recovered; and it is wastefulness [asōtia].

units.la: Obiectio 2. Pejus est dare, quib. non oportet, quam non dare, quibus oportet: Probetur ab ef-sectis: quia mali donatis abutentes redduntur deteriores: boni etiam præteriti non efficiuntur pejores. Respond. negatione antecedentis: quia deterius est, quod per se, quam quod per accidens nocet. Hinc ostendatur fallacia accidentis in probatione: Erogationem per se prodesse, quia virtutis: per accidens nocere, si indignis fiat: liberales per se nocere sibi, appetitum depravantes: & frauda-realios[?].
units.tr: Objection 2. It is worse to give to those to whom one ought not, than not to give to those to whom one ought. It is proved from the effects: because those who abuse gifts from bad people become worse, while good people who are passed over do not become worse. Reply, by denying the antecedent: because that which harms in itself is worse than that which harms by accident. Hence the fallacy of accident is shown in the proof: giving in itself benefits, because it is a matter of virtue; it harms only by accident, if it is done to the unworthy. The liberal man harms himself in itself, by corrupting his appetite; and [withholding...]

units.la: Conclusio. Vitia igitur hæc esse inæqualia: ambo tamen fugienda.
units.tr: Conclusion. These vices, therefore, are unequal; yet both are to be avoided.

units.la: Exercitatio VIII.
units.tr: Exercitatio VIII.

units.la: Vituperatio Ebrietatis in genere mixto.
units.tr: Vituperatio Ebrietatis in genere mixto.
