units.la: Exordium fit querela de abusu donorum Dei, liberaliter concedentis hominibus multa non solum ad necessitatem: sed etiam ad voluptatem.
units.tr: Exordium is a complaint about the abuse of God's gifts, which he gives freely to men, many things not only for necessity but also for pleasure.

units.la: Hypothesis: Sic vini usum per se salutarem & jucundum rapi in fœdum abusum ebrietatis.
units.tr: Hypothesis: In this way the use of wine, in itself healthful and pleasant, is turned into the shameful abuse of drunkenness.

units.la: Amplif. ab indigno: Hoc vitium non modo latissime grassari: sed ob frequentiam varie palliari, & encomiis ornari.
units.tr: Amplification from the unworthiness: This vice not only spreads most widely but, because of its frequency, is variously excused and adorned with praises.

units.la: Propositio per adverf., Sed esse peccatum fœdissimum, perniciosissimum, omnibus fugiendum.
units.tr: Proposition by contrast: But it is a most shameful and most destructive sin, to be avoided by all.

units.la: Probetur 1. fœditas ex loco effectorum.
units.tr: Let it be proved, (1) the shamefulness from the place of its effects.

units.la: I. Quia aufert usum rationis, qua sola differt homo a brutis. Hos. 4. 11. Luc. 21. 34. Explicetur metaphorica phrasis Christi: ne graventur corda vestra: vestra: ex Jef.5.12. Amplificetur ex fine creatio-nis hominis.
units.tr: I. Because it takes away the use of reason, by which alone man differs from the beasts. Hos. 4. 11. Luke 21. 34. Let the metaphorical phrase of Christ be explained: lest your hearts be weighed down; "your": from Isa. 5. 12. Let it be amplified from the end of man's creation.

units.la: II. Quia exstincto rationis usu inflammat cupiditates, iram; odium: libidinem, &c. quibus ebriosi bestiarum more ad scelera abripiuntur & deformantur: Eph.5.18.
units.tr: II. Because, when the use of reason is extinguished, it inflames the desires, anger, hatred, lust, etc., by which drunkards are carried off to crimes and disfigured, like beasts: Eph. 5. 18.

units.la: Illustretur exemplis Sodomitarum, Lothi, Alexandri Magni, Nohę: M. Antonii sępe[?] vomentis pro tribunali;
units.tr: Let it be illustrated by the examples of the Sodomites, of Lot, of Alexander the Great, of Noah, and of Mark Antony vomiting often before the tribunal;

units.la: Addantur dicta Senecæ: Ebrietas voluntaria insania: Et: Habitus ebrietatis extensus in plures dies est furor. Et ejusdem Epiphonema. Multa faciunt ebrii, quorum postea sobrios pudet.
units.tr: Let the sayings of Seneca be added: Voluntary drunkenness is madness; and: A state of drunkenness extended over many days is frenzy. And his epiphonema: Drunken men do many things, of which they later feel ashamed when sober.

units.la: Probetur II. pernicies itidem ab effectis.
units.tr: Let it be proved, II., the destructiveness likewise from its effects.

units.la: I. Quia meretur æternas pœnas.1.Corinth.6. 10.Gal.5.21.
units.tr: I. Because it deserves eternal punishments. 1 Cor. 6. 10. Gal. 5. 21.

units.la: II. Perdit rem domesticam: cum injuria conjugum & liberorum. Prov.21.17.
units.tr: II. It ruins the household, with injury to spouses and children. Prov. 21. 17.

units.la: III. Generat morbos: febrem: podagram, hydropem. Prov.23.
units.tr: III. It produces diseases: fever, gout, dropsy. Prov. 23.

units.la: IV. Accelerat mortem: sæpe violentam ac turpem,
units.tr: IV. It hastens death, often violent and shameful.

units.la: V. Pervertit judicia Prov.31.5. Lex Solonis capitis pœnam irrogavit principi ebrio.
units.tr: V. It perverts judgments. Prov. 31. 5. The law of Solon imposed the penalty of death on a magistrate who was drunk.

units.la: VI. Evertit regna & respub. securitate. Joel, 1.5.Ief.5.Amos 5.7.
units.tr: VI. It overthrows kingdoms and commonwealths through carelessness. Joel 1. 5. Isa. 5. Amos 5. 7.

units.la: Conclusio: sit ὑποδιωξις[?], & dehortatio.
units.tr: Conclusion: let there be a warning and an exhortation to dissuade.

units.la: Exercitatio IX.
units.tr: Exercitatio IX.

units.la: An fœdera cum impiis sint licita.
units.tr: Whether covenants with the ungodly are lawful.

units.la: EXordium ex præcepto Pauli: Nolite trahere jugum cum infideli: Videri omnia foedera cum impiis esse illicita.
units.tr: THE introduction is taken from Paul's precept: Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. It seems that all covenants with the ungodly are unlawful.

units.la: Adversativa: Sed non sic statuendum esse.
units.tr: Adversative: But it must not be determined in this way.

units.la: Ratio 1. quia multa sint necessaria.
units.tr: Reason 1. because many are necessary.

units.la: 2. Quia in Scriptura sint quaedam exempla non illaudata.
units.tr: 2. Because in Scripture there are certain examples that are not unpraised.

units.la: Propositionis pars prima: Pacta & conventiones cum infidelibus vicinis vel hostibus esse licitas de finibus herciscundis, de pace, de commerciis necessariis.
units.tr: First part of the proposition: Pacts and agreements with neighbouring or hostile unbelievers are lawful concerning the dividing of boundaries, concerning peace, and concerning necessary commerce.

units.la: Ratio 1, Quia sine his neque Ecclesia neque Respubl. stare, vel diu stare potest.
units.tr: Reason 1. Because without these neither the Church nor the commonwealth can stand, or stand for long.

units.la: 2. Quia apostolus praecipit, ut pacem colamus cum omnibus. Rom. 12.
units.tr: 2. Because the apostle commands that we cultivate peace with all. Rom. 12.

units.la: 3 Exempla non illaudata Abrahami cum tribus fratribus Emorœis. Gen. 14. 13. & cum Abimelecho: Gen. 21. Isaaci cum eodem. Gen. 26. Iacobi cum Labane. Gen. 31.
units.tr: 3. Unpraised examples: Abraham with the three Amorite brothers, Gen. 14. 13; and with Abimelech, Gen. 21; Isaac with the same, Gen. 26; Jacob with Laban, Gen. 31.

units.la: Propositionis altera pars: Confoederationes cum impiis de societate religionis, nuptiarum, armorum, &c. non esse licitas.
units.tr: Other part of the proposition: Confederations with the ungodly concerning fellowship in religion, marriages, arms, etc., are not lawful.

units.la: Ratio 1. ab inhonesto: quia est species apostasiae a Deo, & conspirationis adversus eum, vel collocatio fiduciae in impiis.
units.tr: Reason 1. From the dishonourable: because it is a kind of apostasy from God and a conspiracy against him, or a placing of trust in the ungodly.

units.la: Ratio 2. ab inhonesto & inutili: quia hoc vere est habere jugum cum infideli, seu participare impiorum peccatis cum laesione gloriae Dei & salutis propriae: quod breviter ostendatur.
units.tr: Reason 2. From the dishonourable and useless: because this truly is to be yoked together with an unbeliever, or to share in the sins of the ungodly, to the injury of God's glory and of one's own salvation; which is briefly to be shown.

units.la: Ratio 3. a minori: quia Paulus prohibet litigare contra fratres ad tribunalia infidelium. 1. Cor. 6. Quanto magis, &c.
units.tr: Reason 3. From the lesser: because Paul forbids going to law against brothers before the tribunals of unbelievers. 1 Cor. 6. How much more, etc.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia ejusmodi foedera perpetuo reprehenprehendit Scriptura etiam in sanctis: & fuerunt infelicia: Vt Asa[?] cum Benhadado: Iosaphati cum Achabo: Iudæorum cum Lacedæmoniis & Romanis.
units.tr: Reason 4. Because Scripture constantly rebukes such covenants even in the saints, and they have been unhappy: as Asa with Ben-hadad; Jehoshaphat with Ahab; the Jews with the Spartans and the Romans.

units.la: Objectio. Deus ipse utitur opera malorum.
units.tr: Objection. God himself makes use of the works of evil men.

units.la: Respond. Dissimilitudo multiplex: Ostendatur: Deus id fecit. 1. absque confœderatione. 2. non ad sui defensionem. 3. ad exsequenda justa sua judicia: ut summus judex: 4. citra periculum inquinationis vel depravationis.
units.tr: Answer. The dissimilarity is manifold. Let it be shown: God did this, (1) without any covenant; (2) not for his own defence; (3) to carry out his just judgments, as the supreme judge; (4) without danger of pollution or corruption.

units.la: Conclusio: Fœdera igitur Christianorum Principum cum Turcis & infidelibus vicinis de finibus: pace: & commerciis verbo Dei & necessitate excusari: Cætera Deum offendere: & homines vana utilitatis specie deludere: ideoque vitanda esse.
units.tr: Conclusion: Therefore the covenants of Christian princes with the Turks and with unbelieving neighbours concerning boundaries, peace, and commerce may be excused by the Word of God and by necessity; the rest offend God and deceive men under the empty appearance of advantage, and therefore are to be avoided.

units.la: Exercitatio X.
units.tr: Exercitatio X.

units.la: An liceat uti dolo.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to use deceit.

units.la: EXordium à causis dubitationis: videri illicitum dolo uti.
units.tr: The introduction, from the grounds of doubt: it seems unlawful to use deceit.

units.la: Ratio 1. quia Scriptura dolum passim detegitur: Addantur breviter testimonia quædam.
units.tr: Argument 1. Because Scripture everywhere condemns deceit. Let some testimonies be added briefly.

units.la: 2. quia sit machinatio ficta, decipiendi causa, quæ sit illicita.
units.tr: 2. Because a contrived scheme, devised for the sake of deceiving, is unlawful.

units.la: Propositio per adversa. Non omnem dolum semper esse illicitum: sed aliquo interdum licere uti. Declaratur distinctione: Bono erga quosvis: malo erga hostes, juxta illud Poëtæ:
units.tr: Proposition, by the contrary. Not every deceit is always unlawful, but sometimes it is lawful to use some kind of it. This is explained by a distinction: deceit that is good, used toward anyone at all; deceit that is bad, used toward enemies, in accordance with that saying of the poet:

units.la: Dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat? Definiatur uterque: Bonus qui nulli nocet, alicui prodest. Malus, qui semper est noxius.
units.tr: Who in an enemy demands deceit or virtue? Let each be defined. Good deceit is that which harms no one and benefits someone. Bad deceit is that which is always harmful.

units.la: Confirmatio I. partis.
units.tr: Confirmation of the first part.

units.la: Ratio 1. quia non pugnat cum veritate, figurate aliquid dicere aut facere, ut aliter accipiatur, quam dicitur aut fit, citra cujusquam læsionem: alicujus autem bono: ut, cum nutrix parvulum placat fictis verbis, crepundiis, &c. vel cum medicus tacitus aut professus aquam pro vino propinat febricitanti, ne noceat.
units.tr: Argument 1. Because it does not conflict with truth to say or do something figuratively, so that it is understood otherwise than it is said or done, without harm to anyone, and for someone's good: as when a nurse soothes a little child with feigned words, rattles, and so on; or when a physician, quietly or openly, gives a feverish patient water instead of wine, so that it will not harm him.

units.la: Ratio 2. quia charitas jubet non modo aperte, sed & tecte, re ita postulante, juvare salutem proximi: ut dare furioso lignum pro gladio depositó: Probetur: quia lex vetat occidere.
units.tr: Argument 2. Because charity commands us to help the health of our neighbour not only openly but also covertly, when the circumstances require it: as to give a madman a piece of wood instead of a sword that he has laid down. Let it be proved: because the law forbids killing.

units.la: Ratio 3. quia exempla non simpliciter illaudata exstant in Scriptura: ut, dolus obstetricum Ægyptiarum, sororculæ Mosis adducentis matré pro nutrice: Davidis simulato furore vitantis periculum in aula Achis, &c.
units.tr: Argument 3. Because examples are found in Scripture that are not simply unpraised: as the deceit of the Egyptian midwives, and the little sister of Moses who brought their mother in as the nurse; David, feigning madness to escape danger at the court of Achish, and so on.

units.la: Confirmat. II. partis.
units.tr: Confirmation of the second part.

units.la: Præmittatur limitatio.
units.tr: Let the limitation be set down first.

units.la: 1. Si hostes sint vel Dei vel reipub. notorii.
units.tr: 1. If the enemies are notorious either to God or to the commonwealth.

units.la: 2. Si non intervenerit jusjurandum, vel pactum de non lædendo, vel non celando.
units.tr: 2. If no oath or agreement not to injure or not to conceal has intervened.

units.la: Addatur utriq; conditioni sua ratio: Priori: quia vindicta privati de privato sit prohibita: Posteriori: quia fallere fidem etiam hosti datam est violatio legis divinæ & juris gentium.
units.tr: Let the reason for each condition be added: for the former, because private revenge of a private person against a private person is forbidden; for the latter, because breaking faith even pledged to an enemy is a violation of the divine law and of the law of nations.

units.la: Ratio I. à minori : quia in hostem licet uti armis, quorum vice est dolus malus.
units.tr: First argument, from the lesser: because against an enemy it is lawful to use arms, in whose place stands bad deceit.

units.la: II. à pari: quia in causa necessitatis licet vim vi repellere: Ergo etiam vim vel dolum dolo.
units.tr: Second, from the equal: because in a case of necessity it is lawful to repel force with force; therefore also force or deceit with deceit.

units.la: III. quia nec veritati nec justitiæ repugnat, celando consilia dictis vel factis figuratis hostem circumvenire.
units.tr: Third: because it contradicts neither truth nor justice to circumvent an enemy by concealing one's plans with figurative words or deeds.

units.la: IV. Quia Deus jussit Israelitas dolo uti in Ægyptios & Ajenses.
units.tr: Fourth: because God commanded the Israelites to use deceit against the Egyptians and the Ajenses.

units.la: Confutatio.
units.tr: Refutation.

units.la: Ad obiectionem I. quod Scriptura damnet dolum. Resp. 1. malum. 2. erga amicos.
units.tr: To the first objection, that Scripture condemns deceit. Reply: 1. bad deceit; 2. deceit toward friends.

units.la: Ad II. Machinationem fictam decipiendi causa esse illicitam. Resp. non omnem: sed qua fit deceptio. 1. cum laesione proximi: 2. contra legem veritatis vel justitiæ. Probetur: quia quædam sit præcepta lege: Diliges proximum ut te ipsum: ut fallere puerum vel furiosum vel febricitantem suo bono.
units.tr: To the second, that a contrived scheme devised for the sake of deceiving is unlawful. Reply: not every such scheme, but one by which deception is effected: 1. with injury to a neighbour; 2. against the law of truth or justice. Let it be proved: because a certain deceit is commanded by the law: You shall love your neighbour as yourself: as to deceive a child, or a madman, or a feverish man, for his own good.

units.la: Instantia: Diligite inimicos. Respond. remis-sione vindictæ privatæ: non intermissione ossi-cii legibus nobis injuncti.
units.tr: Instance: Love your enemies. Reply: by the remission of private revenge, not by the omission of the duty enjoined on us by the laws.

units.la: Conclusio: Dolum quidem vel veniam vel lau-dem aliquando mereri: sed in omnibus candorē magis probari, & sectandum esse.
units.tr: Conclusion: Deceit may indeed sometimes deserve pardon or even praise, but in all things candour is more to be approved and pursued.

units.la: Exercitatio XI.
units.tr: Exercitatio XI.

units.la: Reprehensio Amici utentis in morbo magorum opera.
units.tr: Reproof of a friend who uses the work of magicians in sickness.

units.la: EXordium testetur συμπαθείαν[?] ob amici morbum: bum : magis verò dolorem, quòd audiveris cum à medicis ad magos confugere.
units.tr: The Exordium expresses sympathy for the illness of a friend; but more grief, because you have heard that he has fled from physicians to magicians.

units.la: Propositio : Nefaciat.
units.tr: Proposition: He should not do it.

units.la: Ratio I. quia fit horribilis Idolplatria[?] lege prohibita.
units.tr: Reason I. Because it becomes a horrible idolatry, forbidden by the law.

units.la: Probetur : quia salutem à magis petere, sit fiduciam, spem, invocationem, & cultum Deo debitum ad Satanam transferre.
units.tr: To be proved: because to seek health from magicians is to transfer to Satan the trust, hope, invocation and worship due to God.

units.la: Exaggerentur prohibitiones, & comminationes divinæ ex lege : Levit. 19. 31. & 20. 6. 27. Num. 23. 23. Deut. 18. 10. &c.
units.tr: The prohibitions and divine threats from the law are to be emphasised: Lev. 19.31, and 20.6, 27; Num. 23.23; Deut. 18.10, etc.

units.la: II. quia, fit φαρμακεία[?] & perfidia : ostendatur ex obligatione Baptismi : Occupetur excusatio : frustra eum sibi blandiri, quod salva conscientia & professione faciat : ex dictis : Nemo potest duobus, &c. Quid Christo cum Belial?
units.tr: II. Because it is sorcery [pharmakeia] and treachery. This is shown from the obligation of Baptism. The excuse is to be refuted: that it is vain for him to flatter himself that he may do this with a good conscience and without breaking his profession. From what has been said: No one can serve two masters, etc.; What fellowship has Christ with Belial?

units.la: III. Quia sit stultitia summa, salutem ab homicida, veritatem à mendace petere. Iohan. 8: Diabolus homicida & mendax.
units.tr: III. Because it is the highest folly to seek safety from a murderer and truth from a liar. John 8: The devil was a murderer and a liar.

units.la: IV. Ab exemplo Ahaziæ reprehensi & puniti hoc nomine à Deo. 2. Reg. 1.
units.tr: IV. From the example of Ahaziah, who was reproved and punished by God for this very thing. 2 Kings 1.

units.la: Obiectio. Multis profuisse magorum operam.
units.tr: Objection. The work of magicians has helped many.

units.la: Resp. 1. per concessionem: Id fieri permittente Deo, ut magis seducantur, & in nassam Satanæ trahantur infideles. 2. Thess. 2. Propterea mittit eis, &c. Sed piis servandam regulam : Non facienda mala, ut eveniant bona.
units.tr: Answer 1, by concession: this happens because God permits it, so that unbelievers may be more deceived and drawn into the snare of Satan. 2 Thess. 2: For this reason God sends them, etc. But the rule must be kept by the godly: evil things are not to be done so that good things may come of them.

units.la: 2. Per negationem : quia non prosint, quæ cum læsione Dei & conscientiæ fiunt. Matth. 16. 26. Quid prodest homini : si totum, &c.
units.tr: 2. By denial: because those things do not profit which are done to the injury of God and of conscience. Matt. 16.26: What does it profit a man, if he gains the whole, etc.

units.la: Obiectio 2. Licere ab impiis eleemosynam petere. Ergo etiam à magis sanitatem. Resp. negatione confequ. ob dissimilitudinem. r.[?] quia Diabolus juratus & insanabilis Dei hostis & generis humani: Impii sæpe sint sanabiles. 2. ab impiis eleemosyna peti & accipi potest citra fidu-ciam in ipsos: à Diabolo & magis non item. 3. De magis & Diabolo fugiendis extat mandatum. De eleemosyna impiorum non item.
units.tr: Objection 2. It is lawful to ask alms from the impious; therefore also health from magicians. Answer: by denial of the consequence, on account of dissimilarity. First, because the Devil is a sworn and incurable enemy of God and of the human race, whereas the impious are often curable. Second, alms may be sought and received from the impious without trust placed in them; this is not so with the Devil and magicians. Third, there is a command concerning fleeing from magicians and the Devil; there is no such command concerning the alms of the impious.

units.la: Conclusio: Renunciet itaque magorum operæ: resipiscat: ac toleret patienter, vel mediis licitis curet mala à Deo immissa: nisi eum Zelotem ac vindicem experiri velit.
units.tr: Conclusion: Let him therefore renounce the work of magicians, return to repentance, and bear his evils patiently, or cure the evils sent by God by lawful means, unless he wishes to try God as a jealous avenger.

units.la: Exercitatio XII.
units.tr: Exercitatio XII.

units.la: Dehortatio Amici à κακοζηλία in vestitu.
units.tr: Dissuasion of a friend from bad taste (κακοζηλία) in dress.

units.la: EXordium sit gratulatio, quod audiveris eum de consilio Patris totum se Theologiæ studio dedisse: ac Principis beneficio liberaliter foveri.
units.tr: Let the introduction be a congratulation, that you have heard he has devoted himself wholly to the study of theology, in accordance with his father's counsel, and that he is generously supported by the favour of the Prince.

units.la: Collaudationis ratio: quia pro tuo in ipsum amore de ejus commodis sis sollicitus.
units.tr: The reason for praise: because, out of your love for him, you are concerned for his welfare.

units.la: Adversat. Sed displicere tibi, quod audiveris, cum sub specie elegantiæ se deformare κακοζηλία in vestitu.
units.tr: Objection. But it displeases you, as you have heard, that under the appearance of elegance he disfigures himself by bad taste (κακοζηλία) in dress.

units.la: Declaratur: ut intelligat te loqui de prava affectatione vestium exoticarum, deformium ac indecentium, quas vulgò videat: ut sunt pilei ὠ-μοπλατ[?], fasciæ coruscantes: circuli dodrantales, collaria luxuriosa, thoraces prægnantes, &c. calcei fenestrati, &c.
units.tr: Explanation: that he may understand that you are speaking of the perverse affectation of outlandish, misshapen and unseemly clothing, which is commonly seen: such as caps of (?) shape, glittering sashes, circular ruffs of nine inches, luxurious collars, bulging doublets, etc., slashed shoes, etc.

units.la: Propositio: Hortari te, ne amet has ineptias.
units.tr: Proposition: I exhort you not to love these follies.

units.la: Ratio I. ab inhonesto: Quia hæc κακοζηλία[?] fit index animi variis vitiis corrupti: Enumerentur aliquot vitia: Levitas abjiciens res consuetas sine causa: nec habens studium retinendi famam honestam.
units.tr: First reason, from dishonour: because this bad taste (κακοζηλία) becomes a sign of a mind corrupted by various vices. Some of the vices are listed: Levity, casting aside customary things without cause and not having a care to keep an honourable reputation.

units.la: Curiositas, arripiens nova sine judicio:
units.tr: Curiosity, seizing on novelties without judgement.

units.la: Immodestia, negligens decorum personæ suæ.
units.tr: Immodesty, neglecting the decorum of one's own person.

units.la: Superbia, efferens se supra alios, & se ostentans.
units.tr: Pride, raising oneself above others and showing off.

units.la: Stultitia, amans & eligens indecora, & invisa prudentibus.
units.tr: Folly, loving and choosing things unbecoming and hateful to the prudent.

units.la: Lascivia: prodens & irritans pravas animi cupiditates.
units.tr: Lasciviousness, revealing and provoking wicked desires of the mind.

units.la: Probetur minor authoritate Bernhardi: Vestium curiositas deformitatis mentium & morum indicium est. Et vulgari dicto: vestis virum indicat.
units.tr: Let the minor premise be proved by the authority of Bernard: The curiosity of clothing is a sign of deformity of minds and morals. And by the common saying: clothing shows the man.

units.la: Amplificetur I. ex descriptione κακοζηλίας[?], quod sit prava affectatio ejus, quod est ultra virtutem, judicio carens, & specie boni fallens.
units.tr: Let the first point be amplified from the description of bad taste (κακοζηλία) [?], that it is a perverse affectation of what goes beyond virtue, lacks judgement, and deceives by the appearance of good.

units.la: II. a contrario, h. e., a fine vestium, qui est tegumentum turpitudinis.
units.tr: Second, from the contrary, that is, from the end of clothing, which is a covering of shame.

units.la: Ratio II. ab inhonesto: Quia fit aliena a professione tua, quam suscepseris. Probetur ex fine Theologiæ: & ex dictis, Tit.2.7.2.Tim.2.22. Juveniles cupiditates fuge.
units.tr: Second reason, from dishonour: because it is foreign to your profession, which you have taken up. Let it be proved from the end of theology, and from the words of Titus 2.7 and 2 Timothy 2.22: Flee youthful desires.

units.la: Amplificetur a minori: Ethicam requirere auditorem non indulgentem animi perturbationibus & affectibus. Multo magis Theologiam.
units.tr: Let it be amplified from the less: ethics requires a hearer who does not indulge in disturbances and passions of the mind. Much more so theology.

units.la: Ratio IV. ab inutili. 1. quod offendere posset oculos sui Principis. 2 quod violet disciplinam scholasticam. 3. quod corrumpat alios malo exemplo. 4. quod
units.tr: Fourth reason, from uselessness. (1) because it could offend the eyes of his Prince; (2) because it violates scholastic discipline; (3) because it corrupts others by bad example; (4) because

units.la: 4. quòd incurrere possit indignationem praeceptorum.
units.tr: (4) because it may incur the indignation of his teachers.

units.la: 5. quod periculum sit, ne ipse sibi minuat bona praesentia & futura.
units.tr: (5) because there is a danger that he may diminish for himself his present and future goods.

units.la: Conclusio: Orare te, ut hortationi obtemperet, & in vestitu ac moribus decorum, honestatem, ac modestiam sectetur.
units.tr: Conclusion: I ask you to obey the exhortation, and in dress and conduct to pursue what is becoming, honourable and modest.

units.la: Exercitatio XIII.
units.tr: Exercitatio XIII.

units.la: De Ludis: ad Amicum. Utrum ludere homini Christiano liceat. PARS NEGANS.
units.tr: On Games: to a Friend. Whether it is permitted for a Christian man to play. The NEGATIVE part.

units.la: EXordium ab occasione: Querelam Augustini petentis à Deo veniam lusuum adolescentiæ suæ, nuper tibi movisse scrupulum de ludis.
units.tr: Introduction from the occasion: Recently your complaint, in which Augustine asks God for forgiveness for the games of his youth, has stirred in you a doubt about games.

units.la: Ratio dubitationis exponatur dilemmate: quia si sint liciti, frustra ille petierit eorum veniam: si illiciti, male permittantur inter Christianos.
units.tr: The ground of the doubt is set out as a dilemma: if they are lawful, he sought their forgiveness in vain; if unlawful, they are wrongly tolerated among Christians.

units.la: Adversat. Etsi excusentur, quod sint recreationes: tamen multis de causis videri, Christianis ludere non licere.
units.tr: Objection: Although they may be excused on the ground that they are recreations, nevertheless, for many reasons, it seems that it is not permitted for Christians to play.

units.la: PROPOSITIO: Te igitur hujus sententiæ tuæ explicaturum rationes.
units.tr: PROPOSITION: Accordingly, I shall set out the reasons for this opinion of yours.

units.la: Ratio 1. quia non ad lusum, sed ad seria homo est conditus.
units.tr: Reason 1. Because man was created not for play but for serious things.

units.la: Ratio 2. quia finis actionum humanarum est gloria Dei, ad quam ludi nihil faciunt.
units.tr: Reason 2. Because the end of human actions is the glory of God, to which games contribute nothing.

units.la: Ratio 3. quia ludorum nulla potest Deo reddi ratio in extremo judicio. Matth.12. Amplificetur ab adiunctis & effectis: ocio, nugis, blasphemiis, fraudibus, rixis, caedibus: Illustretur etiam exemplo populi Israelitici surgentis ad ludendum. Exod.32.
units.tr: Reason 3. Because no account of games can be rendered to God at the final judgment. Matt. 12. The point is enlarged from the accompanying circumstances and effects: idleness, trifles, blasphemies, frauds, quarrels, slaughter. It is also illustrated by the example of the people of Israel rising up to play. Exod. 32.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia ludendo tempus preciosissimum male perditur: contra præceptum: Redimentes tempus.
units.tr: Reason 4. Because by playing, precious time is wastefully lost, contrary to the precept: Redeeming the time.

units.la: Exaggeretur jactura temporis debiti officiis necessariis & utilibus infinitis: quorum aliqua enumerentur.
units.tr: The loss of time is magnified, which is owed to countless necessary and useful duties; some of these are listed.

units.la: Ratio 5.[?] Quia patres Ecclesiastici fere omnes improbarunt. Ambrosius: Non solum profusos, sed omnes etiam iocos declinandos arbitror. Nam licet interdum honesta ioca ac suavia sint, tamen ab Ecclesiastica abhorrent regula.
units.tr: Reason 5. [?] Because almost all the ecclesiastical Fathers have disapproved of it. Ambrose: I judge that not only excessive jesting but all jokes should be avoided. For although at times jests may be honest and pleasant, nevertheless they are out of keeping with the ecclesiastical rule.

units.la: Conclusio: Sic multa pro peccatis non haberi, quia ad regulam verbi Dei non satis conferuntur.
units.tr: Conclusion: Thus many things are not regarded as sins, because they are not sufficiently compared with the rule of the Word of God.

units.la: Addatur petitio sententiæ amici: si diversum sentiat.
units.tr: The opinion of your friend is requested to be added: if he thinks otherwise.

units.la: Pars affirmans.
units.tr: The affirmative part.

units.la: De ludis licitis & illicitis.
units.tr: On permitted and forbidden games.

units.la: EXordii propositio partitione constet: Appro-bare te amici studium, atque affectum: sed non sententiam in propositā quæstione de Lu-dis: Repetatur breviter utraque.
units.tr: The proposition of the introduction consists of a division: I approve your friend's zeal and feeling, but not his opinion on the question proposed about games. Let each be briefly repeated.

units.la: Ratio I. Nimis durum esset, omnem lusum è vita tollere. Probatio: quia tollerentur multæ recreationes honestæ, & exercitia necessaria.
units.tr: Reason I. It would be too harsh to remove all play from life. Proof: because many honest recreations and necessary exercises would be taken away.

units.la: II. Quia leges, Patres, & concilia tantùm quosdam ludos damnant.
units.tr: II. Because laws, the Fathers, and councils condemn only certain games.

units.la: III. Quia Augustinus non deprecatur simpliciter, quòd pila luserit, sed quòd luserit. 1. faciendo contra præcepta parentum. 2. cum neglectu studiorum. 3. amans in certaminibus superbas victorias.
units.tr: III. Because Augustine does not simply deprecate that he played ball, but that he played: 1. doing so against the commands of his parents; 2. with neglect of his studies; 3. loving proud victories in contests.

units.la: IV. Quia omnes amici rationes tantùm concludunt de ludis illicitis, vel de abusu licitorum.
units.tr: IV. Because all the reasons of my friend conclude only about forbidden games, or about the abuse of permitted ones.

units.la: Transitio per adversat. Esse argumentum satis lubricum: de quo fere tantùm sit judicandum ex circumstantiis.
units.tr: Transition by way of objection. The matter is slippery enough, and it must be judged almost entirely from the circumstances.

units.la: Conclusio: Tamen te petenti sententiam tuam breviter explicaturum.
units.tr: Conclusion: Nevertheless, since you ask for my opinion, I shall explain it briefly.

units.la: Partitio: Judicare te, ludos quosdam licitos, quosdam illicitos esse. Subjiciatur declaratio seu distinctio, cujus partes sint totidem argumenta ad confirmandum utrumque partitionis membrum.
units.tr: Division: You judge that some games are permitted and some forbidden. Let a declaration or distinction be added, whose parts shall be as many arguments to confirm each member of the division.

units.la: De ludis licitis.
units.tr: On permitted games.

units.la: Ostendatur quosdam esse licitos.
units.tr: Let it be shown that some games are permitted.

units.la: Argumentum I. seu primum genus ludorum licitorum.
units.tr: Argument I, or the first kind of permitted games.

units.la: Recreatio pueritiæ: ut blandimenta, risus, crepundia, collusiones puerorum cum nutricibus, parentibus, vel inter se.
units.tr: The recreation of childhood: such as caresses, laughter, rattles, and the playing of children with their nurses, parents, or with one another.

units.la: Probetur esse licitos: 1. à communi sensu: quia hoc nemo sanus reprehendit: cum partim sint ψυχαγωγίαι[?], partim recreatio ætati conveniens & necessaria non minus quam cibus & somnus.
units.tr: Let it be proved that they are permitted: 1. from common sense, because no sane person finds fault with this; since, partly, they are psychagogiae [?], and partly a recreation suited to that age and necessary no less than food and sleep.

units.la: 2. à divina approbatione. Zach. 8. 5. Platea ci-vitatis vitatis replebuntur pueris & puellis, ludentib. in plateis ejus. Offendatur approbatio: quia promittitur ut beneficium Dei.
units.tr: 2. From divine approval. Zech. 8:5: The streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets. Let the approval be noted: because it is promised as a blessing of God.

units.la: Occupatio: Non defendi lasciviam vel petulantiam accidentem: quam peccatum esse, deprecatio Augustini docet.
units.tr: Objection: I do not defend the wantonness or petulance that sometimes occurs, which Augustine's deprecation teaches is sin.

units.la: Argum. II. seu II. genus ludorum licitorum: Gymnastici corporis vel animi. Enumerentur aliqui additis alicubi brevissimis descriptionibus, quales fuerint vel sint: Pila: discus: saltus: cursus: cestus: Par impar: Latrunculi: Astragali five taxilli, &c.
units.tr: Argument II, or the second kind of permitted games: the gymnastic games of body or mind. Let some be enumerated, with very brief descriptions added where needed of what they were or are: ball; discus; leaping; running; boxing; odd or even; checkers (latrunculi); dice (astragali, or taxilli), etc.

units.la: Addantur conditiones: quibus sint liciti: 1. non sint noxii fortunis aut valetudini nostrae vel alienae. 2. sint moderati. 3. tempestivi.
units.tr: Let the conditions be added under which they are permitted: 1. they must not be harmful to our own or others' fortunes or health; 2. they must be moderate; 3. they must be timely.

units.la: Probetur sic esse licitos. 1. quia reparant vires animi laboribus fessi. Amplif. à necessario: Hominis animum requirere aliquam relaxationem & oblectationem [?] ἕσης δὲ καὶ ἀναπαύσεως ἐν τῷ βίῳ, καὶ ἐν ταύτῃ Διαγωγῆς μετὰ παιδιᾶς. Et: δο-κεῖ δὲ ἡ ἀνάπαυσις καὶ ἡ παιδιὰ ἐν τῷ βίῳ εἶναι ἀ-ναγκαῖον.
units.tr: Let it be proved that they are thus permitted. 1. Because they restore the strength of the mind wearied by labours. Amplification from necessity: the human mind requires some relaxation and delight [?]: "There is a need, in life, of rest and relaxation, and in it of a pastime accompanied by play." And: "Rest and play seem to be necessary in life."

units.la: Illustretur simili arcus
units.tr: Let it be illustrated by a simile:

units.la: Arcus & arma tua tibi sint metuenda Diana:
units.tr: Let your bow and arms be a fear to Diana:

units.la: Si nunquam cesses tendere: mollis erit.
units.tr: If you never cease to bend it, it will become slack.

units.la: II. Quia augent & conservant valetudinem. Aristot. Eth. lib. 2. cap. 2. γυμνάσια σύμμετρα ποιεῖ καὶ αὔξει καὶ σώζει τὴν ὑγίειαν.
units.tr: II. Because they increase and preserve health. Aristotle, Eth. book 2, ch. 2: "Moderate exercises produce, increase and preserve health."

units.la: III. Quia juvant agilitatem, quae est utile & decorum corporis bonum.
units.tr: III. Because they aid agility, which is a useful and becoming good of the body.

units.la: IV. à concessione Legum. Cod. lib. 3. tit. 43. in constitutione nova Justinianus prohibito alearum lusu substituit, luctam, discum, cursum, saltum, cestum.
units.tr: IV. From the permission of the laws. Cod. book 3, title 43: in a new constitution, Justinian, in place of the prohibited game of dice, substituted wrestling, the discus, running, leaping, and boxing.

units.la: Addatur restrictio Imperatoris: Sed nec permittimus etiam in his ludere ultra unum solidum, etiamsi multum dives sit: ut si quem vinci contigerit, casum gravem non sustineat.
units.tr: Let the restriction of the Emperor be added: "But we do not permit them even in these games to play for more than one solidus, however wealthy a man may be, so that if he happens to lose, he does not suffer a serious loss."

units.la: Argumentum III. seu III. genus ludo-rum licitorum: Progymnastici militia. Exponantur aliqui veteribus usitati: Saltatio Pyrrhica: certamen equestre vel currule: ναυμαχία: Et hodie: Palastrica: jaculatoria, &c.
units.tr: Argument III, or the third kind of permitted games: the preliminary exercises of military service. Let some be set out that were in use among the ancients: the Pyrrhic dance; equestrian or chariot racing; naval battle [naumachia]. And today: palaestra, javelin-throwing, etc.

units.la: Accommodentur etiam his conditiones: ne sint 1. lucrosi. 2. Immoderati. 3. Intempestivi. 4. periculosi.
units.tr: Let the conditions also be applied to these: they must not be 1. for gain; 2. immoderate; 3. untimely; 4. dangerous.

units.la: Probetur sic esse licitos: 1. Quia sunt exercitia tractandorum armorum civibus & Reipub. utilia & necessaria ad defensionem. Maior probetur: quia ipsa militia: & defensio Reipub. est licita. Minor exornetur a commodis peritiae armorum, ex Arist. Eth. lib. 3. c. 8. ποιῆσαι καὶ μὴ πα-θεῖν μάλιστα ἀλλ' ἀνδρικῶς [?] ... ἀπὸ τῆς ἐμπειρίας [?], &c. Et ab incommodis imperitia, ibidem.
units.tr: Let it be proved that they are thus permitted: 1. Because they are exercises in handling arms, useful and necessary for citizens and the commonwealth for its defence. The major premise is proved, because military service itself and the defence of the commonwealth are lawful. The minor premise is embellished by the advantages of skill in arms, from Aristotle, Eth. book 3, ch. 8: "to act and not to suffer most of all, but manfully ... from experience" [?], etc. And from the disadvantages of inexperience, in the same place.

units.la: II. quia excitant studium virtutis & gloriae.
units.tr: II. Because they stir up zeal for virtue and glory.

units.la: Amplificetur a praemiis propositis industriam excitantibus, & victori gloriosis.
units.tr: Let it be amplified from the prizes offered, which stir up industry, and which are glorious for the victor.

units.la: Per occupationem ostendatur: non esse inhonesta lucra:
units.tr: Let it be shown by an objection that the gains are not dishonourable:

units.la: 1. quia proponuntur a magistratu, vel magistratus authoritate a privatis. 2. quia fere sunt vilia, ut pannus, aries, &c. olim olea, pinus, apiū, pomum. Plutarch. quaest. Symp. quaest. 3. lib. 5. & quaest. 4. lib. 8. Item Herod. lib. 8. de oleagena corona praemio Olympici certaminis. Inseratur generosa sententia Tigranis ad Mardonium: Papa Mardoni, in quos viros induxisti nos, ad pugnandum, qui non pecuniarum certamen agitant, sed virtutum?
units.tr: 1. because they are offered by the magistrate, or by private persons with the magistrate's authority; 2. because they are mostly cheap things, such as cloth, a ram, etc.; formerly olive, pine, parsley, or apple. Plutarch, Quaestiones convivales, book 5, question 3, and book 8, question 4. Likewise Herodotus, book 8, on the olive-wreath as the prize of the Olympic contest. Let there be inserted the noble saying of Tigranes to Mardonius: "Father Mardonius, what men have you led us to fight, who contend not for a contest of money, but of virtues?"

units.la: III. quia legibus Impp. sint concessi: loco supra citato.
units.tr: III. Because they have been granted by the laws of the emperors, in the passage cited above.

units.la: Conclusio: primi partitionis membri sit transitio:
units.tr: Conclusion: let there be a transition to the second member of the division:

units.la: Hactenus de licitis: nunc ostendendum quosdam esse illicitos.
units.tr: So far concerning permitted games; now it must be shown that some are forbidden.

units.la: De ludis illicitis.
units.tr: On illicit games.

units.la: I. CONFIRMATIO sit distributio in illicitos per se, & per accidens: & praemittantur illiciti per accidens cum definitione & argumentis, quae sint totidem genera illicitorum per accidens.
units.tr: I. The confirmation shall consist of a division into illicit games in themselves and illicit games by accident. First, the illicit games by accident are to be set out, with their definition and arguments, which are as many kinds of illicit games by accident.

units.la: Definitio: quod sint vitiosi ex aliqua circunstantia.
units.tr: Definition: they are vicious because of some circumstance.

units.la: ARGUM. I. Omnes liciti prius approbati, neglectis conditionib. additis.
units.tr: ARGUMENT I. All games that are otherwise permitted, when the conditions attached to them are neglected.

units.la: Probatio 1. quia sic alant vitia: lasciviam, otium, avaritiam, &c.
units.tr: Proof 1: because in this way they feed vices: wantonness, idleness, avarice, etc.

units.la: 2. quia sic laedant vitam vel fortunas.
units.tr: 2: because in this way they harm life or property.

units.la: 3. quia sic fiunt jactura temporis, & neglectus officij.
units.tr: 3: because in this way time is lost and duty neglected.

units.la: II. ARGUM II. ἀδιάφοροι[?], sed more aut lege civitatis nostrae omnino vel ad tempus veriti juxta rationem, circumstantiis loci, temporis & personarum accommodata, ut cum vetantur gymnastici, palaestrici, scenici non turpes, musici, &c. Addatur ratio interdicti: luctus, caritas, atrox casus ex ludo, vel enormis abusus, &c.
units.tr: II. ARGUMENT II. Games that are indifferent (ἀδιάφοροι[?]), but which, by the custom or law of our state, are either altogether or for a time forbidden, in accordance with reason and suited to the circumstances of place, time and persons: as when gymnastic, wrestling, and theatrical games that are not shameful, and musical games, etc., are prohibited. The reason for the prohibition is to be added: mourning, charity, a dreadful accident arising from the game, or a gross abuse, etc.

units.la: Probetur tunc esse abstinendum.
units.tr: It is to be proved that they must then be abstained from.

units.la: 1. quia leges positivae magistratus, necessaria vel probabili nitentes ratione, obligant conscientias. Rom.13.5.
units.tr: 1. Because positive laws of the magistrate, resting on a necessary or probable reason, bind consciences. Rom. 13.5.

units.la: Ratio 1 a genere, quod est morale, a Deo praeceptum: obedientia nimirum erga magistratus.
units.tr: First reason, from the genus: it is a moral matter, commanded by God, namely obedience towards the magistrates.

units.la: Ratio 2. a fine: quia sunt determinationes circumstantiarum utiles vel necessariae ad servanda praecepta moralia secundae tabulae, h.e,ad confservandum ordinem & decorum: & societatem ac pacem civilem.
units.tr: Second reason, from the end: because they are determinations of circumstances useful or necessary for keeping the moral precepts of the second table, that is, for preserving order and decorum, and civil society and peace.

units.la: II. quia vitanda sunt scandala, & turbatio ordinis ac decori civilis.
units.tr: II. Because scandals and the disturbance of civil order and decorum are to be avoided.

units.la: Transitio ad illicitos per se: qui describantur, quod sint ludi suo genere impii, naturae vel Dei lege damnati.
units.tr: Transition to the illicit games in themselves: which are described as games that are impious by their very kind, condemned by the law of nature or of God.

units.la: Confirmationis argumenta sint ipsa genera.
units.tr: The arguments for the confirmation are the kinds themselves.

units.la: ARGUM. I. Ludi sacri Ethnicorum omnes.
units.tr: ARGUMENT I. All the sacred games of the heathens.

units.la: Ratio probans impietatem 1. a fine, quia erant cultus idolorum, contra praeceptum: Non habe-bis Deos alienos, &c.
units.tr: The reason proving impiety: 1. from the end, because they were a worship of idols, against the precept: "You shall have no other gods, etc."

units.la: Enumerantur aliquot species: Actia[?], Dionysia, Lupercalia, Juvenalia, Olympia, Pythia, Heraclea, Seculares, Taurii, &c. Et addatur breviter, qui quibus idolis fuerint sacri.
units.tr: Some kinds are listed: Actia[?], Dionysia, Lupercalia, Juvenalia, Olympia, Pythia, Heraclea, Secular games, Taurian games, etc. And it should be briefly added to which idols each was sacred.

units.la: 2. a forma: quia plerique erant licentia scelerum, quod parce ostendatur. Opponatur sententia Scripturae de fugiendis operibus tenebrarum & carnis. 2.Cor.6.14. Gal.5.19. Rom.8.13. &c.
units.tr: 2. From the form: because most of them were licence for crimes, which is to be shown briefly. Let the statement of Scripture be set against them, about shunning the works of darkness and of the flesh: 2 Cor. 6.14; Gal. 5.19; Rom. 8.13, etc.

units.la: ARGUM. I I. Amphitheatrici. Vt venatio-nes & gladiatorii.
units.tr: ARGUMENT II. Amphitheatrical games: such as hunts and gladiatorial contests.

units.la: Describantur breviter: Ratio impietatis petatur ex præcepto. Non occides.
units.tr: These are to be described briefly. The reason for their impiety is to be drawn from the precept: "You shall not kill."

units.la: Amplificetur indignitas, quod fit contra naturam, per ludum vitam homini eripere: ex fine & forma hominis ad Dei imaginem conditi.
units.tr: The indignity is to be enlarged upon: that it is against nature, by way of a game, to take life from a man; and this from the end and form of man, who was created in the image of God.

units.la: Inseratur epiphonema Lactantii. Hos tamen ludos vocant, in quibus humanus sanguis funditur.
units.tr: Let the epiphonema of Lactantius be inserted: "Yet they call these games, in which human blood is poured out."

units.la: Alia amplificatio ab authore Diabolo. Joh. 8. Chrysost.homil.6.in Matth.
units.tr: Another amplification is from the author, the Devil: John 8; Chrysostom, homily 6 on Matthew.

units.la: ARGUM. III. Theatrici sive scenici ethnicorum.
units.tr: ARGUMENT III. The theatrical or scenic games of the heathens.

units.la: Distinguantur in Comicos & Tragicos: ac de-scribantur breviter.
units.tr: They are to be distinguished into comic and tragic, and briefly described.

units.la: Ratio impietatis 1. à firma: quia repræsentabant res suo genere turpes & impias, stupra, amores, incestus, parricidia, &c. etiam Deorum.
units.tr: The reason for their impiety: 1. from the form: because they represented things shameful and impious in their kind, fornications, loves, incests, parricides, etc., even of the gods.

units.la: 2. ab effectu: erant faces & incendia libidinū: irritamenta vitiorum. 1. Cor.15: Colloquia prava corrumpunt mores bonos. Videatur Lactantius ibidem.
units.tr: 2. From the effect: they were torches and fires of lusts, incitements to vices. 1 Cor. 15: "Evil conversations corrupt good manners." Let Lactantius be consulted in the same place.

units.la: Transfertur hypothesis ad Thesin: Simul damnari omnes illiberales ludos, in quibus est aliqua obscoenæ rei repræsentatio, fictio, imitatio aut pronunciatio. 1. Thess.5.22: Abstinete ab omni specie mali.
units.tr: The hypothesis is transferred to the thesis: at the same time, all illiberal games are condemned in which there is any representation, fiction, imitation or delivery of an obscene matter. 1 Thess. 5.22: "Abstain from every appearance of evil."

units.la: Πόρνευμα[?]: Comœdias ergo & Tragœdias turpes vel idololatricas non decere Christianos.
units.tr: Fornication [πόρνευμα[?]]: therefore comedies and tragedies that are shameful or idolatrous do not befit Christians.

units.la: ARGUM. IV. Choreæ lascivæ & turpes. Per occupationem probationi præmittantur duo:
units.tr: ARGUMENT IV. Wanton and shameful dances. Two things are premised to the proof by way of preoccupation:

units.la: 1. Choream per se non esse vitiosam.
units.tr: 1. That dancing in itself is not vicious.

units.la: Ratio 1. à forma: quia est motus & agilitas quædam corporis decora vel artificiosa, quæ est bonum naturale.
units.tr: First reason, from the form: because it is a certain graceful or skilful motion and agility of the body, which is a natural good.

units.la: 2. à fine: quia est vel exercitatio corporis, vel testificatio lætitiæ animi: quod posterius ostendatur ex etymo: quia χορεία dicitur ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς.
units.tr: 2. From the end: because it is either an exercise of the body, or a witness of joy of the mind; the latter is shown from the etymology: because χορεία is said to derive from χαρά [joy].

units.la: Amplificetur a pari: Licet cantu testari lætitiam: & Deum celebrare: Ergò & saltatione.
units.tr: Let it be amplified by parity: one may witness joy by song and celebrate God; therefore also by dancing.

units.la: 3. ab exemplis laudatis piorum: Mariæ. Exod. 15: puellarum. 1. Sam. 18. Davidis. 2. Sam. 6. &c.
units.tr: 3. From the praised examples of the pious: of Mary, Exod. 15; of the maidens, 1 Sam. 18; of David, 2 Sam. 6, etc.

units.la: Clausula cum restrictione: Pertinere igitur choream per se ad secundum genus licitorum: modo sit tempestiva, moderata & absque offensione.
units.tr: Conclusion with a restriction: dancing in itself therefore belongs to the second kind of permitted things, provided it is seasonable, moderate and without offence.

units.la: I I. Distinctio Choreæ in πολεμικὴν, quæ referatur ad I I I. genus licitorum: & in εἰρηνικὴν: Et hujus, in ἐμμέλειαν & χορδακισμόν. Illa statua-tur genus licitarum: iste illicitarum seu inhonestarum: tum veterum: ut erant comicæ: tum re-centium: seu sint solitariæ, ut saltant Itali, Hispa-ni, Galli aliquando, &c. seu γυναικανδρικὴν [?], ut saltant Germani & populi Septentrionales, &c.
units.tr: II. A distinction of dancing into the warlike (πολεμικὴν), which is referred to the third kind of permitted things, and into the peaceful (εἰρηνικὴν); and of this, into the graceful (ἐμμέλειαν) and the lewd (χορδακισμόν). The former is to be set as a kind of permitted things; the latter as a kind of illicit or dishonourable things: both that of the ancients, such as the comic dances, and that of more recent times, whether they are solitary, as the Italians, Spaniards and sometimes the French dance, etc., or mixed of men and women (γυναικανδρικὴν [?]), as the Germans and the northern peoples dance, etc.

units.la: Sequatur probatio: totum hoc genus esse illicitum.
units.tr: Let the proof follow: that this whole kind is illicit.

units.la: Ratio 1. à forma: quia sunt motus per se deformes & lascivi.
units.tr: First reason, from the form: because they are motions that are in themselves deformed and lascivious.

units.la: 2. ab effectu: quia irritamenta & occasiones luxuriæ & libidinum tam spectantibus quam saltantibus: lege Dei prohibitæ.
units.tr: 2. From the effect: because they are incitements and occasions of lust and lusts, both for the spectators and for the dancers, which are forbidden by the law of God.

units.la: Ostendatur ex V I I. præcepto: & amplificetur periculum a pravitate & propensione natu-rali ad lasciviam.
units.tr: Let it be shown from the Seventh Commandment, and the danger be amplified from its wickedness and natural proneness to lasciviousness.

units.la: Item dicto Siracidę. Qui amat periculum, in-eo peribit.
units.tr: Likewise by the saying of the son of Sirach: "He who loves danger shall perish in it."

units.la: 3. ab authoritate Scripturæ prohibentis omnem lasciviam, Rom.13.13.Gal.5.19.Eph.5.11.
units.tr: 3. From the authority of Scripture, which forbids all lasciviousness: Rom. 13.13; Gal. 5.19; Eph. 5.11.

units.la: 4. ab authoritate Patrum: & conciliorum prohibentium tales choreas. [?]Augustl. contra Petil. cap.6.Et in Psal.32.Chrysost.homil.48.&56.supr. Genes.Et in cap.14. Matthæi de saltatione Herodiadis. Concil.Laodic.& Ilerdens.
units.tr: 4. From the authority of the Fathers and of the councils, which forbid such dances: Augustine, against Petilian, chapter 6; and on Psalm 32; Chrysostom, homily 48 and 56 on Genesis; and on chapter 14 of Matthew, concerning the dancing of Herodias. The Council of Laodicea and of Lérida.

units.la: [?]Addatur testimonium Ethnicorum: Cic.3.off. &pro Muræna. Item Senecę.
units.tr: Let the testimony of the heathens be added: Cicero, On Duties, book 3, and Pro Murena. Likewise Seneca.

units.la: Clausula à minori: Multo magis Christianis detestandas esse.
units.tr: Conclusion from the lesser: much more ought they to be detested by Christians.

units.la: Confutatio duarum objectio-num pro choreis.
units.tr: Refutation of the two objections in favour of dances.

units.la: Objectio I. Choreas nocere moribus & accendere libidines tantum per accidens.
units.tr: Objection I. Dances harm morals and kindle lusts only incidentally.

units.la: [?]Minor probetur: quia non semper faciant: quod ostendatur 1. exemplo Aristippi gloriantis, se saltantem in purpura animum Philosophicum nihilominus retinere. 2. quia casti spectatores non moveantur illecebris.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved: because they do not always do so. This is shown first by the example of Aristippus, who boasted that, though he danced in purple, he nonetheless kept a philosophical mind. Second, because chaste spectators are not moved by allurements.

units.la: [?]Maior addatur: & amplificetur à Thesi: De rebus judicandum ex iis, quæ per se insunt; non quæ per accidens accedunt.
units.tr: The major premise is added and enlarged from the thesis: Things are to be judged by what belongs to them through themselves, not by what attaches to them incidentally.

units.la: Respond. 1. negatione minoris de choreis lascivis sub χορευτικισμῷ [?] comprehensis. 2 concessa minore per distinct.majoris, & thescos: nisi accidentia ἀπὸ τὸ πολύ [?] & inseparabiliter insint: ut lascivia inest istis choreis.
units.tr: Reply. First, by denying the minor premise concerning wanton dances comprised under the dancing art. Second, by granting the minor premise and distinguishing the major and the thesis: unless the accidents are present in the usual manner and inseparably, as wantonness is present in those dances.

units.la: Ad probationem minoris & exempla. 1. negatione: quę probetur authoritate Salomonis Proverb. 6. 27. Item Platonis recusantis saltare. Laertius ibid. 1 1. negatione consequentiæ: quia una hirundo non facit ver.
units.tr: To the proof of the minor premise and the examples. First, by denial, which is proved by the authority of Solomon, Proverbs 6:27. Likewise of Plato, who refused to dance (Laertius, in the same place). Second, by denying the consequence, because one swallow does not make a spring.

units.la: Amplif. Ob unius vel alterius integritatem nō oportere reliquos omnes periclitari.
units.tr: Amplification. It is not right that all the rest should be endangered on account of the integrity of one or two.

units.la: Objectio I I. Choreis sæpe conciliari honesta matrimonia. Non ergo damnandas.
units.tr: Objection II. Honourable marriages are often arranged through dances. Therefore they should not be condemned.

units.la: Respond. 1. Fallacia non causæ: ex dicto: Non facienda sunt mala, ut eveniant bona.
units.tr: Reply I. The fallacy of non-cause, by what is said: Evils are not to be done so that good things may come of them.

units.la: Amplificetur à thesi: Peccata non excusari bonis per accidens ea comitantibus vel sequentib: Addantur quædam exempla: Venditio Josephi, adulterium Davidis, scortatio Simsonis: Proditio Judæ, &c.
units.tr: The thesis is enlarged: Sins are not excused by the good things that incidentally accompany or follow them. Some examples are added: the selling of Joseph, the adultery of David, the whoredom of Samson, the betrayal by Judas, etc.

units.la: Respond. 2. à negatione minoris: 1. quia sæpius stupra & adulteria sequuntur quam honesta matrimonia. 2 quia honesta matrimonia etiam honestè sint contrahenda.
units.tr: Reply II, by denial of the minor premise: first, because fornication and adultery follow more often than honourable marriages; second, because honourable marriages ought to be contracted honourably in any case.

units.la: ARGUM. V. seu V. genus ludorum per se illicitorum: ALEA. Definitur: quòd sit ludus cuborum vel chartarum merè fortuitus, in periculum rei nostræ vel alienæ.
units.tr: ARGUMENT V, or the fifth kind of games unlawful in themselves: DICE. It is defined as a game of dice or cards, purely a matter of chance, endangering one's own property or another's.

units.la: Probationi præmittatur distinctio per ἀ πολλαχῶς[?] utriusque differentiæ: Non damnari, nec proprie dici alcam:
units.tr: Before the proof, a distinction is premised, by the various senses of the term, of each difference: such dice-play is not condemned, nor is it properly called dice-play:

units.la: I. Vbi casus ab arte pendet, vel corrigi potest: observatis conditionibus secundi generis ludorum licitorum: ad quod referatur talis alea.
units.tr: I. Where the outcome depends on skill, or can be corrected, with the conditions of the second kind of lawful games observed; to this class such dice-play is referred.

units.la: I I. Vbi sola est recreatio: cum ratione probabilitatis, ut si animo vel corpore ægr sic ludendo se recreet.
units.tr: II. Where there is only recreation, with a reasonable probability, as when someone who is sick in mind or body refreshes himself by playing in this way.

units.la: Probationis ratio I. quia omnis fortitio in re levi aut futili est abusus nominis divini tertio præcepto prohibitus. Deducatur ex eo, quod Deus Prov.16.fortem peculiariter gubernare dicitur.
units.tr: The first argument of the proof: because every casting of lots in a light or trifling matter is an abuse of the divine name, forbidden by the third precept. This may be deduced from the fact that God is said in Proverbs 16 to govern the lot in a particular way.

units.la: Ratio II. quia per aleam fortunæ conjiciuntur in casum recta ratione dispensandæ. Amplificetur ex fine propter quem à Deo dantur hominibus.
units.tr: Second argument: because by dice-play the lots of fortune are cast into a case that ought to be governed by right reason. This is amplified from the end for which God gives them to men.

units.la: Ratio III. ab effectis: quorum quædam exponantur: 1. cupiditas ludendi. 2. avaritia. 3. inertia. 4. blasphemiæ. 5. rixæ & cædes, &c.
units.tr: Third argument, from its effects, of which some are set out: (1) the desire to gamble; (2) avarice; (3) idleness; (4) blasphemies; (5) quarrels and slaughter, etc.

units.la: Ratio IV. à judicio Ethnicorum, qui aleam & alcatores semper probro habuerunt. Cicero Phil. 2. objicit Antonio aleam. Suetonius in Augusto. cap.71.&c.
units.tr: Fourth argument, from the judgement of the heathen, who always held dice and gamblers in disgrace. Cicero, in the second Philippic, reproaches Antony with dice-play. Suetonius, in the life of Augustus, chapter 71, etc.

units.la: Ratio V. à prohibitione Impp. Cod.lib.3.tit.43 Commodis igitur subiectorum prospicientes hac lege decernimus, ut nulli liceat in publicis vel privatis domibus vel locis alea ludere: neque spectare. Sic lib.1. ff.tit.5.&c.
units.tr: Fifth argument, from the prohibition of the emperors. Code, book 3, title 43: Therefore, looking to the advantage of our subjects, we decree by this law that no one be permitted to play dice in public or private houses or places, nor to watch. So too book 1, Digest, title 5, etc.

units.la: Approbentur leges: à causa: quia Reipub. interest, ne quis re sua male utatur. Instit.l.1.t.8. §. sed & maior, &c.
units.tr: The laws are approved from their cause: because it is in the interest of the commonwealth that no one misuse his own property. Institutes, book 1, title 8, section "but also the greater," etc.

units.la: Obiectio I. Tantum abusum aleæ damnari.
units.tr: Objection I. Only the abuse of dice is condemned.

units.la: Respond. per negationem 1. quia leges simpliciter damnant aleam: h.e, ludum, locum, & ludentes. 2. quia rei per se malæ non potest esse bonus usus: (nisi ex accidenti) 3. quia effectus lucrandi, h.e, avaritia est inseparabile accidens aleæ, quia in pecuniam luditur. 4. quia effecta reliqua ὅτι τὸ πλὴν [?] eam sequuntur. Obiectio I I. Aleam nusquam damnari in scriptura.
units.tr: Reply, by denial: first, because the laws condemn dice-play absolutely, that is, the game, the place, and the players. Second, because a thing that is evil in itself cannot have a good use (except incidentally). Third, because the effect of gain, that is, avarice, is an inseparable accident of dice-play, since it is played for money. Fourth, because the remaining effects follow it, as the rest of it does. Objection II. Dice-play is nowhere condemned in Scripture.

units.la: Respond. per negationem: 1. quia genus damnatur: Sortitio impia: & abusus nominis divini. 2. quia effecta ejus per se sunt opera carnis, quæ damnantur. Gal. 5. 20. 3. quia exemplum aleæ damnatur. Psal. 22. 19. & Joh. 19. 24.
units.tr: Reply, by denial: first, because the genus is condemned: an impious casting of lots, and an abuse of the divine name. Second, because its effects are in themselves works of the flesh, which are condemned (Galatians 5:20). Third, because an example of dice-play is condemned (Psalm 22:19 and John 19:24).

units.la: Transitio ad conclusionem: Ex his amicum intelligere. 1. ludorum differentias. 2. argumentorum suorum limitationem: quæ breviter in singulis offendatur.
units.tr: Transition to the conclusion: From these points one understands, first, the differences between games, and second, the limitation of his own arguments, which is briefly indicated in each case.

units.la: Ad 1. Hominem ad feria conditum.
units.tr: To the first: Man was made for the holiday.

units.la: Resp. 1. principaliter. 2. Etiam ad honestas recreationes.
units.tr: Reply: first, principally; second, also for honest recreations.

units.la: Probetur ex fine hominis secundario. Item: quia sine his feria non diu fieri possunt.
units.tr: It is proved from the secondary end of man. Likewise: because without these, holidays cannot long be kept.

units.la: Ad II. Resp. 1. Concessione de ludis illicitis. 2. licitos ad gloriam Dei facere mediatè, ut vitam & valetudinem ipsam.
units.tr: To the second, reply: first, by granting the point about unlawful games; second, that lawful games are made mediately for the glory of God, as life and health themselves are.

units.la: Ad III. IV. V: Respond. per concessionem de illicitis, & de licitorum immoderato usu.
units.tr: To the third, fourth and fifth, reply: by granting the point about unlawful games, and about the immoderate use of lawful ones.

units.la: Conclusio: Damnandos ergo & vitandos Christianis esse ludos turpes & periculosos. Addatur antithesis cum restrictione: Ludos honestos, & moderatam corporis vel animi exercitationem habentes concedi: sed ita ne ab officio nos avocent, &c.
units.tr: Conclusion: Therefore base and dangerous games are to be condemned and avoided by Christians. The antithesis is to be added with a restriction: honest games, having a moderate exercise of body or mind, are to be allowed; but so that they do not draw us away from our duty, etc.

units.la: Exercitatio XIV.
units.tr: Exercitatio XIV.

units.la: Hortatio ad Scholasticum, ne literis ad amicoi traducat Præceptores, veritatis nomine.
units.tr: An exhortation to a scholar, that he should not, under the name of truth, bring his teachers into disrepute with his friend.

units.la: EXordium sit πάθος. Dolere tibi, quod de ipso mutare cogaris judicium.
units.tr: Let the exordium be an appeal to the emotions: it grieves you that you are forced to change your opinion of him.

units.la: Ratio: quia hactenus cum habueris pro modesto juvene: nunc deprehendas arrogantem, inq; præceptores ingratum esse.
units.tr: Reason: because until now you had thought him a modest young man; now you find him arrogant and ungrateful towards his teachers.

units.la: Narratio habens αὐλολογίαν: Incidisse te nuper in literas ipsius ad familiarem scriptas: quibus de severitate disciplinæ graviter conqueratur, & de præceptoribus parum honorificè scribat.
units.tr: Narrative, with a touch of irony: you recently came across a letter of his to a friend, in which he complains bitterly of the strictness of the discipline and writes rather disparagingly of his teachers.

units.la: Propositio. Hortari te cum, ne disciplinam & præceptores traducat:
units.tr: Proposition. I exhort you not to disparage the discipline or the teachers:

units.la: Ratio 1. quia diligens legum defensio præceptoribus incumbat ex officio. Amplificetur a necessitate hujus diligentiæ ob crescentem petulantiam & vanitatem juventutis. Item a contraria Thesi: licentiam stultidis adolescentibus gratam, sed perniciosam esse.
units.tr: First reason: because the diligent defence of the laws falls to the teachers as part of their duty. This is strengthened by the necessity of such diligence, given the growing wantonness and vanity of young people. Likewise, from the contrary thesis: that a licence pleasing to foolish young men is harmful.

units.la: Ratio II. quia nullam habeat conquerendi causam.
units.tr: Second reason: because he has no cause for complaint.

units.la: Probatio 1. quia scias, in schola ejus disciplinam longe arctiorem legib. sanciri, & olim utiliter viguisse, quam nunc sit.
units.tr: First proof: because you know that in his school the discipline is governed by far stricter laws than now prevail, and that it once flourished to good effect.

units.la: Prob. 2. quia ex aliis cognoveris, præceptores ejus erga bonos benevolos esse: severos tantum erga petulantes, ex quibus ipse esse non debeat.
units.tr: Second proof: because you have learned from others that his teachers are kind towards good students and severe only towards the wanton, which he ought not to be among.

units.la: Ratio III. Quia fit ingratus erga præceptores bene de ipso merentes, contra præceptum: Honora patrem, &c.
units.tr: Third reason: because he is ungrateful towards teachers who have deserved well of him, contrary to the precept: "Honour your father," etc.

units.la: Ratio IV. Quia declaret animum suum arrogantem & superbum.
units.tr: Fourth reason: because he reveals his arrogant and proud spirit.

units.la: Ratio V. Quia sit improbum, honestis legibus se obstringere, nec velle obedire: exactionem vero obedientiæ ut severitatem traducere.
units.tr: Fifth reason: because it is wicked to bind oneself to honourable laws and then refuse to obey them, and to call the demand for obedience mere severity.

units.la: Ratio VI. Quia corrumpat tibi discipulos ad quos scribit, & alios, cum quibus isthic talia hauddubie communicat.
units.tr: Sixth reason: because he corrupts the students to whom he writes, and others with whom he doubtless discusses such things there.

units.la: Obiectio: Benevolentia potius quam severitate discipulos esse continendos in officio. Resp. utraque. Ratio 1. quia benevolentia sine metu pœnæ sepe vincitur pravis cupiditatibus. 2. quia multi sunt pravi metu regendi, cum benevolentia contineri in officio non possint.
units.tr: Objection: students should be held to their duty by kindness rather than by severity. Reply: both. Reason 1: because kindness without fear of punishment is often overcome by wicked desires. 2. Because many are wicked and must be governed by fear, and cannot be kept to their duty by kindness alone.

units.la: Conclusio. Abstineat ergo ab hoc scribendi argumento, quo & opinionem modestiæ & probitatis apud bonos amittere, & commodis suis periculum creare possit.
units.tr: Conclusion. Let him therefore refrain from this subject of writing, by which he could both lose the reputation for modesty and integrity among good people and put his own advantages at risk.

units.la: Exercitatio XV.
units.tr: Exercitatio XV.

units.la: Censura Apophthegmatis Epicuri:
units.tr: Censura Apophthegmatis Epicuri:

units.la: λάθε βιώσας[?]
units.tr: λάθε βιώσας[?]

units.la: Exordium à contrariis iudiciis: Vulgò celebrari apophthegma Epicuri: λάθε βιώσας[?].
units.tr: Introduction from contrary judgments: The saying of Epicurus is commonly celebrated: λάθε βιώσας[?] (live hidden).

units.la: Addantur authoritates: Crede mihi bene, &c. Stet quicunq; voler[?] potens, &c.
units.tr: Let authorities be added: Believe me well, &c. Let him stand who wishes to be powerful, &c.

units.la: Antithesis: Plutarch. id graviter reprehendere.
units.tr: Antithesis: Plutarch reprehends it severely.

units.la: Propositio : Esse partim approbandum : partim vituperandum.
units.tr: Proposition: It is partly to be approved, partly to be condemned.

units.la: Ἐκθεσις approbationis : sit brevis explicatio virtutum in quarum commendationem usurpa-vi possit: ut sunt: Modestia, φιλησυχία : αὐτάρκεια cujusque in sua vocatione : & vitiorum : quae reprehendit, ut sunt: φιλοπμία, πολυπραγμοσυνη, πλεονεξία. Applicetur dictum Apostoli. φιλοπμεῖσθαι ἡσυχάζειν καὶ ἴδια πράττειν. 1. Thess. 4.11.
units.tr: Ἐκθεσις of approbation: there should be a brief explanation of the virtues in whose commendation it can be used: such as modesty, φιλησυχία (love of quiet), αὐτάρκεια (self-sufficiency) of each person in his own calling; and of the vices which it reprehends, such as φιλοπμία (love of busyness? / φιλοπονία, industry), πολυπραγμοσυνη (meddlesomeness), πλεονεξία (greed). Let the saying of the Apostle be applied: φιλοπμεῖσθαι ἡσυχάζειν καὶ ἴδια πράττειν (to make it your ambition to be quiet and to mind your own affairs). 1 Thess. 4.11.

units.la: Ἐκθεσις vituperationis sit explicatio sententiae Epicuri: Ita vivendum, ut nemo sciat te vivere aut vixisse: & ejus reprehensio.
units.tr: Ἐκθεσις of condemnation should be an explanation of the saying of Epicurus: Live in such a way that no one knows that you live or have lived, and a reprehension of it.

units.la: I. quia sic vivere est contra mandatum Christi: Luceat lux vestra, &c. & parabolam de non defodiendo talento.
units.tr: I. Because to live thus is contrary to the command of Christ: Let your light shine, &c. and the parable of not burying the talent.

units.la: II. quia tollit communionem officiorum in Ecclesia & Republica.
units.tr: II. Because it removes the fellowship of duties in the Church and the commonwealth.

units.la: Amplificetur a necessitate. Ita a fine hominis.
units.tr: Let it be amplified from necessity. So also from the end of man.

units.la: III. quia suadet ocium: & contemtum virtutum ac vitae.
units.tr: III. Because it recommends idleness and contempt of virtues and of life.

units.la: IV. per dilemma Plutarchi ab inutili. Mali latentes non possent corrigi: boni latentes non praestarent officia Ecclesiae & Reipub. Illustretur exemplis Josuae: Davidis: Lycurgi: Themistoclis.
units.tr: IV. By the dilemma of Plutarch, from uselessness. Bad men who lie hidden could not be corrected; good men who lie hidden would not render the duties of the Church and commonwealth. Let it be illustrated by the examples of Joshua, David, Lycurgus, and Themistocles.

units.la: Conclusio reprehensionis: Epicurum ipsum hoc apophthegmate latere non voluisse. Latendum ergo esse intra vocationis & fortunae metas: sed etiam Deo & Reipub. fideliter serviendum: atque vocanti ad res secundas obtemperandum.
units.tr: Conclusion of the reprehension: Epicurus himself did not wish to lie hidden by this saying. One must therefore lie hidden within the limits of one's calling and fortune, but also serve God and the commonwealth faithfully, and obey the one who calls to prosperous things.

units.la: Exercitatio XVI.
units.tr: Exercitatio XVI.

units.la: Παραίνεσις ad discipulos de colenda modestia, & adhibenda in studiis diligentia.
units.tr: Exhortation to the students on cultivating modesty and applying diligence in their studies.

units.la: Exordium exponat querelam bonorum de vanitate mundi praesertim juventutis nostri tē-poris.
units.tr: The exordium sets out the complaint of good men about the vanity of the world, especially of the young people of our time.

units.la: Hypothesis: Etiam te cum dolore experiri in hac schola, quæ olim laude disciplinæ floruerit.
units.tr: Hypothesis: You too experience this with grief in this school, which once flourished with the praise of its discipline.

units.la: Ratio: quia non pauci quidem modesti probi & seduli: sed & multi superbuli & indecori in vestitu; dissoluti in moribus: ignavi in studiis, ocio & cibo alieno abutentes.
units.tr: Reason: for indeed not a few are modest, upright and diligent, but many are also arrogant, indecorous in dress, dissolute in morals, idle in their studies, and they abuse leisure and the food of others.

units.la: Propositio sit hortatio pathetica: Præstent quæso modestiam & diligentiam se dignam.
units.tr: The proposition is a passionate exhortation: Please display the modesty and diligence that befits you.

units.la: Ratio I. ab honesto: Quia Deus mandat. 1. Tim.4.2. Thess.3. Qui non laborat, non manducet.
units.tr: First reason, from what is honourable: Because God commands it. 1 Tim. 4.2; 2 Thess. 3: "If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat."

units.la: Amplif. ab ipsorum conditione: Versamini in schola pietatis & honestatis: candidati liberalium artium, & S. Theologiæ.
units.tr: Amplification from their own condition: You live in a school of piety and honour; you are candidates in the liberal arts and in sacred theology.

units.la: Item à Scopo studiorum: Ut pietatem & literas tandem doceatis alios in Ecclesiis & Scholis: Itē[?] à scientia legum Collegii, quibus vos obstrinxi-stis.
units.tr: Likewise from the aim of your studies: that you may at last teach piety and learning to others in the churches and schools; likewise from the knowledge of the laws of the college, to which you have bound yourselves.

units.la: II. ab aquo: hoc debetis Ecclesiæ, in cujus spē hic alimini. Exaggeretur necessitas: cur debeant se præparare ad veritatis ac pietatis propagatio-nem: à præsentibus & ingruentibus Ecclesiæ pe-riculis, mundi ingratitudine pro luce veritatis; motibus ac ruinis regnorum, scholarum & Ec-clesiaclesiarum: morte piorum principum & Doctorum: paucitate bonorum successorum: conspiratione hostium in oppressionem melioris partis: furore vulgi contra Orthodoxos: depravatione doctrinae: ac defensione manifestorum errorum, metu denique periculorum ingruentiū.
units.tr: Second reason, from what is fitting: you owe this to the Church, in whose hope you are nourished here. The necessity should be stressed: why they ought to prepare themselves for the propagation of truth and piety. From the present and impending dangers of the Church: the world's ingratitude towards the light of truth; the upheavals and ruins of kingdoms, schools and churches; the death of pious princes and teachers; the scarcity of good successors; the conspiracy of enemies to oppress the better part; the rage of the common people against the Orthodox; the corruption of doctrine and the defence of manifest errors; and finally the fear of dangers that are coming.

units.la: III. ab æquo: Etiam benefactoribus hoc debetis.
units.tr: Third reason, from what is equitable: you owe this also to your benefactors.

units.la: Commendetur & exaggeretur clementia & mu-nificentia Palatinorum Electorum in hanc scho-lam, & novum beneficium Illustrissimi Electoris Friderici I V. quod nuper tertium præceptorem dedit, & collegii amplificationem decrevit.
units.tr: Let the clemency and generosity of the Palatine Electors towards this school be commended and magnified, and the new benefit of the most illustrious Elector Frederick IV, who lately gave a third teacher and decreed the enlargement of the college.

units.la: Addatur epiphonema cum voto: O pietatem laudabilem: suscitet Deus Ecclesiæ multos ejusmodi nutricios, & hunc nobis servet.
units.tr: Add an epiphonema with a wish: O commendable piety! May God raise up many such nurturers for the Church and preserve this one for us.

units.la: IV. a facili: habetis præclaras occasiones: quæ declarentur ab ipsorum ætate: ab Academiæ commodis: a præceptorum fide diligentia, cura: a liberali educatione: a disciplinæ domestica moderatione.
units.tr: Fourth reason, from what is easy: you have excellent opportunities, which are made clear by your age, by the advantages of the Academy, by the faithfulness and diligence and care of your teachers, by your liberal education, and by the moderation of discipline at home.

units.la: Amplificetur a voto plurimorum: qui talibus destituuntur: & ipsorummet, postquam aliquā-do amiserint.
units.tr: Let it be amplified by the wish of many who are deprived of such things, and of yourselves, once you have lost them at some time.

units.la: Ratio V. ab utili: Sentietis benedictionem divinam juxta promissiones: Pietas ad omnia est utilis. Deus humilibus dat gratiam. Quaerentes invenient. Honorantes me honorabo.
units.tr: Fifth reason, from what is useful: you will feel the divine blessing according to the promises: "Piety is useful for all things." "God gives grace to the humble." "Those who seek will find." "Those who honour me I will honour."

units.la: Amplificetur a benevolentia præceptorum & Mecœnatum, quam modestia & diligentia sibi conciliantes, ad honestas & sibi utiles conditiones promoventur.
units.tr: Let it be amplified by the goodwill of teachers and patrons, which those who win favour by modesty and diligence will secure, so that they are advanced to honourable conditions and ones useful to themselves.

units.la: VI. ab utili: Evitabitis pœnas superbiæ, igna-viæ & ingratitudinis apud Deum & homines.
units.tr: Sixth reason, from what is useful: you will avoid the punishments of pride, idleness and ingratitude before God and men.

units.la: Explicetur ex dictis: Deus resistit superbis. Dormiens in messe est filius confusionis. Adomo ingrati nō recedet malum, &c. Serve nequam, &c.
units.tr: Let it be explained from the sayings: "God resists the proud." "He who sleeps at harvest is a son of shame." "The evil of the ungrateful will not depart from his house," etc. "Wicked servant," etc.

units.la: Conclusio: sit obtestatio ut obsequantur recta monentibus, & laudem scholæ tueantur.
units.tr: Conclusion: let there be an earnest appeal that they comply with those who give right counsel, and that they guard the praise of the school.

units.la: Exercitatio XVII
units.tr: Exercitatio XVII

units.la: Paraphrasis Orationis Aiacis, petentis sibi à Græcis decerni arma Achillis. Ovid. 13. Metam.
units.tr: Paraphrase of the speech of Ajax, asking that the arms of Achilles be awarded to him by the Greeks. Ovid, Metamorphoses book 13.

units.la: PROPOSITIO figurata indignatione à re & à loco: Indignum esse, sibi litem intendi de armis Achillis: præsertim eo loci, ubi classem Græcorum contra Hectorem nuper admodum fortiter defenderit.
units.tr: PROPOSITION, figured by indignation from the matter and from the place: It is an outrage that a lawsuit should be brought against me concerning the arms of Achilles, especially in that very place where I lately defended the fleet of the Greeks so bravely against Hector.

units.la: Item: à persona sua & adversarii: Turpe esse, se virum fortem conferri cum Ulysse homine timido, classis desertore in periculo.
units.tr: Likewise, from his own person and that of his opponent: It is shameful that a brave man like me should be compared with Ulysses, a cowardly fellow, a deserter of the fleet in the time of danger.

units.la: Adversativa per occupationem: Facundiam adversarii nihil sibi præjudicare debere.
units.tr: Adversative, by anticipation: The eloquence of my opponent ought not to prejudice me in any way.
