units.la: Ratio à thesi: quia fortitudo militaris, qua i-pse polleat, præstet loquacitati:
units.tr: Reason from the thesis: because military courage, in which I myself excel, is better than glib talk.

units.la: Probetur ironia: quoniam lingua tutius pu-gnetur quàm manu.
units.tr: Let irony be proved: since the tongue is fought with more safely than the hand.

units.la: Transitio ad confirmationem ἐπιδιώξει[?], movens invidiam adversario: Non esse cur res gestas suas commemoret, cum sint illustres adversarii con-trà obscuræ. Item: occupatione de praestantia armorum Achillis.
units.tr: Transition to the confirmation (ἐπιδιώξει[?]), stirring up envy against the adversary: There is no reason for him to recount his own deeds, since the deeds of my opponent are obscure, while mine are illustrious. Likewise: by anticipation, concerning the excellence of the arms of Achilles.

units.la: Item: extenuatione adversarii, cui debeat sufficere laus certaminis cum Aiace.
units.tr: Likewise: by belittling the adversary, for whom the praise of having contended with Ajax ought to be enough.

units.la: Confirmationis argumenta duo.
units.tr: The two arguments of confirmation.

units.la: Argumentum I. per dilemma: Arma debentur vel haeredi vel praestantiori. Ergo mihi: quia sum Achillis patruelis: & Vlysse praestantior.
units.tr: Argument I., by dilemma: the arms are owed either to the heir or to the more excellent man. Therefore to me, since I am Achilles' cousin on the father's side, and more excellent than Ulysses.

units.la: Probetur cognatio recitatione Genealogiae: Praestantia comparatione originis Aiacis a Jove, & Vlyssis a Sisypho.
units.tr: Let the kinship be proved by the recital of the genealogy; the excellence by comparing the origin of Ajax from Jove with that of Ulysses from Sisyphus.

units.la: Item: rerum gestarum utriusque:
units.tr: Likewise: from the deeds done by each.

units.la: Primo Ajacis: Quod sponte profectus sit ad hoc bellum:
units.tr: First, those of Ajax: that he set out of his own accord for this war;

units.la: Quod servaverit Vlyssem sub clypeo:
units.tr: that he saved Ulysses under his shield;

units.la: Quod Hectorem ruentem in castra superarit duello:
units.tr: that he overcame Hector in single combat when he rushed against the camp;

units.la: Quod contra Trojanos mille naves corpore suo protexerit.
units.tr: that he alone, with his own body, protected the thousand ships against the Trojans.

units.la: Amplificetur per ἀντιμεταβολὴν: Majorem armis, quàm sibi gloriam: non Aiaci arma, sed Aiacem armis quæri.
units.tr: Let it be amplified by antimetabole: Ajax seeks greater glory from his arms than they from him; the arms are not sought for Ajax, but Ajax is sought for his arms.

units.la: Deinde Vlyssis: Quod simulato furore militiam detrectarit:
units.tr: Then, those of Ulysses: that he shirked military service by feigning madness;

units.la: Quod Philoctetes ejus suasu in Lemno relictus:
units.tr: that Philoctetes was left behind on Lemnos at his persuasion;

units.la: Quod Quòd Palamedes falsa ejus criminatione oc-cisus:
units.tr: that Palamedes was put to death through his false accusation;

units.la: Quòd Nestor ab eo in acie desertus:
units.tr: that Nestor was deserted by him in battle;

units.la: Quòd si quid utile gessit, non solus, sed à Dio-mede adjutus gesserit:
units.tr: that if he did anything useful, he did it not alone but with the help of Diomedes.

units.la: Argumentum II. à pondere & præstantia armorum Achillis.
units.tr: Argument II., from the weight and excellence of Achilles' arms.

units.la: 1. quòd sint majora, quàm ut corpusculo adversarii conveniant.
units.tr: 1. Because they are too large to fit the little body of his opponent.

units.la: II. quòd sint ei nocitura potiùs quàm profutura, impediendo hominem timidum in fuga: & illiciendo hostem ad prædam.
units.tr: II. Because they would harm him rather than help him: they would hinder a timid man in flight, and they would tempt the enemy to seize the spoil.

units.la: Conclusio abrupta: Omissis verbis arma mittē-da in medios hostes, & iis ornādum, qui retulerit.
units.tr: Abrupt conclusion: leaving out the words, the arms are to be thrown into the midst of the enemy, and the man who brings them back is to be adorned with them.

units.la: Exercitatio XVIII.
units.tr: Exercitatio XVIII.

units.la: Paraphrasis Orationis contrariæ Vlyssis Petentis sibi, non Aiaci, arma Achillis decerni.
units.tr: Paraphrase of the Speech Against Ulysses, Who Asks That the Arms of Achilles Be Awarded to Himself, Not to Ajax.

units.la: Ibidem:
units.tr: Ibidem:

units.la: EXord. habeat πάθῳ[?] de Achillis fato: quod malit eum superstitem esse, quam de armis ejus contendere.
units.tr: The exordium should contain a pathetic appeal concerning the fate of Achilles: that he would rather have him alive than contend over his arms.

units.la: Propositio subiiciatur per adversat: habeatque elevationem argumenti primarii Aiacis, quod arma debeantur vel hæredi vel præstantiori, per inversionem διαλλακτικῶς[?].
units.tr: The proposition is to be added by way of contrast, and it should carry the elevation of Ajax's primary argument, that the arms are owed either to the heir or to the more excellent man, by inversion, in a conciliatory manner.

units.la: Si hæredi, non Aiaci: sed Peleo patri, Pyrrho filio: Teucro patrueli:
units.tr: If to the heir, then not to Ajax, but to Peleus the father, to Pyrrhus the son, to Teucer the cousin.

units.la: Si præstantiori: Ergo mihi Vlyssi.
units.tr: If to the more excellent, then to me, Ulysses.

units.la: CONFIRMATIO 1. Quia stemmate paterno non sum inferior : materno superior Aiace.
units.tr: CONFIRMATION 1. Because I am not inferior to him in paternal descent, and superior to Ajax in maternal descent.

units.la: Transitio ad I I. & praecipuum argumentum per ἀποδείξιν: Non stemmate majorum: sed virtute Nobilitatem censeri:
units.tr: Transition to the second point, and the principal argument by demonstration: nobility is judged not by the lineage of ancestors but by virtue.

units.la: Argum. II. à rebus gestis, quae breviter narrentur. I. Achillis adductio ad bellum ex Gynecaeo. II. Agamemnonis & Clytemnestrae persuasio, ut Iphigeniam sacrificarent Dianae in Aulide. III. Legatio ad Priamum. IV. Ἀρετῶν[?] officiorum exercitui utiliter praestitorum usque ad annum belli decimum, cum nulla esset hostis oppugnandi copia. V. Dissuasio discessus ab oppugnatione. VI. Res gestae cum Diomede: Caedes Dolonis, Rhesi, Sarpedonis.
units.tr: Argument II, from the deeds performed, which shall be briefly related. I. Achilles' summons to the war from the women's quarters. II. The persuasion of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra to sacrifice Iphigenia to Diana at Aulis. III. The embassy to Priam. IV. The services of the soldiers rendered usefully over the ten years of the war, when there was no opportunity of attacking the enemy. V. The dissuasion from abandoning the assault. VI. Deeds done against Diomedes: the slaughter of Dolon, Rhesus and Sarpedon.

units.la: Amplific. ab ἐνδείξει[?] vulnerum adversariorum. VII. Interceptio Heleni: & ereptio Palladii ex arce Troiana.
units.tr: Amplification, from the display of the wounds of the adversaries. VII. The interception of Helenus and the seizure of the Palladium from the citadel of Troy.

units.la: CONFUTATIO habeat: Primo elevationem fortitudinis & rerum gestarum Aiacis.
units.tr: The refutation should contain, first, a diminution of Ajax's courage and deeds.

units.la: I. Quod pro classe pugnârit. Respon. 1. sed non solus. 2. non ultrò. 3. sine victoria.
units.tr: I. That he fought for the fleet. Reply: 1. but not alone. 2. not voluntarily. 3. without victory.

units.la: II. Quod valeat robore militari, cui cedat Eloquentia. Resp. 1. Negatione consequentiae: quia praeter ipsum etiam alii viri fortes sint in exercitu, qui tamen non petant arma. II. Negatione theseos[?]: quia sapientia praestet peritiae militari.
units.tr: II. That he is strong in military vigour, to which eloquence yields. Reply: 1. By denying the consequence, because besides himself there are other brave men in the army who nevertheless do not seek the arms. II. By denying the thesis, because wisdom excels military skill.

units.la: SECUNDO dilutionem criminum objectorum.
units.tr: SECONDLY, the rebuttal of the crimes objected against him.

units.la: I. De imbecillitate & exilitate corporis. Resp.
units.tr: I. Concerning his weakness and the slightness of his body. Reply:

units.la: Per negationem à minori: Tuli ipsum Achillem cum armis : multo magis ferre possum ipsa arma.
units.tr: By denying from the lesser: I carried Achilles himself with his arms; much more, then, can I bear the arms themselves.

units.la: Addatur πάθος pietatis erga Achillem defunctum.
units.tr: Let a pathetic appeal of piety towards the dead Achilles be added.

units.la: II. De simulato furore. Resp. 1. Per communicationem facti cum Achille.
units.tr: II. Concerning his feigned madness. Reply: 1. By sharing the deed with Achilles.

units.la: III. De Palomede circumvento, Resp. 1. Per communicationem criminis cum ipsis. 2. Per defensionem juris à probatione sufficiente.
units.tr: III. Concerning Palamedes, who was entrapped. Reply: 1. By sharing the charge with them. 2. By defending the right against proof that is insufficient.

units.la: IV. De Philacte. Resp. 1. Per communicationem criminis cum ipsis. 2 Pollicitatione officii sui ad eum adducendum, absque cujus sagittis Troja expugnari nequeat.
units.tr: IV. Concerning Philoctetes. Reply: 1. By sharing the charge with them. 2. By promising my service in bringing him to the camp, without whose arrows Troy cannot be taken.

units.la: Conclusio sit petitio armorum pro tot meritis.
units.tr: The conclusion is to be a petition for the arms in return for so many services.

units.la: Exercitatio XIX.
units.tr: Exercitatio XIX.

units.la: Narratio belli Siculi ab Atheniensibus ad Syracusas infeliciter gesti ex Thucydidis l.6.& 7.
units.tr: Narrative of the Sicilian war, unsuccessfully waged by the Athenians against Syracuse, from Thucydides, books 6 and 7.

units.la: Observentur leges bonæ narrationis, nec insistatur orationibus aut circunstantiis non necessariis.
units.tr: The rules of good narration are observed, and no insistence is placed on speeches or on unnecessary circumstances.

units.la: I. EXponatur ἀφορμὴ belli Siculi: quæ fuit Legestanorum legatio ad Athenienses de impetrandis auxiliis contra Selinuntios & Syracusanos: & legatorum oratio, quod Syracusani, nisi reprimerentur, Siciliam viderentur in suam redacturi potestatem, posteaque junctis armis cum Peleponensibus imperium Atheniensium eversuri.
units.tr: I. The occasion [ἀφορμή] of the Sicilian war is set out: this was the embassy of the Egestans to the Athenians to obtain aid against the Selinuntines and the Syracusans, and the speech of the envoys, that the Syracusans, unless checked, would seem to bring all Sicily under their own power and afterwards, joining arms with the Peloponnesians, would overthrow the empire of the Athenians.

units.la: II. Atheniensium consilium, cogitantium præpraetextu juvandi socios invadere imperium Siciliae: & plebiscitum de instituenda ac mittenda classe in Siciliam.
units.tr: II. The counsel of the Athenians, who planned under the pretext of helping their allies to attack the empire of Sicily; and the decree of the people about setting up and sending a fleet to Sicily.

units.la: III. Niciae designati Ducis prudentiam in dissuadendo bello non necessario & periculoso: contrà Alcibiadis προτρεπτικὰ[?] in eodem urgendo.
units.tr: III. The prudence of Nicias, the appointed commander, in dissuading from an unnecessary and dangerous war; on the other hand, the exhortations [προτρεπτικά?] of Alcibiades in urging it on.

units.la: IV. Decretum de bello gerendo: & apparatus potentissimae classis (134.triremium: 30.navium onerariarum, 5100.armatorum) & navigatio in Aeginam, Corcyram, Italiam, Siciliam: ducibus Nicia, Alcibiade & Lamacho.
units.tr: IV. The decree about conducting the war, and the preparation of a very powerful fleet (134 triremes, 30 transport ships, 5,100 armed men), and the voyage to Aegina, Corcyra, Italy and Sicily, under the commanders Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus.

units.la: V. Infausta belli initia: exclusio è civitatibus Italiae ad quas appulerant. Recusatio Rheginorum, quos in belli societatem trahere tentabant. Egestanorum inopia pecuniae, & commentum, quo legatos Atheniensium deluserant: Ducum dissensio & consilia diversa de bello gerendo: Exclusio à sociis Catanensibus item Carmarinensibus. Alcibiadis quoque revocatio ad respondendum criminibus objectis: ejusdem fuga, condemnatio, & defectio ad Lacedaemonios.
units.tr: V. The unlucky beginnings of the war: exclusion from the Italian cities at which they had landed. The refusal of the Rhegians, whom they tried to draw into alliance in the war. The lack of money among the Egestans, and the pretence by which they had deceived the Athenian envoys. The dissension of the commanders and their differing plans for conducting the war. Exclusion from the allied Catanaeans, likewise from the Camarinaeans. The recall of Alcibiades too, to answer the charges brought against him; his flight, condemnation, and defection to the Lacedaemonians.

units.la: VI. Exponatur belli epitasis varia: ac primū strictim narrentur Atheniensium fortiter & prospere gesta ad Syracusas usque ad adventum Gylippi cum auxiliis Peloponesiis in Siciliam, quae usque ad finem libri 6. Thucydidis describuntur.
units.tr: VI. The varied course of the war should be set out; and first, briefly, the Athenians' bold and successful deeds are to be related, up to the arrival of Gylippus with Peloponnesian aid in Sicily; these are described up to the end of the sixth book of Thucydides.

units.la: Ingressus classis Atticae in portum magnum ante Olympicum, & obsidio Syracusarum terra marique.
units.tr: The entry of the Attic fleet into the great harbour before the Olympieum, and the siege of Syracuse by land and sea.

units.la: Victoria in primo conflictu de Syracusanis, & hybernatio in Naxo.
units.tr: Victory over the Syracusans in the first clash, and winter quarters at Naxos.

units.la: Legatio Syracusanorum ad Lacedaemonios: horumque decretum de auxiliis mittendis in Si-ciliam suasu Alcibiadis.
units.tr: The embassy of the Syracusans to the Lacedaemonians, and their decree about sending aid to Sicily at the persuasion of Alcibiades.

units.la: Occupatio Epipolarum, quod erat propugnaculum loco prærupto urbi imminens: & Labda-lum castellum ibi excitatum.
units.tr: The occupation of Epipolae, which was a stronghold on a steep place overhanging the city, and the fort of Labdalum built there.

units.la: Equestris victoria & Trophęum de Syracusanis apud Syram: Spes victoriæ Atheniensibus præsumta: periculum: colloquia Syracusanorum inter se & cum Nicia de paciscendo.
units.tr: A cavalry victory and a trophy over the Syracusans at the Syra; the Athenians' hope of victory presumed upon; the danger; the conferences of the Syracusans among themselves and with Nicias about making terms.

units.la: Adventus auxiliorum Peloponefiorum in Siciliam Ducibus Gongylo & Gylippo.
units.tr: The arrival of Peloponnesian auxiliaries in Sicily under the commanders Gongylus and Gylippus.

units.la: VII. Dehinc exponatur inclinatio fortunæ Atheniensium usque ad adventum Demosthe-nis cum nova classe Attica: nempe: Inhibitio pacificationis facta à Gongylo.
units.tr: VII. Next, the turn of fortune against the Athenians should be set out, up to the arrival of Demosthenes with a new Attic fleet: namely, the stopping of a peace agreement made by Gongylus.

units.la: Edictum Gylippi jubentis Athenienses intra quintum diem Sicilia decedere.
units.tr: The edict of Gylippus ordering the Athenians to leave Sicily within five days.

units.la: Castellum Labdalum cum Epipolis à Syracu-sanis expugnatum & receptum.
units.tr: The fort of Labdalum, together with Epipolae, taken and recovered by the Syracusans.

units.la: Navale prælium primo infeliciter gestum imprudentia Gylippi,
units.tr: A naval battle, first unsuccessfully fought through the imprudence of Gylippus.

units.la: Victoria terrestris Syracusanorum, munitiones excitatæ contra hostes.
units.tr: A land victory of the Syracusans; fortifications built against the enemy.

units.la: Auxilia Corinthia XII. navium.
units.tr: Corinthian aid of twelve ships.

units.la: Imminutio copiarum Atticarum: & episto-la Niciæ ad Athenienses de mittenda nova classe.
units.tr: The diminution of the Attic forces, and Nicias's letter to the Athenians about sending a new fleet.

units.la: Auxilia Peloponefia XXV. navium pro Sy-racusanis.
units.tr: Peloponnesian aid of twenty-five ships for the Syracusans.

units.la: Alia pugna navalis & victoria Syracusanorū: expugnatum & recuperatum Plemmeriū: quod erat promontorium è regione Urbis prominens in portum magnum, & fauces ejus coarctans, muro prius septum ab Athenien-sibus: & muni-tiones Athenien-sium captæ cum omni pecunia & instrumento.
units.tr: Another naval battle and a victory of the Syracusans; Plemmyrium, which was a promontory jutting out opposite the city into the great harbour and narrowing its mouth, previously fortified by the Athenians with a wall, was taken and recovered; and the Athenian fortifications were captured with all their money and equipment.

units.la: Syracusanorum audacia è successibus conce-pta: Congressus alius cum hoste navalis & pede-stris, primum quidem ambiguus, postridie strata-gemate Aristonis Athenienses in fugam acti.
units.tr: The boldness of the Syracusans, conceived from their successes; another encounter with the enemy by sea and land, at first indeed doubtful, but on the following day the Athenians were put to flight by a stratagem of Ariston.

units.la: Adventus Demosthenis & Eurimedontis in Siciliam cum classe LXXIII [?] navium.
units.tr: The arrival of Demosthenes and Eurymedon in Sicily with a fleet of seventy-three [?] ships.

units.la: VIII. Infelix belli catastrophe.
units.tr: VIII. The unhappy catastrophe of the war.

units.la: Demosthenis temeraria & infelix oppugna-tio Epipolarum in tenebris: mox, Consilium ejusdem de reditu: & de maturandi fuga cum classe: &, Niciæ cunctatio territi Lunæ defectu.
units.tr: The rash and unlucky attack of Demosthenes on Epipolae in the darkness; soon after, his counsel about returning home, and about hastening a flight with the fleet; and the hesitation of Nicias, frightened by the eclipse of the moon.

units.la: Syracusanorum conatus prohibendi fugam hostium, conflictus, & victoria navalis.
units.tr: The attempt of the Syracusans to prevent the flight of the enemy, the clash, and the naval victory.

units.la: Trepidatio Athenien-sium, & conclusio clas-sis eorum in portu magno:
units.tr: The alarm of the Athenians, and the confinement of their fleet in the great harbour.

units.la: Conatus erumpendi cum tota classe reliqua CX. navium frustra tentatus cum ingenti clade.
units.tr: An attempt to break out with the whole remaining fleet of 110 ships, tried in vain with great slaughter.

units.la: Consilium de classe & castris deserendis: fuga pedestris: viæ à Syracusanis undique obstructæ: tandem Demosthenes & Nicias cum exercitu su-gitivo capti & interfecti: reliqui venditi.
units.tr: The plan to abandon the fleet and camp; flight on foot; the roads on every side blocked by the Syracusans; at last Demosthenes and Nicias, with the fugitive army, captured and put to death; the rest sold.

units.la: Claudatur gnoma: Tales exitus bella non ne-cessaria plerunque merito sortiuntur, ut πολυ-πραγμοσύνη [?] & φιλονεικία [?] ambitiosorum co-herceatur.
units.tr: Let the maxim be drawn: Such ends generally and deservedly befall wars that were not necessary, so that the meddling [πολυπραγμοσύνη?] and the contentiousness [φιλονεικία?] of the ambitious may be restrained.

units.la: Exercitatio X X.
units.tr: Exercitatio XX.

units.la: Vtrum inventio argumentorum praecedat Judicium in doctrina Logica. PARS AFFIRMANS.
units.tr: Whether the invention of arguments precedes judgement in the doctrine of Logic. AFFIRMATIVE PART.

units.la: EXordium sit commendatio studii amici, quod de materiis Theologicis variis familiariter & docte hactenus responderit:
units.tr: Exordium: a commendation of the study of a friend, who has hitherto answered familiarly and learnedly on various theological matters.

units.la: Et petitio sententia de quaestione Logica:
units.tr: And a request for his opinion on the logical question.

units.la: Ratio I. quia operam suam etiam in aliis tibi amice promiserit.
units.tr: Reason I. because he has promised you his labour in other matters too, as a friend.

units.la: II. quia judicium ejus magnifacias.
units.tr: II. because you esteem his judgement highly.

units.la: Exponatur quaestio: cum ἀπολογίᾳ [?] à dissidio docentium:
units.tr: The question is to be set out: with an apology [?] for the disagreement of the teachers.

units.la: PROPOSITIO: Tibi videri rationes probabiles, quod Inventio argumentorum praecedat: Judicium sequatur.
units.tr: PROPOSITION: It seems to you that there are probable reasons why invention of arguments comes first and judgement follows.

units.la: Confirmatio sit ἔνστασις [?] rationum.
units.tr: The confirmation is to be an objection [?] to the reasons.

units.la: I. Quia ordine naturae est prius invenire, quā de inventis judicare.
units.tr: I. Because in the order of nature it is prior to invent than to judge what has been invented.

units.la: II. Quia inventio versatur circa simpliciora, quae sunt priora naturâ.
units.tr: II. Because invention is concerned with simpler things, which are prior in nature.

units.la: Declaretur & ostendatur, quod argumenta in-ventionis sint simpliciora enunciatione & syllo-gismo:ex definitione Ramea argumenti, quia ar-gumentum est vocabulum affectum ad aliquid arguendum.
units.tr: It is to be declared and shown that the arguments of invention are simpler than the proposition and the syllogism, from the Ramist definition of argument, since an argument is a word disposed to prove something.

units.la: Amplificetur maior : exemplo Aristotelis in Physicis prius de principiis & horum affectioni-bus: bus.posterius de ipsis naturalibus rebus differentis: Item aliarum artium.
units.tr: The major premise is to be amplified: by the example of Aristotle in the Physics, who treats first of principles and their affections, and afterwards of natural things themselves, which differ; likewise of the other arts.

units.la: III. Quia materia est prior formâ. Materiam autem suppeditat Inventio: formam Judicium.
units.tr: III. Because matter is prior to form. Invention supplies the matter; judgement, the form.

units.la: IV. Ab authoritate Ciceronis in Topicis, & Scholarum.
units.tr: IV. From the authority of Cicero in the Topics, and of the schools.

units.la: Responsio ad quæstionem Logicam.
units.tr: Reply to the logical question.

units.la: Pars negans.
units.tr: Negative part.

units.la: Exordium sit levis purgatio, quod hactenus non responderis. 1. propter negocia graviora: 2. quia potuerit consulere præceptores, & libros Logicorum veterum. 3. quia nunc videatur quæstio eristica, de qua in tanta opinionum diversitate non libenter pronuncies.
units.tr: Exordium: a slight apology, that you have not answered hitherto. (1) on account of more serious business; (2) because you could have consulted teachers and the books of the older logicians; (3) because the question now seems contentious, and in such great diversity of opinions you would not willingly pronounce.

units.la: Adversativa cum αἰ[?]τιολογία: Cum tamen videas, eum discendi cupidum, & dubium hærere: te paucis explicaturum tuam sententiam.
units.tr: Adversative clause with aetiologia [?]: Since, however, I see that you are eager to learn and hang in doubt, I will briefly explain my opinion.

units.la: Transitio ad propositionem: Non posse recte judicari de ordine partium Logices, nisi de partitione prius constet.
units.tr: Transition to the proposition: It cannot rightly be judged concerning the order of the parts of Logic unless first it is agreed about the partition.

units.la: Propositio I. Etsi partitio Stoica Logices in Inventionem & Judicium sit vetus & vulgata: doctioribus tamen non videri probandam.
units.tr: Proposition I. Although the Stoic partition of Logic into Invention and Judgement is old and common, it does not seem to the more learned to be worthy of approval.

units.la: Ratio 1. quia multis modis sit ambigua. Ostendatur ambiguitas in utraque parte:
units.tr: Reason 1. because it is ambiguous in many ways. The ambiguity is to be shown on each side:

units.la: I. De Inventione, quod aliis sit doctrina in-venienveniendi argumenta seu medios terminos: aliis doctrina inveniendi vocabula simplicia.
units.tr: I. Concerning Invention: for some it is the doctrine of inventing arguments or middle terms; for others, the doctrine of inventing simple words.

units.la: Approbetur significatio prior ut propria, authoritate Aristotelis, Ciceronis & omnium sanorum Logicorum veterum: item significatione & etymo Argumenti, quod ab arguendo dictum, ratio est, rei dubia faciens fidem:
units.tr: The former meaning is to be approved as proper, on the authority of Aristotle, Cicero and all the sound logicians of old; likewise from the meaning and etymology of argument, which is said from arguing: it is a reason, making trust in a doubtful matter.

units.la: Altera improbetur 1. quia nova. 2. quia prava propter catachresin argumenti. 3. quia falsa: eo quod Logici non fit invenire vocabula, sed rationes: Vocabula autem exhibita vel judicare seorsum vel componere ad ratiocinandum.
units.tr: The other is to be disapproved: (1) because it is new; (2) because it is faulty on account of the catachresis of argument; (3) because it is false, since it is not the business of the logician to invent words but reasons: words that are given are either to be judged separately or put together for reasoning.

units.la: II. De Judicio, ostendatur triplex significatio:
units.tr: II. Concerning Judgement, a threefold meaning is to be shown:

units.la: 1. generaliter pro ipsa intelligentia doctrinæ, sensum & usum præceptorum recte percipiens & dijudicans: de quo Quintilianus lib. 6. capit. 6. Non magis arte traditur, quam gustus, odor, &c.
units.tr: 1. generally, for the very understanding of the doctrine, rightly perceiving and discerning the sense and use of the precepts: on which Quintilian, book 6, chapter 6: Art does not teach this any more than taste, smell, etc.

units.la: 2. improprie pro dispositione, quam Aristoteles vocat τάξιν[?] Syllogismi. Improbetur catachresis, & confusio rerum diversissimarum: & ostendatur discrimen: quia disponuntur judicanda; judicantur disposita.
units.tr: 2. improperly, for the arrangement which Aristotle calls the order [?] of the syllogism. The catachresis is to be disapproved, and the confusion of very different things; and the difference is to be shown: because things to be judged are arranged; things arranged are judged.

units.la: 3. proprie pro examine operis logici, quod examen Aristoteles vocat ἀνάλυσιν[?]. Approbetur ex proprietate vocis.
units.tr: 3. properly, for the examination of a logical work, which examination Aristotle calls analysis [?]. To be approved from the proper use of the word.

units.la: Conclusio 1. rationis: Cum ὁμωνυμία[?] sit mater erroris, partitionem necessario esse vitiosam: & quæstionem de ordine partium Sophisticam, nisi accedat distinctio.
units.tr: Conclusion of the 1st reason: Since homonymy [?] is the mother of error, the partition is necessarily faulty, and the question about the order of the parts is sophistical, unless a distinction is added.

units.la: Ratio II. quia est manca: omittens multas necessarias partes Logices: Ut: doctrinam prædicabilium, Categoriarum, Demonstrationis, Sophisticorum Elenchorum.
units.tr: Reason II. because it is defective, omitting many necessary parts of Logic: such as the doctrine of the predicables, the Categories, Demonstration, and the Sophistical Elenchi.

units.la: Obiectio 1. Praedicabilia non sunt necessaria.
units.tr: Objection 1. The predicables are not necessary.

units.la: Resp. Negatur. Ostendatur necessitas praecipua, ad definitiones & divisiones construendas.
units.tr: Reply. It is denied. The chief necessity is to be shown, for constructing definitions and divisions.

units.la: Obiect. 2. Nec Categoriae. Respond. Sunt materia Logices.
units.tr: Objection 2. Nor are the Categories. Reply. They are the matter of Logic.

units.la: Obiect. 3. Demonstratio Aristotelica non est in rerum natura.
units.tr: Objection 3. Aristotelian demonstration is not in the nature of things.

units.la: Resp. 1. per negationem: quia datur concludere proprium πιϑ&[?] de primo subiecto per primam causam, in omnibus scientiis, atq; etiam in Theologia: quod proprie est demonstrare.
units.tr: Reply 1. by denial: because it is possible to conclude a proper pithanon [?] about the first subject through the first cause, in all sciences, and also in Theology: which is properly to demonstrate.

units.la: Probetur exemplis aliquibus ex lib. 2. poster. cap. 16.17.&c. & Theologico: verbi gratia: Omnes electi salvantur: Omnes credentes in Christum sunt electi, omnes igitur credentes in Christum salvantur, &c. Amplific. Imo est finis & proprium opus Logici. 2. Etsi non esset: tamen ideo est necessaria, ut ad eam probationes dirigantur. Illustretur exemplo perfecti oratoris à Cicerone descripti: quales nulli sunt, omnes tamen esse contendunt.
units.tr: Let it be proved by some examples from the second book of the Posterior Analytics, chapters 16, 17, etc., and from theology: for instance: All the elect are saved; all who believe in Christ are elect; therefore all who believe in Christ are saved, etc. Amplification. Indeed it is the end and proper work of the logician. 2. Even if it were not so, it is nevertheless necessary, so that proofs may be directed to it. Let it be illustrated by the example of the perfect orator described by Cicero: there are no such men, yet all contend that they exist.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Doctrina Elenchorum non est Logicae: quia Elenchi sunt vitia. Respond. Etiam de vitiis docendum, non ut admittantur, sed ut agnoscantur, corrigantur & vitentur: sicut de venenis medicina tradit: ex principio: Contrariorum eadem scientia.
units.tr: Objection 4. The doctrine of the Elenchi does not belong to Logic, because the Elenchi are faults. Reply. Faults too must be taught, not so that they may be admitted, but so that they may be recognised, corrected and avoided; as medicine teaches about poisons, from the principle: The knowledge of contraries is the same.

units.la: Instantia: Rectum est sui & curvi index.
units.tr: Instance: The straight is the judge of itself and of the crooked.

units.la: Resp. 1. Potestate non semper actu.
units.tr: Reply 1. By power, not always in act.

units.la: 2. Peritis, non pueris.
units.tr: 2. For the skilled, not for children.

units.la: 3. Beneficio artis.
units.tr: 3. The benefit of the art.

units.la: Ostende necessitatem in logicis ex scopis sophi-starum, varietate fallaciarum: artificiosa redu-ctione omnium ad unam: dexteritate solutionis, &c.
units.tr: Show the necessity in logic from the aims of the sophists, the variety of fallacies, the skilful reduction of all of them to one, the dexterity of solution, etc.

units.la: Ratio III. Quia perturbata, confundens propria communib.
units.tr: Reason III. Because it confuses and mixes up the proper with the common.

units.la: Ratio IV. Quia nimis lata: & non καθόλου[?], proinde ad ipsorum metregulam non congruēs.
units.tr: Reason IV. Because it is too broad, and not καθόλου [?], and therefore does not fit their own rule.

units.la: Probatio, quia etiā Rhetorica, Poetica, Musica suam habet Inventionem & Judicium.
units.tr: Proof: because rhetoric, poetics and music too have their own invention and judgement.

units.la: Ratio V. Quia est alia melior & perfectior divisio in partem generalem & specialem, seu communem & propriam.
units.tr: Reason V. Because there is another, better and more perfect division into a general and a special part, or a common and a proper part.

units.la: Definiatur utraq.: Generalis, quæ principia & formam generalem syllogismi tradit. Specialis quæ de tribus syllogismi speciebus materiæ qualitate distinctis præcipit.
units.tr: Let each be defined. The general is what hands down the principles and the general form of the syllogism. The special is what teaches about the three species of syllogism, distinguished by the quality of their matter.

units.la: Probetur hujus divisionis perfectio: quia per-sectè tradit partes essentiales finis seu operis lo-gici: quæ sunt materia & forma syllogismi.
units.tr: Let the perfection of this division be proved: because it fully hands down the essential parts of the end or work of logic, which are the matter and the form of the syllogism.

units.la: Declaretur I. quid per formam intelligatur: mentis nempe discursus à noto ad ignotius, cum suis principiis: & ostendatur eius perfectio: quia secundum tres mentis operationes docet notiones simplices apprehendere: apprehensas componere vel dividere, ex compositis vel divisis viâ syllogismi ratiocinari. Item: qua perfectè tradit syllogismi [illegible, ~24 letters] καὶ [illegible, ~12 letters].
units.tr: Let it be explained, first, what is meant by the form: namely, the movement of the mind from the known to the less known, together with its principles; and let its perfection be shown, because according to the three operations of the mind it teaches to apprehend simple notions, to combine or divide the apprehended notions, and from the combined or divided notions to reason by way of syllogism. Likewise: which fully hands down the syllogism [illegible, ~24 letters] καὶ [illegible, ~12 letters].

units.la: II. quid per Materiam: nempe conditiones essentiales materiæ syllogismi: & similiter o-stendatur stendatur perfectio; quia tantum est triplex. Neces-sario vera, probabiliter vera: & falsa apparenter vera, quæ totidem efficit syllogismi materiati differentias. Hæc omnia illustrentur distinctione Organi Aristotelis in has partes; & partium singularum ostensione secundum libros Organi.
units.tr: II. What is meant by the matter: namely, the essential conditions of the matter of the syllogism; and likewise let its perfection be shown, because it is only threefold: necessarily true, probably true, and false but apparently true. These make as many differences of the syllogism in matter. Let all this be illustrated by the division of Aristotle's Organon into these parts, and by the showing of the individual parts according to the books of the Organon.

units.la: Per ὑπόληψιν[?] remittatur amicus ad libros ipsos & interpretes: & claudatur prima propositio: Cum tot modis sit vitiosa partitio Stoica, frustra de partium ordine disputari.
units.tr: Through ὑπόληψις [?] let the friend be referred to the books themselves and their interpreters, and let the first proposition be closed: since the Stoic partition is faulty in so many ways, it is vain to dispute about the order of its parts.

units.la: Transitio per advers. Tamen de hoc te aliquid additurum.Præmittantur tres hypotheses:
units.tr: Transition through the objection. Nevertheless, I will add something to you about this. Let three hypotheses be put forward:

units.la: 1. Distinguendum inter Logicen docentem & utentem.
units.tr: 1. A distinction must be drawn between logic as teaching and logic as used.

units.la: 2. Inventionis significatio propria sola retinenda.
units.tr: 2. Only the proper signification of invention is to be retained.

units.la: 3. Tria significata Judicii discernenda & in conspectu habenda.
units.tr: 3. The three significations of judgement are to be distinguished and kept in view.

units.la: Propositio II. Judicium prima significatione nec sequitur nec præcedit Inventionem in arte, sed totum ubique comitatur.
units.tr: Proposition II. Judgement in its first signification neither follows nor precedes invention in the art, but always accompanies the whole of it.

units.la: Ratio: quia non est pars artis, sed facultas naturæ:
units.tr: Reason: because it is not a part of the art but a faculty of nature.

units.la: Declaretur & ostendatur authoritate Quintiliani, lib.3.cap.3. His adiecerunt quidam sextam partem, ita ut inventioni judicium subnecterent: quia primum esset invenire, deinde judicare: Ego vero ne invenisse quidem credo eum, qui non judicavit, &c. Et Cicero quidem in Rhetoricis judicium subjecit inventioni. Mihi autem adeo primis tribus partib. videtur permixtum, &c.
units.tr: Let it be declared and shown by the authority of Quintilian, book 3, chapter 3: Some have added a sixth part, so that judgement is attached to invention, because first one must find and then judge. But I do not think that he has even found who has not judged, etc. And Cicero, in the Rhetoric, indeed subjoined judgement to invention. But to me it seems so mixed up with the first three parts, etc.

units.la: Propositio III. Judicii secunda significatione pro dispositione non sequitur, sed præcedit Inventionem medii.
units.tr: Proposition III. Judgement in its second signification, as disposition, does not follow but precedes the invention of the middle term.

units.la: Anterationes[?] ostendatur, quod hic agatur de dispositione docente, quæ est [illegible, ~7 letters] seu doctrina generandi syllogismum ex suis principiis: non de operante, quæ est actus generandi seu conficiendi syllogismum.
units.tr: Let it be shown that here we are dealing with disposition in its teaching sense, which is [illegible, ~7 letters], or the doctrine of generating the syllogism from its principles; not with disposition in its operative sense, which is the act of generating or making the syllogism.

units.la: Ratio 1. Quia idea operis præcedit operationem.
units.tr: Reason 1. Because the idea of the work precedes the operation.

units.la: Hæc maior declaretur Thesi, quod in omni arte præposterus & irritus sit conatus generandi, operis artificio nondum tradito vel cognito. Item, exemplo sutoris, fabri, &c. & ad Logicum applicetur. Probetur authoritate Aristotelis Metaph. lib. 7. c. 7. Sanitas fit ex sanitate: domus ex domo: Ut: Intellectio (i. ars docens) procedit a principio & idea (i. a notione finis) ad ultima intellectionis (i. ad singularia, proxima sensui, remotissima ab intellectu, principia operationis.) Minor bipartita: Dispositio est doctrina idea: Inventio operationis. Probetur pars utraque ex definitione seu à conjugatis: Prior: quia disponere, h. e., tradere vel discere principia, naturam, & leges syllogismi est idem operis Logici menti imprimere. Hoc vero est prius. Posterior: quia quærere & invenire medium est se ad operandum, h. e., ad problema syllogismo adstruendum vel destruendum accingere. Hoc vero est posterius.
units.tr: This major premise is to be declared by the thesis that in every art an attempt to generate something is preposterous and vain when the art's workmanship has not yet been handed down or known. Likewise, by the example of the shoemaker, the smith, etc., and let it be applied to the logician. Let it be proved by the authority of Aristotle, Metaphysics book 7, chapter 7: Health comes from health; a house from a house. Thus: understanding (that is, the teaching art) proceeds from the principle and the idea (that is, from the notion of the end) to the last things of understanding (that is, to the singulars, nearest to sense and most remote from the intellect, the principles of operation). The minor is twofold: Disposition is the doctrine of the idea; invention is the operation. Let each part be proved from the definition, or from the conjugates. The former: because to dispose, that is, to hand down or learn the principles, nature and laws of the syllogism, is the same as to impress the work of logic on the mind. This, however, is prior. The latter: because to seek and to find the middle term is to prepare oneself for operating, that is, for establishing or overturning the problem by a syllogism. This, however, is posterior.

units.la: Addatur conclusio: Jure igitur Logica de structura syllogismi ejusque principiis prius quam de operatione præcipit.
units.tr: Add the conclusion: rightly, therefore, logic teaches the structure of the syllogism and its principles before the operation.

units.la: Ratio 2. Maior. Sine quo inventio medii intelligi non potest,id natură præcedit. Probetur ex fine ordinis, qui est, cujusque disciplinæ partes ad meliorem ac faciliorem cognitionem convenienter apteque disponere.
units.tr: Reason 2. Major premise. That without which the invention of the middle term cannot be understood, precedes it by nature. Let it be proved from the end of order, which is to arrange fittingly and suitably the parts of each discipline for better and easier knowledge.

units.la: Minor. sine præcognita ὁρίσει[?] Intentio me-dii non intelligitur.
units.tr: Minor premise. Without a prior definition [?] the intention of the middle term is not understood.

units.la: Probatio 1. quia medium est syllogismi & ex-tremorum medium. 2. quia inventio fit ex an-tecedentibus consequentibus & repugnantibus extremorum. 3. quia talem requirit antecedentium consequentium & repugnantium combi-natione cū extremis, qua propositiones duæ in-de nascentes ad utilem syllogismi formā quantitate & qualitate sint legitimè dispositæ.
units.tr: Proof 1. because the middle term belongs to the syllogism and is the middle of the extremes. 2. because invention is made from the antecedents, consequents and contraries of the extremes. 3. because it requires a combination of the antecedents, consequents and contraries with the extremes, by which the two propositions arising from it are legitimately disposed in quantity and quality into a useful form of syllogism.

units.la: Conclusio. Ergo de extremis (nomine & verbo, subjecto & prædicato) propositionibus, forma & modo syllogismi prius docendum est.
units.tr: Conclusion. Therefore, the extremes (name and verb, subject and predicate), the propositions, and the form and mode of the syllogism must be taught first.

units.la: Ratio 3. ab authoritate Aristotelis, qui συλλογι-σμῶν[?] syllogismi cum necessariis protheoriis prius: methodum inventionis posterius tradidit, quod ex Organo ostendatur.
units.tr: Reason 3, from the authority of Aristotle, who handed down the syllogisms first, with their necessary preliminary theories, and the method of invention afterwards; this is to be shown from the Organon.

units.la: Protheoria operis logici sunt. Isagoge quinque vocum Porphyrii: Decem Categoriæ Aristotelis cum annexis definitionibus, regulis, distinctionibus: Genesis operis Logici sive syllogismi est liber περὶ ἑρμηνείας & primi Priorum Anal. sectio prima: Inventionis methodus est ejusdem sectio secunda. (περὶ διαλεκτικῶν[?].)
units.tr: The preliminary theories of the logical work are these. The Isagoge of Porphyry on the five words; the ten Categories of Aristotle with their attached definitions, rules and distinctions. The genesis of the logical work, or of the syllogism, is the book On Interpretation and the first section of the first Prior Analytics. The method of invention is the second section of the same (on dialectical matters).

units.la: Transitio ad tertiam significationem Judicii, pro ἀναλύσει operis Logici. Declaratur quod sit.
units.tr: Transition to the third signification of judgement, as the analysis of the logical work. Let it be declared what this is.

units.la: 1. Examen syllogismi & medii investigati ad suas normas,
units.tr: 1. The examination of the syllogism and of the middle term investigated according to its rules;

units.la: 2. Reductio orationis syllogisticæ potentia ad syllogismum actu.
units.tr: 2. The reduction of syllogistic discourse from the potential to the actual syllogism;

units.la: 3. Et hujus ex imperfectiore figura & modo ad perfectiorem.
units.tr: 3. And of this, from the more imperfect figure and mood to the more perfect.

units.la: Propositio IV. Hoc judicium sequitur inventionem medii:
units.tr: Proposition IV. This judgement follows the invention of the middle term.

units.la: Ratio 1. petatur ex descriptione: quia non possunt, nisi prius inventa, sic judicari.
units.tr: Reason 1. Let it be taken from the description: because things cannot be judged in this way unless they have first been invented.

units.la: Ratio 2. ab authoritate Aristotelis: qui hoc judicium tradit post [illegible, ~10 letters], seu inveniendi artificium libri primi Priorum sectione tertia, toto libro secundo Priorum.
units.tr: Reason 2. From the authority of Aristotle, who hands down this judgement after [illegible, ~10 letters], or the art of invention in the third section of the first book of the Prior Analytics, and throughout the second book of the Prior Analytics.

units.la: Transseatur[?] ad confutationem per occupationem.
units.tr: Let us pass to the refutation by the way of occupation.

units.la: Non tamen hoc modo approbari Stoicam partitionem.
units.tr: Yet the Stoic partition is not approved in this way.

units.la: Ratio ostendatur ex abusu vocabulorum prius declarato.
units.tr: The reason is to be shown from the abuse of words, declared earlier.

units.la: Ad argumentum I. Respond. 1. per concessionem de judicio proprie dicto. Item de improprie dicto in Logica utente. 2. negatur de improprie sumto pro [illegible, ~5 letters] in Logica nocente.
units.tr: To the first argument. I answer: 1. by conceding it of judgement properly so called, and likewise of judgement improperly so called in logic as used. 2. It is denied of the improperly taken sense as it is applied in logic as misused.

units.la: Probatio petatur ex tertia propositione: quia doctrina ideæ est prior doctrina operationis, &c.
units.tr: Proof is to be sought from the third proposition: because the doctrine of the idea is prior to the doctrine of the operation, etc.

units.la: Ad II. per negationem minoris: quia argumentum seu medium est quiddam compositum & posterius: idque quia relatum: habens respectum ad sua extrema & ad situm in forma syllogistica: sine quo intelligi nequit.
units.tr: To the second, by denying the minor premise: because the argument, or middle term, is something composite and posterior, and that because it is relative, having regard to its extremes and to its place in the syllogistic form, without which it cannot be understood.

units.la: Doctrina vero simplicium pertinet ad [illegible, ~4 letters]; cujus est
units.tr: The doctrine of the simple things, however, belongs to [illegible, ~4 letters]; of which it is

units.la: 1. denomine & verbo 2. de enunciatione 3. desyllogismo 1. denomine & verbo} tradere 2. de enunciatione } tradere 3. de syllogismo
units.tr: 1. of name and verb; 2. of the enunciation; 3. of the syllogism. 1. of name and verb: to hand down; 2. of the enunciation: to hand down; 3. of the syllogism.

units.la: Ad probationem ex definitione Ramæa, per negationem: quia definitio est vitiosa: Probetur
units.tr: To the proof from the Ramist definition, by denial: because the definition is faulty. Let it be proved

units.la: 1. quia argumentum est definiendum actu non potentia.
units.tr: 1. because the argument is to be defined in act, not in potency.

units.la: 2. alioqui sex & pluribus argumentis sæpe cōstabit syllogismus, quoniam tot sæpe vocabulis syllogismus constat.
units.tr: 2. otherwise a syllogism will often consist of six or more arguments, since a syllogism often consists of that many words.

units.la: 3. Authoritate Ciceronis, Quintiliani & omnium recte loquentium.
units.tr: 3. By the authority of Cicero, Quintilian and all who speak correctly.

units.la: 4. Ramo opponatur Ramus in prioribus omnibus dialecticis: ubi recte definivit argumentum esse quod aliquid arguit.
units.tr: Let Ramus be opposed to Ramus in all his earlier dialectics, where he rightly defined the argument as that which proves something.

units.la: Ad III. per concessionem in natura, & arte operante, æmula naturæ: non autem in arte docente, quæ ab idea necessario incipit.
units.tr: To the third, by conceding it in nature, and in the operative art, which imitates nature; but not in the teaching art, which necessarily begins from the idea.

units.la: Ad IV. Resp. 1. Cicero sequitur Stoicorum partitionem, cujus incommoda supra sunt ostensa.
units.tr: To the fourth, I answer: 1. Cicero follows the Stoic partition, whose inconveniences have been shown above.

units.la: 11. Opponitur authoritas Aristotelis, cui ut maiori artifici in sua arte magis credendum est.
units.tr: 11. The authority of Aristotle is opposed, to whom, as to the greater master in his own art, more credit must be given.

units.la: Conclusio: sit hortatio, ut de his sedulo cogitet, & veterem Logicam prius recte intelligere, quā cum novatoribus fastidire discat.
units.tr: Conclusion: let there be an exhortation that they should think carefully about these matters, and learn first to understand the old logic rightly, before they take up a disdain for it with the innovators.

units.la: Exercitatio XXI.
units.tr: Exercitatio XXI.

units.la: An Musica instrumentalis, quàm vocant, recte toleretur in scholis.
units.tr: Whether instrumental music, as it is called, may rightly be tolerated in the schools.

units.la: Propositio: Non male Musicam instrumentalem aliquam tolerari, quę nimirum scholasticis conveniat: sed his conditionibus.
units.tr: Proposition: It is not wrong that some instrumental music be tolerated, which indeed suits scholars, but on these conditions:

units.la: 1. Vt sit moderata.
units.tr: 1. That it be moderate.

units.la: 2. Vt decora, nec levis.
units.tr: 2. That it be decorous and not frivolous.

units.la: 3. Vt tempestiva, non impediens studia & res necessarias, ipsorum & aliorum.
units.tr: 3. That it be timely, not hindering studies or necessary business, either of the students themselves or of others.

units.la: Confirmationis rat. 1. Quia sit pars poëtices, digna literatis, qui eam discere possint.
units.tr: Reasons for the confirmation. 1. Because it is a part of poetics, worthy of learned men, who are able to learn it.

units.la: Exemplis illustretur Lini, Orphei, &c. & contrario Alcibiadis, &c.
units.tr: Let it be illustrated by examples of Linus, Orpheus, etc., and by the contrary example of Alcibiades, etc.

units.la: II. Est assuefactio affectuum & morum ad harmoniam, h.e. justitiam, æqualitatem, & moderationem.
units.tr: II. It is a habituation of the emotions and morals to harmony, that is, to justice, equality and moderation.

units.la: III. Est recreatio animi post labores & res ferias. Exempla Davidis, Achillis, Alexandri, &c.
units.tr: III. It is a recreation of the mind after labours and holidays. Examples of David, Achilles, Alexander, etc.

units.la: IV. Habet vim mitigandi dolores animi, & cruciatus corporis: propter συμπαθείαν[?]: Exemplum Saulis.
units.tr: IV. It has the power to soothe the pains of the mind and the torments of the body, on account of sympathy: the example of Saul.

units.la: V. Fuit olim Dei jussu adhibita in cultu ceremoniali ad excitandos affectus convenientes in celebratione Dei.
units.tr: V. It was formerly employed by God's command in ceremonial worship, to stir up the emotions fitting for the celebration of God.

units.la: VI. Etiam nunc adhiberi potest ad celebrandum Deum hymnis & odis divinis, privatim & publicè, sicut fert ædificatio. Col. 3. 16.
units.tr: VI. It can even now be used to celebrate God with hymns and divine odes, privately and publicly, as edification requires. Col. 3. 16.

units.la: Conclusio. Abusum omnem præsertim ad luxū & lasciviam vitandum esse.
units.tr: Conclusion. Every abuse must be avoided, especially abuse leading to luxury and wantonness.

units.la: Exercitatio XXII.
units.tr: Exercitatio XXII.

units.la: De Hominis Praestantia: & de quaestione: An bruta sint ratione praedita.
units.tr: On the Excellence of Man, and on the question: whether brute animals are endowed with reason.

units.la: Exordii propositio: Dicendi exercitia in scholis sunt necessaria.
units.tr: Proposition of the exordium: Exercises in speaking are necessary in the schools.

units.la: Ratio ab usu: quia sunt praecipua exercitatio styli & sermonis.
units.tr: Reason from use: because they are the chief exercise of style and speech.

units.la: Anthypophora: Requirunt ea non levem rerum cognitionem & usum, quae cum mihi desint, vereor, ne videar temerarius. Adversat. Attamen cathedram nunc conscendi fretus. 1. auditorum benevolentia, qui sunt commilitones. 2. loci conditione, qui est privatus, tyrannum palaestra[?], ubi non turpe est hallucinari. 3. praecipue au-thoritate praeceptorum, quorum iussui obtemperandum fuit.
units.tr: Objection: Such exercises require no slight knowledge and experience of things, which, since I lack them, I fear I may seem rash. Reply: Nevertheless I have now mounted this chair, relying (1) on the goodwill of the hearers, who are my fellow soldiers; (2) on the condition of the place, since I am a private man, and the tyro's wrestling-ground, where it is no shame to go astray; (3) and above all on the authority of the teachers, whose command I was bound to obey.

units.la: Conclusio. Rogo igitur, ut docentem patienter audiatis.
units.tr: Conclusion. I ask, therefore, that you hear the teacher patiently.

units.la: Transitio habeat docilitatem, & occasionem ar-gumenti: Jussus cogitare de argumento, digna explicatione judicavi quaestionem de Ratione, utrum homini sit communis cum brutis, nec ne.
units.tr: Transition, which contains both the modesty and the occasion of the argument: Bidden to think about a subject, I judged the question of Reason worthy of explanation, namely whether it is common to man and the brutes or not.

units.la: Ratio: quia nuper in lectione Plutarchi incidi in disputationem Grylli & Ulyssis, qua videtur e-verti recepta sententia de ratione hominis pro-pria.
units.tr: Reason: because recently, while reading Plutarch, I came upon the disputation of Gryllus and Ulysses, which seems to overturn the accepted opinion about the reason proper to man.

units.la: Amplif. 1. ab experientia, quod bruta multa calliditate, prudentia, fortitudine, temperantia, &c. homines aequare, imo superare videntur. 2. a testimonio Lactantii, quod in multis brutis et-iam[?] loquendi & ridendi vis, aliaque rationis signa deprehendantur.
units.tr: Amplification: (1) from experience, since brute animals seem to equal, and even to surpass, men in cunning, prudence, courage, temperance and so on. (2) from the testimony of Lactantius, that in many brutes the power of speaking and laughing, and other signs of reason, are detected.

units.la: PROPOSITIO I. Quæ & quanta sit Hominis præstantia. II. Confutatio argumentorum de ratione brutorum. De Primo.
units.tr: PROPOSITION I. What and how great is the excellence of man. II. Refutation of the arguments concerning the reason of the brutes. Concerning the first.

units.la: De præcellentia Hominis variæ sententiæ: alii eam collocarunt in ratione, alii in risu, alii in sermone, alii in numerandi facultate: alii in erecta corporis figura, &c.
units.tr: Various opinions have been held about the pre-eminence of man: some placed it in reason, others in laughter, others in speech, others in the faculty of counting, others in the upright bodily form, and so on.

units.la: Dic esse præclara & vera hominis elogia, sed non explicare veram ejus Præstantiam.
units.tr: Say that these are fine and true praises of man, but that they do not explain his true excellence.

units.la: Opponatur sententia SCRIPTURÆ: Hominem, & quidem solum esse conditum ad Imaginem Dei: ex historia creationis. Hanc esse veram Præstantiam.
units.tr: Set against them the opinion of Scripture: that man, and he alone, was created in the image of God, from the history of the creation. This is the true excellence.

units.la: Explicetur, & ostendatur: Imaginem Dei non esse corporis formam, cum Deus sit incorporeus: sed consistere 1. in hominis forma essentiali ejusque operationibus: II. in finis præstantia.
units.tr: Let it be explained and shown: that the image of God is not the form of the body, since God is incorporeal; but that it consists (I) in man's essential form and its operations, and (II) in the excellence of his end.

units.la: Persequere utrunque hoc ordine.
units.tr: Pursue both in this order.

units.la: Primò, Formam esse ipsam animam: cujus præstantia.
units.tr: First, the form is the soul itself, whose excellence lies as follows.

units.la: 1. Insubstantia, quia non ex crasi corporum vel elementorum orta: non harmonia ex compage viscerum & vigore membrorum existens: sicut in fidibus ex intentione nervorum efficitur concors sonus: Vide Lactantium lib.7.c.13. qui opinionem hujusmodi cuidam Aristoxeno tribuit: Sed spiritualis essentia, separabilis a corpore, viva a Deo corpore inspirata: Gen.2.7: Inspi-ravit homini spiraculum vitae. Ratio: quia Deus est Spiritus, Joh.4.24.
units.tr: (1) Its immateriality: because it does not arise from the blending of bodies or elements, nor is it a harmony existing from the joining of the organs and the vigour of the limbs, as in the lyre a harmonious sound is produced by the tension of the strings. See Lactantius, book 7, chapter 13, who ascribes this opinion to a certain Aristoxenus. Rather it is a spiritual essence, separable from the body, living, breathed into the body by God: Genesis 2:7, "He breathed into man the breath of life." Reason: because God is Spirit, John 4:24.

units.la: II. In immortalitate: Abjiciatur sententia Platonis de animorum aeternitate, quasi fuerint antenatos homines, Deo coaeterni: quia sic non imago Dei, sed Deus essent.
units.tr: (II) In immortality: let the opinion of Plato be rejected, that souls are eternal, as if men had existed before birth, coeternal with God; for thus they would be not the image of God, but gods themselves.

units.la: Afferatur brevissime: Immortalitas ex scriptura: Platone: & Aristotelis loco citato: ubi intellectum agentem vocat φῶς & ἐνέργειαν χωρι-στὴν, ἀμιγῆ, καὶ ἀπαθῆ τὴν οὐσίαν.
units.tr: To be given very briefly: immortality from Scripture, from Plato, and from the passage of Aristotle cited above, where he calls the active intellect light and an activity separate, unmixed, and impassible in its essence.

units.la: III. In facultate intelligendi & volendi: quae utraque ex operationibus asseratur. 1. Intellectus operationes, cognitio singularium & universalium: compositio, divisio, ratiocinatio, actus reflexus, cognitio sui ipsius & propriae excellentiae. 2. Voluntatis operationes: Spontanea electio vel repudiatio objecti ab intellectu monstrati, persecutio, fuga, suspensio actionis, gubernatio locomotivae.
units.tr: (III) In the faculty of understanding and willing: both of which are established from their operations. (1) The operations of the intellect: knowledge of particulars and universals, composition, division, reasoning, reflexive act, knowledge of itself and of its own excellence. (2) The operations of the will: spontaneous choice or rejection of an object shown by the intellect, pursuit, flight, suspension of action, direction of the locomotive faculty.

units.la: IV. In harum facultatum rectitudine & perfectione: quia in mente lux & agnitio vera Dei: In voluntate & appetitionibus rectitudo, conformitas cum Deo. Ephes.4.v.23.24. Col.3.8. Occupatio: Etsi haec rectitudo per peccatum sit amissa: & secuta horribilis caecitas atque aversio a Deo, & omnium virium ἀταξία: tamen per Christum naturam instaurari nunc in renatis, donec in altera vita perficiatur: & in homine etiam lapso manmansisse formam essentialem, qua homo est: a-nimam immortalem cum facultatibus & opera-tionibus divinissimis.
units.tr: (IV) In the rectitude and perfection of these faculties: because in the mind there is light and true knowledge of God; in the will and the appetites there is rectitude, conformity with God. Ephesians 4:23–24; Colossians 3:8. Objection: although this rectitude was lost through sin, and there followed a dreadful blindness and aversion from God, and disorder in all the powers; nevertheless through Christ nature is now restored in the regenerate, until it is perfected in the other life; and even in fallen man the essential form by which man is man has remained: an immortal soul with its most divine faculties and operations.

units.la: Secundo, Finis hominis explicetur 1. brevi-ter ex disputationibus Philosophorum: de bono præstantissimo: arguatur eorum cæcitas & lan-guor in assensu. 2. ex Scriptura: Vera Dei agnitio, cultus, celebratio, Felicitas, &c. 2.Cor.3.18 Col.3.10. Eph.4.24.
units.tr: Secondly, the end of man is to be explained: (1) briefly from the disputations of the philosophers about the highest good, and their blindness and feebleness in assent is to be refuted; (2) from Scripture: the true knowledge of God, worship, celebration, happiness, and so on. 2 Corinthians 3:18; Colossians 3:10; Ephesians 4:24.

units.la: Colligatur ex his, quę & quanta sit hominis præstantia: quanta fuisset, si non peccasset: quanta deniq; futura sit in vita cœlesti: Addatur [illegible, ~4 letters] Lactantius de instauratione per Christum: qua homo denuo incipiat vere esse homo. Et πλάσμα[?], In sola Ecclesia recte explicari & intelligi istam humanæ naturæ præstantiam: quia sola intelligit præstantiam sui ortus, & instaurationem naturæ.
units.tr: Let it be gathered from these what, and how great, the excellence of man is: how great it would have been had he not sinned, and how great it will finally be in the heavenly life. Add Lactantius on the restoration through Christ, by which man begins anew to be truly man. And [illegible], the excellence of this human nature is rightly explained and understood only in the Church, since only the Church understands the excellence of its origin and the restoration of its nature.

units.la: Ἀ'πιώξις[?] per adversativam: Sed de reliquiis tantum Imaginis Dei & præstantiæ Hominis, te orationem instituisse: quibus natura humana à brutis & animantibus aliis separatur.
units.tr: Aposiopesis, by way of adversative: But you have undertaken to speak only of the remnants of the image of God and the excellence of man, by which human nature is separated from the brutes and other living creatures.

units.la: Removeantur ordine sed breviter à brutis par-tes imaginis Dei prius expositæ: in forma & fine.
units.tr: Let the parts of the image of God be set aside in order, but briefly, first expounded from the brutes: in form and in end.

units.la: Remotio rationis ostendatur ex remotione propriarum operationum utriusque facultatis: & explicetur, qualis sit cognitio in brutis, & qualis appetitus movens ea ad agendum secundum na-turam: monstrato discrimine inter sensum tum externum, tum internum communem, quo singularia objecta præsentia cognoscunt: Et ipsum intellectum[?]: Item: inter appetitum tum naturalem, tum sensitivum: & inter voluntatem, quæ appetitus rationalis dicitur.
units.tr: The denial of reason is to be shown from the denial of the proper operations of each faculty; and it is to be explained what kind of knowledge there is in the brutes, and what kind of appetite moves them to act according to nature; the distinction being shown between the external sense and the common internal sense, by which they know present particular objects, and the intellect itself. Likewise between natural appetite and sensitive appetite, and between the will, which is called the rational appetite.

units.la: Claudatur prima pars per hæc πογίσματα.
units.tr: The first part is closed by these syllogisms.

units.la: I. Hominem ergo solum ratione & voluntate uti.
units.tr: I. Man alone, therefore, uses reason and will.

units.la: II. Solius hominis esse virtutem tum ἀγαθ-νομικῶ, tum φυσικῶ: quia solus habet utriusq; subjecta: & principia scientiarum & artium capax: docere ac discere potest: Solus etiam habet organa: intellectum, sermonem, electionem, civitatem, leges, &c.
units.tr: II. Virtue, both moral and natural, belongs to man alone: because he alone has the subjects of both, and is capable of the principles of the sciences and arts; he can teach and learn. He alone also has the instruments: intellect, speech, choice, the state, laws, and so on.

units.la: III. Solus homo contemplatur, agnoscit, miratur, reveretur, celebrat Deum: ex fine suo. Vide quomodo Lactantius lib.3. cap. 10. ostendat religionem solam propriam esse hominis: cum in ceteris omnibus bruta homini quodammodo communicare videantur. Ex notitiis item naturalib. testimonio Ciceronis; ex corporis figura: Vide rursus Lactantium lib.7.cap.4.5.8.9.
units.tr: III. Man alone contemplates, acknowledges, admires, reveres and celebrates God, in accordance with his end. See how Lactantius, book 3, chapter 10, shows that religion alone is proper to man, since in all other respects the brutes seem in some way to share with man. Likewise from the natural notions, from the testimony of Cicero; from the bodily form. See again Lactantius, book 7, chapters 4, 5, 8 and 9.

units.la: De Secundo.
units.tr: On the Second Thing.

units.la: Revocentur omnia argumenta, quibus ratio brutis vendicari posse videtur ad duas classes. 1. sit eorum, quæ intelligentiam & voluntatem. II. eorum quæ virtutem brutis inesse docent.
units.tr: Let all the arguments by which reason seems to be claimed for the brutes be brought back to two classes. (1) Those that show that the brutes have understanding and will; (2) those that teach that virtue is present in the brutes.

units.la: Argumentum pro ratione & voluntate brutorum.
units.tr: Argument for the reason and will of the brutes.

units.la: I. Argumentum Autobuli apud Plutarchum. Quicquid sentit est rationale: Bruta habent sen-sum. Ergo,&c. Maioris prob,quia sentire est in-telligere. Sola mens videt,audit: Exemplo Cleo-menis non audientis in convivio loquentes ho-spites,cum mente absens in Peleponnefo esset.
units.tr: I. The argument of Autobulus in Plutarch. Whatever perceives is rational. Brutes have sense. Therefore, etc. The major premise is proved because to perceive is to understand. Only the mind sees and hears: as in the example of Cleomenes, who did not hear the guests speaking at the banquet, since in mind he was absent in the Peloponnese.

units.la: Respond. negetur probatio: non mens videt, sed intelligit se videre per oculum, &c: quod deest brutis. Mens avocat Phantasiam & sensum communem, sine quibus non fit sensus externus.
units.tr: Answer. The proof is denied: it is not the mind that sees, but it understands that it sees through the eye, etc., which the brutes lack. The mind calls away the phantasy and the common sense, without which external sense does not occur.

units.la: II. Argum. Affectus sunt opiniones: & sunt in brutis: Canis gaudet conspecto hero vel cibo: bruta irascuntur, metuunt, dolent reprehensa, respiciunt: deliniuntur tibiis, &c. Ergo, &c. Resp. negatur major: quia differunt genere & subjectis: contra Stoicos. 2. ad minorem: In brutis esse affectus ultimos communes: qui fiunt ex contactu & comitantur sensum: Ut Delectatio & dolor: non autem appetitiones sequentes cognitionem.
units.tr: II. Argument. Passions are opinions, and they are present in the brutes: a dog rejoices when it sees its master or food; brutes grow angry, fear, grieve when rebuked, look back, are soothed by flutes, etc. Therefore, etc. Answer. The major is denied, because they differ in genus and subjects; against the Stoics. 2. To the minor: in the brutes there are only the common final affections, which arise from contact and accompany sense, such as delight and pain; but not the appetites that follow cognition.

units.la: III. Argumentum. Privatio praesupponit habitum: Bruta privantur ratione: dicuntur enim canes, equi, vulpes, &c. erraro, insanire, furere: Ergo praesupponitur ea prius habuisse rationem. Respond. Rabies brutorum non est mentis error, sed Phantasiae & sensus communis turbatio ex humorum intemperie.
units.tr: III. Argument. Privation presupposes a habit. The brutes are deprived of reason: for they are called dogs, horses, foxes, etc. who wander, go mad, rage. Therefore it is presupposed that they previously had that reason. Answer. The rage of the brutes is not an error of the mind, but a disturbance of the phantasy and the common sense arising from an intemperance of the humours.

units.la: IV. Argumentum. Ovis videns lupum, fugit: audiens vocem nati balantis, intelligit defectum pabuli: Gallina invento grano convocat pullos: qui eliciunt ex voce matris praesentiam pabuli & accurrunt: Canis in bivio odoratur & eligit rectam viam, qua lepus fugit,&c. Ergo est in brutis compositio, divisio, ratiocinatio, electio, &c. Respond. Non via ratiocinationis fit compositio & divisio in brutis: sed vel naturali quodam instinctu, συμπαθεία [?] vel ἀντιπαθεία [?], vel phantasia conservante species: & præsente tantum objecto in sensibus externis: non vero absente [?]: nec eliciente intentiones non sensatas, quod facit ratio humana.
units.tr: IV. Argument. A sheep seeing a wolf flees; hearing the bleating of its young, it understands the lack of pasture; a hen, having found a grain, calls her chicks, who, from the mother's voice, perceive the presence of food and run up; a dog at a crossroads sniffs and chooses the straight road by which the hare fled, etc. Therefore there is in the brutes composition, division, reasoning, choice, etc. Answer. Composition and division in the brutes do not come about by way of reasoning, but by a certain natural instinct, sympathy [?] or antipathy [?], or by a phantasy preserving the species, and only when the object is present to the external senses, not when it is absent [?]; nor do they draw out unperceived notions, which human reason does.

units.la: Argumenta pro virtute brutorum
units.tr: Arguments for the virtue of the brutes.

units.la: Argumentum I. Bruta possunt docere & discere artes & sermonem. Perdices docent pullos fugientes se occultare, ac resupinos jacentes se gleba terræ pedibus apprehensa cooperire: Ciconiæ docent pullos volare: Lusciniæ cantare: Psittacus discit loqui. Ergo habent usum rationis. Respond. Est hæc ἀγχίνοια [?] quædam naturalis: non in artibus, sed in operationibus determinatis à natura: Psittacus reddit voces, sine intellectu significationis & rerum.
units.tr: Argument I. The brutes can teach and learn arts and speech. Partridges teach their chicks to hide when fleeing and, when they lie on their backs, to cover themselves with a clod of earth grasped in their feet; storks teach their young to fly; nightingales to sing; a parrot learns to speak. Therefore they have the use of reason. Answer. This is a certain natural quickness of wit, not in arts but in operations determined by nature: the parrot repeats sounds without understanding their meaning or the things.

units.la: Argumentum II. Bruta in morbis quærunt salutaria remedia. Canes nausea correpti gramen appetunt: Sues ad fluviatiles cancros properant: Testudo origanum arrodit: Ursus languidus formicas mandit, &c. Hæc vero sunt Prudentiæ. Respon. 1. Odore, non cogitatione utilitatis trahuntur. 2. Temperamenta corporum eis afferunt certas appetitiones: Ostende prudentiam non esse; ex definitione. Ethic.l.6.c.5. Virtutem Moralem non modo inesse sed etiā magis inesse brutis quam homini probare conatur Gryllus ille porcus Cyrces ex homine factus apud Plutarchum: præferens animam & vitam porcorum animæ & vitæ hominum: &c.quia virtutem habeat natura, & sine labore. Similiamplif. Terram sponte sua omnia proferētem,præferendam esse ci,quę cultu magno indiget:ut terra Cyclopum, Ithaca Vlyssis, &c.
units.tr: Argument II. In sickness the brutes seek healing remedies. Dogs seized with nausea seek out grass; swine hasten to the river crabs; the tortoise gnaws oregano; the sluggish bear eats ants, etc. These, however, are works of prudence. Answer. 1. They are drawn by smell, not by thought of usefulness. 2. The temperaments of their bodies bring them certain appetites. Show that it is not prudence, from its definition: Ethics, book 6, chapter 5. He tries to prove that moral virtue is not only present in the brutes but is even more present in them than in man: that famous pig of Circe, made from a man, in Plutarch, who prefers the soul and life of pigs to the soul and life of men, etc., because nature has virtue, and without labour. Similarly, in amplification: a land that yields all things of its own accord should be preferred to one that needs great cultivation, as the land of the Cyclopes is preferred to Ithaca of Ulysses, etc.

units.la: Argumentum III. Fortitudo inest brutis à natura: & quidem major quam hominibus.
units.tr: Argument III. Courage is present in the brutes by nature, and indeed greater than in humans.

units.la: 1. quia pugnant secum & contra homines ad mortē usque, nec victa supplicant, &c. 2. æque fœminis & maribus inest. 3. Poetę robur hominum amplificantes leonibus eos comparant, non contra. Resp.ex cap.8.lib.3.Ethicorum: Esse in brutis non veram fortitudinem sed animositatē ex iracundia. Probetur ex causa impulsiva: quæ fortitudini est τὸ καλὸν: Iracundiæ ἡ λύπη: unde est assinorum fortitudo. 2. Poetæ notantes timidum vocant leporem, cervum: Achilles de Agamem. Iliad.α: Canis oculos habes: cor cervi.
units.tr: 1. Because they fight among themselves and against men even to death, and when conquered do not beg for mercy, etc. 2. It is equally present in females and males. 3. Poets, magnifying the strength of men, compare them to lions, not the reverse. Answer. From chapter 8 of book 3 of the Ethics: in the brutes there is not true courage but a spirit of boldness arising from anger. Let it be proved from the impulsive cause: for the cause of courage is the noble [to kalon], that of anger is grief [lype]; hence the courage of asses. 2. Poets who note a timid man call him a hare or a deer. Achilles, of Agamemnon, in Iliad 1: You have the eyes of a dog, the heart of a deer.

units.la: Argumentum IV. Temperantia major brutis quam hominibus: Quia voluptates naturales necessarias sectantur ordinatē: non necessarias non quærunt: non argentum, ebur, vestes preciosas admirantur ut homines.
units.tr: Argument IV. Temperance is greater in the brutes than in humans, because they pursue natural and necessary pleasures in an orderly way; they do not seek unnecessary ones; they do not admire silver, ivory, precious garments as men do.

units.la: Resp. 1. Bruta moderantur voluptates non recta ratione, sed naturali instinctu: Non igitur habent temperantiam virtutem quæ est actio secundum rectam rationem. 2. Non moderantur: sed explent ardentissime: nec minus sæpe peccant excessu in pabulo & ivenere: nisi cohibeantur. 3. Brutorum propria est intemperantia: quia fit circa sensum brutum, infimum & ignobilissimum TACTUM: Hominibus vero accidit, non qua homines, sed qua corrupti: vel qua animalia, videl. 3. c. 10. Ethic. 4. Bruta non appetunt res preciosas, propter stuporem: Homines vero appetunt tanquam naturae suae ornamenta propria: & virtus servat mediocritatem in appetitione.
units.tr: Answer. 1. The brutes moderate their pleasures not by right reason but by natural instinct. They therefore do not have temperance, which is a virtue, the action according to right reason. 2. They do not moderate; they gratify their desires most ardently, and no less often sin by excess in food and in venery, unless they are restrained. 3. Intemperance is proper to the brutes, because it occurs in the brutish sense, the lowest and most ignoble, touch. But it befalls humans not as humans but as corrupted, or as animals, namely Ethics book 3, chapter 10. 4. The brutes do not desire precious things, because of their dullness; but humans desire them as ornaments proper to their nature, and virtue keeps a mean in desire.

units.la: CONCLUSIO breviter repetat propositionem: habeat detestationem Gryllii Cyrcæi, & similium, vitam brutam agentium sub hominum figura. Hortetur ad cognoscendam hominis praestantiam originalem: ad deplorandum lapsum, quo illa excidimus, & subsecutam caliginem, pravitatem: ad excolendas imaginis divinæ reliquias doctrina, virtute, pietate, fide, & precibus: donec rursus in perfectam Imaginem Christi gloriosi transformetur, ac luce illa inaccessa circumfusi in cœlis Deum sine fine celebremus.
units.tr: CONCLUSION: briefly repeats the proposition; let it instil detestation of Gryllus, the Circean, and of those like him who lead a brutish life under the figure of a man. Let it exhort us to recognise the original excellence of man, to lament the fall by which we dropped from it and the darkness and depravity that followed; to cultivate the remnants of the divine image by learning, virtue, piety, faith and prayers, until we are again transformed into the perfect image of the glorious Christ, and, surrounded by that inaccessible light, celebrate God in heaven without end.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: DAVIDIS PAREI Exercitationum Philosophicarum & Theologicarum LIBER II.
units.tr: DAVID PAREUS' Philosophical and Theological Exercises, BOOK II.

units.la: Exercitationes Theologicas continens. Exercitatio I. Consultatio ad amicum de quaestione:
units.tr: Containing theological exercises. Exercise I. A consultation with a friend on the question:

units.la: An liceat emere & possidere res preciosas Idololatriae dicatas.
units.tr: Whether it is lawful to buy and possess precious things dedicated to idolatry.

units.la: PARS NEGANS.
units.tr: THE NEGATIVE PART.

units.la: EXordium ab occasione: Quod nuper No-vesio expugnato milites quidam vestimenta & vasa preciosa, Idololatrica, bello direpta,civibus vestrae urbis venalia, & quidem viliore precio obtulerint.
units.tr: Introduction from the occasion: Recently, after Novesium was taken, some soldiers offered for sale to the citizens of your city garments and precious vessels, idolatrous spoils of war, and indeed at a rather low price.

units.la: Adversativa. Te verò suasisse, ne emerent.
units.tr: Adversative: But you advised them not to buy.

units.la: Ratio continens propositionem: Quia judices nō licere.
units.tr: Reason containing the proposition: Because judges that it is not lawful.

units.la: Argumentum I. Ab interdicto Dei Deut.7. 25: Sculptilia deorum ipsorum igni comburite, non concupisces aurum & argentum, quæ super ea sunt.
units.tr: Argument I. From God's prohibition, Deut. 7.25: The graven images of their gods you shall burn with fire; you shall not covet the silver or gold that is on them.

units.la: Amplif.à causis: 1. Abominatio est Jehovæ.
units.tr: Amplification from causes: (1) It is an abomination to Jehovah.

units.la: 11. Nesis[?] abominatio sicut illud.
units.tr: (2) Nesis[?] is an abomination, as that is.

units.la: Obiect. Esse hanc legem forensem, Mosaicam.
units.tr: Objection: That this is a law of the courts, Mosaic.

units.la: Respon. Etiam Christianis dicitur: Fugite i-dola.
units.tr: Answer: It is also said to Christians: Flee from idols.

units.la: Argumentum II. à Thesi: Quia res Eccle-siæ publicis usibus semel dicatas, quantum vis su-perstitione inquinatæ sint, in privatos usus con-vertere non liceat.
units.tr: Argument II, from the thesis: Because things once dedicated to the public uses of the Church, however much they may be polluted by superstition, may not be turned to private uses.

units.la: Probatio Majoris ab authoritate Ambrosii l.2 off. cap. 28. Et Augustini Epistola 154. dicentis, vel in communes usus, vel in honorem Dei veri convertendas esse.
