But this is uncertain: (1) because those passages can be understood of the Jewish Pentecost; (2) by the testimony of Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 21, who says that neither the Saviour nor the Apostles prescribed laws concerning festivals, nor imposed a yoke of servitude: "But the feast of Easter and the other feasts," he says, "they left to be kept by the free judgment of those who had received benefits in those days. For it was not the Apostles' purpose to enact laws about the celebration of feasts, but to be for us authors of the right manner of living and of piety."

units.la: Origo tamen ad tempora Apostolis vicina referatur: quia vetustissimi Scriptores eius mentionem faciunt. Tertull. de corona mil. Origen. l.8. cont. Cels. Irenaeus apud Iustin. quaest. 115. ubi expresse ad tempora Apostolorum refert August. Epist.118.&c.
units.tr: Its origin, however, is to be referred to times close to the Apostles, since the most ancient writers make mention of it: Tertullian, On the Crown of the Soldier; Origen, book 8 against Celsus; Irenaeus, as cited in Justin, Question 115, where he expressly refers it to the times of the Apostles; Augustine, Letter 118, etc.

units.la: II. Solennitatis modo. Ad veterem omnes Iu-dæi lege convocabantur Hierosolymam, fiebant sacrificia, epulae: movebatur de feria in feriam, cum secundo die azymorum.
units.tr: II. As to the manner of the solemnity: for the old feast all Jews were summoned by law to Jerusalem; sacrifices and banquets were made; it was moved from day to day, as with the second day of the unleavened bread.

units.la: Nova non est alligata uni loco: celebratur co-cionibus sacris precibus & hymnis de misso Spi-ritu Sancto:
units.tr: The new feast is not tied to one place; it is celebrated with sacred sermons, prayers and hymns concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Obiter dic de geniculatione in Pentecoste in-ter precandum: cum a Paschate ad Pentecosten stantes precarentur veteres.
units.tr: Incidentally, mention should be made of kneeling during prayer on Pentecost, whereas the ancients prayed standing from Easter to Pentecost.

units.la: Causam exponit Iustinus ibidem.
units.tr: Justin explains the reason in the same place.

units.la: Reiiciantur nugae Papisticae de columbis è fornice templi missis ad Spiritum Sanctum repraesentandum.
units.tr: The Papist trifles about doves sent down from the vault of the temple to represent the Holy Spirit are to be rejected.

units.la: Dies stata Dominica septima post pascha.
units.tr: The fixed day is the seventh Sunday after Easter.

units.la: Occupat. Etsi ex loco dicto Iustini patet, olim non semper fuisse in Dominica celebratam (quia dicit: ἐνδιωχμεῖ[?] τῇ κυριακῇ[?]) tamen sunt causae probaprobabiles receptæ Dominicæ. 1. quia quinquagesima dies à resurrectione Domini semper incidit in Dominicam. 2. quia missio Spiritus Sancti facta est in Dominica.
units.tr: Concerning its origin: although it is clear from the passage of Justin cited that at one time it was not always celebrated on the Lord's day (since he says "on the Sunday" as a particular day), yet there are probable reasons for which the Sunday was received: (1) because the fiftieth day from the Lord's resurrection always falls on a Sunday; (2) because the sending of the Holy Spirit took place on a Sunday.

units.la: Reiciatur eorum opinio qui feria quinta vel sexta factam volunt: & probetur quod in Dominica: quia anno passionis Domini secundus dies azymorum fuit feria prima, postridie Sabbathi, in quod Iudæi Pascha in feriam sextam tunc incidens reiecerant ex consuetudine ne cogerentur continuatas ferias agitare: de qua cum inter eruditos sit quæstio non levis, hoc loco prætereatur.
units.tr: The opinion of those who want it to have been on a Thursday or a Friday is to be rejected, and what is held to be that it was on a Sunday is to be approved: because in the year of the Lord's passion the second day of the unleavened bread was the first day of the week, the day after the Sabbath, upon which the Jews, as a custom, had put off the Passover that then fell on the Friday, so that they would not be forced to keep the days in succession. As this is a question of no small difficulty among the learned, it is passed over at this point.

units.la: III. Finibus. Vetus instituta ad recolendam vindicationem populi à servitute: necnon promulgationem legis: & agebantur gratiæ Deo pro messe.
units.tr: III. As to the purposes: the old feast was instituted to commemorate the deliverance of the people from servitude, and also the promulgation of the law; and thanks were given to God for the harvest.

units.la: Nova, est memoria effusi Spiritus Sancti super omnem carnem juxta oraculum Ioel. 2. quod primum & summum beneficium fuit Christi ad dextram Patris exaltati.
units.tr: The new feast is the memory of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh, according to the oracle of Joel 2, which was the first and greatest benefit of Christ, exalted at the right hand of the Father.

units.la: Ratio à thesi per occupationem. Etsi semper sint recolenda Dei beneficia: tamen utiliter stata tempora eorum meditationi tribui.
units.tr: The reasoning from the thesis, through the reason for the occupation: although God's benefits are always to be commemorated, yet it is useful to assign fixed times for their meditation.

units.la: 1. quia omnia debent fieri in Ecclesia ordine.
units.tr: 1. Because all things ought to be done in the Church in good order.

units.la: 2. ut solennitate stata & publica omnes magis excitentur.
units.tr: 2. So that all are more stirred up by a fixed and public solemnity.

units.la: 3. ut publice sonet confessio fidei contra infideles, & ab his Ecclesia discernatur.
units.tr: 3. So that the confession of faith may sound publicly against unbelievers, and the Church be distinguished from them.

units.la: 4. ut servetur consensus in doctrina de præcipuis patefactionibus & beneficiis Dei Ecclesiæ in Christo exhibitis.
units.tr: 4. So that consensus is preserved in the doctrine of the chief revelations and benefits of God exhibited to the Church in Christ.

units.la: Conclusio per applic. Cum his de causis etiam nova Pentecoste celebretur: Ecclesiam non Iu-daizare, nec libertatem suam imminuere.
units.tr: Conclusion by application: for these reasons the new Pentecost too is celebrated, the Church not thereby Judaizing nor diminishing her liberty.

units.la: Transeatur ad collationem beneficiorum Veteris & Novae Pentecostes.
units.tr: Let us pass over to the comparison of the benefits of the old and the new Pentecost.

units.la: II. Collatio beneficiorum utri-usque Pentecostes, datae nimirum Legis, & donati Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: II. The comparison of the benefits of each Pentecost, namely of the law given and of the Holy Spirit bestowed.

units.la: Praemitte causas collationis. 1. quia Deus eodem die utrunque ideo haud dubie praestitit, ut inter se conferri possent: approbetur sententia Augustini, facientis ἀναγωγὴν[?], &c.
units.tr: First, the causes of the comparison: (1) because God, on the same day, granted both, undoubtedly so that they might be compared with each other; the opinion of Augustine is approved, who makes an allegorical interpretation, etc.

units.la: 2. quia etiam Paulus 2. Cor. 3. ea inter se con-fert, & quidem, ut novum veteri longe antefe-rat.
units.tr: (2) Because Paul in 2 Cor. 3 also compares them with each other, and indeed so that he far prefers the new to the old.

units.la: 3. Ut intellecta praestantia novi beneficii ma-gis grati simus.
units.tr: (3) So that, the excellence of the new benefit being understood, we may be more grateful.

units.la: Collationis instituantur tria membra, & in singulis ostendatur praestantia maior novi quam veteris beneficii.
units.tr: Three heads of comparison are to be set up, and under each it is to be shown that the excellence of the new benefit is greater than that of the old.

units.la: 1. In symbolis.
units.tr: (1) In the signs.

units.la: 2. In donis ipsis.
units.tr: (2) In the gifts themselves.

units.la: 3. In usu & effectis.
units.tr: (3) In the use and effects.

units.la: 1. Symbola olim fuisse tremenda: mōs totus flagrat, perstrepunt tubae, tonitrua, fulgura, populus arcetur, &c. vide Exod. 19. Sunt signa praesentis quidem Dei, sed inaccessi, tremendi: Ego ignis consumens, &c.
units.tr: (1) The signs were formerly terrifying: the whole mountain blazes, trumpets sound, thunders, lightnings, the people are kept back, etc. See Exod. 19. They are signs of God's presence indeed, but of a God inaccessible and terrible: "I am a consuming fire," etc.

units.la: Hic symbola non terribilia: ventus vehemes, sed non lædens nec terrens: ignis sed non urens, linguarum divisio sed non dolens, &c. Sunt signa præsentis Spiritus Sancti, accedentis ad homines, & coniungentis cum Deo: Sedit super unumquemque, &c.
units.tr: Here the signs are not terrifying: a violent wind, but one that neither harms nor frightens; fire, but not burning; a division of tongues, but not painful, etc. They are signs of the presence of the Holy Spirit, coming near to men and joining them to God: "He sat upon each one," etc.

units.la: 2. Collatio donorum. Vetus erat promulgatio Legis totius: cuius beneficii præstantia commendetur.
units.tr: (2) Comparison of the gifts. The old was the promulgation of the whole Law; the excellence of this benefit is to be commended:

units.la: 1. ab illustri patefactione Dei & voluntatis eius in lege.
units.tr: (1) from the illustrious revelation of God and of his will in the law;

units.la: 2. à causa promulgati Decalogi: ut esset instauratio Legis naturæ per peccatum corruptæ: & regula perfectæ obedientiæ, iustitiæ & conformitatis cum Deo.
units.tr: (2) from the purpose of the promulgated Decalogue: that it should be a restoration of the law of nature, corrupted by sin, and a rule of perfect obedience, righteousness and conformity with God;

units.la: 3. Ceremoniales & forenses leges monebant de beneficiis spiritualibus Messiæ: discernebant populum Dei ab aliis, & serviebant conservationi Ecclesiæ usque ad Messiam.
units.tr: (3) the ceremonial and judicial laws pointed forward to the spiritual benefits of the Messiah, distinguished God's people from others, and served the preservation of the Church until the Messiah.

units.la: Per adversativam extolle beneficium missionis Spiritus Sancti in Pentecoste.
units.tr: Through the contrast, extol the benefit of the mission of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

units.la: 1. Propter illustrem in ea patefactionem Trinitatis.
units.tr: (1) On account of the illustrious revelation of the Trinity in it.

units.la: Pater mittit Spiritum Sanctum iuxta promissionem: Effundam de Spiritu meo. Quem mittet vobis Pater in nomine meo.
units.tr: The Father sends the Holy Spirit according to the promise: "I will pour out my Spirit." "Whom the Father will send you in my name."

units.la: Filius mittit Spiritum Sanctum à Patre: Ego mittam eum vobis à Patre: Iesus exaltatus effudit hoc quod videtis, &c.
units.tr: The Son sends the Holy Spirit from the Father: "I will send him to you from the Father"; "Jesus, exalted, has poured out this which you see," etc.

units.la: Spiritus Sanctus adest specie venti, ignis, & linguarum.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit is present in the form of wind, fire and tongues.

units.la: Est ergo nō motus aut qualitas, sed ὑφιστάμενον.
units.tr: It is therefore not a motion or a quality, but a subsisting being (ὑφιστάμενον).

units.la: Sedet super unum quenque: implens donis dans eloqui, &c.
units.tr: He sits upon each one, filling them with gifts, giving them to speak, etc.

units.la: Ergo Deus immensus, propria Dei operas, &c.
units.tr: Therefore God is immense, the proper works of God, etc.

units.la: II. Propter Evangelium in Pentecoste publicatum in universum orbem. Prob. Apostoli illustrantur, confirmantur, ducuntur in omnem veritatem, juxta promissionem: Ille te statuitur de me. Inducemini virtute ex alto: loquuntur linguis magnalia Dei ad omnes nationes sub caelo: Postea praedicatione implent universum orbem: juxta mandatum: Eritis mihi testes a Jerosolymis, &c.
units.tr: (2) On account of the Gospel published throughout the whole world at Pentecost. Proof: the Apostles are enlightened, strengthened, led into all truth, according to the promise: "He shall be taught concerning me"; "You shall be endued with power from on high"; they speak in tongues the great works of God to all nations under heaven; afterwards by preaching they fill the whole world, according to the command: "You shall be my witnesses from Jerusalem," etc.

units.la: Ergo in Pentecoste primum facta est publicatio Evangelii in universum orbem, cuius praedicatio prius inclusa fuerat Judaeis, &c.
units.tr: Therefore at Pentecost the publication of the Gospel throughout the whole world was first made, whose preaching had before been confined to the Jews, etc.

units.la: Amplifica declaratione discriminum Legis & Evangelii seu veteris & novi foederis ex 2. Cor. 3.
units.tr: Amplify by the declaration of the differences between the Law and the Gospel, or the old and the new covenant, from 2 Cor. 3.

units.la: I. Lex scripta in tabulis lapideis. Evangelium Spiritu Dei vivi in tabulis carneis cordis ver. 3. Ierem. 31. Non secundum pactum.
units.tr: I. The law written on tablets of stone; the Gospel written by the Spirit of the living God on tablets of the heart of flesh, ver. 3; Jer. 31: "not according to the covenant."

units.la: Obiect. Etiam lex inscripta cordibus. Rom. 2.
units.tr: Objection: the law is also written on hearts, Rom. 2.

units.la: Resp. 1. Erat inscripta naturae integrae. Post lapsum secuta horribilis caecitas & αντιξια in mentibus & cordibus: reliquiae notitiarum languidae supersunt ad hoc, ut omnes sint αυτολογητοι.
units.tr: Answer: (1) It was written on the nature of man while it was whole. After the fall there followed a dreadful blindness and hardness in minds and hearts; the remnants of knowledge that remain are faint, so that all are without excuse.

units.la: 2. Inscriptio legis est nuda notitia: Evangelii salutaris agnitio Dei & Mediatoris, coniuncta cum fide & obedientia nova per Spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: 2. The inscription of the law is bare knowledge: the knowledge of God and of the saving Mediator of the Gospel, joined with faith and new obedience through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 2. Lex litera occidens, minisferium mortis, condemnationis: Evangelium Spiritus vivificans, ministerium justitiae, vitae, &c. ver. 6. Declaratur utrunque breviter.
units.tr: 2. The letter of the law kills, is the ministry of death and of condemnation; the Gospel is the Spirit who gives life, the ministry of righteousness, of life, etc. 2 Cor. 3.6. Both are set out briefly.

units.la: Occup. Etiam lex est doctrina justitiæ: sed pro-priæ & impossibilis. Item vitæ: sed cum condi-tione obedientiæ perfectæ: Illustretur compara-tione promissionum legis & Evangelii.
units.tr: Objection: The law too is a teaching of righteousness, but of its own kind, and impossible. Likewise it is a teaching of life, but on condition of perfect obedience. Illustrate this by comparing the promises of the law and of the Gospel.

units.la: Obiect. Etiam Lex est spiritualis. Rom.7. Resp. Sed non ut Evangelium spiritus vivificans. Declara quod sit spiritualis 1. quatenus spiritualem obedientiam exigit. 2. quatenus cum Evangelio coniuncta præparat corda ad conversionem, & conversis est norma vitæ,&c.
units.tr: Objection: The law too is spiritual. Rom. 7. Answer: But not as the Gospel is the Spirit who gives life. Explain in what sense it is spiritual: (1) inasmuch as it requires spiritual obedience; (2) inasmuch as, joined with the Gospel, it prepares hearts for conversion, and for the converted it is the rule of life, etc.

units.la: Instantia: Etiam Evangelium occidit 2.Cor. 2. Sumus Christi fragrantia in his qui pereunt. Resp. per accidés propter infidelitatem hominum: per se vivificat, accendens fidem & convertens corda.
units.tr: Objection: The Gospel too kills, 2 Cor. 2. "We are the fragrance of Christ among those who perish." Answer: It does so incidentally, on account of the unbelief of men; in itself it gives life, kindling faith and converting hearts.

units.la: 3. Lex est temporaria : usque ad Christum: Matth.11. 23. Hebr.8.13. Evangelium æternum: Apoc.14.6.
units.tr: 3. The law is temporary, until Christ: Matt. 11.13; Heb. 8.13. The Gospel is eternal: Rev. 14.6.

units.la: Obiect. Etiam lex æterna. Resp. Moralis: quo ad notitias & obligationem naturæ rationalis: sed abrogata per Christum 1. quo ad condemnationem & coactionem: Deus non iudicat nos amplius secundum legem, &c. Non sumus sub lege sed sub gratia. 2. quo ad Ceremonias & forensia; quia maceries est diruta. Eph.2.
units.tr: Objection: The law too is eternal. Answer: As a moral law, with respect to the knowledge and obligation of rational nature, but it has been abrogated by Christ: (1) with respect to its condemnation and compulsion: God no longer judges us according to the law, etc. "We are not under the law but under grace." (2) with respect to the ceremonies and judicial matters, because the dividing wall has been broken down. Eph. 2.

units.la: 4. Ministerium legis tectum, obscurum, Velamen impositum in facie Mosis manet: constans vaticiniis & typis. Hebr. 10.1. Evangelium clarum,retectum, transformans nos in imaginem Christi de gloria in gloriam. 2.Cor.3.18.
units.tr: 4. The ministry of the law is covered, dark, "the veil laid upon the face of Moses remains," consisting of prophecies and types. Heb. 10.1. The Gospel is clear, uncovered, "transforming us into the image of Christ from glory to glory." 2 Cor. 3.18.

units.la: Claudatur collatio hæc cum Apostolo: Si igitur gloriosum fuit ministerium cõdemnationis;&c. quanto magis,&c.
units.tr: Let this comparison be concluded with the Apostle: "If therefore the ministry of condemnation was glorious, etc., how much more ...," etc.

units.la: Tranfeatur ad tertium membrum collationis in fructibus seu effectis.
units.tr: Let us pass to the third member of the comparison, in the fruits or effects.

units.la: Fructus seu usu promulgatae Legis perstringe paucis.
units.tr: Briefly describe the fruits or use of the law as promulgated.

units.la: 1. Accusabat peccata: Rom.3.4. & 7. hinc metus, contumacia, poenae.
units.tr: 1. It accused of sins: Rom. 3.4 and 7. Hence fear, obstinacy, punishments.

units.la: 2. Eratiugum intolerabile Act.15.
units.tr: 2. It was a yoke intolerable: Acts 15.

units.la: 3. Paedagogia ad Christum. Gal.3.
units.tr: 3. It was a schoolmaster leading to Christ: Gal. 3.

units.la: Contra extolle fructus novi beneficii: & often-de 1. Exhiftoria, quid in Apostolis effecerit Spiritus: loquuntur linguis: magnalia Dei: praedicat in nomine Iesu μετὰ παῤῥησίας[?], intrepide se opponunt hostibus: gaudent in afflictionibus, martyria subeunt, &c.
units.tr: On the other hand, extol the fruits of the new benefit, and first (1) from history: what the Spirit effected in the Apostles: they speak with tongues, "the mighty works of God," they preach in the name of Jesus with boldness, they fearlessly oppose their enemies, they rejoice in afflictions, they undergo martyrdom, etc.

units.la: 2. Ex promissionibus: quid in omnibus electis.
units.tr: (2) From the promises: what is effected in all the elect.

units.la: 1. Illuminat mentes nostras veram agnitionem Dei & Servatoris, &c. accendens fidem, movens corda per Evangelium, &c. Ief.11. Spiritus Sapientiae. Ostende ex promissionibus. Ioel. 2. Omnes prophetabunt Ier.31. Omnes cognoscent me, &c. Ioh.16. Ducet vos in, &c.
units.tr: (1) He enlightens our minds with the true knowledge of God and of the Savior, etc., kindling faith and moving hearts through the Gospel, etc. Isa. 11: the Spirit of wisdom. Show this from the promises. Joel 2: "All shall prophesy." Jer. 31: "All shall know me, etc." John 16: "He will lead you into, etc."

units.la: 2. Purificat corda nostra per fidem, regeneras, sanctificans, &c. Ief.11. Spiritus pietatis. Ezech.36 ver.25. Effundam aquam mundam, &c. Per verbum & usum Sacramentorum. Eph.5. & Tit.3.
units.tr: (2) He purifies our hearts through faith, regenerating, sanctifying, etc. Isa. 11: the Spirit of piety. Ezek. 36:25: "I will pour clean water, etc." Through the Word and the use of the Sacraments. Eph. 5 and Titus 3.

units.la: 3. Dicit & excitat preces: clamat Abba Pater. Zach.12.10. Effundam Spiritum gratiae & precum. Rom.8. Nescimus quid precemur: Spiritus est, &c.
units.tr: (3) He stirs up and kindles prayers: he cries "Abba, Father." Zech. 12:10: "I will pour out the Spirit of grace and of prayer." Rom. 8: "We do not know what to pray for; the Spirit, etc."

units.la: 4. Consolatur, confirmat & obsignat electos: quia Paracletus: Est arrhabo salutis Ephef. 1. 2. 2.Cor.1. Manet nobiscum. Spiritus consilii & fortitudinis, Ief.11[?].
units.tr: (4) He comforts, strengthens and seals the elect, because he is the Paraclete: he is the pledge of salvation, Eph. 1; 2 Cor. 1. "He abides with us." The Spirit of counsel and of strength, Isa. 11.

units.la: 5. Non modo hæc dona salutis, sed & dona vocationis necessaria in omnibus operatur sicut vult,1.Cor.12.
units.tr: (5) He works not only these gifts of salvation but also the gifts of calling, which are necessary, in all, as he wills, 1 Cor. 12.

units.la: Fiat generatim antithesis legis & Evangelii fecundum effecta. Non igitur accusat, terret, &c. sed absolvit, erigit: non imponit jugum, sed liberat: non monstrat Christum in umbris sed in speculo, &c.
units.tr: Let there be made, in general, an antithesis of law and Gospel according to their effects. The law therefore accuses, terrifies, etc.; but the Gospel absolves and raises up; the law imposes a yoke, but the Gospel frees; the law shows Christ in shadows, but the Gospel in a mirror, etc.

units.la: Conclusio: Ex his manifestum, quanto gloriosior fit promulgatio Evangelii in Pentecoste facta per Spiritum sanctum super Apostolos effusum, quam promulgatio legis fuit in môte[?] Sinai: quia Deus fe clarius patefecit, & beneficia Spiritus S. in Ecclesiam redundarunt.
units.tr: Conclusion: From these things it is evident how much more glorious is the promulgation of the Gospel made at Pentecost, through the Holy Spirit poured out upon the Apostles, than the promulgation of the law was on Mount Sinai: because God revealed himself more clearly, and the benefits of the Holy Spirit overflowed into the Church.

units.la: Hortare ad gratiarum actionem pro donato Ecclesiæ Spiritu S. pro Evangelio ad nos etiam propagato, per quod sibi inter nos colligit veram Ecclesiam. Ad gratitudinem vitæ: ad preces: ut confervet hæc tanta beneficia, defendat Ecclesiam contra furores hostium, tueatur Germaniæ tranquillitatem: fervet Ecclesiarum & Scholarum nutritios: & in his Serenissimum Electorem Fridericum 1 V. quem regat Spiritu sapientiæ, consilii, roboris, &c. ut &c.
units.tr: Exhortation to give thanks for the gift of the Holy Spirit bestowed on the Church, and for the Gospel also spread abroad to us, through which he gathers for himself the true Church among us. To thankfulness of life; to prayers, that he may preserve these great benefits, defend the Church against the rages of enemies, and guard the tranquillity of Germany; that he may foster the nurseries of Churches and Schools; and in these, the most serene Elector Frederick V, whom he may rule with the Spirit of wisdom, counsel, strength, etc., so that, etc.

units.la: DAVIDIS PAREI Exercitationum Philosophicarum & Theologicarum LIBER IV.
units.tr: DAVIDIS PAREI Exercitationum Philosophicarum & Theologicarum LIBER IV.

units.la: Orationes sacras de anniversariis Ecclesiæ festis continens.
units.tr: Containing sacred orations on the annual festivals of the Church.

units.la: ORATIO I. DE NATIVITATE D. N. Jesu Christi.
units.tr: ORATIO I. ON THE NATIVITY OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.

units.la: Recitata publicè in Academia Heidelbergensi. à J. Georgio Wendelino Geyero Sapientia alumno. 24. Decemb. 1584.
units.tr: Delivered publicly in the Academy of Heidelberg, by J. Georgius Wendelinus Geyer, a student of wisdom, 24 December 1584.

units.la: MIRAMINI forsan, Auditores, quid sit, quòd ego, vix ab ulla re, quæ ad præsentem locum tempusque requiritur, instructus, verba factu-rus huc prodeam. Etenim hoc tempus pus doctrinam exactam, judicium maturum: locus vero facultatem dicendi non mediocrem postulat, quorum quam in me sit nihil, vel sane exiguum, libenter agnosco & fateor. Accedit amplissimae hujus doctissimorum virorum & juvenum coronae eruditio, & acre judicium, cui respondere, quantum sit satis, perdifficile esse intelligo. Argumenti enim de quo dicendum est hoc tempore, tanta est magnitudo, tanta majestas, ut nullius hominis, quantumvis ingeniosissimi oratione exhauriri possit. Et sane si in mea potestate situm fuisset, alium quemvis ex hoc loco dicentem audire, quam ad alios verba facere maluissem.
units.tr: Perhaps you wonder, listeners, why I, who am scarcely equipped with anything that this place and occasion require, come forward to speak. For this occasion demands exact learning and mature judgment, and this place demands no small facility in speaking; how little of these I possess, I gladly acknowledge and confess. Add to this the learning of this most ample crown of very learned men and young scholars, and their keen judgment, to which I understand it is extremely difficult to give an adequate reply. For the subject on which I must speak at this time is so great and so majestic that it cannot be exhausted by the speech of any man, however gifted. And indeed, if it had been in my power to hear someone else speak from this place, I would much rather have heard another than speak myself.

units.la: Sed quia leges collegii Theologici volunt, ut aliquis ex numero juvenum hoc tempore ex hoc loco dicat: Et mihi a doctissimis, & quibus nunquam par gratia rependi a me possit, fi-delissimis praeceptoribus hoc muneris impositū est: non potui non illis, tum pro summa, quam illis debere me sentio, reverentia & obedientia, tum pro laudabili hujus scholae consuetudine morem gerere, & onus, quanquam impar humeris meis suscipere, vestra fretus, Auditores, facilitate atque prudentia, quod minime ignorare vos existimem, Theologiae tyronum haec exercitia esse, plenéque mihi persuasum habeam, vos in solenni hac Nativitatis Iesu Christi Domini & Servatoris nostri celebritate, cujus repetitio vetusto & laudabili sane amplissimi Facultatis Theologicae Collegii decreto, hodierno debetur diei, rem ipsam magis, quam facultatem dicentis spectare & perpendere solere. At haec molesta erit & ingrata repetitio: Quid vero homine Christia-no dignius, quā ea beneficia, quæ Deus, miseris abjectis, planeq; immeritis nobis pro immensa sua misericordia contulit, summa cum laude sem percelebrare? Inprimis vero illud, quod æterni Dei æternus Filius ꝓ summa in nos φιλανθρωπία carnem nostram assumpsit, ut nos miseros peccatores sempiternę morti & damnationi obnoxios, æterno Patri reconciliaret, ac λντῳ[?] suo æternam nobis justitiam & vitam restitueret. Quid ista consideratione nobis & piis omnib.: hoc potissimum tempore possit vel jucundius esse vel utilius? Aut quę pię meti[?] major cōtingeret delectatio, quam versari in diligēti meditatione harum rerū, quas tum ad servatoris sui gloriam, tum ad suam ipsius salutem facere manifestum est? Vt vero ad majore etiam alacritate animi præstemus, ipsa naturæ nostræ pravitas movere debet. Videmus enim adeo corruptam & in divinis rebus oscitantem, tantis denique tenebris offusam & irretitam esse naturam nostram, ut nisi incredibilia illa beneficia Christi mediatoris nostri merito & obedientia nobis parta, quotidie aures nostras circumsonent: innatus ille lethargus & sopor spiritualis vix unquam satis excuti aut curari in nobis possit. Hoc sane consilio Spiritus sanctus in sacra Scriptura promissiones de Messia, generis humani servatore passim repetit, inculcat, ut nusquam non occurreret materia tum de salute nostra cogitandi, tum vero immensam Dei patris erga humanum genus misericordiam laudandi & celebrandi.
units.tr: But since the statutes of the Theological college require that one of the young men speak from this place at this time, this duty has been laid upon me by the most learned and most faithful teachers, to whom I can never repay the favour. I could not refuse them, both out of the great reverence and obedience I feel I owe them and to comply with the praiseworthy custom of this school. Trusting in your kindness and wisdom, listeners, I have undertaken a burden, though unequal to my shoulders; I am well aware that you know these are exercises of beginners in theology, and I am fully persuaded that you, on this solemn celebration of the Nativity of Jesus Christ our Lord and Saviour, to which, by the ancient and commendable decree of the most ample College of the Theological Faculty, today's day is devoted for repetition, are accustomed to regard and weigh the matter itself rather than the ability of the speaker. But this repetition will be tedious and unwelcome. Yet what is more worthy of a Christian than to celebrate with the highest praise those benefits which God, in his immense mercy, has bestowed upon us, wretched, rejected and wholly undeserving as we are? Above all, that the eternal Son of the eternal God, out of his supreme love for mankind, took on our flesh, so that he might reconcile us wretched sinners, liable to eternal death and damnation, to the eternal Father, and restore to us, by his own merit and obedience, eternal righteousness and life. What could be either more pleasing or more useful to us and to all the godly than to consider these things, especially at this time? Or what greater delight could a pious mind have than to dwell in careful meditation upon these things, which clearly serve both the glory of their Saviour and their own salvation? And so that we may act with even greater eagerness of mind, the very wickedness of our nature ought to move us. For we see that our nature is so corrupted, so sluggish in divine matters, and finally so clouded and ensnared by such darkness, that unless those incredible benefits won for us by the merit and obedience of Christ our Mediator daily sound in our ears, that innate lethargy and spiritual drowsiness can hardly ever be sufficiently shaken off or cured in us. With this purpose indeed the Holy Spirit in Sacred Scripture repeats and inculcates everywhere the promises concerning the Messiah, the Saviour of the human race, so that there is nowhere a lack of matter both for thinking about our salvation and for praising and celebrating the immense mercy of God the Father toward mankind.

units.la: Etsi vero quæ de Filii Dei nativitate & beneficiis in sacra Scriptura prædicantur, omnia brevi oratione comprehendi non possint: ac tanta mihi dicturo, rerum cum magnitudo tum copia in hoc argumento se quasi effundat, ut vel unde exordiar, vel quo ordine aut modo singula complectar, videre difficile sit: Attamen ut ipse ille, cujus natales celebramus, æterni & immensi patris, æternus & immensus Filius, naturaque incomprehensibilis, carnem nostram induendo, se veluti in arctum contraxit: ita & mea oratio in explicandis ejus laudibus, quæ modum nesciunt, modum sibi ipsa faciat oportet, & ea tantum attingat, quæ mihi pro ingenii mei tenuitate, præcipua & cognitu maximè necessaria videntur. In tribus ergo potissimum summam totius historiæ de Nativitate Christi Domini nostri consistere existimo.
units.tr: Although indeed the things which are proclaimed in Sacred Scripture concerning the birth of the Son of God and his benefits cannot all be comprehended in a short speech; and although, as I am about to speak on such great matters, the greatness and abundance of the subject so pour themselves out that it is difficult to see either where I should begin or in what order or manner I should embrace the individual points, nevertheless, just as he himself, whose birth we celebrate, the eternal and immense Son of the eternal and immense Father, whose nature is incomprehensible, drew himself, as it were, into a narrow compass by putting on our flesh, so my speech too must, in setting forth his praises, which know no measure, impose a measure upon itself, and touch only those points which seem to me, given the slenderness of my ability, most important and most necessary to know. I think therefore that the sum of the whole history of the Nativity of Christ our Lord consists chiefly in three things.

units.la: Primò, quis sit ille, quæ ex virgine nobis esse natû prophetę & Evangelistę testantur: Deinde quis modus nativitatis fuerit: Postremò, cur nasci & cur talis nasci Filius Dei voluerit.
units.tr: First, who he is, whom the prophets and Evangelists testify to have been born for us of a virgin; secondly, what the manner of his birth was; lastly, why and why in such a manner the Son of God willed to be born.

units.la: Ac primum quidem cum antiqua & omnium temporum orthodoxa Ecclesia credimus & pfite-mur, λόγον æt. Filium Dei, Deum, Patri & Spiritui Sancto ὁμοούσιον[?], tempore secundum promissiones patribus à Deo factas definito, verum hominem ex Maria virgine, operante Spiritu, factum esse, non deitatis in carnem conversione, sed naturæ nostræ in DEUM assumtione, ut esset unus Christus θεάνθρωπος[?], non confusione substantiæ, sed unitate personæ, perfectus Deus, perfectus homo. Hoc enim nos docent vaticinia prophetarum, Evangelistarum historiæ, & Apostolorum testimonia innumera, in quibus utrumque nomen Dei & hominis Messiæ tribuitur: & unus idemque nominatur filius hominis, Davidis, Mariæ: & Filius Altissimi: ex quib. præcipua breviter nunc attingere satis fuerit.
units.tr: And first, indeed, we believe and confess with the ancient and orthodox Church of all times that the Word, the Son of God, God, consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, was in time, according to the promises made by God to the fathers, made true man from the virgin Mary, the Spirit working, not by a conversion of his deity into flesh, but by the assumption of our nature into God, so that there is one Christ, God-man, not by a confusion of substance but by the unity of person, perfect God and perfect man. For the prophecies of the prophets, the histories of the Evangelists and the countless testimonies of the Apostles teach us this, in which both the name of God and the name of man are attributed to the Messiah, and one and the same is named Son of man, of David, of Mary, and Son of the Most High; of these it will suffice to touch briefly upon the chief ones now.

units.la: Ecce, inquit Iesaias: Virgo concipiet & pariet filium, & vocabit nomen ejus Immanuel: butyrum & mel comedet, ut sciat reprobare malum & eligere bonum. In Christo, de quo vaticinatur, utramque naturam evidentissime nobis declarans. Deum prædicat, cum in ipso & per ipsum Deum nobis-cum fore testatur. Cum enim hoc nobis præstare debuerit Messias, ut nos, qui per reatum ab Adamo protoplasto contractum, à Deo hostiliter dif-sidebamus, eidem corporis sui sacrificio & inter-cessione reconciliaret, ac spiritus sancti interve-niente nexu in æternum conjungeret: manife-stum est, Immanuelem, cujus virtuti ista attribuuntur, verum Deum à propheta nuncupari. Hominem vero eundem fatetur, dum filium virgi-nis agnoscit, comedentem butyrum & mel, malum spernere & bonum eligere discentem, nosq; homines ejusdem naturæ socios cum Deo reconciliantem: interprete angelo apud Matthæum & Lucam Evangelistas.
units.tr: Behold, says Isaiah: A virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and she shall call his name Immanuel: butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good. In Christ, of whom he prophesies, declaring to us most evidently both natures. He proclaims him God, when he testifies that God will be with us in him and through him. For since the Messiah ought to accomplish this for us, that he should reconcile to God by the sacrifice and intercession of his body us, who by the guilt contracted from Adam the first-formed man were hostile and estranged from God, and should join us to him for ever by the bond of the intervening Holy Spirit, it is plain that Immanuel, to whose power these things are attributed, is called by the prophet the true God. But he confesses him to be man as well, while he acknowledges him as the son of a virgin, eating butter and honey, learning to reject evil and choose good, and reconciling us men, companions of the same nature, with God, as the angel interprets in the Evangelists Matthew and Luke.

units.la: Obstrepunt hic Pseudoiudæi, non esse genuinum hujus loci sensum, quem exposui: sed hoc potius significari, fore ut Deus per eum fit no-biscum, seu fore hunc ministrum & vicarium ju-stitiæ[?] Dei: sæpe enim in sacra Scriptura Dei nomen ad ea monumenta transferri,in quibus se fi-delibus suis adesse testatus est,ut cum Moyses al-tare extructum nominat Iehovah vexillum suu: Ezechiel Hierusalem vocat Iehovah illic. Sed ve-lint nolint fateri coguntur, nomen Immanuelis specialem quandam Dei praesentiam in Christo nobis exhibitam significare ab universali multũ diversam, qua ante ejus adventum populo Israelitico sese patefecerat. Nam si tunc hujus nominis ratio vere constare coepit,cum apparuit Christus in carne,sequitur olim non in solidum, sed ex parte tantum Deum conjunctum fuisse cum patribus. Unde certissime confici potest, Christum esse Deum in carne patefactum. Deinde si nihil nisi homo hic Immanuel esset,quorsum attinebat propheta sequenti versu de butyro & melle,quibus hic puer educandus erat, deque incremento judicii ac sensuum mentionem facere? Voluit certe propheta ista restrictione innuere, Immanuelem hunc verum quidem Deum fore, sed & verum hominem, qui butyrum & mel comedat,cibum infantibus nutriendis consuetum, qui fastiditis amaris, suavibus delectetur & recreetur: qui denique certa animi & corporis incrementa sit habiturus. Quare ut cibus & pueritia incrementa corporis & intelligentiae, verum hominem arguunt: Sic Immanuel verum & aeternum Deum convincit. Quid? quod in tota sacra Scriptura beneficia, quae, unico Messiae tanquam fonti & authori tribuuntur, non sunt finitae aut creatae potentiae, sed solius Dei opera propria,ut sunt:colligere sibi ex universo genere humano certum salvandorum cœtum, instituere & conservare ministerium verbi, remittere peccata, flectere mentes, illuminare mentes, mutare corda, justitiam & vitam reparare atque conferre, &c. Quæ cum Christo sacra Scriptura passim ad-scribat, utique non tantum hominem, sed & Deū esse necesse est. Neque verò Deus appellatur eo modo, quo interdum Dei nomen rebus creatis metaphoricè propter officium aliquod divinum tribuitur: ut cum Angeli & magistratus Dii: Moses Deus Pharaonis: Satan Deus sæculi: venter Deus impiorum nominatur: sed proprie & absolutè Christo Dei nomen in sacra Scriptura attribui, non modò evidentia dicta quàm plurima testantur, sed ex idiomatis quoque divinis soli Deo propriis, longè est evidentissimum. Manet enim immotum axioma Theologicum: Cuicunque tribuitur proprium, quod uni soli essentiæ convenit, eidem essentiam ipsam tribui necesse est. Omnipotentiam Immanueli nostro Propheta aperte hic tribuit, cum in Immanuele nobis defensionem & salutem promittit. Cum igitur Omnipotentia solius Dei adeo propria fit, ut de eo prædicetur convertibiliter, & Deus fit, quicunque omnipotens est, & omnipotens fit, qui Deus est: contra verò Deus non fit, qui omnipotens non est, nec omnipotens fit, qui Deus non est: Sequitur immutabiliter in Christo divinam naturam esse, & Christum secundum eam naturam Deum esse: Et rursus Christum secundum humanam naturam, seu humanam naturam Christi, sicut non est Deus, sic nec omnipotentem esse. Considerent hoc, qui divinæ naturæ ꝓprietates, humanæ realiter cōmunicatas, inque eam transfusas imaginantur: & humanam naturam Omnipotentem, & ubiq; præsentem, h.e, immensam faciunt. Quidni eandem dicunt Deum esse? Et si Deum esse dicunt, cur non æternam etiam dicunt? An Dei nomen de humana natura præ-dicabitur, propria non prædicabuntur? An aliud verè dicetur Deus, de quo propria Dei dici nequeant? Sed redeo ad institutum, & alium ejusdē prophetæ locum profero, quo Immanuelis natu-rā, potentiā, & admirandas vires clarius describit, unde firmissima demonstratione efficitur, explicationem superioris loci à nobis adductā, conve-nientissimam fuisse. Postquam Propheta liberationem populi & urbis per angelum exercitus Assyriaci ꝑdixerat futuram ad consolationem piorū progrediens, etiam æternam libe-rationem per Messiā illis promittit, dicens: Quo-niā puer natus est nobis, & Filius datus est nobis, & factus est principatus super humerum eius, & vocabitur nomen eius Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis, pater futuri seculi, princeps pacis. Quib. propheta utramq; Christi naturā præclarè iterū describit. Humana, quia puerū: divinam, quia filium vocat, filium, inquam, illū, [illegible, ~12 letters] ab æterno genitum & nobis datum. De filio enim illo Dei unigenito & æterno se loqui, propheta non modò absoluta Filii appellatione, inconsueto loquendi more, innuit: sed & attributis omnibus aliis planè divinis & illustribus testatum fa-cit. Quid enim quæso regnum ejus æternum, quod sine fine humeris suis sustentat? quid augustissimi tituli, Admirabilis, Consiliarii, Dei fortis, patris æternitatis, principis pacis, &c. quibus Iehova pater hunc filium nobis datum appellat, quid, inquam, aliud ista denotant, quam præstantius quiddam, ac omni vi, sapientia ac potentia humana majus in hoc puero spectari oportere?
units.tr: Here the Pseudo-Jews raise an objection: that the sense I have set out is not the genuine meaning of this passage, but that it signifies rather that God will be with us through him, or that he will be this minister and vicar of God's justice. For in holy Scripture the name of God is often transferred to those monuments in which he has testified that he is present with his faithful people: thus Moses names the altar he built "Jehovah is my banner," and Ezekiel calls Jerusalem "Jehovah is there." But whether they will or not, they are compelled to admit that the name Immanuel signifies a special presence of God, exhibited to us in Christ, which is very different from the universal presence by which he had made himself known to the Israelite people before his coming. For if the reason for this name truly began to hold only when Christ appeared in the flesh, it follows that God was not joined with the fathers wholly, but only in part. From this it can be most certainly concluded that Christ is God revealed in the flesh. Furthermore, if this Immanuel were nothing but a man, why would the prophet, in the following verse, make mention of butter and honey, with which this child was to be nourished, and of the growth of judgment and of the senses? The prophet certainly wished, by this qualification, to indicate that this Immanuel would indeed be true God, but also a true man, who eats butter and honey, the food customary for nourishing infants, who, having rejected the bitter, takes delight and refreshment in the sweet, and who will finally have a definite growth of mind and body. Therefore, just as food and childhood growth of body and understanding prove a true man, so Immanuel proves the true and eternal God. What is more, throughout the whole of holy Scripture, the benefits that are attributed to the Messiah alone, as to the sole fount and author, are not the works of finite or created power but the proper works of God alone: such as gathering to himself from the whole human race a certain assembly of those to be saved, instituting and preserving the ministry of the Word, forgiving sins, bending minds, enlightening minds, changing hearts, restoring and bestowing righteousness and life, and so on. Since holy Scripture everywhere ascribes these things to Christ, he must necessarily be not only man but also God. Nor is he called God in the way in which the name of God is sometimes metaphorically given to created things on account of some divine office: as when angels and magistrates are called gods, Moses is called God of Pharaoh, Satan is called god of this age, and the belly is named the god of the impious. Rather, the name of God is attributed to Christ in holy Scripture properly and absolutely; this is attested not only by very many plain sayings, but also, most evidently, by the divine idioms proper to God alone. For the theological axiom remains unshaken: whatever is attributed to one thing that belongs to one essence alone, the essence itself must necessarily be attributed to that thing. Here the prophet plainly attributes omnipotence to our Immanuel, when he promises defense and salvation in Immanuel. Since, therefore, omnipotence is so proper to God alone that it is predicated of him convertibly, and whoever is omnipotent is God, and whoever is God is omnipotent, while on the contrary, whoever is not omnipotent is not God, and whoever is not God is not made omnipotent, it follows unchangeably that the divine nature is in Christ, and that Christ according to that nature is God. And again, that Christ according to the human nature, or the human nature of Christ, just as it is not God, so is not omnipotent. Let those consider this who imagine the properties of the divine nature to be really communicated to the human nature and poured into it, and who make the human nature omnipotent and everywhere present, that is, immense. Why should they not also call it God? And if they call it God, why do they not also call it eternal? Will the name of God be predicated of the human nature while the proper attributes are not predicated? Or will something else be truly called God, of which the proper attributes of God cannot be said? But I return to my purpose, and bring forward another passage of the same prophet, in which he describes more clearly the nature, power, and admirable strength of Immanuel, whereby it is most firmly demonstrated that the explanation of the previous passage which I have brought forward was most fitting. After the prophet had foretold that the deliverance of the people and city would come through the angel of the Assyrian army, going on to console the pious, he also promises them eternal deliverance through the Messiah, saying: For a child is born to us, and a Son is given to us, and the government is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. In these words the prophet again describes both natures of Christ most clearly: the human, because he calls him a child; the divine, because he calls him a Son, that Son, I say, [illegible, ~12 letters] begotten from eternity and given to us. For that the prophet speaks of that only-begotten and eternal Son of God is shown not only by the absolute title Son, in an unusual manner of speaking, but also by the testimony of all the other attributes that are plainly divine and illustrious. For what, I ask, does his eternal kingdom, which he sustains upon his shoulders without end, signify? And what do the most august titles, Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, and so on, by which Jehovah the Father names this Son given to us, signify, I say, other than that something more excellent, and greater than all human power, wisdom, and might, must be regarded in this child?

units.la: Ad Ieremiam veniamus, qui cum multa de instauratione Ecclesiæ ad consolationem fidelium prædixisset, pastoresque, fideliter officium suum exsecuturos promisisset: tandem de unico illo pastore, æterni fœderis sequestro: Ecce, inquit, dies veniunt, dicit Iehova, quibus suscitabo Davidi germen justum, qui regnabit rex, & secundabitur, faciet judicium & justitiam in terra. Diebus ejus servabitur Iuda, & Israel habitabit secure, & hoc nomen quo vocabunt eum, Iehovah justitia nostra. Quo vaticinio Christum Messiam nostrum rursus Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν describi animad vertimus. Commendat enim nobis in eo propheta tam deitatis gloriam, quam humanæ naturæ veritatem. Homo est, quia Davidis germen: Deus est, quia Iehova justitia nostra, & Rex cœlestis ac spiritualis, qui nos externa Evangelii voce & interna Spiritus virtute regenerat atque gubernet, qui Ecclesiam adversus hostes quoscunque tueatur, beneficiis, dignitatibus & præmiis ornet: ad vitam & gloriam resuscitet æternam: hostes contra in pœnas æternas abjiciat. Fiduciam nostram fore in hoc germine testatur propheta. Atqui idem alibi clamat: Maledictus omnis qui fiducian collocat in homine: Benedictus vir qui confidit in Deo. Ipse Christus non semel promittit vitam æternam in ipsum credentibus. Si igitur benedicti, qui confidunt in germine: utique germen Deus est. Secus maledicti erunt, qui confidunt in germine, quod est CHRISTUS. Denique cum Iehova iustitiam nostram vocat. Atqui Iehova non est alius præter unum, nec alia iustitia aut salus est præter una, quæ à Deo donatur. Christus igitur cum ille Iehova, illa salus & iustitia nostra sit, consequens est, verum & unum cum patre Deum esse. Ego, dicit Iehova, Dominus Deus hoc nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Hic vero iterum audio obganientes Iudaeos, non hinc obtineri divinitatem Messiæ, quod dicatur Iehova iustitia nostra: cum eodem nomine & Hierosolyma civitas nuncupetur ab eodem propheta cap. 33.16. Sed quid verat nomen, Christo datum, ipsique soli competens quadam κοινωνίαν [?] transferri ad Ecclesiam, cum, quod capitis proprium est, etiam corpori commune fiat? Quid enim caput membris suis denegare posset? Notum est, Christo nihil esse suum, quia, dicit Apostolus, Factum est nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. Quod igitur supra de Messia proprie dictum fuit, hoc loco metonymice de Ecclesia dicitur, quatenus iustitiam & omnia Messiæ bona participat. Hoc inquam sensu à propheta dicitur nomen, quod Christo indiderat, fore etiam Hierosolymæ, id est, Ecclesiæ commune, quia Christus ibi regnat cum omni iustitia, & quia iustitia ejus ad singulos fideles sese diffundit, unde etiam Ecclesia ab Apostolo vocatur ipse Christus:
units.tr: Let us come to Jeremiah, who, after he had foretold much about the restoration of the Church for the consolation of the faithful, and had promised that the ministers would faithfully carry out their office, at last spoke of that one unique Shepherd, the mediator of the eternal covenant: Behold, the days come, says Jehovah, when I will raise up to David a righteous branch, who shall reign as king and prosper, and shall do judgment and justice in the land. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely, and this is the name by which they will call him: Jehovah our righteousness. In this prophecy we observe that Christ our Messiah is again described as Jesus Christ [Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν]. For the prophet commends to us in him both the glory of his deity and the truth of his human nature. He is man, because he is the branch of David; he is God, because he is Jehovah our righteousness, and the heavenly and spiritual King, who regenerates and governs us by the external voice of the Gospel and the inward power of the Spirit, who protects the Church against all enemies, adorns it with benefits, dignities and rewards, raises it to life and eternal glory, and on the contrary casts its enemies into eternal punishments. The prophet testifies that our trust will be in this branch. And indeed the same prophet elsewhere cries out: Cursed is everyone who places his trust in man; blessed is the man who trusts in God. Christ himself more than once promises eternal life to those who believe in him. If therefore they are blessed who trust in the branch, then certainly the branch is God. Otherwise those will be cursed who trust in the branch, which is CHRIST. Finally, since he calls him our righteousness, Jehovah, and since Jehovah is not another besides the one, nor is there another righteousness or salvation besides the one that is given by God, it follows that Christ, since he is that Jehovah, that salvation and righteousness of ours, is the true and one God together with the Father. I, says Jehovah, am the Lord God; my name, and I will not give my glory to another. Here, however, I hear again the Jews objecting that the divinity of the Messiah is not established by the fact that he is called Jehovah our righteousness, since the city of Jerusalem is named by the same prophet with the same name, in chapter 33, verse 16. But what forbids that a name given to Christ, and belonging to him alone, should be transferred by a certain communion to the Church, since what is proper to the head also becomes common to the body? For what could the head deny to its members? It is well known that nothing is Christ's own, because, says the Apostle, wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption have been made to us from God. Therefore what was said properly above of the Messiah is said here metonymically of the Church, insofar as it participates in the righteousness and all the good things of the Messiah. In this sense, I say, the name that the prophet had given to Christ is said to be also of Jerusalem, that is, shared by the Church, because Christ reigns there with all righteousness, and because his righteousness spreads to each of the faithful, whence also the Church is called by the Apostle Christ himself:

units.la: Porrò ad confirmandam divinam Christi maiestatem facit dulcissima & modis omnibus convenientissima illa harmonia Malachiæ, Zachariæ, Lucæ, Gabrielis Archangeli, uno ore attestatium, Ioannem Baptistam fuisse θεσβρομον Christi Domini nostri, qui sit ipse Iehova. Si enim ratum firmumque est axioma: In ore duorum aut trium testium stabit omne verbum: quanto magis hoc verissimum erit, ubi non duorum aut trium, sed plurium, non vulgarium hominum, sed prophetarum & angelorum testimonia tam concinnè sibi respondent, quasique conspirant. Huc referri debent ejusdem archangeli verba, ad virginem Mariam dicentis, Quod in te nascetur, vocabitur Filius Dei: Et mox: Hic erit magnus, & Filius altissimi vocabitur. Quibus evidenter testatur cœlestis præco, non modò virginis, sed & altissimi Filium, esse illum, cujus nativitatem prænunciabat. Nec Filium modo Altissimi, sed & Altissimum, h. e, Deum ipsum futurum Zacharias in Cantico suo aperte testatur, ita filium suum Baptistam compellans: Et tu puer propheta Altissimi vocaberis, cuius faciem præcedes, &c. Cujus vero faciem præcessit Baptista? Certe Christi. Christus igitur ita filius est altissimi, ut & ipse altissimus sit, Deus verus & æternus, verè magnus, adeoque cœlis ipsis superior. Hoc enim volunt sequentia verba: Invisit nos oriens ex alto, quasi dicat, æternus Dei filius, qui verus sol justitiæ & lux mundi adventu suo omnem hominem illuminat, de cœlo descendit, massa carnis nostræ assumta. Dixi de persona nascentis Christi.
units.tr: Moreover, to confirm the divine majesty of Christ, that most sweet and in every way most fitting harmony of Malachi, Zechariah, Luke, and the archangel Gabriel, who bear witness with one voice that John the Baptist was the forerunner [θεσβρομον] of our Lord Christ, who is himself Jehovah, is of great help. For if this axiom is valid and firm: "in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand," how much more true will it be where the testimonies are not of two or three, but of many, and not of ordinary men, but of prophets and angels, and they answer one another so harmoniously and, as it were, agree together. To this must be referred the words of the same archangel, spoken to the virgin Mary: "That which shall be born in you will be called the Son of God." And soon after: "He will be great and will be called the Son of the Highest." By these words the heavenly herald plainly testifies that the one whose birth he foretold is not only the Son of the virgin but also the Son of the Most High. Nor does Zechariah in his Canticle declare only that he will be the Son of the Most High, but also that he will be the Most High, that is, God himself, openly testifying this as he addresses his own son the Baptist: "And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High, for you shall go before his face," etc. Whose face, however, did the Baptist go before? Surely Christ's. Christ, therefore, is so the Son of the Most High that he is himself the Most High, true and eternal God, truly great, and so exalted even above the heavens. For this is what the following words mean: "The dayspring from on high has visited us," as if to say: the eternal Son of God, who is the true sun of righteousness and the light of the world, by his coming enlightens every man, descending from heaven, having taken on the mass of our flesh. I have spoken of the person of Christ at his birth.

units.la: De modo Nativitatis sequitur ut dicam: ubi dulcissimus omnium propheticorum de venturo Messiæ oraculorum & historiæ Evangelicæ concentus & παναρμονία[?] nobis observanda venit. Ea enim piis mentibus vel sola satisfacit, ut credant firmiterque statuant puerum, qui natus est nobis, Messiam & redemptorem esse, quem juxta promissiones nascitu-rum hominem, fideles olim crediderunt, quem carne sua indutum videre summo patres desiderio exoptarunt, de quo denique testati sunt omnes prophetæ, remissionem peccatorum accepturos esse per nomen ejus, quicunque in eum crediderint. Hic igitur Jesus, quem nasciturum ex virgine prædixit Jesaias, prædixerunt prophetæ, prædixit virgini Archangelus, nunciavit chorus angelorum pastoribus, Bethlehemæ, in urbe Davidis jam natum esse: Hic inquam, & non alius, est Messias ille promissus: est semen illud mulieris conterens caput serpentis: est Redemtor & Salvator mundi; quandoquidem in hoc solo, quicquid unquam de Messia in Ecclesia notum fuit, impletum esse constat. Sed operæ pretium fuerit, aliquanto clarius idipsum demonstrare, & nativitatis historiam à duobus Evangelistis recitatam cum manifestioribus prophetarum oraculis conferre.
units.tr: Next I must speak of the manner of the Nativity, where the most sweet concert of all the prophetic oracles concerning the coming Messiah and of the Gospel history, and a [panharmonia], must be observed by us. For this alone satisfies pious minds, so that they believe and firmly hold that the boy who is born to us is the Messiah and Redeemer, whom the faithful of old believed would be born according to the promises, whom the fathers longed with the greatest desire to see clothed in his flesh, and concerning whom finally all the prophets testified that those who believe in him will receive remission of sins through his name. This, then, is Jesus, whom Isaiah foretold would be born of a virgin, whom the prophets foretold, whom the archangel announced to the virgin, and whom the host of angels proclaimed to the shepherds as already born at Bethlehem, in the city of David. This one, I say, and no other, is the promised Messiah: he is that seed of the woman who crushes the head of the serpent; he is the Redeemer and Savior of the world; since it is certain that in him alone has been fulfilled whatever has ever been known in the Church about the Messiah. But it will be worth the effort to demonstrate this somewhat more clearly, and to compare the history of the birth, as recounted by the two Evangelists, with the plainer oracles of the prophets.

units.la: Ac primum familiam Messiæ quod[?] attinet, promiserat Deus Davidi: & juramento confirmaverat, fore ut ex semine ejus prodiret Christus Salvator mundi: Cum, inquit, exalti fuerint dies tui, dordormierisq, cum patribus tuis, suscitabo semen tuum post te, quod egredietur e visceribus tuis, & firmabo regnum tuum. Ego ero ei in patrem, & ille erit mihi in filium. Hinc prophetae Messiam quotiescunque de adventu ejus vaticinati sunt, Davidem, Davidis germen, furculum & florem cognominarunt. Hoc in puerulo nostro adimpletum esse quis non videt? Mittitur archangelus ad virginem Mariam ex regia Davidis prosapia oriundâ: conceptus miraculosus denunciatur, & expressè significatur, nasciturum ex ea semen illud benedictum Davidi & caeteris patribus promissum: Hic, inquit angelus, erit magnus & filius altissimi vocabitur, & dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris sui. Quod quid aliud est, quam in hoc Mariae filio, altissimi in quam & Davidis filio, impletum iri, quodcunque Deus olim de Messia pollicitus fuerat?
units.tr: And first, as far as the family of the Messiah is concerned, God had promised David, and confirmed it with an oath, that Christ, the Savior of the world, would come forth from his seed: "When," he says, "your days are fulfilled, and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your bowels, and I will establish your kingdom. I will be a Father to him, and he shall be a Son to me." Hence the prophets, whenever they prophesied of his coming, called him David, the shoot, the twig and the flower of David. Who does not see this fulfilled in our little child? The archangel is sent to the virgin Mary, who sprang from the royal line of David; a miraculous conception is announced, and it is plainly signified that the seed blessed to David and the other fathers will be born of her: "He," said the angel, "will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father." What else is this than that in this son of Mary, who is both the Son of the Most High and of David, will be fulfilled whatever God had once promised concerning the Messiah?

units.la: Tempus nascituri Messiae patriarcha Iacob praedixerat: qui cum moriturus ex Spiritus sancti suggestione filiis suis fausta precaretur, & de Ecclesiae successu vaticinaretur, dixit: Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, neque Legislator de pedibus ejus, donec veniat Siloh, & ad illum confluent gentes. Cui vaticinio quàm concinnè conveniant ea, quae ab Evangelista Luca narrantur, intelligunt omnes. Etenim tempore nativitatis Christi Domini nostri Augustus Caesar totum orbem ipsamque Iudaeam Romani Imperii provinciam descripsit. Iam si Caesaris Augusti mandatu totius orbis census actus fuit, & huic Iudaei etiam subjecti fuerunt: confectum jam arbitror, sublatum tunc fuisse sceptrum de Juda, cum subditi non nisi à suis Dominis censeantur. Jacet nunc in cineribus regnum Judaicum: & caruit sceptro ac Legislatore posteritas Jacobi non multò pauciori-bus annis adhuc, quam regia dignitate prius floruerat: id quod impleti vaticinii & exhibiti Messiæ testimonium est evidentissimum.
units.tr: The patriarch Jacob had foretold the time of the coming Messiah: when, dying, and under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, he was pronouncing blessings on his sons and prophesying the success of the Church, he said: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and to him the nations shall gather." How well the things related by the Evangelist Luke agree with this prophecy, everyone understands. For at the time of the birth of our Lord Christ, Augustus Caesar registered the whole world, and Judea itself, a province of the Roman Empire. Now if by the command of Augustus Caesar a census of the whole world was taken, and the Jews too were subject to it, I hold it already established that the scepter was then taken from Judah, since subjects are counted only by their own lords. The Jewish kingdom now lies in ashes, and the posterity of Jacob has lacked scepter and lawgiver for not many fewer years than it had flourished before with royal dignity; and this is most evident proof of the fulfilled prophecy and of the Messiah who has appeared.

units.la: Locum nativitati Messiæ præfinitum divinitus Micheas indigitavit his verbis: Et tu Bethle-hem Ephrata parvula es in millibus Juda, ex te egredietur mihi, qui sit dominator in Israel, & exitus eius a diebus æternitatis. Quæ quam pulchrè nativitati Domini nostri respondent? Josepho enim cum sponsa gravida Bethlehemum urbem tribus suæ primariam, tribulis sui Davidis patriam, census deponendi gratia proficiscere, nascitur illic puer promissus, egreditur de utero virginis dominator Israelis: eventu sane mirabili. Habet enim exemplum providentiæ divinæ admodum memorabile, omnes res humanas præter hominum opinionem ad finem præstitutum dirigentis, nec non impiorum opera ad exsequendum consiliũ suum utentis. Quis enim Augustum, edictum censorium promulgantem, suoque imperio singulos ad tribuum suarum mediomatrices urbes pertrahentem de Messia cogitasse existimet? Nihilominus Deus ejus consilia sic regit, moderatur, frenat, ut ad divinum decretum adimplendum, & ad promissionum veritatem illustrandam facere cogantur. Sic fere fieri monemur, ut ea, quæ Ecclesiæ Christianæ maximè obfutura, imò regnum Christi oppressura videbantur, ejus cõmodis atque salūti tandem serviant: & ut tyrān-norum conatibus plerunque promoveatur, excitetur & instauretur Ecclesia.
units.tr: Micah, divinely inspired, pointed out the place fixed for the birth of the Messiah in these words: "And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and whose goings forth are from of old, from everlasting." How beautifully do these words correspond to the birth of our Lord! For when Joseph, with his pregnant betrothed, set out for Bethlehem, the leading city of his tribe, the native town of his David, to register, there the promised child was born, and the ruler of Israel came forth from the virgin's womb: a truly wonderful outcome. For it offers a most memorable example of divine providence, which directs all human affairs to the end appointed, beyond human expectation, and uses the works of the impious to carry out its own counsel. For who would think that Augustus, issuing the decree of the census and compelling each man by his command to go to the cities of his tribe, had the Messiah in mind? Yet God so guides, governs and restrains his counsels that they are compelled to serve the fulfilment of the divine decree and the confirmation of the truth of the promises. We are thus taught that, in this way, the things which seemed most likely to harm the Christian Church, and even to overthrow the kingdom of Christ, at last serve his advantage and salvation; and that the Church is for the most part advanced, roused and restored by the attempts of tyrants.

units.la: Iam quod de conceptu dicit Iesaias: Ecce virgo concipiet & pariet filium: annon & hoc in miraculosa Christi conceptione & nativitate impletū videmus? Imò Evangelistæ apertè testantur, Mariam esse adolescentulam & illibatam illam virginem matrem Immanuelis, in quo divinitas sic se humanæ naturæ conjunxit, ut firma fide gloriari possimus, esse nobiscum Deum. Neque conceptionis modum insuetum ac miraculosum tacuerunt prophetæ. Iesaias enim partum virginis vocat signum, hoc est, miraculum a consue-to naturę ordine alienum. Alibi dicit, Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini: Et zelus Iehovæ faciet hoc. Hæc quàm bene ad conceptionem Christi Domini nostri quadrant? Nā Marię de verbis angeli hęsitāti, &, q est imbecillitas humana, fidei remoras objicieti, respondet angelus: S.S. superveniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit te. Idē postea Iosephum à Maria gravida clanculū divertere volente, in somniis ab instituto retrahēs, Ioseph, inquit, fili David, ne metuas tibi adiungere Mariam, nam quod in illa conceptū est, è S.ō profectum est [?]. Fuit igitur conceptio Domini nostri Iesu Christi vere miraculosa, quam altius ingenii nostri acumine scrutari velle, nefas fuerit. Neque verò hic fingendum est cum vetustis quibusdam hæreticis, carnem Christi Domini nostri ex substantia Spiritus S. decisione aliqua conceptam & natam esse.
units.tr: Now as to what Isaiah says of the conception: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son," do we not see this also fulfilled in the miraculous conception and birth of Christ? Indeed, the Evangelists plainly testify that Mary was the young and undefiled virgin mother of Immanuel, in whom the divinity so joined itself to human nature that we may boast with firm faith that God is with us. Nor did the prophets pass over the unusual and miraculous manner of the conception. For Isaiah calls the virgin's childbearing a sign, that is, a miracle, foreign to the usual order of nature. Elsewhere he says: "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, and the zeal of Jehovah will do this." How well do these words fit the conception of our Lord Christ? For when Mary hesitated at the words of the angel, and objected obstacles to faith, as human weakness does, the angel answered: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you." Likewise, when Joseph wished to put Mary away secretly because she was pregnant, the angel in a dream called him back from this purpose: "Joseph, son of David," he said, "do not fear to take Mary to you, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit." The conception of our Lord Jesus Christ was therefore truly miraculous, and it would be wrong to wish to probe it too deeply with the keenness of our intellect. Nor indeed must we imagine, with certain ancient heretics, that the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ was conceived and born from some severance of the substance of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Mundior hoc loco, ut Cypriani verbis utar, auditus requiritur, & purior sensus. Hunc enim quē dudum de patre natum ineffabiliter didicimus, nunc à Spiritu Sancto templum fabricatum intra secreta uteri virginalis intelligere debemus. Et sicut in Sancti Spiritus sanctificatione nulla sentienda est fragilitas: ita in partu virginis nulla est intelligenda nascentis corruptio. Non enim, sicut omnis homo est, ex virili erat & fœmina permixtione generatus, sed operante Spiritu Sancto immaculatum corpus susce-perat, quod non solum nulla vitia maculaverant, sed nec generationis aut conceptionis concretio iniuriosa fuscaverat, ut Ambrosius alicubi loquitur.
units.tr: "More pure hearing is required in this place," to use Cyprian's words, "and a purer sense. For we must understand that He whom we long ago learned was born of the Father, ineffably, is now built as a temple by the Holy Spirit within the secret recesses of the virginal womb. And just as no frailty is to be perceived in the sanctification by the Holy Spirit, so in the virgin's giving birth no corruption of the one being born is to be understood. For He was not generated, as every man is, from the mixing of male and female, but by the working of the Holy Spirit He had taken up an immaculate body, which not only no stains had defiled, but which the conjoining of conception and generation had not darkened with any harm," as Ambrose says somewhere.

units.la: Pauper & omnium rerum egenus describitur Messias à Zacharia dicente: Exulta filia Sion, laetare filia Ierusalem, ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus & Salvator, ipse pauper, ascendens super asinam & pullum eius. Et Isaias, Inglorius, inquit, erit inter viros aspectus eius, & forma eius inter filios hominum. Et alibi: Non est species eius neque decor: & vidimus eum, & non erat aspectus eius. Haec omnia Domino nostro probe competere, qui dubium esse possit? Ipse enim cum in forma Dei, in sinu patris, & Dominus omnium & Dei filius esset, forma servi assumpta, seipsum exinanivit, & sua se veluti maiestate atque gloria exuens, eius quam induit humanae naturae infirmitates & miserias experiri, abiectissimique hominis conditionem subire non dubitavit: cum esset dives, factus est pauper, quia Deus nasci dignatus est homo, virtutem potestatis suae humilians, ut hominibus divinitatis divitias acquireret. Quam primum ex utero materno egreditur, en summa cum excipit mendicitas. Nascitur non in regali palatio, non in conclavibus concameratis, sed in stabulo, non inter suae naturae consortes homines, sed inter jumenta, non aulaeis Vermiculatis insternitur, sed fasciis lineis involvitur, cunabula ei praebet vilissimum praesepe: mox etiam a tyranno Herode in exilium eiicitur. Neque toto humiliationis tempore meliorem fortem expertus est, atque conquestus, miserias suas, quamvis durissimam etiam bestiarum conditionem excedere. Vulpibus, inquit, sua sunt foveae, volucribus caeli, nidi: at filius hominis ne quidem habet, quo caput suum reclinet. Neque hoc satis erat, quin insuper contemtus accederet, ac mundi totius ludibrio mundi conditor haberetur. Pontifices, sacerdotes, scribæ, & pharisæi, populi Iudaici [illegible, ~5 letters] oracula de Messia susque deque habebant, Messiā quidem verbis crepabant, Christum ignorabant, præsentem alto supercilio despiciebant & persequebantur. Pauci admodum & quos fere memorat Scriptura, Maria, Ioseph, Zacharias, Elisabetha, pastores, Anna, &c. consolationem Israelis cum Simeone exspectabant verbum Dei reverenter amplectentes: ut vere de eo prædixerit propheta, despectum fore, contemtissimum virorum, virum dolorum & scientem infirmitatem, absconditum vultum eius atque despectum.
units.tr: The Messiah is described as poor and lacking all things by Zechariah, who says: "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your king comes to you, just and a Saviour, himself poor, riding on an ass and on its colt." And Isaiah says: "His appearance will be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men." And elsewhere: "He has no beauty or comeliness; and we saw him, and he had no appearance that we should desire him." Who could doubt that all these things fitly belong to our Lord? For though He was in the form of God, in the bosom of the Father, and Lord of all and Son of God, taking the form of a servant He emptied Himself, and, as it were, stripping off His majesty and glory, He did not hesitate to experience the infirmities and miseries of the human nature which He had put on, and to undergo the condition of the most abject man: though He was rich, He became poor, because God deigned to be born a man, humbling the power of His might, so that He might win for men the riches of His divinity. As soon as He comes forth from His mother's womb, there at once he meets with the utmost beggary. He is born not in a royal palace, not in vaulted chambers, but in a stable; not among men, companions of His nature, but among beasts of burden; He is laid not on embroidered hangings but wrapped in linen swaddling clothes; the vilest manger provides Him a cradle; soon afterwards he is driven into exile by the tyrant Herod. Nor during the whole time of His humiliation did He experience a better lot, complaining that His miseries exceeded even the most wretched condition of the beasts. "Foxes," He says, "have their dens, and birds of the air their nests; but the Son of Man has not even where to lay his head." Nor was this enough, but contempt was added on top, and the Creator of the world was held in mockery by the whole world. The high priests, priests, scribes and Pharisees, and the oracles about the Messiah among the Jewish people, they held in little regard; they indeed cried up the Messiah with their words, but they did not know Christ; they looked down on Him, present among them, with haughty disdain and persecuted Him. Very few, whom Scripture mentions, Mary, Joseph, Zechariah, Elizabeth, the shepherds, Anna, and so on, waited with Simeon for the consolation of Israel, reverently embracing the word of God; so truly did the prophet foretell of Him that He would be despised, most contemptible of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity, His face hidden and His person despised.

units.la: Sed quid tum? Talis cum esset, nequaquam caruit testimoniis divinis. De oraculorum [illegible, ~6 letters]-via dictum est. Adsunt in ipsa conceptione & nativitate cœlitus angelici testes. Gabriel divino-rum consiliorum internuncius testatur, esse eum Filium Dei, Messiam & Salvatorem populi sui: In ipsa nativitate pastoribus idem denunciat, natum ipsis esse salvatorem, Christū Dominū, hoc est, Messiam, Iehovam. Denique omnes angelorum exercitus una voce nascenti testimonium perhibent suavissime concinentes: Gloria Deo in ex-celsis, in terra pax, & hominibus beneplacitum. Huc accedunt miracula, conceptus ex Spiritu Sancto miraculosus, partus ex virgine insuetus, Spiritus propheticus in Zacharia; Portenta etiam externa, Romæ Ianiculum clausum: fons olei largissi-mus totum diem fluxit: Augustus se Dominum vocari vetuit: 30000[?] servorum manumisit: Augustus quaerens ex Pythia, quisnam post se esset regnaturus: audivit responsum:
units.tr: But what then? Although He was such, He was by no means lacking divine testimonies. The way of the oracles has been spoken of. In His very conception and birth there are angelic witnesses from heaven. Gabriel, the messenger of the divine counsels, testifies that He is the Son of God, the Messiah and Saviour of His people. At His very birth he proclaims the same to the shepherds, that a Saviour has been born to them, Christ the Lord, that is, the Messiah, Jehovah. Finally, all the hosts of angels with one voice bear witness to the newborn, singing most sweetly: "Glory to God in the highest, peace on earth, and good will toward men." Added to these are miracles: the conception by the Holy Spirit a miracle, the birth from a virgin unheard of, the prophetic Spirit in Zechariah; also external portents: at Rome the Janiculum was closed; a most abundant fountain of oil flowed through the whole day; Augustus forbade himself to be called Lord; he freed 30,000 slaves; Augustus, inquiring of the Pythia who would reign after him, heard this answer:

units.la: Me puer Hebræus superum Rex, linquere tecta Hac iubet, & Ditis caecas remeare sub umbras: Ergo silens aris tu nunc abscedito nostris:
units.tr: "A Hebrew boy, the King of the heights, bids me leave these dwellings and return to the blind shades of Dis. Therefore, silent, now depart from our altars."

units.la: Aram itaq; transtulit in capitolium, cum hac inscriptione:
units.tr: So he transferred the altar to the Capitol, with this inscription:

units.la: Ara hæc est primogeniti Dei. Orosius: Suidas.
units.tr: "This altar is of the firstborn God." Orosius; Suidas.

units.la: Quæ omnia argumento sunt, hunc puerum Iesum esse Messiam primis parentibus in paradi-so promissum.
units.tr: All these things are evidence that this boy Jesus is the Messiah promised to our first parents in paradise.

units.la: Quare agite opponamus hæc Iudæorum scan-dalo[?], sarcasmis & subsannationibus, quibus certam, manifestam & totius scripturæ divino con-sensu, testimoniis, miraculis confirmatissimam doctrinam de exhibito Messia calumniari magis quam refellere conantur. Erigamus nos vera fi-de, firmaque animi fiducia nobis persuadeamus, hunc puerum, cuius natales ex Bethlehemo patria Davidis anniversaria hodie celebramus memoria, esse Christum illum Dominum, qui nos unico corporis sui sacrificio servat ab omnibus peccatis nostris, sanctificat, tuetur, & contra potestatem diaboli mortisque æternæ defendit: qui denique pro nobis iam apud patrem in cœlis intercedit, omnique benedictione cœlesti ac spiritu-ali Ecclesiam suam perfundit.
units.tr: Therefore come, let us set these things against the scandal, sarcasms and mockeries of the Jews, by which they try to slander rather than refute the certain, manifest doctrine concerning the Messiah already exhibited, most firmly confirmed by the divine consent of all Scripture, by testimonies and by miracles.
