Let us raise ourselves up with true faith and firm confidence of mind, and persuade ourselves that this boy, whose birth from Bethlehem, the homeland of David, we celebrate today in an annual remembrance, is that Christ the Lord, who by the one sacrifice of His body saves us from all our sins, sanctifies us, protects us, and defends us against the power of the devil and eternal death; who finally already intercedes for us before the Father in heaven, and floods His Church with every heavenly and spiritual blessing.

units.la: Restat ut de fine nativitatis aliquid dicam. Dicam ergo breviter, cur æternus Dei patris filius, forma servi assumpta, in hunc mundum venerit. Hoc enim probè perspecto cognitoque, luce meridiana clarius apparebit, universam salutis no-stræ rationem hoc unico mysterio contineri. Constat autem vel ex Iesaiæ oraculo aliquoties reci-tato, cum non propter semetipsum, sed propter nos miseros peccatores hominem factum esse.
units.tr: It remains that I say something about the purpose of the nativity. I will say briefly why the eternal Son of God, taking the form of a servant, came into this world. For when this has been thoroughly grasped and understood, it will appear clearer than midday light that the whole plan of our salvation is contained in this one mystery. It is established, indeed, both from the oracle of Isaiah, recited several times, that He was made man not for His own sake, but for us wretched sinners.

units.la: Nobis enim, inquit propheta, filius datus est, non sibi, nobis est natus, non sibi: quo etiam spectantes angeli, vobis, inquiunt, pastoribus hodie natus est servator Christus Dominus.
units.tr: "For to us," says the prophet, "a son is given," not to himself; "to us he is born," not to himself: looking to which also the angels, saying, "To you, shepherds, today a Saviour, Christ the Lord, is born."

units.la: Quorsum vero nobis natus est puer? quorsum datus Filius? Audiamus Iesaiam, ex muneris, ꝓ[?] infanti nascituro assignat, ratione, causas nativitatis nobis suggeretē[?]. Iugū, inquit, oneris illius & virga humeri illius, sceptrum opprimentis illū (de Ecclesia loquitur) cōtrivisti, ut in die Midianitarum. Nomē infantis vocat Iehova patrē æternitatis, principē pacis, q[?] stabiliet regnum Davidis in perpetuū: qui sit iudicaturus in iustitia pauperes, qui portavit iniquitates nostras, & cuius livore sanati sumus. Sic angelus ad Mariam dicit; vocabis nomē eius Iesum, quia salvum faciet populum suum à peccatis: Ad pastores vero: Hodie natus est vobis Christus Dominus: Gloria in excelsis, pax in terra, hominibus beneplacitum. Non iam sanè obscurum esse potest, quorsū nobis puer sit natus: Filius nobis sit datus. Eramus omnes propter peccatum à Deo alienati, filii iræ, æternæ maledictioni obnoxii, ab omni spe salutis exclu-si, Satanæ exactori mancipati, peccati jugo op-pressi, horribili denique exitio destinati atq; im-pliciti. Sed nobis ille natus puer, nobis ille datus Immanuel virgam exactoris confregit, jugum oppressoris nostri contrivit, sicut in die Midian. Excussit enim à cervicibus nostris jugum gravis-simum legis, peccati, mortis & Satanæ divina sua potentia & merito, ita ut credentibus nihil am-plius ad condemnationem intentare valeant. Sic uti enim in die Midian victoria parta est clango-re tubarum, & collisione lagenarum, ut in histo-ria Iudicum habetur c. 7. ita contra vim mortis, legis, & peccati Christus victoriam obtinuit clangore cœlestis tubæ, quæ est prædicatio Evange-lii, & vasculorum sanctissimorum animæ & corporis sui cruenta collisione, factaque per mortem distractione.
units.tr: But for what purpose has a boy been born to us? For what purpose has the Son been given? Let us hear Isaiah, who assigns to the infant about to be born, by reason of his office, the causes of his nativity. "The yoke," he says, "of that burden and the rod of his shoulder, the staff of the one oppressing him, you have broken, as in the day of Midian." He calls the name of the infant: Jehovah, Father of eternity, Prince of peace, who will establish the kingdom of David forever; who will judge the poor in righteousness, who has borne our iniquities, and by whose bruises we have been healed. So the angel says to Mary: "You shall call his name Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins." And to the shepherds: "Today there is born to you Christ the Lord: glory in the highest, peace on earth, good will toward men." Surely it cannot now be obscure why the boy has been born to us, the Son given to us. We were all, on account of sin, alienated from God, sons of wrath, subject to eternal curse, excluded from every hope of salvation, enslaved to Satan the exactor, oppressed by the yoke of sin, and finally destined and entangled in dreadful destruction. But that boy was born to us, that Immanuel was given to us, and He broke the rod of the exactor, and crushed the yoke of our oppressor, as in the day of Midian. For by His divine power and merit He threw off from our necks the most grievous yoke of the law, of sin, of death and of Satan, so that they can no longer threaten condemnation to believers. For just as in the day of Midian the victory was won with the clangour of trumpets and the crashing of pitchers, as is related in the history of Judges, chapter 7, so against the power of death, of the law and of sin Christ obtained the victory with the clangour of the heavenly trumpet, which is the preaching of the Gospel, and by the bloody crashing of His most holy vessels of soul and body, and by the dismemberment effected through death.

units.la: Hic est ille pater æternitatis nobis à Deo patre in patrem datus, ut in eo & per eum iustificati, & adoptionem filiorum consecuti, sempiternæ vitæ cohæredes efficeremur.
units.tr: Here is that father of eternity, given to us by God the Father as a Father in him, so that in him and through him we might be justified, obtain the adoption of sons, and be made heirs of everlasting life.

units.la: Hic est ille princeps pacis, qui in pristinam nos gratiam, qua omnes per inobedictiam excideramus, apud patrem suū cœleste reposuit, nostrasq; cōscietias miseradis modis à peccato & morte divexatas, æterna tranquillitate & lætitia in Deo acquiescente pacavit. Hic est pax nostra, ex quo omnis paternitas in cœlo & in terra denominatur. Per hunc justificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum: Extra hunc frustra cum morte & inferis pacisc[?]untur impii, ut propheta loquitur.
units.tr: Here is that Prince of peace, who restored us in heaven to our former grace with his Father, the grace from which we had all fallen through disobedience, and who pacified our consciences, troubled in wretched ways by sin and death, so that they rest in God with eternal tranquillity and joy. Here is our peace, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth takes its name. Through him we are justified by faith and have peace with God. Apart from him the wicked make a covenant with death and hell in vain, as the prophet says.

units.la: Hic est ille rex & caput Ecclesiæ, qui regnum Davidis judicio & justitia stabilit in æternum; non sanè collapsa, & iam pridem in cineres reda-cta, ventisque dissipata externi regni Iudaici ru-dera instaurans (quod stulti Iudæi somniant) sed juxta promissiones Davidi factas spirituale regnum, hoc est, Ecclesiam ex universo genere humano, per vocem Evangelii & Spiritum Sancti colligens, regenerans, gubernans & conservans, atque hanc tandem à morte vindicatam, æternâ vita & gloria cœlesti exornans.
units.tr: Here is that King and Head of the Church, who establishes the kingdom of David with judgment and justice for ever; not restoring the ruins of an external Jewish kingdom, long since collapsed, reduced to ashes and scattered by the winds (which foolish Jews dream of), but, according to the promises made to David, a spiritual kingdom, that is, the Church, gathering, regenerating, governing and preserving it from the whole human race through the voice of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit, and finally adorning it, once freed from death, with eternal life and heavenly glory.

units.la: Hic est qui judicat pauperes in justitia: mise-riæ ac pravitatis suæ sensu oppressos, & in conspectu Dei deiectos, intercessione sua, & Spiritus Sancti virtute contra Satanam, peccatum & mundum defendens, consolationibus semper erigens, tandemque in æternam libertatem asserens.
units.tr: Here is he who judges the poor in righteousness: defending those oppressed by a sense of their misery and wickedness, and cast down in the sight of God, by his intercession and by the power of the Holy Spirit against Satan, sin and the world, always raising them up with consolations, and at last asserting them into everlasting liberty.

units.la: Hic est qui servat populum suum à peccatis tegens obedientia sua peccata nostra in Dei conspectu: & Spiritus sui virtute ad novam obedientiam nos regenerans, magisque ac magis, quic-quid in carne restat sordium, eluens atque expur-gans, donec in conspectum patris gloriosos, non habentes maculam aut rugam aut tale aliquid, sed sanctos & inculpatos (ut Apostolus loqui-tur) producat.
units.tr: Here is he who saves his people from their sins, covering our sins in the sight of God by his obedience; and by the power of his Spirit regenerating us to a new obedience, and more and more washing away and cleansing whatever filth remains in the flesh, until he presents us glorious before the face of the Father, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but holy and blameless (as the Apostle says).

units.la: Hic est verus ille Servator, omnibus numeris absolutissimam salutem & felicitatem nobis præstans, nosque ab omnibus malis protegens, ex cuius manibus oves ipsi à Patre traditas rapere nemo in æternum potest.
units.tr: Here is that true Saviour, bestowing upon us salvation and happiness most perfect in every respect, and protecting us from all evils, out of whose hands no one can snatch the sheep given to him by the Father for ever.

units.la: Hic est Christus nobis à patre ordinatus summus propheta, qui nos de Deo & voluntate eius erudiat, atque promissionem Evangelii de remissione peccatorum, & vitæ æternæ patefaciat: summus pontifex, qui seipsum pro nostris peccatis victimam offerat, suaque intercessione in æternum nos patri reconciliet: summus denique rex & caput Ecclesiæ, qui nos virtute Spiritus sui regat, defendat & conservet, in hac vita contra hostes tueatur, ornet beneficiis & præmiis, ac tandem resuscitatos, municipes regni cœlestis faciat.
units.tr: Here is Christ, appointed for us by the Father as the chief prophet, who teaches us about God and his will, and reveals the promise of the Gospel concerning the forgiveness of sins and eternal life; the chief priest, who offered himself as a victim for our sins, and by his intercession reconciles us to the Father for ever; and finally the chief King and Head of the Church, who rules, defends and preserves us by the power of his Spirit, protects us against enemies in this life, adorns us with benefits and rewards, and at last, raising us up, makes us citizens of the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Hic est qui verè gloriam Deo in excelsis asserit. Nam in quo unquam immensa Dei sapientia & potestas, justitia & bonitas, misericordia & veritas gloriosius sese extulit, quam in missione & nativitate Filii Dei?
units.tr: Here is he who truly ascribes glory to God in the highest. For in what has the immeasurable wisdom and power, justice and goodness, mercy and truth of God ever shown itself more gloriously than in the mission and birth of the Son of God?

units.la: Hic denique est, qui verè pacem terris, gratiam hominibus apud Deum restituit: ex Deo irato, propitium nobis reddidit, nos ex hostibus Dei infensissimis, filios Dei & hæredes cœlestis gloriæ fecit: quin etiam insuper Spiritus sui virtute hoc nobis præstitit, ut Deum nos amantem redamemus, ipsi soli toto corde fidamus, nos ipsi dedamus, voluntario animi obsequio totos subiiciamus.
units.tr: Here, finally, is he who truly restored peace on earth and grace among men before God: from an angry God he made him favourable to us, from enemies most hostile to God he made us sons of God and heirs of heavenly glory. Moreover, by the power of his Spirit he has further granted us this, that we love God in return for his love, trust in him alone with our whole heart, give ourselves up, and submit ourselves wholly in willing obedience of mind.

units.la: Sed quid (inquiet hic aliquis) necesse fuit, Filium Dei, ut hæc omnia nobis præstaret, hominem nasci, ut qui patri ὁμοούσιῳ[?] erat deitatis æter-nitate, nobis etiam consubstantialis fieret huma-nitatis veritate?
units.tr: But why (someone here will ask) was it necessary for the Son of God, in order to bring about all these things for us, to be born a man, so that he who was of one essence with the Father in the eternity of his deity might also become consubstantial with us in the truth of humanity?

units.la: Omnino inquam ita fieri oportuit. Cum e-nim ex ordine justitiæ cardo nostræ cum Deo re-conciliationis in eo versaretur, ut homo, qui sua inobedientia perierat, pœnas peccati luedo, Dei judicio satisfaceret, necesse erat, Messiam, purum quidem & à peccatoribus segregatum, sed verum hominem ex Adami posteris prodire, & in carne nostra satisfactionis pretium Dei judicio præsta-re, ut homo pro hominibus satisfaceret. De quo præclarè alicubi Ambrosius, Caro, inquit, Christi, damnavit peccatum, quod nascendo non sensit, quod moriendo crucifixit, ut in carne nostra esset justifica-tio per gratiam, ubi erat ante colluvio per culpam. Quod illi considerent, qui carnem Christi ubi-quitariam faciunt, & in Deitatem factitiam trans-formant. Si enim nostram carnem non assum-psisset Christus, profecto nec natus, nec mortuus, nec suscitatus, nec in cœlum susceptus vere esset: nec nos à peccatis nostris liberati vere essemus. Omnia enim illa per umbram aut fasci-num quoddam mendaciter egisset, atque adeò miseris nobis imposuisset. Quod quanto est absurdius, & à Christiana pietate alienius, tantò magis mirandum est, inveniri etiam hodie quosdam posse, qui Christo, corpus ab omni proprietate veri corporis abstractum affingunt, & præter φυ-σικὰ & ὑπερφυσικὰ ornamenta, quæ cum scriptu-ra omnes orthodoxi in eo agnoscunt, etiam im-mensas illas Deitatis proprietates, quas ne cogitatione quidem ab ipsa Dei essentia separare licet, carni non uniant modò, sed & realiter infundant, quasique exuvias deitatis induant, neque aliud, præter nudum hominis nomen in Immanuele nostro nobis relinquant. Scimus quæ nūc illi σοφὰ φάρμακα[?] huic vulneri admoveant, & quod loqui cum vetustate & nobiscum incipiant, ut novo dogmati antiquitatis reverentiâ, authoritatem concilient. Sed retractandæ illis priùs erant manifestissimæ plurimorū fidei Christianæ articulorum corruptelæ, ad quas pii omnes merito cohorrescunt: Deinde fatendum erat cum antiqua & orthodoxa Ecclesia, Christū carnem nostram ex virgine Maria veram, visibilem, contrectabilem, finitam, carni nostræ per omnia similem excepto peccato, assumisse, as-sumtam nunquam deposuisse: carne pro peccatis nostris verè mortuum esse: verè à mortuis revixisse, & pedem ex sepulchro posuisse: verè ex hoc mundo ascendisse in cœlum: verè in cœlis thronum dextræ Dei conscendisse, ut imperium cœli ac terræ gloriôsus administret: neque gloriam hanc capitis nostri naturæ veritatem ademisse, sed carni immortalitatem dedisse, ut Augustinus loquitur: denique cum carne nostra è cœlo rediturum esse ad iudicium: Hæc inquam fatendū est eis non uno modo vera altero falsa, sed simpli-citer & omni modo vera esse.
units.tr: I answer: it was indeed necessary that it should be so. For since the hinge of our reconciliation with God turned, in the order of justice, on this, that man, who had perished by his disobedience, should satisfy the judgment of God by paying the penalty of sin, it was necessary that the Messiah should come forth from the posterity of Adam, pure indeed and separated from sinners, but a true man, and in our flesh should render the price of satisfaction to the judgment of God, so that a man might make satisfaction for men. Ambrose says well of this somewhere: "The flesh of Christ, he says, condemned sin, which it did not feel in being born, which it crucified in dying, so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace, where before there had been defilement through guilt." Let those consider this who make the flesh of Christ ubiquitous and transform it into a made-up deity. For if Christ had not assumed our flesh, he would truly not have been born, nor died, nor been raised, nor taken up into heaven; and we would not truly have been freed from our sins. For he would have done all those things falsely, through a kind of shadow or phantom, and so would have deceived us wretched people. And as this is more absurd, and more alien to Christian piety, so much the more is it to be wondered at that there are found even today certain people who ascribe to Christ a body stripped of every property of a true body, and who, besides the physical and supernatural ornaments which all orthodox people acknowledge in him from Scripture, attribute to the flesh not only the immense properties of the deity, which cannot even be separated from the essence of God by thought, but actually pour them into it; and, as it were, clothe the flesh with the trappings of deity, leaving us nothing in our Immanuel but the bare name of man. We know what clever remedies they now apply to this wound, and how they begin to speak with antiquity, so that they may win authority for their new doctrine by the reverence due to antiquity. But first they ought to have retracted the most manifest corruptions of many articles of the Christian faith, against which all the pious rightly shudder. Then it had to be confessed with the ancient and orthodox Church that Christ assumed our flesh, true, visible, tangible, finite, in all things like our flesh except sin, from the Virgin Mary; that he never laid down the flesh once assumed; that in the flesh he truly died for our sins; truly rose again from the dead, and set foot outside the tomb; truly ascended from this world into heaven; truly mounted the throne at the right hand of God in the heavens, so that he might gloriously administer the rule of heaven and earth; and that he did not take away from the nature of our Head this glory and truth, but gave immortality to the flesh, as Augustine says; and finally that he will return from heaven with our flesh to judgment. These things, I say, must be confessed to be true for them not in one way and false in another, but simply and in every way true.

units.la: Porrò autem cum solus homo mortem superare non posset, apprimè necessarium erat, simul verum Deum esse, qui redemptor noster futurus esset, & carnem Deitati personaliter unitam habere, ut alterius imbecillitatem ad expianda pec-cata morti subiiceret: alterius virtute de morte victoriam nobis acquireret. Quis enim mor-tem absorbere poterat nisi vita? Quis peccatum vincere, nisi iustitia? Quis mundi & aeris pote-states profligare, nisi qui mundo & aere superior erat? Penes quem autem vita est, aut iustitia, aut coeli imperium & potestas, nisi penes solum Deū? Quare clementissimus Deus in persona unige-niti Filii redemtorem nostrum sese fecit, dum nos ab æterna pœna redimere voluit.
units.tr: Furthermore, since man alone could not overcome death, it was most necessary that he should at the same time be the true God who would be our Redeemer, and have a flesh personally united to deity, so that the weakness of the one might be subjected to death to atone for sins, and the power of the other might win for us the victory over death. For who could swallow up death except life? Who could conquer sin except righteousness? Who could overthrow the powers of the world and of the air, except one who was superior to the world and the air? In whom, moreover, is life, or righteousness, or the empire and power of heaven, except in God alone? Wherefore the most merciful God made himself our Redeemer in the person of his only-begotten Son, when he wished to redeem us from eternal punishment.

units.la: Hæc sunt, Auditores, quæ oratione qualicun-que in præsentia vestra de Christi servatoris no-stri natalibus, repetere libuit, in consolationem nostram & laudem æterni Filii Dei, qui mirando Trinitatis consilio propter salutem humani ge-neris secundum oracula, assumtam ex substantia virginis Mariæ humanam massam personali unione[?] sibi copulavit, ut esset verus Immanuel, Deus & homo verus, mediator, redemtor, iustificator & salvator, seque in extremas humanæ vitæ mise-rias demersit, non sui utique sed nostra causa. Fa-ctus enim est filius hominis, ut nos filios Dei, fratres & coheredes suos constitueret: iniustitiam nostram in se recepit, ut nos eius iustitiæ participes fieremus: infirmitatem nostram atque mise-riam omnem in se transtulit, ut nos summa per-sectione & beatitudine donaret: pauperrimus natus est, ut in nos divinitatis divitias effunderet: peregrinus factus est in mundo, ut nos cœlestis civitatis municipes redderet: denique in præsepi reclinatus est, ut animabus nostris æternæ vitæ pabupabulum exhiberet. Hinc de summa Dei patris φιλανθρωπίας certi sumus, qui nobis, cum essemus hostes, Filium suum unigenitum, & in eo omnia ad salutem consequendam necessaria plenè exhibere non est dedignatus. Non pudeat nos ergo communis ignominiæ participes fieri, nec dubitemus cum ipso crucem ferre, ut & gloriæ cœlestis olim participes facti, cum eo in omnem æternitatem regnemus. Interim dum huius miseræ vitæ usura nobis concedditur[?], ut pro exhibito Messia nos gratos Deo exhibeamus, cum sanctis angelis in excelsis gloriam divinæ sapientiæ, iustitiæ & misericordiæ perpetuo decantemus: pacem in terra cum Deo, cum angelis, cum fratribus, cum omnibus, quantum in nobis est sectemur[?] atque colamus: de Dei denique in hominibus benevolentia per Immanuelem hunc stabilita læti semper congratulemur. Tibi igitur omni potens, misericors, æterne Deus & Pater, cum Filio tuo unigenito Domino nostro Iesu Christo & Spiritu Sancto paracleto, gratias ex imis pectoribus agimus, quod adeo nos dilexeris, ut filium tuum unigenitum pro salute nostra hominem nasci, nostras infirmitates suscipere, in cruce victima fieri, dolores inferorum pro nobis sentire, nosque ipsi vera fide per Spiritum Sanctum insitos, de æterna vita & gloria per ipsum confidere voluerit: Quod etiam in his regionibus & inter nos colligere dignaris veram Ecclesiam, quæ te recte agnoscat colat & celebret: quod denique scholis & Ecclesiis nostris per omnipotentem illum Immanuelem nostrum, sedentem à dextris tuis, & dominantem in medio inimicorū suorum, invitis & stridentibus inferorum portis, statum mediocrem hactenus cocessisti. Oramus te etiam clementissime Deus, ut veritatis tuæ lu-cem nobis accensæ porrò conserves, technas ho-stium & falsorum fratrū impedias, blasphemias, quas Diabolus per organa sua ad te & Filium tuū contumelia afficiendum evomit potenter elidas: Annum hunc ineuntem nobis faustum & felicem, Ecclesiæ, Reipublicæ & scholis tranquillum ac salutarem largiaris, & clementer efficias, ut cū veteris anni exuviis, veterem quoque hominem deponamus, justitiæ vivamus, teque omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ, & post in omnem æternitatem celebremus.
units.tr: These things, hearers, I have wished to repeat in my present address, however slight, concerning the birth of Christ our Saviour, for our consolation and the praise of the eternal Son of God, who, by the wonderful counsel of the Trinity, for the salvation of the human race, according to the oracles, joined to himself in personal union the human mass taken from the substance of the Virgin Mary, so that he might be the true Immanuel, God and true man, mediator, redeemer, justifier and saviour; and he plunged himself into the extreme miseries of human life, not for his own sake but for ours. For he became the Son of Man so that he might make us sons of God, his brothers and co-heirs; he took our unrighteousness upon himself so that we might become partakers of his righteousness; he transferred our weakness and all our wretchedness into himself, so that he might bestow upon us the highest perfection and blessedness; he was born most poor, so that he might pour the riches of divinity upon us; he became a stranger in the world, so that he might make us citizens of the heavenly city; finally, he was laid in a manger, so that he might set before our souls food for eternal life. From this we are certain of the highest philanthropy of God the Father, who, when we were enemies, did not disdain to give us fully his only-begotten Son, and in him all things necessary for obtaining salvation. Let us not be ashamed, then, to share in the common disgrace, nor let us doubt to bear the cross with him, so that, having at some time become partakers of heavenly glory, we may reign with him for all eternity. Meanwhile, while the use of this wretched life is granted to us, so that we may show ourselves pleasing to God for the Messiah who has been shown to us, let us sing without ceasing with the holy angels in the highest the glory of divine wisdom, justice and mercy; let us pursue and cultivate peace on earth with God, with the angels, with our brothers, with all, as far as lies in us; and let us always rejoice and give thanks for the goodwill of God towards men, established through this Immanuel. To you therefore, almighty, merciful, eternal God and Father, together with your only-begotten Son our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit the Comforter, we give thanks from the depths of our hearts, that you have so loved us as to will that your only-begotten Son should be born a man for our salvation, take up our infirmities, become a victim on the cross, feel the pains of hell for us, and that he should wish us, implanted by the Holy Spirit in true faith, to trust through him in eternal life and glory. We thank you also that you deign to gather in these regions and among us a true Church, which may rightly acknowledge, worship and celebrate you; and finally that you have hitherto granted to our schools and churches a moderate state through that almighty Immanuel of ours, who sits at your right hand and rules in the midst of his enemies, the gates of hell being unwilling and gnashing. We pray you also, most merciful God, that you would preserve for us the light of your truth now kindled, that you would frustrate the snares of enemies and false brothers, and powerfully crush the blasphemies which the Devil vomits through his instruments to insult you and your Son; grant that this coming year may be prosperous and happy for us, and peaceful and salutary for the Church, the commonwealth and the schools; and mercifully grant that, with the remnants of the old year, we may also put off the old man, live in righteousness, and celebrate you all the days of our life, and afterwards for all eternity.

units.la: Deinde gratias, quas animis concipere possu-mus, maximas agimus Illustrissimo principi ac Domino, D. Iohanni Casimiro Com. Palatino Rheni, &c. Electoralis palatinatus Ad-ministratori, & Illustrissimi pupilli D. FRIDE-RICI IV. tutori dignissimo ac fidelissimo, Do-mino & Patrono nostro clementissimo, ꝑ libe-ralitate & munificentia sua amplissimam hanc scholam fovet, seque liberalium studiorum Mœ-cenatem clementissimum præstat liberalissimè: Ac Deum Opt. Max. precamur, ut Celsitudini ipsius consilia recta & eventus salutares, & diu-turnam gubernationē largiatur: Inprimis verò, ut summū illud prudentiæ ac fortitudinis in ani-mo illius robur ne sinat laguescere, ut ne patroci-niū, ꝙ[?] semel pro afflicta Ecclesia & periclitate ve-ritate suscepit, unquā deponat: Sed potius cōtra oēs potētiæ humanæ minarumq; & terrorū impetus constanter & sincerè pergat & perseveret.
units.tr: Next, we offer the greatest thanks that our minds can conceive to the most illustrious prince and lord, Lord John Casimir, Count Palatine of the Rhine, etc., administrator of the Electoral Palatinate, and most worthy and faithful guardian of the most illustrious ward, Lord Frederick IV, our lord and most gracious patron, who by his generosity and munificence cherishes this very ample school and generously shows himself its most gracious patron of the liberal studies.

units.la: Præterea gratias agimus Illustri ac Generoso Domino Comiti, Rectori inclytæ huius Academiæ Magnifico, quod sepositis multis gravieri-bus occupationibus pro eo, quo pietatis & liberalium artium studia, inprimis verò Sacrosanctam Theologiam complectitur amore, Illustri sua præsentia cœtum hunc ornare ac decorare non fuerit dedignatus.
units.tr: Moreover, we thank the illustrious and noble Lord Count, the magnificent rector of this renowned Academy, who, setting aside many weighty occupations, has not disdained to adorn and grace this assembly with his illustrious presence, because he embraces with love the studies of piety and the liberal arts, and above all sacred Theology.

units.la: Gratias denique agimus Reverendis & Clarissimis Dominis Doctoribus, præceptoribus nostris perpetua observatia honorandis, nec nō reliquis Dominis Professoribus, Magistris, studiosis adolescentibus, & aliis q; ad ornandū hunc nostrū congressum, & ad declarandam suam erga nos benevolentiam huc convenerunt: Quibus omnibus & singulis vicissim perpetuam gratitudinem, & in omni officiorum genere promtissimā paratissimamque voluntatem detulimus: Omnes insuper precamur, ut quemadmodum antea, ita denuo sua vota nobiscum coniungant, & æternum Dei Filium salvatorem nostrum, in cuius laudem & gloriam oratio hæc instituta fuit, toto cordis affectu sic nobiscum invocent:
units.tr: Finally, we thank the reverend and most distinguished Lords, the Doctors, to be honoured with perpetual respect as our teachers, as well as the other Lords Professors, Masters, young students, and others who have come here to adorn this our gathering and to show their goodwill toward us. To all of them, both singly and together, we in turn have offered perpetual gratitude and the most ready and willing readiness in every kind of duty. Furthermore, we all pray that, as before, so now again they will join their prayers with ours, and with their whole heart call upon the eternal Son of God, our Saviour, in whose praise and glory this oration has been undertaken, in this way with us:

units.la: Vnigenite Fili & verbū Dei, qui cum immortalis, assumsisti humanā naturā propter nostra salutem: Et ex sancta Dei genitrice homo factus pro nobis mori dignatus es: Christe Deus, qui morte mortem conculcasti, & simul cū patre & Spiritu Sancto glorificaris: Salva nos. Amen, Dixi.
units.tr: Only-begotten Son and Word of God, who, though immortal, didst assume human nature for our salvation, and, made man of the holy Mother of God, didst deign to die for us: Christ God, who by death didst trample down death, and art glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit: Save us. Amen, I have spoken.

units.la: ORATIO II. DE NATIVITATE DOMINI NOSTRI IESU CHRISTI.
units.tr: ORATIO II. ON THE NATIVITY OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.

units.la: Pridie Natalitiorum Anno 1586.
units.tr: The Day Before the Birthday Festival, Year 1586.

units.la: A
units.tr: A

units.la: M. Ioh. Philippo Roskopff in Acad. Heidelb. publicè recitata.
units.tr: Delivered publicly by M. Johann Philipp Roskopff in the Academy of Heidelberg.

units.la: Etsi consuetudine receptum est, auditores; ut ii, quibus hoc tempore dicendi provincia demandatur, vel de more repetendi salutarem de Nativitate Servatoris nostri doctrinam, vel de ipsa argumenti dignitate atq; praestantia, vel denique de propria persona nonnihil praefen-tur, quo auditorum benevolentiam sibi con-cilient: ego tamen hoc labore in augustissimo hoc doctissimorum virorum conventu supersedendum mihi esse existimo: Non quod veluti quidam Aristarchus consuetam pluribus-que communem dicendi consuetudinem impro-bare velim: sed quod illa ipsa, praesertim si pluribus exponatur verbis, non admodum necessaria hoc tempore mihi esse videatur. Etenim morem Scholae nostrae in recolendis hoc die Christi Domini nostri Natalibus positum alte repetere, vel à superstitionis opinione vindicare, quid quæso opus est? cùm non solum nulla cum superstitiosa observatione coniunctus sit, sed & omni superstitiosę observationis suspicione apud nos careat. Ad hæc ut rei dignitatem & præstãtiam vobis vel commendem vel amplificem, nulla prorsus necessitas me inducit: Quandoquidem eam per se vobis esse gratissimam, adeoque ad excitandum in vobis audiendi studium quàm efficacissimam minimè dubito. Quid enim ista tàm frequens congregatio, in cuius medio CHRISTUS est, sibi vult? quid exspectatis? quid exoptatis? nisi ut animi vestri, qui iam in meditationem nativitatis Christi Domini nostri iterum incumbunt, ex eius pleniore consideratione inflammentur, inque verâ eius cognitione, quam Satan varie corrumpere & obscurare omnibus temporibus conatus est, indies magis magisque crescant & corroborentur. Denique cur de me dicam non video, quoniam meam in dicendo tenuitatem & infantiam hæc ipsa oratio rebus quidem per se gravissima, sed ornatu verborum parum perpolita satis declarabit. Quapropter his omnibus omissis rem ipsam aggrediar, hac spe fretus, de Filio Dei ante mille quingentos & amplius annos in carne nostra manifestato orationem, etiam [?] pios omnes gratam & acceptam habituros esse. Ne vero in dicendo absq; certa lege & ordine vagemur, primùm λόγον Filium Dei patri ὁμοούσιον [?] καὶ συναΐδιον non mutatione naturæ suæ, sed assumtione naturæ humanæ in næ in personæ suæ unitatem ex Maria virgine, virtute Spiritus Sancti hominem factum esse demonstrabo. Deinde ad officiū & beneficia Christi θεανθρώπῳ[?] Redemtoris nostri me convertam.
units.tr: Although it has become customary, listeners, that those to whom the task of speaking is assigned at this season either repeat from long habit the wholesome teaching about the Nativity of our Saviour, or speak of the dignity and excellence of the subject itself, or finally say something about their own person so as to win the goodwill of the listeners, I think that I must forgo this labour in this most distinguished gathering of learned men. Not that I wish, like some Aristarchus, to condemn the customary and common manner of speaking practised by most people; but because those very things, especially if they are set out at length, seem to me to be not very necessary at this time. For what need is there, I ask you, to trace at length the custom of our school in observing the birthday of Christ our Lord on this day, or to defend it from the opinion of superstition? Since it is not only not joined with any superstitious observance, but is also free among us from any suspicion of superstitious practice. Moreover, I am under no necessity at all to recommend or enlarge upon the dignity and excellence of the matter for you; since I have no doubt that it is in itself most welcome to you, and so most effective in stirring up in you a desire to listen. For what does this so frequent gathering, in the midst of which Christ is, mean? What are you expecting? What are you desiring? Except that your minds, which now again apply themselves to meditation on the Nativity of Christ our Lord, may be kindled by a fuller consideration of him, and may daily grow and be strengthened in the true knowledge of him, which Satan has always tried in various ways to corrupt and obscure. Finally, I do not see why I should speak about myself, since this very speech will sufficiently show my slightness and inexperience in speaking, a speech weighty indeed in its subject matter, but not very polished in its verbal ornament. Therefore, setting all these things aside, I shall come to the matter itself, relying on the hope that a discourse about the Son of God, made manifest in our flesh more than fifteen hundred years ago, will be welcome and acceptable to all the pious. Lest we wander in speaking without a fixed rule and order, I shall first demonstrate that the Word, the Son of God, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, was made man, not by a change of his nature, but by the assumption of human nature into the unity of his person, from the Virgin Mary, by the power of the Holy Spirit. Then I shall turn to the office and benefits of Christ, our God-man Redeemer.

units.la: Quæ duo dum brevi sermone persequor, vos ut auribus & animis benevolis dicentem audiatis, oro. Principiò igitur licet tanta vis sit veritatis, ut contra omnem sophisticam facile se ipsam defendere queat: rursus tamen ea humanæ mentis pravitas est, ut eam falsis & effictis rationibus ob-scurare? & labefactare nunquam non audeat: Un-de Democritus eam tam variis procellarum flu-ctibus agitari dicebat, ut non raro in profundum submersa esse videatur. Et sane ad hoc ipsum co-probandum ut Ethnicos ex mortuis excitemus haud est necesse. Ad Ecclesiam respiciamus, & erunt nobis testes eius rei locupletissimi. Ut enim de aliis non dicam, quæ homines fanatici vel pror-sus tollere tanquam non existentia, vel maxima ex parte labefactare sunt ausi: de Filio Dei incarnato cogitate, quot quantæque hæreses? quot quantæque corruptelæ extiterint? Nonnulli qua[?] infinitum finiti capax fieri non posse statuerunt, secundam personam Trinitatis nullo modo incarnatam esse concludebant. Alii imbecillitatem & corruptionem humanæ naturæ perpendentes divina maiestate indignum iudicarunt, si quicquam de substantia Mariæ virginis peccati originalis lue & sordibus inquinata assumsisse diceretur, ideoque Filium Dei carnem coelitus detulisse somniarunt. Alii denique Christo corpus omnibus verae carnis proprietatibus & affectionibus destitutum, h.e, phantasma hominis assinxerunt. At hoc stolidum est rationis humanæ iudicium, cui sacra Scriptura passim reclamat. Nusquam enim illa nobis Christum proponit hominem imaginaria vel inani corporis specie prædi-tum, nec carnem ejus cœlitus delapsam docet: sed hominem verum ex Mariæ virginis substantia factum asseverat. Cur enim quasi eum ex Iudæorum progenie secundum carnem natum esse? cur filium Davidis? cur semen mulieris ipsum esse toties inculcat? Cur Christus ipse toties se hominem & filium hominis prædicat: Nisi ut se non in cœlo, aut in aëre creatum: sed in utero Mariæ virginis conceptum, indeque verè prognatum demonstret? Nam λόγον Filium Dei unigenitum carnem factum esse Iohannes Evangelista testatur. Eundem participasse car-nem & sanguinem nostrum habituque compertum ut hominem disertis verbis D. Paulus ostendit: Eum denique omnibus veri corporis partibus præditum, ac pedum beneficio de loco in locum progressum esse, reliqui Evangelistæ prodiderunt. Jam vero fieri carnem nostram, participare carnem & sanguinem nostrum, habere latera, manus & pedes, cui nisi humano corpore & natura prædito conveniunt? Quod si eam animi facultatem, quam θρεπτικὸν[?] seu vegetativum Philosophi vocant, quis spectet: hunc puerum in præsepi repositum, statim lacte materno, melle item, ut propheta inquit, & butyro nutritum fuisse in tota reliqua vita ad famem si-timq; restinguendam cibum potumq; adhibuisse,eundem denique incrementa aetatis & staturæ per gradus sumsisse ex Evangelica historia est no-tissimum. Si αἰσθητικῶ [?] seu sensitivam facultatem quis consideret, oculis vidit, auribus audivit, gustu gustavit, tangens leprosos tangiq; à Thoma cupiēs tactus sensu se minime carere ostendit. Si superiorem animæ facultatem λογικῶ [?] seu mentis δυνάμεως [?] & affectiones apud se expendere quis velit, Christum hac in parte cæteris hominibus non modo non inferiorem fuisse, sed & omnes longè superasse intelligit. Hunc enim perfecta illa & omnibus numeris absoluta scientia repro-bandi malum & eligendi bonum imbutum fuisse, sapientia profecisse, modò tristitia affectum esse, modò infremuisse spiritu, atque turbatum fuisse, modò spiritu exultasse ex Scriptura liquidò constat. Denique de θελήσει [?] seu voluntate humana in Christo si quis ambigat, Christum, qui ipsissima veritas est, loquentem audiat, Descendi, inquit, non ut voluntatem meam faciam, sed voluntatem eius, qui misit me. Vbi expresse inter divinam, quam cum patre communem ab æterno habuit, & inter humanam suam voluntatem distinguit. Quapropter cum in universa hominis substantia à Deo Opt. Max. fabricata nihil plane reperiri possit, quod non æque Christo tribuatur in Scriptura: cum verum perfectumq; hominem esse quis nō videt? Sed agedum concedamus paulùm hæreticis atq; faciamus ita, Christū non esse verum hominem, quid futurum est? nimirum gravissima illa infirmitatū moles, passio ac mors ejus pretiosissima in dubiū vocata prorsus abnegabitur: gabitur: Qua abnegata quid relinquetur? nempe veritatis, h. e, Christi ipsius destructio necessario est consecutura. Si n. Christus acerbissimas illas in anima pariter & corpore passiones neutiquam sustinuit, sed externa tantum larva hominum ocu-los delusit: non est, inquit Irenæus, veritas in eo, nec est ipse veritatis doctor, sed sophista aliquis, quorum proprium est, Φάντασμα μὴ εἶναι [?]: quod de Christo pronunciare, imo suspicari impium & blasphemum merito censetur. Quis n. ab omni pietate tam alie-nus est, ut mendacii arguat eum, qui est ipsissima veritas? de quo Pater cœlestis e cœlo clamat: Ipsum audite. Quis impostorem habebit, in cujus ore non est inventus dolus, non fraus, non fallacia depre-hensa qua nobis imponeret: Notę sunt [?] ipsius lacrymę, noti squalores, quib. cū nostri causa in hac miseriarū valle cōflictatus fuit: notę sanguinolen-tę de corpore ejus manantes guttę: nota vox ejus tristissima: Tristis est anima mea usq; ad morte. Nō igitur Christū ꝑ [?] vero corpore quasi corpus, pro vero sanguine quasi sanguine, ꝑ vera anima quasi animā prę se tulisse, sed carne sua infirmitates humanas vere passus esse, patiendoq; se verū hominē demonstrasse statuendum est. Ac licet post opus Redemptionis pactū in cœlū evectus infirmitates, qb. antea obnoxiꝰ fuerat, universas deposuerit, itaq; deposuit, ut natura hum. nō abolevert aut destruxerit. Hac n. statim post resurrectionē discipulis suis palpandā & contrectandā exhibuit dicē: Videte & palpate, Spiritus carnē & ossa nō habet. Hanc visibiliter in cœlū ascendentē conspexerūt Apost. Hāc in cœlo stātē à dextris Dei & sūma majest. & gloria refulgentem vidit Stephanus: hanc deniq; in extremo judicio homines universi pii & impii videbunt. Hæc Auditores pura est & syncera illa de humanitate Christi doctrina, quam tot seculis pii omnes crediderunt, martyres suo sanguine roboraverunt, hæretici magnis torrentibus oppu-gnarunt. Sed væ illis, qui tenebras lucem & lucem tenebras dicunt, qui ex Christo homine perfecto, visibili, finito, circumscripto, imperfectum, invisibilem, infinitum, incircumscriptum h. e, non hominem facere, & scripturis apertissimis furenter obstrepere non cessant. Atqui durum erit illis contra stimulum calces. Desinant ergo tandem isti [?] alios convitiis lacessere, & diligentius animo perpendant, quod cadè substantia animæ & corporis nequaq; sit simul finita & infinita, infirma & omnipotens: aliqua aliquando nescien, ordine cognoscens & cogitans, simulque omnisci[?]a, & uno actu omnia intuens atque intelligens. At inquiunt, nisi humanam naturam etiam proprietatibus æqualem divinæ faciamus abnegabitur Christi Deitas & Christus homo non erit Deus. Falsum hoc est. Homo enim Christus Deus est non quia humanitas est Deificata aut Deitati exæquata, sed quia est à Filio Dei vero Deo in unitatem personæ assumta: salvis atque distinctis naturis, & naturarū proprietatibus. Manente hac unione manet homo Deus verus, & Deus homo verus. Homo inquam Christus Deus est non secundum humanitatem, sed secundum Deitatem suam: sicut Christus Deus est homo non secundum Deitatem sed secunsecundum humanitatem suam. Sic loquitur Scriptura, dicens Christum Filium Dei etiam factum sive prognatum ex femine Davidis secundum carnem: declaratum Filium Dei potenter secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, &c. Rom.1.3. Divina tribuit homini Christo non secundum humanitatem sed secundum divinitatem, quod descendit de coelo: quod in coelo exstiterit cum loqueretur Nicodemo in terra, quod fuerit ante Abrahamum, &c. Vicissim humana tribuit Deo non secundum humanitatem: quod conceptus & natus, quod ambulaverit, esurierit, quod passus[?], mortuus, sepultus fuerit, quod resurrexerit, sursum ascenderit, &c. per loquendi modum quem Damascenus τρόπον ἀντιδόσεως[?], scholae communicationem idiomatum vocarunt, propter naturarum personale commercium. Quemadmodum igitur homine, quia Deus est, æternum, infinitum, creatorem & conservatorem rerum omnium, datorem Spiritus S. resuscitatorem mortuorum propter unitatem personæ nominamus: ita Deum, quia homo est, mori, resurgere, in coelum ascendere affirmamus. O admirabile commercium, Deus carnem nostram assumere dignatus est. O ter beatos nos, si fide illibata hoc mysterium tenuerimus, ut & Deum verum in carne manifestatum, & carnem veram in Deum assumtam confiteamur. Sed nunc ad alterum instituti membrum nostra se convertat oratio. Dixi de personæ nascentis subsistentia, q[?] duab. naturis divina & humana inseparabiliter unitis mirando mysterio subsistit. De ejusdem officio breviter etiam dicam, ut cur à Filio Dei assumta fit natura nostra seu cur facta, duarum naturarum unio, recte intelligatur. Hic quidem alii secundum humanitatem, alii secundum Deitatem solum Christum redemptorem nostrum esse contendunt: Sed enim tam hos quam illos à vera Mediatoris cognitione longissime aberrare manifestum est: quandoquidem nec divina tantum nec humana tantum sed utraque simul natura ad opus Redemtionis peragendum necessario requirebatur. Primum enim necesse erat, ut Mediator fieret victima pro peccatis nostris: Quomodo autem victima fieri absque sanguinis effusione, & sanguinis effusio, quomodo ab eo, qui verus homo non esset fieri poterat? Vt ergo pati & mori possit redemtor noster, verum hominem esse eum oportuit. Hinc particeps factus esse dicitur carnis & sanguinis, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, Diabolum: Deinde victima redemtoris pro nobis hominibus valere debuit.
units.tr: These two points I pursue in a short discourse, and I beg you to listen to me with kind ears and minds. First, then, although the force of truth is so great that it can easily defend itself against every sophistry, yet the perversity of the human mind is such that it never ceases to dare to obscure and undermine it with false and fabricated arguments. Hence Democritus said that it is tossed about by such varied waves of storms that it often seems to have been submerged in the depths. And indeed, to prove this, we need not raise the heathen from the dead. Let us look to the Church, and there will be most abundant witnesses of this thing. For, not to speak of others, which fanatical men have dared either to remove altogether as if they did not exist, or for the most part to undermine: think of the Son of God made flesh, how many and how great heresies and corruptions have arisen! Some, holding that the infinite cannot become capable of the finite, concluded that the second person of the Trinity was in no way incarnate. Others, weighing the weakness and corruption of human nature, judged it unworthy of the divine majesty if it were said that he had assumed anything from the substance of the Virgin Mary, who was defiled by the stain and filth of original sin; and so they dreamed that the Son of God had brought the flesh down from heaven. Finally, others fashioned for Christ a body stripped of all the true properties and affections of flesh, that is, a phantom of a man. But this is a foolish judgment of human reason, against which Holy Scripture cries out everywhere. For Scripture nowhere presents Christ to us as a man endowed with an imaginary or empty appearance of a body, nor does it teach that his flesh came down from heaven; rather it asserts that he was a true man made from the substance of the Virgin Mary. For why does it so often insist that he was born according to the flesh from the progeny of the Jews, as it were? Why the son of David? Why that he himself is the seed of the woman? Why does Christ himself so often proclaim himself a man and the Son of man? Unless to show that he was not created in heaven or in the air, but was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and thence truly born. For John the Evangelist testifies that the Word, the only-begotten Son of God, was made flesh; and that he partook of our flesh and blood, and was found in appearance as a man, St. Paul plainly shows in express words; and finally the other Evangelists have related that he was endowed with all the parts of a true body and by the help of his feet progressed from place to place. Now, to whom do the words 'made flesh,' 'partook of flesh and blood,' 'had sides, hands and feet' apply, if not to a body and nature endowed with a human body? And if one considers that faculty of the soul which the philosophers call the nutritive or vegetative, it is most well known from the Gospel history that this child, laid in a manger, was at once nourished with his mother's milk, also with honey and butter, as the prophet says, and throughout the rest of his life took food and drink to quench hunger and thirst, and finally took on increases of age and stature by degrees. If one considers the sensitive faculty, he saw with his eyes, heard with his ears, tasted with taste, touching lepers and desiring to be touched by Thomas, showed that he was in no way lacking in the sense of touch. If one wishes to weigh the higher faculty of the soul, that of the mind and its powers and affections, one understands that Christ in this respect was not only not inferior to other men, but far surpassed them all. For it is plainly clear from Scripture that he was imbued with that perfect knowledge, complete in every respect, of rejecting evil and choosing good; that he advanced in wisdom; that at times he was affected with sadness, at times he groaned in spirit and was troubled, and at times he exulted in spirit. Finally, if anyone doubts the human will in Christ, let him hear Christ, who is very truth, speaking: "I came down," he says, "not to do my own will," but "the will of him who sent me." Here he expressly distinguishes between the divine will, which he had from eternity in common with the Father, and his own human will. Wherefore, since in the whole substance of man, fashioned by God the Best and Greatest, nothing at all can be found which is not equally attributed to Christ in Scripture, who does not see that he is a true and perfect man? But come, let us concede a little to the heretics and suppose that Christ is not a true man: what will follow? Surely that heavy mass of infirmities, his most precious suffering and death, will be called into doubt and entirely denied. Once these are denied, what will remain? Certainly the destruction of truth, that is, of Christ himself, must necessarily follow. For if Christ did not truly undergo those most bitter sufferings in soul as well as in body, but only deluded men's eyes with an external mask, "there is no truth in him," says Irenaeus, "nor is he himself a teacher of truth, but some sophist, whose characteristic it is to be a phantom"; and to pronounce this of Christ, or even to suspect it, is rightly judged impious and blasphemous. For who is so alienated from all piety as to charge with lying him who is very truth, of whom the heavenly Father cries from heaven: "Hear him"? Who will hold him an impostor, in whose mouth no deceit, no fraud, no trickery was found, by which he might impose upon us? His tears are known, his sorrows are known, with which he struggled for our sake in this valley of miseries; known are the drops of blood flowing from his body; known is his most sorrowful voice: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." Therefore it must be affirmed that Christ did not present a true body merely as a body, nor a true blood merely as blood, nor a true soul merely as a soul, but that he truly suffered human infirmities in his flesh, and by suffering showed himself to be a true man. And although, after the work of redemption, having been taken up into heaven, he laid aside all the infirmities to which he had previously been subject, and so laid them aside, yet he did not abolish or destroy human nature. For immediately after the resurrection he showed this to his disciples to be handled and touched, saying: "See and touch; a spirit does not have flesh and bones." The Apostles beheld this as he ascended visibly into heaven. Stephen saw this standing in heaven at the right hand of God, shining with supreme majesty and glory; and finally all men, pious and impious, will see it at the last judgment. This, hearers, is the pure and sincere doctrine concerning the humanity of Christ, which all the pious have believed for so many centuries, which martyrs have confirmed with their blood, and which heretics have assailed with great torrents. But woe to those who call darkness light and light darkness, who, from Christ a perfect, visible, finite, circumscribed man, do not cease to make an imperfect, invisible, infinite, uncircumscribed one, that is, not a man, and furiously clamour against the most open Scriptures. Yet it will be hard for them to kick against the goad. Let them therefore at last cease to assail others with reproaches, and let them more carefully consider in their minds that the same substance of soul and body cannot at once be finite and infinite, weak and omnipotent, sometimes ignorant, knowing and thinking in order, and at the same time all-knowing, and beholding and understanding all things in one act. But they say that unless we make the human nature equal to the divine in its properties, the Deity of Christ will be denied and Christ as man will not be God. This is false. For Christ as man is God not because his humanity is deified or made equal to the Deity, but because it was assumed by the true God, the Son of God, into the unity of person, the natures and the properties of the natures remaining safe and distinct. While this union remains, the man is true God, and the God is true man. The man Christ, I say, is God not according to his humanity but according to his Deity; just as Christ is God, man, not according to his Deity but according to his humanity. So Scripture speaks, saying that Christ, the Son of God, was also made or born from the seed of David according to the flesh, and was declared the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, etc. Rom. 1.3. It ascribes divine things to Christ as man, not according to his humanity but according to his divinity: that he came down from heaven; that he was in heaven when he spoke to Nicodemus on earth; that he was before Abraham, etc. Conversely, it ascribes human things to God, not according to his divinity: that he was conceived and born, that he walked, hungered, suffered, died, was buried, rose again, ascended on high, etc. by the mode of speaking which Damascene calls the mode of exchange, and the schools call the communication of idioms, on account of the personal communion of the natures. Just as, therefore, because he is God we call the man eternal, infinite, the creator and preserver of all things, the giver of the Holy Spirit, and the raiser of the dead, on account of the unity of person; so, because he is man, we affirm that God died, rose again, and ascended into heaven. O wonderful communion! God deigned to take on our flesh. O thrice blessed are we, if with unshaken faith we hold this mystery, so as to confess both the true God manifested in the flesh and the true flesh assumed into God. But now let our discourse turn to the other member of our undertaking. I have spoken of the subsistence of the person who was born, which subsists by a wonderful mystery in the inseparable union of the two natures, divine and human. Of his office I will also speak briefly, so that it may rightly be understood why our nature was assumed by the Son of God, or why the union of the two natures was made. Here indeed some contend that Christ our Redeemer is so only according to his humanity, others only according to his Deity; but it is plain that both these and those wander very far from the true knowledge of the Mediator, since for carrying out the work of redemption not the divine nature alone nor the human alone, but both natures together, were necessarily required. For first it was necessary that the Mediator should become a victim for our sins. But how could he become a victim without the effusion of blood, and how could the effusion of blood be made by one who was not a true man? Therefore, that our Redeemer might be able to suffer and die, he had to be a true man. Hence he is said to have become a partaker of flesh and blood, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil. Then the victim of the Redeemer had to avail for us men.

units.la: Valere autem quomodo potuisset, nisi ex genere humano idem redemtor fuisset? Non enim justitia Dei pro hominibus satisfactionem acceptare poterat, nisi ab homine præstitam. Hinc ergo apostolus: qui inquit sanctificat & qui sanctificantur ex uno sunt omnes. Porro cùm Deus non nisi in infinito merito acquiescere velit & possit, quomodo victima & ἀντίτυπον[?] ejus, qui nihil nisi homo esset, sufficiens esse potuisset? Quo-modo modo gravissimû iræ divinæ onus ipse sustinere, & pœnam temporalem æternis peccatorum no-strorum pœnis æquipollentem persolvere qui-visset, nisi excellentiore quadam quàm sit ho-minis natura præditus fuisset. Quomodo dia-bolum, infernum, mortem vincere, gratiam ju-stitiam & vitam æternam reparare ac restituere nobis posset, qui verus Deus non esset? Non hæc, credite mihi, nudi hominis opera sunt, sed potentissimi ac sapientissimi Dei. Quid enim eo potentius, qui mortem omnibus creaturis invictam sua morte devicit, Satanæ potentiam virtute sua superavit? Quid eo gloriosius, qui perfractis ac spoliatis infero-rum portis, victor cœlos adiit? Quid eo sapientius, qui nobis arcanum Dei consilium & sanctam Evangelii doctrinam è sinu Patris cœ-litus revelavit? Vtique non fuit hic nudus ho-mo, sed λόγος ille Dei σαρκωθεὶς[?], qui ἀπ' ἀρχῆς[?] & ab æterno existens apud Patrem, tandem ho-mo factus Evangelii doctrinam consolationis plenissimam nobis patefecit, multis stupendis miraculis confirmavit, Sacramentis veluti cer-tissimis sigillis obsignavit. Quid illustrius eo, qui est lux mundi illuminans omnem homi-nem venientem in hunc mundum, regenerans electos per Spiritum sanctum, regeneratos nos donans vita æterna. Ego inquit do ovibus meis vitam æternam: regeneratos ad vi-tam æternam conservans?
units.tr: But how could he have been able to be of value, unless the same Redeemer had been of the human race? For the justice of God could not accept satisfaction for men unless it was rendered by a man. Hence the apostle says: "He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one" [Heb. 2.11]. Since God wills and is able to rest only in an infinite merit, how could a sacrifice and antitype of him who was nothing but a man have been sufficient? How could he have been willing to bear the most grievous burden of divine wrath himself, and to pay a temporal punishment equal to the eternal punishments of our sins, unless he had been endowed with a certain nature more excellent than the nature of man? How could he have been able to conquer the devil, hell and death, and to recover and restore grace, righteousness and eternal life to us, if he were not true God? Believe me, these are not the works of a mere man, but of the most powerful and most wise God. For what is more powerful than he who by his death conquered death, which is invincible to all creatures, and by his own strength overcame the power of Satan? What is more glorious than he who, having broken and despoiled the gates of the lower world, entered heaven as victor? What is wiser than he who revealed to us from the bosom of the Father, from heaven, the secret counsel of God and the holy doctrine of the Gospel? Surely this was not a bare man, but that Word of God who was made flesh, who, existing from the beginning and from eternity with the Father, at last became man and revealed to us the doctrine of the Gospel, most full of consolation, confirmed it by many wonderful miracles, and sealed it with the sacraments as with most certain seals. What is more illustrious than he who is the light of the world, enlightening every man coming into this world, regenerating the elect through the Holy Spirit, and giving us who are regenerated eternal life? "I," he says, "give to my sheep eternal life" [John 10.28]; preserving the regenerated unto eternal life.

units.la: Ego non relinquam vos orphanos: Ego feci: Ego feram: Ego gestabo ad extremam usque canitiem. O infinitam & inæstimabilem tuam misericordiam, qui miserrimam nostram vice commiseratus in carnem venisti. O adorandam tuam bonitatem, qui nos miseros homunculos immenso amore prosequeris. Quid non egisti? Quid non pertulisti nostri causa? ultro temeti-plum ex cœlesti domicilio in hoc nostrum exilium demisisti, ut nos paradiso exclusos cœli cives redderes: Nostram naturam assumisti, ut nos in tuæ divinitatis consortium asciscerec: Nostrum hunc limum induisti, ut nos immortalitatis gloria vestires: Nostra tecta forma nobiscum in hoc calamitoso mundo complures annos agere voluisti, ut nos in tui agnitionem adduceres: Nudus in hanc lucem, imo noctem prodiisti; nobiscum & pro nobis vagiisti, sitivisti, esurivisti, alsisti, æstuasti, laborasti, delassatus es, eguisti, vigilasti, jejunasti, miseriis ac malis nostris obnoxius esse voluisti, ut nos ab omnibus exemtos miseriis ac malis in tui, hoc est, summi boni communionem asseresces. O investigabilem tuam charitatem, qua nos immeritos, indignos, imo transfugas & hostes complexus es. Si mediocribus officiis homines ad hominem amandum accendimur, hunc conditorem, Salvatorem nostrum tam impense amantem, tam bene promeritum, non redamabimus? Atqui hanc solam ille gratiam a nobis reposcit, Hanc ipsam immensō nostro lucro compensat. Adamas sanguine mollescit hircino: Aquilæ, Leones, Pardi, Delphines, Dracones agnoscunt gnoscunt & referunt beneficium. Et ô duritiam cordis humani plusquam Adamantinam, si tanta charitate non mitescit: O ingratitudinem plusquam beluinam, si tantorum beneficiorum potest oblivisci. O singularem impudentiam dicam an potius dementiam, si sic restitutus, sic locupletatus, tanta obrutus beneficentia, ad tantas spes vocatus quicquam amare potest homo praeter illum unum, in quo & à quo sunt omnia, quique nobis se ipsum & omnia impertit. Nos igitur tantorum memores beneficiorum salutis nostrae reparatorem sanctè agnoscamus, omnem in illo fiduciam collocemus, synceram de ejus persona & officio doctrinam firmiter teneamus, constanter profiteamur, omnibus rebus fluxis mundi hujus anteponamus: propter quam ipse Judæorum furore in crucem actus est: quam in mundo voce & literis promulgarunt ac sanguine apostoli obsignarunt: apostolici viri ad nos usque transmiserunt: Testis est Theodoretus, ex scriptis Ignatii martyris Episcopi Antiocheni, qui fuit auditor Johannis hæc verba citans: Certissima verò fiducia credentes in Dominum nostrum, qui est ex genere Davidis secundum carnem: Filius Dei secundum Deitatem & potentiam, natus ex virgine, baptizatus à Johanne, ut impleretur omnis justitia ab ipso, qui verè sub Pontio Pilato & Herode Tetrarcha crucifixus est pro nobis. Testis est Justinus Martyr, qui annos circiter quadraginta, post mortem Johannis Apostoli, & centum post Christi ascensionem in cœlum floruerit: Quando visum fuit λόγῳ propriarum creaturarum reparationi[?] fieri, tunc è cœlo descendens discedens ad eos descendit, firmavitque templum fil[?] ipsi perfectum hominem, massam sumens humanae naturae, ex qua substantiam templi conformavit, quo indutus secundum arctissimam unionem filius Dei prodiit secundum utramque naturam. Ex illo enim est filius & Deus & homo, & quatenus quidem homo voluntariam mortem subiit, quatenus autem Deus dissolutum templum resuscitavit, & mortem ipsam prorsus abolet. Unus igitur est filius Dei & qui solutus fuit, & qui quod solutum erat, resuscitavit. Testis est Irenaeus Episcopus Lugdunensis, qui non suam tantùm sed omnium totius orbis Ecclesiarum sententiam, quam se à Polycarpo praeceptore, hanc ex ore Iohannis Apostoli accepisse dicit, his verbis recitat: Vnivit igitur sicut prius diximus hominem Deo. Nisi enim homo vicisset adversarium hominis, non recte fuisset victus inimicus. Rursus autem nisi Deus donasset nobis salutem, firmam eam non haberemus. Et nisi homo unitus esset Deo, non-potuisset particeps fieri corruptibilitatis. Oportebat enim Mediatorem Dei & hominum per suam cum-utraq; cognationem, ad amicitiam & concordiam utrosque adducere, & Deo quidem adjungere homines, hominibus autem patefacere Deum. Et alibi: Sicut enim erat homo ut tentaretur, sic & λόγος erat, ut glorificaretur: requiescente quidem λόγῳ cum-tentaretur, & crucifigeretur, & moreretur, humani-tati tamen unitus dum vivebat & sustinebat & benefaciebat & resurgebat & ascendebat. Testis est Irenaeo σωτῆρ[?] Clemens Alexandrinus in Paedagogo suo sic dicens de filio Dei: Noster autem Paedagogus sanctus Deus, totius generis humani dux, dux, λόγῳ ipse hominum amans Deus Paedago-gus, de quo dicit Spiritus sanctus in Cantico Moy-sis: Prospexit populo in deserto, in siti æstus[?], in siccita-te circumduxit eum, erudiit eum & custodivit tanquam pupillam oculi: Dominus solus duxit eos, & non erat Deus alienus cum eis.
units.tr: "I will not leave you orphans" [John 14.18]. "I have made, I will bear, I will carry, even to extreme old age" [Isa. 46.4]. O your infinite and inestimable mercy, who, moved with compassion for our most wretched state, came down into flesh! O your adorable goodness, who pursue us poor little men with immense love! What have you not done? What have you not suffered for our sake? Of your own accord you sent yourself down from your heavenly dwelling into this our exile, so that you might make us, shut out from paradise, citizens of heaven. You took on our nature, so that you might admit us to the fellowship of your divinity. You put on this our clay, so that you might clothe us with the glory of immortality. You were willing to live with us for many years in this calamitous world, in our own form, so that you might bring us to the knowledge of yourself. You came forth naked into this light, or rather darkness; with us and for us you wailed, you thirsted, you hungered, you were cold, you sweated, you labored, you were weary, you lacked, you kept watch, you fasted; you were willing to be subject to our miseries and evils, so that you might free us from all miseries and evils and assert us to the communion of yourself, that is, of the highest good. O unfathomable charity, by which you embraced us who were undeserving, unworthy, indeed deserters and enemies! If by ordinary services we are kindled to love a man, shall we not love in return this Creator and Savior of ours, who loves us so eagerly and has deserved so well? Yet he asks from us this one grace alone, and repays it with our immense gain. The adamant is softened by goat's blood; eagles, lions, leopards, dolphins and dragons recognize and return a kindness. And O hardness of the human heart, harder than adamant, if it is not softened by so great a charity! O ingratitude more than beastly, if it can forget so great benefits! O singular impudence, or rather, shall I say, madness, if, having been restored, enriched and overwhelmed with so great a beneficence, called to such great hopes, a man can love anything beyond that one in whom and from whom are all things, who gives us himself and all things. Let us therefore, mindful of such great benefits, rightly acknowledge the Restorer of our salvation, place all our trust in him, firmly hold fast the sincere doctrine concerning his person and office, constantly profess it, and set it before all the fleeting things of this world. For its sake he himself was driven to the cross by the fury of the Jews. It was proclaimed in the world by voice and writings, and sealed with blood by the apostles; apostolic men have handed it down to us even to this day. Theodoret is a witness, citing these words from the writings of Ignatius, martyr and bishop of Antioch, who was a hearer of John: "With most certain confidence we believe in our Lord, who is of the race of David according to the flesh, the Son of God according to the Godhead and power, born of the virgin, baptized by John, that all righteousness might be fulfilled by him, who truly was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate and Herod the Tetrarch." Justin Martyr is a witness, who flourished about forty years after the death of the apostle John, and a hundred after Christ's ascension into heaven: "When it seemed good to the Word to effect the restoration of his own creatures, then descending from heaven he came down to them, and he established in the womb a perfect man, taking the mass of human nature, from which he formed the substance of the temple, in which, clothed, the Son of God came forth, according to the closest union, in both natures. For from that one is both Son and God and man; and insofar as he is man he underwent voluntary death, and insofar as he is God he raised up the dissolved temple and utterly abolished death itself. Therefore there is one Son of God, who was dissolved and who raised up what had been dissolved." Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, is a witness, who recites not only his own opinion but that of the churches of the whole world, which he says he received from his teacher Polycarp, who had it from the mouth of the apostle John, in these words: "He united man to God, as we said before. For unless man had conquered the adversary of man, the enemy would not have been rightly defeated. Again, unless God had granted us salvation, we would not possess it firmly. And unless man had been united to God, he could not have become a partaker of incorruptibility. For it was necessary that the Mediator between God and men, through his own kinship with both, should bring both together into friendship and concord, and on the one hand join men to God, and on the other hand reveal God to men." And elsewhere: "For as he was man, that he might be tempted, so also he was Word, that he might be glorified; the Word resting while he was tempted and crucified and died, yet united to humanity while it lived, and suffered, and did good, and rose again, and ascended." Clement of Alexandria is a witness, who, in his Paedagogus, speaks thus of the Son of God, the Irenaeus-like savior: "Our Paedagogus, however, is the holy God, the leader of the whole human race, the Word himself, God the Paedagogus who loves men, of whom the Holy Spirit says in the Song of Moses: 'He watched over the people in the desert, in thirst and heat, in dryness he led him about, he instructed him and kept him as the pupil of his eye; the Lord alone led them, and there was no strange god with them.'"

units.la: Testes denique sunt alii Patres, qui ante Samosateni & Arrii furores, & ante oppositam illis Synodum Nicenam vixerunt: Sed cum temporis habenda sit ratio, hæc pauca breviter attingere visum fuit, tum ut nostram cum doctrina veteris Ecclesiæ consensionem testatam facerem, tum etiam ut de veritate doctrinæ huius magis confirmaremur adversus hostium filii Dei impudentiam, qui doctrinam de duabus naturis in Christo à Patribus Concilii Niceni primum inventam & publicatam esse calumniantur.
units.tr: Finally there are other Fathers who lived before the raging of Samosatenus and Arius, and before the Nicene Synod was set against them. But since account must be taken of time, it seemed right to touch briefly on these few points: partly so that I might show the agreement of our doctrine with the teaching of the ancient Church, and partly so that we might be more confirmed in the truth of this doctrine against the impudence of the enemies of the Son of God, who slander the doctrine of two natures in Christ as having first been devised and published by the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea.

units.la: Nos igitur de filio Dei Servatore nostro vero Deo veroque homine, & de parta nobis i-psius merito liberatione, à peccatis & morte, secundum oracula prophetarum & Apostolorum cum certa quadam [illegible, ~4 letters] φύσεως[?] sentientes, impias veterum & recentium hæreticorum opiniones detestemur[?], ac præcisa illarum prolixiore refutatione hoc potius agamus, ut immensum amorem Dei erga genus humanum, cujus redimendi causa filium unigenitum misit in carnem: & beneficia Filii Dei colligentes atque servantis in mundo Eccle-siam suo sanguine redemtam, nosque fratres &c. membra sua efficientis, ut inquam haec omnia considerantes, gaudio illo magno, solido, & aeter-no, quod pastoribus angeli annunciabat, in cor-dibus nostris perfundamur ac perfruamur : & celebremus gloriam Dei in altissimis: pacem in terra, benevolentiam in homines: celebremus inquam non sermone tantum, sed factis etiam & vita: sic instituentes consilia & actiones no-stras, ut ei, qui tanto nos precio nos sibi acquisivit, propriosque dicavit, non possessio ingrata, o-ciosa, infrugifera: sed ut luceat lux nostra coram hominib. ut glorificetur pater noster qui in cœ-lis est.
units.tr: Therefore we, who think about the Son of God, our Saviour, true God and true man, and about the deliverance from sin and death that he has won for us by his own merit, and who feel this in keeping with the oracles of the prophets and Apostles, [illegible, about four letters] φύσεως[?], should reject the impious opinions of the ancient and recent heretics. Setting aside a lengthy refutation of them, let us rather do this: consider the immeasurable love of God towards the human race, for whose redemption he sent his only-begotten Son into the flesh; and gather up the benefits of the Son of God, who preserves in the world the Church redeemed by his blood and makes us, too, brothers and members of his body. Considering all these things, I say, let us be filled and refreshed in our hearts with that great, solid and eternal joy which the angel announced to the shepherds, and let us celebrate the glory of God in the highest, peace on earth, and goodwill towards men. Let us celebrate, I say, not only with words but also with deeds and our way of life, arranging our plans and actions so that our possession, given to him who acquired us at so great a price and dedicated us as his own, is not ungrateful, idle or unfruitful; but so that our light may shine before men, that our Father who is in heaven may be glorified.

units.la: Tibi igitur omnipotens æterne Deus cum Fi-lio tuo unigenito, Domino nostro Jesu Christo, & Spiritu sancto paracleto, gratias agimus totis pectoribus, quod sic dilexisti nos, ut propter sa-lutem nostram voluerit Filium tuum hominem fieri, nostrasque infirmitates expertum, in cruce mori, & dolores inferorum sentire pro nobis: quodque Filius tuus coæternus λόγῳ[?] & sapien-tia tua, cum esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapi-nam, parem esse Deo, sed ipse se exinanivit, for-ma servi accepta, habitu compertus ut homo, fa-ctus obediens patri usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis pro nobis: cumque esset dives, fa-ctus est pauper propter nos, ut nos ipsius pauper-tate ditesceremus: ex hostibus tuis acerrimis filii tui charissimi fieremus: ex peccato, morte, miseria æterna, in justitiam, vitam & beatitudinem æternam restitueremur: Quodque is tuo suoque Spiritu sancto veram tui & sui agnitionem in no-bis accendit, & hactenus conservavit. Oramus te misericors & omnipotens Deus ut lucem ve-ritatis tuae puram & incorruptam deinceps in nobis & inter nos serves: exstingue blasphemias, quas Diabolus per organa sua ad te & Filium tuum contumelia afficiendum spargit: reprime ty-rannos & hostes saevientes in Ecclesiam tuam, eosque ferrea tua virga veluti figulinas testas confringe ne se adversum te & Filium tuum diutius efferant: Tuere inter nos sanctam in veritate tua concordiam & rege nos Spiritu tuo, ut con-stanti veritatis professione, & universa vita no-stra pro immensis beneficiis per Filium tuum in nos collatis, nos tibi gratos exhibeamus: Et sicut ille paupertatem, ignominiam & mortem propter salutem nostram ferre non detrectavit: sic nos in omni fortuna ejus sequi vestigia propter gloriam ejus nunquam recusemus: Excita nobis, & quos excitasti tuere, rege & fortuna Ec-clesiae tuae nutritios, pios Principes: & in primis illustrissimum atque fortissimum Principem Jo-HANNEM CASIMIRUM Tutorem & Administratorem, &c. nec non Illustrissimum Princi-pem FRIDERICUM Electoralis Palatinatus haeredem. Protege eos sub umbra alarum tuarum: Da ut ipsorum cura doctrinarum studia hic floreant, ipsorumque administratione Res-publica salva & incolumis perfistat: da etiam doctores fideles, qui sciant, ὀρθοτομεῖν[?] recte secare verbum tuum: Averte ab Ecclesia tua omnia præpræsentia & imminentia, hæresium, bellorum, famis, pestilentiæ, & alia pericula, ut colligi & foveri cœtus docentium & discentium, ac propagari doctrinarum studia possint: serva inter nos & in hac dilectissima patria nostra Ecclesiam te rectè agnoscentem & invocatem, & fac nos omnes vasa misericordiæ tuæ, salutaria nobis & aliis, ut te cum Filio tuo & Spiritu sancto in æternum celebremus.
units.tr: To you therefore, almighty eternal God, with your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, we give thanks with our whole hearts, that you so loved us that for our salvation you willed your Son to become man, to experience our weaknesses, to die on the cross, and to suffer the pains of hell for us; and that your Son, co-eternal with the [illegible, λόγῳ?] and your wisdom, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being found in human appearance, made obedient to the Father even unto death, the death of the cross, for us; and though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might be made rich; that from your most bitter enemies we might become the dearest of your dearest Son; that from sin, death and eternal misery we might be restored to righteousness, life and eternal blessedness; and that he, by your Holy Spirit and his own, has kindled in us a true knowledge of you and of himself, and has preserved it until now. We pray you, merciful and almighty God, that you would keep the light of your truth pure and uncorrupted in us and among us from now on; quench the blasphemies which the Devil spreads through his instruments to insult you and your Son; restrain the tyrants and enemies who rage against your Church, and break them with your iron rod like potters' earthen vessels, so that they may no longer exalt themselves against you and your Son. Preserve among us, in your truth, holy concord, and rule us by your Spirit, so that by a steadfast profession of the truth and by our whole life we may show ourselves grateful to you for the immense benefits bestowed upon us through your Son. And just as he did not shrink from bearing poverty, disgrace and death for our salvation, so may we never refuse, in every fortune, to follow his footsteps for his glory. Raise up for us, and protect those whom you have raised up, rule and nourish, in the fortunes of your Church, the pious princes as nursing fathers: and especially the most illustrious and most valiant Prince, JOHN CASIMIR, guardian and administrator, etc., and likewise the most illustrious Prince FREDERICK, heir of the Electoral Palatinate. Protect them under the shadow of your wings.
