Grant that, through their care, the study of the doctrines may flourish here, and that through their administration the commonwealth may remain safe and unharmed; grant also faithful teachers, who know [ὀρθοτομεῖν?] to rightly divide [recte secare] your word. Turn away from your Church all present and impending dangers: of heresies, wars, famine, pestilence and other perils, so that the assemblies of teachers and learners may be gathered and cherished, and the study of the doctrines may be propagated. Preserve among us, and in this most beloved fatherland of ours, a Church that rightly acknowledges and invokes you, and make us all vessels of your mercy, salutary to ourselves and to others, so that we may celebrate you with your Son and the Holy Spirit for ever.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: ORATIO III. CONCIO NATALIS EX Jesa. 9. habita
units.tr: ORATIO III. CONCIO NATALIS, delivered on Isaiah 9.

units.la: A BENIAMINE KOBERO Anno 1592
units.tr: BY BENJAMIN KOBER, in the year 1592

units.la: DIES hos festos, Auditores, in lætitia agita-re debebamus: quando universa Ecclesia memoriam nati ex virgine Servatoris, singulari religione celebrat, quod gaudium Angeli maximum ducebant humano generi. Sed ea est, (proh Deum Immortalem) temporum horum tristitia, à qua haud scio an revocare animos possit illius nuncii, quamvis optatissimi, recordatio. Quid e-nim dicam de cruentis & acerbissimis bellis, quæ contra pios in Belgio, in Galliis, in Pannonia & in conspectu Palatinatus nostri geruntur? quid de sectis detestabilibus, quæ per calumniam religio-nis, naturalem hominum conjunctionem diri-munt? Accedit quòd qui has pestilentissimas pe-stes vel armis vel voce avertere debebant, & pro sua fortitudine ac doctrinâ, Deo benè juvante poterant, illi diem suum obierunt; eorum verò vices, qui obire & tueri queât, vix aliq inveniûr. Sed enim magna populi improbitas & incredibi-lis superstitionum obstinatio tam luculentis plagis vindicatur a Deo, atque ut deinceps vindicetur, utinam non sit metuendum! nihil enim ad probitatem isthæc vindicta adhuc profecit. De quo cogitanti mihi veniunt in mentem Iesaiæ tempora, quæ sunt tanquam exemplar aliquod nostrorum. Nam etiamsi decem tribus, quod commentitios Deos coluissent, in exilium projicerentur à Iehova, libertate & patria & fortunis amissis: neutiquam tamen Iudæi vicinorum exemplo à protervitate sua deterrebantur. Conciones habebat Iesaias plenas minationum gravissimarum, ut pervicaces animos ad pœnitudinem contorqueret. Sed nullius erant apud illos ponderis: &, quod ad contumaciam addi poterat, beneficia Dei maleficiis suis vincere contendebant. Creabat ipsis reges, Vziam & Iothamum, summa tum pietate in retinenda religione, tum felicitate in tuendo regno, præditos: ut respublica majestate & potentia præter modum cresceret. At illi, in impietate obfirmati, quo tantorum beneficiorum, ipsiusque adeo veri Dei memoria delectetur, pro libidine improbi Achazi gentilicios & falsos Deos, introducere, his fana excitare, sacra facere, postremo omnia divina humana-que jura pervertere. Idem post mortem piorum regum Hizkiæ & Iosiæ factitatum. Inde consequuta tempestas turbulentissima, bellum horribile, vastatio patriæ miserabilis, servitus durissima, denique exsilium calamitosissimum, quibus malis pœnas impietatis dependerunt. Similiter nunc hunc severè ulcisciturs Deus cùm cætera peccata, tum vel maxime avitam superstitionem & veritatis renascentis, quàm in vulgus promulgat, cõ-temtionem. Tamen nihilo sanctior hominum vita est; imò vitiosior: ut dubium non sit, quin maiora mala impendeant, nisi iam nunc incide-runt, quando Germaniam nostram charissimâ truculentissimorum hostium multitudine cir-cumplicatam atque irretitam propè videmus.
units.tr: Today's festivals, listeners, ought to be kept in joy, since the whole Church with particular devotion celebrates the memory of the Saviour's birth from the Virgin, which the Angels regarded as the greatest joy for the human race. But such is (good God!) the sadness of these times that I do not know whether even the recollection of that most welcome message can lift our minds. For what shall I say of the bloody and most bitter wars waged against the godly in the Netherlands, in France, in Pannonia, and before the eyes of our Palatinate? What of the detestable sects which, under the pretext of religion, tear apart the natural bond of human fellowship? Add to this that those who ought to have averted these most pestilential plagues, whether by arms or by voice, and who, by their courage and learning, could have done so with God's good help, have departed this life; and of those who could take up their duties and defend them, scarcely any can be found. But the great wickedness of the people and the incredible obstinacy in superstitions are punished by God with such striking blows; and I pray that there is no cause to fear they will be punished further in the future! For this punishment has so far achieved nothing toward uprightness. As I think on this, the times of Isaiah come to mind, which are like a certain model of our own. For even though the ten tribes, because they worshipped fictitious gods, were cast into exile by Jehovah, with liberty, fatherland and fortunes lost, the Jews were by no means deterred from their wilfulness by the example of their neighbours. Isaiah preached sermons full of the gravest threats, to turn stubborn minds to repentance. But they carried no weight with them; and, adding to their obstinacy, they strove to overcome God's benefits by their own wrongdoings. God set over them kings, Uzziah and Jotham, endowed with the highest piety in maintaining true religion and with good fortune in protecting the realm, so that the commonwealth grew beyond measure in majesty and power. But they, hardened in impiety, so that they might take pleasure in forgetting such great benefits and even the memory of the true God himself, at the wicked Ahaz's whim introduced heathen and false gods, raised shrines to them, offered sacrifices, and at last overturned all divine and human law. The same was done after the death of the pious kings Hezekiah and Josiah. From this followed a most turbulent storm, a dreadful war, the miserable devastation of the fatherland, the harshest slavery, and finally the most calamitous exile, by which evils they paid the penalty for their impiety. In like manner God now severely punishes us, both for our other sins and above all for our ancestral superstition and our contempt for the newly reborn truth, which he proclaims abroad. Yet the lives of men are no holier; rather they are more sinful, so that there is no doubt that greater evils are impending, if they have not already fallen, since we see our Germany almost encircled and entangled by the dear and most savage multitude of enemies.

units.la: In his tantis Eccle-siæ malis, quis adeò ferreus, qui non de mœsto ducat suspiria corde? quis nisi vulnera propria non sentiens vel non curans læ-tari possit? Quærenda igitur aliunde, atque adhi-benda est consolatio, quà à tristissima præsentium atque instantium malorum cogitatione ad san-ctam ac salutarem lætitiam traducamur. Cæ-terum cùm Iesaias in simili positam fortuna Eccle-siam consolatione sustentarit, ad nostrum insti-tutum accommodata:non est cur longius eamus.
units.tr: In such great evils of the Church, who is so iron-hearted as not to draw sighs from a sorrowing heart? Who, not feeling or not caring for his own wounds, could rejoice? We must therefore seek comfort elsewhere and apply it, by which we may be led away from the most sad thought of present and impending evils to holy and saving joy. Since Isaiah sustained the Church, placed in a similar fortune, with consolation, let us adapt it to our purpose: there is no reason to go further.

units.la: Insistamus prophetæ vestigiis, atque ad nos trans-lato illius argumento de Emmanuele nascituro, discamus, quod primum erit nostræ orationis ar-gumentum, ut ruat, fremat, insaniat mundus, tu-multuentur ac furant Tyranni, stridant & crepi-tent omnes inferorum portæ: haud tamen oppor-tere pios homines tantopere commoveri, ut vel publicis Ecclesiæ miseriis, vel privatis suis ani-mos despondeant: quippe qui sciunt sibi natum esse Christum, Servatorem illum, cuius potentiâ inde ab initio stetit & servata est semper Ecclesia.
units.tr: Let us follow the footsteps of the prophet, and, transferring to ourselves the subject of his prophecy about Emmanuel who is to be born, let us learn what will be the first theme of our address: let the world rage, roar and go mad, let tyrants riot and rage, let all the gates of hell grind and crackle; yet godly people ought not to be so greatly moved as to lose heart over the public miseries of the Church or over their own private troubles. For they know that Christ, that Saviour by whose power the Church has stood and been preserved from the beginning, has been born for them.

units.la: Operæpretium verò fuerit toto illo oraculo paulò altius repetito hæc comprobare. Iesaias ergo trepidationem Iudæorum nō mi-tigavit, promissâ peccatorum impunitate, quæ fere origo est contumaciæ & interitus, sed salutari pœnæ temperatione. Non, inquit, erit ei obscu-ratio secundum angustiam priorem ab eo, qui allevi-are fecit terram Zebulon, &c. Confirmavit nimirum hoc ex voluntate Dei, tolerabilore Iudæos fore conditione, quàm Israëlitas, qui à Tiglat-Pi-lassare, & post à Salmanassare captivi in Assyriam abducti fuerant, Pekâ & Hoseâ regibus: quæ promissio plurimum contra desperationem Iudæorum valebat, si in illorum intuerentur miseriam. Verum enimvero in exilio, dixisset aliquis Iudæus, oraculorum ignarus: graviores nos, quam Israëlitæ, pœnas dedimus: quando apud nos Templum sanctitatis Dei, quod portus & aura fuit miserorum, evertetur, & una delebitur regnum Davidis, cuius ex posteris Rex ille Opt. Max.serva-tor noster nasci debuit. Tam tragica Israëlitæ nō sunt passi, qui nec Templum perdiderunt, quod non habuerant, nec spe tanta exciderunt promissionum quas nō acceperant, licet cum regno libertatem amiserint. Ita equidem se res habebat: nō tamen idcirco melior Israëlitarum, quàm Iudæorum fortuna fuit, his enim Deus exsulibus & stirpis propagationem in ipsa captivitate, & post annorum 70 decursum, in patriam reditum, nec non Templi, cultus urbis ac politiæ instaurationem promisit ac præstitit; Decem-vero Tribus semel eversas, perpetuo exsilio multavit. Sic & hodie miserrima desperatissimaque videtur esse Ecclesiæ fortuna: hostium contrà si non o-ptima: ptima; at tolerabilior: nempe quòd eventus non prævidetur, & beatitudinem plerique non divitiis promissis, sed humanis oculis metiuntur. Verum enim si recta ratio valeat: nullo modo est Ecclesiæ sors, cum extremo reprobæ multitudinis fato comparanda. Nam quemadmodum Ecclesia olim Iudaica, castigata quidem exsilio Babylonio, & aliquandiu in tenebris ac terra umbrosa mortis, uti loquitur Iesaias, quasi sepulta jacuit, sed mox in patriam tanquam ad respiciendam lucem, reducta est, magnaque perfusa lætitia ex insperato liberationis beneficio: ita nunc Ecclesia Christiana quamvis jaceat densis circumfusa tenebris calamitatum corporalium & spiritualium, peccati & mortis; accepit tamen à DEO IESUM, suam lucem, suum desiderium, suam salutem, ut neque in miseriis misera sit, neque in morte mortua. Idcirco lucem hanc magnam dixit Propheta, Populus, inquiens, in tenebris vidit lucem magnam: quòd hac una consolatione sustentare se possunt in ærumnis pii: sine hac nulla uspiam desperationi medicina reperitur. Sed quomodo magnitudinem lucis huius extollat Propheta, audiamus. Multiplicasti gentem, non magnificasti lætitiam. Lætati sunt enim coram te iuxta lætitiam quæ est in messe, & quemadmodum exultant milites, cum dividunt spolia. Confert propheta lucem, hoc est lætitiam piorum & impiorum. Hæc sola etiam sine aliis ad animi tranquillitatem sufficit. Quid est igitur quòd homo sanctus, si illa luce perfusus, propter turbidas mundi præsentis tempestates, animo consternetur? aut hostes huic luci ex fucosa prosperitate, felices judicet? Magna fuit Decem-tribuum multitudo & flores respublica. Sed cum se a vera religione abdicassent, & Judeis, Dei cultoribus infelicitæ essent[?]: miseras judicavit Propheta: quòd lætitia & beata tranquillitate animi carerent. Sic nimirum impii pollent quidem honoribus, opulentia, multitudine & fortunâ: verum (ô misera vita) abest optata animi securitas: adsunt interni carnifices conscientiæ stimuli, quibus tacitè perpetuò agitantur, ut ne ea quidem fallaci lætitia, quam sibi ex voluptatibus faciunt, perfrui queant. Et huiusmodi illis fortunam pii invidebunt? qui pauci sint licet & speciem habeant miserae gentis, ut olim Judæi; tamen magnificatur lætitia ex aspectu beatæ illius lucis, ut humana infra se ducant omnia. Nam solidam constantemque lætitiam, utpote ex veris & summis bonis, percipiunt, atque, ut loquitur Isaias, coram Deo lætantur: nempe quòd se in gratiam Dei restitutos, & regni coelestis hæredes scriptos esse in Christo confidunt. Ad horum bonorum vel possessionem vel spem si revocetur animus, non immoderatè feret molestias, quæ foris exhibentur. Sicut in messe, inquit Propheta, & victoria lætabuntur. Ostendit elegantissimè salutarem & iucundissimam futuram esse liberationem, quemadmodum messis copiosa rusticani; aut divisio prædæ opimæ post victoriam bellatoribus fructuosa & iocunda est. Nos quoq; cogitemus, quando famelicæ animæ in miseriis sen-su peccati & iræ Dei contabescunt, aut hostium potentia intus & foris nos premit, sustineri nos spiritali esca, CHRISTO scilicet & omnibus beneficiis eius, contra beatæ vitæ desperationem; finem autem ac miseriarum triumphum fore gloriosissimum. Iam unde lætitiam Iesaias p. omittat, sequitur: Iugum oneris eius, & virgam humeri eius, sceptrum exactoris confregisti secundum diem Midian. Hæc nimirum lætitiæ causa Iudæis & nobis. Nam sicut Iudæi à iugo servitutis acerbissimo & ab exactionibus Babyloniorum, Dei beneficio, liberati sunt: ita à nostris cervicibus iugum peccati & mortis & legis confractum est; ira Dei mitigata; malæ conscientiæ vulnera sanata; tyrannis Diaboli, cuius libidini obstricti tenebamur, comminuta: denique Tyrannorum & mundi vis omnis attrita, ut quicquid in nos mali hostes quicunque moliantur; miseros tamen ex beatis facere nequeant. Tantorum malorum liberatione quis pius non exultet? cùm præsertim sine sua cura & labore sublata sint? cuiusmodi liberationis modum Propheta Iudæis, porrò etiam promittit. Cum enim bella alia & victoriæ non cō-ficiantur & parentur absque strepitu & tumultu bellico, ac voluntatis in sanguine vestibus & armis: hoc tamen bellum, quo Deus defendet ac vindicabit Ecclesiam, erit, inquit, in combustionem & cibum ignis, q. d., non humanis viribus, sed divina potentia quasi flamma hostes consumente conficietur: quando Deus miseris exulibus reditum in patriam, ὡς ἄνευ μηχανῆς[?] sine vi vel armis patefaciet, non miraculo obscuriore, quàm quo olim à cervicibus Israelitarum durissimam sustulit tyrannidem, cùm Midianitarum exercitum, Gideone Imperatore non confligente, sed in proximo inspectante cum paucis suis perterruit & concidit. Similiter nos singulari & summo beneficio clementiffimus Deus, nullo nostro merito vel sudore, à peccati & mortis servitio liberos asseruit, id solù à nobis postulàs, ut quëadmodum milites Gideonis circù hostê facesin tectis & tubas ferebát; itaRedemtore nos tû fide illustri circù plectamur, tû vocis tuba prædicemus, fine metu, utcumq; hostes stomachêtur & côtra consistant. Nam cp[?] Iefaias alias quidé victorias dicit parari in prælio virtute militari; illâ non ite:id ad cômunem Ecclesiæ victoriâ transferre licet. quin pe ut olim Ahafiæ emissarii in Eliam, cœlesti igne crematî, subito absumti sunt: ita terribilibus exéplis, Ecclesiæ hostes perdit ac delet, nunc Tyrannos & Hæreticos inter fe cômittens, aut suis ipso rum consiliis & viribus evertens, nunc aliis modis e medio tollens, tandemque in æternas abiiciens pœnas, ut eorum molitiones non sint extimescendæ.
units.tr: Yet it will be worthwhile to trace the whole of that oracle back a little further and confirm these points. Isaiah, then, did not soften the Jews' alarm by promising impunity for sins, which is almost always the source of obstinacy and ruin, but by tempering the punishment with salvation. "There will not be gloom for her," he says, "as in the former distress, when he made the land of Zebulun light, etc." He surely confirmed by God's will that the Jews would be in a more bearable condition than the Israelites, who under Pekah and Hoshea kings had been taken captive by Tiglath-Pileser and afterwards by Shalmaneser and led away into Assyria. This promise greatly served against the despair of the Jews, if they looked at the misery of those others. Yet truly, a Jew ignorant of the oracles might have said in exile: "We have suffered heavier penalties than the Israelites, since among us the Temple of God's holiness, which was the harbour and breath of the wretched, will be overthrown, and at the same time the kingdom of David will be destroyed, from whose descendants that Ruler, the Best and Greatest, our Saviour, ought to be born." The Israelites did not suffer such tragedies, for they lost no Temple, since they had none, nor did they fall from such great hopes of promises which they had never received, although they lost their liberty along with the kingdom. So indeed the matter stood; yet the fortune of the Israelites was not for that reason better than that of the Jews. For to these exiles God promised and granted the propagation of their stock even in captivity itself, and after seventy years had run their course, a return to their homeland, and also the restoration of the Temple, the worship, the city and the commonwealth; but the Ten Tribes, once and for all overthrown, he punished with perpetual exile. So too today the fortune of the Church seems most wretched and most desperate; that of its enemies, if not the best, yet more bearable, namely because the outcome is not foreseen, and most people measure happiness not by promised riches but by human eyes. But truly, if right reason prevails, the lot of the Church is in no way to be compared with the final fate of the reprobate multitude. For just as the Jewish Church of old, indeed chastised by the Babylonian exile, and for a time in darkness and in the shadowy land of death, as Isaiah says, lay as if buried, yet soon was led back into its homeland, as if to see the light again, and was filled with great joy from the unhoped-for benefit of deliverance: so now the Christian Church, although it lies surrounded by thick darkness of bodily and spiritual calamities, of sin and of death, has nevertheless received from God Jesus, its light, its desire, its salvation, so that it is neither wretched in miseries nor dead in death. Therefore the Prophet called this light great, saying: "The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light"; because by this one consolation the godly can sustain themselves in their troubles; without it no remedy for despair is found anywhere. But let us hear how the Prophet extols the greatness of this light: "You have multiplied the nation, you have not magnified the joy. For they rejoice before you according to the joy that is in the harvest, and as soldiers exult when they divide the spoils." The Prophet sets off the light, that is, the joy of the godly and of the impious. This alone, even without other things, suffices for tranquillity of mind. What then is it, that a holy man, if bathed in that light, should be dismayed in spirit on account of the troubled storms of the present world, or judge enemies of this light happy by reason of a deceptive prosperity? The multitude of the Ten Tribes was great and their commonwealth flourishing. But when they had renounced true religion, and had become unhappy for the Jews, the worshippers of God, the Prophet judged them wretched because they lacked joy and the blessed tranquillity of mind. Thus indeed the impious flourish with honours, wealth, numbers and fortune; but (O wretched life) the desired security of mind is absent; there are present the inner executioners, the goads of conscience, by which they are constantly harassed in secret, so that they cannot enjoy even that deceptive joy which they derive for themselves from pleasures. And will the godly envy them such a fortune? Though they be few and bear the appearance of a wretched people, as once the Jews did, yet their joy is magnified from the sight of that blessed light, so that they count all human things beneath themselves. For they perceive a solid and constant joy, as it springs from true and supreme goods, and, as Isaiah says, they rejoice before God: namely because they trust that they have been restored into the favour of God and written in Christ as heirs of the heavenly kingdom. If the mind is recalled to the possession or the hope of these goods, it will not bear immoderately the troubles that are inflicted from without. "As in the harvest," says the Prophet, "and as in victory they will rejoice." He shows most elegantly that the coming deliverance will be healthful and most pleasant, just as an abundant harvest is fruitful and joyful for the countryman, or the division of rich spoil after victory is profitable and delightful for the warriors. Let us too consider that when hungry souls waste away in miseries, through the sense of sin and the wrath of God, or the power of enemies presses us both within and without, we are sustained by spiritual food, namely CHRIST and all his benefits, against despair of a blessed life; and that the end and triumph over miseries will be most glorious. Now that Isaiah goes on to name the cause of joy: "You have broken the yoke of his burden, and the rod of his shoulder, the sceptre of the exactor, as in the day of Midian." This is surely the cause of joy for the Jews and for us. For just as the Jews were freed, by God's benefit, from the most bitter yoke of servitude and from the exactions of the Babylonians, so from our necks the yoke of sin and death and of the law has been broken; the wrath of God has been appeased; the wounds of an evil conscience have been healed; the tyranny of the Devil, to whose lust we were bound, has been crushed; finally the whole power of tyrants and of the world has been worn down, so that whatever evil enemies of whatever kind may plan against us, they cannot make us wretched out of blessed. Who that is godly would not exult at deliverance from such great evils, especially since they have been removed without any care or labour of his own? The Prophet further promises the Jews this manner of deliverance. For while other wars and victories are not accomplished and prepared without the din and tumult of battle, and without garments and weapons rolled in blood, yet this war, by which God will defend and avenge the Church, "will be," he says, "for burning and food of fire": that is to say, it will be accomplished not by human strength but by divine power, as a flame consuming the enemies; when God will open to the wretched exiles a return to their homeland without force or arms, as it were without machinery, by no more obscure a miracle than that by which of old he took the most harsh tyranny from the necks of the Israelites, when, with Gideon as commander not fighting but looking on from close by, he terrified and cut down the army of the Midianites with his few. Similarly, the most merciful God, by a singular and supreme benefit, without any merit or sweat of ours, has set us free from the servitude of sin and death, asking of us only this: that as Gideon's soldiers carried torches hidden in jars and trumpets around the enemy, so we, clothed with the illustrious faith of our Redeemer, should be girded about, and proclaim with the trumpet of our voice, without fear, however the enemies may rage and resist. For although Isaiah elsewhere says that victories are won in battle by military valour, this is not so here; this may be transferred to the common victory of the Church. Just as of old the emissaries of Ahaziah against Elijah, consumed by heavenly fire, were suddenly swallowed up, so by terrible examples he destroys and blots out the enemies of the Church, now setting the tyrants and heretics against one another, or overthrowing them by their own counsels and strength, now removing them from the midst by other means, and at last casting them into eternal punishments, so that their schemes need not be feared.

units.la: Porrò ne locus relinqueretur Iudæis dubitandi de reductione ab exsilio Babylonio, ostendit Iefaias, Deum velle, ut Seruator exspectatus nascatur, stante regno cultuq; Iudaico, idcirco hæc instaurari oportere; eamque esse maximi gaudii materiam: cùm ab illa instauratione seruatoris repræsentatio, atque adeo peccatorum absolutio & vita pendeat. Hoc fundamentum est consolationis, quod omni cura & cogitatione, summaq; lætitia & voluptate sanctus vates aperuit & commendavit. Quod si Iudæos hilarare in malis debuit exspectatio Redemtoris nondum nati: quà-tò magis nos ipse eius natalis dies, ipsaque adeò redemtio, hæc quippe tollit nobis dubitationem de promissione quam illis nonnunquam afferebat rerum perturbatio. Quamobrem autem propter eum in gaudiis esse debeant pii: demonstrat Vates luculenta eius personæ officiique descriptione. Quoniam, inquit, puer nascetur nobis: Filius dabitur nobis. Puerum nasciturum ait, & sic describit, ut Messiam promitti appareat: quippe quem paulo supra oraculo non minus illustri ex virgine gravida nasciturum prædixerat, quo declaravit, servatorem mortalium hominem futurum esse, & puerum quidem, nobis per omnia ὁμοῖον [?] ac similem, solo excepto peccato: ut ipse quidem pro peccatis hominum ἀντίχρεον [?] debitum Deo persolvere quiret: nobis vero nulla unquam dubitatio de γνησίῳ [?] ipsius in nos amore subiret, sed firma semper fiduciæ spes in eo reposita foret. Nā homo ut in homine, potête liçet [?], parum spei nonnunquam ponat, facit hæsitatio de illius in se benevolentia atq; constantia. At in nostro Servatore quid desiderabimus? voluntatem ad nos servandos? qui tantum amorem erga nos habuit, ut naturæ nostræ mortalis & humilis particeps fieri non dubitârit. An facultatem requirimus? atqui Deus est; non homo duntaxat, nempe ut Poëta pie cecinit:
units.tr: Moreover, so that the Jews should have no room to doubt the return from Babylonian exile, Isaiah shows that God wills the Saviour to be born as expected, while the kingdom and Jewish worship still stand, and that for this reason these things must be restored; and that this is the very matter of greatest joy, since the representation of the Saviour, and indeed the forgiveness of sins and life, depend upon that restoration. This is the foundation of consolation, which the holy prophet set forth and commended with all care and thought, with the greatest gladness and delight. If the expectation of the Redeemer not yet born ought to cheer the Jews in their troubles, how much more should his birthday itself, and the redemption itself, do so for us? For this removes from us the doubt about the promise, which the disturbance of affairs sometimes brought upon them. Why the godly ought to rejoice on account of him, the Prophet shows by a clear description of his person and office. For, he says, a child will be born to us: a Son will be given to us. He says that a child is to be born, and describes him so that it appears he is the promised Messiah; for a little before, by an oracle no less famous, he had foretold that he would be born of a pregnant virgin, by which he declared that the Saviour of mortals would be a human being, and indeed a child, like us in all things (the Greek word here is uncertain), apart from sin alone; so that he himself could pay to God the debt owed for the sins of men in our place, while for us no doubt would ever arise about his genuine love toward us, but a firm hope of trust would always rest in him. For a man, as a man, may sometimes place little hope in another, because of uncertainty about that man's goodwill and constancy toward him. But in our Saviour, what shall we lack? The will to save us? He who had such love for us that he did not hesitate to become a partaker of our mortal and humble nature. Or do we ask for ability? Yet he is God; not merely a man, as the poet has piously sung: who is not contained by the spaces of the earth, nor the waters of the sea, nor by heaven, yet came into small limbs.

units.la: --qui non spacii terræ, non æquoris unda, Nec capitur cœlo, parvos confluxit in artus.
units.tr: --who is not contained by the spaces of the earth, nor the waters of the sea, nor by heaven, yet came into small limbs.

units.la: Nam Iesaias non puerum modo, sed & Filium dixit. At cuius Filium? An Davidis tantum, cuius ex stirpe homo futurus erat? Imò & Dei. Dei enim hoc iam olim de eo testimonium exstabat: Ego ero ipsi in Patrem; & ipse erit mihi in Filium. Et supra Filium virginis Propheta appellavit sua lingua עִמָּנוּאֵל[?] Immanuelem quod est: Nobiscum Deus. Sic ergo hic puer Filius Dei est, ut & ipse sit Deus. Quid est igitur, quod reformidemus vel mundi vel Diaboli potentiam? si propugnator noster est omnipotens Deus? quid est, quòd illorum furoribus conturbemur, &c. Si idé[?] nostri amantissimus? Et quibus puer hic natus? An non nobis? Quibus hic Filius Dei Deus datus? annon nobis? Et quibus nobis? Vtique hominibus. Sed an omnibus? Imò toti mundo datus est, quatenus homo factus communem omnibus naturam induit, & omnibus salus eius offertur, mandato Patris de coelo clamantis: Hunc audite. At cur non bis, inquit Propheta, non mundo datus? Quia solatur fideles, non impios ex hoc mundo. Nobis igitur est datus, qui eū Servatorem agnoscimus, qui fide eum accipimus, qui veri sumus per fidem Abrahæ filii, Nobis, inquam, fidelibus omnibus & solis datus est hic puer virginis, datus est hic Filius Dei, non ut reliquis datus naturæ duntaxat communione, sed efficaci ad salutem donatione. Nobis igitur verè datus ac destinatus est à Patre Filius, qui vera fide & gratitudine datum recipimus. Quid ni igitur certam ex manu eius salutem speremus? Est naturæ communis, imò fraternitatis vinculo nobis colligatus. A fratre igitur fratres quidni omnia expectemus? Qui Mediator ac Redemtor nobis factus est, quomodo clido clientes suos in periculis non curabit? cumq; idem sit Filius Dei: quin & nos filios ac hæredes Dei, sibique coheredes per Filium & Spiritum Sanctum potenter efficiat, nihil quaso addubitemus, attestante Paulo, cum dicit, Deum fecisse nos sibi dilectos in illo dilecto: & Spiritum contestari Spiritui nostro, quòd sumus Filii Dei: cum que filii simus, Deum emisisse Spiritum Filii sui in cordi nostra, clamantem, Abba, h.e, Pater.
units.tr: For Isaiah spoke not only of a child but also of a Son. But whose Son? Of David only, from whose stock he was to be a man? Nay, also of God. For already long ago this testimony concerning him stood: I will be to him a Father, and he will be to me a Son. And above, the prophet called the son of the virgin, in his own tongue, Immanuel, which is: God with us. So then this child is the Son of God, in such a way that he himself is God. Why then should we fear the power of the world or of the devil, if our defender is almighty God? Why should we be troubled by their furies, etc.? If he is most loving toward us? And to whom has this child been born? Is it not to us? To whom has this Son of God, who is God, been given? Is it not to us? And to whom are we? Surely to men. But to all? Nay, he has been given to the whole world, insofar as, made man, he has put on the nature common to all, and his salvation is offered to all, by the command of the Father crying from heaven: Hear him. But why, says the prophet, not twice, not given to the world? Because he comforts the faithful, not the impious of this world. He has therefore been given to us, who acknowledge him as Saviour, who receive him by faith, who are true sons of Abraham through faith. To us, I say, to all the faithful and to us alone, this child of the virgin has been given; this Son of God has been given, not as to the rest, by the common bond of nature only, but by a gift effective for salvation. Truly, therefore, the Son has been given and destined to us by the Father, and we receive him, given, with true faith and gratitude. Why then should we not hope for certain salvation from his hand? He is bound to us by the common bond of nature, indeed by the bond of brotherhood. Why then should brothers not expect all things from a brother? He who has been made our Mediator and Redeemer, how will he not care for his clients in dangers, as a patron does? And since he is the Son of God, and moreover, through the Son and the Holy Spirit, he powerfully makes us sons and heirs of God and fellow heirs with himself, let us, I beg, doubt nothing, as Paul attests when he says that God made us beloved in the Beloved; and that the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God; and since we are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, that is, Father.

units.la: Fiduciam porrò istam, officii Messiæ expositionem nobis confirmat Propheta, Et fiet, inquit, seu constitutus est principatus super humerum eius.
units.tr: Moreover, the Prophet confirms that confidence for us by setting out the office of the Messiah: And it will come to pass, or the rule has been placed upon his shoulder.

units.la: Principem ergo & caput Ecclesiæ futurum esse docet, cui nec potentia deest nec industria ad gubernandum ac servandum regnum suum, hoc est Ecclesiam, cuius a Patre Rex atque caput est constitutus. Et est certè rex ille, qui Ecclesiam suam liberat, servat ac defendit potenter. Est pastor ille impiger, qui ovem perditam humeris imponit. Est armatus ille fortis, qui Satanæ potentiam frangit, ac spolia dividit. Sub hoc igitur Principe in tuto est salus nostra: nec est periculum, cum Deus sit, ne de civibus amittat quenquam, vel a perduellibus opprimatur ipse, regnóve spolietur. Sed qualis sit hic Princeps qualisque Principatus: ex iis, quæ apud Prophetam sequuntur, plenius intelligemus. Nomen, inquit, eius vocabitur (a Patre nimirum & ab Ecclesia) Admirabilis: quippe qui sapientia & robore, operumque magnitudine antecellat omnibus tum hominibus tum Angelis. Sive enim hoc universum intueamur, sive naturarum in illo unionem cogitemus, sive miracula,quæ ipse anteasscensum fecit, quæque post Apostolorum ministerio edidit, reminiscamur; divina eius sapientia & virtus se ostendit, maxi-mamque admirationem movet. Cum primis autem in gubernatione Ecclesiæ admirabilis est. Si enim res & eventus omnium seculorum memoria cognoscamus: Deus bone, quanto in discrimine sæpenumero fuit Ecclesia! at quàm mirabiliter à suo servatore usque defensa! cùm neque in se spem salutis ullam reperiret, utpote pauper-cula & parva, neque in cæteris mortalibus, utpote infensissimis. Nec defensa modò est, sed etiam propagata, contra obstacula inimicorum: quemadmodum ventus nulla mole obiecta cohiberi aut supprimi potest. Hanc admirabilem Servatoris in tuenda Ecclesia potentiam si reputemus cum animis nostris: non tanto timore percelle-mur, ubi de hostium molitionibus & furore allatum fuerit. Accidit enim plerisque, ut nimis admirentur splendorem & robur eorum, ex eaque admiratione in dubitationem de ope sui Servatoris incidant. quasi temeritas imbecillorū mortalium quicquā valeat contra admirabilem, hoc est, sapientissimum & omnipotentem Deum.
units.tr: He teaches, therefore, that he will be the prince and head of the Church, who has neither lack of power nor diligence to govern and preserve his kingdom, that is, the Church, over which he has been appointed king and head by the Father. And certainly he is that king who powerfully frees, saves and defends his Church. He is that tireless shepherd who lays the lost sheep upon his shoulders. He is that strong armed man who breaks the power of Satan and divides the spoils. Under this Prince, therefore, our salvation is safe; nor is there danger, since he is God, that he should lose any of his citizens, or be overwhelmed by enemies himself, or be stripped of his kingdom. But what sort of prince this is, and what sort of principate, we shall understand more fully from what follows in the Prophet. His name, he says, will be called (by the Father and by the Church, of course) Wonderful: since he surpasses all, both men and angels, in wisdom and strength and greatness of works. For whether we look upon this whole universe, or consider the union of natures in him, or call to mind the miracles which he performed before his ascension, and those which he afterward worked through the ministry of the Apostles, his divine wisdom and power show themselves and move the greatest admiration. Above all, he is wonderful in the government of the Church. For if we recognise the events of all ages by memory: good God, how often has the Church been in danger! Yet how wonderfully has it been defended up to now by its Saviour, since it found in itself no ground of hope for salvation, being very poor and small, nor in other mortals, being most hostile. Not only has it been defended, but also propagated, against the obstacles of enemies, just as the wind cannot be checked or suppressed by any mass placed before it. If we reflect in our minds upon this admirable power of the Saviour in preserving the Church, we shall not be struck with such great fear when reports of the plots and fury of enemies are brought to us. For it happens to many that they admire too much the splendour and strength of their foes, and from that admiration fall into doubt about the help of their Saviour, as if the rashness of weak mortals could prevail anything against the admirable, that is, most wise and almighty God.

units.la: Postea Consiliarium nuncupat Propheta, eo ipso consilio, ut certam sibi unusquisque piorum salutis spem in illo positam esse teneat. Nam is consiliarius non modò consilium Patris de commu-nicatione beatitudinis cum hominibus, quod neque natura dictare, neque Angelus quispiam scire & enunciare potuit, cognitum habuit & an-nunciavit, verumetiam per Spiritum Sanctum anianimos Electorum, ut huic assentiantur, flectit & gubernat. Et quoniam multa sunt, quæ nos de hac voluntate abstrahere conantur, ancipitemq; afferunt cogitandi curam: divino consilio instruit, ut quid sequantur, habeant, & ab huiusmo di insidiis periculisque se expediant. In ipso videlicet omnes thesauri sapientiæ reconditi sunt, ac frustra cogitant hostes illum regem suis technis circumvenire: frustra item cives eius metuunt, ne ab illis circumveniantur & beatitudine priventur. Etiamsi enim nulla via ad evadendum se ostendat, & iam hostes in manibus habere victoriam sibi persuadeant: nunquam tamen salutis retinendæ ratio nostrum consiliarium deficiet, ita quidem, ut quanto periculum maius fuerit; tanto liberatio illustrior sit & mirabilior. Et sanè uti[?] illustrior & mirabilior sit, rem in extremum discrimen adduci patitur. Interim tamen suos, ne de gradu deturbentur & de omni spe decidat, per consolatorem Spiritum suum sustentari consolatione curat, usque dum ex malis & periculis omnibus eripiat. Nam Deus est fortis & mirabilis, quod nomen ei etiam Iesaias dedit: quòd omnes mortales ac dæmones fortitudine illi sint inferiores. Quidni enim ille, quos creavit, vincere & eradicare quiret? Quòd si potentior omnibus creaturis est: non est Deus creatus, neque ex honore hoc ei nomen natum est, sed Deus æternus, à quo universum hoc creatum sit. Quæ cogitatio omnem sollicitudinem in malis adimere piis debet. Quid enim volumus amplius? Ut potentes sint hostes; nos imbecilli: Redemtor noster potenpotentior est: siquidem & Deus est & fortissimus, utpote in quo divina fortitudo ineftatque potentia. Idcirco nunquam occumbemus: sed ipse vincet in nobis. quod Paulus etiam in epistola ad Rom. monet. Si Deus, inquit, pro nobis, quis contra nos? & Iohannes Maior qui in nobis, quam qui in mundo. Adhoc Patrem seculi prophe-ta appellat: quia sempiternam & beatam vitam dat. Est enim vitæ æternæ fons, quam communicat cum suis. Quæ enim esset hæc vita, quamvis ab hostibus tuta: si post mortem sit vel nulla vel beatitatis expers? Cum ergo noster Redemptor author sit vitæ æternæ: verendum non est, ne quis hostis hanc nobis eripiat, etiamsi in corpora sæviat. Nam ipse vivificat nos & tuetur, ne perpetuò pereamus. quod si mortem oppetamus: tamen reviviscemus, ipsius virtute, ad vitam sempiternam & beatam. Porrò principem pacis esse Iesaias ait: quod omnium temporum memoriam & ipse abnegare videtur. Quanta enim bella orta sunt, ubi primum pura eius doctrina annunciabatur? quantæ cædes? quanta odia malorum in professores eius? nec vero contra omnem opinionem. Aperte enim prædixit & testificatus est Servator, se non advenisse, ut pacem daret; sed gladium. Verùm quemadmodum hoc intelligendum sit ipse ostendit hoc verbo: Pacem meam do vobis; non sicut mundus dat. Nimirum illius pacis vocatur Princeps, quæ inter Deum & homines facta est & conscientiis tranquillitatem conciliavit, quæque tandem aliquando erit, ubi reditus Christi finem calamitatum & perturbationum afferet. Hæc vera & solida est pax; hæc lux clarissima: hæc lætitia maxima: qua cum nulla ex parte coæquari potest vel societas omnium mortalium, vel solis splendor vel voluptas & gaudium aliud. Eorum bonorum nulla est in piis fa-cietas: hæc spectant: hæc desiderant: in his acquiescunt. In qua cogitatione cum versaretur sanctus Iesaias, atque eiusmodi inde voluptatem caperet: addidit, nullum fore finem multiplicationis principatus & pacis, hoc est, regnum CHRISTI & amplissimum & sempiternum. Nam etsi non universi mortales secum coniungunt, & legibus ipsius parere, beneficiaque accipere volunt: tamen nulla est gens usquam, in qua non aliquos cives ille Rex habuerit, aut adhuc deligat, summisque sibi beneficiis obstringat, licet id cæteri ægre ferant & impedire conentur. Nec enim vel perduellium vis vel ætas ulla regni eius finem af-feret: utcunque in angustum contractum, aut omnino eversum esse[?] sæpenumero videatur. Pacem etiam illam quam diximus, cùm sempiterna sit; nulla hominum vel dæmonum malevolentia labefactare aut dirimere poterit, nulla violentia, quod ipsum spondens olim suis hic pacis princeps, Gaudium vestrum, inquit, nemo tollet. Sed ne se in ocium dedisse & suorum curam deponere existimetur: demonstrat Iesaias, sedere eum super solium Davidis & regnum eius tenere. quo significat eum officium regis facere, rempub. Christianam administrare & ab iniuria tueri. Ecclesiam enim regnum Davidis vocat; non Iudæo-rum regnum, quod typus fuit regni spiritalis, in id à CHRISTO mutatum. quemadmodū ipse ait: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Itaque hoc regnum tenebit usq; dum ponat inimicos suos scabellum pedum suorum; cives suos ex omnibus malis ereptos, gloria cœlesti exornet & perpoliat. Porrò firmum statum regni huius Prophēta notat, cùm dicit, Instaurari & stabiliri in judicio & justitia, id est, subinde Ecclesiam restitui, ubi ad paucos redacta est, aut plane intermortua videtur. Stabilietur in judicio, sic ut repurgetur doctrina, & à corruptelis calumniatorum vindicetur, vitia expurgentur, ubi ab officio discedere cœperint; hostes verò & reprobi exterminentur, uti etiam alio oraculo apud Isaiam refertur: Ecce servus meus quo nitor[?]: electus meus, quo unicè placatur anima mea: dedi Spiritum meum super eum, judicium gentibus proferet. Non clamabit neque efferetur, non faciet audiri in platea vocem suam. Arundinem fractam non conteret, & linum obscurum non extinguet, ad veritatem judicium proferet. Non hallucinabitur, nec præceps erit, donec ponat judicium in terra, & ad legem eius insula expe-ctabunt. Vigebit etiam justitia, tum propter ipsius regis tum propter civium justitiam. Ille enim quicquid aget, justitiæ consentaneum erit, & ne cives sui à perduellibus iniuria afficiantur, providebit: quicquid etiam humano generi promisit aut interminatus est, servabit atque effiet. Hi verò & ipsi justitiæ studebunt, postea quam justitia sui Regis & Redemtoris imputata eis & Spiritus Sanctus donatus fuerit. De ipso enim in alio oraculo Isaias sic loquitur: Servus meus jusius justificabit multos sui cognitione. Et Daniel, ducetur, inquit, justitia sempiterna. Quamobrem exspuamus ex animis nostris omnem solicitudinem & metum: siquidem ille servus Dei iustus nos a peccato & miseriis, quibus adhuc obnoxia est vita nostra, vindicavit & cum Deo reconciliavit. Quis enim intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus is est qui justificat, ait Paulus. Itaque si sentimus nos electos esse regni eius cives in quibus judicium & justitia instaurentur: non est, quod metuamus exitium aut universæ Ecclesiæ eversionem. a quo metu dehortatur Propheta, quod de Rege Christo addit, firmaturum esse regnum suum in perpetuum, hoc est, conservaturum & amplificaturum, ita, ut usque eos, quibus beatitudinem æternō decreto condixit, in regni sui societatem vocet, idque cum iis in omne seculum possideat. Hæc, Auditores, vera & magna bona sunt: hæc lux fidei, quæ apparuit omnibus: hæc messis illa fructuosissima: hæc victoria gloriosissima, ex quibus lætitia capienda est ea, quæ sola contra desperationem valet. Num vero nos peccatum & indignitas nostra vel potentia hostium vel miserabilis Ecclesiæ facies tam topere perterret & perturbat, ut illorum bonorum possessionem desperemus? Sed quid Iesaias? Zelus Iehovæ exercituum, inquit, hæc refaciet. Quid igitur? Iehova exercituum, hoc est, dominus rerum omnium hæc bona nobis pollicitus est & præstat per Christum, qui ipse est Iehova exercituum, ut quicquid decrevit, facere queat. Et quicquam de iis dubitabimus? An voluntatem ei desse ad nos beandos opinamur? atqui Iesaias ait, cum zelo & amore ardentissimo suam Eccle-siam prosequi. De hoc etiam dubitabimus? quasi non satis ex missione Filii elucesceret, atque ex studio depellendi à se contumeliam & eripiendi nos ex malis, cum quibus conflictamur. Recognoscantur enim quæ superioribus seculis egerit. Propter zelum videlicet Iehova exercituum liberavit Iudæos à servitute Babyloniorum; in pa-triam reduxit; fundos & fortunas restituit; cultum antiquum instauravit: Servatorem promis-sum exhibuit; Ecclesiam prædicatione Evange-lii collegit, & quam collegit, defensavit hucusq;, & superstitionibus expurgatam subinde instau-ravit, vel nostris temporibus. Ea voluntas erga Ecclesiam superiorem & hodiernam, cum hacte-nus perspiciatur ex eventibus: quis de ea in po-sterum dubitabit? quasi parum sibi constet in co-filiis & in amore. At vero perpetuo sibi similis est & cuius patrocinium semel suscepit, eam deserct nunquam, sed propter Filium suum & per eum ab hostibus tutabitur. id quod spondet apud hunc ipsum Prophetam his verbis: usque ad senium ego idem & usque ad canitiem ego portabo. Ego feci, & ego feram. ego portabo & servabo. Rursus perduel-les regni sui, quos æterno decreto sempiternis suppliciis adiudicavit, nec adamavit unquam æ-què atque suos, suum peculium, suam hæredita-tem, neque beatos faciet, sed & ante mortem mo-litiones eorum & furorem retundet & post mor-tem pœnis æternis vindicabit.
units.tr: Afterwards the Prophet calls him Counsellor, with this purpose: that each of the godly should hold firmly that their hope of salvation is placed in him. For this counsellor not only knew and announced the Father's counsel concerning the communication of blessedness with men, which no nature could dictate and no angel could know and declare, but also, through the Holy Spirit, bends and governs the minds of the Elect so that they assent to it. And since there are many things which try to draw us away from this will, and bring with them a doubtful care for thought, he instructs them by divine counsel, so that they may know what to follow and how to extricate themselves from such snares and dangers. In him, of course, all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, and the enemies think in vain that they can circumvent that King by their schemes; in vain likewise do his citizens fear lest they be circumvented by them and deprived of blessedness. For even if no way of escape appears, and the enemies persuade themselves that they already hold the victory in their hands, yet the means of keeping our salvation will never fail our Counsellor, so that the greater the danger, the more illustrious and wonderful the deliverance will be. And indeed, in order that it may be more illustrious and wonderful, he permits the matter to be brought to the utmost peril. Meanwhile, however, so that his own may not be thrown from their footing and fall from all hope, he takes care to sustain them with comfort through his Consoling Spirit, until he snatches them from all evils and dangers. For God is strong and wonderful, a name which Isaiah also gave him: that all mortals and demons are inferior to him in strength. For why should he not be able to conquer and root out those whom he created? But if he is more powerful than all creatures, then God is not created, and this name was not born from an honour bestowed on him, but he is the eternal God, by whom this whole universe was created. This thought ought to take away all anxiety in evils from the godly. For what more do we want? Let the enemies be powerful; we are weak: our Redeemer is more powerful, since he is both God and most strong, as one in whom divine strength and power dwell. Therefore we shall never perish, but he himself will conquer in us. This Paul also warns in the Epistle to the Romans: If God is for us, who is against us? and John: Greater is he who is in us than he who is in the world. Moreover, the Prophet calls him Father of the age, because he gives eternal and blessed life. For he is the fountain of eternal life, which he communicates to his own. For what kind of life would this be, however safe from enemies, if after death it were either nothing or devoid of blessedness? Since, therefore, our Redeemer is the author of eternal life, we need not fear lest any enemy snatch this from us, even if he rages against our bodies. For he himself quickens us and keeps us, so that we may not perish forever. And if we should die, yet we shall be revived, by his power, to eternal and blessed life. Furthermore, Isaiah says that he is the Prince of Peace, a title which he himself seems to deny for the whole of time. For how many wars arose as soon as his pure doctrine began to be proclaimed? How many slaughters? How great the hatred of the wicked against its professors? Nor indeed is this contrary to all expectation. For the Saviour foretold and testified plainly that he had not come to give peace, but a sword. But how this is to be understood he himself shows by this word: My peace I give to you; not as the world gives. Clearly he is called the Prince of that peace which has been made between God and men, which has brought tranquillity to consciences, and which will at last be fully realised when the return of Christ brings an end to calamities and disturbances. This is the true and solid peace; this is the brightest light; this is the greatest joy, with which neither the fellowship of all mortals, nor the splendour of the sun, nor any other pleasure or delight can in any way be compared. In the godly there is no satisfaction of these goods: they look to these, they long for these, they rest in these. While holy Isaiah was occupied with this thought and took such delight from it, he added that there would be no end to the increase of the principality and peace, that is, the kingdom of Christ is both most ample and everlasting. For although not all mortals join themselves to him, and wish to obey his laws and receive his benefits, yet there is nowhere any nation in which that King has not had, or does not still choose, some citizens, and bind them to himself with the greatest benefits, even though others bear this with difficulty and try to hinder it. For neither the power of rebels nor any age will bring an end to his kingdom, however often it may seem to have been contracted into a narrow compass or altogether overthrown. Also that peace of which we have spoken, since it is eternal, no malice of men or demons will be able to shake or dissolve, no violence either; the Prince of Peace himself, promising this to his own once, said: No one will take away your joy. But lest he should be thought to have given himself to idleness and to have laid aside the care of his people, Isaiah shows that he sits upon the throne of David and holds his kingdom. By this he signifies that he performs the office of a king, administers the Christian commonwealth and protects it from injury. For he calls the Church the kingdom of David; not the kingdom of the Jews, which was a type of the spiritual kingdom, changed by Christ into that, as he himself says: My kingdom is not of this world. Therefore he will hold this kingdom until he places his enemies as a footstool for his feet; he will adorn and polish his citizens, snatched from all evils, with heavenly glory. Moreover, the Prophet notes the firm state of this kingdom when he says: to be restored and established in judgment and justice, that is, the Church is from time to time restored, when it has been reduced to a few, or seems altogether dead. It will be established in judgment, so that doctrine may be purged and defended against the corruptions of slanderers, faults may be cleansed away when men have begun to depart from their duty; but the enemies and the reprobate are to be cut off, as is also related in another oracle in Isaiah: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; my elect, in whom my soul is wholly pleased; I have put my Spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles. He shall not cry out nor lift up his voice, nor make his voice heard in the street. A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench; he shall bring forth judgment unto truth. He shall not fail nor be discouraged, until he has set judgment in the earth, and the islands shall wait for his law. Justice too shall flourish, both on account of the justice of the king himself and on account of the justice of his citizens. For whatever he does will be consistent with justice, and he will take care that his citizens are not wronged by rebels; whatever he has promised or threatened to the human race, he will also keep and bring about. And these citizens too will apply themselves to justice, after the justice of their King and Redeemer has been imputed to them and the Holy Spirit has been given to them. For Isaiah speaks of him in another oracle thus: My righteous servant shall justify many by his knowledge. And Daniel: everlasting justice, he says, shall be brought in. Wherefore let us cast out of our minds all anxiety and fear; since that righteous servant of God has delivered us from sin and the miseries to which our life is still exposed, and has reconciled us with God. For who shall bring any charge against the elect of God? It is God who justifies, says Paul. Therefore, if we perceive that we are the elect citizens of his kingdom, in whom judgment and justice are restored, there is no reason for us to fear ruin or the overthrow of the whole Church. From this fear the Prophet dissuades us, when he adds concerning King Christ that he will establish his kingdom forever, that is, he will preserve and extend it, so that he calls to fellowship in his kingdom those whom he has destined to blessedness by an eternal decree, and possesses them with himself for all eternity. These, hearers, are true and great goods: this is the light of faith, which has appeared to all; this is that most fruitful harvest; this is the most glorious victory, from which joy is to be taken, which alone avails against despair. But do our sin and unworthiness, or the power of enemies, or the wretched face of the Church so greatly terrify and disturb us that we despair of possessing those goods? But what does Isaiah say? The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. What then? The LORD of hosts, that is, the Lord of all things, has promised these goods to us and bestows them through Christ, who himself is the LORD of hosts, so that he is able to do whatever he has decreed. And shall we doubt any of these things? Or do we suppose that he lacks the will to bless us? Yet Isaiah says that he pursues his Church with zeal and most ardent love. Shall we doubt this too? As if it were not clear enough from the sending of the Son, and from his eagerness to drive away the reproach against himself and to snatch us from the evils with which we struggle. For let what he has done in earlier ages be recalled. Out of zeal, to be sure, the LORD of hosts freed the Jews from the servitude of the Babylonians; he led them back into their country; he restored their lands and fortunes; he re-established the ancient worship; he exhibited the promised Saviour; he gathered the Church by the preaching of the Gospel, and having gathered it, has defended it until now, and from time to time, even in our own times, has restored it purged of superstitions. Since that will towards the Church of former times and of today is seen from the events so far, who will doubt it for the future? As if he were little consistent in counsel and in love! But indeed he is always like himself, and whose patronage he has once undertaken, he never forsakes, but on account of his Son and through him will protect from enemies. This he promises in this same Prophet in these words: Even to old age I am the same, and even to grey hairs I will bear you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and I will save. Again, the rebels against his kingdom, whom he has condemned by an eternal decree to everlasting punishments, and whom he never loved as much as his own, his peculiar people, his inheritance, he will not make blessed, but even before death he will beat back their schemes and fury, and after death he will avenge them with eternal punishments.

units.la: Quamobrem etsi conditio Ecclesiæ multò vi-deatur esse deterior, quàm profanæ multitudinis: tamen cum illa Deum habeat benevolum, me-liore esse animo, quàm haec, potest & debet. Hac enim perpetuò pereunte, de omnibus hostibus triumphum aget. Nimirum natus est & datus ei puer ille Filius Dei, qui humeris suis principatum sustinens admirabili & divino consilio eam po-tentiaque & sapientia & bonitate gubernat & conservat; justitia & vita & pace sempiterna do-nat, idque ex ineffabili zelo & amore, quo ample-ctitur unumquemque fidelium, & is quidem zelus nunquam frigebit. Quod scientes & cogitantes quis separabit à charitate Dei in CHRISTO? num oppressio? num angustia? num persecutio? num fames? num nuditas? num periculum? num gladius? Imo in his omnib. plus quam victores sumus per eum, qui dilexit nos.
units.tr: Therefore, although the condition of the Church may seem much worse than that of the profane multitude, nevertheless, since the Church has God as her benevolent friend, she can and ought to be of better courage than they. For while she perishes continually, she will win a triumph over all her enemies. Indeed, that boy, the Son of God, has been born and given to her; he, bearing the rule upon his shoulders, governs and preserves her by a wonderful and divine counsel, with power, wisdom and goodness; he bestows upon her righteousness, life and everlasting peace, and does so out of an inexpressible zeal and love with which he embraces each one of the faithful; and that zeal will never grow cold. Knowing and considering this, who shall separate us from the love of God in Christ? Shall tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or peril? Or the sword? Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.

units.la: Quare ut id agamus, cujus causa huc conveni-mus, nempe ut publicè testemur, nos gratis animis tanta Dei beneficia agnoscere & celebrare: Agimus gratias Deo æterno Patri, Domino ex-ercituum, per Filium suum coæternum Dominū nostrum Iesum Christum, in Spiritu S. quod nobis nasci voluit hunc puerum, & dedit hunc Filium, admirabilem, consiliarium, Deum fortem, patrem seculi, principem pacis, qui nos gestet suis humeris, & regat, ac servet in æternum, quod colligit sibi Ecclesiam & contra omnium hostium furores & conatus defendit, exsuscitat pios Prin-cipes, quib. cordi sit religio, & Ecclesiæ, scholarū-que salus & amplificatio. Quæsumus eundem, ut hic Princeps noster Iesus Christus, æternæ pacis author, posthac similiter conservet principatum suum, suam hæreditatem, utque in his regionib. Ecclesiam sibi usque colligat, & à sordibus Antichristi purget; cœtus etiam docentium & discentium tueatur, ut in tranquillitate gloriam ejus evulgent & propagent, eorumque patronos tuetur omnes, inprimis Illustrissimum Principem & Electorem Palatinum FRIDERICUM I V. Dominum nostrum clementissimum, ejusque vitam, actiones, gubernationem & consilia suo spiritu gubernet, potentia sua & bonitate fortunet ac locupletet, ut universa cedant in laudem gloriosi nominis ejus, ac serviant multorum hominum æternæ saluti, per eundem Immanuelem Dominum nostrum, cui cum Patre & Spiritu sancto sit laus & gloria in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Wherefore, that we may do what we have come together here for, namely, to bear public witness that we gladly acknowledge and celebrate such great benefits of God, we give thanks to God the eternal Father, the Lord of hosts, through his co-eternal Son our Lord Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit, because he willed that this boy be born to us and gave us this Son: wonderful, counsellor, mighty God, everlasting Father, Prince of peace, who bears us upon his shoulders, rules us, and keeps us for ever; because he gathers the Church to himself and defends her against the rage and attempts of all her enemies; because he raises up godly princes, to whom religion is dear, and the welfare and enlargement of the Church and the schools. We beseech the same Jesus Christ, our Prince, the author of eternal peace, that hereafter he likewise preserve his principality and his inheritance, and that in these regions he gather the Church to himself unto the end and cleanse her from the filth of Antichrist; that he also protect the assemblies of teachers and learners, so that in tranquillity they may spread abroad and propagate his glory; and that he watch over all their patrons, above all the most illustrious Prince and Elector Palatine, Frederick IV, our most gracious Lord; and that he govern by his Spirit his life, actions, rule and counsels, and enrich and bless him with his power and goodness, so that all things may turn to the praise of his glorious name and serve the eternal salvation of many men, through the same Immanuel, our Lord, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be praise and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: ORATIO IV. DE NATIVITATE CHRI-STI ET CELEBRATIONE HUJUS BENEFICII DEI, QUOD Messiam exhibuerit, desumta ex nuncio & cantico Angelorum.Luc.2
units.tr: ORATION IV. ON THE NATIVITY OF CHRIST AND THE CELEBRATION OF THIS BENEFIT OF GOD, THAT HE HAS SENT FORTH THE MESSIAH, TAKEN FROM THE ANNOUNCEMENT AND SONG OF THE ANGELS. Luke 2

units.la: Recitata à GOTHARDO VÖGELINO prid. Natalis Domini Anno 1593.
units.tr: Delivered by GOTTHARD VÖGELIN, the day before the Lord's Nativity, in the year 1593.

units.la: Annuus assuetum Domini natalis honorem, Exigit: Approperant ad pia sacra dies. Cras erit illa dies, quæ si non orta fuisset, Nulla forent miseris festa videnda piis.
units.tr: The yearly day demands the honour customary for the Lord's birth; the days hasten toward the holy rites. Tomorrow will be that day, which, had it not dawned, no festival would be seen by the pious in their wretchedness.

units.la: LICEAT enim mihi versibus penè iisdem affari vos, Clarissimi & Ornatissimi Auditores, quibus se alloquitur Poëta ille, haud ita magnâ in re, sed elegantiæ plenus: Quanquam in eo solennem hunc lætitiæ sensum ipsa rerum natura & consuetudo tulit, Divino autem Ecclesiæ cœtui Spiritus etiam Sanctus certa gaudii vestigia non impressit leviter ad exigui prædicationem temporis, sed fixit ad memoriam nativitatis Messiæ sempiternam; Ut crastinum quotannis diem cogitationibus & vocibus lætissimis celebraret, omnium, nisi quis me fallit, meritissimo. Quid e-nim quisquam potest ex omni memoria sumere illustrius, quàm pro sordidatis de capite, de sub-stantia reis, proprio scelere perditis Filium DEI DEUM mutasse nonnihil gloriæ suæ vestem sple-ndidissimam assumta humanæ carnis & infirmi-tatis togâ, quando eum Deus ante annos adhuc mille quingentos nonaginta tres propter salutem nostram ex iisdem, quibus nos, radicibus natum, eidem mortis & periculorum auræ nobiscum exponere cœpit. Opus profecto tota universi moli-tione longè admirabilius. Nam effector mundi Deus, cùm originem rerum quæreret, ea quidem machinatus est, quæ gloriam suam omnibus modis illustrarent. Bonitatem ostendebat, quia bo-nis omnibus explebat mundum, mali nihil ad-miscebat. Sapientiam declarabat, dum cœlum certa constructum proportione & lutum corpo-ris humani intelligentiis ornabat, dum informe chaos ex inordinato in ordinem adducebat. Ejus tandem in se perfecta & ad summum perducta natura in omnipotentiæ speculo maximè refulge-bat, quòd omnia condebat, cœlum tornabat, ut nihil effici posset rotundius, Solem & Lunam accendebat, errores siderum multitudine infinita, varietate admirabili præditos, è quibus erat motus temporis consignandus, definiebat, ac deniq; præclarâ quadam conditione hominem finge-bat, & ad ejus commoditates atque usus tantam rerum ubertatem largiebatur, quanta terræ & a-nimalium fœtu copiosè adhuc profunditur. Sed idem Deus, quod ad gloriam suam atque ad am-plissimi beneficii in creatione collatam gratiam magis pertinebat, nova dilectionis foedera nobiscum ferire instituit, posteaquam Satan divina-rum humanarumque rerum praedo primos uni-versitatis parentes à foedere pacto quo se soli Deo devoverunt, retraxit, iisque plagam insanabilem atque mortiferam imposuit. Atque hoc foedus, quod Jesu Christi sanguine ictum sanciebatur, summi in nos amoris signum esse debet certissi-mum. Deinde alias quoque, imo omnes virtutes suas exseruit, ut nos quibus omne supplicium atque omnis jure summo poena debebatur, praevari-catione liberaret, atque ita redemtionem no-stri multo excellentiorem creatione esse testare[?]-tur. Igitur immensae potentiae fuit, quod Maria sponsa non naturae consuetudine sed virgo concepit, virgo peperit, virgo mater fuit. Ineffabilis misericordiae, quòd nos tanta charitate complexus est, ut filium unigenitum donaret, qui morte voluntariâ nefarium defectionis crimè æternam-que condemnationem à nobis depelleret. Summæ justitiæ, quòd antequam effrenatum peccandi furorem impunitate aleret, & offensionem sui inultam esse pateretur, cum, quem ex sua mente genuit, quem unicè dilexit Filium pro nob. mortem appetere voluit. Hæc autem duo in unam speciem temperare, id est, strictum justitiæ rigorem & misericordiæ liberalitatem simul exercere, non nisi perfectæ fuit cumulataque; sapientiæ. Plus igitur, Domine Jesu, nativitati tuæ debemus, quòd redemti sumus, quàm operi, quòd creati fumus. Non prodesset nasci, nisi redimi profuisset; exclamat Ambrosius. Hanc majestatis divinae amplitudinem, hanc impensam Dei erga homines voluntatem angeli suspiciunt & admirantur. Viae Bethlehemiticae legatorum multitudine coelitus missorum celebrantur, cantorum voces incredibili gratulatione exultant. Percipite, Auditores, harmoniam angelicam, & omnia diligenter nuncii verba cognoscite, cum alacer laetusque volitat, tripudiat, & ita personat;
units.tr: For I may address you, most distinguished and most honoured hearers, in nearly the same verses with which that poet addresses himself, a poet not in a matter of great weight, but full of elegance. Although nature itself and custom bring this solemn sense of joy to the occasion, the Holy Spirit has also imprinted upon the divine assembly of the Church certain traces of joy, not lightly, for the brief span of preaching, but fixed them in memory for the everlasting birth of the Messiah, so that the Church might celebrate that coming day every year with the most joyful thoughts and voices, deservedly so, unless I am mistaken, for all. For what can anyone take from all memory more illustrious than this: that the Son of God, God, has, for the sake of those who were squalid in head and substance, ruined by their own crime, exchanged somewhat of his glory, putting on a most splendid robe, the toga of human flesh and weakness, when God, some one thousand five hundred and ninety-three years ago, began to share with us, for our salvation, the same breath of death and danger, having been born from the same roots as we are. Surely a work far more admirable than the whole construction of the universe. For God, the maker of the world, when he sought the origin of things, devised indeed those things which illustrated his glory in every way. He showed goodness, because he filled the world with all good things and mixed in nothing evil. He declared wisdom, while he adorned the heavens, constructed with a fixed proportion, and the clay of the human body with understanding, while he brought the formless chaos from disorder into order. Finally, his nature, perfect in itself and brought to its height, shone most brightly in the mirror of omnipotence, because he founded all things, turned the heavens so that nothing more round could be made, kindled the Sun and Moon, defined the courses of the stars, endowed with an infinite multitude and admirable variety, from which the motion of time was to be marked; and at length, under a certain outstanding condition, he formed man, and to his conveniences and uses he bestowed such abundance of things as still flows forth copiously from the fruitfulness of the earth and of animals. But the same God, since it pertained more to his glory and to the grace bestowed in creation as a very great benefit, began to strike new covenants of love with us, after Satan, the plunderer of divine and human things, had drawn our first parents away from the covenant by which they had devoted themselves to God alone, and had inflicted upon them an incurable and deadly wound. And this covenant, which was ratified by the blood of Jesus Christ, ought to be the most certain sign of his highest love towards us. Then he also put forth all his other virtues, and even all, so that he might free us, to whom every punishment and every penalty was owed by highest right, from transgression, and thus bear witness that our redemption is far more excellent than creation. Therefore it was an effect of immeasurable power that Mary, the betrothed, conceived not by the custom of nature but as a virgin, bore as a virgin, and was a virgin mother. It was an effect of ineffable mercy that he embraced us with such charity that he gave his only-begotten Son, who by a voluntary death would drive from us the wicked crime of defection and eternal condemnation. It was an effect of supreme justice that, before he allowed unpunished licence to nourish the unbridled fury of sinning and suffered his offence to remain unavenged, he willed that the Son whom he begot from his own mind, whom he loved alone, should seek death for us. Yet to temper these two into one form, that is, to exercise at once the strict rigour of justice and the liberality of mercy, belonged only to perfect and consummate wisdom. Therefore, Lord Jesus, we owe more to your nativity, by which we have been redeemed, than to the work by which we have been created. "It would not have profited to be born, unless to be redeemed had profited," exclaims Ambrose. The angels look up to and admire this immensity of divine majesty, this lavish will of God toward men. The ways of Bethlehem are celebrated by a multitude of messengers sent from heaven; the voices of singers exult with incredible rejoicing. Hear, hearers, the angelic harmony, and learn carefully all the words of the messenger, when, eager and joyful, he flies, dances, and sounds forth thus:

units.la: Natus est vobis hodie Redemtor: Gaudium magnum, pecoris magistri: Sed tamen toti [?] populo futurum, Nuncio vobis.
units.tr: "A Redeemer is born to you today: great joy for the master of the flock; but it is to be for the whole people; I announce it to you."

units.la: Confestim incredibili celeritate advolat omnes angelorum ordines, frequentissima celebritate laetantur, atque ita concrepant. Gloria in excelsis Deo, et in terra pax, in hominibus benevolentia. Præterveĉta est aures vestras, Auditores, pergravis & perbrevis angelorum symphonia. Annon ex ejus recordatione plus voluptatis, quam quovis concentu videmini vobis capere? Atqui verius ad nostram quàm ad angelorum salutem spectat hoc redemtionis beneficium. Ex nostro igitur ore nulla exibit gratitudinis significatio? Nos singulari honore non decorabimus, quod illi non solum facto suo sed etiam exemplo summis laudibus efferunt? Præsertim vero, qui in scholis versamur, voces & clamore omnes profundere ac symphoniae coelesti applaudere debemus. Sicuti enim angeli in coelis nostram personam & simulacrum quodammodo gerunt, ita nos agminum cœlestium imago quædam in terris sumus. In nos omnium oculorum animorumque contuitus dirigitur, ex nostris factis exempla peti solent. Nostro exempla agūt alii, quod fe dignum est, quod sperare, quod reddere Deo decet. Non igitur strictim à nobis percurrenda est hujus beneficii memoria, ne nō ad aliorum aures permanet, sed perattentè recolenda ejus prædicatio, aliis voce præeundo & nostra eos sedulitate invitando. Intelligitis, Auditores, quo consilio suscepta sit hæc dicendi consuetudo.¦Eâ enim mentes nostræ commodissimè præparantur, & vehementissimè inflammantur ad meditationem & celebrationem nativitatis tot modis admirandæ, pro quâ hoc inprimis anni puncto manibus passis gratiæ Deo sunt agedæ. De me quod maximè à vobis petendum est idcirco non peto, quòd de humanitate vestrâ planè sim persuasus. Irepidè hunc locum attigi & conscendi, audire alios quàm dicere paratior conscientiâ infantiæ meæ, cui spero veniam facilè tributis, si intellexeritis à me in hoc dicendi loco pietatis potiùs quàm orationis, obedientiæ quàm eloquentiæ, officii quàm ingenii partes esse suscepțas, quæ mihi à Reverendis Dominis Præceptoribus meis sunt impositæ. Quicquid verò & quantumcunque dicere conatus fuero, absorbebit, Auditores, orationem meam mysterii tractandi profunditas. Quid meam dico? Imò omnium angelorum & eloquentissimorum hominum linguæ omnes hic tantum balbutiunt. Nulla mens, nulla oratio, cogitatione aut verbis consequi id potest. Video vos attentissimis animis propositionis meæ exspectare initium, & vel le audire domi meditata vobis prælegentem, memoriæ autem suæ adolescentiori nunquam antea exercitatæ plus fortassis in tanto doctorum consessu quàm alibi diffidentem. Itaque non faciam longius: Cùm etiam ex infantium & lactentium ore laudem suam se perficere velle Deus testetur, cur mea me ab hoc obsequio absterreat infantia? Quare, quò minus aberret oratio à via, vestigia cantici illius sequar, quo primum hoc incarnati Filii Dei mysterium à choro angelico est patefactum & celebratum; Expositurus principio, Quid angeli de Christo nato cœlitus annuncient: Post-ea, quali carmine natales ejus & tàm admirandi operis laudes decantent. Vos ad S.Spiritus verba audienda nunc animos erigite, Erant autem pastores (inquit Lucas historiæ suæ capite secundo) in regione prope Bethlehem sita excubantes & agentes noctis vigilias super gregem suum. Et ecce angelus Domini superveniit ipsis, & gloria Domini circumfulsit eos: Et timuerunt timore magno. Tunc dixit eis angelus, Ne timete. Ecce enim evangelizo vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit toti populo: quia natus est vobis hodie Servator, qui est Christus Dominus in urbe Davidis. Et repente adfuit cum angelo multitudo exercituum cœlestium laudantium Deum & dicentium: Gloria in altissimis Deo, & in terra pax, & in hominibus benevolentia.
units.tr: Immediately, with incredible speed, all the orders of angels fly up, rejoice with the most crowded celebration, and thus harmonise: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." The symphony of the angels, very weighty and very brief, has passed into your ears, hearers. Do you not seem to yourselves to draw more pleasure from its remembrance than from any concert whatever? And yet this benefit of redemption concerns our salvation more truly than that of the angels. Shall no sign of gratitude therefore come from our mouth? Shall we not adorn with singular honour what they extol with the highest praises, not only by their deed but also by their example? Especially we who spend our time in schools ought to pour forth voices and shouts and applaud the heavenly symphony. For just as the angels in heaven bear, in a way, our person and likeness, so we on earth are a certain image of the heavenly hosts. Upon us the gaze of all eyes and minds is directed; examples are wont to be sought from our deeds. Others act by our example what is fitting, what is to be hoped for, what is proper to render to God. Therefore the memory of this benefit must not be run through hastily by us, lest it not reach the ears of others, but its proclamation must be recalled with careful attention, going before others with our voice and inviting them by our diligence. You understand, hearers, with what purpose this manner of speaking has been undertaken. For by it our minds are most conveniently prepared, and most vehemently inflamed, for the meditation and celebration of a nativity admirable in so many ways, for which, at this particular point of the year above all, thanks must be rendered to God with hands outstretched. What I most of all must ask of you I do not ask, for the reason that I am quite persuaded of your humanity. I have approached and mounted this place with trembling, more prepared to hear others than to speak, conscious of my youth, to which I hope pardon will readily be granted, if you have understood that in this place of speaking I have undertaken the role of piety rather than of oratory, of obedience rather than eloquence, of duty rather than of talent, which have been imposed upon me by my Reverend Teachers. But whatever and however much I try to say, Hearers, the depth of the mystery to be treated will swallow up my speech. Why do I say mine? Indeed the tongues of all the angels and of the most eloquent men only stammer here. No mind, no speech, can attain it by thought or by words. I see that you, with most attentive minds, await the beginning of my proposition, and perhaps you wish to hear me recite what I have meditated at home, while my memory, never before exercised in its youth, is perhaps more distrustful in so great an assembly of learned men than elsewhere. Therefore I shall not go on longer. Since God also bears witness that he wills to perfect his praise even from the mouths of infants and sucklings, why should my infancy keep me away from this duty? Wherefore, so that my speech may stray less from the way, I shall follow the traces of that song by which this mystery of the incarnate Son of God was first revealed and celebrated by the angelic choir: about to set forth, first, what the angels announce from heaven concerning Christ born; afterwards, in what kind of song they sing his nativity and the praises of so admirable a work. Now raise your minds to hear the words of the Holy Spirit. "There were shepherds," says Luke in the second chapter of his history, "in the region near Bethlehem, keeping watch and keeping the night watches over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them; and they feared with great fear. Then the angel said to them, Do not fear.
