For behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all the people; for there is born to you today a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, and good will toward men."

units.la: O inauditam clementiam, ô incredibilem amorem Dei & nulla unquam ratione satis celebrandum. Unicum coæternum Filium suum non modo in carnem misit ac donavit clementissimus Pater, qui miseris mortalibus salutem redderet; sed angelos etiam legatos cœlitus addidit, qui rem tam mirandam & mundo incognitam aperuerunt, & ad bene sperandum quasi signum aliquod primam Evangelii vocem sustulerunt. Aut enim hominibus, in tenebrarum & ignorantiæ densissima nebula palpantibus, vel potius sepultis, cœlitus hæc nova lux accendenda erat, & novus ac lætissimus hic nuncius afferendus, aut perpetuo delituisset pretiosissima salutis gaza, & obsignatus, clausus, incognitus thesaurus vitæ nihil profuisset. Unde igitur potissimum incipiam? Mirabar, si sileres, ô nasuta humani ingenii ratio. Quæris enim, cur ad pastores missa sit pacificatoria hæc legatio. Cur non magnates illi tui, duces dynastæ, principes tetrarchæ, reges monarchæ, Imperatores Cæsares eo munere digni judicati fuerint, quibus nihil magnificentius? Hic ego tuam loquacitatem similima interrogatione irretitam retardabo. Dic enim nobis, Cur ex paupere matre, cur inter pecora natus, cur infans in præsepi reclinatus, cur fasciis laceris involutus sit rerum omnium Dominus? Est hæc mira res, quæ profanorum ingenio non capitur, sed credentium judicio expenditur. In nostrum commodum miser & egenus fuit, ut paupertate sua in stabulo divites nos redderet in cœlo, utque in hoc mundi ambitu ne quidem vestigium terrestris regni se facere significaret. Tametsi enim laurea ejus cruentis parta laboribus infinito tempore non amittit viriditatem: in hisce tamen imperiis pravitate conflaccescentibus non floret. Divina quippe est non mundana. Commodissimum autem id erat ad salutis mysterium perficiendum. Sic enim latere eum oportuit, ne agnitus ante tempus gloriae Dominus non crucifigeretur. Videri eam passus est, sed quasi per caliginem praestringente animorum aciem misera quidem illa & flebili specie verum ad salutem necessaria, quoad ex morte resurgeret, & redivivus aeternę gloriae adyta in coelis subiret. Ex quo nimirum documentum nos capere Deus monuit, quid ipse moretur sapientiam & potentiam hujus mundi. Evangelii esculenta sapientibus mundi non sapiunt, potentes, apud Deum potentes esse desinunt. Prudentes hujus saeculi pudore suf-funduntur, stulti & ignobiles in sapientiae schola m deliguntur. Prætereo vaticinium, cujus veritatem Christus ut testatam faceret, advenit nobis Rex pauper & abjectus: atque eâ re nobis fratribus suis exempli fuit atque facti author, quo nullus gravior, nullus constantior. Ponamus ante oculos lumen illud & speculum verae humilitatis, ac in eo imaginem cernemus, quam ita fixam animis teneamus, ut in vitae ratione instituenda morteque oppetenda exprimere eam contendamus. Has igitur causas Deum habuisse non dubitemus, quod in tuguria nō in palatia, in caulas non in aulas nativitatis hujus buccinatores ablegaverit. Quos vero illos? Angelorum chori coelitus legati veniunt, hi natales Christi mundo patefaciunt. Cur hoc quaeso inquam? In ipsis primordiis, dum foetus à S. Spiritu fingebatur, dum animabatur, Gabrielem legatum Deus decreverat; Nunc legiones & exercitus angelorum advenire par erat, qui perfectum, qui genitum, qui omnem salutis spem omnem lætitię causam in ejus nativitate nobis propositam esse confirmarent.
units.tr: O unheard-of mercy, O incredible love of God, which can never be celebrated enough in any way! The most merciful Father did not merely send and give his only co-eternal Son in the flesh, to restore salvation to wretched mortals; he also added angels as messengers from heaven, who revealed a matter so wonderful and unknown to the world, and who, as if giving a sign, raised the first voice of the Gospel to encourage good hope. For either this new light had to be kindled from heaven for men groping in the thickest mist of darkness and ignorance, or rather buried in it, and this new and most joyful message had to be brought; or else the most precious treasure of salvation would have remained hidden forever, and the sealed, shut, unknown treasure of life would have profited nothing. Where then should I most fittingly begin? I would have been surprised if you had kept silent, O keen-nosed reason of the human mind. For you ask why this message of peace was sent to shepherds. Why were not those great men of yours, the dukes, lords, princes, tetrarchs, kings, monarchs, emperors and Caesars, judged worthy of that office, to whom nothing is more splendid? Here I shall check your garrulity, caught in a question very like the first. Tell us then: why was the Lord of all things born of a poor mother, why among cattle, why was the infant laid in a manger, why was he wrapped in ragged swaddling clothes? This is a wonderful thing, which is not grasped by the wit of the profane, but is weighed by the judgment of believers. For our benefit he was wretched and needy, so that by his poverty in the stable he might make us rich in heaven, and so that he might show that not even a trace of an earthly kingdom was to be found in this circle of the world. For although his laurel, won by bloody labours, does not lose its greenness through infinite time, yet in these empires, which wither with wickedness, it does not flourish. For it is divine, not worldly. Moreover, this was most fitting for accomplishing the mystery of salvation. For he had to be hidden in this way, so that the Lord, if recognised before the time of his glory, would not be crucified. He allowed himself to be seen, but as if through a mist dulling the sight of minds, in that wretched and mournful appearance which was indeed true and necessary for salvation, until he rose from death and, restored to life, entered the sanctuaries of eternal glory in the heavens. From this, no doubt, God warned us to take a lesson: what he himself disdains, the wisdom and power of this world. The food of the Gospel does not taste of wisdom to the wise of the world; the powerful cease to be powerful before God. The prudent of this age are put to shame, and the foolish and ignoble are chosen in the school of wisdom. I pass over the prophecy, whose truth Christ, to make it witnessed, fulfilled: a King, poor and abject, has come to us; and by this he became for us, his brothers, an example and the author of a deed, than which none is more serious, none more steadfast. Let us set before our eyes that light and mirror of true humility, and in it we shall see an image which we should hold so firmly fixed in our minds that we strive to express it in ordering our life and in facing death. Therefore let us not doubt that God had these reasons, that he sent the heralds of this birth not to palaces but to huts, not to courts but to sheepfolds. But who were they? Choirs of angels, sent from heaven, come, and these reveal the birth of Christ to the world. Why, I ask? In the very beginning, while the offspring was being formed by the Holy Spirit, while it was being animated, God had decreed Gabriel as his messenger; now it was fitting that legions and armies of angels should come, to confirm that the one who was perfect, the one who was begotten, and every hope of salvation and every cause of joy had been set before us in his birth.

units.la: Tum vero non minore gloria aperiri debuit Evangelii patefactio quam legis promulgatio, Majorem certe eventus demonstravit. Lex quidem ipsa, Deo tonante lata, Deo exarante perscripta, Deo dictante iterum in tabulis incisa, cœlesti clamore rogata, sed consternato sed gemen-te populo approbata. Quæ enim illa tempestas? quis ille fragor? cujus vim Israelitæ sustinere non poterant. Lator ipse legis in montis descendit verticem, maximo igne caliginis nubiumque telis stipatur, agmen angelorum sequitur, montis aditus divino mandato sepiuntur, ab ingressione omnes propulsantur. Mons fumat, flagrat, trepidat. Lex inter fulmina & tonitrua tubarumque strepitus proclamatur. Illa igitur omnia auditu horrenda & formidabilia non modo aspectu. At hic lętissimę rei nuncius iis, qui nihil minus exspectabant, ex alto imminet, quibus favore numinis tanta felicitas obtigisset, gratulatur, timorem oem[?] blando alloquio adimit. Quę possumus recordari in vita pastoribus istis illuxisse die lætiorem? Gloriosa oia[?] plena lætitię, plena consolationis. Inquies, Animum illis legati afferre debuerunt, timorem attulerunt. Quæro, si quisquam vestrum eo fuisset loco, quod sensisset aliud? Splendebat nova lux, quę nec Solis erat nec Lunę nec consueti ignis: Oculo: fulgor perstringebat. Hoc cum esset lęti ominis, tamen ob insolitum ac subitum prodigium, quid mirum, homines i-psâ admiratione obstupefactos tàm insperato nuncio percelli? Hic profectò pavor non ex ju-cundissimo angelorum numero, sed ex naturę nostræ igniculos tantæ majestatis ferre non va-lentis infirmitate qua sæpè labimur, exstitit. Li-cet verò in ejusmodi casu maleficiorum conscie-tia obversari soleat, non tamen ad desperationem pastoribus injiciendam tantâ gloriâ angeli com-paruerunt, sed ut illi cœlestis legationis sensu af-secti hos amplius revererentur, & authoritas de-bita his internunciis conciliaretur.
units.tr: Then indeed the revelation of the Gospel ought to have been made known with no less glory than the promulgation of the Law; certainly the event showed it to be greater. The Law itself was given with God thundering, written out with God burning, cut again in tablets with God dictating, proposed with a heavenly clamour, yet approved by a dismayed and groaning people. For what a storm that was! What a crash! Its force the Israelites could not endure. The giver of the Law himself came down to the summit of the mountain, surrounded by the greatest fire of darkness and by the darts of clouds; a host of angels follows, the approaches of the mountain are fenced off by divine command, and all are driven back from entering. The mountain smokes, blazes, trembles. The Law is proclaimed amid lightnings and thunders and the din of trumpets. All those things were terrible and frightful to hear, not merely to see. But here the messenger of a most joyful matter hangs from on high before those who expected nothing less, and to those upon whom such great happiness had fallen by the favour of the divine power he gives congratulations, and he removes fear with a gentle address. What more joyful day could we recall having dawned on those shepherds in their life? Glorious, full of joy, full of consolation. You will say: the messengers ought to have brought them peace, but they brought fear. I ask, if any of you had been in that place, what would you have felt otherwise? A new light was shining, which was neither that of the sun, nor of the moon, nor of ordinary fire; it dazzled the eye with its brightness. Although this was of a joyful omen, yet because of the unusual and sudden portent, what wonder that men, stunned by the very admiration, were struck down by such an unexpected message? Here, surely, the fear arose not from the most pleasant number of angels, but from the weakness of our nature, which cannot bear the sparks of so great a majesty, and by which we so often fall. Although in such a case a consciousness of wrongdoing is wont to stand before the mind, yet the angels appeared with such great glory not to cast the shepherds into despair, but so that, affected by the sense of the heavenly embassy, they might revere these messengers all the more, and that due authority might be won for these heralds.

units.la: Quod ergò nuncium tandem afferunt? Gau-dium magnum, lętitiam perennem universæ Ec-clesiæ futuram sine fine. Et quamnam? De nato nobis Servatore, qui nos sceleribus [?] solutos cum Deo reducit & restituit in gratiam. At quonam illo: De Christo Domino nato in civitate Da-vidis: de quo angelus prædixerat, futurum esse magnum, & filium altissimi, qui thronum Patris sui Davidis teneat, qui collapsum Davidis regnum instauret, qui super domum Iacob in æternum regnet, & cujus regni non sit futurus finis. Ta-lem ac tantum Dominum cùm natum dicunt, utiq; Deum hominem factum esse dicunt. Quis enim omnium rerum Dominus? Deus. Quis verè magnus? Deus. Quis altissimus altissimi fi-lius? Deus. Quis regnum possidet æternum? Deus. Quis, de quo David, Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede à dextris meis? Deus. Quis igi-tur hic tur hic nisi Deus aut esse, aut si ita placet fingi possit?
units.tr: What, then, do they finally bring as news? "Great joy," an everlasting gladness for the whole Church, to be without end. And what joy? That a Saviour has been born to us, who reconciles us to God, releases us from our sins, and restores us into grace. And who is this? Christ the Lord, born in the city of David: of whom the angel had foretold that he would be great, and the Son of the Most High, who would hold the throne of his father David, who would restore the fallen kingdom of David, who would reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of whose kingdom there would be no end. When they say that such and so great a Lord has been born, they assuredly say that God has been made man. For who is the Lord of all things? God. Who is truly great? God. Who is the Son of the Most High? God. Who possesses an eternal kingdom? God. Who is he of whom David said, "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand"? God. Who then could this be, unless God, or, if it so pleases, one who can be imagined to be God?

units.la: Quia tamen naturam assumsit humanam, hodie natus dicitur. Ac ne rem pulcherrimam transiliat oratio, hunc unum diem, hunc unum, inquam, hodiernum diem (cogitate me aut cum angelis aut cras loqui) quo salutis nostrae jacta sunt fundamenta, diligentius quaeso mecum expendite. Comparant angeli tempus datae olim promissionis & longissimae exspectationis cum praesenti utriusque complemento, quasi dicant: Jam olim promissum Patribus fuit semen illud contriturum caput Serpentis; Jam olim Patrum spem & fidem sustentavit Prophetae oraculum de virginis partu, futurum nempe ut virgo concipiat & pariat Filium, cujus nomen vocetur Immanuel. Hodie hodie natus est vobis Servator ille, semen illud, Filius ille virginis.
units.tr: Yet because he assumed human nature, he is said to be born today. And so that my discourse may not pass over this most beautiful matter, I ask you to weigh carefully with me this one day, this one, I say, present day (think of me speaking either with the angels or tomorrow), on which the foundations of our salvation were laid. The angels compare the time of the promise once given and of the very long waiting with the present fulfilment of both, as if they were saying: Long ago it was promised to the fathers that that seed would crush the head of the Serpent; long ago the oracle of the prophet concerning the virgin's birth sustained the hope and faith of the fathers, namely that a virgin would conceive and bear a Son, whose name would be called Immanuel. Today, today there has been born to you that Saviour, that seed, that Son of the virgin.

units.la: Jam nova progenies coelo demittitur alto,
units.tr: Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven,

units.la: Ultima primavi venit jam carminis aetas,
units.tr: Now the last age of the song of Virgil has come,

units.la: Jam puerum virgo peperit, quo ferrea primum
units.tr: Now a virgin has borne a child, by whom the iron

units.la: Desinet ac toto surget gens aurea mundo;
units.tr: Race shall cease, and a golden race shall rise through all the world;

units.la: Quo duce, si qua manent sceleris vestigia vestri
units.tr: Under whose leadership, whatever traces of your wickedness remain,

units.la: Irrita perpetua solvent formidine terras.
units.tr: Shall dissolve the lands, made void, from perpetual dread.

units.la: O diem felicem pastoribus, nobisque omnibus ad posteritatis memoriam gloriosam. Quidni exclamemus cum Augustino? O exspectatum diem, o festum diem & faustum, quem Servator natus de Patre sine die, per quem factus est omnis dies, natalem hunc diem habere voluit ex virgine. Si miramur in die, miremur potius aeternum Servatorem ante omnem diem permanentem, omnem diem createm, tem,in die nascentem, à malitia diei liberantem.
units.tr: O happy day for the shepherds, and for all of us, to be remembered gloriously by posterity! Why should we not cry out with Augustine: O expected day, O festive and auspicious day, which the Saviour, born of the Father without day, through whom every day was made, chose to have as his birthday from a virgin. If we marvel at him in time, let us marvel rather at the eternal Saviour, who abides before every day, who created every day, who was born in time and who delivers from the evil of the day.

units.la: Multa insuper de hoc Prophetæ prædixerunt, Evangelistæ enarrarunt multa. Angelus Davidis urbem appellat, ut Ecclesia hunc Iesum Patribus promissum certâ fide complectatur. Michæas enim Bethlehem in Iudeâ oppidulum ab Ephrata Calebi uxore cognominatum assignat, quod Messiæ ortu futurum sit nobilissimum. Ovantes ac prope triumphantes ingredimur ea, quæ angeli præceperunt & ultra quàm fines terræ peragrarunt, gaudia. Servator non externam salutem nobis contulit, sed interiorem nullis spoliatam ornamentis reddidit: Lethifera peccatorum tela animarum intenta jugulis extorsit, contra mortis æternæ formidines suæ mortis præsidio animum & latera nostra tutatus est, Diabolum exultantè, apud quem vitæ nobis insidiæ erant positæ, repressit, fundamenta denique jecit, quibus tenere cursum justitiæ & capere vitæ illum portum ac dignitatis æternæ ipsius fulti gratiâ & robore valeamus. Quòd si Sacrosanctæ Scripturæ authoritas satis apud nos hac in re ponderis habet, audiamus primò Gabrielem nominis Iesu interpretem, cùm ait: Ipse liberabit populum suum à peccatis ipsius: Et ad Hebræos epistolam: Quoniam pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter factus est particeps eorundem, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis habet imperium, hoc est, Diabolum, & liberos redderet, quotquot per omnem vitam obnoxii erant servituti. Et Iehova apud Iesaiam de filio suo pollicetur: Cognitione sui justificabit justus servus meus multos. De quo eodem Daniel inquit: Æternam justitiam reducet: Et ipse de se: Ego ovibus meis do vitam æternam. Mo-dum scire qui desiderat, officii ejus partes in tria distinctas munera contempletur. Propheta no-ster est, qui e sinu Patris æternam voluntatem de redemtione nostri protulit, qui ministerium Ecclesiæ instituit, qui per id feliciter operatur corda erudiendo non tantum rem docendo. Sacer-dotio fungi intelligitur, quando victimam ultrò sese obtulit, obsequio suo Patris iram mitigavit, salutis deprecator intercedit ne preces & lacrymas piorum repudiet, & pios promovet conatus. Regem agit Ecclesiæ, dum etiam spiritu suo præstat eamque regit ut efficiat, non solum verbo imperat, quod est faciendum, hostes potentia frenat in æternas pœnas mox deturbaturus. Hoc item triplici officio bis servat salutem, semel ærumnâ, iterum gloriâ suâ, aut merito potius suo, ut in scholis loquimur, & efficaciâ. Primum e-nim ipsum verbum mortis corporis & animi o-mnibus modis devoravit, cùm extremum spiritum in victoriam effudit, hoc sacrificio culpæ liberationem nobis promeritus. Deinde reatu sublato errati veniam nobis impetravit, postea-quam omnia beneficia, quæ in sua morte sepulta jacebant, nobis applicavit. S. Spiritus virtute & vi resurrectionis nostræ ac gloriosæ conditionis, in qua vivit. Justitiâ vicit, vitâ vicit, gloriâ vicit: Ju-stitiam dedit, vitam dedit, gloriam dedit. Hoc est illud gaudium, quod honorificentissimis verbis angelus prosequitur, & gaudium magnum appellat.
units.tr: Moreover, the prophets foretold many things about this, and the evangelists related many things. The angel calls it the city of David, so that the Church may embrace with sure faith this Jesus, promised to the fathers. For Micah assigns Bethlehem in Judah, a little town named after Ephrath, the wife of Caleb, to be most noble because the birth of the Messiah would take place there. Exulting and almost triumphant, we enter upon those joys which the angels proclaimed and which spread beyond the bounds of the earth. The Saviour did not bestow on us an outward salvation only, but restored us inwardly, stripped of nothing, adorned with every gift: he wrested the deadly darts of sins, aimed at the throats of souls, away from us; against the terrors of eternal death he protected our spirit and our sides by the defence of his own death; he restrained the Devil, who was exulting, and with whom snares for our life had been laid; and finally he laid the foundations by which we may be able to keep to the course of righteousness and reach that harbour of life and of eternal dignity, supported by his own grace and strength. But if the authority of Holy Scripture carries sufficient weight with us in this matter, let us hear first Gabriel, the interpreter of the name of Jesus, when he says: He himself shall save his people from their sins. And the Epistle to the Hebrews: Since the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise was made a partaker of the same, that through death he might destroy him who has the power of death, that is, the Devil, and set free all who through the whole of life were subject to bondage. And Jehovah, in Isaiah, promises concerning his Son: By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many. Of this same one Daniel says: He shall bring in everlasting righteousness. And he himself says of himself: I give my sheep eternal life. Whoever desires to know his manner, let him contemplate the parts of his office, distinguished into three offices. He is our Prophet, who from the bosom of the Father brought forth the eternal will concerning our redemption, who instituted the ministry of the Church, who through it works happily in hearts, teaching not merely the matter. He is understood to discharge the office of Priest when he offered himself as a victim of his own accord, mitigated the Father's wrath by his obedience, intercedes as the advocate of salvation so that he may not reject the prayers and tears of the godly, and promotes their endeavours. He acts as King of the Church, while by his Spirit he also supplies strength and rules it so that he may bring about what must be done; he does not merely command by word, but restrains enemies by power, about to cast them down soon into eternal punishments. In this same threefold office he preserves salvation twice: once by his suffering, and again by his glory, or rather by his merit, as we speak in the schools, and by his efficacy. For first, he himself, the Word, devoured death of body and soul in every way, when he poured out his last breath in victory, having by this sacrifice merited our deliverance from guilt. Then, the guilt having been removed, he obtained for us pardon of the offence, after he had applied to us all the benefits which lay buried in his death. By the power and force of the Holy Spirit he applies them to us, and of our resurrection and of our glorious condition, in which he lives. He conquered by righteousness, he conquered by life, he conquered by glory: he gave righteousness, he gave life, he gave glory. This is that joy which the angel pursues with most honourable words, and calls it a great joy.

units.la: An vero soli pastores horum beneficiorum continentur communione? Omnia genera ætatum[?], ordinum, summi medii infimi, viri mulie-res, omnis fortunę ac loci invitantur. Etiam ho-stibus recipiendis augetur civitas cœlestis, pace omnibus oblatâ. Multi tamen in eam se non di-cant, sed ad infirmanda divini fœderis & juris sci-ta prorumpunt, & sic suâ pertinaciâ amittunt vi-tam. Iis, qui credunt in nomen suum jus dedit, ut filii Dei fierent: Ita fides in sanctissimo fœdere, quo de Dei cavetur majestate, adjunctum est & requisitum. Ceteris Iesus non venit Servator sed Iudex, ut iis in nostro etiam conspectu seręnonnunquam sed justę tamen & debitę pœnę persolvantur, ad insigneis ultimi judicii cruciatus semper reservatis. Quam sententiam qui obsti-natione opinionis repudiant, nos non medio-criter lacessunt, quòd eos excludamus, quos ipsi recipiunt; cur non se quoque leviter repungūt, quòd eos injiciunt, quos nos exterminamus? Pereant inimici dummodo vivant filii. Eòsne Deus admitteret, qui ipsum proterve oppugnat, in petulantia nequiter se volutant, pios impiè cōtrucidant. O sanctum dogma, ô diligens præ-conium in convocandis ad salutem hominibus sine mentione fidei, quod alios servat, seipsum servare non potest, præ dissidii, qua sponte rum-petur, copia, in omnes Evangelii promissiones injurium. O beata sœcula! Cœlum impios in-greditur, non ullum videmus hominem cœlo va-cuum. Quid enim aliud clamat illa furia? cùm in omnibus concionibus palàm vociferatur; Im-probos probos Calvinistas & infelices, qui in tali multo-rum miseria perfugium tollunt misericordiae. Du-cat age ducat quisque se ad Christum etiam sine manu fidei, aperui portas (Epicureismo arbitror) vivat in diem, ego illum intromittam, Quia haec fere ei semper patent aedes, hunc Deus curet sci-licet. Deus bone! quantum est clementem esse? Nullus accedit, quin verbis abeat beatior. Sed ca-veamus, nescimus, quanto illudamus viro. Quid est aliud vanum ovium pastorem esse quam lu-pum. Ergóne reiicimus homines? Canes, porcos, flagitiosos, incredulos, Audi obsecro. Quorum furore violati sumus, cur eos vocis libertate non perstringeremus? Cum igitur foedus nostrum fi-dei & religionis vinculo maximè teneatur, hac iam cum exultatione faustisque acclamationi-bus Servatorem Christum excipiamus, & quod pietatis nostrae est, omnibus declaremus, quam memores simus, quamque grati in eius nativita-te decorandâ; quòd laus eius, qui nos salvos praestitit, ad nostrum aliquem fructum redun-det. Praesertim vero, cum angeli singulares ei ho-nores exquisiverint, divinos dedicaverint, atque adeo verba ad immortalitatis memoriam conse-crata reliquerint, gloriae ei munus iusto celebra-tionis honore persolvamus. Nā institutus ordo postulat, ut his explicandis sermo concludatur.
units.tr: But are only the shepherds included in the fellowship of these benefits? All ages, orders, high, middle and low, men and women, every fortune and place, are invited. Even by receiving enemies the heavenly city is enlarged, peace being offered to all. Many, however, do not say that they enter it, but break out to weaken the decrees of the divine covenant and right, and so by their obstinacy they lose life. To those who believe in his name he gave the right to become children of God: thus faith is joined to and required by the most holy covenant, by which provision is made for the majesty of God. For the rest, Jesus did not come as Saviour but as Judge, so that punishments, sometimes delayed even before our eyes but yet just and due, may be paid to them, while the notable torments of the last judgment are always reserved. Those who reject this opinion out of obstinacy of belief do not assail us moderately, because we exclude those whom they themselves receive; why do they not also sting us lightly, because they cast out those whom we banish? Let the enemies perish, provided the sons live. Would God admit those who attack him insolently, who wallow wickedly in wantonness, who slaughter the godly impiously? O holy dogma, O diligent proclamation in calling men to salvation without mention of faith, which saves others but cannot save itself, injurious to all the promises of the Gospel because of the abundance of discord it will bring on by its own accord! O blessed ages! Heaven admits the wicked; we see no man empty of heaven. For what else does that fury cry out, when she openly shouts in all the sermons: The wicked are good, the Calvinists are unhappy, who in such a mass of wretchedness take refuge from the mercy of God? Let each one lead himself to Christ, even without the hand of faith; I have opened the gates (in my opinion by Epicureanism), let him live from day to day, I will admit him, since these houses are almost always open to him; God, of course, will take care of him. Good God! How great is it to be merciful? No one approaches who does not depart happier by words. But let us beware: we do not know how greatly we are mocking the man. What else is it to be a vain shepherd of sheep than to be a wolf? Do we then reject men? Dogs, swine, the shameless, the unbelieving, hear, I beg you. By whose rage we have been violated, why should we not hold them to account by the freedom of our voice? Since, therefore, our covenant is held most closely by the bond of faith and religion, let us now receive Christ the Saviour with this exultation and auspicious acclamations, and let us declare to all what is the duty of our piety, how mindful and how grateful we are in adorning his birth; so that the praise of him who has rendered us safe may redound to some fruit of our own. Especially since the angels sought out for him singular honours, dedicated divine ones, and left words consecrated to the memory of immortality, let us pay to the glory of him the due honour of celebration. For the ordered plan requires that the discourse be concluded with the explanation of these things.

units.la: D. Lucas historiam in hunc pertexit modum:
units.tr: Luke weaves the history in this manner:

units.la: Et repente adfuit cum illo angelo multitudo exerci-tuum caelestium laudantium Deum & dicentium: Gloria in altissimis Deo, & in terra pax, in hominibus benevolentia.
units.tr: And suddenly there was with that angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.

units.la: Ante omnia indicat, non unum aliquem angelum has laudes cecinisse, sed totas legiones & myriadas cōspiciendas una se præbuis-se,quæ universæ una mente atque una voce con-clamarint,Filio Dei testes adfuerint,gratiam Dei concelebrarint,natalitia Messiæ condecorarint, hæc autem omnia lætitia & gratulatione publica honorarint. O dulcem harmoniam! O honoris aram ad recordationem & spatia æternitatis po-sitam! Intuemini cœli & terræ fabricam,quæ duo compellant & coagmentant angeli,ut horum et-iam consensu honos augeatur, & Dei cum homi-nibus unio significetur. Nullum opus maius,nul-lum gloriosius, nullum commendatius omnium creaturarum memoriæ increbruit, cuius testifi-catio nullibi silebitur, sed semper & in omnibus versabitur terris. Brutus cordis stupor erit non gaudere Dei isto tàm excellenti dono, nefaria linguæ hæsitantia expeditis laudum vocibus non succinere, extrema pertinacia felicitati suæ non congratulari, scelerata ingratitudo laudem gra-tissimâ omnium memoria inclusam suo suffragio testatam non facere. A gloriæ Deo tribuendæ exordio inductum est carmen angelorum: GLO-RIA IN EXCELSIS DEO. Gloriam Deo tribui-mus,quando omnia effecta eius pro divinis agno scimus, & eiusmodi quandam ad eum institui-mus orationem: Quòd tot ac tantas res, quot & quantæ mundi teguntur circumflexu, ex nihilo evocasti,huius gloriæ,ô Deus, socium habes ne-minem: quòd clavos omnium imperiorum solo nutu tenes, in huius quoque gloriæ societatem veram nemo se offert: Inprimis, quòd guberhacula[?] Ecclesiæ in maximo cursu ac fluctibus persecutionum tum tractantur tum in scopum salu-tarem diriguntur, tibi cedit, tuum esse totum & proprium fatemur: quod terrarum orbis ingen-ti diluvio submersus periit, justissimum judicium tuum ducimus: te duce te comite duro Ægyptio-rum & Babyloniorum servitio Israelitæ exierunt, tot prodigiis educti tot miraculis in Cananæam collocati. Similiter de minutissimis Dei ope-ribus statuendum est, quorum (quia multis & di-versis gradibus ad summum culmen ascenditur) eò semper ampliorem gloriam esse putabimus, quò ipsa sunt illustriora, quò vehementius eorum magnitudo in sui nos rapit admirationem. Ergò totum missionis Filii in carnem opus, quantumcunq; est (est autem maximū & angelorum testimonio gloriosissimum) totum inquam Dei est. Lucet in hoc immensa eius bonitas, justitia, sa-pientia, potentia, quibus non modò extulit ja-centes, sed etiam amplificavit pristinam eorum dignitatem. Ut igitur gloriam Deo integram tribuamus, Filium nobis missum omni cogitatione & tota mente intueamur, hilarè amplexe-mur, & osculo testemur amorem benevolentiam fidem & gratitudinem nostram: Solent hanc glo-riam Turcæ extenuare, Judæi arrodere, Ethnici cum innumerabili Deorum multitudine com-municare, Diabolus maximam eius portionem nequicquam sibi vendicare, omnes summatim impii Filium Dei non agnoscentes pro sua quis-que facultate aliquid ex illa decerpere: Siquidem Patrem non honorant, qui non honorant Filiū: Quod si forte accidat, ut in aliquam justitiæ & misericordiæ divinæ notitiam veniant: eius tamen sensu penitus non perfunduntur, ut ad se pertinere firmiter persuasi sint, eoque quantum in se est, bonam gloriæ partem Deo detrahunt. Hanc Dei gloriam non illi tantum hæretici obscurant, qui veram Filii divinitatem aut mendaciis aut convitiis proscindunt, sed etiam, qui humanam naturam cum divina adæquant, neque aliquid eam esse statuunt, nisi omnia transformet sese in miracula rerum, qui utriusque commiscet proprietates, qui unam tollunt & transfigurant in aliam metamorphosi plusquam Ovidianâ.
units.tr: First of all he indicates that not one angel sang these praises, but that whole legions and myriads appeared to be seen together, which all with one mind and one voice cried out together, were present as witnesses to the Son of God, celebrated the grace of God, and adorned the birthday of the Messiah, and honoured these things with public joy and congratulation. O sweet harmony! O altar of honour placed for the remembrance and the spaces of eternity! Look at the fabric of heaven and earth, which the angels address and join together, so that by their consent too honour may be increased and the union of God with men may be signified. No work is greater, no more glorious, no more commendable, has grown in the memory of all creatures, whose testimony will nowhere be silent, but will always dwell in all lands. It would be the stupidity of a brutish heart not to rejoice in this so excellent gift of God, the wicked hesitation of the tongue not to join in with ready voices of praise, extreme obstinacy not to congratulate itself on its happiness, and a wicked ingratitude not to bear witness, by its vote, to the praise most gratefully enclosed in the memory of all. From the beginning of ascribing glory to God the song of the angels was led in: GLORY IN THE HIGHEST TO GOD. We ascribe glory to God when we acknowledge all his works as divine, and set up for him a prayer of this kind: That you have called out of nothing so many and so great things as the circuit of the world encloses, O God, you have no companion in this glory; that you hold the keys of all empires by a mere nod, no one offers himself as a true partner in this glory either: above all, that the helm of the Church is handled in the greatest course and waves of persecutions, and is directed to a saving goal, we confess belongs to you, wholly and properly yours; that the orb of the lands, submerged by a huge flood, perished, we judge to be your most just judgment; under you as leader, under you as companion, the Israelites went out from the harsh servitude of the Egyptians and Babylonians, led out by so many prodigies, placed in Canaan by so many miracles. In the same way, concerning the smallest works of God we must determine that, since one ascends to the highest summit by many and diverse steps, we shall always think their glory to be the greater the more illustrious they themselves are, and the more vehemently their greatness carries us into admiration of them. Therefore the whole work of the Son's mission into the flesh, however great it is (and it is the greatest, and most glorious by the testimony of the angels), the whole of it, I say, belongs to God. In this his immense goodness, justice, wisdom and power shine forth, by which he not only raised up the lowly, but also increased their former dignity. Therefore, that we may ascribe whole glory to God, let us look upon the Son sent to us with all thought and whole mind, embrace him gladly, and bear witness with a kiss to our love, goodwill, faith and gratitude. The Turks are wont to diminish this glory, the Jews to gnaw at it, the heathens to share it with an innumerable multitude of gods, the Devil in vain to claim its greatest portion for himself, and all the impious in sum, who do not acknowledge the Son of God, each to pluck off something of it according to his own ability: for those who do not honour the Son do not honour the Father. If it should happen that they come to some knowledge of the justice and mercy of God, they are nevertheless not thoroughly imbued with its sense, so that they are firmly persuaded that it pertains to themselves, and so, as far as it lies in them, they take away a good part of the glory from God. This glory of God is obscured not only by those heretics who tear apart the true divinity of the Son either by lies or by reproaches, but also by those who make the human nature equal to the divine, and who hold that it is nothing unless it transforms itself into the miracles of things, who mix together the properties of each, who take away one and transform it into another by a metamorphosis more than Ovidian.

units.la: Nunc demum in mentem venit requirere, cur beneficium redemtionis ad celebrandum in al-tissimis dicatur expositum non etiam in terris, cū eius gloria vix cœlo capi posse videatur. Sed ut exceptio facit ne liceat, ita necesse est licere, ubi non est exceptum. Imò magis in terra laudem eius audiri oportere certum est, quod præreli-quis locis ipsa id acceperit. Nos, qui in terris degimus, una illorum omnium causa soli fuimus. Interim probamus plenioré laudem in cœlo esse & semper fore propter perfectam beneficii completionem. Nam vagaretur modo nomen eius longè atque latè, nisi sedem stabilem & domicilium certum in cœlis haberet.
units.tr: Now at last it occurs to me to ask why the benefit of redemption is said to be proclaimed "in the highest places" for celebration, and not also on earth, since his glory seems scarcely able to be contained in heaven. But just as an exception makes a thing not allowed, so where there is no exception, it must be allowed. Indeed it is certain that his praise ought to be heard more on earth, since the other places have received it from this one. We, who live on earth, were the sole cause of all those others. Meanwhile we grant that the fuller praise is in heaven, and always will be, on account of the perfect completion of the benefit. For his name would wander far and wide, unless it had a stable seat and a fixed dwelling in the heavens.

units.la: Deinde, ut simul revertar ad illud, quod mihi in hoc secundo orationis membro est propositum, expressis verbis angeli annectunt, INTER-RAPAX, ut homines præcipuè ad celebrationem cohortentur. At quam non modo non credibiliter sed ne suspiciosè quidem, fi modò pax appellanda est tràquilla libertas. Vix nato Christo, Herodes Judæorum bimulos ad mortem quærit, & puerulorum cæde cruentat urbem, Serva-tore nostro solum vertente civitatis. Taceo[?] protomartyres Novi Testamenti, quos lapidibus, ferro, facibus, & ipso religionis nomine deletos accepimus. Nec hodie quidam in judicia orthodoxos rapere desistunt, ut eos errore quodam uti volunt justitiæ & misericordiâ, inclusione non contenti patriâ privent. Quæ ibi pax, ubi omnia furore conquassata discordiis pascuntur? Christus utique protestatur: Non veni pacem mittere sed gladium. Ad spem, proh dolor, inanem pacis devolvimur, sub cuius nomine bellum latet. Sic caro dictitat, sic ratio judicat, quid Spiritus regerit? quid Scriptura respondet? Cùm o-mnium peccatorum quæstiones sint, conscientiis nostris Christus pacem affert, quam explora-tam habere & servare opus est, ne spe præsentis perpetuam amittamus. Hæc fideles mutuâ charitate conglutinat, copulat unitate fidei & Spiritus, largitur prosperitatem, ut omnia cooperentur in bonum. Hæc peccatis abolitis nos Deo conciliat. Huius fiduciâ pugnandum est, quæ nō mundi sed Christi pax est.
units.tr: Next, so that I may return at once to that which is set before me in this second member of the oration, the angels expressly add PEACE ON EARTH, so that they may chiefly urge men to celebrate. But how little credible this is, or even suspicious, if indeed freedom in tranquillity is to be called peace! Scarcely was Christ born when Herod sought the lives of the Jews' infants, and stained the city with the slaughter of little boys, while our Saviour fled from the city. I say nothing of the first martyrs of the New Testament, whom we have heard were destroyed with stones, iron, torches, and even in the name of religion. Nor today do some cease to drag the orthodox into courts, so that, not content with banishing them from their country, they may, under some pretext of justice and mercy, deprive them of their homes. What peace is there where all things are shaken by fury and fed by discords? Christ certainly declares: "I came not to send peace but a sword." We are carried down, alas, to a vain hope of peace, under whose name war lies hidden. So the flesh keeps saying, so reason judges; what does the Spirit reply? What does Scripture answer? Since all questions concern sins, Christ brings peace to our consciences, which it is necessary to have and keep examined, lest by hoping for the present we lose the perpetual peace. This peace binds the faithful together in mutual charity, joins them in the unity of faith and of the Spirit, bestows prosperity, so that all things work together for good. This peace, its sins having been abolished, reconciles us to God. We must fight with confidence in it, for it is not the peace of the world but of Christ.

units.la: Hinc illud tertio loco additur, BENEVO-LENTIA IN HOMINES, quæ aliter definiri nequit, quàm gratuitus & pacificus ille Dei amor, quo Pater in Filio acquiescit electis reconciliatus. Chrysostomus tamen & Augustinus vertunt, pax in terra hominibus bona voluntatis, & hanc de iis expoexponunt, qui Christum suscipiunt. Neque enim pax hæc est omnium, sed eos solùm spectat, quos Deus gratiâ bonæ voluntatis dignatur. Quæ est ergò in medio belli causa posita? Mundus, quicquid à sua professione alienum est, Christo teste, odit. At ei quosdam incolas separavit sibi Deus, quorum conscientiæ iisdem cum illo flagitiis non devinciantur, sed præclaris operibus suis ad voluntatem Dei conformatis lætentur. Ita ex hac parte modestia & veritas pugnant illinc mendacium & petulantia, illic virtus hic vitium, hinc pietas illinc libido.
units.tr: Hence, in the third place, is added GOODWILL TOWARDS MEN, which can be defined in no other way than as that free and peaceful love of God by which the Father, reconciled in the Son, rests upon the elect. Chrysostom and Augustine, however, translate it "peace on earth to men of good will," and explain this of those who receive Christ. For this peace is not for all, but looks only to those whom God graciously deigns to favour with good will. What, then, is the cause of war set in the midst? The world, whatever is alien to its profession, hates, as Christ witnesses. But God has set apart for himself certain inhabitants, whose consciences are not bound by the same crimes as the world's, but rejoice in their excellent works conformed to the will of God. Thus on this side modesty and truth fight; on that side lying and wantonness; there virtue, here vice; on this side piety, on that lust.

units.la: Sed veniamus aliquando ad clausulam eamq; brevem. Vix enim egemus hortatore. Quoniam ergò crastinus dies adventu Christi Redemtoris festus est ac solennis, ad Servatorem fide complec-tendum procedamus, debitâ eum reverentiâ su-scipiamus, & caveamus, ne nostra fides reconciliatâ gratiâ secus ac decet infirmior videatur. Expressa deinde signa habeamus non adumbrata castimoniæ & sanctitatis, quæ patientiæ & humilitatis radicibus nitatur. Ideò enim Dominus noster (ait Chrysostomus) virginem sibi requisivit hospitium habitandi, ut nobis ostenderet, in casto corpore Deum portari debere. Ac ne nostra superbia in eius humilitate reprehendatur, angusto simus spiritu & animo submisso, cùm nostra causa in stabulum inter stercora se demiserit. Membrorum præterea eius necessitatibus sublevandis officiosissimos nos offeramus, eadem moti ratione. An enim homulum ex argillâ & luto fictum se implacabilem & inexorabilem præbere par est erga eos,ob quos Deus purpuram, sceptrum, insignia regia, id est, divinam gloriam suam de manibus corpore capite deposuerat? Firmatâ harum virtutum stirpe nullo exilii turbine aut malorum tempestate pervertamur, sed praecellentes & constantes nos exhibeamus. Constantes dico? Nescio an melius patientes possim dicere: Stabulum certè animum nostrum minùs debet offendere. Num igitur praesepe? Æquè minus. Salutis enim nostrae honestam necessitatem utrunque habuit. Praemeditemur, ferendum modicè esse calamitatis pondus, nec pudeat nos crucis, si Deo visum fuerit, libenter suscipiendae. Iniquissimâ servi-tute peccati mortis & Diaboli Christus nos liberavit, nos sibi insertos membra sua fecit, collegit & conservavit Evangelii praedicatione ac sui Spiritus potentiâ, summa tandem gloriae ornamenta in nos congesturus. Quare grati simus, nec laudes eius unquam negligamus, sed gloriae eius in hoc etiam vitae curriculo semper serviamus, ut, postquam in alterum erimus reposi-ti[?], aeterna illa celebrationis memoria hanc possit excipere & continuare.
units.tr: But let us at last come to the conclusion, and a brief one. For we scarcely need an exhorter. Since, therefore, tomorrow is the festive and solemn day of the coming of Christ the Redeemer, let us go forth to embrace the Saviour with faith, receive him with due reverence, and take care that our faith, now that grace is reconciled, does not appear weaker than it ought. Let us then have clear signs, not shadowy ones, of chastity and holiness, which rest on the roots of patience and humility. For this reason, "our Lord (says Chrysostom) sought out a virgin as a dwelling-place for himself, to show us that God ought to be borne in a chaste body." And lest our pride be rebuked in his humility, let us be of a narrow spirit and a submissive mind, since for our sake he lowered himself into a stable among the dung. Moreover, let us offer ourselves most dutifully to relieve the needs of his members, moved by the same reason. For is it fitting that we show ourselves implacable and inexorable towards those on whose account God laid down the purple, the sceptre, the royal insignia, that is, his divine glory, from his hands, body and head? With the root of these virtues made firm, let us not be overturned by any whirlwind of exile or storm of evils, but let us show ourselves steadfast and constant. Constant, I say? I do not know whether I may better say patient: the stable, at least, ought to offend our mind less. Then is it the manger? Equally less so. For each had the honourable necessity of our salvation. Let us premeditate that the weight of calamity must be borne with moderation, and let us not be ashamed of the cross, which, if it seems good to God, is to be taken up willingly. From the most unjust slavery of sin, death and the Devil, Christ has freed us; he has made us members of his own body, grafted into himself; he has gathered and preserved us by the preaching of the Gospel and the power of his Spirit, about to heap upon us at last the highest ornaments of glory. Wherefore let us be thankful, and never neglect his praises, but in this very course of life always serve his glory, so that, after we shall have been placed in the other life, that eternal memory of celebration may receive this one and continue it.

units.la: Ut igitur in voto & precibus terminetur oratio, Maximas tibi omnes gratias agimus & habemus, Omnipotens ac Misericors Deus, primum pro Servatore non tantùm nobis nato sed etiam dato & donato. Deinde; quòd Ecclesia per omnes terrae angulos dispersa congregatur, quòd tandem in portu salva à te collocatur: quòd vocem Evangelii dissipatis errorum nebulis claram excipimus, quòd ex superstitione Pontificiâ ad verum tui cultum rectumque vitæ tramitem tra-ducti sumus: quòd scholas constantissimè tueris & diligis, quòd politias incolumes custodis: quòd magistratus pios, qui literarum dent hospitia, serie certa excitas, inprimis quòd pro Illustrissimo Electore nostro religionis purę propugnaculo illo & tranquillitatis muro excubas ac pervigilas: quòd hoc exacto anno præstitisti, ne cœtus e-lectorū omnibus propugnatoribus spoliaretur, quòd Palatinæ inprimis Ecclesiæ contra periculosissimas potentias providisti, ne possessionibus suis moveretur. Noli in his conservandis defatigari, Deus clementissimè. Ad misericordiam tuam abiecti imploramus, exposcimus & obsecramus opem. Bonorum confirma mentem. Hostium consilia infringe, conatus reprime, quisquilias seditionum contere, Pacem concede. Auge cœtus docentium ac discentium. Sed quos multiplicari petimus.
units.tr: So then, that the oration may end in a vow and prayers: we all give and render most mighty thanks to you, Almighty and Merciful God, first for the Saviour, not only born for us but also given and bestowed. Then, that the Church, scattered through all the corners of the earth, is gathered together; that at last she is safely placed by you in the harbour; that we receive the clear voice of the Gospel, the clouds of error having been dispersed; that we have been led out of Papist superstition to the true worship of you and the right path of life; that you most constantly protect and love the schools; that you keep the commonwealths safe; that you raise up pious magistrates, who give a home to letters, in a fixed succession; above all, that for our most illustrious Elector, that bulwark and wall of pure religion and of tranquillity, you keep watch and stay awake; that in the year just past you provided that the college of electors should not be stripped of all its defenders; that above all you provided for the Palatine Church against the most dangerous powers, lest it be moved from its possessions. Do not grow weary in preserving these things, most merciful God. Cast down before your mercy, we implore, demand and beseech help. Strengthen the minds of the good. Break the counsels of the enemies, restrain their attempts, crush the trifles of sedition, grant peace. Increase the congregations of teachers and learners. But those whom we ask to be multiplied.

units.la: Tu modo nascenti puero clementer in illis Sancta fave Lucina Dei, Divina favoris ô Lux te diffunde, Tuus modo regnet Jesus.
units.tr: "Only, to the newborn child, in those things, be kindly propitious, holy Lucina of God; O Light divine, pour yourself out upon him, let only Jesus reign over you."

units.la: Fortuna illis pios principes, posteaquam tot columina Imperii subito subversa conciderunt.
units.tr: Grant them pious princes, fortune, since so many pillars of the Empire have suddenly fallen down overthrown.

units.la: Conserva suos tuis. Nos te oramus tui. Annum denique instantem Ecclesiæ faustum, Palatinatui felicem, nobis salutarem faxis. Solet tua misericordia supplicibus succurrere non longis etiam precibus evocata.
units.tr: Preserve your own with your own. We pray you, we are yours. Finally, make the coming year fortunate for the Church, happy for the Palatinate, and salutary for us. Your mercy is wont to succour suppliants, even when called upon not even with long prayers.

units.la: Exaudi nos Deus noster.
units.tr: Hear us, our God.

units.la: Exaudi nos Pater noster, Fac valere preces nostras, per DOMINUM NOSTRUM JESUM CHRISTUM
units.tr: Hear us, our Father. Make our prayers prevail, through OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

units.la: AMEN.
units.tr: AMEN.

units.la: ORATIO V.
units.tr: ORATIO V.

units.la: DE PERSONA ET BENEFICIIS CHRISTI, EX 2.Corinth. 8.v. 9. Qui cum esset dives:
units.tr: ON THE PERSON AND BENEFITS OF CHRIST, FROM 2 CORINTHIANS 8:9, "Though he was rich"

units.la: Recitata à WENDLINO SECKLERO Heylbrunnensi. Pridie natalis Domini 1595.
units.tr: Delivered by WENDELIN SECKLER of Heilbronn. On the eve of the Lord's birthday, 1595.

units.la: Pio & gravi Consilio, à Maioribus sancitum usuque receptum est, Auditores, ut quemadmodum aliis festis solennioribus anni circulo revolutis: Ita hoc die tanquam παρεγκλῆ[?] crastinæ solennitatis Natalitiæ de admirando divinæ incarnationis mysterio, in præsentia studiosæ juventutis ex hac cathedra aliquid disseratur, quo ad altiorem divinorum beneficiorum considerationem ac celebrationem mentes nostræ excitentur. Quod igitur à vestra humanitate omnes alii ante me ex hoc loco perorantes facilè impetrarunt, idem me quoque iussu superiorum meorum de occultissimis humanæ redemptionis mysteriis, vel tenuiter aliquid repetere conantem, apud vos obtenturum, plane confido, nempe, ut patienpatienter, ac placidè me audiatis, quo vestra æqua nimitate, ac benevolentia oratio mea, ceu placidis subvecta ventis, facilius portum suum consequatur.
units.tr: It has been established by our forefathers, with pious and serious counsel, and it is customary, listeners, that just as something is discussed from this chair before the studious youth on other more solemn feasts of the year's cycle, so on this day, as a preparation for tomorrow's solemn birthday celebration, something should be said about the wonderful mystery of the divine incarnation, so that our minds may be stirred to a deeper consideration and celebration of the divine benefits. Therefore, what all the others who have spoken from this place before me have readily obtained from your kindness, I confidently expect to obtain from you as well, since I am attempting, by the command of my superiors, to say something, however slight, about the most hidden mysteries of human redemption. Namely, that you hear me patiently and calmly, so that my speech, carried as if by gentle winds, may more easily reach its harbour through your fair indulgence and goodwill.

units.la: De historia verò, & de causis incarnationis Filii Dei ex illibata virgine sæpiusculè antehac dictum, meministis. Ne igitur idem repetendo videar vobis molestus esse velle, ab instituto meo non alienum fore censui: breviter, & pro ingenii mei tenuitate explicandum sumere locum illum Apostoli 2. Corinth. 8. quo Corinthios hortatur proposito Christi exemplo, tanquam limpidissimo ineffabilis gratiæ, ac beneficentiæ speculo, ne segniter, aut parce, sed alacriter ac liberaliter conferant eleemosynas ad necessitatem sanctorum in Iudæa sublevandam hisce verbis: Nostis enim gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, cum videlicet pauperem factum esse, cum esset dives, ut vos illius paupertate ditescerētis. Mira evidentia & brevitate hoc dicto Apostolus doctrinâ integram de Christi tum persona tum beneficiis complexus est, quod priusquam miseræ huius nostræ carnis commercium susciperet Filius Dei, ac pauper nasceretur in stabulo, dives fuerit, rerum omnium Dominus ac Deus; quodque tam grave pauperta-tis jugum non propter se, sed propter nos, & pro-pter nostram salutem subierit, quo videlicet ipse pauper, & egenus, nos miseros famelicos cœlestibus bonis impleret, divitesque redderet. Plura de Apostoli argumento nunc non dicam: sed præ-sentis instituti ratione habita, primum explicabo, quæ fuerint divitiæ illæ, quibus Christus fuit di-ves, ves antequā fieret pauper ; Deinde modum, quo factus est pauper, exponam. Tertio loco, cur fa-ctus sit pauper, & quas nobis divitias sua egestate lucrifecerit, oratione persequar.
units.tr: You remember that the history and the causes of the incarnation of the Son of God from the undefiled virgin have been discussed quite often before. So that I may not seem troublesome to you by repeating the same things, I judged it not foreign to my purpose to take up briefly, and as far as the slenderness of my ability allows, that passage of the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 8, where he exhorts the Corinthians, setting before them the example of Christ as the most clear mirror of his inexpressible grace and beneficence, that they should contribute alms for relieving the need of the saints in Judea not sluggishly or sparingly, but eagerly and generously, in these words: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich." With remarkable clarity and brevity, in this saying the Apostle has comprehended the whole doctrine both of the person of Christ and of his benefits: that before the Son of God entered into fellowship with this wretched flesh of ours and was born poor in a stable, he was rich, the Lord and God of all things; and that he undertook this heavy yoke of poverty not for his own sake but for ours and for our salvation, so that he, being poor and needy, might fill us wretched and hungry ones with heavenly goods and make us rich. I will not now say more about the Apostle's argument, but, having regard to the plan of the present discussion, I will first explain what those riches were in which Christ was rich before he became poor; second, I will set forth the manner in which he became poor; third, I will go on to explain why he became poor and what riches he has gained for us by his poverty.

units.la: Principio Apostolus de Christo, Factus, inquit, est pauper, cum esset dives. Plærique hominū in hac delira hærent opinione, ut quamprimum divitias audiunt mox innumera auri talenta, vel argenti pondo vel nummorum acervos, vel fundorum & servorum possessiones immensas sibi somnient: quoties divitis mentio incidit, mox vel Croesum, vel Midam, vel Crassum aliquem animo concipiendum censeant. Opulētia Croesi Lydorum regis, ut nostis, adeo quondam nobilitata fuit apud Græcos, ut fecerit proverbio locum de quo Martialis
units.tr: First, the Apostle says of Christ: "He became poor, though he was rich." Most people cling to this foolish opinion, that as soon as they hear of riches they at once imagine countless talents of gold, or masses of silver, or heaps of coins, or immense estates of lands and slaves; whenever the mention of a rich man arises, they think at once of Croesus, or Midas, or some Crassus. The wealth of Croesus, king of the Lydians, as you know, was once so famous among the Greeks that it gave rise to the proverb from which Martial says: "Though I had been richer than Croesus..."

units.la: Croesō divitior licet fuissem
units.tr: Though I had been richer than Croesus

units.la: Midas, Rex Phrygiæ ita divitiis undique affluebat, ut quicquid attingeret in aurum converte-tur. Marcus cognomento Crassus, opulentia sua tumens negabat divitem esse, nisi qui reditu annuo legionem posset alere: in agris suis possidens sestertium bis millies, hoc est, ære nostro, quinquagies centena aurearum coronatorum millia: Ingentes sanè opes, quarum possessione quis nō dives censeretur? Verùm rectè quidam; Si (in-quit) animus hominis dives, non arca appellanda est: Fuit Marcus Crassus nunquam dives, licet ho-minum opinione, esset togatorum omnium ditissimus; Fuerunt inquam omnes isti minimè divites, sed pauperes divitiarum servi, quippe quorum inexplebili habendi cupiditate semper fuerunt vexati. Nam ipsis etiam Philosophis pau-peres sunt, non qui parum habent, sed qui plura semper appetunt. Non est ergo, cur hic mente concipiamus talem aliquem πλουτοῦντα [?] qui arcas auro, vel nummis plenas possideat, cum audimus, Christum divitem fuisse. Quid ergo? Divitias immensae potentiae, sapientiae & bonitatis, h. e, verae & aeternae divinitatis Apostolus Christo ascribit, qua unus cum patre & Spiritu Sancto fuit Deus, antequam fieret homo, cum dicit ἐπλουτήσας [?] ὧν, ut sit sensus, antequam humanae carnis massam induceret, fuisse rerum omnium Dominum: hoc est Deum: Quis enim absolute ac vere dives, nisi ille qui dicit apud Moysen: Ego El Schadai: Deus omnis sufficientia solus sibi per omnia sufficiens, nullius indigus, nullius extra se appetens, fons omnis boni, halitum, vitam, & motum omnibus creaturis suppeditans: a quo omne bonum donum descendit desuper; distribuens omnia omnibus sicut vult: Si esuriero, inquit apud Psaltem, non dicam tibi; Meus est enim orbis terrae; & plenitudo eius; Et per prophetam; Meum est argentum & meum est aurum. Quis divitem non dixerit regem, qui aurum & argentum totius orbis solus possideat? At ditior multo ipse universum orbem cum omni argento & auro solus possidens Deus. Sed quid aurum, vel argentum? quid orbem dico? quali hae sint potiores Dei divitiae; quid enim carbones isti ad ineffabiles thesauros immensae potentiae, iustitiae, bonitatis, misericordiae, quos Deo soli passim Sanctus Apostolus attribuit? cum praedicat ἀληθινῶν [?] τῆς τοῦ τῆς χρηστότητος, καὶ τῆς ἀνοχῆς, καὶ τῆς μακροθυ-μίας θεοῦ. divitias benignitatis, & lenitatis, & tolerantiæ Dei. Alibi πλοῦτον τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ [?]; divitias gratiæ eius; cum vocat Deum πλούσιον ὄντα ἐν ἐλέει divitem misericordia, cum denique exclamat: O profundas divitias, tum sapientiæ, tum cognitionis Dei? quam inscrutabilia sunt eius iudicia, & eius viæ inpervestigabiles? Quis fuit ei à Consilio? aut quis prior dedit ei? Nam ex eo, & per eum, & in eo sunt omnia: ipsi sit gloria. Amen.
units.tr: Midas, king of Phrygia, so abounded in riches that whatever he touched was turned into gold. Marcus, surnamed Crassus, swelling with his own wealth, denied that anyone was rich unless he could maintain a legion from his yearly income; possessing in his fields two thousand million sesterces, that is, in our money, five hundred thousand gold crowns. These were indeed huge resources, and who would not be thought rich by possessing them? But someone has rightly said: "If the mind of a man is rich, it is not to be called a chest." Marcus Crassus was never rich, although in the opinion of men he was the richest of all the togaed men; I say that all those men were not rich at all, but slaves of riches, poor, since they were always troubled by an insatiable desire to have more. For even among the philosophers, those are poor not who have little, but who always desire more. There is therefore no reason for us to conceive in our minds of someone of that kind, who is rich, possessing chests full of gold or coins, when we hear that Christ was rich. What then? The Apostle ascribes to Christ the riches of immense power, wisdom and goodness, that is, of true and eternal divinity, by which he, one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, was God before he became man; when he says, being rich, that he was the Lord of all things before he took on the mass of human flesh; that is, he was God. For who is absolutely and truly rich, except he who says through Moses: "I am El Shaddai, God all-sufficient," who alone is sufficient for himself in all things, needing nothing, seeking nothing outside himself, the fountain of every good, supplying breath, life and motion to all creatures, from whom every good gift comes down from above, distributing all things to all as he wills? "If I were hungry," he says in the Psalm, "I would not tell you; for the world is mine, and its fullness." And through the prophet: "The silver is mine, and the gold is mine." Who would not call a king rich, if he alone possessed the gold and silver of the whole world? But far richer is God, who alone possesses the whole world with all silver and gold. But why speak of gold or silver? Why do I speak of the world? How much more excellent are the riches of God; for what are those coals compared with the ineffable treasures of immense power, justice, goodness and mercy, which the Holy Apostle everywhere ascribes to God alone, when he proclaims "the riches of the goodness, and forbearance, and long-suffering of God." Elsewhere "the riches of his grace"; when he calls God "rich in mercy"; when at last he cries out: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! Who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him? For of him, and through him, and to him are all things: to him be glory. Amen."

units.la: Satis his demonstratum arbitror, solum Deum vere divitem esse, & in scriptura τὸν πλούσιον appel-lari. Quid vero Apostolus hic de Christo? ἐπτώχευσεν [?] πλούσιος ὢν [?]: factus est pauper, cum esset dives. Quomodo dives? An auri vel agrorum dives? Imo dives opum, quarum & Deus pater: O-mnia enim (inquit) quæ pater habet mea sunt. Et de Spiritu Sancto, qui est unus cum patre Deus: Ille (inquit) me glorificabit: quia de meo accipiet, & annunciabit vobis. Hic est ille dives, qui (ut Lucas habet) diuitiis suis Oeconomum præfecit, imò qui multos dispensatores constituit. Hic ille spō-sus, cui cœlestis pater nuptias adornat Matth.22. & ut rem in pauca conferam, ex huius plenitudine, tanquam inexhausto divitiarum fonte omnes accepimus gratiam pro gratia, ut Iohannes Evangelista testatur. Quare dubium esse non potest, Christum verum cum patre & Spiritu Sancto Deum prædicari, cum priusquam pauper fieret, dives fuisse dicitur.
units.tr: I think it has been sufficiently shown that God alone is truly rich, and in Scripture is called "the rich." But what does the Apostle say here about Christ? "He became poor, though he was rich." How rich? Rich in gold or in fields? Nay, rich in those riches of which God the Father also is possessed: "For all things (he says) that the Father has are mine." And concerning the Holy Spirit, who is one God with the Father: "He (he says) will glorify me, for he will receive of mine and will declare it to you." This is that rich man who (as Luke has it) set a steward over his riches, indeed who appointed many stewards. This is that bridegroom for whom the heavenly Father prepares the marriage in Matthew 22; and, to sum up briefly, from his fullness, as from an inexhaustible fountain of riches, we have all received "grace for grace," as the Evangelist John testifies. Wherefore there can be no doubt that Christ is preached as the true God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, since it is said that he was rich before he became poor.

units.la: Verum enim vero videre mihi hic videor, quid cogitetis; Miramini quid sibi velit hoc divini[?]tis argumetum: Christus fuit dives: ergo Deus. An non dives etiam celebratur in scripturis Abraham, Loth David, Salomon? ut de multis quos extra Ecclesiam divitiis celebres Apostolus ad Timotheum vocat divites huius mundi nihil dicam; Nonne & Epulo apud Lucam fuit dives? Nonne Cicero omnes sapientes divites facit? quis vero istorum propter divitias fuit vel erit Deus? Nemo sane. Sed & nemo vere dives. Nam omnes isti propter ingenitum cupiditatis vitium, nunquam praesentibus contenti, anxia solicitudine semper pluribus inhiabant, plura requirebant. Tales vero an divites fuisse existimabimus? Certe Ethnicus homo Cicero in paradoxis contrarium defendit, divitem eum solum definiens, qui nihil quaerat, nihil appetat, nihil optet amplius: qualis sane nullus unquam fuit, ne Abraham quidem. Nam & iste professus se hospitem & advenam esse in terra, patriam quaesivit in coelis, civitatem habentem fundamenta, cuius artifex & conditor est Deus, teste Apostolo ad Hebr. Et quomodo obsecro has veras opes quis dixerit, quae momentaneae, incertae, variis casibus & periculis expositae sunt, quae improbo labore acquiruntur, acquisitae molestissima cura conservantur: quae non faciunt bonos, sed saepius de malis deteriores, communes bonis juxta & malis, irritamenta malorum, crepundia stultorum. Videtis ergo, omnes istos divites cum suis divitiis διὰ[?] πασῶν differre a Christo.
units.tr: Indeed, I seem to see here what you are thinking; you wonder what this argument of divinity means: Christ was rich, therefore God. Are not Abraham, Lot, David and Solomon also called rich in the Scriptures? I say nothing of the many well-known men outside the Church whom the Apostle to Timothy calls "the rich of this world." Was not Dives also rich in Luke? Does not Cicero make all wise men rich? But which of these was or will be God because of riches? Certainly no one. Yet also no one is truly rich. For all of them, on account of the innate vice of desire, never content with what they had, always gaped after more with anxious care and sought more. Shall we then think that such men were rich? Certainly the heathen Cicero, in his Paradoxes, defends the opposite, defining him alone as rich who seeks nothing, desires nothing, wishes for nothing more; such a man indeed never existed, not even Abraham. For he too, confessing that he was a stranger and sojourner on the earth, sought a country in heaven, "a city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God," as the Apostle attests in Hebrews. And how, I ask, could anyone call those true riches which are fleeting, uncertain, exposed to various accidents and dangers, which are acquired by wicked labour, and when acquired are kept with most troublesome care; which do not make men good, but more often make bad men worse, common to the good and bad alike, incitements to evil, playthings of fools? You see therefore that all those rich men, with their riches, differ in every way from Christ.

units.la: Poteram hic porro proferre interpretationes Orthodoxorum patrum, Ambrosii, Hieronymi, TheoTheophylacti, & aliorum, qui Christum non aliter divitem fuisse asserûnt, antequam fieret pauper, nisi quia Deus erat, ante assumtam hominis naturam. sed ne humanis authoritatibus niti videar, longè dilucidius sacræ scripturæ testimoniis æterna Christi divinitas ante assumptam humanam naturam ostendi potest. Angelum illum Domini, qui olim locutus est patribus, & cuius frequentissima in historia Mosis fit mentio, certè non alium nisi ipsum Deum intelligi posse, inde manifestum est, quod non solum Dei nomine passim salutatur, sed etiam ea, quæ soli vero Deo competunt, eidem adscribuntur.
units.tr: I could here go on to cite the interpretations of the orthodox Fathers, Ambrose, Jerome, Theophylact and others, who assert that Christ was rich before he became poor only because he was God before he assumed human nature. But so that I may not seem to rest on human authorities, the eternal divinity of Christ before he assumed human nature can be shown much more clearly from the testimonies of Holy Scripture. That the Angel of the Lord who once spoke to the fathers, and who is so often mentioned in the history of Moses, can certainly be understood as none other than God himself is evident from this: he is not only greeted everywhere by the name of God, but also those things which belong to the true God alone are ascribed to him.

units.la: Hic autem erat secunda ὑπόστασις[?] sanctissimæ Triados, nempe filius Dei, quem inde ab initio fuisse legatum patris ad Ecclesiam omnium piorum fide tenetur. Deum enim nemo vidit unquam? Filius qui est in sinu patris ipse enarravit nobis. Porrò Psaltes de eo sic pronunciat: Thronus tuus, Deus, in seculum seculi; Virga recta, virga regni tui: Dilexisti justitiam, & odisti iniquitatem: propterea unxit te Deus præ consortibus tuis. Elogium hoc D. Paulus ad Hebr. 1. de filio Dei, antequam humanam naturam sibi associaret exponit. Huc pertinet quod Salomon Prov. 30. quærens quis sit ille, qui ventos & mare, & terras suo nutu dirigit, quod nomen eius? & quod nomen filii eius? aperte agnoscit, jam tum filium Dei fuisse, qui una cum patre, cuncta manu sua teneret. Hunc verò Dei filium fuisse Christum, testatur Apostolus ad Hebræos, ubi cum verbo suo potenti omnia sustinere dicit: Te status est ipse Dominus, cum mare, & ventos ob-iurgavit, iurgavit, hominibus admirantibus ac dicétibus: Qualis est iste, ut venti quoq; & mare auscultent ei? Multo vero clarissimè D. Iohannes Evangelista cap. 10. filii Dei æternam Divinitatem asserit dū Verbum illud, quod ab initio, ante omnes res creatas, Deus, & apud Deum erat, rerum omniū causam simul cum Deo statuit, quippe per quod omnia creata sint, quod omnem hominem illuminet venientem in hunc mundum, quod venerit in propria, quod deniq; carnem assumpserit, & habitaverit inter nos: quæ omnia, nimis absurdi sunt hæretici, dum verbo evanido attribui posse contendunt. Nam quod sit illud verbum, Evangelista satis indicat, cum filium Dei unigenitum à patre, & in sinu patris nuncupat. Hic autem Filius quis fuit nisi Christus, qui à patre exivit, & venit in Mundum, Abrahami semine assumpto? Deniq; non præterc undus est locus Apostoli ad Philip. 2. Christus cum esset in forma Dei non duxit rapinam, æqualem esse Deo, sed seipsum exinanivit forma servi accepta. Idem hoc & isto, quem tractamus loco Apostolus dicit, estque optimus suorum verborum interpres. Quod enim hic dicit: ὁ πλούσιος[?] ὤν[?], cum esset dives; ibi dicit ὁ ἐν μορφῇ[?] θεοῦ[?] ὤν[?]: Cum esset in forma Dei; quod hic: factus est pauper: ibi: assumpsit formam servi; Iam quid est in forma Dei esse? Quid? nisi Deum esse. Nam in forma Dei esse, & Deo æqualem esse, idem Apostolo valent. At Deo æqualem esse, quid est nisi Deum esse? Quis enim æqualis Deo nisi ipse Deus sibi? Cui assimilabitis Deum? & quam similitudinem disponetis ei? inquit Isaias Iesaias cap.40.18. Audiamus D. Basilium: In forma Dei esse, idem valet, atque in essentia Dei existere. Sicut enim formam servi assumpsisse significat Dominum nostrum factum esse essentia humana natura participem: Ita qui prorsus eum dicit in forma Dei existere, divina natura proprietatem repræsentat. Cum Basilio sentiunt Ambrosius, Augustinus, Hilarius & alii, quorum sententias recitare, brevitatis causa supersedeo. Ex quibus omnibus meridiana luce clarius constare jam arbitror, ꝙ demonstrandum fuit; Christum humanæ salutis instauratorem & vindicem, priusquam infimæ carnis nostræ habitum induceret, æqualis gloriæ, potentiæ, & divinitatis cum cœlesti suo patre fuisse. Hæ igitur ejus erant divitiæ, quas possidebat, antequam onus nostræ paupertatis subiret. O ineffabiles & inpervestigabiles thesauros, quorum amplitudinem & maiestatem nulla angelica natura, nedum humana mens satis æstimare possit.
units.tr: Now this one was the second hypostasis of the most holy Trinity, namely the Son of God, who, as is held by faith by all the pious, was from the beginning the messenger of the Father to the Church. For no one has ever seen God? The Son who is in the bosom of the Father has himself declared him to us. Moreover, the Psalmist pronounces of him thus: Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of your kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your fellows. St. Paul in Hebrews 1 expounds this praise of the Son of God as it stood before he joined human nature to himself. To this pertains what Solomon says in Prov. 30, asking who it is that directs the winds, the sea and the lands by his nod: What is his name, and what is the name of his son? He plainly acknowledges that the Son of God already existed then, who together with the Father held all things in his hand. That this Son of God was Christ the Apostle testifies in Hebrews, where he says that all things are sustained by his powerful word: The Lord himself stood up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and men marvelled and said: What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him? Much more clearly St. John the Evangelist in chapter 1 asserts the eternal divinity of the Son of God, when he establishes that the Word, which from the beginning, before all created things, was God and was with God, is together with God the cause of all things, since all things were created through him, since he enlightens every man coming into this world, since he came to his own, and since at last he assumed flesh and dwelt among us. All these things are too absurd for the heretics, who contend that they can be attributed to a fleeting word. For what that Word is the Evangelist makes sufficiently plain, when he calls him the only-begotten Son of the Father, who is in the Father's bosom. But who was this Son, if not Christ, who went forth from the Father and came into the world, having taken on the seed of Abraham? Finally, the passage of the Apostle in Philippians 2 is not unlike this: Christ, though he was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. The Apostle says the same thing in this passage we are treating, and he is the best interpreter of his own words. For what he says here, being rich, there he says being in the form of God; what here is became poor, there is took the form of a servant. Now what is it to be in the form of God? What, if not to be God? For to be in the form of God and to be equal to God mean the same to the Apostle. But to be equal to God, what is it except to be God? For who is equal to God except God himself to himself? To whom will you liken God? Or what likeness will you set up for him? says Isaiah in chapter 40, verse 18. Let us hear St. Basil: To be in the form of God means the same as to exist in the essence of God. For just as the assuming of the form of a servant signifies that our Lord became a partaker of human nature in essence, so he who says that he simply existed in the form of God represents the property of the divine nature. Ambrose, Augustine, Hilary and others agree with Basil, whose opinions I pass over, for the sake of brevity, without reciting them. From all of these I now judge it to be clearer than the noonday light that what was to be demonstrated has been established: that Christ, the restorer and vindicator of human salvation, before he took on the lowly condition of our flesh, was equal in glory, power and divinity with his heavenly Father. These, then, were the riches he possessed before he undertook the burden of our poverty. O unspeakable and unsearchable treasures, whose greatness and majesty no angelic nature, much less a human mind, can sufficiently estimate!

units.la: Detestanda igitur est Vesania Photini, Samosateni, Serveti, & similium ὁμοουσιανῶν[?] satanicus furor, qui Christum ante assumptam hominis formam ne fuisse quidem, sed exordium in virginis utero demum accepisse, blasphemo ore contendunt. An non enim hoc est Apostolo in os contradicere, & proterve negare Christum fuisse divitem, antequam fieret pauper? quandoquidem certum est, ut mox demonstrabitur, eum tunc cœpisse pauperem fieri, quando cœpit homo esse. Neque minus hoc loco nostri Vbiquitarii sunt reprehendendi, qui praeter mentem Apostoli, & contra communem omnium Orthodoxorum explicationem istas Christi divitias, non tam de ejus æterna divinitate, quam de fictitia Majestate, & omnipræsentia humanæ Naturæ intelligunt; neque considerant, quam hac expositione sua ab impio Sar.ofateni [?] dogmate parum absint. Excipiunt quidem, fe agnoscere Christum non solum ut hominem (ut Photinus sentiebat) sed etiam ut Deum divitem fuisse. Verum nec ita fe expediunt, sed in idem lutum recidunt. Etsi enim concedant Christum re-fpectu divinæ naturæ etiam fuisse divitem, hinc tamen necessario concludi nequibit, Christum hominem fuisse Deum, sed tantum fuisse hominem divitem antequam appareret pauper, cum contra Nativitatis historia testetur; ratione hu-manitatis ne momento quidem divitem, sed inox ab utero pauperem fuisse: unde confici-tur necessario, aut divinitate, aut nullomodo divitem fuisse, antequam pauper fieret.
