units.tr: Therefore the madness of Photinus, Samosatenus, Servetus and the like who hold the consubstantial (homoousian) doctrine is to be detested, a satanic fury, who with blasphemous mouths contend that Christ did not even exist before the assuming of the form of man, but began to be only in the womb of the virgin. For is it not to contradict the Apostle to his face, and to deny shamelessly that Christ was rich before he became poor? Since it is certain, as will soon be shown, that he began to become poor only when he began to be man. Nor are our Ubiquitarians to be censured any less on this point, who, contrary to the mind of the Apostle and against the common explanation of all the orthodox, understand these riches of Christ not so much of his eternal divinity as of a fictitious majesty and omnipresence of the human nature. Nor do they consider how little they differ by this exposition of theirs from the impious dogma of Samosatenus. They do indeed except by acknowledging that Christ was rich not only as man (as Photinus thought) but also as God. Yet they do not extricate themselves in this way, but fall back into the same mire. For even if they grant that Christ was also rich with respect to the divine nature, it cannot nevertheless be necessarily concluded from this that Christ was God as man, but only that the man was rich before he appeared poor; whereas, on the contrary, the history of the Nativity testifies that in respect of his humanity he was not rich even for a moment, but was poor from the womb. From this it necessarily follows that he was rich either by his divinity or in no way at all before he became poor.

units.la: Excipient rursus, Non posse tamen negari quin etiam humanitate a matris utero, hæres omnium proinde & dives fuerit. Sed & nos fatemur jus hæreditatis illum tenuisse qui-dem ab utero ; Addimus vero quod necessa-rio addendum est, quod hujus usu, quamdiu inter homines versaretur carere voluerit in ter-ris, donec suscepta paupertatis completo ter-mino hæreditatem adiret in cœlis. Ac dili-genter est attendendum, quod Apostolus su-isse divitem pronunciat etiam ante assumtam hominis naturam, & non quatenus jam illam assumserat, quia ab eo momento, quo humanitatem suscepit etiam paupertati sese subjecit. Af-sumptione enim humanitatis pauper factus est, id quod altera orationis parte nobis porrò ex-plicandum ac demonstrandum venit.
units.tr: They will object again that it cannot be denied that he was also heir of all by his humanity from the womb, and therefore rich. But we too confess that he indeed held the right of inheritance from the womb; yet we add what must necessarily be added: that, as long as he lived among men, he chose to forgo the use of it on earth, until, the appointed term of his assumed poverty being completed, he entered upon the inheritance in heaven. And it must be carefully noted that the Apostle declares him to have been rich even before he assumed human nature, and not in so far as he had already assumed it; for from the moment he took on humanity he also submitted himself to poverty. For by the assuming of humanity he became poor, which is what we shall have to explain and demonstrate further in the second part of this discourse.

units.la: De modo igitur simpliciter tenemus cum D. Ambrosio, Christum, cum dives esset, pauperem esse factum, quia Deus, nasci dignatus est ho-mo, virtutem potestatis suæ humilians, ut homi-nibus divinitatis divitias acquireret. Hæc Catholica est Doctorum Ecclesiæ sententia: Verbum factum esse carnem, Christum cum esset in forma Dei, æqualis Deo, exinanivisse semetipsum forma servi assumpta: Deum manifestatum esse in carne; assumpsisse non angelos, sed semen Abrahæ. Ex quibus liquido constat, filium Dei pauperem factum, quando est factus homo; Sed explicatius aliquanto paupertatis hujus sive partes sive gradus sunt considerandi. Primus fuit ipla ἐνσαρκωσις, incarnatio, quando æternus λόγῳ[?] Dei filius in utero illibatæ virgi-nis Mariæ Spiritus sancti operatione homo conceptus, sibi in unitatem suæ ὑποστάσεως[?] miran-do fœdere naturam sociavit humanam. Tunc enim primò factus est homo. Homine autem quid miserius. Brevis est diebus, & fatur per-turbatione. Sicut flos egreditur & exciditur, in-quit Jobus; Nec tantum factus est homo, sed & omnes naturæ humanæ infirmitates ac mise-rias suscepit, peccato excepto, ut Apostolus ad Hebræos testatur: qua causa D. Johannes non dixit, λόγον esse factum hominem, sed carnem:& noster Apostolus alibi, non formam hominis suscepisse sed servi: hoc etiam loco [illegible, ~9 letters] potius dixit, quam [illegible, ~10 letters], ut extremam mendicitatem & miseriam ejus exprimeret. Proximus gradus fuit ipsa nativitas, egestatis & miseriæ plena; Nascitur enim ex matre paupercula, non in palatio, sed in stabulo, non inter amicos aut clientes, sed inter pecora: non in æstivo tempore sed in brumali frigore: involutus non purpureaut fasciis Phrygionico opere laboratis, sed vilissimis pannis: reponitur non mollibus culcitris, sed hispido fœno: nō cunis pretiosis, sed inculto præsepi. Tanta paupertas tenellum infantulum excepit. Sed vix initia hæc miseriarum fuerunt; Nam si ad reliquum vitæ decursum tertio loco respiciamus, proh Deum immortalem, quas non miseriarum ærumnas est expertus? quid eo pau-perius? Vulpes (inquit ipse) habent lustra, & volucres cœli nidos: Filius autem hominis non habet, ubi caput reclinet. Quid eo infelicius? qui cum benefaceret omnibus, ab omnibus tamen odiis, calumniis, contumeliis, insidiis, violentia deniq; manifesta, indesinenter petitus est, tandemque oppressus. Exposui vel indigitavi potius: Quis enim exponeret satis? plus quam Telenciam egestatem Christi, quem paulo ante Croeso Crasso-quo ditiorem fuisse ostenderam? Vnum videtur addendum; ne hæreticus aliquis cavilletur, si ex divite factus est pauper, Divitem ergo ac Deum esse desiisse, & pauperem duntaxat hominem fuisse, puta, sicut Crassus ille ex ditissimo tandem factus est egenus, adeo ut ab occurrentibus per jocum dives salutaretur, ejusq; hæreditas nequidem creditoribus satisfacere posset. Non ita Christus est depauperatus, quasi divitias suas vel abliguriverit, vel decoxerit, vel amiserit; sed ἀλλά[?] πλούσιος ὢν, ἐπτώχευσεν, dives existens & permanens, factus est mendicus, non divitiarum jacturam faciendo, sed spontaneam egestatem assumendo. Non enim suscipiendo humanitatem sese divinitate abdicavit, sed manens quod erat, factus est quod non erat. Divitias Divinitatis, paupertate carnis ad tempus contexit, simul Deus & homo, dives & pauper existens: dives ut Deus, pauper ut homo. Hinc Zacharias: Rex tuus venit tibi pauper; Pauperem dicit Christum, sed Regem simul nominat; & Iohannes cum dixisset: Verbum factum est caro; addit: Vidimus gloriam ejus, ut gloriam unigeniti à patre. Et D. Paulus: Deus suo sanguine acquisivit Ecclesiam. Ex his consectarium omnino est, hunc Christum vere esse Messiam illum, qui patribus à Deo tot retro seculis fuerat promissus, & ab illis tanto cum desiderio exspectatus. Hic enim talis est, qualis Prophetarum oraculis fuerat prædictus, Gigas ille fortis, geminę cōsors[?] naturę, verus Deus & homo. Hic est semen illud mulieris, conterens caput serpentis, hoc est, verus homo ex virgine absque virili semine natus, & verus Deus Satanam propria potentia conterens. Hic est ille Immanuel, quem Iesaias Deum & hominem prædicat: Deum; quia vocabitur Immanuel, hoc est, nobiscum Deus; Hominé; quia nascetur puer ex virgine, mel & butyrum comedens. Hic est puer ille nobis natus, & filius ille nobis datus, quem idem Isaias cap.9. ut hominem verum, & ut Deum verum describit, expresse Deum fortem, & patrem æternitatis nominans. Hic est germen illud justum Davidi promissum: homo verus, quia ex Davidis posteritate natus: & Deus verus, quia Iehova justitia nostra, ut habet Hieremiæ vaticinium.
units.tr: Concerning the manner, then, we simply hold with Saint Ambrose: Christ, though he was rich, became poor, because God deigned to be born a man, humbling the power of his majesty so that he might acquire for men the riches of his divinity. This is the Catholic opinion of the teachers of the Church: that the Word was made flesh; that Christ, though he was in the form of God, equal to God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; that God was manifested in the flesh; that he took on not angels but the seed of Abraham. From these things it is clear that the Son of God became poor when he became man. But the parts or degrees of this poverty must be considered somewhat more fully. The first was the very ἐνσάρκωσις, the incarnation, when the eternal Word of God, the Son, was conceived by the operation of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the unblemished virgin Mary as a man, and, by a wonderful covenant, joined human nature to the unity of his own ὑπόστασις. For then he was first made man. And what is more wretched than man? "He is short-lived and full of trouble. Like a flower he comes forth and is cut down," says Job. Nor did he merely become man, but he took upon himself all the weaknesses and miseries of human nature, sin excepted, as the Apostle testifies to the Hebrews. For this reason John did not say that the Word had become a man, but flesh; and our Apostle elsewhere says that he took not the form of a man but of a servant. In this place too he said [illegible, ~9 letters] rather than [illegible, ~10 letters], so as to express his utmost beggary and misery. The next degree was his very birth, full of need and misery. For he is born of a poor mother, not in a palace but in a stable, not among friends or clients but among cattle; not in summer but in the cold of winter; wrapped not in purple or in bands worked with Phrygian embroidery but in the meanest rags; laid not on soft mattresses but on prickly hay; not in precious cradles but in a rough manger. Such poverty received the tender little infant. But these beginnings of misery were scarcely the start; for if we look to the rest of the course of his life, as a third point, good God, what distresses of misery did he not experience? What could be poorer than that? "Foxes," he himself says, "have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head." What could be more unhappy than that? Though he did good to all, he was nevertheless beset without ceasing by hatreds, slanders, insults, plots and finally open violence from all, and at last he was crushed. I have set forth, or rather merely pointed out, these things; for who could set them forth sufficiently? Was not the poverty of Christ greater than that of Telencius, whom I showed a little earlier to be richer than Croesus and Crassus? One thing seems to be added, lest some heretic cavil that, if he became poor from rich, then the rich God ceased to be, and he was only a poor man, as that Crassus, from being very wealthy, at last became so needy that people meeting him would greet him jokingly as "rich," and his estate could not even satisfy his creditors. Christ was not impoverished in such a way, as if he had squandered, or wasted, or lost his riches; but "being rich, he became poor" (ἀλλά πλούσιος ὢν, ἐπτώχευσεν), rich existing and remaining, he became a beggar, not by making a loss of riches but by voluntarily taking upon himself poverty. For by taking on humanity he did not renounce his divinity; but remaining what he was, he became what he was not. For a time he covered the riches of his divinity with the poverty of the flesh, being at once God and man, rich and poor: rich as God, poor as man. Hence Zechariah: "Your king comes to you, poor." He calls Christ poor, yet at the same time names him King; and John, having said, "The Word was made flesh," adds, "We have seen his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father." And Paul: "God acquired the Church with his own blood." From these things there follows, beyond doubt, that this Christ is truly that Messiah who had been promised by God to the fathers through so many past ages, and awaited by them with such longing. For he is such as the oracles of the prophets had foretold: that strong giant, joined in one of two natures, true God and man. He is that seed of the woman who crushes the head of the serpent, that is, a true man born of a virgin without male seed, and a true God crushing Satan by his own power. He is that Immanuel whom Isaiah proclaims as God and man: God, because "he shall be called Immanuel, that is, God with us"; man, because "a child shall be born of a virgin, eating curds and honey." He is that child born to us and that son given to us, whom the same Isaiah in chapter 9 describes both as true man and as true God, expressly naming him "the mighty God" and "the Father of eternity." He is that righteous branch promised to David: a true man, because born of the posterity of David; and true God, because "Jehovah is our righteousness," as the prophecy of Jeremiah has it.

units.la: Porrò si nativitatem Christi secundum carnem videamus, omnes ejus circunstantias similiter ad sanctorum Prophetarum oracula exactissimè congruere deprehendemus. Nam tempus quod attinet, Messias eo tempore nasciturus erat, sub quod sceptrum de tribu Iude[?] ablatum esset, Gen.49: quo certè tempore Christum natum esse Lucas testatur. Messiæ locum natalis Bethlehem esse debuit, juxta Michæ oraculum: ibi vero natus est Christus. Messias ex stirpe Davidis prodire debuit ut Ieremiæ vaticinium ostendit: Suscitabo Davidi germen justum, &c. Christum vero ex familia Davidis procreatum esse, testis est D. Lucas cum dicit: Angelum Gabrielem missum esse à Deo ad Mariam virginem è domo Davidis. Messiam de virgine nasciturum, clarissimè Isaias prædixit cap.7. Ecce virgo concipiet, &c. Christum virgo inviolata concepit & peperit; Messiæ conceptus futurus erat miraculosus, eodem Isaia teste, quoniam conceptus virginis pro signo datur Achazo. Christus non secundum naturæ cursum, sed modo plane divino virtute Spiritus sancti in virginis utero conceptus & efformatus est. Messiam pauperem & despectū inter homines fore prædixit Zacharias: Ecce Rex
units.tr: Furthermore, if we look at the nativity of Christ according to the flesh, we shall find that all its circumstances agree most exactly with the oracles of the holy prophets. As to the time, the Messiah was to be born at the time when the sceptre was taken from the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49), and at that very time Luke testifies that Christ was born. The place of the Messiah's birth was to be Bethlehem, according to the oracle of Micah; and there indeed Christ was born. The Messiah was to come out of the stock of David, as the prophecy of Jeremiah shows: "I will raise up to David a righteous branch, etc." That Christ was born of the family of David is attested by Luke when he says that the angel Gabriel was sent by God to the virgin Mary of the house of David. That the Messiah would be born of a virgin Isaiah foretold most clearly in chapter 7: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, etc." Christ was conceived and brought forth by an inviolate virgin. The conception of the Messiah was to be miraculous, by the same Isaiah's testimony, since the conception of a virgin is given to Ahaz as a sign. Christ was conceived and formed in the virgin's womb not according to the course of nature, but in a manner altogether divine, by the power of the Holy Spirit. Zechariah foretold that the Messiah would be poor and despised among men: "Behold, your king

units.la: tuus mus[?] venit tibi pauper, &c. Quid vero despectius, quid abjectius fuit Christo, dum versaretur in hoc mundo? In stabulo erat natus, à paucis agnitus, iisque contemtis Maria, Iosepho, Elisabetha, pastoribus, Anna, Simeone, piscatoribus; deniq; ab execrabili turba (ut Pharisæi dicebant) qua non norat legem; Ex Pharisæis autem & ex primoribus quis credidit in eum? Denique prædictum fuit, Messiam in contemtissima sorte nihilominus habiturum testimonia divina, quis quantusq; esset. Hæc certe Christo nostro non defuerunt. Nam in veteri Testamento habuit Prophetarum testimonia, ut ostensum est, quibus nihil divinius. In novo habet testes Angelos, qui primò conceptionem Mariæ annunciant, ejusque divinitatem prædicant; postea de Nativitate ejus pastoribus nuncium cœlitus portant, tandemque de ejus resurrectione & ascensione in cœlum, & reditu è cœlo mulieres atque discipulo edocent. Habet testimonia Spiritus sancti prophetantis de eo in Zacharia, Anna, Simeone, & aliis sanctis. Habet denique testimonium cœlestis doctrinæ, & miraculorum, quibus se filium Dei clarissimè demonstravit: Opera enim quæ faciebat, testabantur de eo, quod Deus esset in carne manifestatus. Hactenus de paupertate Christi diximus.
units.tr: your king comes to you, poor, etc." What indeed was more despised, what more abject for Christ while he lived in this world? He was born in a stable, recognized by few, and those despised: by Mary, Joseph, Elizabeth, the shepherds, Anna, Simeon, the fishermen; finally by "that accursed crowd" (as the Pharisees called it) "which does not know the law." "But has any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed in him?" Finally it had been foretold that the Messiah, though in the most despised condition, would nevertheless have divine testimonies showing who and how great he was. These indeed were not lacking to our Christ. For in the Old Testament he had the testimonies of the prophets, as has been shown, than which nothing is more divine. In the New he has angels as witnesses, who first announce Mary's conception and proclaim her son's divinity; afterwards they bring tidings from heaven to the shepherds of his nativity, and finally they teach the women and the disciples of his resurrection, his ascension into heaven, and his return from heaven. He has the testimonies of the Holy Spirit prophesying concerning him in Zechariah, Anna, Simeon, and other saints. Lastly, he has the testimony of his heavenly doctrine and of his miracles, by which he most clearly showed himself to be the Son of God: for the works which he did bore witness of him that God was manifested in the flesh. So far we have spoken of the poverty of Christ.

units.la: Restat tertium orationis nostræ caput, quo causam fructumque paupertatis Christi paucis etiam perstringemus. De hoc Apostolus noster sic habet: Cum esset dives, factus est pauper propter vos, ut vos ejus paupertate ditesceretis. In Corin-thiorum persona nobis hoc dici cogitemus; ac primum hic indicari observemus; Christum pauperem factum non vi, non infortunio, aut casu, aut culpa sua, quomodo multi divites ad egestatem rediguntur; sed voluntaria humilitate, quoniam Deus sponte factus est homo; Dominus sponte factus est omnium servus, sponte est passus, sponte mortuus. Deinde factum pauperem, non propter se, aut sui commodi causa (erat enim [illegible, ~6 letters], Deus benedictus in secula, filius unigenitus & heres omnium) ut nimis putidum sit commentum scholasticorum, eum paupertate sua divitias, humilitate exaltationem sibi promeritum esse. Vera causa divinae hujus dispensationis fuit salus nostra. Propter nos enim, & propter nostram salutem descendit de coelo, & pauper factus est, ut nos paupertate sua ditaret; sicut Zacharias jam olim dixerat Ecclesiae. Ecce Rex tuus pauper venit tibi; Et Jesaias: Puer natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis: Et Angelus apud Lucam; Vobis hodie natus est Salvator, Christus Dominus, in civitate David. Neque sane abs re fuit Christum nostra causa ad tantam usque pauperta-tem sese demittere. Nos enim nudi, & miseri, deficiebamur gloria Dei, & tanquam filii irae, sub potestate tenebrarum constricti tenebamur. Pater igitur coelestis, pro immenso suo in nos amore unigenitum suum filium dedit, qui esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, ut nos viveremus per eum; Nec minus ipse filius dilexit nos tradens semetipsum pro nobis oblationem & victimam Deo, in odorem bonae fragrantiae, ut credentes in eum non percant, sed habeant vitam aeternam. O ineffabilem æterni patris & filii erga nos dilectionem: O nunquam satis pervestigabilem bonitatem. Ingentem Romani laudem tribuerunt Marco Curtio, qui (si Livio creditur) in specum medio foro urbis hiantem pro Republica sese præcipitem dedit. Non minus celebrabant Athenienses Codrum Regem suum, qui pro Attica regione hostium globo se objecit, ut eam suo interitu servaret. At nihil istorum virtus aut pietas ad Christi gloriam. Nam isti pro patria, pro amicis mortem oppetivere; Christus pro hostibus suis mori dignatus est. Istos ostentatio quædam pietatis, & inanis gloriolæ spes instigavit: Christum sola commiseratio, & amor salutis nostræ permovit. Isti ut respublica Romana perpetua staret, & ne Athenæ occiderent, suo interitu effi-cere voluerunt: neutrum effecerunt. Christus ut Ecclesia electorum cœlestibus bonis locupletata in æternum servaretur, sua paupertate certò certius perfecit. Neque enim divitias terrenas, vel opes caducas acquisivit nobis, quas prophani homines in regno ejus frustra quærunt, sed cœlestes, & æternas, de quibus Evangelium concionatur: gratiam nempè, & reconciliationem cum Deo, adoptionem, remissionem peccatorum, justificationem, sanctificationem, fidem, resipiscentiam, pacem, dilectionem: spem, timorem Dei, patientiam, constantiam, vitam denique & salutè æternam: Christus enim à Deo Patre nobis sactus est sapientia, justificatio, sanctificatio & re-demptio. Verum an non (hic aliquis secum cogitet) [illegible, ~8 letters] dicit Apostolus. Quomodo Irus rus Irum, mendicus mendicum ditabit? quomodo nudus nudum vestiet? Equidem nullo, modo. At cogitandum nobis, Christum ita fuisse Irum in mundo ut simul Crœso opulentior esset in coelo; Secundus namque Adam, Dominus de coelo, Facile igitur coelestia bona quæ habuit, nobis conferre: imo & terrena quibus sponte caruit, largiri potest. An vero (inquis) non aliter poterat nos ditare quam paupertate? Imo poterat, si absolutam ejus potentiam spectemus, siquidem apud Deum omnia sunt possibilia; Nec poterat tamen propter obstantem Dei justitiam, & veritatem, siquidem utrique satisfieri oportuit non aliter nisi paupertate & morte Mediatoris. Quomodo autem nos divites effecit?
units.tr: There remains the third head of our oration, in which we shall also briefly touch upon the cause and the fruit of the poverty of Christ. On this our Apostle says: "Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich." Let us consider that this is said to us in the person of the Corinthians; and let us first observe here that Christ was made poor not by force, not by misfortune, by chance, or by his own fault, as many rich men are reduced to want; but by voluntary humility, since God willingly became man, the Lord willingly became the servant of all, willingly suffered, willingly died. Next, he was made poor not on his own account or for his own advantage (for he was [illegible, about 6 letters], the blessed God for ever, the only-begotten Son and heir of all things). So the scholastics' invention is utterly foul, that by his poverty he merited riches for himself, and by his humility exaltation. The true cause of this divine dispensation was our salvation. For on account of us, and for our salvation, he came down from heaven and became poor, so that by his poverty he might enrich us; as Zechariah long before had said to the Church: "Behold, your King comes to you poor." And Isaiah: "A child is born to us, and a son is given to us." And the Angel in Luke: "To you this day is born a Saviour, Christ the Lord, in the city of David." Nor indeed was it without reason that Christ humbled himself to such great poverty for our sake. For we, naked and wretched, were destitute of the glory of God, and, as children of wrath, were bound and held under the power of darkness. Therefore the heavenly Father, out of his immense love towards us, gave his only-begotten Son, who should be the propitiation for our sins, that we might live through him; and no less did the Son himself love us, giving himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God, as a sweet-smelling savour, so that those who believe in him should not perish but have eternal life. O ineffable love of the eternal Father and Son towards us! O goodness that can never be sufficiently searched out! The Romans gave great praise to Marcus Curtius, who (if we believe Livy) threw himself headlong into the gaping chasm in the middle of the Forum for the sake of the Republic. The Athenians no less celebrated Codrus their king, who exposed himself to the onslaught of the enemy to save Attica by his death. But none of these deeds, virtue or piety, can compare with the glory of Christ. For those men died for their country and for their friends; Christ deigned to die for his enemies. A certain display of piety and the hope of empty renown spurred those men on; Christ was moved only by compassion and love for our salvation. Those men wished by their death to make the Roman republic last forever and to keep Athens from perishing: they achieved neither. Christ, by his poverty, has most certainly ensured that the Church of the elect, enriched with heavenly goods, is preserved for eternity. For he did not acquire for us earthly riches or fading wealth, which profane men seek in vain in his kingdom, but heavenly and eternal goods, of which the Gospel preaches: namely grace and reconciliation with God, adoption, forgiveness of sins, justification, sanctification, faith, repentance, peace, love, hope, the fear of God, patience, constancy, and finally life and eternal salvation: for Christ has been made to us by God the Father wisdom, justification, sanctification and redemption. But is it not so (someone here may think to himself) [illegible, about 8 letters] the Apostle says. How shall Irus enrich Irus, a beggar a beggar? How shall the naked clothe the naked? Certainly in no way. But we must consider that Christ was in the world such an Irus that at the same time he was richer than Croesus in heaven; for the second Adam is the Lord from heaven. It was therefore easy for him to confer on us the heavenly goods which he possessed; indeed he can bestow even the earthly goods of which he willingly went without. But (you say) could he not enrich us in any other way than by poverty? Indeed he could, if we look at his absolute power, since with God all things are possible; yet on account of the opposing justice and truth of God he could not, since both had to be satisfied, and this could be done in no other way than by the poverty and death of the Mediator. But how did he make us rich?

units.la: Primum merito, quoniam factus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris.
units.tr: First, by merit, since he became the propitiation for our sins.

units.la: Deinde efficacia: quoniam Spiritu suo nos vivificat, sanctificat, ac tandem nos suscitabit ad vitam æternam. Quos nam vero ditat? Num solos Corinthios? Imo omnes credentes; Gaudium enim magnum de Christo nato. Angelus non uni tantum sed universo populo annunciat: proprio nimirum ejus populo, quia (ut idem Angelus alibi dicit) salvabit populum suum a peccatis suis. Populus autem ejus sunt omnes credentes. Quotquot enim receperunt eum, illis dedit potestatem, ut filii Dei fierent, credentibus scilicet in nomen ejus, &, qui credit in eum non condemnatur, qui vero non credit jam condemnatus est, quia non credit in nomen unigeniti Dei filii; Impium vero commentum est, quod aliqui malemaleferiati homines hac nostra ætate mordicus defendunt: quosvis promiscuè homines etiam non credentes in filium Dei, thesauris spiritua-libus ab eo locupletari, indigni sane, adversus quos verbum amplius faciam : Cum perpetua vox Evangelii nimis aperte furorem eorum redarguat.
units.tr: Second, by efficacy: since by his Spirit he quickens us, sanctifies us, and at last will raise us up to eternal life. But whom then does he enrich? Only the Corinthians? Indeed all believers; for he brings great joy concerning the birth of Christ. The Angel announces it not only to one, but to the whole people: namely to his own people, because (as the same Angel says elsewhere) "he will save his people from their sins." Now his people are all believers. "For as many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, that is, to those believing in his name; and he who believes in him is not condemned, but he who does not believe is already condemned, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God." But it is an impious invention, which certain wicked and mad men in our age stubbornly defend: that whoever, indiscriminately, even those not believing in the Son of God, are enriched by him with spiritual treasures. They are indeed unworthy, and I shall say no more against them, since the constant voice of the Gospel too plainly refutes their madness.

units.la: Quare ut ad finem properet oratio, cum Christus ad nos locupletandos factus sit pauper: Fatendum sanè, omnes nos coram Deo paupertate extrema pressos jacere, & verarum divitiarum inopes esse, quantumvis arcas auro plenas forte possideamus. Quid enim nobis aurum, si non simus divites in Deo, inquit Christus: aut quid dabimus in redemptionem animæ nostræ, si vel totum possideamus mundum? Hanc paupertatem, quæ sola vera & misera paupertas est, ignorare est certum exitium: agnoscere est salutis principium; Beati enim pauperes spiritu, quia saturabuntur, & bonis æternis implebuntur, ut ca- nit sancta virgo, Luc. cap. primo. Hæc bona, has divitias, quibus destituimur omnes avidè quæramus.
units.tr: Therefore, that my oration may hasten to its end: since Christ was made poor to enrich us, we must surely confess that all of us lie before God pressed down by extreme poverty, and are destitute of true riches, however many chests full of gold we may perhaps possess. "For what does gold profit us, if we are not rich in God," says Christ; "or what shall we give in exchange for our soul," if we possessed the whole world? To be ignorant of this poverty, which alone is true and wretched poverty, is certain destruction; to acknowledge it is the beginning of salvation; "For blessed are the poor in spirit, for they shall be satisfied and filled with eternal goods," as the holy virgin sings, Luke chapter one. These goods, these riches, of which we are all destitute, let us all eagerly seek.

units.la: Hæc enim avaritia sola demum honesta est, quærere regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, & parare thesauros in cœlis, quos nec ærugo corrumpit nec fures surripiunt. Cum sola Christi paupertate ditescamus: non in arca nostra di-vitias, hoc est justitiam & salutem in meritis nostris quæramus; Stultum est enim ibi quærere ubi nihil invenias, aut quod invenias nihil spo-rare liceat.
units.tr: For this covetousness alone is at last honourable: to seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and to lay up treasures in heaven, which neither rust corrupts nor thieves steal. Since we are enriched by the poverty of Christ alone, let us not seek in our own chest riches, that is, righteousness and salvation in our own merits; for it is foolish to seek there where you find nothing, or where what you find may not be spent.

units.la: Eant nunc hypocritæ mercenarii papales, & quantum velint jactitent plenisque buccis crepet opera sua præparatoria, meritoria, supererogatoria, & si quæ alia id genus habent σκύβαλα[?] stercora: quo nomine Apostolus preciosissima quæque sua opera indigitare non dubitavit. Cum Christus propter nos terrenam paupertatem su-sceperit, nos quoque crucis ejus propter ipsum in terris non pudeat; Nihil enim hac nobis utilius, nihil salutarius; Nihil opibus, otio, deliciis Ecclesiæ perniciosius. Unde non sine causa Hieronymus in vita Malchi scripsit, Ecclesiam post quam cœpit habere principes Christianos, facta quidem esse opibus majorem, sed virtutibus minorem. Cum deniq; Christus paupertate sua nos ditarit, memores merito sumus hortationis Apostoli, ut & nos pauperum egestati propter Christum subveniamus.
units.tr: Let now the hypocrites, the papal mercenaries, go on, and boast as much as they like, and rattle their works, preparatory, meritorious, supererogatory, with full cheeks, and whatever other dung [σκύβαλα] of that kind they have: by which name the Apostle did not hesitate to designate all his most precious works. Since Christ has taken upon himself earthly poverty for our sake, let us too not be ashamed of his cross in the world for his sake; for nothing is more useful to us than this, nothing more wholesome; nothing is more harmful to the Church than wealth, ease, and luxury. Hence not without cause Jerome wrote in the life of Malchus that the Church, after it began to have Christian princes, was indeed made greater in riches, but less in virtues. Since, finally, Christ has enriched us by his poverty, we are rightly mindful of the Apostle's exhortation, that we too should help the need of the poor for Christ's sake.

units.la: Dixi de hac illustri Apostoli sententia, non ut debui, sed ut potui, quæ & quantæ fuerint Christi divitiæ, antequam fieret pauper; modum quoque quo factus est pauper, exposui: denique cur factus sit pauper, & quas nobis divitias paupertate sua acquisiverit, breviter ostendi. Quod restat, tibi Iesu Christe, æterni patris cœlestis fili, gratias agimus toto pectore, quod cum esses dives, propter nos pauper fieri dignatus es, quodque nos paupertate tua vere ditasti, lavans nos a peccatis nostris pretiosissimo sanguine tuo, & sanctificans nos in templa, in Reges, & Sacerdotes Deo ac patri tuo per Spiritum tuum: quòd denique per eundem spiritum tuum, & ministerium verbi tui in-ter nos accendis lucem cœlestis doctrinæ, & col-ligis ac servas tibi sanctam Ecclesiam. Oramus te, dulcissime IEsu, serva nobis hæc tanta tua dona, & perge clementer benedicere omni be-nedictione spirituali Ecclesiis ac Scholis Palati-natus, ut doctrina veritatis tuæ inter nos magis ac magis efflorescat, cum omni fide, pietate, & charitate, ad laudem gloriosi Nominis tui.
units.tr: I have spoken of this famous sentence of the Apostle not as I ought, but as I was able: what and how great were the riches of Christ before he became poor; I have also set out the manner in which he became poor; finally I have briefly shown why he became poor, and what riches he has acquired for us by his poverty. As for the rest, we give thanks to you, Jesus Christ, Son of the eternal heavenly Father, with our whole heart, that although you were rich, you deigned to become poor for our sake, and that by your poverty you have truly enriched us, washing us from our sins in your most precious blood, and sanctifying us into temples, into kings and priests to God and your Father through your Spirit; and finally that by the same Spirit of yours, and through the ministry of your Word among us, you kindle the light of heavenly doctrine, and gather and preserve for yourself the holy Church. We pray you, most sweet Jesus, to preserve for us these so great gifts of yours, and to continue graciously to bless with every spiritual blessing the Churches and Schools of the Palatinate, so that the doctrine of your truth may flourish more and more among us, with all faith, piety and charity, to the praise of your glorious Name.

units.la: Tibi sit benedictio, & honos, & potentia in secula seculorum,
units.tr: To you be blessing, and honour, and power, for ever and ever,

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: ORATIO VI. DE RESVRRECTIONE CHRISTI.
units.tr: ORATIO VI. ON THE RESURRECTION OF CHRIST.

units.la: Recitata publicè à Christophoro Vulteio Weterano II. April. 1585.
units.tr: Delivered publicly by Christophorus Vulteius of Wetter, 2 April 1585.

units.la: QVàm vellem, Illustris & Generose Comes, Rector Magnifice, Reverendi & Clariss. D. D. & professores, Præceptores venerandi, nobilis deniq; & studiosa juvenum corona: Quàm vellè, inquam, dicendi ex hoc loco partes alii demandatas esse, qui quam sum ego, exactiore doctrina, judicio maturiore, facultate dicendi uberiore, instructus argumentum hujus temporis illustrare, laudabili Academiæ hujus inclytæ[?] consuetudini, vestrumq; omnium exspectationi honestissimæ satisfacere posset? Quanta enim argumenti hujus dignitas? Quanta majestas Christi à mortuis resurgentis, de Satana, peccato & morte triumphum agentis? Contrà verò, quanta doctrinæ meæ tenuitas? quanta ingenii infirmitas, quàm curta in dicendo supellex? Quoniam verò consuetudo Academiæ, ut aliquid hoc tempore, & authoritas fidelissimorum præceptorum, ut à me dicere-
units.tr: How I wish, Illustrious and Noble Count, Magnificent Rector, Reverend and most Distinguished gentlemen and professors, venerable teachers, and the noble and studious crowd of young men, that this topic had been assigned to another, one who, equipped with more exact learning, more mature judgement, and a richer gift of speech, could illustrate the subject of this season and satisfy both the praiseworthy custom of this famous Academy and the very honourable expectation of you all! For how great is the dignity of this subject? How great the majesty of Christ rising from the dead, who triumphs over Satan, sin and death! On the other hand, how slight is my learning, how weak my talent, how meagre my stock of words in speaking! But since the custom of the Academy, and the authority of your most faithful teachers, required that something be said by me at this time, I have taken upon myself a task I would never have undertaken of my own accord, trusting in this hope: that you will lend me an indulgent ear, and will think not so much about the ornament of my speech or my youthful inexperience, as about the dignity of the matter. For this is the aim and purpose of my address: to remind you of the glorious resurrection of the triumphant Christ, and to open up a broad field for your pious meditations, which may then break out into thanksgiving and praise of almighty God.

units.la: diceretur, postulabat, partes dicendi, quas nun-quam sponte sumsissem, in me recepi, hac spe fre-tus, vos aures æquas mihi præbituros, & non tàm de orationis ornatu, meáve infantia, quàm de ma-teriæ dignitate cogitaturos esse. Hic enim ora-tionis meæ scopus, hic finis est, ut de gloriosa tri-umphantis Christi resurrectione vos commone-faciam, & latum piis vestris meditationibus cam-pum aperiam, quæ deinceps in gratiarum actio-nem, laudesque omnipotentis Dei erumpant.
units.tr: There are four things, however, which seem especially to demand discussion at this time: first, that the Lord Jesus rose; second, by what power or virtue he rose; third, in what manner he rose; and finally, what fruit from his resurrection comes back to us.

units.la: Quatuor autem sunt, de quibus hoc tempore potissimùm dicendum videtur: Primum, quòd resurrexerit Dominus Iesus: Deinde, qua vi seu virtute resurrexerit: Tertiò, quomodo resurre-xerit: denique, quis fructus ex resurrectione ipsius ad nos redeat.
units.tr: There are four points that seem most worth discussing at this time: first, that the Lord Jesus rose; second, by what power or virtue he rose; third, in what manner he rose; and finally, what fruit his resurrection brings to us. ## Proof of the resurrection

units.la: Primùm igitur in probanda resurrectione Christi, scriptores historiæ Christi operosos val-dè & diligentes esse cernimus. Nisi enim cre-datur, Christum à mortuis surrexisse, inanis & ir-rita est omnis tùm prædicatio nostra, tùmfides: ut D. Paulus 1. ad Corinth. cap. 15. docet. Quare apud Christianos, qui beneficiorum Christi par-ticipes fieri cupiunt, indubitatam omninò esse oportet resurrectionem Christi, quia sine illa universa Christi beneficia nihil nobis proderunt.
units.tr: First, then, in proving the resurrection of Christ, we see that the writers of the history of Christ were very laborious and diligent. For unless it is believed that Christ rose from the dead, all our preaching and our faith are empty and vain, as the apostle Paul teaches in 1 Cor. 15. Therefore Christians who wish to share in the benefits of Christ must hold the resurrection of Christ to be wholly beyond doubt, because without it all the benefits of Christ would profit us nothing.

units.la: Testes autem resurrectionis Christi sunt Angeli & homines. Angeli enim resurgente Christo de cœlo descenderunt, ut de Domini sui Resurrectione quærentibus testimonium perhiberent.
units.tr: The witnesses of the resurrection of Christ are angels and men. For the angels came down from heaven when Christ rose, to bear witness to those who inquired about the resurrection of their Lord.

units.la: Quare matronis ad monumentum venientibus, Dominumque quaerentibus, Jesum, inquiunt, Nazarenum quaeritis, qui crucifixus fuit, Resurrexit, non est hic: & simul ad majorem rei, quae miranda erat, confirmationem, ad lintea, quibus Jesus involutus fuerat, sedentes, locum in quo Christi corpus jacuerat, digitis demonstrant vacuum: Venite, inquiunt, videte locum, ubi posuerant illum. Item: Praecedet vos in Galilaeam, ibi videbitis eum. Huic angelorum testimonio fidem addidit, divinus, qui illos circumstitit fulgor, vestitus nivis candorem superans. Quis igitur de illorum testimonio dubitet? Quis contradicat?
units.tr: Accordingly, when the women came to the tomb and sought the Lord, the angels said: "You seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified; he has risen, he is not here." At the same time, to confirm more fully the thing that was wonderful, they sat by the linen cloths in which Jesus had been wrapped and pointed with their fingers to the empty place where the body of Christ had lain: "Come," they said, "see the place where they laid him." Likewise: "He goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him." To this testimony of the angels, the divine splendour that surrounded them, their garment outshining the whiteness of snow, added credibility. Who then could doubt their testimony? Who could contradict it?

units.la: Humana testimonia Resurrectionem Christi nobis confirmantia illorum sunt, quibus se Christus resuscitatus patefecit, & per 40. dies, quos ad testandam resurrectionem suam in his terris ante ascensionem in coelos egit, spectandum ac contrectandum exhibuit.
units.tr: The human testimonies that confirm to us the resurrection of Christ are those of the men to whom the risen Christ revealed himself, and whom, during the forty days he spent on earth before his ascension into heaven to attest his resurrection, he showed to be seen and handled.

units.la: Etsi autem permultis se patefecit, quippe 1. ad Cor. cap. 15. quingentis & ultra fratribus simul visus esse dicitur: singulari tamen modo Apostolis suis, mulieribus quibusdam, & duobus discipulis Emaunta euntibus se patefecit.
units.tr: For first he appeared to Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Mary the mother of James, when, having departed from the tomb, they were running at the command of the angels to announce to the disciples that the Lord had risen; he appeared to them, I say, on the way, greeted them with the sweetest words, and sent them away to his disciples.

units.la: Nam primum apparuit Mariæ Magdalenæ, Joannę, Mariæ Jacobi, cum a monumento digressæ jussu angelorum currerent, ut discipulis Dominum resurrexisse renunciarent, apparuit, inquam, illis in itinere, dulcissimis verbis salutavit, & ad discipulos suos ablegavit.
units.tr: Afterwards he appeared to the two disciples going to Emmaus and conferring together about Christ; he walked with them, unrecognised, for a large part of the journey (for their eyes were held, so that they did not know him); and because they were still very weak, and wavered about the resurrection of Christ, of which they had heard from the women, he fully instructed them from Moses and the prophetic Scriptures. At last he also reclined at table with them, and in the blessing, breaking and distributing of the bread, with their eyes opened, he showed himself to be recognised; and again he withdrew from their sight.

units.la: Postea duobus discipulis Emaunta euntibus, & de Christo sermones conferentibus apparuit, magnam itineris partem cum ipsis, ignotus tamen (oculi enim eorum retenti fuerunt, ne ipsū agnoscerent) confecit, & quod valde infirmi adhuc essent, & de resurrectione Christi, de qua a mulieribus audiverant, hæsitarent, plenè illos ex Mose & Prophetica scriptura instruxit, tandem etiam cum illis accubuit, & in panis benedictio-ne, fractione & distributione apertis ipsorum o-culis seipsis agnoscendum præbuit, iterumque se ex ipsorum aspectu subduxit.
units.tr: Soon afterwards, when these two had reported to the other eleven disciples, behold, Christ stood in the midst of them, offered himself to be touched, and showed them the wounds and marks of his passion. Finally, so that he might cut off every occasion for doubt, and remove every scruple still clinging to their minds, which for joy did not yet believe, he ate in their sight; and after he had sufficiently instructed them from Scripture about his passion and death, he breathed on them with the Holy Spirit and appointed them witnesses of his resurrection.

units.la: Mox, cum hi duo reliquis undecim discipulis renunciassent: Ecce Christus in medio illorum stans, se contrectandum ipsis exponit, vulnera & notas passionis suæ monstrat, denique ut omnem dubitandi occasionem præcidat, omnemq; scrupulum ex animis illorum hærentibus adhuc, & præ gaudio non credentibus eximat, in conspe-ctu illorum comedit, & postquam ex Scriptura eos sufficienter de passione ac morte sua instru-xisset, Spiritu Sancto afflat, testesque Resurre-ctionis suæ constituit.
units.tr: Soon after, when these two had reported to the other eleven disciples, Christ suddenly stood in the midst of them, offered himself to be handled, showed his wounds and the marks of his passion, and finally, to cut off every occasion for doubt and to remove every scruple still clinging to their minds, which for joy did not yet believe, he ate in their sight; and after he had sufficiently instructed them from Scripture concerning his passion and death, he breathed on them with the Holy Spirit and appointed them witnesses of his resurrection.

units.la: Sed miretur forsitan aliquis, Dominum his testibus uti voluisse, qui ad rem tanti momenti confirmandam leviores videri poterant, mulieribus videlicet & paucis discipulis, rudibus & ob-scuris, tanquam ex plebis sece collectis, ac non potius Pharisæis & senioribus populi se manife-stasse, quibus maiorem fidem Judaicus populus habiturus fuisset. Hic vero considerandum est, primo, ut maxime de discipulis res ita haberet, Angelorum tamen testimonium omni exceptione maius esset. Deinde neque de discipulis tam obicurè[?] sentiendum est. Esto, ex plebis secè collecti sint, piscatores enim fuêre: nullo splendeant externo seu mundano eloquentiæ vel divitiarum apparatu: At non sunt rudes & obscuri, si divina testimonia, quæ ipsis tributa sunt, si officium, ad quod vocati sunt, consideramus. An enim rudes & obscuri, qui à Deo ipso immediatè vocati, & authoritate ornati sunt, ita, ut, qui illos audit, Deum ipsum audiat, in quos Spiritus Sanctus illapsus est visibiliter, & qui electi fuerunt ad annunciandam omnibus gentibus gratiam Dei, & qui tot miracula passim ediderunt?
units.tr: But perhaps someone will wonder why the Lord wished to use these witnesses, who might seem too weak to confirm a matter of such importance, namely women and a few disciples, rude and obscure, gathered as it were from the common people, and why he did not rather reveal himself to the Pharisees and the elders of the people, whom the Jewish people would have trusted more. Here we must consider, first, that although this was so with regard to the disciples, the testimony of the angels would nonetheless be greater than any objection. Second, we must not think so poorly of the disciples either. Granted that they were gathered from the common people, for they were fishermen, and shone with no external or worldly show of eloquence or riches; yet they were not rude and obscure if we consider the divine testimonies given to them and the office to which they were called. For are they rude and obscure, who were called immediately by God himself and adorned with authority, so that whoever hears them hears God himself; upon whom the Holy Spirit descended visibly; who were chosen to proclaim the grace of God to all nations; and who everywhere performed so many miracles?

units.la: Omittam nunc milites, quibus monumenti custodia demândata fuit, qui Christi resurgentis divina Majestate, in terræmotu, aliisque Resurrectionem comitantibus miraculis se exserente, adeò consternati & exanimati fuerunt, ut cùm ad opprimendum Christum monumento additi essent, illustre de eo testimonium apud Pharisæos dicere necesse habèrent.
units.tr: I will now pass over the soldiers, to whom the guarding of the tomb had been entrusted, who, when the divine majesty of the risen Christ made itself manifest in the earthquake and other miracles accompanying the resurrection, were so terrified and struck senseless that, when they had been posted to suppress Christ in the tomb, they were compelled to give an illustrious testimony about him before the Pharisees.

units.la: Hæc omnia, etsi Resurrectionem Christi per se certam nobis reddunt: tamen certiorem reddit consideratio tum vaticiniorum de illa in Veteri Testamento editorum, tùm Personæ & officii Christi.
units.tr: All these things, although they make the resurrection of Christ certain to us in themselves, nonetheless the consideration both of the prophecies concerning it published in the Old Testament and of the person and office of Christ renders it more certain.

units.la: Ad vaticinia videmus, quomodo Christus ipse de sua Resurrectione dubitantes passim revocet. Sic enim Luc. 24. discipulos Emaunta euntes, de quibus supra quoque dixi, non sine gravi obiurgatione ad scripturam revocat: O stulti, & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus, qua loquuti sunt Prophetæ. Et cap. 20. iterum dubitationem illis excutit, cutit, ad scripturam illos reducens, sic scriptum est, & sic oportebat Christum pati, & tertio die à mortuis resurgere. Vaticinia igitur Prophetarum de Resurrectione Christi ex multis pauca commemorabo. Non derelinques, inquit regius ille Propheta Psal. 16. animam meam in inferno, nec permittes sanctum tuum videre corruptionem: quæ cùm de typo intelligi nequeant, David enim obdormivit, & corruptionem sensit, de antitypo Messia proprie intelligenda esse docet D. Petrus Act. 2. & D. Paulus Act. 13. Sic Esa. 53. de Messia dicitur: Cum seipsam sacrificium posuerit anima eius, videbit semen, quod prolongabit dies: propter laborem animæ suæ videbit & saturabitur. Item: ex judicio & justitia ereptus est. Sic in Iona, qui tres dies & tres noctes in ventre ceti mansit, typus fuit resurrectionis Christi, quemadmodum docet Christus Matth. 12. Hæc & alia oracula Prophetarum certò adimpleta fuisse, atque adeò Christum resurrexisse merito credimus, Neque enim Spiritus, qui per Prophetas loquutus est, fallere potest: & si illa, quæ de passione, ignominia & cruciatibus Christi à Prophetis prædicta sunt, suo tempore omnia evenerunt: quidni & illa, quæ de eius glorificatione & exaltatione prodita sunt, eventum suum sortita essent?
units.tr: As to the prophecies, we see how Christ himself, on many occasions, recalls to Scripture those who doubt his resurrection. Thus in Luke 24 he recalls the disciples going to Emmaus, of whom I spoke above too, to Scripture, not without grave rebuke: "O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!" And in chapter 20 he again removes their doubt, leading them back to Scripture: "So it is written, and so it behoved Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day." I will therefore mention a few of the many prophecies of the prophets concerning the resurrection of Christ. "You will not leave my soul in hell," says that royal prophet in Psalm 16, "nor will you suffer your Holy One to see corruption." Since these words cannot be understood of the type, for David fell asleep and saw corruption, the apostle Peter in Acts 2 and the apostle Paul in Acts 13 teach that they must properly be understood of the antitype, the Messiah. Thus Isaiah 53 says of the Messiah: "When his soul has made itself a sacrifice, he shall see seed, which shall prolong its days; from the travail of his soul he shall see and be satisfied." Likewise: "He was taken away by judgment and justice." So Jonah, who remained three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, was a type of the resurrection of Christ, as Christ teaches in Matt. 12. Since these and other oracles of the prophets were certainly fulfilled, we rightly believe that Christ rose; for the Spirit who spoke through the prophets cannot deceive. And if all the things foretold by the prophets concerning the passion, shame and sufferings of Christ came to pass at their appointed time, why should not those also which were announced concerning his glorification and exaltation have obtained their fulfilment?

units.la: Sed neque dignitati & potentiæ tantæ personæ conveniebat, ut in morte maneret, & ab illa vinceretur. Quî[?] enim ille, cui æternus Pater dixit: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te: & in cuius manus dedit omnia, etiam potestatem suscitandi mortuos, & judicandi, morti succumberet? qua
units.tr: But neither was it fitting for the dignity and power of so great a person to remain in death and be conquered by it. For how could he, to whom the eternal Father said, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you," and into whose hands he gave all things, including the power of raising the dead and of judging, succumb to death?

units.la: ratione ille, qui est ipsa resurrectio & vita, & cui Pater dedit habere vitam in semetipso, à morte absorberetur? Unde verò mortis imperium in eum, qui iustissimus est, qui peccatum non novit. Nam mors est peccati stipendium: & ubi peccatū non est, ibi nec mors imperii quicquam habet.
units.tr: By what reasoning could he, who is the resurrection and the life, and to whom the Father gave to have life in himself, be swallowed up by death? Whence indeed would dominion of death extend over him who is most just, who did not know sin? For death is the wages of sin, and where there is no sin, death has no dominion at all.

units.la: Tum verò & officium Christi propter quod in carnem venit, & quod secundum utramque naturam exsequitur, multis modis, ut à morte resurgeret, postulabat. In æternum enim regnare debebat Mediator iste, seu semè [?] Davidis, sicut dicitur 2. Sam. 7. & Esaias de Christo prophetans cap. 9: Multiplicationis regni, inquit, & pacis non erit finis. Idem Ezechiel c. 37. innuit: & Daniel c. 7. Filio hominis æternam potestatem adscribit. Oportebat igitur hoc semen Davidis, ut regnum administraret, à mortuis resurgere, & ad dextram Dei sedere, donec omnes inimici subiicerentur pedibus eius, quorum ultima mors in novissimo die destruetur. Similiter debebat esse Pontifex in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedec, ut Psal. 110. prædictum fuit, qui semper coram Deo appareret, & pro Ecclesia intercederet. Secundum humanam igitur naturam sic mori oportuit, ut ad illud officium peragendum mortem vinceret, & ut impleretur, quod dictum est: Mors absorpta est in victoriam.
units.tr: Moreover, the office of Christ, on account of which he came in the flesh and which he carries out according to both natures, required in many ways that he rise from the dead. For this Mediator was to reign for ever, the seed of David, as is said in 2 Sam. 7, and Isaiah, prophesying of Christ, in chapter 9: "Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end." Ezekiel likewise hints at this in chapter 37, and Daniel in chapter 7 ascribes eternal power to the Son of man. It was therefore necessary that this seed of David, in order to administer his kingdom, should rise from the dead and sit at the right hand of God, until all enemies are placed under his feet, the last of which, death, will be destroyed on the last day. Similarly he was to be a Priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, as was foretold in Psalm 110, who would always appear before God and intercede for the Church. Therefore, according to his human nature, he had to die in such a way as to overcome death in order to carry out that office, and so that what was said might be fulfilled: "Death is swallowed up in victory."

units.la: Quæ cùm ita sint omnia, sicut à me breviter dicta sunt, neminem esse spero, qui de resurrectione Christi ambigere, aut dubitare amplius possit.
units.tr: Since all these things are as I have briefly set them out, I hope there is no one who can any longer be in doubt or hesitate about the resurrection of Christ.

units.la: Cæterum idem Christus resurrexit, qui ex virgine Maria natus erat, qui in cruce pependerat [?] & transfixus fuerat: Non tamen iisdem obnoxius infirmitatibus, quibus ante resurrectionem in statu humiliationis propter nos fuerat subie-ctus, sed omni humani generis fragilitate & im-becillitate per mortem abolita gloriosus. Ani-mam enim tot tantisque cruciatibus ante expositam, prae tristitia & dolore ex sensu irae divinae contabescentem, videas nunc solutis mortis vinculis prae laetitia exultantem, perfectissimo & incomprehensibili gaudio in conspectu Dei repletam, summa felicitate, quae in perfectione tum sapientiae, tum virtutis ineffabilis omnem angelorum & hominum captum superantis consistit, perfruentem ita, ut non immerito instante redemtione ex huius gaudii & perfectionis post resurrectionem gloriosae consideratione Christus laetari cor suum, & exultare linguam suam dixerit.
units.tr: Moreover, the same Christ rose who had been born of the Virgin Mary, who had hung on the cross and had been pierced. Yet he was not subject to the same weaknesses to which he had been subjected before the resurrection, in the state of humiliation, on our account, but, with all the frailty and feebleness of the human race abolished through death, he is glorious. For his soul, which before had undergone so many and such great torments, and was wasting away with sorrow and grief from the sense of divine wrath, you now see, with the bonds of death loosed, exulting for joy, filled with a most perfect and incomprehensible gladness in the sight of God, enjoying the highest happiness, which consists in the perfection both of wisdom and of ineffable virtue, surpassing all the grasp of angels and men. So it was not without reason that Christ, at the approaching redemption, from the consideration of this joy and of the perfection of his glorious resurrection, said that his heart rejoiced and his tongue exulted.

units.la: Corpus vero, quod ante resurrectionem mortale erat, & cruciatibus ac laesionibus obnoxium, quod defatigationibus, laboribus & huius vitae molestiis conficiebatur, quod fami & siti, aestui [?] & frigori, aliisq; infirmitatibus expositum erat: iis omnibus depositis immortale nunc aspicias & in corruptibile, robore & potentia valens, agilimū [?], fulgore incomprehensibili splendens sicut Sol, tantisque adeo donis ornatum, ut etiam angelorum captum haec Maiestas superet.
units.tr: His body, however, which before the resurrection was mortal and subject to torments and wounds, which was worn down by fatigue, labours and the troubles of this life, which was exposed to hunger and thirst, heat and cold, and other infirmities: having laid all these aside, you now behold it immortal and incorruptible, strong in vigour and power, agile, shining with an incomprehensible brilliance like the sun, and adorned with such gifts that this majesty surpasses even the grasp of angels.

units.la: Neq; tamen ista gloria & maiestas talis est, ut humanum corpus aboleat, & in Spiritum convertat, ut quidam putarunt. Christus enim ut corpus suum a spiritu discernat, seque verum corpus post resurrectionem habere ostendat, discipulis, qui se spectrum vel umbram corporis videre putabant, diserte dicit: Videte, palpate, Spiritus enim carnem & ossa non habet, sicuti me videtis habere.
units.tr: Yet this glory and majesty is not such that it abolishes the human body and turns it into spirit, as some have thought. For Christ, in order to distinguish his body from a spirit, and to show that after the resurrection he has a true body, plainly says to the disciples, who thought they saw a ghost or the shadow of a body: "See, handle me, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have."

units.la: Neque etiam talis est Christi hominis Maiestas, ut corpus in rotundam formam convertat, & homogeneum efficiat, quod totum videat, totum audiat, totum olfaciat, ita ut nullos habeat distinctos oculos, sed totum sit oculatum, non distinctas aures, sed totum sit auritum, cui errori inter alios Origenem patrocinatū esse legimus. Prodit enim historia Evangelica, Christum post resurrectionem suam habuisse corpus, iisdem lineamentis, quibus ante mortem, definitum, & iisdem partibus distinctum. Praeterea Christum ore, dentibus, palato & gula, non autem cranio vel pedibus edisse & bibisse, & ore & lingua, ut antea, non cruribus vel manibus loquutum esse legimus.
units.tr: Nor is the majesty of Christ the man such that it turns his body into a round shape and makes it homogeneous, so that it sees all over, hears all over, smells all over, with no distinct eyes but the whole being an eye, and no distinct ears but the whole being ears; an error which we read Origen, among others, defended. For the Gospel history shows that Christ after his resurrection had a body defined by the same outlines as before death and divided into the same parts. Moreover, we read that Christ ate and drank with his mouth, teeth, palate and throat, and not with his skull or feet, and that he spoke with his mouth and tongue, as before, not with his shins or hands.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem neque in Spiritum, neq; in totundam formam illa gloria Christi corpus convertit, sic neque proprietates corporis essentiales sustulit & evertit, alioquin ipsum corpus sustulisset & evertisset. Qui n. tollit aut negat proprietates, tollit & negat naturas. Licet igitur corpus Christi sit in se gloriosum, & summis ac mirandis dotibus praeditum, tamen ratione essentiae finitum, & suis terminis circumscriptum manet: non dilatatur vel extenditur in multa loca simul, sed ex loco, in quo est, in locum, in quo non est, sese movet, nec simul est in omnibus aut pluribus ribus locis secundum essentiam suam. Atque id docent angeli, cum mulieribus dicunt: Surrexit, Non est hic, id est, ita surrexit, ut non sit hic secundum corpus suum, Item. Praecedit vos in-Galilaeam.
units.tr: But just as that glory did not turn Christ's body into spirit or into a round form, so neither did it take away and overturn the essential properties of the body; otherwise it would have taken away and overturned the body itself. For whoever takes away or denies the properties takes away and denies the natures. Therefore, although the body of Christ is in itself glorious and endowed with the highest and most wonderful gifts, nevertheless in respect of its essence it remains finite and circumscribed within its own limits. It is not spread out or extended into many places at once, but moves from the place where it is into a place where it is not, and it is not at the same time in all or several places according to its essence. This the angels teach when they say to the women: "He has risen; he is not here," that is, he has risen in such a way that he is not here according to his body; likewise, "He goes before you into Galilee."

units.la: Falsum igitur est, si qui volunt, corpus Christi non uno in loco tantum, sed in pluribus locis simul, imo ubique esse. Si enim ubique simul fuit corpus Christi, quomodo in sepulchro fuisse, & quomodo e sepulchro resurrexisse dicetur? & quomodo verum est, quod angelus dicit, eum non esse in sepulchro, sed in Galilaeam praecessisse? Quod si quis putat secundum alium atque alium modum illa de corpore Christi dici posse, ita ut secundum modum naturalem non fuerit in sepulchro, secundum modum autem majestatis seu dextræ Dei, & in sepulchro & ubique fuerit: Sciendum est. Primum majestatem aut dextram Dei non esse ipsum corpus aut substantiam corporis. Deinde ex hac distinctione sequeretur, idem corpus Christi sepultum & non sepultum esse, resurrexisse, & non resurrexisse, & similiter ascendisse, & non ascendisse: natum esse ex Maria virgine & non natum esse: alterum videlicet secundum modum naturalem, alterum secundum modum majestatis vel dextræ Dei. Hæc vero ἀσυγχύτως[?] esse & fidei Christianæ repugnare manifestum est.
units.tr: It is therefore false if some want the body of Christ to be not in one place only but in many places at once, indeed everywhere. For if the body of Christ was everywhere at once, how would it be said that it was in the sepulchre, and how that it rose from the sepulchre? And how is it true what the angel says, that he was not in the sepulchre but had gone before into Galilee? But if anyone thinks that those things about the body of Christ can be said according to one mode and another, so that according to the natural mode it was not in the sepulchre, but according to the mode of majesty, or the right hand of God, it was both in the sepulchre and everywhere: it must be noted, first, that the majesty or right hand of God is not the body itself or the substance of the body. Second, from this distinction it would follow that the same body of Christ was buried and not buried, rose and did not rise, and likewise ascended and did not ascend, was born of the Virgin Mary and was not born: namely, the one according to the natural mode, the other according to the mode of majesty or the right hand of God. But that these things are confused and contrary to the Christian faith is plain.

units.la: Manet ergo corpus Christi visibile & palpabile. Ideo enim post resurrectionem suam se videri & contrectari Christus voluit, ut certitudinem & veritatem corporis sui probaret. Quod autem post resurrectionem quandoque non fuit agnitus, ut à discipulis Emaunta euntibus, id non corpori asscribendum est, quod per se unum & idem, eadem forma, iisdemque lineamentis definitum mansit, sed discipulorum oculis, quos retentos fuisse, ne ipsum agnoscerent, Evangelista manifeste affirmat. Sic quod [illegible, ~8 letters] seu invisibilis factus est, cum ab illis discederet, non in ipso corpore Christi accidisse putandum est, quod per se immutatum mansit, nec in Spiritum conversum aut transformatum est, sed in discipulorum oculis potius, quorum aciem ita obtusam fuisse, ut antea facto erat, piè sentire possumus. Ergo ex his perspicuum est, quod Christus idem, qui passus, mortuus & sepultus erat, è sepulchro resurrexit.
units.tr: The body of Christ therefore remains visible and palpable. For Christ wished to be seen and handled after his resurrection precisely in order to prove the certainty and reality of his body. That he was sometimes not recognised after the resurrection, as by the disciples going to Emmaus, is not to be ascribed to the body, which remained by itself one and the same, of the same form and defined by the same outlines, but to the eyes of the disciples, which, as the Evangelist clearly affirms, were held back so that they should not recognise him. Likewise, that he became unseen when he departed from them is not to be thought to have happened in the body of Christ itself, which remained unchanged in itself and was not turned or transformed into spirit, but rather in the eyes of the disciples, whose sight, we may piously suppose, was dulled in the way it had been before. Therefore it is clear from these things that Christ, the same who had suffered, died and been buried, rose from the sepulchre.

units.la: Nunc, qua vi & virtute resurrexerit, dispiciamus. Hic scriptura docet, Christum propria potentia resurrexisse, id est, animam ad corpus revocasse, & humanam suam naturam è sepulchro resuscitasse. Hoc enim ipse affirmat Iohan. 2. cum inquit, Destruite templum hoc, & tribus diebus erigam illud, quod non de templo Hierosolymitano manufacto, ut Iudaei calumniabantur, sed de corpore ipsius, quod est templum inhabitantis λόγῳ [?] intelligendum esse, D. Iohannes eodem loco perspicue exponit. Sic Ioh. 10. Ego, ego, inquit, pono animam meam, ut eam rursus assumam. Potestatem habeo ponendi eam, & potestatem habeo rursus assumendi eam. Deinde, cur is, qui alios, quos vult, vivificat propria potetia, seipsum vivificare non posset? Christum vero propria sua potentia, quos vult, vivificare posse, tum ex exemplis mor-tuorum tuorum ab illo resuscitatorum constat, tùm ex Ioan. cap. 5. ubi hanc vim communem sibi & aequalem cum patre esse dicit. Sicut enim pater, inquit, excitat mortuos & vivificat (excitat autem & vivificat pater propria vi & authoritate) ita & Filius (propria intellige potentia & authoritate) quos vult, vivificat. Neque hic obstat, quòd eodem capite praemittitur: Amen, amen, dico vobis, non potest filius a semetipso operari, nisi viderit patrem operantem: Non enim hic potentia seu vis operandi, sed operationis ordo nobis demonstratur. Quemadmodū enim Pater fons est Deitatis: sic etiam fons est omnium operum divinorum, ita ut Filius nihil a semetipso sine patre sed omnia & quidem pariter, id est, aequali & pari potentia cum patre faciat, ut loco ante citato subiungitur. Filius enim & pater unum sunt, una est illorum essentia & omnipotentia, ac proinde una operatio & actio, servato tamen personarum ut subsistendi, sic agendi ordine, ut pater a seipso & per Filium, Filius non a seipso, sed a patre agat, &c.
units.tr: Now let us examine by what power and strength he rose again. Here Scripture teaches that Christ rose by his own power, that is, that he called his soul back to his body and raised up his human nature from the sepulchre. For he himself affirms this in John 2, when he says: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." That this is to be understood not of the temple at Jerusalem made with hands, as the Jews misrepresented it, but of his own body, which is the temple of the indwelling Word [λόγῳ ?], St John expressly explains in the same place. Likewise in John 10: "I, I, he says, lay down my life that I may take it up again. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again." Further, why should he who gives life to whom he wills by his own power be unable to give life to himself? That Christ can give life by his own power to whom he wills is clear both from the examples of the dead whom he raised up, and from John 5, where he says that this power is common to him and equal with the Father: "For as the Father, he says, raises the dead and gives them life" (the Father raises and gives life by his own power and authority), "so also the Son" (understand, by his own power and authority) "gives life to whom he wills." Nor does what is prefaced in the same chapter stand in the way: "Verily, verily, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself unless he sees the Father doing it." For here it is not the power or strength of acting that is shown to us, but the order of operation. For just as the Father is the fount of the Godhead, so he is also the fount of all divine works, so that the Son does nothing of himself without the Father, but does all things equally, that is, with the same and equal power as the Father, as is added in the passage cited above. For the Son and the Father are one; their essence and omnipotence are one, and therefore their operation and action are one, yet with the order of the persons preserved, so that in their subsisting and in their acting, the Father acts from himself and through the Son, and the Son acts not from himself but from the Father, etc.

units.la: Deinde nec illud obstat, quod ad Rom. 4. pater illum suscitasse dicitur: Patris siquidem operatio Filii cooperationem nullo modo excludit, Pater enim usq; adhuc operatur, inquit Christus Ioh. 5. & ego operor. Pater igitur filium quidem suscitavit, sed potentia sibi communi cum filio. Itaque filius quoque seipsum resuscitasse dicitur, nempe eadem illa potentia sibi communi cum patre: ac proinde Christus potentia Deitatis suae resurrexit. Quapropter Ioh. 2. resurrectionem futuram tanquam Deitatis suae ἀνάστασιν[?] adduccit. Quærentibus enim Iudæis, quanam authoritate ius in templum sibi vendicaret, & quodnam signum ederet, respondit: Destruite templū hoc & tribus diebus erigam illud. Et similiter Paulus ait ad Rom. 1. Declaratum illum esse filium Dei per resurrectionem a mortuis. Falluntur ergo, qui Christum potentia humanæ naturæ revixisse & resurrexisse dicunt. Nam si omnes Deitatis proprietates, atque adeo omnipotentiam humanæ naturæ ita communicatas esse sentiunt, ut huic tanquam subiecto nunc insint, næ cum Eutychianis aperte sentiunt, & exæquationem atq; confusionem naturarum faciunt. Sin autem propter unionem duarum naturarum, & huic respondentem communionem proprietatum in persona, existimant, quæ Deitatis sunt Idiomata & proprietates, de humana natura dici & prædicari posse: cur non omnia sed quædam tantum Idiomata Deitatis de humana natura prædicari volunt: & si humana natura, ut ipsi volunt, seipsam resuscitavit, cur non humanam naturam Deum esse dicunt? Et si Deum, cur non æternam? cur non creatricem cœli & terræ?
units.tr: Next, what is said in Romans 4, that the Father raised him up, does not stand in the way either. For the Father's operation by no means excludes the Son's co-operation: "For my Father, Christ says in John 5, works even until now, and I work." The Father therefore raised up the Son, but by a power common to the Son. Thus the Son is also said to have raised up himself, namely by that same power common to him and the Father; and therefore Christ rose by the power of his Godhead. Accordingly, in John 2 he brings forward his future resurrection as a proof of his Godhead. For when the Jews asked by what authority he claimed the right to act in the temple, and what sign he would show, he answered: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." Similarly Paul says in Romans 1 that he was declared to be the Son of God by the resurrection from the dead. Those therefore are mistaken who say that Christ revived and rose by the power of his human nature. For if they think that all the properties of the Godhead, and so the omnipotence, are so communicated to the human nature that they inhere in it as in a subject, then they openly agree with the Eutychians and make the natures equal and confused. But if, on account of the union of the two natures and the corresponding communion of properties in the person, they think that the attributes and properties of the Godhead can be said and predicated of the human nature, why do they not want all the attributes of the Godhead, but only some, to be predicated of the human nature? And if the human nature, as they wish, raised up itself, why do they not say that the human nature is God? And if God, why not eternal? Why not the creator of heaven and earth?

units.la: Quod si ex Iohan. 6. ubi caro Christi dicitur panis vivificus, qui de cœlo descendit, colligi posse existimant, humanam naturam seu carnem Christi seipsam vivificare seu resuscitare potuisse: Sciendum est primum, carnem non simpliciter illo loco intelligi, sed quatenus pro mundi vita data est, ac proinde passionem, mortem & meritum, quod inde proficiscitur & dependet, simul intelligi. 'Deinde vivificationem non simpliciter ut actionem Deitatis, seu omnipotentis naturæ propriam, sed ut ἀποτέλεσμα seu effectum personale, quod Christo secundum utramque naturam competit, de carne Christi prædicari, quæ-admodum & salvatio, expiatio, redemtio, & id genus alia. Tertiò, si ut actio Deitatis, seu omni-potentis naturæ propria, non ut ἀποτέλεσμα intelligitur vivificatio, sicut Cyrillus interdum sentire videtur, ita de carne Christi prædicari intel-ligenda est vivificatio, secundum ipsiusmet Cyrilli expositionem, sicut descensus de cœlo de carne Christi prædicatur, aut prædicari intelligendus est. Nam & vivificare & e cœlo descendere Cyrillus eodem modo de carne Christi prædicari existimat. Sic enim de recta fide ad Theodo-sium ait: Quomodo igitur, dic oro, vivificat caro? vel quomodo intelligitur & de cœlo esse, quod de terra? secundum unionem scilicet cum vivente & cœlesti verbo. Si quis igitur vivificationem, quatenus est actio Deitatis propria, de carne Christi proprie prædicari contendet, etiam descensum e cœlo de carne Christi proprie prædicari, atque adeo car-nem Christi proprie e cœlo descendisse conce-dat, necesse est. Quis autem hoc nisi Marcionita aut Valentinianus concedat?
units.tr: But if they think that from John 6, where the flesh of Christ is called the living bread which came down from heaven, it can be concluded that the human nature or flesh of Christ was able to give life to itself or raise itself, it must first be known that the flesh is not to be understood there simply, but as far as it was given for the life of the world; and therefore the passion, death and merit which proceed from and depend upon it are understood at the same time. Second, the giving of life is predicated of the flesh of Christ not simply as an action proper to the Godhead or to the omnipotent nature, but as a personal effect (ἀποτέλεσμα), which belongs to Christ according to both natures, just as salvation, expiation, redemption and other things of that kind are. Third, if giving life is understood as an action proper to the Godhead or to the omnipotent nature, and not as an effect (ἀποτέλεσμα), as Cyril sometimes seems to think, then giving life must be understood to be predicated of the flesh of Christ in the same way as, according to Cyril's own explanation, descent from heaven is predicated, or must be understood to be predicated, of the flesh of Christ. For Cyril thinks that both giving life and descending from heaven are predicated of the flesh of Christ in the same way. For thus he says in his letter on the right faith to Theodosius: "How then, I beg you, does the flesh give life? Or how is it understood to be from heaven, when it is from earth? Namely, according to its union with the living and heavenly Word." If anyone therefore insists that giving life, as far as it is an action proper to the Godhead, is properly predicated of the flesh of Christ, then he must also grant that descent from heaven is properly predicated of the flesh of Christ, and so that the flesh of Christ properly descended from heaven. Yet who would grant this except a Marcionite or a Valentinian?

units.la: Sed instant, actiones θεανδρικὰς[?] ad utramque naturam spectare, & proinde resuscitationem tanquam actionem θεανδρικὴν[?], tam ad humanam quàm ad divinam naturam pertinere. Fatemur tales actiones ad utramque spectare naturam, sed qualibet, quod suum est, secundum essentiales suas proprietates, conferente. Sic quando Christus mortuos resuscitavit, secundum humanam quidem naturam voluit, tetigit mortuos, & vocem tanquam symbolum edidit: Secundum divinam naturam, seu virtute divinæ naturæ effecit, ut mortui reviviscerent. Eodem igitur modo in hac sua resurrectione Christus secundum Dei tatem suam seu vi divinæ naturæ animam ad corpus reduxit, secundum humanam naturam obedivit, & animam cum corpore iterum coniungi voluit & gestivit, ut Sacerdotis & regis officio in æternum fungi posset. Instant nonnulli, hoc modo nullum fore discrimen inter Christum & Petrum. At vero infinitum manet discrimen. Nam Christus non aliena sed sua propria potentia resurrexit, quoniam illud etiam mortuum corpus, erat filii Dei corpus, & quoniam ille homo quāvis mortuus, erat Deus & Filius Dei. Nam morte Christi, id est, separatione animæ & corporis Christi non est soluta personalis unio. Petrus autem & omnes Sancti resurgent, non propria sed aliena, nempe Christi potentia & virtute.
