Sic igitur sua non aliena, & quidem divina potentia Christus templum suum, quod à Iudæis destructum erat, tertio die secundum typum Ionæ, post quam omnia consummata essent, instauravit, & mortuus resurrexit.
units.tr: But they press that the theandric actions [θεανδρικὰς ?] look to both natures, and that therefore the resurrection, as a theandric action, pertains to the human nature as much as to the divine. We admit that such actions look to both natures, but each nature contributes what is its own, according to its essential properties. So when Christ raised the dead, he did so according to his human nature by touching the dead and uttering a word as a sign; but according to the divine nature, or by the power of the divine nature, he brought it about that the dead came back to life. In the same way, then, in this his resurrection, Christ according to his Godhead, that is by the power of the divine nature, brought the soul back to the body, while according to his human nature he obeyed, and willed and desired that the soul be joined again with the body, so that he might be able to exercise the office of priest and king for ever. Some press that in this way there would be no difference between Christ and Peter. But the difference remains infinite. For Christ rose not by an alien power but by his own, since that dead body too was the body of the Son of God, and since that man, however dead, was God and the Son of God. For by the death of Christ, that is, by the separation of the soul and body of Christ, the personal union was not dissolved. Peter, however, and all the saints will rise not by their own but by an alien power, namely by the power and strength of Christ. Thus Christ, by his own and not an alien, and indeed divine, power restored his temple, which had been destroyed by the Jews, on the third day, according to the type of Jonah, after all things had been accomplished, and rose again from the dead.

units.la: Iam quomodo resurrexerit & exiverit Christus è sepulcro sequitur ut dicatur. Hic sunt qui Christum corpore suo monumentum clausum ac lapidem penetrasse affirmant. Sed primum sine scriptura affirmant. Nusquam enim historia Evangelica de hac retradit, aut huius penetrationis mentionem facit. Contrà vero Matthæus: Ecce terræmotus factus est magnus. Ange-lus enim Domini cum descendisset è cœlo, & accessis-set, devolvit lapidem ab ostio, & sedit super eum. Itaque Leo Romanus Episcopus, cui multum sem-per Orthodoxi omnes tribuerunt, hûc respiciēs, Christum revoluto monumenti lapideresurre-xisse dicit. Deinde considerandum est, quod et-iam in morte & post resurrectionem mansit veritas corporis Christi, sicut Christus ipse testatur Luc. 24. Cùm post resurrectionem discipulis ad-huc dubitantibus dicit, Videte, palpate, Spiritus e-nim cārnem[?] & ossa non habet, sicuti me videtis ha-bere. Quod si quis putat per glorificationem in corpore Christi factam esse mutationem, vicissim cogitandum est, quod Augustinus dicit, gloriam-corpori Christi immortalitatem dedisse, non abstulisse naturam. At, inquis, ingressus est Christus per clausas januas, ut eas penetraret corpore suo, & sic ingressum esse etiam ex Patribus nonnulli exi-stimant. At, inquam, sine scriptura hoc dicitur, neque omnes Patres sic sentiunt. Non enim per clausas januas ingressus esse aut penetrasse, sed clausis januis, vel cum clausæ essent januæ, & nemo aperuisset, ingressus esse dicitur: Quomodo? Non exprimitur: Sed tamen januam, id est, creaturam cessisse creatori, & ad eius præsentiam resiliisse, & transitum præbuisse, sicut Hieronymus interpretatur, simplicius est cogitare, quàm cor-pus Christi, in Spiritum, qui penetraret, conver-sum, ac rursus Spiritum in corpus, quod à discipulis videretur & contrectaretur, mutatum esse.
units.tr: Now it follows that we say how Christ rose and came out of the sepulchre. Here there are those who affirm that Christ with his body penetrated the closed tomb and the stone. But first, they affirm this without Scripture. For the Gospel history nowhere reports this, nor does it make any mention of such a penetration. On the contrary, Matthew says: "Behold, there was a great earthquake. For the angel of the Lord, having come down from heaven and approached, rolled back the stone from the door and sat upon it." Accordingly Leo, the Roman bishop, whom all the orthodox have always greatly esteemed, looking to this, says that Christ rose with the stone of the tomb rolled back. Second, it must be considered that the truth of Christ's body remained even in death and after the resurrection, as Christ himself testifies in Luke 24, when after the resurrection, while the disciples were still doubting, he says: "See, touch; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me to have." But if anyone thinks that a change was made in the body of Christ through glorification, then conversely we must consider what Augustine says, that the glory gave immortality to the body of Christ, not taking away its nature. But, you say, Christ entered through closed doors, so that he penetrated them with his body, and some of the Fathers also think that he entered in this way. But I answer that this is said without Scripture, and not all the Fathers think so. For it is not said that he entered or penetrated through closed doors, but that he entered with the doors closed, or although the doors were shut, and no one had opened them. How? It is not expressed. Yet it is simpler to think that the door, that is, the creature, yielded to the Creator and drew back at his presence, and granted him passage, as Jerome interprets it, than to think that the body of Christ was changed into a spirit so that it could penetrate, and then turned back again into a body, which could be seen and handled by the disciples.

units.la: Superest, ut de fructu resurrectionis Christi dicam. Quæ igitur hactenus à me commemorata sunt omnia, præstitit Christus, non tantum propter se, ut per resurrectionem à mortuis, potenter se filium Dei declararet, unigenitum illum & dilectum, verum Deum cum patre & Spiritu Sancto, adeoque verum Messiam: sed propter nostram etiam salutem. Nam sua morte pro omniū nostrum peccatis satisfecisse, omnesque nostros hostes, qui per peccatum imperium aliquod in nos tenebant, profligasse, resurrectione sua testatur. Nisi enim sufficientem & debitam peccatis poenam persolvisset, nisi omnes nostros hostes devicisset, ex morte, quam pro nobis oppetierat, iustitia Dei nunquam eum emergere permisisset, ac proinde nos in peccatis nostris mansissemus, obnoxii horrendæ iræ Dei, & æternæ morti ac damnationi. At quia Christum verè resurrexisse constat, manifestum est, omnia nostra vitia, quæ nos Deo reddebant detestabilia, abolita, ac mortem & infernum vitiorum istorum stipendia profligata esse: Iustitiam verò, quam primi parentes in Paradiso culpa sua amiserant, & salutem æternam restitutam esse: Quam iustitiam obedientia sua partam Christus resuscitatus nobis credentibus nunc imputat, & non secus, ac si ipsi nos eam præstitissemus applicat, nosque Deo patri iustos in sua persona & puros sistit, ita ut nunc in numero Electorum Dei filiorum & hæredum vitæ æternæ censeamur, qui antea hostes eius fuimus: & propter hāc nostri iustificationem, id est, ut de bonis quæ moriendo nobis acquisivit, certos faceret, eaque nobis applicaret, ipsum à mortuis resuscitatum esse Epistola ad Rom.cap.4. af-firmat. Quid verò maiorem nobis consolationem afferre potest quàm cum omnes nostros hostes devictos videmus à Christo, eandemque victoriam nobis communicatam, ut nos triumphũ de illis agamus: Repulit enim ille à se mortem, ut illam à nobis propelleret; ex infernalibus cruciatibus evasit, ut nos ex istis eriperet: Diaboli potentiam fregit, ut nos ab eius Tyrannide vindicaret: de mundo trophæum statuit, ut nos contra eius insidias & furores defenderet. Ablato enim per Christum peccato, propter quod hostiũ machinationibus expositi eramus, quid illis restat, quo nos impetant? Absorpta est mors in victoriam: Vbi tua, ô Mors, Victoria? Vbi tuus, ô sepulcrum, stimulus?
units.tr: It remains for me to speak of the fruit of Christ's resurrection. Christ accomplished all the things I have so far recounted not only for his own sake, so that by his resurrection from the dead he might powerfully declare himself to be the Son of God, his only-begotten and beloved, true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and therefore the true Messiah; but also for our salvation. For by his resurrection he testifies that by his death he made satisfaction for the sins of all of us, and overthrew all our enemies, who through sin held some dominion over us. For unless he had paid the punishment due to and sufficient for sins, unless he had conquered all our enemies, the justice of God would never have allowed him to emerge from the death which he had undergone for us; and consequently we would have remained in our sins, subject to the dreadful wrath of God, and to eternal death and damnation. But because it is established that Christ truly rose again, it is plain that all our vices, which made us detestable to God, have been abolished, and that death and hell, the wages of those vices, have been overthrown; and that the righteousness which our first parents lost in Paradise through their own fault has been restored, together with eternal salvation. This righteousness, which Christ obtained by his obedience, he now, once risen, imputes to us who believe, and applies it to us no differently than if we ourselves had performed it; and he presents us to God the Father as righteous and pure in his own person, so that we who were formerly his enemies are now counted among the number of the elect sons and heirs of God and of eternal life. The Epistle to the Romans, chapter 4, affirms that he was raised from the dead for the sake of our justification, that is, in order to make us certain of the good things which he acquired for us by dying, and to apply them to us. What greater consolation can be brought to us than when we see all our enemies conquered by Christ, and this same victory shared with us, so that we may triumph over them? For he drove death from himself so that he might drive it from us; he escaped the torments of hell so that he might snatch us from them; he broke the power of the devil so that he might free us from his tyranny; he set up a trophy over the world so that he might defend us against its snares and rages. For with sin taken away through Christ, on account of which we were exposed to the machinations of our enemies, what remains for them by which they may attack us? Death is swallowed up in victory. O Death, where is your victory? O grave, where is your sting?

units.la: Atque huius rei consideratio omnibus temporibus contra Satanæ, mundi, & inferorum insidias consolari nos debet, neunquam animum despondeamus. Tumultuentur enim, persequantur nos, minentur exilia, cædes, gladiorum mucrones, restim, ignem & aquam, maledicant, mentiantur de nobis & execrentur. Quid tum? Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est qui justificat. Quis condemnabit? Christus est, qui mortuus est, imò verò, qui etiam excitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui postulat pro nobis, qui deleto, quod adver-sum nos erat, rituum chirographo, quod erat contrarium nobis, sustulit illud e medio, affixum cruci, expoliatosq; principatus & potestates traduxit palam triumphans de illis per semetipsum, ut Apostolus ait.
units.tr: And the consideration of this matter ought at all times to console us against the snares of Satan, the world, and the powers of hell, so that we never lose heart. For they may make an uproar, persecute us, threaten exile, slaughter, the points of swords, the rope, fire and water; they may slander us, lie about us and curse us. What then? Who shall accuse the elect of God? It is God who justifies. Who shall condemn? It is Christ who died, yea rather who also rose again, who is also at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us, who, having blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross, and having spoiled principalities and powers, made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in himself, as the Apostle says.

units.la: Sed ut recte illa resurrectione Christi & victoria fruamur, ex sordibus & inquinamentis huius vitæ assurgendum nobis est ad vitam sanctam & inculpatam. Sepulti enim una cum eo sumus per Baptismum in mortem, ut, sicut excitatus est Christus ex mortuis, in gloriam patris, ita & nos nova vita in-cedamus, ait idem Apostolus. Mori igitur pecca-to, & per fidem resurgere ad novam vitam oportet, qui resurrectionis Christi, & æternæ vitæ participes fieri cupiunt. Hæc enim mors prima, in-quit D. Ioannes in Apocal. Beatus & sanctus, qui habet partem in resurrectione prima, in hos mors se-cunda non habet potestatem, sed erunt sacerdotes Dei & Christi. Talis autem resurrectio est inchoatio vitæ æternæ & initium: & qui sic vivit, non sibi vivit, sed illi, qui pro nobis mortuus est, quemad-modum Paulus de se ait, Vivo ego iam non ego, sed Christus in me vivit. Militate igitur bonam mili-tiam retinentes fidem & bonam conscientiam. Si resurreximus cum Christo, superna quæramus, ubi Christus est ad dextram Dei sedens, superna quæremus[?], non terrestria. Nam mortui sumus, & vita nostra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo: quando Christus vita illa nostra patefactus fue-rit, tum & nos cum eo patefiemus gloriosi. Mor-tificemus membra nostra terrestria, scortationē, impuritatem, mollitiem, cupiditatem malam, & avaritiam, quæ est Idololatria, ob quæ venit ira Dei in filios contumaces. Quibus in vitiis & nos versabamur quondam, quum in iis viveremus. At nunc deponamus etiam nos hæc omnia, iram, excandescentiam, malitiam, maledicentiam, ver-borum borum turpitudinem ab ore nostro, ut D.Paulus Col.3.nos admonet.
units.tr: But if we are to enjoy rightly that resurrection and victory of Christ, we must rise from the filth and defilements of this life to a holy and blameless life. For we are buried together with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead to the glory of the Father, so also we should walk in newness of life, says the same Apostle. Therefore, those who desire to become partakers of Christ's resurrection and of eternal life must die to sin and through faith rise again to a new life. For this is the first death, says St. John in the Apocalypse: Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection; over such the second death has no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ. Such a resurrection is the beginning and the commencement of eternal life; and he who thus lives does not live to himself, but to him who died for us, just as Paul says of himself: I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me. Therefore, fight the good fight, holding fast faith and a good conscience. If we have risen with Christ, let us seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; let us seek the things above, not the things on earth. For we are dead, and our life is hidden with Christ in God; when Christ, who is our life, shall be made manifest, then we also shall be made manifest with him in glory. Let us mortify our earthly members: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry, on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the disobedient sons. We too once walked in these vices, when we lived in them. But now let us also put away all these things: anger, wrath, malice, slander, filthy speech from our mouth, as the Apostle Paul admonishes us in Colossians 3.

units.la: Quod si fecerimus, verè tales erimus, pro quibus Christus Dominus noster resurrexit, & non dubitabimus, quin in novissimo die nos quoque beneficio resurrectionis suę excitaturus sit ad vitam æternam. Nam ille caput nostrum est, & nos ipsius membra, capitis verò gloria maximè postulat, ut membra sibi sint conformia, id est, gloriosa, nullis obnoxia infirmitatibus, sed sibi convenientia.
units.tr: If we do this, we shall truly be such persons for whom Christ our Lord rose again, and we shall not doubt that on the last day he will raise us also, by the benefit of his resurrection, to eternal life. For he is our head, and we are his members; and the glory of the head especially requires that the members be conformed to it, that is, glorious, subject to no infirmities, but fitting to him.

units.la: Dixi hactenus, quod Christus idem, qui pas-sus & mortuus & sepultus est, tertio die è sepul-cro resurrexerit: quod sua, nempe divina poten-tia, non aliena resurrexerit: quod terræmotu fa-cto, concussoque sepulcro & aperto resurrexerit, denique quod propter nos & nostram salutem resurrexerit.
units.tr: So far I have said that Christ, the same who suffered, died and was buried, rose from the sepulchre on the third day; that he rose by his own, that is, divine power, and not by another's; that, with an earthquake occurring and the tomb shaken and opened, he rose; and finally, that he rose for our sake and for our salvation.

units.la: Nunc tibi, ô bone Jesu, perfecta patris imago, totis pectoribus gratias agimus pro tantis benefi-ciis, quod abolito peccato ab omnibus nostris hostibus, Satana, mundo, morte & inferno nos liberasti & resurrectione tua gloriosa tàm certos nos de salute & futura nostra resurrectione ad vitam æternam reddidisti.
units.tr: Now to you, good Jesus, perfect image of the Father, we give thanks with all our hearts for such great benefits: that, having abolished sin, you have freed us from all our enemies, Satan, the world, death and hell, and by your glorious resurrection have made us so certain of our salvation and of our future resurrection to eternal life.

units.la: Exaudi quæso miserorum tuorum membrorum gemitus & preces, quæ à te solo, tanquam à capite suo pendent, & ad te solum confugiunt, conserva Ecclesiam, quam sanguine tuo redemisti, & resurrectione tua justificasti, in vera tui agnitione, puraq; verbi tui doctrina, & libera eâ à persequutionibus, hæresibus, schismatibus & scandalis, serva literarum studia, tuere docentium & discentium coetus. Excita, illumina, & rege spi-ritu tuo, & defende pios gubernatores & salu-tares, qui Ecclesiam foveant & promoveant: inpri-mis autem Illustrissimum nostrum Principem & Dominum, Dn. Johannem Casimirum, Comitem Palatinum, Ducem Bavariæ & Electo-ralis Palatinatus tutorem & administratorem, u-nà cum Illustrissimo pupillo, reliquisque do-mus Palatinæ Principibus, rege gratia & veritate tua, ut te recte agnoscant, & concordi studio fe-licique successu regnum tuum promoveant.
units.tr: Hear, we pray, the groans and prayers of your wretched members, who depend on you alone, as on their head, and flee to you alone. Preserve the Church, which you redeemed with your blood and justified by your resurrection, in the true knowledge of you and the pure doctrine of your Word, and free from persecutions, heresies, schisms and scandals. Preserve the pursuit of letters, protect the assemblies of teachers and learners. Rouse, enlighten and rule them by your Spirit, and defend the pious and salutary governors who cherish and advance the Church; and especially our most illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord John Casimir, Count Palatine, Duke of Bavaria and guardian and administrator of the Electoral Palatinate, together with the most illustrious ward, and the remaining princes of the Palatine house: rule them by your grace and truth, so that they may rightly acknowledge you, and with harmonious zeal and happy success advance your kingdom.

units.la: Concede illis tranquillitatem, & gubernationem Patriæ & Ecclesiæ salutarem. Denique redde nos omnes per Spiritum συμφύτες[?] τῷ ὁμοιώματι τοῦ θανάτου[?], καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως[?] ἐς[?], & da, ut in hac æru-mnosa vita peccatis moriamur, & ad novam vitam resurgamus, in qua non nobis, sed tibi viva-mus, expectantes secundam resurrectionem, in qua conformes tibi facti, tecum regnemus in omnem æternitatem.
units.tr: Grant them tranquility, and a government of the fatherland and the Church that is wholesome. Finally, by your Spirit, make us all conformed to the likeness of your death, and of the resurrection [συμφύτες τῷ ὁμοιώματι τοῦ θανάτου, καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως], and grant that in this troublesome life we may die to sins and rise again to a new life, in which we may live not to ourselves but to you, awaiting the second resurrection, in which, made conformed to you, we may reign with you for all eternity.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: ORATIO VII. DE FRVCTIBVS RESVRRECTIONIS CHRISTI: & ad quos illi pertineant.
units.tr: ORATIO VII. ON THE FRUITS OF THE RESURRECTION OF CHRIST, AND TO WHOM THEY PERTAIN.

units.la: Anno 1590. pridie Paschatis recitata
units.tr: Delivered on the day before Easter, in the year 1590.

units.la: A Josua Zevelio
units.tr: To Josua Zevelius

units.la: IN multis equidem, quæ in celeberrima hac & antiquissima Academia à majoribus nostris præclarè & laudabiliter instituta, & ad nos in hunc usque diem summa religione sunt propagata, mihi nimirum postremum istud habendum est: quod hoc tempore ex hoc loco, gloriosæ resurrectionis Filii Dei, Domini & Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi à mortuis memoria quotannis recoli & gratis[?] animis celebrari solet. Quid enim sanctius? Quid æquius? & ordini nostro scholastico magis conveniens esse possit, quàm ut præcipua Christi beneficia, sub id ipsum anni tempus, quo ecclesiæ parta sunt, commemoremus, neque unquam turpem illorum oblivionem nobis obrepere patiamur. Ac sanè quo illud majorum nostrorum instiinstitutum est præstantius, eò majori cura studio-que est providendum, ne ut illis pulcherrimum fuit tàm laudabilem morem in schola post se re-linquere: sic nobis turpissimum sit, illud, quod quasi per manus accepimus negligere.
units.tr: Among the many things that this most famous and most ancient Academy, established splendidly and commendably by our forefathers and handed down to us to this day with the greatest reverence, has bequeathed to us, the following must surely be counted the last: that at this season, from this place, the memory of the glorious resurrection of the Son of God, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, from the dead is yearly recalled and celebrated with grateful hearts. For what could be more sacred? What could be more fitting, or more suited to our scholastic order, than that we should commemorate the chief benefits of Christ at the very time of the year when they were obtained for the Church, and never allow a shameful forgetfulness of them to creep upon us? Indeed, the more excellent this custom of our forefathers is, the greater the care and zeal with which we must see to it that, just as it was most admirable for them to leave behind in the school so praiseworthy a custom, so it would be most shameful for us to neglect what we have received, as it were, from their hands.

units.la: Etsi vero infantiæ meæ nimis mihi sim con-scius, atque ideo, sicut usus & consuetudo postu-lat, rationes mihi exponendæ essent, cur ego præ aliis, qui dicendi facultate plus possent, has par-tes in me susceperim: tamen etiam sine iis venia me consequi à vobis posse confido. Non enim vel ingenii viribus fretus, vel inanis gloriolæ sti-mulo impulsus, in conspectum vestrum multò jucundissimum prodii: inque hunc locum, qui ad agendum semper amplißimus, ad dicendum ornatissimus visus est, conscendi: sed Præcepto-rum meorum summa observantia colendorum authoritas ac jussus huc me produxit, cui ego ob-temperandum omnino licet non sine magna solicitudine, magnoque in tanta re timore meo existimavi. Verum enim vero eam animi curam illud nonnihil lenire cœpit, quod in sacris hisce juventutis exercitiis, si non omne ingenio perse-ctum, ac industria elaboratum assertur, conatus saltem apud æquos omnes laudem, vel certè ve-niam invenire solet. Ad hoc istud accedit, quod vos non in orationis pigmenta vel ornatum: sed in ipsius rei splendorem: non in dicentis faculta-tem, sed in tàm augusti argumenti dignitatem in-tentos animos huc attulisse confido. Quapro-pter ut omissa prolixiore excusatione ad ipsam rem fausto pede transeam, de gloriosa Servatoris nostri Iesu Christi resurrectione ex mortuis repetentem nonnulla patienter ac benevolè me ut audiatis, oro.
units.tr: Although I am indeed very conscious of my youth, and for that reason, as custom and usage demand, I ought to set out the reasons why I, rather than others who have greater ability in speaking, have undertaken these parts, nevertheless I trust that I may obtain your pardon even without them. For I have not come forward into your sight, most pleasing as it is, relying on the strength of my talent or driven by the spur of empty glory, and I have not mounted this place, which always seems most splendid for acting and most adorned for speaking. Rather, the authority of my teachers, whom I hold in the highest regard, and their command have brought me forward here, and I judged that I had to obey them, not without great anxiety and, in so great a matter, not without my fear. But that care of mind has begun somewhat to ease itself in this: that in these sacred exercises of the young, if not everything is put forward polished by talent and worked out with diligence, the effort at least usually finds praise, or certainly pardon, among all fair-minded people. To this is added that I trust you have brought to this a mind intent not on the embellishments or ornament of speech, but on the splendour of the matter itself, not on the ability of the speaker, but on the dignity of so noble a subject. Therefore, setting aside a longer apology, so that I may cross over to the matter itself with a fortunate foot, I beg you to listen to me patiently and kindly as I recount some things concerning the glorious resurrection of our Saviour Jesus Christ from the dead.

units.la: Te Fili Dei pro nobis miseris peccatoribus mortuæ ac resuscitate veris gemitibus invoco, ut mentes nostras Spiritus tui radiis illustres, & labia nostra aperias, ad laudem gloriosi nominis tui & ædificationem nostram, Amen.
units.tr: O Son of God, who for us wretched sinners didst die and didst rise again, I call upon thee with true sighs, that thou wouldest illumine our minds with the rays of thy Spirit and open our lips, to the praise of thy glorious name and to our edification. Amen.

units.la: Caeterùm ne in hoc argumento pertractando tanquam in ignoto mari versemur: sed ut recto ubique cursum teneamus, de tribus ordine verba facere constitui. Primò præcipuas quasdam historiæ partes ad fidei nostræ confirmationem repetam: Tum quinam sint præcipui resurrectionis dominicæ fructus ad consolationem nostram breviter exponam: Post ad quos hi fructus pertineant ad commonefactionem nostram explicabo.
units.tr: Moreover, lest in treating this subject we wander as on an unknown sea, but may keep a straight course everywhere, I have resolved to speak in an orderly fashion about three things. First, I shall rehearse certain principal parts of the history for the confirmation of our faith; then I shall briefly set out what the chief fruits of the Lord's resurrection are for our consolation; afterwards I shall explain, for our admonition, to whom these fruits pertain.

units.la: Ad historiam quod attinet, ipsi Evangelistarum fontes adeundi nobis sunt, unde quod ad fidei nostræ certitudinem sufficit, haurimus.
units.tr: As for the history, we must go to the very sources of the Evangelists, from which we draw what is sufficient for the certainty of our faith.

units.la: In tota resurrectionis Domini historia tres præcipuè circumstantias annotatas invenio: tempus:modū:patefactiones. De tempore testantur omnes Evangelistæ, Christum tertia mortis die resurrexisse, atque ita prophetarum vaticinia implevisse. Sexto namque die, qui erat Iudæorum Parasceve, in cruce exspiravit: vespere honorificè à Iosepho sepultus est: postero die toto, qui Pascha erat Iudæorum, in sepulcro mortuus requievit. Tandem sequente die, qui à mor-te tertius, hebdomadis primus erat, superata morte redivivus in hanc lucem reversus est. Narrat e-nim cum reliquis Evangelistis Iohannes, Mariam Magdalenam, aliasque mulieres primo die hebdomadis mane ad monumentum venisse: lapidem ab ostio sepulcri devolutum vidisse: discipulos duos in monumentum in ,reflos[?] lintea posita conspexisse, neque Domini corpus invenisse: sed angeli voce de resurrectione ejus edoctos fuisse. Hinc adeo perversam Iudæorum opinionem de venturo adhuc Messia convellere licet: ipsaque rei veritas illis frustrà ringentibus evincit, hunc Iesum tertia die a mortuis resuscitatum, verum esse Messiam, nec alium nobis exspectandum.
units.tr: In the whole history of the Lord's resurrection I find three circumstances especially noted: the time, the manner, and the manifestations. Concerning the time, all the Evangelists bear witness that Christ rose on the third day after his death, and so fulfilled the prophecies of the prophets. For on the sixth day, which was the Jews' Preparation (Parasceve), he expired on the cross; in the evening he was honourably buried by Joseph; on the following whole day, which was the Passover of the Jews, he rested dead in the tomb. Finally, on the following day, which was the third from his death and the first of the week, having overcome death, he returned to life and to this light. For John, together with the other Evangelists, relates that Mary Magdalene and other women came to the tomb early on the first day of the week; they saw the stone rolled away from the door of the sepulchre; they saw two disciples in the tomb and the linen cloths laid out, and they did not find the Lord's body, but were taught of his resurrection by the voice of an angel. Hence it is indeed possible to overturn the perverse opinion of the Jews that the Messiah is still to come, and the very truth of the matter, while they vainly rage against it, proves that this Jesus, raised from the dead on the third day, is the true Messiah, and that we must look for no other.

units.la: Quod si illi in æternis tenebris, quibus jamdudum immersi obtorpuerunt, palpitare, quàm hanc augustissimam veritatis lucem contueri & adorare malunt: valeat saltem apud nos Chri-stianos hoc firmissimum argumentum: Iesum solum & nullum alium esse promissum redemto-rem: quia solus & nullus alius tertio die a mortuis resurrexit: quod de Messia jam olim prophetarum oracula prædixerant, & ipso Christo fidelissimo interprete, typus Ionæ aperte præfigurave-rat. Sicut enim Ionas in ventre ceti tres dies & tres noctes fuit: ita oportuit filium hominis esse in corde terræ tres dies & tres noctes. Nec sanè aliunde factum est, quod primum diem cujusque hebdomadis, tot jam seculorum usu nos Christiani sacrum celebramus, nisi quod ille ipse est, quo Christus triduana morte defunctus gloriosè resurrexit.
units.tr: But if they prefer to stare in the eternal darkness in which they have long been immersed and grown numb, groping about, rather than to behold and adore this most august light of truth, let at least this most firm argument hold among us Christians: that Jesus alone, and no other, is the promised Redeemer, because he alone, and no other, rose from the dead on the third day. This the oracles of the prophets had long ago foretold of the Messiah, and the type of Jonah had plainly prefigured it, Christ himself being the most faithful interpreter. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so it behooved the Son of Man to be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights. Nor indeed has it come about from anywhere else that we Christians, by the custom of so many ages now, celebrate the first day of each week as holy, except that it is the very day on which Christ, having died a death of three days, rose gloriously.

units.la: Sed pergamus, & modum etiam resurrectionis dominicę exponamus. Ac primò quidem cō-tra fanaticos quosdā spiritus, quib. volupe est, oia ea, quę de Christo vere dicuntur, inanib. spectris deludere, firmiter tenendum est, eum vere à mortuis resurrexisse, h.e, animā ipsius ad corpus, à quo per inenarrabiles angustias, cruciatus & terrores avulsa fuerat, verè rediisse, illiq; unitā fuisse: atq; idem illud corpus, quod paulò ante à furiosis militib. indignis modis tractatum, ac flagris laceratum fuerat, quodq; vi mortis ceciderat, verè resurrexisse: id quod cum ex aliis, tum praecipuè ex his causis fit manifestum. Quod n. λόγῳ[?] naturalis æterni Dei filius ex definito patris sui consilio ad liberandum genus humanum semel assumsit, hoc nunquam ac ne in morte quidem deposuit, nec in æternum deponet: sed omnipotenti sua virtute in cœlum evexit: ac in extremo judicio omnibus hominibus reprobis simul & electis adspiciendum dabit: his in perpetuum gaudium & felicitatem: illis in æternum mœrorem & cruciatū. Quid? quod natura nostra justissimo & immoto judicio Dei propter peccata mori debuit, ac rursum è terra suscitari? Per hominem n. mors, inqt Apostolus, per hominem quoq; resurrectio. Quin & ipse Christus multoties prædixit, eundem Filium hominis moriturum & resurrecturum esse: Et angelus diserte verbis mulieribus fatetur, illum ipsum surrexisse, qui cum illis loquutus fuerat, cum adhuc in Galilæa esset: Surrexit, inquit, non est hic: præcedet vos in Galilæam. Quis igitur verbis ipsius CHRISTI fidem non habeat? Quis nisi summa cum animi obstinatione angeli testimonium respuat? Ac ne dubiū quod sit, quomodo, quaso, resurrexisse dicetur Chri-stus, si aliud corpus mortuum fuit aliud revixit? Hæc enim est resurrectio, ait Ambrosius, sicut verbi ipsius sono exprimitur, ut quod cecidit, hoc resurgat, quod mortuum fuerit, hoc revivisçat[?]. Ex quibus omnibus perspicuum fit, neque animam, neque corpus Christi, saltem eo mortis triduo ubique fuisse, ut quidam falso docent, jam inde ab utero naturam humanam à λόγῳ assumtam vi unionis ubique in omnibus locis & extra omnia loca perpetuò fuisse: nobisque propterea, quod non credimus grandem dicam impingunt. Si enim corpus Christi, uti somniant, communibus naturæ legibus, sicut nostra corpora sunt, nunquam subjectum fuit, qua, quaso, ratione mori, crucifigi, manibus palpari, monumento condi, ex eo prodire, seque de loco in locum movere potuit? Hęc qui faciat, ut certè Christum fecisse omnes Evangelistæ testantur, non ego eum hominem ubiquitarium, sed cum Apostolo fratrib. suis per omnia excepto peccato, similem, h.e, suis definitum terminis & loco esse judico. Nec moror hic Sophi-sticen, fuisse definitum naturali modo: majesta-tico non item.
units.tr: But let us proceed, and set out also the manner of the Lord's resurrection. First, indeed, against certain fanatical spirits, who delight in deluding everything that is truly said of Christ with empty phantoms, it must firmly be held that he truly rose from the dead, that is, that his soul truly returned to his body, from which it had been torn away through unspeakable anguish, torments and terrors, and was united with it again; and that the very same body, which shortly before had been treated shamefully by the savage soldiers and torn with scourges, and which had fallen by the force of death, truly rose again. This is made plain both from other causes and especially from these. For the Son of the eternal God, who in accordance with the definite counsel of his Father once took up the Word [λόγῳ] for the deliverance of mankind, never laid this aside, not even in death, and will never lay it aside for eternity; but by his almighty power he raised it into heaven, and at the final judgment he will give it to be seen by all men, both the reprobate and the elect: to the former for eternal joy and felicity, to the latter for eternal sorrow and torment. What more? Our nature was bound to die because of sin by the most just and unchangeable judgment of God, and again to be raised up from the earth. "For by man," says the Apostle, "came death; by man also came the resurrection." Indeed Christ himself many times foretold that the same Son of Man would die and rise again; and the angel plainly tells the women in words that he who had spoken with them, while he was still in Galilee, had himself risen: "He is risen," he says, "he is not here; he will go before you into Galilee." Who, then, would not believe the words of Christ himself? Who, except with the greatest stubbornness of mind, would reject the testimony of the angel? And lest there be any doubt how, I ask, could it be said that Christ rose again, if one dead body was one thing and what revived was another? "For this is the resurrection," says Ambrose, "as is expressed by the very sound of the word itself: that what fell should rise again, that what was dead should come back to life." From all these things it is clear that neither the soul nor the body of Christ was everywhere, at least not during those three days of death, as some falsely teach, namely that from the womb onwards the human nature assumed by the Word had by virtue of the union been present everywhere, in all places and outside all places continually; and they fall upon us with a great charge because we do not believe this. For if, as they dream, the body of Christ was never subject to the common laws of nature, as our bodies are, by what reason, I ask, could he die, be crucified, be touched with hands, be laid in a tomb, come forth from it, and move himself from place to place? Whoever does this, as all the Evangelists certainly testify that Christ did, I judge him not to be a man who is everywhere, but, like his brethren in all things except sin, as the Apostle says, to be limited to his own terms and place. Nor do I linger here over the sophistry that he was limited in a natural way, but not in a majestic way.

units.la: Quid enim hoc aliud est dicere, quam Christum modo naturali verum homine, majestatico spectrum fuisse: angeli verba natu-rali modo vera majestatico falsa fuisse: fidem de-nique Christianam de nativitate, passione, mor-te, sepultura, resurrectione, ascensione & reditu Christi naturali modo veram, majestatico com-mentitiam esse? Neque porro existimandum est,dum hoc contendimus, nos Christi corpus post resurrectionem iisdem infirmitatibus, quibus ante eam obnoxium fuit subjicere, aut gloriosum esse negare. Liberè enim & constanter, id quod res est, profitemur: idem corpus quidem resurrexisse: sed glorificatum, incorruptibile, immortale, gloria & donis cœlestibus ornatum: nō tamen deificatum, non immensum, non ubiquitarium, non proprietatibus naturę humanę essentialibus destitutum. Ipse enim angelus, qui nobis instar mille testium merito esse debet, Christum discipulos in Galilæam præcessurum esse affirmat. Qua verò ratione se eò recipere poterat, ubi, ut adversariis placet, jam ante erat? Quod si ne huic quidem tàm amplo angeli testimonio locum dare, sed sententiam suam mordicus tenere volunt, quid prohibet, quo minus etiam nostra corpora in mortuorum resurrectione immensa & ubiquitaria fore concedant: siquidem mor-talia nostra corpora glorioso corpori Christi conformia erunt? Atqui corpora nostra, etsi erunt incorrupta, gloriosa, spiritualia: vera tamen corpora manebunt, trina dimensione terminata. Non enim, ut Apostolus loquitur, cupimus exui, sed superindui, ut absorbeatur mortalitas à vita, hoc est, non cupimus naturæ destructionem: sed tantum à mortalitate liberationem. Quare viderint illi, qua ratione, quo jure, aut quo scripturæ testimonio freti, Christi carnem veris humanæ naturæ proprietatibus privent, ipsíque ubiquitatem assingant. Gloria enim, ut Augustinus ad Dardanum inquit, immortalitatem carni dedit, na-turam non abstulit.
units.tr: For what else is it to say that Christ was a true man in a natural way but a phantom in a majestic way; that the angel's words were true in a natural way but false in a majestic way; and, finally, that the Christian faith concerning Christ's birth, passion, death, burial, resurrection, ascension and return is true in a natural way but fictitious in a majestic way? Nor must it be supposed, when we contend this, that we subject Christ's body after the resurrection to the same infirmities to which it was liable before it, or deny that it is glorious. For we freely and steadfastly profess what is the case: that the same body indeed rose again, but glorified, incorruptible, immortal, adorned with glory and heavenly gifts; yet not deified, not immense, not ubiquitous, and not deprived of the essential properties of human nature. For the angel himself, who ought rightly to be to us as a thousand witnesses, affirms that Christ would go before the disciples into Galilee. But by what reasoning could he betake himself there, if, as our opponents would have it, he was already there before? But if they will not even give place to so ample a testimony of the angel, but wish to hold their opinion stubbornly, what prevents them from also conceding that our bodies in the resurrection of the dead will be immense and ubiquitous, since our mortal bodies will be conformed to the glorious body of Christ? Yet our bodies, although they will be incorruptible, glorious and spiritual, will nevertheless remain true bodies, bounded by three dimensions. For, as the Apostle speaks, we do not desire to be stripped, but to be clothed upon, so that mortality may be swallowed up by life; that is, we do not desire the destruction of nature, but only the liberation from mortality. Wherefore let them see by what reasoning, by what right, or relying on what testimony of Scripture, they deprive Christ's flesh of the true properties of human nature and ascribe ubiquity to it. For "glory," as Augustine says to Dardanus, gave immortality to the flesh; it did not take away its nature.

units.la: Cæterum in describendo dominicæ resurre-ctionis modo, illud nequaquam est prætereundum, quod non aliena, sed propria potentia Christus resurrexit. Cum autem caro ejus, quæ sensu, motu, & vita omni destituta jacebat hoc tàm magnificum, tàm divinum, tàm admirabile suscitationis opus peragere in seipsa potuerit minimè: divinitati ipsius omnino id adscribendum esse, quanta possumus vocis contentione asserimus: idque vel ex terræ motu, in quo Dominus haud dubie resurrexit nō obscurè confirmamus. Quæ enim humana vis aut potentia terram & saxa concutiat? An emortua caro id faciat? Dubium ergo non est, ejusdem divinæ potentiæ effecta fuisse, tum terræ illam concussionem tum Christi redivivi è sepulcro egressum. Illo enim tàm repentino terræ motu, non tàm animos truculentorum militum concutere & ferociam compescere, quâ divinam suam potentiam toti mundo declarare Dominus voluit. Ex fi vero angelus Domini de cœlo descendisse, lapidemque ab ostio sepulcri devolvisse legitur: hoc tamen non eò factum esse existimemus, ut Christum ceu captivum aliquè ex ergastulo lib-raret[?]: sed potius, ut præco divinæ ipsius potentiæ & resurrectionis esset, gloriam resurgentis illustraret, & Domino suo quasi è prælio, Satana, morte, inferno reliquisque hostibus fusis ac superatis, revertenti victoriam gratu-laretur. Quid enim? an non Christus omnipotens Dei filius, æternus cum patre Deus & rerum omnium creator vel solo nutu lapidem illum ingentem non dico removere, sed in nihilum redigere poterat? Sed & alia non minus evidens ratio in promtu est, quæ Christum divinitatis suæ potentia resurrexisse probat. Surrexit, inquit angelus, sicut dixit. At quænam illa sunt quæ dixe-rat? Habeo potestatem ponendi & sumendi animam. Item: Destruite templum hoc, & tribus diebus eri-gam illud. Quæ de divinitatis potentia intelligen-da esse, quis non animadvertit.
units.tr: Moreover, in describing the manner of the Lord's resurrection, this must by no means be passed over: that Christ rose not by another's power but by his own. Since, however, his flesh, which lay destitute of sense, motion and all life, could by no means accomplish in itself so great, so divine and so admirable a work of raising up, we assert with as much vehemence as we can that this must wholly be ascribed to his divinity; and we confirm this not obscurely from the earthquake, in which the Lord undoubtedly rose. For what human force or power could shake the earth and the rocks? Could dead flesh do it? It is therefore beyond doubt that both that earthquake and Christ's egress from the sepulchre, now restored to life, were effects of the same divine power. For by that sudden earthquake the Lord willed to shake the minds of the fierce soldiers and to restrain their ferocity, and so to declare his divine power to the whole world. Moreover, we read that the angel of the Lord descended from heaven and rolled the stone away from the door of the sepulchre; yet let us not think this was done so that he might free Christ, as a captive from some prison, but rather that he might be a herald of his very divine power and of the resurrection, might illustrate the glory of the one rising, and might congratulate his Lord, returning as from battle with Satan, death, hell and the remaining enemies routed and overcome, on his victory. For what? Could not Christ, the almighty Son of God, eternal with the Father, God and creator of all things, reduce that huge stone to nothing, not to say remove it, by a mere nod? But there is also another reason, no less evident, at hand, which proves that Christ rose by the power of his divinity. "He has risen," says the angel, "as he said." But what were the things he had said? "I have power to lay down and to take up my life." Likewise: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." Who does not see that these must be understood of the power of the divinity?

units.la: At excipiunt illi, qui jamdudum contra Filium Dei insurrexerunt, eumque de summo divinitatis gradu deturbare conati sunt, Scripturam passim expressis verbis hoc opus patri tri-buere, dum Christum à Deo excitatum esse affirmat.
units.tr: But those who long ago rose up against the Son of God, and have tried to thrust him down from the highest degree of divinity, object that Scripture everywhere, in express words, attributes this work to the Father, since it affirms that Christ was raised up by God.

units.la: Petrus enim in actis apostolorum aliquoties Iudæis: Quem, inquit, vos trucidastis, hunc Deus excitavit a mortuis: Et Paulus, Pater ille-glo-ria potentiam suam exeruit, cum eum excitavit ex mortuis. Sed plumbeum hoc telum retundere haud quaquam difficile est. Cùm enim Chri-stus ipse, quem in hac lite merito judicem con-stituimus, diserte fatetur, se cum patre suo sem-per operari, & quæcunque Pater facit, Filium similiter facere: & Petrus testatur, Christum mortificatum esse carne, sed vivificatum Spi-ritu, nempe suo, & non alieno, hoc est, propria divinitatis suæ potentia: quis non nisi summo cum scelere Filium ab hoc opere excludat? Quare cum Christus divina sua virtute mortem à se depulerit, atque ita sævissimorum hostium victor extiterit : constanter & intrepidè ipsum verum Deum, & Dei Filium, per resurrectionem à mortuis, potenter, ut apostolus loquitur declaratum, etiam in mediis mundi furoribus prædicemus ac celebremus, quo freti nullius creaturæ vim aut minas pertimescamus, sed certissima hac consolatione suffulti stemus, fore, ut ipse, qui vitam suam à morte vindicare potuit, cùm sit caput nostrum etiam nos sua membra, quemadmodum promisit, ex terræ pulvere tandem exsuscitet, & ad se in patriam cœlestem ac sempiternam gloriam traducat.
units.tr: For Peter in the Acts of the Apostles, speaking several times to the Jews, says: "Whom you slew, God raised up from the dead." And Paul: "That Father of glory exerted his power when he raised him up from the dead." But this leaden weapon is by no means difficult to blunt. For since Christ himself, whom we rightly constitute judge in this dispute, plainly confesses that he always works together with his Father, and that whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does; and since Peter testifies that Christ was put to death in the flesh but quickened in the Spirit, namely his own, and not another's, that is, by the proper power of his divinity; who, unless with the greatest wickedness, would exclude the Son from this work? Wherefore, since Christ by his divine power repelled death from himself, and so stood forth as victor over the most savage enemies, we shall constantly and fearlessly proclaim and celebrate him as the true God and Son of God, declared powerfully, as the apostle speaks, by the resurrection from the dead, even in the midst of the world's rages; relying on which we shall not fear the strength or threats of any creature, but, supported by this most certain consolation, we shall stand, knowing that he who was able to vindicate his own life from death will, since he is our head and we are his members, as he has promised, at length raise us up from the dust of the earth and bring us to himself into the heavenly fatherland and everlasting glory.

units.la: Verum enim vero, haud scio an hæc tam eximia fides tamque excellens consolatio, cui ne inferorum quidem portæ prævalere possunt, an ea, inquam, nobis suppeteret, nisi & Christus post resurrectionem se ipsum patefecisset & conspiciendum præbuisset. Cui enim thesaurus in terra defossus prodesse possit? Talis sane fuisset, Christi resurrectio, nisi mundo innotuisset. Quomodo igitur, & quibus, thesaurus iste primum innotuerit, audiamus. Extremo sabbatho cum lucesceret in primum diem hebdomadis Maria Magdalena & altera Maria egressæ ad ungendum pro gentis more corpus Domini in sepulcro: primæ lætissimum hoc nuncium ab angelo cœlesti præconé acceperunt. Quid, inquit ille, quæritis viventem cum mortuis? Surrexit: præcedet vos in Galilæam sicut dixit, venite, videte locum, ubi jacebat Dominus. O exoptatum miseris mortalibus nuncium! O inexpectatum gaudium! Hoccine mulierculas primò percipere erat æquum? Sanè erat æquum, mirando Dei consilio, ut quę pecca-tum & mortem primæ in mundum invexerant, etiam primæ nuncium vitæ acciperent. Nec minus hoc ipsa ratio & æquitas postulabat, ut quæ maximè doluerant, quæque discipulis fugienti-bus, & sese præ metu in nescio quos angulos pro-ripientibus, Christum ad crucem usque secutæ fuerant, eumque solicitè in sepulcro quæsierant, ut, inquam, hæ primæ tanti gaudii participes fierent.
units.tr: Indeed, I do not know whether this so remarkable faith and so excellent consolation, against which not even the gates of hell can prevail, could be ours, I say, unless Christ, after the resurrection, had himself made himself known and presented himself to be seen. For what good could a treasure buried in the earth do anyone? Such indeed would Christ's resurrection have been, had it not become known to the world. Let us hear, therefore, how and to whom that treasure first became known. At the end of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went out to anoint the body of the Lord in the sepulchre, according to the custom of the people; and they first received this most joyful news from a heavenly herald, the angel. "Why," he says, "do you seek the living among the dead? He has risen; he will go before you into Galilee, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay." O message longed for by wretched mortals! O unexpected joy! Was it fitting that women, mere women, should first perceive this? Certainly it was fitting, by the wondrous counsel of God, that those who had first brought sin and death into the world should also first receive the message of life. Nor did reason and equity demand this any less, that those who had grieved most, and who had followed Christ even to the cross, when the disciples fled and hurried away in fear to I know not what corners, and who had anxiously sought him in the sepulchre, should, I say, be the first partakers of so great a joy.

units.la: Huic angeli testimonio apparitiones Chri-sti redivivi complures per totos 40. dies accesse-runt. Primò enim ipso mane resurrectionis Ma-riæ Magdalenæ in horto specie hortulani apparuit, mox & agnoscendum se dedit, eamque de ascensu suo ad patrem familiariter edocuit. Eodem die discipulis duobus Emaunta proficiscen-tibus, ac multa de Christi passione & morte am-bigentib. sese adjunxit, eorum incredulitate re-prehendit, suam tum mortem tum resurrectione oraculorum propheticorum autoritate ipsis con-firmavit. Eadem vespera discipulis, metu Iudæo-rum loco ab hominum frequentia remotiore conclusis, medius adstitit, manus ac latus suum o-stendit, afflatu oris Spiritum sanctum eis dedit. Octiduo elapso ibidem in discipulorum conspectu Thomæ incredulo sese non modo visendum, sed & manibus contrectandum exhibuit. Tan-dem & Petro ac sociis ejus piscantibus ad mare Tyberiadis apparuit, atque ut plenius infirmitati eorum mederetur, illustri miraculo insolitæ capturæ, sumptoque ex piscibus prandiolo fidem eorum id temporis confirmavit. Harum ac multo plurium apparitionum etiam Apostolus catalogum contexit, ubi mortem sepulturam & resurrectionem Christi secundum scripturas factam esse pluribus ostendens. Visus est, inquit, Cephae: deinde duodecim illis: postea visus est amplius quam quingentis fratribus semel: visus est etiam Jacobo: deinde apostolis omnibus: ultimo vero omnium, velut abortivo visus est etiam mihi. Quod vero Christus non mox in coelum ascenderit: sed toties se patefecerit: id haud temere, sed in usum & consolationem nostram factum esse existimemus. Cum enim resurrectio Christi, ut Apostolus passim ac praecipue loco illo ad Corinthios jam citato satis demonstrat, basis ac fundamentum sit, in quo omnis nostra consolatio consistit, & sine quo salutis aeternae spes prorsus jacet: non alia causa ille redivivus toties apparere voluit, nisi ut ea ratione fidem nostram modis omnibus confirmatam redderet: quae sane tam est infirma, tamque languida, ut nisi undique illustribus argumentis fulciatur, facile dubitationum fluctibus obruatur: id quod in discipulorum exemplo videre est. Non eos tot prophetarum vaticinia officii admonent: non tot Christi praedictiones consulantur: non angeli testimonium erigit: alii dubitant: alii de regno Israelis prorsus actum esse putant: alii lugent, plorant, Dominumque sublatum queruntur. Ipse ergo Christus redivivus apparet, fratribus suis haec omnia, ut credant, annunciari jubet, & incredulitatem eorum taxans: O stulti, inquit, ac tardi corde, ad credendum omnibus, quæ locuti sunt Prophetæ, nonne oportuit Christum hæc pati & intrare in gloriam suam. Tot ac tàm illustria resurrectionis Christi testimonia certiora profectò sunt, quàm ut à Iudæis negari: augustiora, quàm ut in contemtum adduci possint. Quod si eo audaciæ vel potius impudentiæ prolabantur, ut mulieres & discipulos tanquam viles & abjectos testes irrideant, en adsunt ipsi angeli è cœlo missi, qui oculos eorum cœlesti fulgore præstringūt, & ora obturant, ne vel hiscere quidem audeant: Si apparitionibus fidem derogent: adest Paulus qui Christum non uni, sed omnibus apostolis, imò quingentis fratribus apparuisse testatur: Si denique historiam tanquam fictam calumnientur: adsunt quatuor Evangelistæ, qui eam cum publicè nota res esset, nemine contradicere ausō descripserunt, atque ita eos in conscientiis suis dudum convicerunt. In ore enim duorum & trium omnis veritas consistit. Nec quisquam miretur Christum non in medio templo & foro illustria victoriæ suæ trophæa statuisse, inque conspectum Pilati, Herodis & Sacerdotum prodiisse, iisque se redivivū probasse. An nō enim divinis testimoniis potius quam humanis fidem nostram niti oportuit? An non Deus elegit ea, quæ stulta sunt in mundo, ut sapientiam carnis confunderet? Sed & aliam non minus gravem causam habuit Christus, cur discipulis toties visendum se exhiberet, ut nimirum de veritate resurrectionis suæ nobis certò constaret, contra Marcionis, Eutychis, aliorumque fanafanaticorum hominum somnia de spectro deificato & ubiquitario, quæ Diabolum suo tempore in Ecclesia disseminaturum[?] esse præscivit. Hæc enim causa est, cur discipulis consternatis ac metuentibus, quasi spectri aliqua imagine objecta, dixerit: Quid turbati estis, & quare disceptationes subeunt in corda vestra? Videte manus meas. Nam ego ipse sum. Contrectate me & videte me. Nam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout conspicitis me habere. A proprio corporis demonstrat, sed verum h.e. finitum & palpabile corpus habere, non spiritum esse. Spiritus enim carnem & ossa non habet. Spiritus videri nequit: contrectari nequit. Utrumque Dominus à resurrectione in se ostendens, non spectrum evanidum sed verum hominem se esse, qui ante fuerat firmiter probat. Argumentum hoc D. Ignatius, referente Hieronymo in vita ejus, ex Epistola ad Polycarpum similiter intellexit: Ego, inquit, & post resurrectionem cum vidi, & credo, quia fit, quoniam venit ad Petrum & ad eos qui cum Petro erant: & dixit eis: Ecce palpate me & videte me quia non sum Daemonium incorporale.
units.tr: To this testimony of the angel, many appearances of the risen Christ followed during the whole forty days. First, on the very morning of the resurrection, he appeared to Mary Magdalene in the garden in the appearance of a gardener; soon he also made himself recognised and familiarly taught her about his ascension to the Father. On the same day, when two disciples were setting out for Emmaus and were doubting about many things concerning Christ's passion and death, he joined them, rebuked their unbelief, and confirmed for them by the authority of the prophetic oracles both his death and his resurrection. The same evening, when the disciples had shut themselves in, in a place remote from the crowds of men, for fear of the Jews, he stood in their midst, showed them his hands and side, and by breathing on them gave them the Holy Spirit. After eight days had passed, he showed himself in the same place, in the sight of the disciples, to the unbelieving Thomas, not only to be seen but also to be handled with the hands. Finally, he appeared to Peter and his companions as they were fishing at the sea of Tiberias, and, so that he might more fully heal their weakness, he confirmed their faith at that time by an illustrious miracle of an unusual catch and by a little meal taken from the fish. The Apostle also set out a list of these and of many more appearances, showing that Christ's death, burial and resurrection took place according to the Scriptures. He was seen, he says, by Cephas; then by the twelve; afterwards he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once; he was seen also by James; then by all the apostles; and last of all, as by one born out of due time, he was seen by me also. That Christ did not ascend into heaven at once, but revealed himself so many times, we judge to have been done not without reason, but for our use and comfort. For since the resurrection of Christ, as the Apostle shows throughout and especially in that passage to the Corinthians already cited, is the foundation on which all our consolation rests, and without which the hope of eternal salvation lies utterly prostrate, the risen one wished to appear so many times for no other cause than to make our faith, by this means, confirmed in every way. Indeed it is so weak and so feeble that, unless it is propped up on every side by illustrious arguments, it is easily overwhelmed by the waves of doubts; as may be seen in the example of the disciples. The many prophecies of the prophets did not remind them of their duty; the many predictions of Christ were not consulted; the testimony of the angel did not raise them up. Some doubted; some thought that the kingdom of Israel had been wholly abandoned; some mourned, wept, and complained that the Lord had been taken away. So the risen Christ himself appears, bids his brothers to announce all these things to them so that they may believe, and, rebuking their unbelief, says: O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken, ought not Christ to have suffered these things and entered into his glory? So many and so illustrious testimonies to the resurrection of Christ are surely too certain to be denied by the Jews, and too weighty to be brought into contempt. But if they proceed to such audacity, or rather impudence, as to mock the women and the disciples as worthless and despised witnesses, behold, the angels themselves sent from heaven are present, who dazzle their eyes with heavenly brightness and stop their mouths, so that they do not even dare to open them. If they disparage the appearances, the Apostle Paul is present, who testifies that Christ appeared not to one, but to all the apostles, and even to five hundred brethren. If finally they slander the story as invented, the four Evangelists are present, who, since the matter was publicly known, described it without anyone daring to contradict them, and so have long since convicted them in their own consciences. For in the mouth of two or three witnesses every truth stands. Nor should anyone wonder that Christ did not set up the illustrious trophies of his victory in the middle of the temple and the forum, and come forward before the eyes of Pilate, Herod and the priests, and prove himself risen before them. Ought not our faith rest on divine testimonies rather than on human ones? Did not God choose the things that are foolish in the world, to confound the wisdom of the flesh? But Christ also had another no less weighty reason why he presented himself to be seen by the disciples so often: namely, that we might be certain of the truth of his resurrection, against the dreams of Marcion, Eutyches, and other fanatical men about a deified and ubiquitous phantom, which the Devil foresaw he would spread abroad in the Church in his own time. For this is the reason why, when the disciples were dismayed and afraid, as if some image of a ghost had been put before them, he said: Why are you troubled, and why do doubts rise in your hearts? See my hands. For I myself am here. Handle me and see me. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have. He shows from his own body that he has a true, that is, finite and tangible body, and is not a spirit. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones. A spirit cannot be seen; it cannot be handled. By showing both of these in himself from the resurrection, the Lord firmly proves that he is not an evanescent phantom but the true man he had been before. Saint Ignatius, as Jerome reports in his life, understood this argument in the same way from the Epistle to Polycarp: I, he says, also after the resurrection saw him and believe that he is in the flesh; and when he came to Peter and to those who were with Peter, he said to them: Behold, handle me and see me, for I am not an incorporeal demon.

units.la: Sed hîc adversariis contrà sententib. breviter occurrendum est. Principio ut commentis suis fucum inducant, & Christum redivivum, non eandem carnem sed diversam habuisse ostendat, eum à Maria & discipulis non agnitum fuisse objectant. Sed quò se vertent, quidve causæ suæ prætexent, si oculos Mariæ & discipulorum retentos fuisse, ne agnoscerent eum, quem norant, cum Luca respondeamus? An neiterum eum repen-te evatē[?] evanuisse excipient, ac proinde corpus invisibile, aerium, spirituale habuisse? Atqui eundem clypeum eis opponimus, & rursus oculos eorum retentos esse, ut quem prius non agnoverant, eum amplius plane non viderent, repente alio se recipientem, cum Evangelistis asserimus. Quin etiam cum Augustino Christum quidem corpus spirituale, h.e, spiritualibus dotibus praeditum habuisse libenter agnoscimus: sed Spiritum fuisse negamus. Nihilo plus coloris illud habet, in quo praecipuum causae suae robur ponunt, cum ex eo corpus illocale & ubiq; existens nituntur probare, quod saxum & fores clausas penetrarit. Ut n. in eo multum est falsitatis: ita parum firmamenti positum habent. Ostendant vel unum epicem[?], qui penetrationem saxi[?] adstruat. Quod si adeo sibi in suis figmentis blandiuntur: cur non etiam angelos ubique esse profitentur, siquidem & hi corpora solida penetrare possunt? Sed abest ut penetrationem concedamus, cum ea directe cum apparitionis scopo confligat, eumq; destruat, atque etiam cum Christi verbis aperte pugnet, qui se Spiritum esse negat. Quapropter cum Christū in utroque miraculo in certo VBI fuisse, locum mutasse, nec simul in conclavi & foris fuisse sciamus: putidis illorum commentis valere jussis, cum verum humanum corpus retinuisse statuamus, & cum Hieronymo creaturam creatori cessisse libere dicamus.
units.tr: But here we must briefly meet our adversaries who hold the contrary opinion. First, in order to put a gloss on their inventions and to show that the risen Christ had not the same flesh but a different one, they object that he was not recognised by Mary and the disciples. But where will they turn, or what pretext will they offer for their cause, if we answer, with Luke, that the eyes of Mary and of the disciples were held so that they did not recognise him whom they knew? Or will they claim that he afterwards suddenly vanished, and therefore had an invisible, aerial, spiritual body? Yet we oppose them with the same shield, and assert with the Evangelists that their eyes were held again, so that they no longer at all saw him whom they had not recognised before, withdrawing suddenly elsewhere. Moreover, with Augustine we gladly acknowledge that Christ had a spiritual body, that is, one endowed with spiritual gifts, but we deny that he was a spirit. Their chief strength is no more colourful in this, that from it they strive to prove a body not confined to a place and existing everywhere, because he passed through a rock and closed doors. For as there is much falsehood in this, so they have set little firmness in it. Let them show even one epigram which affirms the penetration of a rock. But if they flatter themselves so much in their fictions, why do they not also profess that angels are everywhere, since these too can penetrate solid bodies? But we are far from conceding penetration, since it directly conflicts with the purpose of the appearance and destroys it, and also openly clashes with the words of Christ, who denies that he is a spirit. Therefore, since we know that Christ in each miracle was in a definite place, that he changed place, and that he was not at the same time in the room and outside it, let us bid farewell to their foul fictions, and let us hold that he kept a true human body, and say with Jerome that the creature has freely yielded to the Creator.

units.la: Cæterum, cum Christus non sibi, sed nobis resurrexerit omnia siquidem, quæ in his terris fecit, nostri non sua causa præstitit: nobis, teste angelo, natus, nobis passus, nobis denique mortuus est: consequens est, ut fructus etiam resurrectionis, quantum fert instituti nostri ratio breviter explicemus. Etsi autem scriptura plurimos eosque praestantissimos tanquam ex refertissimo penu nobis suppeditat: trium tamen praecipuorum explicatione in praesentia contenti erimus.
units.tr: Moreover, since Christ rose not for himself but for us (for all the things he did on this earth he performed for our sake, not his own), since, as the angel testifies, he was born for us, suffered for us, and died for us, it follows that we should briefly explain the fruits of the resurrection, as far as the plan of our work allows. Although Scripture supplies us with very many and most excellent ones, as if from a richly stocked storehouse, we will be content for the present with the explanation of three principal ones.

units.la: I. Primus itaque resurrectionis Christi fructus est, quod nos miseras perditaque, Diaboli, peccati & mortis mancipia, Christi victoria in libertatem asseruit, Deo reconciliavit, & iustitiam illam in Adamo per lapsum amissam postliminio nobis restituit. Nam (ut primo liberationem illam adstruamus) quid mors eius nisi cruentissima fuit lucta, cum peccato, Diabolo, & morte: resurrectio autem de his omnibus devictis laetissimus triumphus? Hinc peccatum ei, ceu horrendas quasdam Gorgones, iram Dei & aeternam condemnationem obiiciens graviter instabat: illinc Diabolus variis dubitationum telis & machinis gravius oppugnabat: mox ipsa mors spiculis suis confectum omnino prosternebat. Ipse nihilominus, quem hostes iam oppressum iacere putabat, ex morte vitam, & ex sepulcro victoriam proferens, hostibus cunctis devictis & contritis tertia die resurrexit, laetissima trophaea de illis reportavit, peccatum abolevit, mortem deglutivit, Diaboli regnum destruxit, & potentiam omnem attrivit. Audiamus huius victoriae testem Apostolum selectum illud Dei organum. Mortuus est, inquit, propter peccata nostra. Sed clarius alibi. Absorpta est mors in victoriam. ubi tua o mors victo-ria? ria? ubi tuus o inferne stimulus? stimulus vero mortis est peccatum: vis autem peccati lex. Sed Deo sit gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Et alibi eandem victoriam praedicans: Carnis, inquit, & sanguinis particeps factus est, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui habebat mortis imperium, hoc est Diabolum: & redimeret, quicunq; metu mortis per omnem vitam obnoxii erat servituti. Ab hoc ergo mortis & damnationis aeternae metu, Christus nos liberavit, dum mortem sua sustulit, quod in morte formidabile erat. Etsi enim mors omnibus etiamnum dominari videtur: revera tamen exitus piorum non mors est: sed erumnarum omnium malorum q; perfugium, & fida statio ac portus quietis: sepultura vitiorum, virtutum suscitatio, atq; in vitam aeternam transitus: ut Ambrosii verbis utar. Atque hunc fructum A- postolus loco prius memorato, egregie explicas. Si, inquit, Christus non est excitatus, adhuc estis in peccatis vestris, & inanis est fides vestra: fides, inquam, de liberatione a peccato & morte, per mortem eius. Hinc enim a contrario nos vult colligere, cum Christus sit excitatus, primitiae eorum, qui obdormiverunt, factus: firmam & immotam stare fidem nostram de redemtione per Christū, nec amplius nos esse in peccatis nostris. Quod de reparatione iustitiae dixi, necessario cum illis cohaeret. Si enim morte & resurrectione Christi, attrita est Diaboli & mortis potentia: si maledictio legis & peccati reatus expiatus: Utique nos, qui in Christum credimus ab omni noxa absoluti & coram Deo justi sumus. Ubi enim est satisfactio, ibi est absolutio: & ubi absolutio, ibi & justitia; Beati enim, inquit ex Psalmis Apostolus, quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, & quorum obtecta sunt peccata. Beatus vir cui non imputat Deus peccatum. Et ibidem: Christus, &c. sed resurrexit propter justificationem nostri. Et alio loco: Commendat suam caritatem erga nos Deus, qui cum adhuc essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus sit. Justificati igitur eius sanguine, servabimur nunc multo magis, &c.
units.tr: I. The first fruit of Christ's resurrection, therefore, is that his victory has asserted us, who were wretched and lost, the slaves of the Devil, of sin and of death, into liberty; it has reconciled us to God, and restored to us by right of postliminium that righteousness which was lost in Adam through the fall. For (to establish that deliverance first) what was his death but a most bloody wrestling with sin, the Devil and death? And what was the resurrection but a most joyful triumph over all these enemies defeated? Sin, setting before him like horrible Gorgons the wrath of God and eternal condemnation, pressed him hard on one side; on the other the Devil assailed him more grievously with the various darts and engines of doubt; and presently death itself, with its missiles, laid him low, quite worn out. Yet he himself, whom the enemies thought already overcome and lying prostrate, brought life out of death and victory out of the sepulchre; the enemies being conquered and crushed, he rose on the third day, bore off most joyful trophies over them, abolished sin, swallowed up death, destroyed the kingdom of the Devil, and broke all his power. Let us hear the Apostle, that chosen instrument of God, as witness of this victory: "He died," he says, "for our sins." But more clearly elsewhere: "Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy victory? O grave, where is thy sting? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." And again, proclaiming the same victory elsewhere: "He himself likewise partook of flesh and blood, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil, and might deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to bondage all their lives." From this fear of death and of eternal damnation, therefore, Christ has delivered us, since by his own death he took away what was dreadful in death. For even if death still seems to rule over all, in truth "the departure of the godly is not death, but a refuge from all evils and a faithful station and haven of rest: the burial of vices, the raising up of virtues, and a passage into eternal life," to use the words of Ambrose. And the Apostle, in the passage mentioned above, explains this fruit admirably: "If Christ is not raised," he says, "you are still in your sins, and your faith is vain": faith, I say, concerning deliverance from sin and death through his death. For from the contrary he wishes us to conclude that, since Christ has been raised, having become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, our faith concerning redemption through Christ stands firm and unmoved, and that we are no longer in our sins. What I have said concerning the restoration of righteousness necessarily coheres with these things. For if by the death and resurrection of Christ the power of the Devil and of death has been broken, and the curse of the law and the guilt of sin have been expiated, then surely we who believe in Christ are absolved from every harm and are just before God. For where there is satisfaction, there is absolution; and where there is absolution, there is also righteousness. "For blessed," says the Apostle, quoting the Psalms, "are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom God does not impute sin." And in the same place: "Christ ... was raised again for our justification." And in another place: "God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Being therefore justified by his blood, we shall be saved much more now," and so on.

units.la: Quod si quis quaerat, cur Apostolus justitiam nostram modo sanguini & morti, modo resurrectioni adscribat: explicatio facilis est: non esse dis-sentanea quae dicit. Sunt enim eadem utriusque, mortis nimirum & resurrectionis Christi beneficia, & eadem recte tribuuntur utrique ab Apostolo. Nec tamen hoc impedit, quo minus inter ea alicubi distinguat, ac morti ἀνάστασιν[?]: resurrectioni vero δικαίωσιν[?] recte attribuat. Id enim facit, tum ut gradibus victoriae, beneficiorum quoque gradus respondeant: tum quia ab ipsa resurrectione pendebat mortis perfectio. Qualis enim satisfactio mortis fuisset, si Christus mortis victor non emersisset? Oportebat enim Mediatorem hominem & mereri & conferre justitiam & vitam Apostolo teste, cum inquit: Per hominem mors, per hominem quoque resurrectio.
units.tr: But if anyone asks why the Apostle ascribes our righteousness at one time to the blood and death, at another to the resurrection, the explanation is easy: what he says is not inconsistent. For the benefits of both, namely of the death and the resurrection of Christ, are the same, and the same are rightly attributed by the Apostle to each. Nor does this prevent him from distinguishing between them in some places, and rightly assigning "resurrection" [anastasis] to death and "justification" [dikaiosis] to the resurrection. He does this both so that the degrees of benefits may correspond to the degrees of victory, and because the perfection of death depended on the resurrection itself. For what kind of satisfaction would his death have been, had Christ not emerged as the conqueror of death? For the Mediator, being a man, had to both merit and confer righteousness and life, as the Apostle testifies when he says: "By man came death, by man also came the resurrection."

units.la: Huic tam praestanti fructui alius non minus pretiosus individuo nexu adhaeret: Mortificatio veteris & vivificatio novi nostri hominis: dum nimirum Christus virtute resurrectionis suae membra nostra terrena mortificat, ne suas in posterum actiones exerceant: dum veterem nostrum homihominem enecat, ne posthac vigeat & fructi-ficet, dum denique cor novum per Spiritum Sanctum in nobis creat, ut justificati & sanctificati, in vitæ puritate Deum colentes, dulcissimos gratitudinis fructus proferamus. Cum enim ipse caput, nos vero membra eius simus: profecto non tantum in se, sed etiam in membris suis mortuus est & resurrexit. Quidni ergo etiam in nobis peccata aboleret, & per Spiritum Sanctum vitam novam inchoaret? Mors ergo eius efficax est, ad nequitiam carnis nostræ exstinguendam ac profligandam: resurrectio vero ad melioris naturæ novitatem suscitandam & instaurandam. Secus si quis statuat, non ego hunc minus absurdum dixero, quam qui membra emortua, & fœtida capiti vivo & gloriosò copularet. Hunc fructum in Christi resurrectione nobis ostendit ipse Apostolus cum inquit: Consepulti sumus ei per Baptismum in mortem, ut quemadmodum suscitatus est Christus ex mortuis per gloriam patris: sic & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus. Nam a mortis societate trãsitum merito facit ad vitæ participationem. Hæc enim duo arctissimè sanè inter se cohærent, veterem hominem Christi morte aboleri, ut eius resurrectio justitiam instauret, & nos creaturas novas efficiat. Et sanè cum nobis in vitam datus sit Christus, quorsum, quæso, referret, nos cum ipso emori, nisi etiam in meliorem vitam inque ipsam justitiam resurgeremus? Non enim alia ratione, quod in nobis mortale est, occidit, nisi ut verè nos vivificet & justificet. Nam si insitu[?] fa-cti sumus similitudini mortis eius, inquit Paulus, ni-
units.tr: Another fruit, no less precious, clings inseparably to this so excellent fruit: the mortification of our old man and the quickening of our new man. For Christ, by the power of his resurrection, mortifies our earthly members, so that they may no longer exercise their actions; he kills our old man, so that he may no longer flourish and bear fruit; and finally, through the Holy Spirit, he creates in us a new heart, so that, justified and sanctified, worshipping God in purity of life, we may bring forth the sweetest fruits of gratitude. For since he is the head and we are his members, surely he has died and risen not only in himself but also in his members. Why then should he not also abolish sins in us, and through the Holy Spirit begin a new life? His death is therefore efficacious for extinguishing and crushing the wickedness of our flesh, and his resurrection for raising up and restoring the newness of a better nature. If anyone should hold otherwise, I would not call him less absurd than one who would join dead and foul limbs to a living and glorious head. The Apostle himself shows us this fruit of Christ's resurrection when he says: "We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so also we might walk in newness of life." For he rightly makes the passage from fellowship in death to participation in life. These two things cohere very closely together: that the old man is abolished by the death of Christ, so that his resurrection may restore righteousness and make us new creatures. And indeed, since Christ has been given to us for life, to what purpose, I ask, would it be for us to die with him, unless we also rose again into a better life and into righteousness itself? For it is not by any other means that what is mortal in us perishes, except that he may truly quicken and justify us.
