Apostolus, quoniam videlicet longè ante illud propheta prædixerit, cum in hanc vocem: Quis credit auditui nostro: gemens erumperet. Multò illustrius est, quod in actis cap. 8. Candaces Reginæ Eunuchus Æthiops, non intelligēs, de quo sermo prophetæ esset, à Philippo Diacono de Christo crucifixo & mortuo, iterumque ex mortuis suscitato, oraculum intelligendum esse didicit. Sic languores nostros portare apud Matthæum, livore suo nos sanare apud Petrum, cum sceleratis numeratus esse apud Marcum dicitur Christus dominus noster, petitis ex hoc oraculo verbis. His fundamentis certis & immotis, ut vos perspicere arbitror, veritas nititur. Quid Iudæi contra?cum servum Jehovæ nominat scriptura, sæpè populum Iudaicum intelligi aiunt: ut in illo eiusdem prophetæ cap. 42. Quis est cæcus, nisi servus meus? Hoc amētes & verè cæci Iudæi arripiunt, & hoc quoque loco servum Iehovæ populum Israëliticum esse contendunt. Sed q; præpostera hæc, Deus bone, inepta & absurda est colligendi ratio? quā ridicula & Iudæis id est hominibus bonarum artium omnium non minus ignaris, quam pietatis expertibus, digna probatio. Vocetur sane alicubi populus servus Iehovae: at non ubique servus Iehovae populi Iudaici appellatio est. Multa alia quod Iudaeos scire, aut potius non dissimula-re oportebat, isthoc nomine dicuntur. Ex cir-cumstantiis enim iudicium faciendum est, non cum Iudaeis Andabatarum more clausis oculis pugnandum. Populum appellari servum Iehovae in isto, quo Iudaei male sani abutuntur loco, li-benter fatemur, quia praecedit: audite caeci (Iudaeos sui temporis, noistris[?] improbitate haud dissimiles alloquitur propheta) & sequitur: At iste est populus direptus. In nostro autem hoc oraculo Messiam servum Iehovae vocari, ex eo cyncimus[?], quod servus Iehovae, qui hic dicitur, a populo, tanquam redemtor ac iustificator, a redimendis & iustificandis expresse discernitur. Quemadmodum necillud de populo accipere licet, quod in eodem cap. 42. legimus. Ecce servus meus quem sustento, ubi rursus Chaldaeus paraphrastes nomen Messiae expresse addit: Et recte quidem. Nam de Messia loqui propheta patet ex collatione loci cum 11. cap. Ubi quae in cap. 42. de servo Iehovae dicebantur: Dabit Deus Spiritum suum super eum: iudicabit ipse gentes: calamum quassatum non conteret: linum fumigans non exstinguet, & quae sequuntur: de virga egrediente e radice Iessae, id est, de Messia e femine Davidis nasciturus[?], in cap. 11. satis aperte referuntur. Quocirca etiam ad Christum a Matthaeo cap. 12. verissime transferuntur. Stat igitur immota & inconcussa veritas, quod de Messia oraculum loquatur, & eo quidem solo & unico: primum humili, deinde ex-altando: id quod rursus contra Iudæos, non tam recentes quam veteres tenendum est. Isti enim cum de Messia hoc vaticinium accipiendum esse intelligerent, neque aliter illud cum suis phantasiis de mundano Messiæ regno conciliare possent, duos finxere Messias, unum qui iam olim venerit, & etiamnum in terris obam-bulet [?], specie mendici, ut pro peccatis Iudæorum satisfaciat: atque de hoc primam oraculi partem interpreta-ti sunt. Alterum vero regem gloriosum & mundanum Monarcham, quem adhuc exspectant: & de hoc alteram oraculi partem acceperunt. Som-nium est hominum, ad fabulas nescio quo fatali malo proclivium. Unus enim tantum servus Iehovæ, unus Ecclesiæ Messias est promissus, unum est semen mulieris, unus Emmanuel, unus mediator Dei & hominum, ut pleno ore clamat Apostolus 1. ad Timoth.2.
units.tr: That the whole prophecy must be understood of the Messiah, the supreme servant of Jehovah and our only Saviour, those who are not utterly deluded readily agree; those who dare to deny it are most strongly refuted by unanswerable arguments. First, it can be obscure to no one on what occasion the prophet came to speak of him, what he looked at in the whole discourse, and what goal he aimed at. He comforts the captive people with the promise of a spiritual and eternal deliverance, a deliverance, I say, from sin and from death, and he holds out the hope of reconciliation with God, of righteousness and of everlasting life. If you ask a Jew in whom this promise, so great and so many blessings, is fulfilled, in whom it has its foundation, he, however shameless and hard-faced he may be, will never, I am quite sure, name Ezra, Joshua the high priest, or any other man; but even against his will he will confess that it belongs to the Messiah alone, in whom alone all the promises of God are also "yea and amen." Next, with what shame do those wretched and blinded Jews dare to thrust upon us the name of a mere man, when the attributes of this servant of Jehovah belong not to a mere man but to the God-man [θεανθρώπῳ] alone? For who could bear our sins, expiate and take them away by his death? Who could heal our wounds? Who could restore peace with God, except the Messiah alone? Who of men was free from all sin and stain? Who by the knowledge of himself was able to justify many? To be called the high priest and king of the Church, to intercede for it and to save it: who could do this? Only the Messiah, surely. Therefore the prophet, who ascribes all these things to the servant of Jehovah, understands the Messiah to be true God and true man. Nor indeed did the ancient Hebrews, who either just preceded or just followed the age of Christ, understand this prophecy otherwise; there is no point in reciting their testimonies here, since in place of them all there can and should be for us Jonathan the son of Uzziel, a hearer of Hillel and a fellow disciple of Simeon the Just, who received this servant of Jehovah, a newborn infant, into his arms. This Jonathan, I say, in his Chaldee paraphrase, expressly calls this servant of Jehovah the Messiah. Moreover, this paraphrase has such authority among all the Jews that they wish faith to be given to it no less than to the text itself. And yet, although the Jews have no testimony of the Evangelists and Apostles in any place, among us Christians it rightly carries the greatest weight, and it can suffice by itself to open the genuine sense of the prophet. Therefore we take the oracle to be about Christ alone, because the sacred writers of the New Testament everywhere testify that what Isaiah foretold was fulfilled in him alone. Thus Paul writes in Phil. 2 that the form of a servant was assumed by the Son of God. Thus John, in the Gospel history, chap. 12, explains from this oracle why the fruit of so many and so great miracles and teaching of Christ among the Jews was so small, and why the obstinate Jews were unwilling to believe in him; and the Apostle in Rom. 10 explains why not all obey the Gospel, since, as is evident, the prophet had foretold it long before, crying out in these words: Who has believed our report? Much more illustrious is what we read in Acts chap. 8: the Ethiopian eunuch of Queen Candace, not understanding of whom the prophet spoke, learned from Philip the Deacon that the oracle must be understood of Christ crucified and dead and raised again from the dead. So too, in Matthew, it is said that our Lord Christ "bore our infirmities," and in Peter, "by his stripes we are healed"; and in Mark, that Christ was numbered among the wicked, the words being taken from this oracle. On these certain and immovable foundations, as I think you clearly see, the truth rests. What do the Jews say against this? When Scripture names "the servant of Jehovah," they say it often means the Jewish people, as in that passage of the same prophet, chap. 42: Who is blind but my servant? The mad and truly blind Jews seize on this and contend that here too the servant of Jehovah is the Israelite people. But what a perverse, foolish and absurd method of inference is this, good God! What a ridiculous proof, worthy of Jews, that is, of men as ignorant of all the liberal arts as they are strangers to piety! Let a people indeed be called the servant of Jehovah somewhere; but the name "servant of Jehovah" is not everywhere the designation of the Jewish people. Many other things are called by this name, which the Jews ought to know, or rather not to pretend ignorance of. For judgment must be made from the circumstances, and one must not fight with the Jews with eyes shut, as the Andabatae did. We freely admit that the people is called the servant of Jehovah in that passage which the mad Jews abuse, because it is preceded by: Hear, you blind (the prophet addresses the Jews of his own time, who in wickedness are not unlike ours), and it is followed by: But this is a people spoiled. But in this our oracle we conclude that the Messiah is called the servant of Jehovah from the fact that the servant of Jehovah who is here spoken of is expressly distinguished from the people, as redeemer and justifier, from those to be redeemed and justified. Nor can we take to the people what we read in the same chap. 42: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, where again the Chaldee paraphrast expressly adds the name of the Messiah; and rightly so. For that the prophet speaks of the Messiah is evident from comparing this passage with chap. 11. There, what was said in chap. 42 of the servant of Jehovah: God will give his Spirit upon him; he will judge the nations; a bruised reed he will not break; smoking flax he will not quench, and what follows, and the branch growing out of the root of Jesse, that is, the Messiah who is to be born of the seed of David, is quite plainly referred to in chap. 11. Wherefore also Matthew, in chap. 12, most rightly applies these words to Christ. Therefore it stands firm and unshaken that the oracle speaks of the Messiah, and of him alone and uniquely: first lowly, then exalted. This must again be held against the Jews, and not only the recent ones but the ancient ones as well. For when they understood that this prophecy had to be taken of the Messiah, and could not otherwise reconcile it with their fancies about a worldly kingdom of the Messiah, they invented two Messiahs: one who came long ago and still wanders on earth in the guise of a beggar, to make satisfaction for the sins of the Jews; and they interpreted the first part of the oracle of him. The other they make a glorious king and worldly monarch, whom they still await; and of him they took the second part of the oracle. It is a dream of men, prone to fables by some fatal evil. For only one servant of Jehovah, only one Messiah of the Church, is promised; there is one seed of the woman, one Immanuel, one mediator between God and men, as the Apostle cries out with full voice in 1 Tim. 2.

units.la: Hactenus, auditores, quod Messias solus & verus sit ille servus Iehovæ, de quo Iesaias loquitur, edocuimus. Nunc ut institutum à principio ordinem servemus expendendum est, qualia de hoc servo Iehovæ propheta prædicet, atque oraculum cum implicatione [?] conferendum ut futura ex factis investigemus. In singulis hic circum-stantiis, quoniam multæ sunt ac variæ: haud diu nobis immorandum esse video. Itaque in pleris-que summa tantum vestigia sequemur: cumque propheta hæc duo potissimum agat, ut primum de humilitate, deinde de glorificatione Messiæ vaticinetur, cum ordinem nos quoque secuti; quasi bivio quodam ad metam praefixam, hinc quæ prophetæ futura prædixere, illinc quæ impleta Evangelistæ ostendere, exponentes, sermone nostro decurremus.
units.tr: Thus far, listeners, we have shown that the Messiah alone is the true servant of Jehovah of whom Isaiah speaks. Now, to keep the order we set at the beginning, we must consider what the prophet foretells about this servant of Jehovah, and compare the oracle with the (?) to learn from the facts what is to come. Since the circumstances here are many and varied, I see that we must not linger long over each one. So for the most part we shall follow only the main traces. Since the prophet mainly does two things, first foretelling the humility of the Messiah and then his glorification, we too shall follow this order, and in our discourse run through, as it were on a fork in the road toward a fixed goal, setting out on one side what the prophet foretold and on the other what the Evangelists show to have been fulfilled.

units.la: Principio abiectam Messiæ sortem & summam humilitatem, illustrissimis picturis & metaphoris adumbrans propheta, ascendit, inquit (hoc est ascensurus, seu nasciturus est. Omnia enim hæc præterita oraculi verba, intelligi debere per futurum doctissimus Vatablus monet) ut surculus coram eo, nempe infideli populo Iudaico, non adhibente aures auditui prophetæ de Messia: & sicut radix e terra solitaria, deserta vel arida, vigore ad germinandum destituta. Cur furculum vocet Messiam liquere potest, si hic locus cum oraculo altero conferatur, ubi eadem similitudine utens, prædicit egressurum furculum e trunco Isai, hoc est, nasciturum Messiam e familia Davidis jam effœta, omnique regio splendore exuta. Cur radicem e terra solitaria germinantem, ipse interpres est alibi, cum futurum prædicit, ut virgo concipiat, & pariat filium cuius nomen vocet Emmanuel. Ex matre igitur virgine virum non passa, præter communem naturæ modum nasciturum esse Messiam, sub iis imaginibus propheta prædicit. Id vero sic evenisse testis est Evangelistarum historia. Natus est Christus ex virgine Maria, quæ viri nondum habuerat notitiam, ut Lucas perhibet, ac tametsi ad Davidem regem, fama pietatis & rerum gestarum super æthera notissimum, per multos reges potentissimos (quod ex Genealogia, quæ Lucæ 3. cap. texitur, apparet) originem referret, in summa tamen inopia vitam egenam difficilemque degebat. Sic quod Bethlehemi oppidulo ut his incunabulis celebratissimo, sic cætera obscuro, quod sub censu servitutis indicio natus est, quod in stabulum detrusus, quod in præsepi inter pecora vagiens fasciis involutus est, totidem sunt extremæ egestatis & miseriæ argumenta.
units.tr: At the start, the prophet, sketching the Messiah's abject lot and extreme humility with the most striking pictures and metaphors, says: "He shall grow up" (that is, he is about to grow up, or to be born; for the most learned Vatablus warns that all these past-tense words of the oracle must be understood in the future sense), "as a tender shoot before him," namely before the unbelieving Jewish people, who did not give ear to the prophet concerning the Messiah, "and as a root out of a dry ground," a desert or arid land, lacking the strength to put forth shoots. Why he calls the Messiah a shoot can be made clear if this place is compared with another oracle, where, using the same likeness, he foretells a shoot coming out of the stump of Jesse, that is, the Messiah to be born from the family of David, now worn out and stripped of all royal splendour. Why he describes the root sprouting out of a dry ground, the interpreter himself explains elsewhere, when he foretells that a virgin shall conceive and bear a son whose name she shall call Immanuel. Therefore, under these images, the prophet foretells that the Messiah is to be born from a virgin mother who has not known a man, beyond the common manner of nature. That this came to pass in this way the history of the Evangelists bears witness. Christ was born of the virgin Mary, who had not yet known a man, as Luke reports. And although she traced her origin to King David, most famous for the reputation of his piety and his deeds, through many most powerful kings (as appears from the genealogy woven in the third chapter of Luke), nevertheless she lived a needy and difficult life in extreme poverty. Thus, that he was born in the little town of Bethlehem, so celebrated for its cradle yet otherwise obscure; that he was born under a census, a sign of servitude; that he was thrust into a stable; that he was wrapped in swaddling clothes and cried out in a manger among the cattle: these are so many proofs of extreme want and misery.

units.la: Ad prophetam redeamus, & picturam Messiæ humilis omnem intentis oculis perlegamus. Forma ei esse propheta negat, abiectissimum virorum nominat, hoc indicans, fore Messiæ speciem humilem & contemtam, conditionem & vitam servilem, abiectam, miseram, quovis denique catharmate magis invisam. Unde in Psal. 22. vermem quoque humi repentem se appellat ipse, & Zacharias filiam Zionis regem suum pauperem ac vilem aspicere jubet adventantem. Hæc vero mox ab ipsa matris alvo Christo ita evenisse, testis est Evangelistarum historia. Vix enim auras vitales hauserat, cum puerulus a Tyranno Herode ad necem postulatus, in Ægyptum fugatur, ad huc infans tenellus a Simeone sene signum contradictionis appellatur, sic prædicente quod evenit: non minus videlicet omnes mortales adversos exinde habiturum esse, quam scopus a sagittariis certatim ferientibus creberrimè impetitur, configitur, perfunditur. Huc pertinet quod formam servi assumpsisse, ministraturus venisse, nō habuisse quo caput reclinaret, passim in historia Evangelica legimus. Fabrum, humilem sortem exprobraturi, fastuosi ipsum vocant Iudæi, dæmoniacum etiam scelerati calumniantur, heluo-nem vocitant, impostorem clamitant, eum ceu lapidem reprobum, cum suo Evangelio Pharisæi & Scribæ reiiciunt. Si quis hic quærat, quomodo forma Christo non fuerit, neque decor: cum in canticis sponsa de eo dicat: Botrus Cypri dilectus meus mihi. Ecce pulcher es dilecte mi & decorus: Et Nicephorus scribat, servatorem fuisse ὡραῖον τὴν ὄψιν[?], hoc est, asspectu venustum casarie, barba, & oculis subflavescentibus, supercilis nigris, totaque denique corporis forma haud inelegantem, ac persimilem divinæ immaculatæ genetrici, &c. Sed nulla mihi cum isthoc erit dissensio, nec productos formæ domini sat bonæ testes refellere opus habebo. Non enim tam de externa corporis & personæ forma, quam de conditionis & regni abiectissima specie loqui prophetam tenendum est, in qua nec forma, nec decor, nec aspectus est ullus, ut mundus desiderio eius teneatur. Nec absolutè negat formam ei futuram, sed ascensurum dicit ut virgultum coram eo, nempe infideli mū-do, ut supra monui: significans quale sit perpetuo futurum mundi de Christo eiusque regno judicium. Quia enim mundus terrenum, magnificum & gloriosum Messiam sibi falsò imaginatur, Christi humilitatem & mortem corrupto cerebri sui judicio non congruentem fastidit.
units.tr: Let us return to the prophet, and read through with attentive eyes the whole picture of the humble Messiah. He says that he has no form, and calls him the most abject of men, indicating that the Messiah's appearance will be lowly and despised, his condition and life servile, abject, wretched, and, in short, more hateful than any kind of outcast. Hence in Psalm 22 he calls himself a worm creeping on the ground, and Zechariah bids the daughter of Zion behold her poor and base king coming to her. That these things came to pass for Christ just so, from the very womb of his mother, the history of the Evangelists bears witness. For scarcely had he drawn the breath of life, when the little child, sought for death by the tyrant Herod, was driven into Egypt; and while still a tender infant he was called by the aged Simeon "a sign of contradiction," thus foretelling what came to pass: that he would have no less opposition from all mortals than a target is struck, pierced and drenched by archers shooting eagerly from every side. To this belongs what we read throughout the Evangelical history: that he took the form of a servant, came to minister, and had nowhere to lay his head. The Jews, wishing to reproach his humble lot, call him a carpenter and proud; the wicked accuse him of being demon-possessed; they call him a glutton and cry out that he is an impostor; the Pharisees and Scribes reject him with his Gospel as a reprobate stone. If anyone here asks how Christ had no form or beauty, when in the Song of Songs the bride says of him: "My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus. Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely"; and when Nicephorus writes that the Saviour had an appearance that was ὡραῖον (lovely in face), that is, pleasing in aspect, with curly hair, a beard, eyes slightly tawny, black eyebrows, and in short a form of body not unlovely, and very like the divine immaculate mother, etc.: I shall have no quarrel with this, nor need I refute the testimonies brought forward about the fairly good form of the Lord. For the prophet must be understood to speak not so much of the outward form of body and person as of the most abject appearance of his condition and kingdom, in which there is no form, no beauty, no look, that the world should be held by desire for him. Nor does he deny absolutely that he will have a form, but says he will grow up as a tender shoot before him, namely before the unbelieving world, as I have pointed out above, signifying what kind of judgment the world will for ever make concerning Christ and his kingdom. For because the world falsely imagines for itself an earthly, magnificent and glorious Messiah, it despises the humility and death of Christ, which do not agree with the corrupt judgment of its own brain.

units.la: Ac quandoquidem ad mortem Christi ipsa iam nos deduxit orationis series, quam miro consensu oraculum in omnibus circumstantiis cum Evangelica historia conspiret, æquis animis attendite. Authores mortis Messiæ aperiens propheta, ex defectione populi mei plaga ei, inquit. Defectionem vocat apostasiam à Deo, depravationem doctrinæ cœlestis & cultus, impietatem summam Judæorum, ipsumque adeo proditionis crimen, quo interveniente plaga sit futura Messiæ.
units.tr: And since the very sequence of our discourse has now brought us to the death of Christ, attend with open minds to how wonderfully the oracle agrees in every circumstance with the Evangelical history. The prophet, revealing the authors of the Messiah's death, says: "For the transgression of my people was he stricken." He calls "transgression" the apostasy from God, the corruption of heavenly doctrine and worship, the supreme impiety of the Jews, and indeed the very crime of betrayal, by whose intervention the stroke was to fall upon the Messiah.

units.la: Architectos ergo indignissimæ necis futuros prędicit non hostes, sed amicos, non exteros sed gentiles Messiæ Judæos, quos populum suum Jesaias vocat eo sensu, quo angelus dicit Danieli: septuaginta septimanæ decisæ sunt super populum tuum, hoc est, ex quo tu natus es, cuius civis es & propheta.
units.tr: He therefore foretells that the architects of the most unworthy death will be not enemies but friends, not foreigners but the Jews, the Messiah's own race, whom Isaiah calls his people in the sense in which the angel says to Daniel: "Seventy weeks are determined upon your people," that is, from the time you were born, whose citizen and prophet you are.

units.la: Fore igitur ex Jesaiæ verbis cognoscimus, ut Judæorum flagitio ac scelere Christus impiè proditur, insidiosè capitur, & iniquè trucidetur.
units.tr: We learn, then, from the words of Isaiah that through the wickedness and crime of the Jews Christ is impiously betrayed, craftily seized, and unjustly slaughtered.

units.la: Ingredere nunc exhibiti in carne Messiæ ætatem & qualis temporum eorum status fuerit considera: reperies profecto ne latum quidem unguem à veritate eventuum aberrare prædictionem. An non tunc defectio populi grassabatur. Ea certè depravatio cultum publicum invaserat, ea lues more, omnium occupaverat, superstitio in omnium animis tam altas radices egerat, ut pristinæ sinceritatis & veræ pietatis vix tenuis umbra superesset.
units.tr: Now enter into the age of the Messiah who appeared in the flesh, and consider what the state of their times was: you will certainly find that the prediction has not strayed from the truth of the events even by the breadth of a nail. Was not the defection of the people then rampant? That corruption had certainly invaded public worship; that plague had by custom taken hold of everyone; superstition had struck such deep roots in all minds that scarcely a thin shadow of the former sincerity and true piety remained.

units.la: Columina habebantur Ecclesiæ & primi omnium rerum Pharisæi, qui docendi munus ad se rapuerant, ut miseros homines publica authoritate infatuarent. Capitales & jurati hi Christi hostes erant, populum ad traditiones & frigidas inanium rituum nænias, quasi ad proram puppimque salutis, abducebant, insidias domino innumerabiles[?] struebant, donec tandem à Juda nefarè proditum, atque à satellitio armato nocturnis in tenebris captum, scelerate trucidarent.
units.tr: The pillars of the Church and the chief of all things were considered to be the Pharisees, who had seized the office of teaching to themselves, so that they might infatuate wretched men with public authority. These men were capital and sworn enemies of Christ; they led the people, as to the prow and stern of salvation, to traditions and the cold lullabies of empty rites, they laid countless snares for the Lord, until at last, having been wickedly betrayed by Judas and seized in the night-time darkness by an armed guard, they wickedly slew him.

units.la: Sed quo modo id futurum praevidit vates no-ster? Per coarctationem, inquit, & per judicium tol-letur. Qui hunc locum ita recitant: de angustia & de judicio sublatus est, de resurrectione intelligunt: Sed absq; dubio modus poenae significatur, fore nimirum, ut sistatur judicio, accusetur, conspuatur, colaphis caedatur, e medio tollatur. Iudicium ergo notatur incompositum, iniquum, tumultuarium, in quo non fori legitimi consuetudo observetur, sed omnia sint plena coarctatione, iniuriis, cotumeliis, crudelitate. Haec enim expressius alibi idem propheta noster, in persona Messiae exponit, cum inquit: Exposui corpus meum percutientibus, & genas meas vellentibus: faciem meam non abscondi ab ignominia & sputo. Neque ab hac sententia multum recedit, quod nonnulli particulam Hebræa privative interpretantur: sine carcere & judicio tolletur: violenter ad mortem rapiendum dominum intelligentes, nec claudendum carceri captivum, sed mox damnatum judicio e medio tollendum. Sed de hoc etiam Evangelistas audiamus. Qui ceperat dominum, vinctum Cajaphae mox sistere, alii accusare & crimina confingere, alii faciem caedere, colaphos infringere, venerandum os spurcissime conspuere, pontifices ipsi damnare, praesidem Romanum importunis clamoribus tande huc impellere, ut non convictum morti adiudicaret, damnatumq; contra jus fori profanissimis scurris illudendum, conspuendum, coronandum, deniq; carnificibus immanissimis crucifigedum traderet.
units.tr: But how did our prophet foresee that this would happen? "By restraint," he says, "and by judgment he shall be taken away." Those who read this place thus, "he was taken away from distress and from judgment," understand it of the resurrection. But undoubtedly the manner of punishment is signified: namely, that he is to be brought before judgment, accused, spat upon, struck with blows, and removed from the midst. A judgment is therefore noted that is disordered, unjust, tumultuous, in which the custom of a lawful court is not observed, but all things are full of restraint, injuries, insults and cruelty. For the same prophet expresses these things more plainly elsewhere, in the person of the Messiah, when he says: "I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them; I did not hide my face from shame and spitting." Nor does it differ much from this opinion that some interpret the Hebrew particle as privative: "he shall be taken away without prison and judgment," understanding that the Lord was to be violently dragged off to death, not to be shut up in prison as a captive, but soon condemned and removed from the midst without judgment. But let us hear the Evangelists on this as well. Those who had seized the Lord quickly brought him bound before Caiaphas; others accused him and invented crimes; others struck his face, dealt blows, most foully spat upon that venerable countenance; the high priests themselves condemned him; at last, by importunate clamours, they drove the Roman governor to this point, so that he would adjudicate to death a man not convicted, and, contrary to the law of the court, hand the condemned over to the most profane buffoons to be mocked, spat upon, crowned, and finally to the most savage executioners to be crucified.

units.la: Porro etiam qualem se Messias in tanto hostium furore gesserit, quam mitem se præbuerit, quâ in victa patientia fuerit propheta noster non tacet: cum inqt: Tanquam ovis coram tonsoribus suis ob-mutescet, & non aperiet os suum. Quâ verè hoc dixerit, ipsi scitis, q in historia nec pontifici, cp crimina impudentissimè confictâ refutatione opˢ nō haberet, nec Pilato, cp satis superq; iñocetiâ perspectâ sciret, multa respodisse dominum legistis.
units.tr: Moreover, what kind of person the Messiah showed himself to be amid such fury of his enemies, how gentle he proved himself, and with what patient endurance he bore it, our prophet does not pass over in silence. He says: "As a sheep before its shearers is dumb, so he does not open his mouth." How truly he said this you yourselves know, for you have read in the history that the Lord answered many things: not to the high priest, who had no need of refutation of such shamelessly invented charges, nor to Pilate, who, having perceived his innocence well enough and more than enough, knew it.

units.la: Etiam illud convenit, quod ait propheta: ovis instar ad mactationem ducetur: &, quod in historia extra urbem ad necem eductus esse, crucem ipse baiulasse, & mulieres sortem eius indignam lugentes blandissimè consolatus esse narratur. His enim omnibus testatum fecit, se mitissimum esse illum Dei agnum, qui peccata nostra tolle-ret.
units.tr: The words of the prophet also agree with this: "As a lamb is led to the slaughter." And it is related in the history that he was led out of the city to his death, that he himself carried the cross, and that he consoled most tenderly the women who lamented his unworthy fate. For by all these things he showed that he is that most gentle Lamb of God who takes away our sins.

units.la: Iam quid de supplicii genere præcinant prophetæ audiamus. Vulnerabitur, inquit noster hic, propter iniquitates nostras, & succidetur de terra viventium. Et Daniel: post hebdomadas 62 excidetur Christus, & non erit ei. David verò: Perfoderunt manus meas, & pedes meos. Numerabo omnia ossa mea. Luiturum ergo cruentum supplicii genus in cruce, non obscuré significant. Quid verò Evangelistæ? Ad crucem postulatum Christum à furiosa plebe, clamante: crucifige, crucifige: damnatum à Pilato ac traditum, ut crucifigeretur, tandemque in Golgotha, loco supplicii facinorosorum nobilitato, medium inter duos latrones cruci affixum esse: quod ipsum etiam prophetam nostrum haud fugit. Nam quasi medium inter latrones pendentem intuens dixit: cum iniquis reputatus est, illud simul significans, quod paulo ante Pilatus, ut furorem popularem mitigaret, cum Barraba sceleratissimo latrone ac nebulone cum composuerat.
units.tr: Let us now hear what the prophets sing about the kind of punishment. "Our one," he says, "will be wounded for our iniquities, and will be cut off from the land of the living." And Daniel: "After sixty-two weeks Christ will be cut off, and shall have nothing." But David says: "They have pierced my hands and my feet. I can count all my bones." They clearly signify, then, that the death was to be a bloody kind of punishment on the cross. And what do the Evangelists say? That Christ was demanded for the cross by the raging crowd, crying: "Crucify, crucify"; that he was condemned by Pilate and handed over to be crucified; and that at last, on Golgotha, a place made famous as the place of punishment for criminals, he was fixed to the cross between two robbers. Our prophet did not overlook this either: for, looking upon him as hanging between the robbers, he said: "He was reckoned with the wicked," signifying at the same time what Pilate had arranged shortly before, when, to calm the people's fury, he set him side by side with Barabbas, the most wicked robber and scoundrel.

units.la: Acerbitas hostium crucifixo insultantium non solum a nostro propheta notatur, cum dicit: aestimabitur ut plaga affectus, & percussus a Deo: sed clarius etiam a Davide in Psalmis: omnes videntes me, subsannant me, diducunt labium, movent caput: speravit in Iehova, eripiat eum, liberet eum, quia bene vult ei. Posuerunt in escam meam fel, & in siti mea potaverunt me aceto. Diviserunt sibi indumenta mea, & super vestem meam miserunt sortem: Quae singula ad literam Christo evenisse Evangelistae testantur. Certe aestimabatur ut percussus a Deo, cum Iudaei blasphemas eructarent voces, & Christo Dei opem in cruce imploranti Sarcasmo plane Diabolico illuderent: Vah qui destruis templum Dei: Eliam vocat iste, sinite, videamus an veniat Helias liberans eum: Deo confidit, is opituletur ei: cum miles accurrens acceptam spogiam impleret aceto, & calamo appositam ori sitientis in cruce admoveret: cum carnifices in oculis eius sub cruce partirentur vestes eius, jacta sorte super iis, quid quisque tolleret.
units.tr: The bitterness of the enemies insulting the crucified one is noted not only by our prophet, when he says: "He will be esteemed as one struck and smitten by God," but more clearly still by David in the Psalms: "All who see me mock me; they open the lip, they shake the head: 'He trusted in Jehovah; let him deliver him, let him rescue him, since he delights in him.' They put gall in my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. They divided my garments among themselves, and over my vesture they cast lots." The Evangelists testify that each of these things happened to Christ to the letter. Certainly he was esteemed as one struck by God, when the Jews belched forth blasphemous words and, with a truly diabolical sarcasm, mocked Christ as he implored God's help on the cross: "Ah, you who destroy the temple of God! This man calls Elijah; let him be, let us see whether Elijah comes to rescue him. He trusts in God; let God help him." When a soldier ran up, filled a sponge with vinegar, and put it on a reed and brought it to the mouth of the thirsting one on the cross; when the executioners, beneath the cross, before his eyes, divided his garments, casting lots over them to decide what each should take.

units.la: Sed acerbissimos istos sarcasmos dominum de gradu patientiae nequaquam deiecturos prophetam etiam praevidit, quin potius oraturum ipsum pro transgressoribus: quod & summo affectu Christus praestitit, cum patrem coelestem rogaret in cruce pendens, condonaret blasphemantibus culpam, quippe nescientibus quid agerent. Oraverat etiam pro pio suo grege paulo ante-quam mortem adiret, & pro nobis omnibus ad dexteram patris in summa sua gloria teste Apostolo ad Rom.8 continenter interpellat.
units.tr: But the prophet also foresaw that these most bitter sarcasms would by no means drive the Lord from the step of patience, and that he would rather pray for the transgressors himself. This Christ also accomplished with the greatest affection, when, hanging on the cross, he asked the heavenly Father to pardon the blasphemers their guilt, since they did not know what they were doing. He had also prayed for his faithful flock shortly before he went to death, and, as the Apostle testifies in Romans 8, he continually intercedes for all of us at the right hand of the Father in his supreme glory.

units.la: Quæ de sepultura Christi Isaias dicit, ex historia clarius intelligntur: Lectio genuina verborum hæc est: Populus meus dabit sepulchrum eius impius, & diviti in mortibus eius. Id in historia ita narratur, cum ne morte quidem Domini bilem Diabolicam exsaturassent Iudæi: sed & resurrectionem eius, quam prædixisse cum meminerant, prohibere conarentur, à Pilato militare præsidium obtinuerunt, homines impios, quibus custodiendum commisere Christi sepulchrum, in quod à Iosepho Arimathæensi viro consulari & divite, paulo ante fuerat repositus. Sic impiis expositum est sepulchrum eius: & diviti in morte eius. Quod aliis placet [illegible, ~5 letters]: mortuum esse ut impium, sepultum ut divitem, duriusculum videtur: tametsi ad historiam aliquo modo conveniat.
units.tr: What Isaiah says about the burial of Christ is understood more clearly from the history. The genuine reading of the words is this: "They will give his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his deaths." This is related in the history in such a way that the Jews, not even by the death of the Lord, were satisfied in their diabolical rage; but they also tried to prevent his resurrection, which they recalled he had foretold, and obtained from Pilate a military guard: impious men to whom they entrusted the guarding of Christ's sepulchre, into which he had been laid shortly before by Joseph of Arimathea, a man of consular rank and rich. Thus his grave was exposed to the impious, and he was with the rich in his death. That some prefer [illegible, about five letters]: "dead as the wicked, buried as the rich," seems rather harsh, although in some way it agrees with the history.

units.la: Sed unum hic restat caput, silentio minimè prætereundum: Innocentiam dico Christi, quæ vel maximè in passione ac morte eius observanda venit. De hac sic noster propheta: Iniquitatem non fecit, nec fuit dolus in ore eius: Et David in Mes-siæ persona Psal. 69. Multiplicati sunt super pilos capitis mei, qui oderunt me gratis, aucti sunt, qui me perdere cupiunt, adversarii mendaces, & quæ non rapui tunc exsolvi. Quid verò Evangelistæ? Ipse Dominus apud Iohannem Iudæos hostes acerbissimos non dubitans innocentiæ suæ testes appel-lare. lare. Quis ex vobis, inquit, arguet me de peccato? Petrus agnum vocat immaculatum & incontaminatum, cuius pretioso sanguine redemti simus. Idem dicit mortuum esse justum pro iniustis. Paulus ad Hebræos pontificem vocat pium, innocentem, impollutum, segregatum a peccatoribus. Sed in ipso passionis dominicæ actu, quot, quamque illustria innocentiæ huius testimonia elucent? Testis est Pilatus initio intellecta Iudæorum calumnia ex-clamans: Nullam invenio noxam in homine hoc.
units.tr: But one point remains here, which must by no means be passed over in silence: I mean the innocence of Christ, which above all comes to be observed in his passion and death. Our prophet speaks of this thus: "He did no iniquity, nor was there guile in his mouth." And David, in the person of the Messiah, in Psalm 69: "They are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, those who hate me without cause; they are increased, those who desire to destroy me, my lying adversaries; what I did not steal, I then have to restore." And what do the Evangelists say? The Lord himself, in John, does not hesitate to call the bitterest Jewish enemies as witnesses of his innocence: "Which of you," he says, "will convict me of sin?" Peter calls him a lamb unblemished and undefiled, by whose precious blood we have been redeemed. The same Peter says that he "died, the just for the unjust." Paul in Hebrews calls him a high priest "holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners." But in the very course of the Lord's passion, how many and how illustrious testimonies to this innocence shine forth? Pilate is a witness, who at the start, having understood the calumny of the Jews, cried out: "I find no fault in this man."

units.la: Testis idem est rursus exclamans postquam ab Herode rege reductus esset Iesus ad eius tribu-nal, neque se, neque Herodem, noxam ullam in-venire in eo, etiam in eorum conspectu quæstio-ne habita. Testis idem est tertio de flagellato & coronato spinis sic dicens Iudæis: Ecce adduco eum vobis foras, ut noveritis me nullum in eo crimen invenire. Testis idem est quarto Iudæis furenter clamantibus: crucifige, respondens apud Iohannem: Accipite vos eum & crucifigite. Ego enim non invenio in eo crimen. Testis idem est quinto & sexto, Iudæis furenter clamare pergentibus: Tolle, Tolle, crucifige, crucifige, respondens: Regem vestrum crucifigam? tandemque tumultu invalescente, voce & ritu externo, lotione manuum de innocentia protestans: Innocens ego sum a sanguine huius iusti, vos videritis. Marito assistipulatur u-xor, testis innocentiæ Christi divinitus excitata, dehortans sedentem pro tribunali: Nihil tibi sit cum iusto isto. Testis innocentiæ est titulus cruci impositus: HIC EST IESUS NAZARENUS REX IUDÆORUM: qui proinde etiam à Iudæis improimprobatus, & ægrè admissus est. Testis est latro dexter in cruce: nos, inquiens socio, iuste patimur. Nam digna factis nostris recipimus. Hic verò nihil mali gessit. Testis est centurio crucis custos, qui cum moriente domino velum templi scinderetur, terra concuteretur, petræ scinderentur, monimenta aperirentur, mortui prodirent, ingemiscens exclamat: Certe hic homo iustus fuit. Addamus his Pilati ad Tiberium imperatorem epistolam apud Egesippum, & Iosephi hominis Iudæi, scriptoris clarissimi testimonium de innocentia Iesu. Quid his omnibus obganniet Iudæus?
units.tr: He is a witness again when, after Jesus had been led back by King Herod to his tribunal, he cried out that neither he nor Herod had found any fault in him, even after an examination held in their presence. He is a witness a third time, of the one who was scourged and crowned with thorns, when he said to the Jews: "Behold, I bring him out to you, so that you may know that I find no crime in him." He is a witness a fourth time, when the Jews were clamoring furiously, "Crucify," and he answered in John: "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no crime in him." He is a witness a fifth and sixth time, while the Jews kept on furiously shouting, "Take him away, take him away, crucify, crucify," and he answered: "Shall I crucify your King?" And at last, when the tumult grew stronger, by voice and by outward rite, by washing his hands, he protested his innocence: "I am innocent of the blood of this just man; you will see to it." His wife, a witness of Christ's innocence raised up by God, supports her husband, urging the man sitting on the tribunal: "Have nothing to do with that just man." A witness of his innocence is the title placed on the cross: "THIS IS JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS," which was therefore also disapproved by the Jews and admitted with reluctance. A witness is the robber on the right on the cross: "We," he says to his companion, "suffer justly, for we receive what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong." A witness is the centurion, the guard of the cross, who, when the veil of the temple was torn as the Lord was dying, the earth shook, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, and the dead came forth, groaning, cried out: "Surely this man was just." To these let us add Pilate's letter to the emperor Tiberius, as given by Hegesippus, and the testimony of Josephus, a Jewish man and most famous writer, concerning the innocence of Jesus. What will the Jew snarl against all these?

units.la: Perspexisse vos hactenus arbitror Auditores, sacrū in omnibus & singulis humiliationis Christi partibus, inter vates antiquos: Iesaiamque inprimis nostrum, & Evangelistas consensum. Eundem in glorificatione quoque reperietis sum-mum & plane admirabilem.
units.tr: I think, hearers, that you have so far perceived the harmony of the ancient seers, and above all of our Isaiah and the Evangelists, in all and each of the parts of Christ's humiliation. You will find in his glorification also a harmony that is supreme and truly admirable.

units.la: Primus gloriæ huius quasi solis purissimi, di-scussis perpessionum tenebris exorientis effulgen-tisque gradus est, quod morte superata in omnem æternitatem victurum esse Messiam prædixit Iesaias, cum ait: Generationem eius quis enarrabit? quasi dicat: Etiamsi scelere Iudæorum per coarctationem & iudicium morte omnium a-cerbissima tollatur: futurum tamen, ut in æter-num vivat. Videbit, inquit, semen: id quod viven-tium est non mortuorum. Prolongabit dies: post mor-tem molestia exemptus semetipsum videbit: Ergo ex morte resurrecturum prædicit. Prædam cum iu-stis partietur. Prædam ergo & spolia hostibus eripiet: hostes ergo vincet, peccatum nempe, diabolum & mortem resurgendo ex morte. Sic Mes-sias ipse in Psalmis: Caro mea requiescet in spe. Quoniam non derelinques animam meam in inferno, nec sines sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Iam quid Evangelistae de Christi nostri resurrectione testentur quis ignorat? Tertia die nimirum invitis hostibus eum e sepulchro vivum prodiisse, apparuisse discipulis, apparuisse mulieribus, videndum, palpandum, contrectandum se praebuisse, per mortem abolevisse eum, qui mortis imperium habet, hoc est diabolum, & liberos reddidisse quotquot metu mortis per omnem vitam obnoxii erant servituti: Chirographum legis nobis ad versum sanguine suo delevisse, & cruci affixum e medio sustulisse: traduxisse exspoliata imperia & potestates, palam triumphatis illis per eam: Denique spiritu vivificatum in aeternum nunc vivere Deo nec mori amplius.
units.tr: The first step of this glory, like that of the purest sun rising and shining forth after the darkness of sufferings has been dispelled, is that Isaiah foretold that the Messiah, having overcome death, would live for all eternity, when he said: "Who will declare his generation?" as if to say: even if, through the wickedness of the Jews, he is taken away by restraint and judgment, by the most bitter death of all, it will nevertheless happen that he lives forever. "He will see," he says, "a seed; that which is of the living, not of the dead. He will prolong his days; after death, freed from trouble, he will see himself." Therefore he foretells that he will rise from death. "He will divide the spoil with the strong." He will therefore snatch the booty and spoils from the enemies, and so conquer the enemies: namely sin, the devil, and death, by rising again from death. So the Messiah himself says in the Psalms: "My flesh will rest in hope, for you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you suffer your Holy One to see corruption." Who does not know what the Evangelists testify about the resurrection of our Christ? That on the third day, against the will of his enemies, he came forth alive from the sepulchre; that he appeared to the disciples, appeared to the women, and showed himself to be seen, touched, and handled; that through death he abolished him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free all who, through fear of death, were subject to servitude all their lives; that he blotted out for us, by his blood, the handwriting of the law against us, and nailed it to the cross, and removed it from the midst; that he led captive stripped principalities and powers, openly triumphing over them through it; and finally, quickened by the Spirit, he now lives forever with God and dies no more.

units.la: Sed an nihil sublimius de gloria Messiae propheta noster? imo pontificem & regem aeternum Ecclesiae futurum, non obscure indicat: cum ait fore, ut servus Jehovae exaltetur, elevetur, & sit sublimis valde, aspergat gentes multas, cognitione sui justificet multos, deniq; delectatio & opus Dei per manum eius prosperetur. David item fore, ut in altum ascendat, captivam ducat captivitatem, donet hominibus, gloria & honore coronetur, sedeat ad dextram Dei, donec ponat inimicos suos scabellum pedum suorum: denique principatum teneat super solium Davidis, & super regnum eius, ut disponat & stabiliat ipsum in judicio & justitia, ab hoc tempore usque in perpetuum. Hæc omnia in Christo nostro impleta esse atque impleri Evangelistæ testantur. Nam post xl dierum à resurrectione cū discipulis dulcissimam conversationem aspectā-tibus ipsis sursum receptus est in cœlum, & con-sedit ad dextram throni majestatis cœlestis, lon-gè supra omne imperium, ac potestatem & potentiam & dominium, & omne nomen, quod nominari potest, in hoc & in futuro seculo, fa-ctus caput & rex Ecclesiæ super omnia, subiectis sibi angelis, & potestatibus, ac virtutibus, & in-terpellat pro nobis. Inde iuxta oraculum Ioëlis die quinquagesimo copiosè effudit Spiritum suum super Apostolos, quorum ministerio sibi collegit & colligit ex genere humano æternam Ecclesiam, regens eam verbo & Spiritu, ac implens donis ad ædificationem, mittens Spiritum suum in corda credentium, iustificans, regene-rans, ac suscitans electos ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: But does our prophet say anything more sublime about the glory of the Messiah? Indeed, he plainly indicates that he will be the eternal high priest and king of the Church. For he says that the servant of Jehovah will be exalted, raised up, and made very lofty; that he will sprinkle many nations, justify many by the knowledge of himself; and finally that the good pleasure and work of God will prosper through his hand. David likewise says that he will ascend on high, lead captivity captive, give gifts to men, be crowned with glory and honour, sit at the right hand of God until God makes his enemies his footstool; and finally that he will hold the sovereignty over the throne of David and over his kingdom, to order and establish it in judgment and justice from this time forth, even for ever. The Evangelists bear witness that all these things have been fulfilled, and are being fulfilled, in our Christ. For after forty days from his resurrection, spending most delightful time with his disciples, while they looked on, he was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of the throne of heavenly majesty, far above every rule, authority, power and dominion, and every name that can be named, in this age and in the age to come; made the head and king of the Church over all things, with angels, powers and virtues made subject to him; and he intercedes for us. Then, according to the oracle of Joel, on the fiftieth day he poured out his Spirit abundantly upon the apostles, through whose ministry he has gathered and still gathers for himself an eternal Church out of the human race, ruling it by the Word and the Spirit, and filling it with gifts for edification, sending his Spirit into the hearts of believers, justifying, regenerating, and raising the elect to eternal life.

units.la: Quæ omnia cum ita sé[?] habeant, concludamus nunc contra cæcam Iudæorum gentem, Iesum filium Dei & virginis, passum, crucifixum, mortuum, suscitatum & evectum in cœlos ad dextrā patris, solum esse illum Iehovæ servum Messiam, cum in hoc solo Isaiæ omniumque aliorum prophetarum oracula impleta esse, sole meridiano clarius demonstretur.
units.tr: Since all these things stand thus, let us now conclude against the blind nation of the Jews that Jesus, the Son of God and of the virgin, who suffered, was crucified, died, was raised, and was taken up into heaven to the right hand of the Father, is alone that Messiah, the servant of Jehovah, since it is demonstrated more clearly than the midday sun that in him alone the oracles of Isaiah and of all the other prophets have been fulfilled.

units.la: Sed & contra Marcionem atque Eutychen & horum fratres ubiquitarios hinc concludamus: servum Iehovæ Messiam verum hominem esse ac manere in æternum, nobis per omnia ὁμοούσιον teste Apostolo ad Hebr. peccato excepto. Verè e-nim nim humilis fuit, vere doluit, vere passus est, mortuus ac suscitatus, neque depositit naturam no-stram in gloria, quam assumpsit in ignominia: gloria quippe mortalitatem carni ademit: veri-tatem non abstulit, ut Augustinus vere ad Dar-danum scripsit.
units.tr: But let us also conclude from this against Marcion, Eutyches, and their brothers, the ubiquitarians: that the Messiah, the servant of Jehovah, is a true man and remains so for ever, of one substance with us in all things, as the Apostle witnesses in Hebrews, sin excepted. For he was truly humble, truly grieved, truly suffered, died and was raised; nor did he lay aside our nature in glory, which he took up in shame. For glory took away the mortality of the flesh, but did not take away its truth, as Augustine truly wrote to Darius.

units.la: De Ario vero quid dicemus, an verum Deum verumque Iehovam esse negabit, quem opera Iehovæ propria potentia edere, tollere ac remittere peccata, sanare vibices nostras, justificare ac vivificare electos propheta noster testatur. Excipiunt Ariani, Messias servus est Iehovæ: non ergo ipse Iehova. Sed plumbeus est pugio. Utrumque enim est diverso respectu: Iehova est secundum deitatem, quia opera Iehovæ facit, justificans & servans electos: atque ut ipse apud Iohannem de se testatur, ὁμοίως omnia cum patre operatur. Tu[?] apud Ieremiam expresse vocatur Iehova justitia nostra: & apud Iesaiam nostrum cap. 15. Ecclesia Novi Testamenti Messiam in carne exhibitum gratulabunda sic alloquitur: Ecce Deus noster iste: Expectavimus eum & salvabit nos. Iste Iehova, expectavimus eum: exultabimus & lætabimur in salute eius. Hinc etiam Paulus Dominum gloriæ à Iudæis crucifixum esse, & Deum sanguine suo redemisse Ecclesiam testatur. Servus vero Iehovæ appellatur, tum assumptæ humanitatis, quam Paulus formam servi vocat, tum officii ratione, quoniam opus Iehovæ, ut noster Iesaias loquitur, per manum eius prosperabitur. Neque vero tollit inæqualitas officii (ut Cyrillus ait) æqualitatem naturæ. Denique Nestorium quoq;, qui naturas in Chri-sto distrahebat, illud confutat, quod non alium & alium, sed unum eundemque servum Iehovæ mortuum esse, resurrexisse, & justificare constat, quod ipsum Deum & hominem eundem esse probat. Neque enim duos habemus servos Ieho-væ, quod iudæi aliqui olim fingebant, ut supra dixi: sed unum, proinde nec duos Christos, sed unum: mortificatum quidem carne, ut Petrus ait, vivificatum vero spiritu: unum eundemque Christum pati oportuit, & ingredi in gloriam suam. Nec redemisset sanguine suo Ecclesiam Deus, si corpus quod illum cruorem fudit, non Dei proprium, sed alterius fuisset.
units.tr: But what shall we say of Arius? Will he deny that he is the true God and the true Jehovah, whom our prophet testifies performs by his own power the works of Jehovah, takes away, and forgives sins, heals our stripes, and justifies and quickens the elect? The Arians object: the Messiah is the servant of Jehovah, therefore he is not Jehovah himself. But this is a leaden dagger. For both statements hold in different respects: he is Jehovah according to his deity, because he does the works of Jehovah, justifying and saving the elect; and as he himself testifies of himself in John, he works all things in the same way as the Father. Moreover, in Jeremiah he is expressly called Jehovah our righteousness; and in our Isaiah, chapter 15, the Church of the New Testament, rejoicing at the Messiah revealed in the flesh, addresses him thus: "Behold this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us. This is Jehovah; we have waited for him; we will exult and rejoice in his salvation." Hence also Paul testifies that the Lord of glory was crucified by the Jews, and that God redeemed the Church with his own blood. But he is called the servant of Jehovah both by reason of the humanity he assumed, which Paul calls the form of a servant, and by reason of his office, since the work of Jehovah, as our Isaiah says, will prosper through his hand. Nor indeed does the inequality of office (as Cyril says) remove the equality of nature. Finally, he also refutes Nestorius, who separated the natures in Christ, by this: it is clear that it was not another and another, but one and the same servant of Jehovah who died, rose again, and justifies, which proves that he is the same God and man. For we do not have two servants of Jehovah, as some Jews once imagined, as I said above; but one, and therefore not two Christs, but one: put to death indeed in the flesh, as Peter says, but made alive in the Spirit; it was necessary that one and the same Christ should suffer and enter into his glory. Nor would God have redeemed the Church with his own blood, if the body that shed that blood had not been God's own, but another's.

units.la: Nunc ut ad finem nostra properet oratio, auditores, tertium instituti nostri caput aggressi, quid de causis fructibusque tum mortis tum resurrectionis Messiæ Iesaias noster doceat, breviter dispiciamus. Etsi ultra hominem sapere videatur, qui vel tenuem mysteriorum paulo ante explicatorum cognitionem adeptus est: parum tamen prodesset scire hæc omnia, nisi etiam causas & fructus tantæ humilitatis & subsecutæ gloriæ intelligeremus: Quos quoniam non intelligunt nec pervestigant miseri Iudæi, nec quicquā vident, nisi infamem crucem, vulnera & pendentem in ligno fœdè lancinatum confectumque plagis hominem, offensi miserabili specie auditui prophetæ non credunt, & se ab hac gratia incredulitate sua excludunt. Itaque in tantarum rerum causas penitissimè nos introspicere oportet, ut earum consideratione animos nostros ab hoc scandali genere immunes confervemus. Principio igitur Iefaias ad æternum omnipotentis Dei beneplacitum tanquam ad fontem primum, causamq; principem rei gestæ mentes nostras evehit, docetq; totum opus admirabili Dei consilio, sic prædestinatum & gubernatum fuisse cũ ait: Iehova deleƫatus est eum sic conterere, atq; infirmitati subjicere. Sic & apud Zachariam Iehova ipse, Ogladie (inquit organa cõsilii sui alloquens) percute pastorem, & dispergentur oves. Hoc æternum Dei consilium, cum his aliisq; prophetarum oraculis retectum fuerit, & non potuerit non definito tempore impleri: à Christo ipso & historiæ Evangelicæ scriptoribus crebro discipulis inculcatum legimus. Sic enim Christus: Filius hominis vadit κατὰ τὸ ὡρισμένον[?]: & clarius Petrus: Hunc definito consilio & providentia Dei deditum cum accepissetis manib. sceleratis, cruci affixum interemistis.
units.tr: Now, that our discourse may hasten to its end, hearers, having turned to the third head of our subject, let us briefly examine what our Isaiah teaches about the causes and fruits both of the death and of the resurrection of the Messiah. Although it may seem to be wiser than man, if one has gained even a slight knowledge of the mysteries explained a little while ago, it would nevertheless profit little to know all these things unless we also understood the causes and fruits of so great a humiliation and of the glory that followed it. Since the wretched Jews do not understand or investigate these, and see nothing but the infamous cross, the wounds, and a man hanging on a tree, foully mangled and worn out with blows, they are offended by the pitiable appearance and do not believe the prophet's word, and by this unbelief they shut themselves out from this grace. Therefore it is necessary for us to look deeply into the causes of such great matters, so that by considering them we may keep our minds free from this kind of stumbling-block. First, then, Isaiah lifts our minds to the eternal good pleasure of almighty God as to the first source and the principal cause of the event, and teaches that the whole work was so predestined and governed by the admirable counsel of God when he says: "Jehovah was pleased to crush him thus and to subject him to infirmity." So too in Zechariah, Jehovah himself, addressing the instruments of his counsel, says: "O sword (he says), strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." When this eternal counsel of God had been revealed by these and other oracles of the prophets, and could not fail to be fulfilled at the appointed time, we read that Christ himself and the writers of the Evangelical history repeatedly impressed it upon the disciples. For thus Christ: "The Son of man goes according to what has been determined"; and more clearly Peter: "Him, delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you took and by wicked hands crucified and slew."

units.la: Clarissimè apostoli, quando Pilatum reliquosq; necis Christi authores, quasi ex præscripto egisse, eaq; exsecutos docet, quæ consilii & manus Dei definierit facienda. Nemo igitur existimet cæco fortunæ casu rem tantã evenisse, vel rabie Judæorum superatum Dominum nostrum, ad tam dirũ supplicii genus fuisse pertractum. Patris hæc fuit æterna & sanctissima voluntas q hora & momentũ morti Filii sui certum præfixerat: cujus ꝓinde[?] Filius ipse minimè ignarus, cũ adesse horam illã videret, spote summaq; cũ voluntate se patris decreto subjecit, ut oracula impleret, & genus humanũ patri reconciliaret. Quod si n.ne pilus quidem de nostro capite sine voluntate Dei potest cadere, quomodo sine ea Filius Dei crucifixus est, opusq; omnium, quæ facta sunt ab æternitate, multò maximum est effectum ?
units.tr: The apostles most clearly teach that Pilate and the other authors of Christ's death acted, as it were, according to a prescribed plan, and carried out those things which the counsel and hand of God had determined should be done. Let no one therefore think that so great a thing happened by blind chance, or that our Lord was overcome by the rage of the Jews and dragged to so dreadful a kind of punishment. This was the eternal and most holy will of the Father, who had fixed the certain hour and moment for the death of his Son; and the Son himself, by no means ignorant of this, when he saw that the hour was at hand, of his own accord and with the highest will submitted himself to the Father's decree, so that he might fulfil the oracles and reconcile the human race to the Father. But if not even a hair of our head can fall without the will of God, how could the Son of God be crucified without it, and the greatest of all the works that have been done from eternity be accomplished?

units.la: Sed nodus hîc vindice dignus incidit. Quid n? (inquiet aliqs) passus est Christus dirissimâ morte decreto & voluntate patris cœlestis? An non igitur extra culpam Iudæi, consilio Dei obtemperantes? imo an non Pater crudelis qui Filium? an non injustus qui innocentem? an nō Ἀπχαιρέτικος[?] qui afflictū cōterere delectatus est? Minimè verò, auditores, in Dei consilio inveniūt Iudæi, qui sceleri suo prætexant. Quid n. ad ipsos Domini voluntas, quæ nec intellexerunt, nec respexerunt, cum Messiæ sceleratas injiceret manus, ut odiū ac bilem suam Diabolicam ejus nece explerent? Deū ꝙ attinet, sentire vos oēs intelligo, nihil illorū in ejus majestatem cadere posse. Aliam igitur adorando huic consilio causam subesse oportet: quā Iesaias noster non tacuit, sed multis verbis iteratò inculcavit: Jehova, inquiens traduxit in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Languores nostros ipse tulit & dolores nostros ipse portavit: vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter peccata nostra. Non igitur crudelitas, non injustitia, non Ἀπχαιρετικία[?] Dei: sed peccata nostra Filiū Dei miserū fecerūt, ac Iudæorū libidini subjecerunt. Sed quid ad ipsum, inquit aliquis, peccata nostra? Non vos istud dicere audi tores scio, sed tamen quia quæri potest, solvi etiā potest. De Messia ac Salvatore mundi nobis sermonem esse meministis. Messiam autem admirādo Dei consilio à peccatis & morte liberare populum suū debuisse, in oculis oīm situ est. Oportuit igitur Christum nostrorum peccatorum pœnam propterea luere, quia illa in fe derivarat, ut nos a reatu & morte liberatos justitiae ac vitae restituere-ret. Docet hoc angelus, nomen Iesu ei imponens: quia, inquit, servabit populum suum a peccatis ipsorum. Nec tacent hoc Evangelistae & Apostoli passim testantes: patrem non pepercisse filio suo, sed pro nobis omnibus dedisse illum: Ipsumque adeo filium summa voluntate tradidisse se-metipsum pro peccatis nostris, ut nos eximeret ex praesenti saeculo malo secundum voluntatem Dei & patris nostri, atque ut propheta noster loquitur, seipsum exposuisse sacrificium pro reatu, nostro videlicet non suo, seque ipsum in mortem profudisse pro nobis.
units.tr: But here a knot arises that deserves a champion. For what (someone will say), did Christ suffer the most dreadful death by the decree and will of the heavenly Father? Are not the Jews therefore free from blame, as obeying the counsel of God? Nay, is not the Father cruel who delivered up his Son? Is he not unjust who delivered up the innocent? Is he not... who took pleasure in crushing the afflicted? Not at all, hearers: the Jews find no excuse for their wickedness in the counsel of God. For what has the will of the Lord to do with them, which they neither understood nor regarded, when they laid their wicked hands on the Messiah, so that they might satisfy their hatred and diabolical rage by his death? As far as God is concerned, I know you all perceive that none of those things can fall upon his majesty. It must therefore be that a different cause lies beneath this counsel, which our Isaiah did not pass over, but repeatedly impressed on us in many words: "Jehovah, he says, has laid upon him the iniquities of us all. He himself bore our sicknesses and carried our sorrows: he was wounded because of our iniquities, he was bruised because of our sins." Therefore it was not the cruelty, not the injustice, not the [partiality?] of God; but our sins made the Son of God wretched, and subjected him to the lust of the Jews. But what has our sin to do with him, someone may say? I know you do not say this, hearers, but since it can be asked, it can also be answered. You remember that our discourse concerns the Messiah and the Saviour of the world. Now it is plain to all that the Messiah, by God's admirable counsel, had to free his people from sins and from death. It was therefore necessary for Christ to pay the penalty of our sins, because they had been transferred to him, so that he might free us from guilt and death and restore us to righteousness and life. The angel teaches this, giving him the name Jesus: because, he says, he will save his people from their sins. The Evangelists and Apostles, testifying everywhere, do not keep silent about this either: that the Father did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all; and that the Son himself so willingly delivered himself up for our sins, that he might rescue us from this present evil age according to the will of God and our Father; and, as our prophet says, that he offered himself as a sacrifice for guilt, namely our guilt and not his own, and poured himself out to death for us.

units.la: Caeterum hic non quiescit ratio humana: sed scrutari pergit ac sciscitari: ecquid hoc sit consilii? an non alio pacto hominum peccata expiari, mors superari, vita reparari, quam morte Messiae potuerit? Sed desinat scrutari quod capere nequit. Consilia Dei sunt abyssus multa. Adoremus sapientiam Dei, quae tale consilium invenit, cujus executione primum justitiae ejus satisfieret, deinde veritas salva tecta maneret, denique im-mensus erga nos amor declararetur. Tantum est malum peccatum, ut ordine justitiae Dei non expiari nisi aeterna destructione peccantis queat: teste Paulo, qui ait, Stipendium peccati mors est. Cum vero neque homo peccator, neque creatura ulla pro homine tantum supplicium citra aeternam sui destructionem sustinere potuerit vel debuerit: placuit sacrosanctae Trinitati, ut Filius aeterni patris homo factus ἱλαστήριον [?] fieret pro hominis peccato,poenamque luendo, finitam quidem tempore, sed infinitam virtute, ob divinæ personæ dignitatem, nec non ob dolorum ipsorum,quos corpore pariter & anima sustinuit, im mensam gravitatem , λύτρον[?] æquivalens culpæ hominis justitiæ Dei dependeret. Veritas quo-que divina salva manere aliter non potuit, quam si in hominis redemtione à morte æterna, hominis quoque mors æterna, vel certè æternæ æquivalens interveniret. Dixerat enim Deus: Quæ-cunque die comederis morte morieris. Violato itaque Dei interdicto ab homine, mori oportuit hominem vel mediatorem pro homine, ut hominem citra veritatis divinæ læsionem à morte liberaret. Sed & charitatem suam Deus, Apostolo teste, commendare ac testatam facere sic voluit, quod cum essemus peccatores æternæ mortis rei, filium illum suum unigenitum pro nobis tradidit, ut per sanguinem ejus servati Deoque reconciliati justitiam & vitam æternam consequeremur.Sic enim dilexit mundum clementissimus pater, inquit servator ipse, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Denique veritatem typis & oraculis respondere par fuit. Nam victimæ olim in figura Messiæ cædebantur: serpens æneus de palo suspendebatur, & prænuncius ille Spiritus Christi, qui in prophetis erat, teste Petro, per-pessiones Christo eventuras, nec non gloriam illas consecuturam jam olim declaraverat. His causis contenti, desinamus mirari, qui conveniat in mensa æterni patris amori, ut Filium unigenitū ita conterere fit delectatus. Non contrivit Filiu, sed Messiam: non multavit innocentem, sed vadem alienae culpae de satisfactione postulavit: nō. cruciatib.morientis est delectatus: sed generi humano per mortem resurgentis placatus. Fecit n. inquit Apostolus, ut qui non norat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum esset, ut nos efficeremur justitia Dei in eo.
units.tr: Yet human reason does not rest here; it keeps probing and inquiring: is there any purpose in this? Could men's sins not have been expiated, death overcome, and life restored in some other way than by the death of the Messiah? But let us stop searching into what we cannot grasp. The counsels of God are a great deep. Let us adore the wisdom of God, which devised such a counsel, by whose carrying out, first, his justice would be satisfied, then his truth would remain safe and intact, and finally his immense love towards us would be displayed. Sin is so great a evil that, under the order of God's justice, it cannot be expiated except by the eternal destruction of the sinner: the witness is Paul, who says, The wages of sin is death. But since neither a sinful man nor any creature could have endured, or ought to have endured, so great a punishment without their own eternal destruction, it pleased the most holy Trinity that the Son of the eternal Father should be made man and become a propitiatory [?] for man's sin; and by bearing the penalty, finite indeed in time but infinite in power on account of the dignity of the divine person, and also on account of the immense weight of the sufferings which he endured in body and soul alike, a ransom [?] equivalent to the guilt of man should hang upon the justice of God. Likewise the divine truth could not remain otherwise safe, unless in the redemption of man from eternal death an eternal death, or at least something equivalent to eternal death, of man intervened. For God had said: On whatever day you eat of it you shall surely die. Therefore, since the divine prohibition had been violated by man, it was necessary for man to die, or for a mediator to die on man's behalf, so that man might be freed from death without any injury to divine truth. But God also willed to commend his charity, as the Apostle witnesses, and make it manifest, in that while we were sinners liable to eternal death, he delivered up his only-begotten Son for us, so that, saved through his blood and reconciled to God, we might obtain justice and eternal life. For God the most merciful Father so loved the world, says the Saviour himself, that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. Finally, it was fitting that the types and oracles should correspond to the truth. For in former times victims were slain as a figure of the Messiah; the bronze serpent was hung upon a pole; and that prophetic Spirit of Christ, which was in the prophets, as Peter testifies, had already declared long ago that sufferings would befall Christ and that he would afterwards attain glory. Content with these causes, let us cease to wonder how it befits the love of the eternal Father to have been pleased to crush his only-begotten Son in this way. He did not crush the Son but the Messiah; he did not punish the innocent, but demanded a surety for another's guilt as satisfaction; he was not delighted by the torments of the dying, but was appeased for the human race by the death and rising again. For, says the Apostle, he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might be made the justice of God in him.

units.la: Jam vero auditores, ex his causis uberrimi nobis fructus emergunt, quos etiam brevissima oratione explicare non pigebit. Reconciliatos primum nos esse Deo documento certissimo deprehendimus. Quoniam n. ipse Deus Filium suum percussit, mortique per os judicis addixit propter nos: poenam ejus mortemq; haud dubie λύτρον[?] pro nostris peccatis acceptat. Docet hoc Iesaias noster cum ait: Castigatio pacis nostrae super eum, q.d. ipse pro peccatis nostris vapulabit, ac pretium pacis nostrae persolvet, ut per eum gratis reconciliemur Deo: & clarius Apostolus ad Rom. 5: Si reconciliati, inquit, fumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus: multo magis reconciliati per vitam ipsius servabimur. Alter fructus est justificatio nostra in remissione peccatorum consistens: Nam justus ille servus meus, inquit hic Iehova, cognitione sui justificabit multos, quorum peccata ipse portavit. Et Apostolus: mortuus est propter peccata nostra, & resurrexit propter justificationem nostram. Nec obscura est ratio. Quoniam enim servus ille Iehovae Messias animam suam sacrificium posuit pro reatu: utique Deus pro sua justitia, quae eandem culpam bis puniri non finit, propter satisfactione Filii sui ab omni reatu nos absolabsolvit & justos pronunciat. Unde etiam à mor-te, quæ peccato sublato necessario aboletur, nos liberatos esse constat, licet animę & corporis dis-solutionem adhuc patiamur, non ut moriamur, sed ut in vitam sempiternam transferamur, quę beneficia tam morti quam resurrectioni tribuū-tur, quoniam illa parta, hac confirmantur & con-feruntur. Accedit his tertius fructus, quod virtute mortis ac resurrectionis Christi natura nostra in-stauratur, & nos toti ad novam vitā regeneramur per Spiritum sanctum: quod beneficium paucis quidem verbis indicat propheta noster, cum ait: nos livore eius sanatos esse: Apostolus vero ad Rom. 6. illustrius exponit. Gloriosam denique, corporum ex morte suscitationem, propter Christi resurrec-tionem credimus & speramus. Nisi n. ipsi quoq; ad vitam beatè in omnem æternitatem degēdam excitaremur, irrita fieret Iesaię promissio, quādo visurum Messiam semē, & habituū generationē æt. pollicetur, propterea q; ipse caput nostri ū cum sit, nobis membris suis carere non poterat. Ac valde illustris est Pauli illa inter Adamū & Christum oppositio, quando perinde in Christo vivificari oēs nos oportere demonstrat, atq; in Adamo oēs sumus mortui. Verū, auditores, sentio me copia argumenti hujus ita obrui, ut quasi in vastum pelagus abreptus, quo me expediam modo, aut quo modo paucis multa, nedum oīa dicam, nō videā[?]. Superant sanè beneficia Christi omnem humanā eloquentiam, & video hic ante oculos abyssum magnam omnigenæ consolationis: quoniam omnia, quæ CHRISTUS fecit, saluti nostræ
units.tr: Now indeed, hearers, from these causes the most abundant fruits spring forth for us, which I shall not be reluctant to set out even in a very brief discourse. We perceive, first, by the most certain proof, that we have been reconciled to God. For since God himself struck his Son and handed him over to death through the mouth of the judge on our behalf, he undoubtedly accepts his punishment and death as a ransom [?] for our sins. Our Isaiah teaches this when he says: The chastisement of our peace was upon him, that is, he himself will be scourged for our sins and pay the price of our peace, so that we may be reconciled to God freely through him. And the Apostle says more clearly in Romans 5: If we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, he says, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. The second fruit is our justification, consisting in the remission of sins. For my righteous servant, says this Jehovah, by his knowledge shall justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities. And the Apostle: He was delivered for our sins, and rose again for our justification. The reason is not obscure. For since that servant of Jehovah, the Messiah, laid down his soul as a sacrifice for guilt, God, on account of his justice, which does not allow the same guilt to be punished twice, absolves us from all guilt on account of the satisfaction of his Son and pronounces us just. Hence it is also clear that we have been freed from death, which is necessarily abolished once sin is taken away, although we still undergo the dissolution of soul and body, not so that we may die, but so that we may be transferred into eternal life. These benefits are ascribed as much to his death as to his resurrection, since the former procures them and the latter confirms and bestows them. To these is added the third fruit, that by the power of Christ's death and resurrection our nature is restored, and we are wholly regenerated to a new life through the Holy Spirit. Our prophet indicates this benefit in a few words when he says: by his bruise we were healed; and the Apostle in Romans 6 explains it more clearly. Lastly, we believe and hope for the glorious raising of bodies from death on account of Christ's resurrection. For unless we too were roused to live blessedly through all eternity, the promise of Isaiah would be void, when it promises that the Messiah would see his seed and that the generation of his days would be prolonged; and since he is the head of us, he could not be without his members. And that antithesis of Paul between Adam and Christ is very striking, when he shows that all of us ought to be made alive in Christ just as in Adam we have all died. But, hearers, I feel that I am so overwhelmed by the abundance of this subject that, as though carried off into a vast sea, I cannot see how to make my way through it, or how to speak of many things briefly, let alone of all. The benefits of Christ certainly surpass all human eloquence, and here before my eyes I see a great abyss of every kind of consolation: since all the things that Christ did, he willed to serve our salvation

units.la: [Remainder of the final line is partly covered by the margin note; no further printed text.] servire voluit. Ascendit ut surculus, ut nobis daret edere ex arbore vitæ, quæ est in Paradiso: factus est pauper, ut nos ditaret: abjectissimus viro-rum esse voluit, ne nos abjiceremur a Deo: vir do-lorum, ut sanaret dolores nostros: percussus a Deo, ut ejus iram a nobis in se derivaret: productus, ut nos reciperemur: captus est, ut nos in libertatem vindicaret: per coarctationem & judicium sublatum est, ne judicio Dei nos coarctaremur: Accusatus os non aperuit, non consentiens tacendo, sed de-spiciens non refellendo, ut gloriemur nos ejus potentiâ servatos. Ovis instar ad mactationem du-ctus est, ut obedientiâ suâ nostram expiaret contu-maciam: opprobria pertulit, ut improperia detra-hentium electos non moverent: Damnatus est a judice, ut damnatos a Dei judicio liberaret: edu-ctus extra urbem, ut ex mundo in cœlum nos duceret: Deputatus est inter impios, ut nos filios Dei faceret: crucifixus est, ut maledictionem tolleret, veteris hominis nostri occasum offenderet, atque omnia ad se traheret. Vulneratus est, ut nos sana-ret, & obligaret confractos; Portavit in ligno pec-cata nostra, ut nos a peccatis absolutos justificaret: Innocens passus est, ut esset victima pro peccatis nostris, & nos a reatu absolveret: clamavit in cruce, ut nos exaudiremur in morte. Oravit pro transgressoribus, ut nos clamemus Abba pater. Mor-tuus est, ut mortuos vivificaret: sepultus, ut sepulturam nobis sanctificaret: Resurrexit, ut se victorem mortis, inferni, diaboli, & mundi declararet. Prolongat in æternum dies suos, ut opus Iehovæ, quod est collectio, defensio & glorificatio nostra, per eum prosperetur. Quid amplius? Reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii ejus. Spem ergo minimè vacillantem concipimus, nihil esse quod à dilectione Dei nos separet: pacemque nobis cum Deo intercedere inviolabilem novimus. Peccatis enim sublatis sublatam intelligimus omnem irę Dei in nos causam.
