Nam delicta quæ nec opinantibus interdum obrepunt, periculum nobis creare non possunt, quoniam Christi sanguis instar rapidissimi fluminis quotidie nos inundat & contractas sordes eluit. Peccata nostra solus ille Ichovæ servus portavit, solus calcavit torcular iræ Dei, ut alibi idem noster propheta testatur. Caveamus ergo, uspiam alibi nisi in sola hac satisfactione ac morte remissionem, justitiam & vitam æternam quæramus. Aliud enim nomen (teste Apostolo Petro) sub cœlo nullum est datum, per quod oporteat nos servari. Facessant ergo qui merita & satisfactiones alias jactitant vel quærunt. Resurrexit ex morte hic servus Ichovæ. Hostes ergo nostros, mortem, infernum, diabolum, ac mundum, veré devictos esse oportet, & nos ab eorum servitio liberatos. Opus Ichovę in manu ejus prosperabitur. Nihil ergo dubitemus Ecclesiam contra Tyrannorum insultus & diaboli fraudes ac technas, dum hæc mundi stabit machina, potentia Messiæ incolumem permansurum esse. Tantum enim abest ut rabies hostilis consilium Dei reddere queat irritum, ut tum vel maximè opus Domini prosperetur, quando in furorem vel maximè hostes exardescunt. Ut enim palma contra pondus in altum nititur, aurumque igni, quò coquitur magis, eò fit purius: sic ecclesia quantò premitur magis, tanto prosperatur magis, quod omnium seculorū historiæ ecclesiasticæ testatur. Denique generationem Messiæ nemo enarrabit.
units.tr: [Remainder of the final line is partly covered by the margin note; no further printed text.] He ascended like a shoot, to give us to eat of the tree of life, which is in Paradise; he became poor, so that he might enrich us; he willed to be the most abject of men, lest we should be cast off by God; a man of sorrows, to heal our sorrows; smitten by God, so that he might turn God's wrath away from us onto himself; led forth, so that we might be received; he was taken, so that he might deliver us into liberty; by distress and judgment he was taken away, lest we should be straitened by the judgment of God; when accused he did not open his mouth, not assenting by silence, but despising without refuting, so that we might glory that we were saved by his power. He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, so that by his obedience he might expiate our stubbornness; he endured reproaches, so that the taunts of those who slander would not move the elect; he was condemned by the judge, so that he might free the condemned from God's judgment; led outside the city, so that he might lead us from the world into heaven; he was reckoned among the wicked, so that he might make us sons of God; he was crucified, so that he might take away the curse, destroy the downfall of our old man, and draw all things to himself. He was wounded, so that he might heal us and bind up the broken; he bore our sins on the tree, so that he might justify us, absolved from sins; the innocent suffered, so that he might be a victim for our sins and absolve us from guilt; he cried out on the cross, so that we might be heard in death. He prayed for the transgressors, so that we might cry Abba, Father. He died, so that he might make the dead alive; buried, so that he might sanctify the burial for us; he rose again, so that he might declare himself the victor over death, hell, the devil and the world. He prolongs his days to eternity, so that the work of Jehovah, which is our gathering, defence and glorification, may prosper through him. What more? We have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son. Therefore we conceive a hope by no means wavering, that nothing can separate us from the love of God; and we know that peace with God between us is inviolable. For with sins taken away we understand that every cause of God's anger against us is taken away too. For faults which sometimes creep upon us even unawares cannot create danger for us, since the blood of Christ, like the swiftest river, floods us daily and washes away the defilements we have contracted. The Servant of Jehovah alone bore our sins, alone trod the winepress of God's wrath, as our same prophet bears witness elsewhere. Let us therefore take care that we seek remission, justice and eternal life nowhere else than in this satisfaction and death alone. For there is no other name under heaven given (as the Apostle Peter witnesses) by which we must be saved. Let those then who boast of or seek other merits and satisfactions be gone. This Servant of Jehovah rose again from death. Our enemies, therefore, death, hell, the devil and the world, must truly be overcome, and we freed from their servitude. The work of Jehovah will prosper in his hand. Let us therefore have no doubt that the Church, against the assaults of tyrants and the frauds and snares of the devil, will remain unharmed for as long as this machine of the world stands, by the power of the Messiah. For the hostile rage is so far from being able to render God's counsel void, that the work of the Lord prospers most of all just when the enemies blaze up most in fury. For as the palm tree struggles upward against the weight, and as gold becomes purer the more it is heated in the fire in which it is refined, so the Church, the more it is pressed, the more it prospers, as the history of the Church in all ages bears witness. Finally, no one will tell the generation of the Messiah.

units.la: Ergo plena fiducia aspirare licet ad beatam illam spem, quam in altera vita obtinebimus. Neque enim fieri potest, ut ipse solus in æternum vivat, ac non simul etiam nos ex morte suscitet, & gloria æterna donet. Nos enim omnes, qui in ipsum credimus, [illegible, ~6 letters] illa fumus quam ei propheta p-mittit, prognati virtute ejus ex immortali femine, membra ejus, os de ossibus ejus.
units.tr: Therefore we may with full confidence aspire to that blessed hope which we shall obtain in the other life. For it cannot be that he alone should live for ever, and not also raise us from death and grant us eternal glory. For all of us who believe in him [illegible, about six letters] are that offspring which the prophet promises to him, begotten by his power from an immortal seed: his members, bone of his bones.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt, auditores, quæ hoc tempore de oraculi Iesaiæ celeberrimi, cum narratione Evangelica admirabili consensu, & de fructibus mortis ac resurrectionis Christi repetenda duxi. Sed parum tamen hæc quamvis luculentissima & fructuosissima, parum tamen, inquam, profuerint, nisi ea per fidem nobis applicemus & gratissimus. Soli enim credentes & grati beneficia Christi percipiunt, & consolatione salutari fruuntur: Infideles & ingrati vana spe seipsos lactant. Idcir-co non universos sed multos justificaturum esse Messiam, testatus est Iesaias, eos nimirum, qui vera vivaque cognitione ejus donati fuerint. Ea vero cognitio nequaquam in sola personæ officiique; Messiæ notitia consistit, qua scitureum[?] Filiū Dei esse missum in carnem, servatorem promissum, propter peccata nostra mortuum, propter justificationem suscitatum, factum denique nobis à patre sapientiam, justitiam, sanctificationem & redemptionem. Sed fides quoq; exigitur, quæ Servatorem hunc cum omnibus beneficiis certa cordis fiducia amplectatur, quoniam fides sola perfectissimum Christi meritum sibi applicans, nos coram Deo justos facit. Hic novæ vitæ puritas, sanctitas, & gratitudo pro tantis beneficiis necessario accedit. Hac n. destituti utut verbis cognitionem veram Christi jactitent, ipso tamen opere fa&isq;, ut Apostolus loquitur, salvatorem eū negant. Atq; hæc est vera illa & salutaris cognitio Dei & Salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi, in qua Dominus ipse Ioh. 17. vitam æternam sitam esse pronunciat. Quamobrem qui nostro hoc tempore, nescio quo malo genio suasore, etiam impiis, incredulis, & palam ingratis, ipsisq; adeo damnatis, fructus cruentæ mortis Filii Dei, cū Petro Paulo aliisque fidelib. communes facere non dubitant, eò quod Evangelii promissiones universales, universis promittere salutem, ipsis quidem videantur, errorem haud dubiè perniciosissimū fovent. Quid n. cognitione Messiæ, quid fide, quid gratitudine opus foret, si infideles perinde ac fideles, vi mortis Christi remissione peccatorum, justitiam & vitâ recuperarunt, inque sinum[?] & gratiâ Dei, ut scribere non verentur, recepti sunt? Vbi vero legerunt universale promissione, q omnib. fidelib. pariter & infidelib. vitam pmittat[?]? An nō totum Evangelium est doctrina fidei, arcens à gratia infideles oēs? Nos vero his missis teneamus Iesaiæ oraculum: Servus meus justus cognitione sua justificabit multos, quorum peccata ipse portavit. Atque ut in nos quoq; tanta beneficia magis magisque redundent: primum fide hunc servū Iehovæ, & Iehovam ipsum, in carne manifestatum ample &tamur: inq; hoc solo adversus tétationes omnes remedia quæramus. Si negant hunc esse Messiam blasphemi Judæi, suo malo negent, nos ad cõsen-sum historiæ Evangelicæ cum prophetarum oraculis respiciamus. Si peccatorū conscientia nos urget, spectemus agnum hunc Dei, qui peccata nostra in ligno portavit, qui cum ad mactatione pro nobis duceretur os non aperuit. Si ira Dei terret, cogitemus a Deo propter iniquitates nostras contritum, & percussum, ut nos livore suo sanaret. Si deest justitia, hic servus Jehovæ justificat omnes cognoscentes ipsum. Si peccatorū nos cruciant reliquiæ, scimus factum hunc esse sacrificiū pro omni reatu, nec quicquam esse damnationis in iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Si anxios nos habet infirmitas nostra, & defectionis, qua tantis beneficiis spoliemur, metus: cogitemus eum pro trāf-gresforibus etiam orasse, & perpetuo apud patre cœlestem intercedere, ne fides nostra deficiat unquam, neminem etiam quantumvis potentem, oves ipsius rapere posse de manu ejus. Si rugit leo nisi instar Diabolus, furit mundus, fremunt Ty-ranni, minantur, tumultuantur: meminerimus per mortē Christi ademptam potestatem ei, qui mortis habebat imperiū, ereptum morti ne pungat aculeum, mundum denique victum esse: sicut dixit: confidite ego vici mundum. Ridet ille in cœlis conatus Ty-rannorum, quo nos freti, ne pili quidem inanes eorum minas facere debemus, certi, quod opus Domini, ringentibus licet hostibus, ac stridentibus omnibus inferorum portis per manum ejus prosperabitur perpetuò. Sed of-ficio nostro nondum sic satrsfecimus, nisi in id quoque sedulò incumbamus omnes, ut pro im-mensis his beneficiis, nos Deo gratos exhibeamus. Id vero fiet si cum Christo liberatore nostro in novam vitam magis magisque resurgentes, nō ea quæ in terris sunt caduca & momentanea, defixis humo animis, sed quę sursum cœlestia bona nos mánent, omni studio quæramus, optimoq; redé-ptori nostro, in novitate spiritus, non in vetusta-te literæ serviamus. Iugiter quoque corde & ore immensam hanc Dei patris φιλανθρωπίαν, filiiqué ipsius ineffabilem erga nos amorem celebremus.
units.tr: These, listeners, are the things which at this time I have judged fit to repeat concerning the most celebrated oracle of Isaiah, together with the Gospel narrative, which agree admirably, and concerning the fruits of Christ's death and resurrection. But these things, however very clear and very fruitful, will profit us little, I say, little, unless we apply them to ourselves through faith and gratitude. For only believers and the grateful receive the benefits of Christ and enjoy saving consolation; unbelievers and the ungrateful flatter themselves with vain hope. Therefore Isaiah testifies that the Messiah will justify not all but many, namely those who have been endowed with a true and living knowledge of him. Yet this knowledge does not consist at all in mere acquaintance with the person and office of the Messiah, by which one knows that the Son of God was sent in the flesh, the promised Saviour, who died for our sins and was raised for our justification, and who has been made for us by the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Faith is also required, which embraces this Saviour with all his benefits by the certain trust of the heart, since faith alone, applying to itself the most perfect merit of Christ, makes us righteous before God. Here the purity of the new life, holiness, and gratitude for such great benefits necessarily follow. For those who lack these, however much they boast in words of a true knowledge of Christ, deny him by their deeds, as the Apostle says, as Saviour. And this is that true and saving knowledge of God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, in which the Lord himself in John 17 declares eternal life to consist. Wherefore those who in our time, by I know not what evil genius as persuader, do not hesitate to make the fruits of the bloody death of the Son of God common even to the impious, the unbelieving, the openly ungrateful, and those so condemned, together with Peter, Paul and other faithful, because they seem to them to hold the universal promises of the Gospel to promise salvation to all, certainly cherish a most pernicious error. For what need would there be of knowledge of the Messiah, of faith, of gratitude, if the unbelievers, just as the faithful, have by the power of Christ's death recovered remission of sins, righteousness and life, and have been received, as they do not hesitate to write, into the bosom and grace of God? But where have they read of a universal promise that would grant life to all the faithful and unbelieving alike? Does not the whole Gospel stand as a doctrine of faith, excluding all unbelievers from grace? But let us now set these aside and hold to the oracle of Isaiah: "My righteous servant by his knowledge shall justify many, whose iniquities he shall bear." And so that such great benefits may flow more and more upon us also: first, let us embrace by faith this servant of Jehovah, and Jehovah himself manifested in the flesh, fully; and in this alone let us seek remedies against all temptations. If the blasphemous Jews deny that this is the Messiah, let them deny it to their own harm; we, for our part, let us look to the agreement of the Gospel history with the oracles of the prophets. If the consciousness of sins presses upon us, let us look upon this Lamb of God, who bore our sins on the tree, who when he was led to the slaughter for us did not open his mouth. If the wrath of God terrifies us, let us consider him crushed and smitten by God for our iniquities, so that by his bruises he might heal us. If righteousness is lacking, this servant of Jehovah justifies all who know him. If the remnants of sins torment us, we know that this has been made a sacrifice for every guilt, and that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. If our weakness and the fear of falling away, by which we might be despoiled of such great benefits, make us anxious, let us reflect that he prayed even for transgressors and makes continual intercession before the heavenly Father, so that our faith may never fail, and that no one, however powerful, can snatch his sheep out of his hand. If the lion roars like the devil, the world rages, tyrants snarl, threaten and make tumult: let us remember that through the death of Christ the power was taken away from him who had the dominion of death, that death was robbed of its sting, and that the world has been finally conquered, as he said: "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." He who sits in the heavens laughs at the attempts of tyrants; relying on him, we ought not to make even the least account of their threats, certain that the work of the Lord will prosper for ever by his hand, though the enemies gnash their teeth and all the gates of hell hiss. But we have not yet satisfied our duty in this way unless we all also apply ourselves diligently to this, that we show ourselves pleasing to God for such immense benefits. This will happen if, rising ever more and more into a new life with Christ our deliverer, we seek with all zeal not the things on earth which are frail and fleeting, our minds fixed on the ground, but the heavenly goods which await us above, and serve our most excellent Redeemer in newness of spirit, not in the oldness of the letter. Let us also continually celebrate with heart and mouth this immense philanthropy of God the Father, and the ineffable love of his Son towards us.

units.la: Tibi igitur, æterne Deus, gratias toto pectore agimus, quod ineffabilem tuum amorem, tam p-lixè[?] ac cumulatè in nos effudisti, Filium tuum u-nigenitum propter nostram salutem, post exan-tlatas innumeras vitę ærumnas, pœnam nostris peccatis debitam, corpore animaq; luere: posta-cerbissimos ac dirissimos cruciatus & dolores, quos in æternum nos luere oportebat, mortem omnium ignominiosissimam oppetere: sangui-ne suo preciosissimo per multa vulnera effuso fœdissimas nostras maculas eluere, & quæcunq; in Adamo amiseramus recuperare nobis voluisti: eundem etiam perafto redemptionis opere gloriosè resuscitavisti, ut parta morte beneficia suis fidelibus communicaret. Neque id solum, sed et-jam, quod nos pro immensa tua misericordia, ad cognitionem ejusdem filii tui vocasti, & viva ejus membra per fidem fecisti, nec non sanctissimi e-jus meriti dulcissimos in animis nostris fructus sentire, & beatam, ad quam omnes pii aspirant, gloriam, certa spe expectare voluisti. Oramus te clementissime Pater, ut haec beneficia indies in nobis amplifices, animos nostros in vera pietate, assiduaque tuorum in nos meritorum consideratione confirmes, Ecclesiam potenti tua dextera defendas, studia literarum, & scholas doctrinae coelestis, earumque pios doctores in his praesertim regionibus benigne ferves. Inprimis autem, serenissimum nostrum & clementissimum Principem ac Dominum, D. FRIDERICUM IV. Electorem Palat.tanquam pupillam oculi tui custodias, omnibus corporis atque animi bonis locupletissime expleas, diuturnam ac longaevam in aurea pace, in felici ac tranquilla patriae florentis gubernatione, in fideli Ecclesiae defensione, ejus Celsitudinem vitam concedas, minaces hostium in gregem pusillum tuum furores compescas, ut te in hac vita, inter ruentis mundi fragores conservati, & in aeterna illa, gloriam immortalem adepti, immortalibus tibique gratissimis laudib.cum aeterno tuo filio, Spirituque sancto benignissimum patrem, fortissimumque Deum celebremus.
units.tr: To you therefore, eternal God, we give thanks with our whole heart, because you have poured out your ineffable love upon us so abundantly and fully, that you willed your only-begotten Son, for our salvation, after he had endured innumerable hardships of life, to pay with body and soul the punishment due to our sins; after the most bitter and dire torments and pains which we were bound to suffer for ever, to undergo death, the most ignominious of all; by shedding his most precious blood through many wounds, to wash away our most foul stains; and to restore to us whatever we had lost in Adam. You also gloriously raised the same Son after the work of redemption was accomplished, so that he might share the benefits won by his death with his faithful people. Not only this, but now also, because by your immense mercy you have called us to the knowledge of the same Son of yours, and have made us living members of him through faith, and have willed that we should both feel the sweetest fruits of his most holy merit in our souls and await with certain hope the blessed glory to which all the pious aspire. We pray you, most merciful Father, that you would increase these benefits in us day by day, confirm our minds in true piety and in the constant consideration of your merits toward us, defend the Church with your mighty right hand, and graciously preserve the study of letters, the schools of heavenly doctrine, and their pious teachers, especially in these regions. Above all, may you keep as the apple of your eye our most serene and most merciful Prince and Lord, Lord FREDERICK IV, Elector Palatine; fill him most abundantly with all good gifts of body and soul; grant that his Highness may live long and to old age, in golden peace, in the happy and tranquil government of a flourishing fatherland, in the faithful defence of the Church; restrain the threatening fury of enemies against your little flock; so that we, preserved in this life amid the crashing of the falling world, and in that eternal life having obtained immortal glory, may celebrate with immortal praises most grateful to you, together with your eternal Son and the Holy Spirit, the most kindly Father and most mighty God.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: ORATIO IX. DE MISSIONE SPIRITUS SANCTI.
units.tr: ORATIO IX. ON THE SENDING OF THE HOLY SPIRIT.

units.la: Publicè recitata ab OTTHONE GYSONE Marchiaco. 29. Maij. 1585.
units.tr: Publicly recited by OTTHO GYSO of Marchiaco, 29 May 1585.

units.la: LAUDABILI ac inveterata consuetudine hujus celeberrimæ & antiquiss. Academiæ, viri Amplis. patres in Christo Reverendi. Nobilissimi ac doctissimi auditores, receptum est, ut hoc solenni ac faustissimo Pentecostes tempore, (quod iterum Dei gratia nobis illuxit) aliquid vestris auribus dignum, in hoc laudatissimo congressu, dicatur, uti omnium nostrum animi, ad considerationem summi & ineffabilis beneficii, quod ante annos plus minus quinquaginta supra millesimum quingentesimum, Filius Dei apud Ecclesiam suam benignissimè posuit, misso in Apostolos visibili specie Spiritu S. inflamme-tur. Est certè id miraculum accuratiore consideratione dignissimum: quia consolationis ac doctrinæ plenissimum: Itaq; imminente nuper hoc solenni festo, certè non dici potest, quanto gau- diorum cumulo, quasi sim perfusus, quod piis votis sæpius optâdo sperarim huic negotio satis arduo ac difficili, præficiendum aliquem, qui pro dignitate rem tantam tractando, vestræ meæque exspectationi cumulatissimè satisfaceret: quemque omnes nos magna cum voluptate ac utilitate doctissimè differentem audiremus. Verum ubi sensi has dicendi partes mihi deferri sustinendas, non inficias eo, meum mihi gaudium aliquanta ægritudine perturbari cœpisse: siquidem spe me frustratum colligebam: ac profectò conscius mihi meæ ruditatis curtæque supellectilis, (ut verum fatear) nunquam mihi has partes imponi passus essem, nisi me paterna fidelissimorum doctissimorumque præceptorum authoritas, laudatissima loci hujus consuetudo, summaque temporis necessitas permovissent. Quare præclari juvenes, nolite quaso arbitrari, me captandæ gloriæ causa in cathedram hanc ascendisse. Quinimò quod res est, cogitate, præceptoribus obtemperare in tam sancto instituto, pium esse, quibus idcirco verecundè ac modestè potius obsequium præstare, quàm morosè debitam obedientiam detrectare volui, ut hoc pacto mihi æque atque vobis, quod citharœdus ille dicebat, canerem. Minimè itaque dubito, quin vestrum omnium summa æquanimitas, qua antehac alios, qui in hunc locum dicturi prodiere, vos vidi complexos fuisse, mihi quoque veniæ locum aliquem sit relictura, si forte minus, quàm pro rei dignitate, vestraque expectatione dicam, vel etiam oneri imposito succumbam[?]. Verum ne nimia prolixitate, vestræ benignitati diffidere videar, age uno verbo, si possum dicam quod volo.
units.tr: Following the praiseworthy and long-established custom of this most celebrated and most ancient Academy, reverend fathers in Christ, distinguished and most learned hearers, it has been agreed that at this solemn and most auspicious season of Pentecost, which by the grace of God has once again dawned upon us, something worthy of your ears should be spoken in this most distinguished assembly, so that the minds of us all may be inflamed by the consideration of the supreme and unspeakable benefit which the Son of God most graciously bestowed upon his Church about fifty years after the year one thousand five hundred, when the Holy Spirit was sent upon the Apostles in visible form. Certainly this miracle is most worthy of closer consideration, because it is full of comfort and instruction. Therefore, as this solemn festival drew near, I cannot say with what great heap of joy I was, as it were, overwhelmed, because I had often hoped with pious prayers that someone would be appointed to this rather arduous and difficult task, who, handling so great a matter as it deserves, would satisfy to the fullest both your expectation and mine, and whom we would all hear discoursing most learnedly, with great pleasure and profit. But when I perceived that this part of speaking was being transferred to me to bear, I do not deny that my joy began to be disturbed by a certain distress, since I gathered that I had been cheated of my hope. And indeed, conscious of my own lack of skill and my meagre equipment (to tell the truth), I would never have allowed these duties to be laid upon me, had not the authority of my most faithful and most learned teachers, the most praiseworthy custom of this place, and the great necessity of the time moved me. Therefore, distinguished young men, I beg you, do not think that I have mounted this chair for the sake of seeking glory. Rather, as is the case, consider that it is a pious thing to obey teachers in so holy an institution; to them I preferred to render obedience modestly and respectfully rather than refuse the owed submission peevishly, so that in this way I might sing, as that citharist said, equally to myself and to you. I have no doubt, therefore, that the great equanimity of all of you, which I have seen you show to the others who previously came forward to speak in this place, will leave me some room for pardon, should I perhaps speak less than the dignity of the matter and your expectation require, or even succumb to the burden laid upon me. But lest I seem to distrust your kindness by excessive lengthiness, come, in a word, I will say what I wish, as far as I can.

units.la: Recolit hoc tempore grata mente universa Christi Ecclesia memoriam admirandæ historiæ quo pacto Filius Dei, dominus ac redemptor no-ster, postea quam definito patris consilio pro peccatis nostris victima factus, devicta morte imperium & gloriam dextræ Dei in cœlis occupasset, quinquagesimo resurrectionis die, hoc est, ipso Pentecostes festo, cœlitus, inaudito miraculo, ac munere ineffabili Spiritum Sanctum misit Apostolis. Agebant tum Hierosolymis ex lege patria Iudæi totius orbis festum conventum, quos omnes Filius Dei incredibilis alioqui rei spectatores ac testes esse voluit. Apostolis enim eodem loci congregatis, extitit repente è cœlo sonitus tanquam venti flatus violenti, totamq; replevit domum, qua convenerant. Mox & linguæ singulorum, flammarum radiantium instar: dispertitæ apparuerunt, Spiritu Sancto hac visibili specie unicuique illorum insidente & variis linguis loquendi facultatem conferente. Hæc illi videntes, partim quidem, quos à pietate sacra historia laudat, attoniti, incredibili admiratione miraculum extulerunt: partim vero quibus mens levior erat, absurdo ἐμπαιγμῷ[?] & calumnia nimis impudenti rem sole meridiano clariorem eludentes, ebrietatis ac vesanæ mentis Apostolos insimula-runt. At istorum proterviam D. Apostolus Pe-trus argumento populari à temporis circumstā-tia, inprimis vero oraculi divini authoritate satis convellit, non esse hanc differendi de rebus coelestibus admirandam facultatem, variarumque linguarum in hominibus alioquin illiteratis peritiam dulcis musti ructus, sed potius ipsissimi Spiritus Sancti ex Ioelis Prophetae oraculo coelitus a Christo effusi in Apostolos adorandum beneficium demonstrans.
units.tr: At this time the whole Church of Christ gratefully recalls the memory of the wonderful history of how the Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer, after being made a victim for our sins according to the settled counsel of the Father, and having overcome death, had taken possession of dominion and glory at the right hand of God in heaven, on the fiftieth day after the resurrection, that is, on the very festival of Pentecost, sent the Holy Spirit to the Apostles from heaven, with an unheard-of miracle and an ineffable gift. Then, according to the law of their country, the Jews of the whole world were keeping a festive assembly at Jerusalem, all of whom the Son of God wished to be witnesses and spectators of a thing otherwise incredible. For when the Apostles had gathered together in one place, suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing wind, and it filled the whole house in which they were sitting. Presently tongues also appeared, divided like shining flames, the Holy Spirit taking up residence in each of them in this visible form and bestowing upon each the ability to speak in various tongues. Some of those who saw these things, namely those whom sacred history praises for piety, were astonished and extolled the miracle with incredible wonder; but others, whose minds were lighter, mocked the thing, which was clearer than midday sun, with a foolish jest and a most shameless slander, and accused the Apostles of drunkenness and a deranged mind. But the Apostle Peter sufficiently refuted their insolence by a popular argument drawn from the circumstances of the time, and above all by the authority of the divine oracle, showing that this admirable ability to speak of heavenly things, and the skill in various tongues in men otherwise unlettered, was not the belching of sweet wine, but rather a benefit to be adored: the very Spirit of God poured out from heaven by Christ upon the Apostles, according to the oracle of the prophet Joel.

units.la: Est haec de missione Spiritus Sancti historia, quemadmodum ipsi metanimadvertitis, doctrinae ac consolationis plenissima, continentur enim in ea res maximi momenti de utilitate seu fructu Ascensionis Domini in coelum, quarum enarrationem hic instituere nō fertanimus. Nos vero iis contenti nunc, quae huius temporis videntur esse maxime, auxiliante Deo optimo maximo, Primum monstrabimus, effusione Spiritus Sancti in Apostolos confirmari, & ceu sigillo quodam obsignari doctrinam Evangelii, cuius πίστις nititur salus nostra. Hinc ostendemus, miraculo hoc veram tam Filii quam Spiritus Sancti Deitatem liquido demonstrari, ac doceri, quod uterque sit verus, immensus ac perfectus Deus, Patri ὁμοούσιος. Tandem eodem miraculo, quae & quanta sint Spiritus Sancti in Ecclesiam beneficia luculenter ostendi, ea qua fieri poterit brevitate docebimus. Faxit ille coelestis Spiritus, ut & omnis mea in gloriam eius cedat oratio, & vos dicentem me benigne atque utiliter audiatis.
units.tr: This is the history of the sending of the Holy Spirit, as you yourselves are aware, and it is most full of teaching and comfort, for it contains matters of the greatest moment concerning the usefulness and fruit of the Lord's Ascension into heaven, the explanation of which we do not intend to undertake here. But being content for now with those points which seem to be most pressing for this time, with the help of God, best and greatest, we will first show that the effusion of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles confirms the doctrine of the Gospel, and seals it as with a certain seal, the faith of which our salvation rests upon. Next we will show that by this miracle the true Deity of both the Son and the Holy Spirit is clearly demonstrated and taught, namely that each is true, immeasurable and perfect God, of one substance with the Father. Finally, by the same miracle, what and how great are the benefits of the Holy Spirit to the Church will be clearly shown, and we will teach them with as much brevity as possible. May that heavenly Spirit grant that all my speech may turn to his glory, and that you may hear me speaking kindly and profitably.

units.la: Divus Augustinus lib. 12. Confess. cap. 2. non minus pie quam erudite scripsit, verbo Dei miraculis auctoritatem conciliari, qua insigni sententia tia haud dubiè innuere voluit, homines ex mira- culorum consideratione & admiratione firmius discere, quanta debeat esse apud mortales omnes doctrinæ eorum, qui miraculis divinis insignes fuerunt, authoritas. Quæcunque enim miracula Deo optimo Max: naturæ conditori ac Domino per ministros suos unquam edere visum fuit, in eum præcipuè finem sunt facta, ut illis ceu datis pignoribus & arrhis veritas doctrinæ cœlestis in mentibus hominum confirmaretur. Id quod vel unius Iohannis sententia satis manifestè testa-tur, sub finem Evangelii sui dicentis, quædam tantum insigniora Domini miracula descripta ef se eius libro, ut credamus, Iesum esse Christum, & credentes per nomen eius vitam habeamus. Est verò hæc de qua dicimus, Spiritus Sancti effusio, non uno, sed pluribus miraculis divinis adeò illustris, uti profecto in maximis sapientiæ ac potentiæ Dei operibus, quibus unquam hominibus sese patefecit, numerari haud postremo loco debeat. Quid enim?De cœlo flatus violentus in Apostolos repente irruit. De cœlo flamma linguas Apostolorum adurit sine dolore, dispescit sine læsione: Deus igitur operis tàm mirandi authorem se profitetur. Evidentius eius rei testimonium est illud, quod in historia sequitur, repletos fuisse omnes Spiritu Sancto, præsentiam nimirum suam, flatu flammisque quasi symbolis testante, cœpisseque omnes loqui linguis aliis, nec loqui tantum, sed loqui de magnalibus Dei, hoc est, immensis illis beneficiis, quæ Deus juxta Prophetarum oracula in Filio redemptore universo generi humano pro admirabili sua bonitate exhi-buerit. Quis hic miracula divina non agnoscat? Quis non cum piis illis Iudæis hæsitet? admiretur? obstupescat? Quid hoc sit rei? homines de infima plebe piscationibus assuetos, vix patriæ linguæ satis gnaros, inter doctorum pulpita nunquam versatos, vicinorum Arabum, Ægyptiorū, Lybiorum, &c. gentem ac linguam vix fama tenentes, repente nullo accedente studio in confertissima hominum corona summa omnium ad miratione cœlestis sapientiæ verba fundere, patriumque Idioma cum remotissimis Parthorum, Medorum, Ponticorum, aliarumque extremi orbis gentium linguis commutare suo arbitratu? Vnde id vero? Spiritu Sancto suggerente singulis peritiam quarum vis linguarum, quibus apud obvios quosvis, pro necessitate docendo uterentur. Sedit enim super unumquenque eorum, ac dedit eis loqui linguis aliis. Deum ergo miraculi huius authorem agnoscamus oportet: Cuius unius est, per Spiritum Sanctum agere, linguarumque donum miraculosè infundere. Quis enim posuit os in homine, aut quis ponit surdum vel mutum vel videntem, vel cæcum? Nonne ego (inquit Deus Mosi) qui sum Iehova? Exod. 4.11.
units.tr: Saint Augustine, in book 12 of the Confessions, chapter 2, wrote no less piously than learnedly that miracles lend authority to the word of God. By this notable saying he undoubtedly wished to indicate that men learn more firmly, from the consideration and admiration of miracles, how great the authority of those should be among all mortals whose teaching was distinguished by divine miracles. For whatever miracles it has ever pleased almighty God, the Creator of nature and the Lord, to perform through his ministers, they were done chiefly for this end: that the truth of the heavenly doctrine might be confirmed in the minds of men by them as given pledges and earnests. This is attested quite plainly even by the saying of John alone, who at the end of his Gospel says that certain of the Lord's more remarkable miracles were described in his book, that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, and believing may have life through his name. Now this effusion of the Holy Spirit of which we speak is so illustrious, not by one but by several divine miracles, that it ought certainly to be counted not in the last place among the greatest works of God's wisdom and power by which he ever revealed himself to men. For what? A violent wind suddenly rushed upon the Apostles from heaven. A flame from heaven set the tongues of the Apostles on fire without pain, divided them without injury: God therefore professes himself the author of so wonderful a work. Even clearer testimony of this is what follows in the history: that all were filled with the Holy Spirit, his presence being attested, of course, by the wind and flames as if by signs, and that all began to speak in other tongues, and not only to speak but to speak of the mighty works of God, that is, of those immense benefits which God, according to the oracles of the prophets, has for his wonderful goodness displayed to the whole human race in the Son, the Redeemer. Who here would not recognise divine miracles? Who would not, with those pious Jews, hesitate, marvel, be astonished? What is the matter here? Men from the lowest common people, accustomed to fishing, scarcely knowing their own native tongue well, never before conversant with the pulpits of the learned, hardly knowing by report the people and language of the neighbouring Arabs, Egyptians, Libyans, and so on, suddenly, with no study intervening, in a most crowded gathering of men, pour forth words of heavenly wisdom to the great admiration of all, and at their own will exchange their native language for the tongues of the most distant Parthians, Medes, Pontians, and other peoples of the farthest parts of the world? Whence is this truly? From the Holy Spirit suggesting to each the skill in whatever tongues they used with whomever they met, as needed for teaching. For he sat upon each one of them, and gave them to speak in other tongues. We must therefore acknowledge God as the author of this miracle: it is his alone, through the Holy Spirit, to act and to pour into men the gift of tongues by miracle. For who made the mouth of man, or who makes the dumb, or the deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? Is it not I (says God to Moses) who am Jehovah? Exod. 4.11.

units.la: Nunc itaque manifestum esse arbitror, hanc admirandam Spiritus Sancti effusionem habere hunc usum cum aliis miraculis communem, uti testetur de doctrina Christi & Apostolorū, quod sit vera, & à Deo profecta: siquidem Deus [illegible, ~8 letters] ergo, addidit arrhabonem Sanctum Spiritum. Non enim ei doctrinæ testimonii causa addit miracula, quam minimè approbet. Est enim Deus nolens iniquitatem aut mendacium: & Spiritus omnis veritatis. Huic verò doctrinæ de Filio testimonium perhibet tali edito miraculo, quod omnium creaturarum vires & captum superat. Est ergo doctrina illa, quam Spiritu Sancto suggerente, & viva voce sonuerunt, & libris consignarunt Apostoli, cœlitus à Domino nobis manifestata.
units.tr: It seems to me now clear that this wonderful outpouring of the Holy Spirit has a purpose in common with the other miracles: to attest that the teaching of Christ and of the Apostles is true and comes from God. For God, [illegible], has added the Holy Spirit as a pledge. He does not add miracles to a teaching in order to bear witness to it unless he approves of it; for God is not willing iniquity or lying, and the Spirit is the Spirit of all truth. Moreover, by such a miracle he bears witness to the teaching concerning the Son, a miracle which surpasses the powers and comprehension of all creatures. That teaching, therefore, which the Apostles proclaimed by the living voice under the suggestion of the Holy Spirit and committed to books, was revealed to us from heaven by the Lord.

units.la: Neque verò hic mihi quis obiiciat, etiam Sa-tanam consuevisse non raro per homines obses-sos loqui linguis, quas non didicerint: Cuius rei exempla fortasse vestrum aliqui experientia ob-servarunt: Illud enim si fiat, huic admirando o-peri Dei nequaquam simile videri debet. Quis enim ignorat Satanam sæpè præstigiis suis illu-dere miseris hominibus, atque eosdem cachin-no satyrico irridere? Quis nescit impurum illum Spiritum transformari quandoque in angelum lucis? Quamvis autem mira solertia instar pro-tervæ similis conetur imitari opera Dei, & ina-nia etiam εἴδωλα ad illa obscuranda & deforman-da hominibus offundat: Tamen (vel si iupatur[?]) miracula Dei illi prorsus sunt ἀσωσία[?] & ἡ ἀμι-χανία. Garrit, blasphemat, fremit, ridet Deum & homines, in obsessis idiomate ignoto Satan: Fa-ctor. Hoccine verò est linguis loqui? an verò est veteratorie imperitis illudere? Nihil enim videas miseros homines intelligere eorum, quæ blate-rant. Itaque sine cognitione linguarum linguis loquuntur, Diabolo inanem strepitum buccis eorum concitante, quasi qui tibiam inflat. Apo [?]stolis autem revera illarum linguarum, quibus usi sunt, cognitionem atque verum intellectum collatum fuisse, testatur manifeste historia. Subi-to enim callebant linguas omnes, quibuscunque uti ad quamcunque gentem exteram liberet. Te-stantur pii illi Iudæi, cum admiratione dicentes, audimus eos loquentes nostris linguis magnifica Dei facta: Testantur deniq; libri Apostolorum exo-tico Iudæis, id est, Græco Idiomate exarati, & ad nos usque transmissi. Nihil igitur cum hoc divino opere habent commune Diabolicæ præstigiæ, ac meridiana luce est clarius, à Deo linguarum formatore atque authore mirandum illud donum Apostolis fuisse collatum, quo tum suam potentiam declarare, tum vero doctrinam de Fi-lio suo traditam confirmare sategerit.
units.tr: Nor let anyone here object to me that Satan too has not infrequently been accustomed to speak through possessed men in tongues they had never learned. Some of you have perhaps observed examples of this from experience. For if that were to happen, it ought not to seem at all similar to this wonderful work of God. Who does not know that Satan often mocks miserable men with his tricks and laughs at them with a satyr-like cackle? Who does not know that the impure spirit sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light? Although, with remarkable skill, he like a wanton ape tries to imitate the works of God, and pours out empty idols to obscure and deform those works for men, nevertheless the miracles of God are wholly unlike his, and [...] lack of power. He babbles, blasphemes, roars, and mocks God and men; in the possessed he speaks in an unknown idiom, "Factor." Is this speaking in tongues? Or is it rather a crafty deceiving of the ignorant? For you would see that the wretched men understand nothing of what they babble. Thus they speak in tongues without knowledge of the tongues, the Devil stirring up empty noise in their mouths, like one who blows on a pipe. But history plainly testifies that the Apostles truly possessed both knowledge and true understanding of those tongues which they used. For at once they knew all the tongues, whichever they wished to use for any foreign nation. Those pious Jews testify, saying with wonder, "We hear them speaking in our tongues the magnificent deeds of God." Finally, the books of the Apostles testify, written in a foreign language for the Jews, that is, in the Greek idiom, and handed down even to us. Diabolical tricks therefore have nothing in common with this divine work, and it is clearer than the noonday light that this wonderful gift was conferred on the Apostles by God, the former and author of tongues, by which he sought both to declare his power and to confirm the doctrine concerning his Son handed down.

units.la: Congruit vero etiam hæc historia cum vaticiniis ac prædictionibus Prophetarum, Ioelis & Christi. Effunditur enim hic visibili & corporali quodam modo in semen Israelis Apostolos Spi-ritus Sanctus, cuius illi virtute instructi mox de mysteriis divinis supra vulgarem modum splen-didissime disserunt, quod Ioël per Prophetias & somnia designabat, quemadmodum illa omnia D. Petrus liquido ac prolixe ad historiam præsentem referri debere ostendit. Quis enim dubita-ret, prædictiones illas rerum futurarum, quibus exacte respondent eventus, qui non possunt præsciri nisi à solo Deo, divinas esse? Harum itaque impletione, non aliam, quàm divinam cœlestem quæ doctrinam confirmari necesse est? Cedo au-tem: quæ quæso est illa doctrina, cuius patefa[illegible, ~1 letter]ctionem servis & ancillis Iehovæ Propheta sub ultima tempora promittit? Quæ illa, quam Dominus Iesus Apostolis suis toties pollicetur? Nulla sanè alia, quam cuius intelligentia Apostoli mi-raculoso Spiritus Sancti magisterio imbuti fue-runt, & quam præclaro illo diversarum lingua-rum dono instructi, per omnes universi orbis partes deinceps propagarunt. Quare cum dubium amplius non sit, quin Filius Dei exaltatus, de throno cœlestis gloriæ effuso in Apostolos, Spiri-tu Sancto, non tàm suis promissis satisfecerit, quàm Ioëlis illud oraculum, de admiranda Evangelicæ doctrinæ per effusum Iehovæ Spiritu pa-tefactione impleverit: liquidò satis me iam de-monstrasse illud confido, quod primum fuit orationis nostræ caput: firmissimam nempe doctrinæ Apostolicæ totiusque religionis nostræ Chri-stianæ [?]ἀπόδειξιν καὶ ἐπίδειξιν[?], contra Diaboli Ethnicorum & hæreticorum Sarcasmos hoc oraculo nobis suppeditari: Cuius sanè fidem dubiam fa-cere, quid aliud esse potest, quàm lingua, quod dicitur, cœlum impetere? Vix enim, si palàm de cœlo descendisset Deus, clarius conspici potuisset eius maiestas. Neque aliud spectasse Filium Dei existimandus est, cum non occulta suggestione, sed manifesto miraculo doctrinam suam cœlitus patefaceret, quam ut testes sibi adscisceret totius mundi oculos, non hominum placita, sed cœlestem sapientiam esse doctrinam eam, quam tradituri erant Apostoli. Hinc D. Ambrosius non minus acutè, quàm pie veritatem doctrinæ Chri-sti de ascensione & gloria eius aliisque capitibus eo miraculo comprobari docet. Credendum enim est, inquit, ad patrem pervenisse Christum, cum vidimus ad Apostolos descendisse paracletum, Credendum inquam est, sicut ait de Salvatore David, in Dei dextra considere, quia cernimus Spiritum Sanctum, sicut promisit dominus, in discipulis exultare.
units.tr: This history also agrees with the prophecies and predictions of the Prophets, Joel, and Christ. For here the Holy Spirit is poured out in a visible and bodily manner upon the seed of Israel, upon the Apostles, who, instructed by his power, at once discourse most splendidly about divine mysteries beyond the common manner. This Joel signified through prophecies and dreams, just as St. Peter clearly and at length showed that all those things ought to be referred to the present history. For who would doubt that those predictions of future things, to which the events correspond exactly, which cannot be foreknown except by God alone, are divine? Therefore, from their fulfilment, must not the doctrine be confirmed as divine and heavenly? But tell me: what, I ask, is that doctrine whose revelation the Prophet promises to the servants and handmaids of Jehovah in the last times? What is that which the Lord Jesus so often promises to his Apostles? Surely none other than that whose understanding the Apostles, imbued by the miraculous teaching of the Holy Spirit and equipped with that splendid gift of diverse tongues, afterwards propagated through all parts of the whole world. Therefore, since there is no longer any doubt that the Son of God, exalted, poured out from the throne of heavenly glory upon the Apostles the Holy Spirit, he fulfilled not so much his own promises as that oracle of Joel concerning the wonderful revelation of the Evangelical doctrine through the outpouring of the Spirit of Jehovah. I trust I have now shown clearly enough what was the first head of our discourse: namely, that this oracle supplies us with the most firm demonstration and display of the Apostolic doctrine and of our whole Christian religion, against the sarcasms of the Devil, of the Gentiles and of heretics. What else can make its faith doubtful than to attack heaven with the tongue, as they say? For if God had descended openly from heaven, his majesty could hardly have been seen more clearly. Nor should the Son of God be thought to have aimed at anything else, when he revealed his doctrine from heaven by a manifest miracle rather than by a hidden suggestion, than to take to himself as witnesses the eyes of the whole world, so that it might be seen that this doctrine, which the Apostles were to hand down, is not the opinions of men but heavenly wisdom. Hence St. Ambrose teaches no less acutely than piously that the truth of Christ's doctrine concerning his ascension and glory and other heads is confirmed by that miracle. "It must be believed," he says, "that Christ has reached the Father, since we have seen the Paraclete descend upon the Apostles. It must be believed, I say, that, as David said of the Saviour, he sits at the right hand of God, because we perceive the Holy Spirit, as the Lord promised, exulting in the disciples."

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Nunc ut ad illud, quod secundo loco nobis explicandum sumsimus, concedamus, miraculosa hac & visibili Spiritus Sancti in Apostolos effusione, non solum universam Evangelii doctrinam confirmari: Sed & veram atque aeternam Filii & Spiritus Sancti Deitatem comprobari docebimus. Credit Ecclesia Christiana, aeterna generatione Filium ex patre natum ineffabiliter, sententia aeterno patri aequalem ac ὁμοούσιον: subsistendi autem modo ordineque agendi ab eodem distinctam personam esse. Credit Spiritum Sanctum aeterna processione a Patre & Filio emanantem ineffabiliter utrique aequalem ac ὁμοούσιον Deum: ab utroque vero subsistendi ratione ordineq; agendi distinctam personam esse. Hanc fidem nostram tanto impensius Satan per haereticos, ad blasphemandum ludo ipsius edoctos, hodie non minus quam olim impugnat: quanto eius professione maiorem ab omnibus illorum sectis secessionem facimus, firmiusque illi universa salus nostra innititur. Est ergo, optimi auditores, cur hic contra Satanam probe nos muniamus, in quem usum breviter, quae ad confutandas tam πλανῶν quam βλασφημιας, quos vetus Ecclesia vocabat, blasphemias pertinere videntur ex historia illa nunc repetenda duximus.
units.tr: Now, as to the second point we have undertaken to explain, let us grant that by this miraculous and visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, not only is the whole doctrine of the Gospel confirmed, but we will also show that the true and eternal Deity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is proved. The Christian Church believes that the Son was ineffably born of the Father by eternal generation, of the same substance as the eternal Father and homoousios with him, yet distinct as a person by the mode of subsistence and the order of action. It believes that the Holy Spirit, proceeding eternally from the Father and the Son, is ineffably God, equal to both and homoousios with both, yet distinct as a person from both by the mode of subsistence and the order of action. Satan, taught by his own cunning to blaspheme, attacks this faith of ours through heretics today no less than in the past, and the more so because by professing it we separate ourselves further from all their sects, and because our whole salvation rests more firmly upon it. There is therefore good reason, most excellent hearers, for us to fortify ourselves well here against Satan. To this end we have decided to recall briefly from that story the points which seem to bear on refuting the errors (planai) and blasphemies (blasphemiai), as the ancient Church called them.

units.la: Ac primum quidem D. Petrus, volens auditorum animis persuadere, miraculum hoc quod videbant, esse divinum, magna animi constantia asseverat, à Christo illo crucifixo & resuscitato, inque gloriam coelestem ad dextram Patris evecto, iam effusum esse Spiritum promissum, ipsis videntibus & audientibus: promissum inquam, istum à Ioële, tum vero ab ipso Christo nō semel. Ego enim (inquit discipulis aliquoties) Si abiero, mittam eum vobis à patre, & Baptista apud Matthaeum, ille inquit vos baptizabit Spiritu Sancto & igni. Christus igitur est, qui mittit Spiritum Sanctum, qui Spiritu Sancto baptizat & regenerat Ecclesiam suam. Hinc & Deum esse, & distinctum personâ esse à patre & Spiritu Sancto elice-re promptum est. Quis enim mittere Spiritum Sanctum potest, nisi Deus, cuius ille Spiritus est proprius, qui etiam per Prophetam dixerat: Ego effundam de meo Spiritu. Sed & mittentem seu effundentem à misso atque effuso Spiritu Sancto distinctum esse, manifestum est, Filius igitur Dei mittens Spiritum Sanctum, & per eum agens, in mentibus, cordibus, & linguis Apostolorum, ve-rus & omnipotens Deus est. Praeclarum hoc argumentum est, quod non modo Arianorum ac Sabellianorum blasphemiis, sed Nestorii etiam deliriis opponamus. Ut enim τῇ[?] λόγῳ Deitatem veram, meridiana luce clarius, evincit: sic cum eodem λόγῳ veram & hypostaticam humanae massae unionem liquidò confirmat. Non enim alius quàm Filius Dei, & quidem homo ille Dei filius incarnatus, passus, mortuus, resuscitatus, & in gloriam dextræ Dei evectus, divino hoc bene-ficio ornat Ecclesiam suam. Non dicimus, ut quidam hodie volunt, ab humana natura dari Spiritum Sanctū. Absit enim ut dicamus à creatura procedere Spiritum creaturam dare creatorem suum creaturis: Absit ut credamus, creatuaram agere per creatorem suum. Hæc enim sunt ἐθεολογικώτεροι[?]. Tum satis etiam convenit inter Theologos, non nisi eam naturam agere per Spiritum Sanctum, à qua etiam procedit. Est enim per Spiritum Sanctum agere nihil aliud, nisi ordine personarum voluntatem agentis per eum præire, ipsius autem voluntatem comitari. Atqui humanæ naturæ voluntas non præcedit voluntatem Spiritus Sancti, sed ab hac potius informatur ac regitur. Adde quod Christus secundum eam naturam (humanam dico) Spiritu Sancto donari, ungi, obsignari, passim in scripturis dicitur. Non ergo secundum humanam, sed secundum divinam naturam mittit Spiritum Sanctū: quanquam unus idemque sit Christus unctus atque ungens seipsum atque Ecclesiam. Necesse est (inquit Lutherus locum Psalmi 45. in Epistola ad Hebræos 1. cap. explicans) verum Deum esse qui ungit. Jam vero etiam ille, qui ungitur, verus Deus est, eo quod thronum habet & in æternum regnat. Atqui Deus seipsum ungere non potest, sed qui ungitur inferior est ungente. Nam ungere hic est Spiritum Sanctum una cum suis donis infundere, idque creaturæ tantum convenit. Hactenus Lutherus. Hæc adiicere atque modeste aspergere libuit, ut cogitemus, sobrie hic philosophādum ef-fe,ne se,ne fugientes charybdin in scyllam incidamus: neve pro deificatione humanae Christi naturae in consideratè contraque Scripturae mentem propugnantes, aeternum λόγον de throno ὁμοουσίας cū patre praecipitemus, ac ludos de nobis ipsis praebeamus haereticis: quibus nihil unquam profuarum blasphemiarum defensione visum est esse compendiosius, quam quod hodie audiunt à nonullis ut καθολικὸν defendi, creaturam finitam, quae natura Deus non sit, nec Deo patri, sed hominibus nobis ὁμοούσιος, non tantum unione hypostatica, sed & reali communicatione omnium divinarum proprietatum essentialium, totiusque adeo Deitatis, sine tamen aeternitate, spiritualitate, immensitate, hoc est, sine veritate capacem esse. Sed stat illud Damasceni satis tritum ac verum dictum: Quomodo una natura contrariarum susceptiva subsistentialium differentiarum fuerit? aut quomodo possibile est, eandem naturam secundum idem creatam & increatam, mortalem & immortalem, circumscriptam & incircumscriptam?
units.tr: And first, St. Peter, wishing to persuade his hearers that the miracle they were witnessing was divine, asserts with great firmness of mind that the Spirit promised, now poured out, is the one promised by Joel and then by Christ himself, not once: with Christ, crucified and raised, and exalted to heavenly glory at the right hand of the Father, while they saw and heard it. Promised, I say, by Joel, and by Christ himself more than once. For he says to his disciples on several occasions, "If I go away, I will send him to you from the Father"; and the Baptist in Matthew says, "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire." It is Christ, therefore, who sends the Holy Spirit, and who baptizes and regenerates his Church with the Holy Spirit. From this it is easily inferred that he is God and is distinct as a person from the Father and the Holy Spirit. For who can send the Holy Spirit except God, whose proper Spirit he is, as he also said through the prophet: "I will pour out of my Spirit"? But that the one who sends or pours out is distinct from the Spirit who is sent and poured out is also plain. The Son of God, therefore, sending the Holy Spirit and working through him in the minds, hearts and tongues of the Apostles, is the true and almighty God. This is a splendid argument, which we may oppose not only to the blasphemies of the Arians and Sabellians but also to the delusions of Nestorius. For just as it proves clearly, brighter than midday light, the true Deity of the Word, so with the same Word it firmly confirms the true and hypostatic union of the human mass. For it is none other than the Son of God, and indeed that same Son of God made flesh, who suffered, died, was raised, and was exalted to the glory of God's right hand, who adorns his Church with this divine benefit. We do not say, as some want today, that the Holy Spirit is given by human nature. Far be it from us to say that the Spirit proceeds from a creature, that a creature gives the Spirit to creatures, its own Creator, or that we believe a creature acts through its Creator. For these are more theological subtleties. Moreover, theologians generally agree that only that nature acts through the Holy Spirit from which the Spirit also proceeds. For to act through the Holy Spirit is nothing other than that, in the order of persons, the will of the agent goes before through him and accompanies his will. But the will of the human nature does not go before the will of the Holy Spirit; rather it is shaped and governed by it. Add that Christ is said throughout the Scriptures to be given, anointed and sealed with the Holy Spirit according to that nature (I mean the human one). Therefore he sends the Holy Spirit not according to the human but according to the divine nature, although Christ is one and the same, both anointed and anointing himself and the Church. "It is necessary," says Luther, explaining the passage of Psalm 45 in the first chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, "that the one who anoints be true God. Now indeed the one who is anointed is also true God, since he has a throne and reigns forever. But God cannot anoint himself, and the one who is anointed is inferior to the anointer. For to anoint here means to pour in the Holy Spirit together with his gifts, and this belongs to a creature alone." Thus far Luther. We have been pleased to add these remarks and to touch on them with moderation, so that we may consider that we must philosophize soberly here, lest, fleeing Charybdis, we fall into Scylla; lest, in defending carelessly the deification of the human nature of Christ and against the mind of Scripture, we hurl the eternal Word from the throne of homoousia with the Father, and provide sport for the heretics about ourselves. Nothing has ever seemed more convenient to them for defending their blasphemies than what they now hear from some people defended as orthodox: that a finite creature, which is not God by nature, and is homoousios not with God the Father but with us human beings, is capable, not only by hypostatic union but also by real communication of all the essential divine properties, and of the whole Deity, yet without eternity, spirituality and immensity, that is, without truth. But that well-worn and true saying of Damascene stands: "How could one nature be capable of receiving contrary subsistent differences? Or how is it possible for the same nature to be, in the same respect, created and uncreated, mortal and immortal, circumscribed and uncircumscribed?"

units.la: Vidimus quam validis rationibus adversus hostes Filii Dei ex miraculosa Spiritus Sancti missione pugnare possimus: nunc quae arma nobis eadem adversus πνευματομαχῆς[?] suggerat, breviter quoque disputiamus. Spiritum Sanctum non esse motus tantum creatos in cordibus electorum, sed vivum, intelligens ac voluntarie agens ὑφιστάμενον[?], haud obscure ex historia eiusdem missionis ostendi potest. Primum enim visibili specie instar ignis ac flatus violeti coelo descendisse, & corporeis hominum oculis quasi conspicienspiciendum se praebuisse dicitur, quod certe de motione animi, seu asflatu aliquo divino intelligi nullo modo potest. Visibil' enim specie sub as-spectum humanum cadere non qualitatis alicuius aut motus creati, sed substantiae est. Idem etiam Spiritus Sanctus suggessisse dicitur suo arbitratu res & verba, quae eloquerentur Apostoli. Motus autem animorum & cordium non dicuntur nobis suggerere, sed idipsum sunt quod a causa motrice suggeritur, inque animis nostris generatur. Hinc igitur colligere est, esse illum certe quoddam subsistens, vivum, intelligens, a be-neficiis suis tanquam causa ab effectibus diffe-rens.
units.tr: We have seen with how strong arguments we can fight against the enemies of the Son of God from the miraculous mission of the Holy Spirit. Now let us briefly discuss also what weapons the same mission supplies against the fighters against the Spirit (pneumatomachoi). That the Holy Spirit is not merely created motions in the hearts of the elect, but a living, intelligent and voluntarily acting subsistent being, can be shown clearly from the history of this same mission. For first it is said to have descended from heaven in visible form, like fire and a violent blast of wind, and to have presented itself so as to be seen, as it were, by human bodily eyes. This certainly cannot be understood in any way as a motion of the mind or some divine inspiration. For to fall under human sight in visible form belongs to substance, not to some quality or created motion. The same Holy Spirit is also said to have suggested, at its own discretion, the things and words the Apostles were to speak. But the motions of minds and hearts are not said to suggest things to us; they are themselves what is suggested by a moving cause and generated in our minds. From this one may gather that there is certainly a subsistent, living, intelligent being, differing from its benefits as a cause differs from its effects.

units.la: Porro distinctam personam a Patre & Filio esse, historia testatur, dum non Patrem, non Filium, sed tantum Spiritum Sanctum specie ignis, ac venti ruentis apparuisse dicit. Non tamen distinctus ita est ab utroque ut sit divisus, aut Deitate inferior: sed aequalem potentia, essentiaque ὁμοούσιον[?] utrique Deum esse, eodem miraculo docemur[?]: Quis enim inficiabitur? esse id divinae & infinitae naturae atque potentiae opus, si nul[?] in diversis locis praesentem esse, in coelis aeque atque in terris, in Deo simul atque in hominibus? Cum enim Spiritus in Deo semper maneat, utiq; non discedebat a Patre & Filio in coelo, etiam tunc, cum visibili specie super unumquemque Apostolorum sederet, totus ac individuus idem, essentia & donis eos implens.
units.tr: Further, the history bears witness that he is a person distinct from the Father and the Son, since it says that not the Father, not the Son, but only the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of fire and of a rushing wind. Yet he is not so distinct from each that he is divided or inferior in Deity; rather, by the same miracle we are taught that he is God, equal to both in power and essence, homoousios with both. For who will deny that this is a work of divine and infinite nature and power, that he should be present in diverse places at once, in heaven as well as on earth, in God as well as in human beings? For since the Spirit always remains in God, he certainly did not depart from the Father and the Son in heaven, even when, in visible form, he sat upon each of the Apostles, wholly and undivided the same, filling them with his essence and gifts.

units.la: Sed obieceris mihi forsan, sedere illud, potius igni coelitus delapso, quam Spiritui Sancto tri-buenbuendum[?] esse. Quasi verò insolitum sit, sacris literis signo tribuere, quod rei est signatæ, quam illud sensibus nostris quasi percipiendam offert. Rursus autem ex te quæro, cuinam putes adscribendum illud, quod homines rudes ac illiterati tanta facundia, atque idiomatum varietate de rebus divinis ac cœlestibus repente disseruerint, tantum nō mundo universo ad divinam illorum cloquentiam obstupescente? Profecto miraculum cœlitus à Deo patratum id esse supra satis ostendimus. Quis enim tam profanus est, qui non vel hodie etiam in summis Dei donis numerandam esse existimet notitiam linguarum ac cœlestis sapientiæ, quarum alii aliis pleniorem cognitionem, nullam tamen sine labore ac studio in Ecclesia consequimur. Quantò igitur magis est consentaneum, homines illiteratos variarum linguarum idiomatis, quæ ante non didicerant, sapientissimè de rebus maximis loqui posse, id non fragilitatis humanæ, sed omnipotentis naturæ miraculosum opus existere, quod cum insolidum[?] tribuitur[?] Spiritui Sancto, dubia esse non potest, vera & æterna eius Deitas. Sed & verè [illegible, ~3 letters] Patri ac Filio eundem esse, loëlis verba testantur. De Spi-ritu meo (inquit Iehova) effundam super omnem carnem. Atqui in Deo, cuius simplicissima est essentia, accidens, aut aliud aliquid fingere, quod Deo in totum sit [illegible, ~3 letters], nefas est, ipsis hæreticis testibus. Spiritus igitur Sanctus sic à Deo effunditur, ut & in Deo sit, & de ipsius essentia sit, verus & coæternus cum Patre & Filio Deus. Quid? quod unicum duntaxat verum Deum, Iehovam æternum, immensum, omnipotentem, Scriptura sacra contra Tritheitarum, vel potius Atheorum deliria nobis confirmat. Eadem vero Scriptura teste, Spiritus Sanctus est idem ille Iehova æternus, immensæ potentiæ & sapientiæ Deus: cœ'li ac terræ conditor, & gubernator:apparens super propitiatorium, ac responsa dans populo: Faciens electos sibi templa, in quibus habitet: Irritatus ab Israelitis in deserto: eosdem hortatione excitans, ne audientes vocem eius obdurent corda: mittens prophetas & per illos oracula edens: cui mé-ticebatur Ananias: Denique omnem illam χα-ρισμάτων καὶ διακονιῶν καὶ ἐνεργημάτων varieta-tem, de qua Apostolus ad Corinthios disputat, in omnibus ad utilitatem Ecclesiæ pro libera sua voluntate efficiens. Sed quid multis? citius dies, quàm Scriptura in hoc argumento nos deficiet. An non enim Iehova is erat, qui dicebat Isaiæ: vade, excæca cor populi huius. Hic quid respondebunt Apostolo πνεύματι ἁγίῳ[?] Spiritui Sancto, eadem verba in Actis extremo capite aperte tribuenti? Maneat igitur piis mentibus rata & fixa Christiana illa & orthodoxa fides: cum patre & filio Spiritum Sanctum verum & æternum Deum esse.
units.tr: But perhaps you will object to me that the sitting was to be attributed to the fire that came down from heaven rather than to the Holy Spirit. As if it were unusual for Scripture to attribute to the sign what belongs to the thing signified, which the sign presents to our senses as if to be perceived. Again, I ask you in turn: to whom do you think that should be ascribed, that uneducated and unlettered men suddenly spoke about divine and heavenly things with such eloquence and variety of languages, the whole world almost astonished at their divine eloquence? Clearly we have already sufficiently shown that this is a miracle wrought by God from heaven. For who is so profane as not to think that even today the knowledge of languages and of heavenly wisdom must be counted among the highest gifts of God, which some of us acquire more fully than others, yet in the Church we acquire none without labour and study? How much more fitting, then, is it that uneducated men should be able to speak most wisely about the greatest things in the idioms of various languages they had not learned before, and that this is a miraculous work not of human frailty but of almighty nature. When this is attributed to the Holy Spirit, there can be no doubt that his true and eternal Deity is meant. Moreover, the words of Joel also testify that he is the same with the Father and the Son: "I will pour out my Spirit (says Jehovah) upon all flesh." Now, in God, whose essence is most simple, it is impermissible, even by the testimony of the heretics themselves, to imagine an accident or anything else that is not wholly God. The Holy Spirit is therefore so poured out from God that he both is in God and is of his essence, the true God and co-eternal with the Father and the Son. What more? Holy Scripture confirms for us, against the fancies of the Tritheists, or rather the Atheists, that there is only one true God, Jehovah, eternal, immense and almighty. And by the same Scripture's testimony, the Holy Spirit is that same eternal Jehovah, God of immense power and wisdom, creator and governor of heaven and earth, appearing above the mercy seat and giving answers to the people; making for himself the elect temples in which he dwells; provoked by the Israelites in the desert; stirring up the same people by exhortation not to harden their hearts when they hear his voice; sending prophets and uttering oracles through them; whom Ananias feared to lie to; and finally, effecting in all things, for the benefit of the Church, at his own free will, that whole variety of gifts, ministries and workings about which the Apostle disputes to the Corinthians. But why say more? The day would end sooner than Scripture would fail us on this subject. Was it not Jehovah who said to Isaiah, "Go, blind the heart of this people"? What will they answer to the Apostle, who in the last chapter of Acts openly attributes these same words to the Holy Spirit? Let therefore that Christian and orthodox faith remain firm and fixed in pious minds: that the Holy Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, is the true and eternal God.

units.la: Postremum distributionis nostræ membrum de officio & beneficiis Spiritus Sancti, sequitur. Neque enim tantum quis sit, sed etiam, quod ha-beat officium, & qualia, quantaq; beneficia con-ferat Ecclesiæ, hac patefactione luculenter ostenditur. Etsi vero immensum esse eius donorum cumulum, atque inexhaustum beneficiorum sontem, non modo scriptura sancta passim nos docet: Sed etiam oculi & sensus piorum testantur: Tamen docendi causa universa illa ad certa quaedam & summa quasi capita revocare studebimus.
units.tr: The last part of our division, concerning the office and benefits of the Holy Spirit, follows. For it is shown clearly by this exposition not only who he is, but also what office he has, and of what kind and how great the benefits are that he confers on the Church. Although Scripture everywhere teaches us not only that the store of his gifts is immense and the source of benefits inexhaustible, but also the eyes and feelings of the pious bear witness to it, nevertheless, for the sake of teaching, we shall strive to reduce all that to certain definite and principal heads.

units.la: Primum est, propter quod à Christo veritas ac doctor veritatis nuncupatur. Docet enim Ecclesiam, abstergens caliginem mentis nostræ, ac fulgore cœlestis sapientiæ, eandem ita illustrans, ut ex tanto suo beneficio Dei scholasticos seu θεοδ-διδάκτ[?]ς ipse nos vocare non dubitet. Hujus vero magisterii exemplum cum primis illustre Apostoli ipsi hic nobis exhibent. Quid enim hactenus miseris istis piscatoribus fuerat rudius & ineptius ad intelligendum ea, quæ Christus toties de regno spirituali, de morte, de resurrectione, de ascensu denique suo in cœlos, ad tædium usque illis inculcârat? Jam vero Spiritu Sancto mentes eorum illuminante ac docente ad quævis percipienda & discenda adeo redduntur faciles, ut illa omnia, quæ antea cymmeriis tenebris visa fuerat ipsis obscuriora, videantur nunc meridiei luce clariora. Itaque hactenus de rebus illis divinis non dico loqui, sed nec balbutire poterant, jam adeo promtè, erudite ac sapienter de iis differunt, uti argutissimos pharisæos, pontifices, totamque Hierosolymorum urbem in summam sui admirationem abripiant. Hæc enim erant illa oracula, hæ visiones & somnia, quæ propheta ex illustri illa Spiritus Sancti effusione Ecclesiæ fuerat pollicitus. Renovat idem Spiritus Sanctus, rege-nerat corda credentium, beneficio non minus admirabili, quam ad salutem necessario. Hic enim baptismus ille est ignis & Spiritus, quem Io-hannes & Christus Ecclesiae promiserant: sic nunc cupantes Spiritus Sancti donationem, ut de spirituali renascentia per externum aquae baptismū nos confirmarent. Neque vero alia causa factum putabimus, quod flammae speciem Spiritus San-ctus hic induit, Apostolis insidens, quàm ut hujus nos beneficii similitudine quadam commonefaceret. Ut enim ignis fulgore suo pulsis tenebris aërem illustrat, corpora frigida reficit & recreat, scoriam expurgat, sordes excoquit, vi caloris separans [illegible, ~9 letters], congregans [illegible, ~9 letters]: Sic Spiritus Sanctus discussis mentium nostrarum tenebris eadem caelestis sapientiae radiis illustrat atque illuminat, mortua cord a vivificat, ex lapideis carneā facit, sordida à scoriis peccatorum excoquit, frigida suo calore igneo fovet, & accendit amore Dei & studio pietatis uti verus Deicul-tus in nobis instauretur ac reparetur. Neque ve-rò ita regenitos nobis nos relinquit, sed cū Christo capite nostro nexu spirituali coniungit, ut ipso quasi aeterni vigoris vehiculo intervenien-te, κοινωνία nostra sit cum Deo patre, & cum filio eius Iesu Christo. Est enim ille in nos effusus Spiritus patris & filii, qui in nos de suo Spiritu effusuros esse promiserant. Per hoc ait Iohannes cognoscimus, nos in eo habitare quod de suo Spiritu dedit nobis. Hinc adeo est, quod Apostolus nos templa Dei, & Sancti Spiritus ναὸν vocat, qua dignitate homini maior contingere nulla potest.
units.tr: The first is that for which Christ is called the truth and the teacher of truth. For he teaches the Church, dispelling the darkness of our mind and illuminating it with the brightness of heavenly wisdom, so that, from so great a benefit, he does not hesitate to call us the taught of God (θεοδίδακτοι). The apostles themselves present here the most illustrious example of this teaching. For what had been more rude and unfit for understanding than these wretched fishermen regarding those things which Christ had so often impressed upon them, to the point of weariness, concerning the spiritual kingdom, his death, his resurrection, and finally his ascension into heaven? But now, with the Holy Spirit illuminating and teaching their minds, they are rendered so ready to perceive and learn anything that all those things which before, in Cimmerian darkness, had seemed more obscure to them now appear clearer than the light of noon. Thus, those who until then could not speak of, nor even stammer about, those divine matters now speak of them so readily, learnedly and wisely that they carry away the keenest Pharisees, the high priests, and the whole city of Jerusalem into great admiration. For these were those oracles, these visions and dreams, which the prophet had promised to the Church from that illustrious outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The same Holy Spirit renews and regenerates the hearts of believers, by a benefit no less admirable than it is necessary for salvation. For this is that baptism of fire and of the Spirit which John and Christ had promised to the Church, desiring the gift of the Holy Spirit in such a way as to assure us of spiritual rebirth through the outward baptism of water. Nor indeed should we think that the reason the Holy Spirit took on the appearance of a flame here, resting upon the apostles, was anything other than to remind us, by a certain likeness, of this benefit. For just as fire, by its brightness, drives away darkness and illuminates the air, warms and revives cold bodies, purges dross, and by the force of its heat separates [illegible, about nine letters] and gathers [illegible, about nine letters]: so the Holy Spirit, dispersing the darkness of our minds, illuminates and enlightens them with the same rays of heavenly wisdom, makes dead hearts alive, turns stony hearts into fleshly ones, purges the filth of sins from the dross, warms the cold with his fiery heat, and kindles us with love of God and zeal for piety, so that true worship of God may be restored and renewed in us. Nor does he leave us thus regenerated, but joins us to Christ our head by a spiritual bond, so that, with him acting as a kind of vehicle of eternal vigour, there may be our fellowship (κοινωνία) with God the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. For that Spirit which was poured out upon us is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, who had promised that they would pour out their Spirit upon us. "By this," says John, "we know that we dwell in him, because he has given us of his Spirit." Hence it is that the Apostle calls us the temples of God and the sanctuary (ναός) of the Holy Spirit, a dignity than which none greater can befall a human being.

units.la: Idem porrò Spiritus divino quodam instinctu quasi freno fideles perpetuo sic ducit, gubernat & conservat, ne à verae pietatis tramite in avia de-flectant, instruit salutaribus consiliis in actioni-bus vitae & vocationis rectè peragendis, ut salu-tares etiam successus sortiantur: Flectit animos, ut quae recta sunt, iusta, & Deo placentia, sequan-tur, promptique officia dilectionis in Deum & proximos faciant. Hic enim est ille Spiritus, qui Apostolis dabat eloqui, variis linguis magnalia Dei: perpetuumque se illis ducem & gubernatorem deinceps praebuit, ne vel in docendi munere usquam exorbitarent, vel metu periculorum la-bascerent: Spiritu in hora illa, ut Christus pro-miserat, semper suggerente & defensionis argu-menta, & tolerantiae vires.
units.tr: Moreover, the same Spirit, by a certain divine impulse, as it were a bridle, continually leads, governs and preserves the faithful so that they do not turn aside from the path of true piety into byways; he instructs them with salutary counsels to carry out rightly the actions of life and of their calling, so that they may also obtain salutary outcomes; he bends their minds so that they follow what is right, just and pleasing to God, and makes them ready to perform the duties of love toward God and neighbour. For this is that Spirit who gave the apostles to speak the great works of God in various tongues; and he continually showed himself to them as their leader and governor thereafter, so that they should not go astray in the office of teaching anywhere, nor waver through fear of dangers; the Spirit, as Christ had promised, always suggesting in that hour both arguments for defence and strength for endurance.

units.la: Accedit tandem quasi omnium φυλακτήριον confirmatio & consolatio Sanctorum. Cum enim militia nostra Christiana adeo sit plena maximarum calamitatum, ingentium periculorum ac miseriarum, ut stationem absque illius auxilio tueri minime nobis sit possibile: Ille ne malorum pondere pressi succumbamus, consolatur nos, pavidos confirmat, timidos ac vacillantes ita cor-roborat, ut non solum, quaevis in mundo dis-crimina, pro Christi nomine intrepide adeamus: sed in ipsis etiam tribulationibus immensum gaudeamus, ac triumphemus. Est enim dulcis ille παράκλητος nobis promissus, ut in aeternum nobis-cum maneat, non sane ἄχρεος[?]; sed consolatione perfundens fidelium animos, omnem intellectū superante, longeque diversissima à mundi larvis, quae in lucta tentationum protinus evanescunt, & pro thesauris carbones miseris hominibus re-linquunt. Cum è contrario pii etiam in mediam mortis voraginem demersi, vera & solida semper consolatione fruantur, cum Apostolo exclamantes: ut morientes reputati sumus, sed ecce vivimus: castigamur [?]: sed non occidimur: ut dolentes, sed semper gaudemus: ut pauperes, sed multos ditamus, tan-quam nihil habentes, omnia tamen possidemus. Non hæc auditores credite, est Gnathonica μεγαλαυ-χία, nec stolida Zenonicorum παραδοξολογία [?] aliqua, sed invictum illud Sanctorum robur cœlitus ipsis afflatum, quo cum mundo sint crucifixi, mundum sibi vicissim crucifigunt. Videte enim quæso Apostolos, nova repente παρρησία [?] in medium prodeuntes ad docendum, ad propugnan-dum pro veritate, ad patiendum denique cum summa alacritate ac gaudio pro Christi gloria, quibus prius nihil fuerat meticulosius. Fugerant ad solum hostium conspectum, abnegarant ad unius mulierculæ impetum, metu Iudæorum oc-cultis claustrorum latebris sese abdiderant.
