These so great and so inestimable virtues the Holy Spirit produced in the apostles from the promises of Christ.

units.la: Verum enim vero ut beneficentia Dei nullis limitibus includitur, sed ultra spem nostram & ultra promissa sese plerumque extendit; sic præ-ter hæc eximia dona, aliud quoque admirandum sed nec promissum nec speratum ipsis collatum est, facultas nempe variis loquendi linguis quæ talis erat, ut quovis peregrino sermonis idio-mate æquè expedite ac vernaculo, quando opus erat, verba facerent, & æquè perspicuè docerent. Absurdum enim est quod quidam opinantur, ipsos sua tantum lingua locutos esse: auditorum vero aures ejusmodi sonis percussas fuisse, ac si his propria lingua uterentur: sic quippe non in Apostolis sed in auribus auditorum miraculum factum fuisset: quod cum historia prorsus non congruit. Quorsum enim linguæ igneæ dissectæ in ipsis apparuerunt? Quorsum stupor & admiratio audientium? Qui certè nullam in se mutationem animadverunt, sed aperte fatentur, quod unusquisque eorum audiat sua lingua Apostolos magnifica Dei loquentes. Magnum igitur etiam hoc donum fuit Spiritus effusi. Per id enim Evangelium omnibus linguis personuit, & toti mundo innotuit; per id etiam ad nos Germanos penetravit non multò post, quemadmodum testatur Irenæus, jam suo tempore Ecclesias in Germania fundatas & fidem Apostolicam amplexas fuisse. Quanta autem est illa Dei sapientia, bonitas ac potentia, qui quod olim pœna fuit impiorum & Θεομαχούντων, id tum convertit in bonum piorum & Θεοφίλων. Nam pœna sanè justa fuit stultitiæ & superbiæ mortalium, quando ad turrim Babylonis, cujus summitatem in cœlum usque evehere insano conatu moliebantur, confusa sunt eorum labia, cum prius esset universa terra labii unius. Sed ut diversitas ista linguarum non intellectarum olim pœnæ rationem habuit: ita tunc peritia loquendi variis linguis, quæ ab Apostolis & aliis cum quibus versabantur intelligerentur præclarum beneficium & utile donum fuit Spiritus S. At illud donum, inquis, desiit in Ecclesia, quid ergo ad nos? Imò verò ꝓ[?] Christum agnoscimus, quodque in Ecclesia sumus, Apostolis semel collato debetur dono. Pluri-mum igitur nō solum ejus memoria sed & ipsum nobis prodest. Sed enim non tam ipsum donum hoc desiit, quam miraculum, cujus ut aliorum omnium miraculorum post doctrinam Evangelii satis confirmatam & per totum orbem sparsam in Ecclesia usus amplius non erat. Datur enim multis etiamnum Ecclesiæ membris callere exteras linguas, veluti Hebræam, Græcam, Latinam & alias ad colligendam & docendam Ecclesiam necessarias, licet non miraculosè ut Apostolis infundatur ea facultas, sed institutione & studio acquiratur, quod studium tamen absque Spiritus sancti gratia, irritum esse solet nec salutare. Ideo Apostolus linguarum non minus quam aliorum donorum Spiritum sanctum authorem facit. Alii, inquit, datur prophetia, alii discretio spirituum; alii genera linguarum, alii interpretatio linguarum. Sed hæc omnia efficit unus ille & idem Spiritus distribuens privatim illa singulis sicut vult. Neque hoc scribit suorum tantum respectu temporum, quibus miraculosè multa dona multis dabantur, sed & omnium Ecclesiæ temporum ratione. Loquitur enim ibi de donis quovis tempore ad colligendam, docendam & ædificandam Ecclesiam necessariis. Quare hic primus missionis Spiritus sancti fructus non modo in Apostolis eximius fuit, sed in universæ Ecclesiæ commodum & salutem tanquam uberrimus rivulus exundavit.
units.tr: Indeed, just as the beneficence of God is bounded by no limits, but for the most part extends beyond our hope and beyond the promises, so besides these excellent gifts, another thing also admirable, yet neither promised nor hoped for, was conferred upon them: namely, the faculty of speaking various tongues, of such a kind that, whenever there was need, they spoke in any foreign idiom of speech as readily as in their native one, and taught with equal clarity. For it is absurd to think, as some do, that they spoke only in their own tongue, and that the ears of the hearers were struck by such sounds as if they used their own language; for in that case the miracle would have been wrought not in the apostles but in the ears of the hearers, which does not at all agree with the history. For why did tongues of fire, divided, appear upon them? Why the amazement and admiration of the hearers? These certainly observed no change in themselves, but openly confess that each of them heard the apostles speaking the magnificent works of God in his own tongue. This also, therefore, was a great gift of the outpoured Spirit. For through it the Gospel sounded forth in all tongues and became known to the whole world; through it, too, it penetrated to us Germans not long after, as Irenaeus testifies, that already in his time churches had been founded in Germany and had embraced the apostolic faith. How great, however, is that wisdom, goodness and power of God, who turned into the good of the godly and God-loving what once was the punishment of the impious and God-fighting. For the punishment was indeed just for the folly and pride of mortals, when at the tower of Babylon, whose summit they laboured with mad effort to raise up to heaven, their lips were confused, although before the whole earth had one lip. But just as that diversity of tongues, not understood, once had the purpose of punishment, so then the skill of speaking in various tongues, which might be understood by the apostles and by the others with whom they dealt, was an excellent benefit and useful gift of the Holy Spirit. "But that gift," you say, "has ceased in the Church; what then is it to us?" Indeed, we acknowledge Christ, and that we are in the Church, is owed to the gift once conferred on the apostles. Therefore not only its memory but also the gift itself profits us very much. For, indeed, it is not so much this gift that has ceased as the miracle, whose use in the Church no longer existed, as with all other miracles, after the doctrine of the Gospel had been sufficiently confirmed and spread throughout the whole world. For even now many members of the Church are given to know foreign tongues, such as Hebrew, Greek, Latin and others necessary for gathering and teaching the Church; although that faculty is not infused miraculously as it was into the apostles, but is acquired by instruction and study, which study, however, without the grace of the Holy Spirit, is wont to be vain and not salutary. Therefore the Apostle makes the Holy Spirit the author of tongues no less than of the other gifts. "To one," he says, "is given prophecy, to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of tongues. But all these one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each one individually as he wills." Nor does he write this with respect only to the times of his own, when many gifts were miraculously given to many, but also with respect to all the times of the Church. For he speaks there of gifts necessary at any time for gathering, teaching and building up the Church. Wherefore this first fruit of the mission of the Holy Spirit was not only distinguished in the apostles, but overflowed for the advantage and salvation of the whole Church like a most abundant stream.

units.la: Alter fructus est fidei nostræ contra hæreticos & infidelis illustris demonstratio, quod Spiritus sanctus cum Patre & Filio sit unus & æternus Deus. Non recitabo hic variorum hæreticorum prodigiosas blasphemias. Simoniani dixerunt SpiriSpiritum sanctum esse tantum nomen energiæ & virtutis: non autem essentiæ: Hierachitæ esse Melchisedecum: Helcesaitæ esse sororem Chri-sti: Arriani, Macedoniani & alii esse creaturam, non Deum: & partes atque essentiam ejus per omnes creaturas esse diffusas. Tritheitæ hodie blasphemant esse Deum Patre & Filio inferiorem. Contra has blasphemias fides nostra miraculosâ istâ patefactione Spiritus sancti evidentissimè confirmatur. Primo quod sit vera vivensque hypostasis. Deinde quod non sit creatura, sed Deus: Denique quod sit Patri & Filio consub-stantialis Deus. Quomodo enim Spiritus sanctus si tantum est motus sanctus, vel operatio Dei sancta, corpoream speciem ignis sustinuit? quomodo magnifica Dei variis linguis eloqui Apostolis dedit? quomodo effector est χαρισμά-των omnium in Ecclesia, distribuens ea singulis prout vult? Nec refert quod ipse etiam χάρισμα[?] seu donum appellatur. Donatur enim à Patre per Filium, sed tanquam donorum aliorum effector; neque ideo ipse filius hypostasis vera non est, eo quod à Patre donatur & donum Dei à se-[?]ipso appellatur. Sed jam ostendamus non esse eum spiritum creatum sed Deum. Opera sunt Dei propria quæ ipse in Apostolis efficit. Infundit mentibus Apostolorum cum luce doctrinæ & sapientiæ cœlestis etiam variarum linguarum notitiam: movet & regit linguas & corda prout vult: quæ certè non sunt nisi solius Dei opera. Sed & sedet totus ac indivisus super unumquemque eorum. Est ergo immensæ essentiæ & Deus.
units.tr: The second fruit is the clear demonstration, against heretics and unbelievers, that the Holy Spirit is, together with the Father and the Son, one and the same eternal God. I will not recount here the monstrous blasphemies of the various heretics. The Simonians said that the Holy Spirit is merely a name of energy and power, not of essence; the Hierakites said that he is Melchizedek; the Helkesaites said that he is the sister of Christ; the Arians, the Macedonians and others said that he is a creature, not God; and they said that his parts and essence are diffused through all creatures. The Tritheites today blaspheme that he is God inferior to the Father and the Son. Against these blasphemies our faith is most evidently confirmed by this wonderful manifestation of the Holy Spirit: first, that he is a true and living hypostasis; then, that he is not a creature but God; and finally, that he is God, consubstantial with the Father and the Son. For how could the Holy Spirit, if he were merely a holy motion or a holy operation of God, have taken on the bodily appearance of fire? How could he have given the Apostles to speak the magnificent works of God in various tongues? How is he the author of all the charismata in the Church, distributing them to each one as he wills? Nor does it matter that he himself is also called a charisma, or gift. For he is given by the Father through the Son, but as the author of the other gifts; and for that reason the Son is not a true hypostasis, because he is given by the Father, and because the gift of God is called by his own name. But let us now show that he is not a created spirit but God. The works that he performs in the Apostles are God's own works. He pours into the minds of the Apostles, together with the light of doctrine and heavenly wisdom, also the knowledge of various tongues; he moves and governs tongues and hearts as he wills; these are certainly the works of God alone. Moreover, he sits whole and undivided upon each one of them. He is therefore of immense essence and God.

units.la: Nam cum Didymo sic firmiter colligimus: Si Spiritus sanctus unus de creaturis esset saltem circumscriptam haberet substantiam, sicut universa quæ facta sunt. Etsi enim non circumscribantur loco & finibus invisibiles creaturæ: tamen prorietate substantiæ finiuntur. Spiritus sanctus vero non habet circumscriptam substantiam cum simul sit in cœlo & in terra & in pluribus sanctis: siquidem effusus super omnem carnem manet nihilominus in Deo, non discedens à patre & filio & sedet super unumquemque Apostolorum indivisus licet symbolum divisum appareat, quo testificatur se esse iis præsentem & dona illa efficere, non tunc modo cum Hierosolymis essent congregati sed & deinceps cum alii in alias essent nationes dispersi & longissimis spaciis in Asia, in Scythia, in India disjuncti. Præterea solius Dei est replere omnia substantia sua: Spiritus sanctus per naturam sanctificantem & implentem bonis universa bonus ipse subsistit. Nam de Apostolis dicitur: Repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto. Et hortatio D. Pauli est ad omnes fideles: Implemini Spiritu sancto. De Stephano πρωτομάρτυρι dicitur, cum esset plenus Spiritu sancto. De Paulo: Saulus, a. qui & Paulus, repletus Spiritu sancto. At nemo plenus dicitur creatura, angelo, throno, dominatu, inquit idem Didymus, nec angeli præsentia, sive alicujus alterius excellentis naturæ implet mente atq; sensum, quia & ipsa aliunde completur. Quemadmodum enim ex plenitudine qs [?] accipiens Salvatoris, plenus efficitur sapientia & virtute & justitia & sermone Dei: sic etiam qui Spiritu S. plenus est statim universis donationi-bus Dei repletur, sapientia, scientia, fide caeterisque virtutibus. Qui igitur implet universas creaturas, quae tamen possunt virtutem & sapientiam capere non est ex his quae ipse complet. Ex quo concludit Spiritum sanctum omnia replentem alterius esse substantiae quam sint omnes creaturae:
units.tr: For with Didymus we thus firmly conclude: if the Holy Spirit were one of the creatures, he would at least have a circumscribed substance, as all things that have been made do. For although invisible creatures are not circumscribed by place and boundaries, they are nevertheless limited by the property of their substance. But the Holy Spirit does not have a circumscribed substance, since he is at once in heaven and on earth and in many saints; indeed, though poured out upon all flesh, he nonetheless remains in God, not departing from the Father and the Son, and he sits undivided upon each of the Apostles, although he appears as a divided symbol, by which he testifies that he is present to them and produces those gifts, not only then when they were gathered together at Jerusalem but also afterwards, when they were scattered among different nations and separated by the greatest distances, in Asia, in Scythia, and in India. Furthermore, it belongs to God alone to fill all things with his substance; the Holy Spirit, being good, subsists himself by sanctifying and filling all things with good things through his nature. For it is said of the Apostles: "They were all filled with the Holy Spirit." And the exhortation of St. Paul is to all the faithful: "Be filled with the Holy Spirit." Of Stephen, the first martyr [πρωτομάρτυρι], it is said, "being full of the Holy Spirit." Of Paul: "Saul, who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit." But no creature, angel, throne, or dominion is called full, says the same Didymus; nor does the presence of an angel, or of any other excellent nature, fill the mind and senses, because that presence is itself filled from elsewhere. For just as those who receive from the fullness of the Saviour are made full of wisdom and virtue and righteousness and the word of God, so also he who is full of the Holy Spirit is at once filled with all the gifts of God: wisdom, knowledge, faith, and the other virtues. He therefore who fills all creatures, which nonetheless are able to take in virtue and wisdom, is not one of those things which he fills. From this he concludes that the Holy Spirit, who fills all things, is of a different substance from all creatures.

units.la: Porro ipsum quoque effusionis nomen increatā Spiritus sancti substantiam probat. Neque enim Deus cum mittit angelum aut aliam creaturam dicit: Effundam de angelo meo, aut principatu, aut throno. In solis quippe his quae ab aliis participantur, hic sermo consentit. De spiritu autem sancto dicitur: Effundam de spiritu meo. Nomine vero effusionis largam attributionem Spiritus & divitem muneris abundantiam significat, teste Apostolo, qui dicit Spiritum sanctum effusum esse super nos abundanter. Neque enim cum unus aut duo Spiritum sanctum accipiunt, effusus dicitur Spiritus sanctus, sed tunc quando in universas gentes munus Spiritus sancti redundaverit. Unde consequitur capabilem esse Spiritus S. substantiam: & ex hoc increatam. Capabilem autem vocat substantiam Didymus, interprete Hieronymo, quae capitur a pluribus & eis sui consortiū tribuit: Capacem vero eam quae communicatione substantiae alterius completur & capiens aliud ipsa non capitur ab alio. Denique si creatura est Spiritus S. vel corporea erit vel incorporalis. Non est corpus, quia a sensu & mente capitur, & sermonis, scientiae & sapientiae est effector. Nec incorporalis: Quia nec anima nec angelus est. Non anima, Quia non suscipit sanctificatio-nem, & virtutes alias ut anima sed efficit. Nec an-gelus, tum quia non est spiritus administratorius ut sunt omnes angeli tum quia angeli non sunt ex propria substantia sancti, sed ex participatione Spiritus Sancti & inhabitatione filii Dei, qui est sanctitas & communicatio patris. At Spiritus S. naturae proprietate est sanctus, angelos & homi-nes sanctificans. His itaque argumentis alterius substantiae ab omnibus creaturis & in propria sub-sistit essentia, increatus & ineffectus, proindeque Deus esse demonstratur.
units.tr: Moreover, the very name of effusion proves the uncreated substance of the Holy Spirit. For when God sends an angel or another creature, he does not say, "I will pour out of my angel, or of my principality, or of my throne." Indeed, this expression fits only those things which are shared by others. But of the Holy Spirit it is said, "I will pour out of my Spirit." By the name of effusion is signified a generous imparting of the Spirit and an abundant richness of his gift, as the Apostle witnesses, who says that the Holy Spirit has been poured out upon us abundantly. For when one or two receive the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit is not said to be poured out, but only when the gift of the Holy Spirit has overflowed upon all nations. Hence it follows that the substance of the Holy Spirit is capable, and from this uncreated. Didymus, as Jerome translates him, calls a substance "capable" which is received by many and imparts itself to those who share it; but he calls it "capacious" which is filled by the communication of another substance, and, receiving another, is not itself received by another. Finally, if the Holy Spirit is a creature, he will be either corporeal or incorporeal. He is not a body, because he is grasped by the senses and the mind, and is the author of speech, knowledge and wisdom. Nor is he incorporeal, because he is neither a soul nor an angel. Not a soul, because he does not receive sanctification and other virtues as a soul does, but produces them. Nor an angel, both because he is not a ministering spirit as all angels are, and because angels are not holy from their own substance, but by participation in the Holy Spirit and the indwelling of the Son of God, who is the holiness and communication of the Father. But the Holy Spirit is holy by the property of his nature, sanctifying angels and men. By these arguments, therefore, it is shown that he subsists in his own essence, of a substance different from all creatures, uncreated and unmade, and therefore is demonstrated to be God.

units.la: Neque vero Deus est a Patre & Filio diversus aut Deus inferior, sed Deus unus cum Patre & Filio eiusdem essentiae potentiae & gloriae. Est.n. Patris & Filii Spiritus, sicut dicit Iehova apud Ioelem: Effundam Spiritum meum, quod Petrus de Christo interpretatur: neque rarum aut obscurum est in scripturis Spiritum Sanctum tam Filii quam Patris Spiritum appellari. Atqui Spiritus Dei [illegible, ~5 letters] Deo esse non potest, & necessario est Deo coaeternus, cum Deus sine Spiritu suo nunquam fuerit. Quod si Patris & Filii est Spiritus ab utroque igitur procedit, h. e. ab utroque communicatam sibi essentiam habet, nec diversum ex scripturis ostendi potest. Sicut enim dicitur quod a patre procedat, sic etiam dicitur quod a filio mittatur: Ego mittam eum vobis a Patre inquit Christus: A nullo autem mittitur nisi a quo procedit. Quare non levis fuit error Graecorum quorundam, praesertim recentium qui Spiritum à Filio procedere negarunt. Sic enim non esset filij Spiritus: nec mitti à filio posset: nec esset utrique ὁμοούσιον[?] quod voluit hæresis Samosatenianorum & Macedonianorum. Neque verò in hoc errore versati sunt veteres græci Doctores, Athanasius, Cyrillus, Didymus, Epiphanius & alii, qui Spiritum Sanctum à patre & filio procedere orthodoxè passim scripserunt, id quod authoritatibus haud paucis demonstrari posset, nisi prolixitas obstaret. Quomodo autem Spiritus Sanctus esset Deus inferior, aut diversus à Patre & Filio cum sit Iehova, qui non nisi unus est. Iehovam verò esse omnia ea scripturæ loca testantur quibus Apostoli ea quæ à prophetis de Iehova dicuntur, ad Spiritum Sanctum accommodant. Ex multis unum dūtaxat adducam. Non-na Apostolus Actor. 28. Spiritui tribuit hæc verba: Vade, excæca cor populi huius. At Iehovam ea dixisse Iesaias expresse testatur. Plura non addam de hoc altero fructu cum ex his fides nostra satis confirmetur.
units.tr: Nor is he a God different from the Father and the Son, or a lesser God, but one God with the Father and the Son, of the same essence, power and glory. For he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, as Jehovah says through Joel: "I will pour out my Spirit," which Peter interprets of Christ; nor is it rare or obscure in the Scriptures that the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father. And yet the Spirit of God [illegible, about 5 letters] cannot be other than God, and he is necessarily co-eternal with God, since God was never without his Spirit. But if he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, then he proceeds from both, that is, he has his essence communicated to him by both; nor can it be shown from the Scriptures that it is otherwise. For just as it is said that he proceeds from the Father, so also it is said that he is sent from the Son: "I will send him to you from the Father," says Christ. But no one is sent except by him from whom he proceeds. Therefore the error of certain Greeks, especially recent ones, who denied that the Spirit proceeds from the Son, was no slight one. For then he would not be the Spirit of the Son, nor could he be sent by the Son, nor would he be homoousios with both, which the heresy of the Samosatenes and the Macedonians wanted. Indeed the ancient Greek teachers did not fall into this error: Athanasius, Cyril, Didymus, Epiphanius and others, who wrote everywhere, in orthodox fashion, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, which could be demonstrated by no small number of authorities, were it not for the length of the discussion. But how could the Holy Spirit be a lesser God, or different from the Father and the Son, since he is Jehovah, who is not other than one? That Jehovah he is, all those passages of Scripture testify in which the Apostles apply to the Holy Spirit what the prophets say of Jehovah. I will adduce just one of many. Does not the Apostle in Acts 28 attribute to the Spirit these words: "Go, make the heart of this people blind"? Yet Isaiah expressly testifies that Jehovah spoke them. I will add no more about this second fruit, since our faith is sufficiently confirmed by these things.

units.la: Huic accedit tertius, quod Spiritus Sanctus super omnem carnem adeoque super nos etiam & liberos nostros effusus est, juxta Ioelis prophetiam. Quod enim prophetamus, nos, & filii no-stri, & filiæ nostræ, quod juvenes nostri visiones vident, & seniores nostri somnia somniant, hoc est, quod uberiore & clariore mysteriorum divinorum cognitione omnes à minimo ad maximū imbuti sumus (Hoc enim sub tropis veteri Testamento convenientibus significatum fuit) unde quæso habemus nisi ex illo thesauro, quem Filius Dei semel in Ecclesiam profudit? Neque hoc totum est beneficium quod inde obtinemus: Si-mul renascimur eius gratia ad novam vitam: glu-tine Spiritus coalescimus cum Christo capite no-stro in unum corpus, eodemque attestante spiri-tui nostro de adoptione nostra in filios certi su-mus, adeo ut nihil sit quod nobis solatium æter-næ vitæ eripere possit. Ipse enim Spiritus Sanctus arrhabonem se nobis præstat supernæ hæreditatis, nobiscum iuxta Christi promissionem in æ-ternum manens.
units.tr: Added to this is a third benefit: the Holy Spirit has been poured out upon all flesh, and so upon us too, and upon our children, according to the prophecy of Joel. For what the prophecy says, that "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams," is fulfilled in us: all of us, from the least to the greatest, have been imbued with a richer and clearer knowledge of the divine mysteries. (This was signified under tropes suited to the Old Testament.) From where, I ask, do we have this, if not from that treasure which the Son of God poured out once for all into the Church? Nor is this the whole benefit we obtain from it. At the same time we are reborn by his grace to a new life; by the bond of the Spirit we are joined with Christ our head into one body; and by the same Spirit bearing witness to our spirit, we are certain of our adoption as sons, so that nothing can snatch from us the comfort of eternal life. For the Holy Spirit himself gives us a pledge of the heavenly inheritance, abiding with us for ever, according to Christ's promise.

units.la: Postremò neque hic fructus miraculi tacendus venit, quod inde certa fiducia & consolatione hac fruimur: Christum vere in cœlum ascendisse: ad Patrem abiisse: Patrem rogare: locum nobis parare: ad dextram maiestatis Dei sedere; Ecclesiam in genere humano sibi voce Evangelii colligere, defendere & servaturum esse, donec ad judicium redeat eam perfecte glorificaturus. E cœlo enim se missurum esse Spiritum Sanctum promisit, qui cum iam ante multa sæcula non tantum missus, sed effusus sit copiose in Ecclesiam, certum hoc est τρόπαιον[?] veri ascensus & gloriæ Christi. In quam sententiam præclarè Ambrosius: Credendum est, inquit, Christum in Dei dextra considere, quia cernimus Spiritum Sanctum, sicut promisit Dominus, in discipulis exultare. Et Chrysostomus. Impletio oraculi Ioelis est fidelis confirmatio Christi in cœlos assumti, ut absque hæsitatione credamus illum sedere à dextris oblata nostra natura patri & in an-tidotum tidotum ac remunerationem Spiritu Sancto nobis de-missó. Vnde patet & hunc fructum miraculiam-pliffimum esse. Nisi enim certi simus Christum in coelesti gloria regnare, nescimus ubi sit noster thesaurus in quo omnis spes & fiducia nostra posita esse debet, nescimus quo vota nostra sint di-rigenda, unde exspectanda sit nobis liberatio, ac ubi deniq; nostra futura post hanc vitam sit mansio. Ex quo etiam illi omnem consolationem piorum convellunt, penitusque eradicant, qui assce-sionem Christi in coelos in allegoriam nescio quam transformant & disparitionem interpretantur.
units.tr: Finally, the fruit of this miracle must not be passed over in silence: from it we enjoy a firm confidence and consolation, that Christ truly ascended into heaven, went away to the Father, asks the Father, prepares a place for us, and sits at the right hand of the majesty of God; that he gathers the Church from the human race to himself by the voice of the Gospel, and that he will defend and preserve it until he returns to judgment, there to glorify it perfectly. For he promised that he would send the Holy Spirit from heaven, and since the Spirit was sent, and indeed poured out abundantly into the Church many centuries ago, this is a sure trophy of the true ascension and glory of Christ. To this effect Ambrose nobly says: "We must believe that Christ sits at the right hand of God, because we see the Holy Spirit, as the Lord promised, exulting in the disciples." And Chrysostom: "The fulfilment of Joel's oracle is the faithful confirmation that Christ was taken up into the heavens, so that without hesitation we may believe that he sits at the right hand of the Father, having offered our nature, and that he has sent down the Holy Spirit to us as an antidote and reward." Hence it is clear that this fruit too is most important of miracles. For unless we are certain that Christ reigns in heavenly glory, we do not know where our treasure is, in which all our hope and trust ought to be placed; we do not know where our prayers are to be directed, from where we are to expect deliverance, or where, finally, our dwelling is to be after this life. Those also overthrow and utterly root out all the comfort of the godly, who turn Christ's ascension into the heavens into I know not what allegory and explain away his departure.

units.la: Atq; haec sunt, auditores, quae de causis & fructibus effusi in Pentecoste Spiritus Sancti, hoc tempore breviter repetenda duxi. Nostrum est sedulo meditari & perpetua gratiarum actione amplecti tanta divinae misericordiae beneficia: quo non tantum firmam & sinceram de persona & officio Spiritus Sancti contra hostes veritatis retineamus fidem, sed & congruentem ei insti-tuamus vitam, omnium virtutum studio nos totos consecrando, ardentibusque votis auxilium Spiritus Sancti implorando, ut dona eius nobis collata conserventur & augeantur: ne forte ingrati ea effundamus & contristemus eum quo su-mus obsignati in diem redemtionis.
units.tr: And these are the things, hearers, that I have thought it right to briefly recall at this time concerning the causes and fruits of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. It is our duty to meditate on them diligently and to embrace with constant thanksgiving such great benefits of divine mercy: so that we may keep a firm and sincere faith concerning the person and office of the Holy Spirit against the enemies of the truth, and also order our life in harmony with it, devoting ourselves wholly to the pursuit of every virtue, and with burning prayers imploring the help of the Holy Spirit, so that the gifts bestowed on us may be preserved and increased; lest perhaps, being ungrateful, we squander them and grieve him by whom we have been sealed for the day of redemption.

units.la: Tibi itaque clementissime Deus, Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, gratias, quas possumus, maximas agimus, pro immenso tuo erga Ecclesiam favore, quod non solum per Filium tuum a peccatis & æterna damnatione eam redemisti, sed & Spiritum Sanctum tuum super eam effudisti, cuius virtute colligitur, docetur, regitur & in semita tendente ad cœlestem beatitudinem ducitur. Fac ut & nobis singulis hæc gratia tua sit salutaris. Conserva pios magistratus nutritios tuæ Ecclesiæ: defende scholas pietatis & honestatis seminaria: Reprime conatus hostium, ne turbent fidelium tuorum in his regionibus halcyoniam, ut tibi soli, uni & trino Deo Patri, Filio & Spiritui Sancto omnis laus & gloria in solidum tribuantur, & salus electorum tuorum magis magisque promoveatur,
units.tr: To you therefore, most merciful God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, we give the greatest thanks we can, for your immense favour toward the Church: that you have redeemed it through your Son from sin and eternal damnation, and have also poured out your Holy Spirit upon it, by whose power it is gathered, taught, governed and led along the path that leads to heavenly blessedness. Grant that this your grace may be saving for each of us. Preserve the pious magistrates, the nurses of your Church; defend the schools of piety and the seminaries of honesty; restrain the attempts of enemies, lest they disturb the calm of your faithful in these regions; so that all praise and glory may be given wholly to you alone, the one and triune God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and the salvation of your elect may be promoted more and more.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: ORATIO XI. DE PENTECOSTE VETERI ET NOVA: ET DE beneficiis Ecclesiæ in ea præstitis.
units.tr: ORATIO XI. CONCERNING THE OLD AND NEW PENTECOST, AND CONCERNING THE BENEFITS BESTOWED ON THE CHURCH IN IT.

units.la: Recitata pridie Pentecostes anno 1595. A IOHANNE ROTTENGATTERO Mosbacensi.
units.tr: Delivered on the day before Pentecost, in the year 1595. BY JOHANN ROTTENGATTER of Mosbach.

units.la: SI quis vestrum est, Auditores, qui miretur, quod cum plerique Oratores in more positum habeant, ut prius, quàm rei caput attingant, seu ingenio suo, seu causæ, quam adgrediuntur, seu auditorum judiciis, quæ extimescunt, diffisi, multa solicitè præfentur, quibus vel sese purgèt, vel benevolentiam auditorum sibi concilient: Ego contra nihil jam horum operosius faciam; sed omnibus prætermissis, ad rem ipsam potius acce-dam: Is si instituti mei causam rationemque co-gnoverit, simul id quod facio, sat scio, probabit, & si facerem secius, peccaturum me esse fortasse existimabit. Id enim minimè facio eò, quòd ingenio meo tantum confidam, aut quod dicendi vi aliqua, usúve polleam. Ab utroque enim nimis me imparatum fateor. Sed eorum potius me voluntati præbeo, qui ut dicerem hoc tempore, ex hoc loco, voluerunt, & quorum jussui refragari mihi religio fuit. Ad hoc tyronum hæc esse exer-citia, (in quibus τὸ ἀ[illegible, ~5 letters] requiri nec solet nec potest)vos, quæ sapientia vestra singularis est & æquitas, non ignorare, persuasum habeo. Imò quanti hæc scholastica faciatis exercitia, quantum ametis, hac frequentia vestra satis testari vos video, & antehac alios, ex hoc loco dicentes, quâ benignè, quàm patienter, quàm attente audieritis recordor. Argumentum denique, quod tra-ctandum suscepi, vobis haud ingratum futurum confido. Est enim tempori huic accommodum, quo tota, ut nostis, Ecclesia, grata memoria cele-brat Pentecostes solennitatem, quâ Deus olim quidem in monte Sinai legem suam cœlitus promulgavit: Christus verò tandem Hierosolymis Spiritum Sanctum visibiliter super Apostolos suos effudit. Unde postea omnis generis χαρίσ-μάτα[?], tanquam uberrima viventis aquæ flumina in totam Ecclesiam dimanarunt. Horum inquâ beneficiorum anniversaria repetitio Ecclesiæ jucunda: nobis cumprimis gratissima esse debet: non solum, ut pro iis gratum nostrum publice declaremus animum, & nostram cum universâ Ecclesiâ lætitiam contestemur: sed quòd id etiam maximè nostrum decet ordinem, qui enarrandis Dei beneficiis & celebrandis, tum voce, tum exemplo in Ecclesiâ & scholis aliis aliquando prae-ituri sumus.
units.tr: If there is any one of you, Listeners, who wonders why most orators make it their custom, before they come to the heart of the matter, to spend much effort on preliminaries, distrustful either of their own talent, or of the cause they take up, or of the judgment of the audience, which they dread: in order either to clear themselves or to win the goodwill of their hearers, I on the contrary will do nothing more laboured than these things; but, setting all such aside, I will come rather to the matter itself. If he has learned the reason and purpose of my undertaking, I am sure he will also approve what I am doing now, and if I were doing otherwise, he will perhaps judge that I would be at fault. For I do not do this at all because I trust in my own talent, or because I am strong in any power or practice of speaking. For I confess that I am far too unprepared for either. But I yield rather to the wishes of those who wanted me to speak at this time, from this place, and whose command it would have been a scruple for me to refuse. Moreover, I am persuaded that you, whose remarkable wisdom and fairness they are, know that these are the exercises of beginners (in which τὸ ἀ[illegible] neither is nor can be required). Indeed, I see from your so great attendance how much you value these scholarly exercises and how much you love them, and I remember how kindly, how patiently, and how attentively you have listened to others speaking from this place before. Finally, I trust that the subject I have undertaken to treat will not be unwelcome to you. For it is fitting for this season, in which the whole Church, as you know, gratefully celebrates the solemnity of Pentecost, on which God once proclaimed his law from heaven on Mount Sinai, and Christ at last in Jerusalem poured out the Holy Spirit visibly upon his Apostles. From that time onward every kind of χαρίσματα [gifts] flowed out over the whole Church like the most abundant rivers of living water. The yearly recollection of these benefits is pleasant to the Church, and should be most welcome to us above all: not only so that we may publicly declare our thankfulness for them and bear witness to our joy together with the whole Church, but also because this especially befits our order, which will one day take the lead in recounting and celebrating God's benefits, both by voice and by example, in the Church and in the other schools.

units.la: Etsi autem cogitanti mihi de quibusnam po-tissimum nunc verba facerem quàm latissimus se se de Spiritus Sancti persona & divinitate, deque eius cū æterno patre & filio ὁμοουσίας[?], officio item & beneficiis dicēdi campus offerebat; tamen in praesentia oratione haec nō prosequar. Nā & saepius de iis ab aliis dictū esse, memini, & ea mentibus[?] vestris atq; cordibus pridē cognita, probeq; inscri-pta & cōfirmata nō dubito. Cæterum duo haec de-legi, in quibus nostra nūc versaretur oratio: Vnū, de veteri & de nova Pentecoste:alterum, de benefi-ciis in utraque à Deo collatis.
units.tr: Although, as I thought about which of these I should most of all speak about now, a very broad field presented itself, namely the person and divinity of the Holy Spirit, and his consubstantiality [ὁμοουσία] with the eternal Father and the Son, and likewise his office and benefits; nevertheless, in the present oration I will not pursue these. For I remember that these things have been spoken of many times by others, and I do not doubt that they are already well known to your minds and hearts, and firmly impressed and confirmed there. Instead, I have chosen these two topics, on which our present discourse will turn: first, the old and the new Pentecost; second, the benefits conferred by God in each of them.

units.la: Principio igitur, Auditores, de pentecoste u-traque & veteri Iudaeorum, & nova Christianorum dicēdū aliquid, nō absq; causâ, mihi video. Scribit.n. Lucas, completo Pentecostes die effusum super Apostolos Spiritum S. ubi de Iudaeorū Pentecoste eū loqui constat: Haec vero cum Christi adventu cum festis reliquis Iudaicis sit abroga-ta; & nihilominus à nobis Christianis nostra quoq; annis adhuc celebretur Pentecoste: Cogitatio haec animum hauddubiè vobis subit: Numquid ergo Iudaizamus? an non illam Apostoli incurri-mus reprehensionem: Dies observatis & menses & tempora & annos? Omninò igitur qualis tum vetus olim fuerit, tum nova nostra sit Pentecoste explicandum videtur.
units.tr: To begin, then, Listeners, I see that I must say something, and not without reason, about both Pentecosts: the old one of the Jews and the new one of the Christians. For Luke writes that when the day of Pentecost was fully come, the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the Apostles, where it is clear that he is speaking of the Jewish Pentecost. But since, with the coming of Christ, this feast, like the other Jewish festivals, has been abrogated, and yet we Christians still celebrate our own Pentecost in our years, this thought doubtless comes to your minds: Do we then Judaize? Or do we not fall under that rebuke of the Apostles: You observe days and months and times and years? Therefore it seems necessary to explain altogether what sort of Pentecost the old one was, and what sort our new one is.

units.la: Pentecoste vetus erat ex tribus anniversariis festis maximè solennibus, quibus omnes Iudaei, ubiçunq; degerent locorū, ex Dei praecepto Ierosolymis solymis convenire tenebātur, ad recolēdam præ-çipuorū Dei beneficiorū memoriā, & ad testan-dam certis oblationib° erga Deū ꝑ illis gratitudi-nem. Passim.n.occurrit in lege, hæc Dei sanctio: Tribus vicibus in anno comparebit omne masculum tuum in conspectu Domini Dei tui in loco quē elegerit: in solennitate azymorum, & in solennitate hebdomadarum, seu Pentecostes: & in solennitate tabernaculorum, non comparebis coram Domino vacuus. Omissis vero iam aliis festis, de Pentecoste, quando, quo modo, & quare ex Dei instituto celebrata fuerit, præcipuè considerandum venit.
units.tr: The old Pentecost was one of three most solemn annual feasts, to which all Jews, wherever in the places they lived, were bound by God's command to come together at Jerusalem, to recall the memory of the chief benefits of God, and to bear witness by certain offerings to their gratitude towards God. For everywhere in the law this decree of God occurs: Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God in the place which he shall choose: at the feast of unleavened bread, and at the feast of weeks, or Pentecost, and at the feast of tabernacles; they shall not appear before the Lord empty. But, setting aside the other feasts now, what needs to be considered chiefly is when, how, and why Pentecost was celebrated by God's appointment.

units.la: Tēpus festivitatis huius passim definitū legitur. Exod. 34. Solennitate hebdomadarū facies tibi in primitiis frugū messis tuæ triticeæ. Et Deut. 16. Septē hebdomadas numerabis tibi, ab eâ die, quâ falcem in-segetē miseris, & celebrabis diē festū hebdomadarum Domino Deo tuo. Expressius vero Levit. 23. Numerabitis ab altero die Sabbathi, quo obtulistis manipulū primitiarum, septem hebdomadas plenas: usque ad alterū die expleta hebdomada septima, h. e, sq dies.
units.tr: The time of this festival is everywhere read as fixed. Exod. 34. You shall keep the feast of weeks, of the first fruits of the wheat harvest. And Deut. 16: You shall count seven weeks for yourself, from the day on which you put the sickle to the standing grain, and you shall keep the feast of weeks to the Lord your God. More expressly, however, Lev. 23: You shall count from the day after the Sabbath, on which you offered the sheaf of the first fruits, seven full weeks: until the morrow of the seventh week is complete, that is, fifty days.

units.la: Hinc liquet post messis triticeæ initium, seu post oblatas frugum primitias, seu post pascha, ab altero sive postero die Sabbathi Paschalis, septimanis septem integris sive quinquaginta diebus numeratis, veterem Pentecosten celebratam fuisse. Quo etiam nomine ab Hebræis חג שבעות festum septimanarum, à Græcis πεντηκοστή[?] quinquagesima est dicta.
units.tr: From this it is clear that, after the beginning of the wheat harvest, that is, after the first fruits of the crops were offered, after the Passover, from the second or following day of the Passover Sabbath, seven full weeks, that is, fifty days, being counted, the old Pentecost was celebrated. By this name also the Hebrews call it חג שבעות [the feast of weeks], and the Greeks call it πεντηκοστή [the fiftieth], that is, the fiftieth day.

units.la: Verum enim vero, quis dies ille alter, sive posterus Sabbathi fuerit, à quo septem septimanæ erant numerandæ, non est eadem omnium sententia. Sunt enim qui eum de feriâ primâ post Sabbathum à paschate proximum, hoc est, de die quæ nobis Dominica est, capiunt: sunt alii, qui per pascha totum paschatis festum seu septem illos dies paschales intelligunt, & posterum diem Sabbathi, feriam octavam post pascha, seu post agnum manducatum fuisse existimant. Verum optima & verbis Mosis convenientissima eorum sententia est, qui diem illum posterum de die secundo azymorum accipiunt. Numeratio enim expresse jubetur fieri ab eo die, quo primitiarum manipulus oblatus est. Oblatus est autem secundo die azymorum, luna nempe decimâ sextâ. Nâ decimâ quartâ exeūte, erat pascha Iehovæ: Quintâ decimâ primus dies azymorum, postridie hoc est, secundo azymorum manipulus frugum offerebatur. Nam secundo die azymorum, ut Iosephus ait, frugibus demessis & hactenus intactis incipiebat frui; æquumq; rati Deum eius ubertatis authorem per gratitudinem honorari, hordei primitias offerebant. Ab eâ igitur die numerandæ septem septimanæ fuêre. Sic Iosephus lib. antiq. lud. 3. cap. 9. Sic Rabini, sic etiam Lyranus.
units.tr: But truly, what that second, or following, day after the Sabbath was, from which the seven weeks were to be counted, is not the same opinion for everyone. For there are those who take it from the first day of the week after the Sabbath next after Passover, that is, the day which is for us the Lord's Day; there are others who understand the whole festival of Passover, or those seven paschal days, to be meant, and think the following day of the Sabbath was the eighth day after Passover, that is, after the lamb was eaten. But the best opinion, and the most agreeable to the words of Moses, is that of those who take that following day to be the second day of unleavened bread. For the counting is expressly commanded to begin from the day on which the sheaf of first fruits was offered. Now it was offered on the second day of unleavened bread, that is, on the sixteenth day of the moon. For on the fourteenth, when it came out, was the Passover of Jehovah; on the fifteenth was the first day of unleavened bread; on the day after, that is, on the second day of unleavened bread, the sheaf of the crops was offered. For, as Josephus says, on the second day of unleavened bread, when the crops had been reaped and had until then been untouched, they began to enjoy them; and thinking it right that God, the author of their abundance, be honoured with gratitude, they offered the first fruits of barley. From that day, therefore, the seven weeks were to be counted. Thus Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 3, chapter 9. Thus the rabbis, and thus also Lyra.

units.la: Nec est, quod hîc quis cogitet, quomodo septem septimanæ hoc modo numeratæ quinquaginta dies fuerint, cum constet septem septimanas dies tantum quadraginta novem conficere. Quinquagesima enim erat dies proximè sequens septimanas septem completas, quod expresse monet Deus Levit. 23. inquiens: Numerabitis ab altero die cessationis paschatis septem septimanas inte-gras, usque ad posterum diem septimæ septimanæ complecompleta, hoc est, quinquaginta dies.
units.tr: Nor is there any reason for anyone here to wonder how seven weeks counted in this way could come to fifty days, since it is plain that seven weeks make only forty-nine days. For the fiftieth was the day immediately following the seven completed weeks, as God expressly warns in Lev. 23, saying: You shall count from the day after the cessation of the Passover seven complete weeks, until the day after the seventh week is completed, that is, fifty days.

units.la: De tempore hactenus: jam de ritu solennitatis huius aliquid porrò cognoscite. Agitata fuit Pentecoste, magna totius Iudææ celebritate, universali omnium conventu, solennitate non minore quam ipsum Pascha, hoc solum excepto, quod non dies septem continuata, ut Pascha, sed unius diei festivitate absoluta fuit, epulis, lætitiâ, & plausu maximo totius populi. Neque enim placet, quod nonnulli illam septem dies durasse volunt. A laboribus omnibus religiosè tunc cessatum est, oblationibus verò & victimis lege præscriptis cuncta etiam augusta. Septem agni, iuvencus unus, arietes duo, hircus, agni rursus duo, à toto populo, à singulis familiis duo ex horno[?] tritico cocti fermentati panes oblati. de quibus legatur Moses Levit.23. & Num.28.
units.tr: So far concerning the time. Now learn something further about the ritual of this solemnity. Pentecost was kept with great celebration throughout all Judea, with a universal gathering of all people, and with a solemnity no less than that of the Passover itself, except that it was not continued for seven days, as the Passover was, but was concluded with the festivity of a single day, with feasting, joy, and the greatest applause of the whole people. For it does not please me that some want it to have lasted seven days. On that day all labours were religiously set aside, and all things were done with the solemn offerings and sacrifices prescribed by the law. Seven lambs, one bullock, two rams, a he-goat, and again two lambs were offered by the whole people, and from each family two loaves of leavened wheat bread, baked. On these see Moses, Lev. 23, and Num. 28.

units.la: Quorsum verò, inquis, spectabant hæc omnia? Principio fuit isthæc legitima liberalitatis Dei, & largitatis agnitio; fuit sancta grati animi testificatio; fuit divinæ benedictionis celebratio. Maturitatem enim frugum agrorum, messis ubertatem, felicem anni proventum, omne denique quod terra gignit, quod sidus alit, quod annus profert, soli acceptum se Deo ferre, testati sunt Iudæi, eoque munus ipsi ex primis collectis frugibus panes illos duos fermentatos cōsecrarunt. Unde & festum primitiarum & messis appellatum fuit.
units.tr: But why, you may ask, did all these things aim at? First of all, this was the lawful acknowledgment of God's liberality and bounty; it was a holy testimony of a grateful spirit; it was the celebration of God's blessing. For the Jews bore witness that the ripening of the fields' fruits, the abundance of the harvest, the happy yield of the year, in short everything that the earth brings forth, that the heavens nourish, that the year produces, is to be credited to God alone; and so from the first gathered fruits they consecrated to him, as a gift, those two leavened loaves. Hence the feast was also called the feast of firstfruits and of harvest.

units.la: Etiam secundâ azymorum die primitiæ offerebantur, & tabernaculorum festo pro frugibus gratiæ agebantur Deo: sed non sine discrimine evidenevidenti. Nam in pafchate tantum manipulus u-nus spicarum triticearum jam maturescentium, ante messem offerebatur. In Pentecoste, messe iam demessa, non spicarum, sed panum duorum ex novis frugibus oblatio fiebat: In tabernaculorum festo pro frugibus omnib²[?], ex agris, hortis, vineis collectis gratiarum actio habebatur. Quare & hoc collectionis festum nominabatur.
units.tr: On the second day of unleavened bread too, firstfruits were offered, and at the feast of tabernacles thanks were rendered to God for the fruits; but not without a clear distinction. For at the Passover only one sheaf of ripening wheat was offered, before the harvest. At Pentecost, with the harvest already cut, the offering was not of sheaves but of two loaves from the new fruits. At the feast of tabernacles thanksgiving was made for all the fruits gathered from the fields, gardens and vineyards. Therefore this feast was also called the feast of ingathering.

units.la: Fuit porrò Pentecoste solenne quoque μνημό-συνον lætissimi illius in terram promissionis introi-tus. Quoties enim populus festivitatem eam perageret, recordari debuit, ex quo deserto, quam in terram! quam ex horrido & inhospito loco, in quàm fœcundam esset & amœnam deductus regionem! ibi demum quos tum agros colere, quos serere, quos metere cœpisset? qui quotânis[?] tantis segetibus, tantis omnis generis frugibus induc-rentur, ut cum feracissimis quibusq; terris certa-rent. Imò ut scriptura loquitur, lacte & melle verè diffluerent. Atq; hoc est, quod Levit.23.[?] dicitur: cũ ingressi fueritis terrâ, quam ego dabo vobis, & messueritis segetem, feretis manipulos spicarum, primitias messis vestræ ad sacerdotem, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, Pentecost was also a solemn memorial of that most joyful entry into the land of promise. For whenever the people kept that festival, they ought to call to mind from what a desert, into what a land, from what a rough and inhospitable place, they had been led into a region so fruitful and pleasant! There, at last, they had begun to till the fields, to sow, to reap, fields which every year would yield such crops and such fruits of every kind that they could vie with the most fertile lands of all. Indeed, as Scripture says, they would truly flow with milk and honey. And this is what is said in Lev. 23: when you have entered the land which I shall give you, and reaped its harvest, you shall bring a sheaf of the first ripe grain of your harvest to the priest, etc.

units.la: Fuit præterea recordatio durissimæ servitutis, quam Ægyptiis serviisset populus ille, & liberationis admirabilis, quâ Dei potentissimâ manu Pharaonis ereptus tyrannide, in Iehovæ solius transiisset potestatem, eiusque leges accepisset. Quò facit, quod dicit Deus: Memento quod ser-vus fueris. Deut.16.
units.tr: There was also a remembrance of the hardest slavery which that people had served in Egypt, and of the wonderful deliverance by which, snatched from Pharaoh's tyranny by God's most mighty hand, they had passed under the power of Jehovah alone and received his laws. To this God's words apply: Remember that you were a servant. Deut. 16.

units.la: Fuit igitur &[?] data in Sinai lege gratiarum a-ctio, eiusq; solennis celebratio: idq; vel maximè, quod in ipsum illud septimanarū seu Pentecostes festum promulgatio legis olim incidit: siquidem die quinquagesimo ab exitu facta creditur.
units.tr: Thus the thanksgiving for the law given at Sinai, and its solemn celebration, belonged to this feast; and this above all, because the promulgation of the law fell upon that very feast of weeks, or Pentecost: for it is believed to have taken place on the fiftieth day after the exodus.

units.la: Fuit deniq; Spiritus S. in Pentecoste super Apostolos, novamq; Ecclesiā totam, venturi[?] figura. Vt.n.cætera festa omnia, & cærimoniæ rerū futurarū spiritualiū, & Messię beneficiorum typi fuerunt & umbræ: Ita hoc etiā sua significatione nō caruit, & figurā, q; iccirco Paulus ipse, haud obscure innuere videtur, quando posteriori ad Corinth. epistolā cap. 3. duo illa lōge maxima, veteri & novæ Ecclesiæ, die Pentecostes exhibita beneficia, legis promulgationem & Evangelii publicationem prolixè inter se confert.
units.tr: Finally, the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles at Pentecost, and upon the whole new Church, was a figure of things to come. For just as all the other feasts and ceremonies were types and shadows of spiritual things to come and of the benefits of the Messiah, so this feast too had its significance and figure. Paul himself seems to hint at this quite plainly, when in the second epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 3, he compares at length those two very great benefits, given on the day of Pentecost, to the old and new Church: the promulgation of the law and the publication of the Gospel.

units.la: At nusquam legis latæ causā Pentecosten institutam fuisse legimus, inquiet aliquis? Fateor equidem: Expressis verbis sancitum hoc non reperitur: implicitè verò indicari non est dubium, ubi Deus jubet festo septimanarum recordari, quod fuisset servus populus in Ægypto. Nam id dicere omninò voluit, latā lege in Sinai vindicatum sibi populum illum à servitute & legibus Ægyptiorum fuisse, & in suam potestatem redactum, ut sibi deinceps servus esset, suisque legibus viveret, cuius proinde rei ut ne interiret unquam memoria, quotannis solennitatem Pentecostes gratis ac lætis mentibus celebrandam Deus instituit.
units.tr: But someone will say: we nowhere read that Pentecost was instituted on account of the giving of the law? I admit it: this is not found sanctioned in express words; but it is undoubtedly indicated implicitly, where God bids them remember at the feast of weeks that the people had been slaves in Egypt. For God wished to say this plainly: that by the law given at Sinai that people had been claimed for himself, delivered from slavery and from the laws of Egypt, and brought under his own power, so that thereafter they would be his servants and live by his laws. So that the memory of this should never perish, God instituted that the solemnity of Pentecost be celebrated every year with glad and grateful minds.

units.la: Pascha quidem, in recordationem solennem liberationis ex Ægypto sancitum fuit: sed Pentecoste amplius etiam renovabat memoriam de liberationis modo, quod nempe Deus lata lege in Sinai hunc populum à legibus Ægyptiis vindi-catum, sibi proprium fecisset. Neque alia est Augustini, & multorum aliorum veterum sententia, quàm ideo sancitam fuisse Pentecosten, quia quinquagesimo die, ab exitu ex Ægypto lex fuerat promulgata: quippe quibus absurdum videtur, aliorum beneficiorum, & operum divinorũ suam à Deo inolituram festivitatem: huius summi beneficii, nullam anniversariam celebrationem, sancitam fuisse.
units.tr: The Passover was indeed ordained as a solemn remembrance of the deliverance from Egypt; but Pentecost renewed even more the memory of the manner of that deliverance, namely that God, by giving the law at Sinai, had claimed this people for himself, freeing them from the laws of Egypt and making them his own. Nor is the opinion of Augustine and of many other ancient writers different: that Pentecost was ordained because the law had been promulgated on the fiftieth day after the exodus from Egypt. For it seems absurd to them that the festival of other benefits and divine works should have received its annual observance from God, while this greatest benefit should have been ordained without any yearly celebration.

units.la: Hîc tamen nodus se offert, in cuius solutione veteres & recentiores interpretes non pauci laborarunt. Eum ne curiosè potius obiecisse, quàm modestè explicasse videar, quaeso, patienter aures advertite.
units.tr: Here, however, a knot presents itself, in the untying of which many of the ancient and more recent interpreters have laboured. Lest I seem to have raised it rather in a spirit of curiosity than to have explained it with modesty, I beg you, listeners, to attend patiently.

units.la: Quasi pro confesso accepimus, legem quinquagesimo die ab exitu, seu à paschate in monte à Deo promulgatam fuisse. Id verò, si in dubium nonnulli revocent, quid dicemus? Nam certè ex loco Exod.19.ver.1.& 11. confici videtur, nō quinquagesimo, sed quadragesimo octavo die, ab exitu, legem latam fuisse. Dicitur namque ibi, populus primo die tertii mensis, qui est Sivan, in desertum Sinai venisse: tertio die post Deum descendisse in montem, ac legem Mosi dedisse. Sic tertio die Sivan lata lex fuit, ad quem à primo paschate, hoc est, à decimo quarto die mensis primi, (qui est Nisan) non sunt plures, quàm quadraginta octo dies. Sic igitur promulgatio legis non videtur in Pentecoste facta.
units.tr: We have taken it as agreed that the law was promulgated by God on the fiftieth day from the exodus, or from the Passover, on the mountain. But if some call this into doubt, what shall we say? For it seems certainly to be concluded from Exod. 19:1 and 11 that the law was given not on the fiftieth but on the forty-eighth day from the exodus. For it is said there that the people came into the desert of Sinai on the first day of the third month, which is Sivan; that on the third day God came down onto the mountain and gave the law to Moses. Thus the law was given on the third day of Sivan, and from the first Passover, that is, from the fourteenth day of the first month (which is Nisan), to that day there are no more than forty-eight days. So the promulgation of the law does not seem to have taken place at Pentecost.

units.la: Cæterum, Auditores, absit, ut hæc ratio à communi receptaque sententia nos dimoveat. Sic enim illa legis latio nec in Pentecosten, nec in festum aliud ullum, incidisset Iudæis, nec tanti tamque præclari & divini operis celebritas ulla fuisset, aut recordatio solennis.
units.tr: For the rest, listeners, far be it from us that this argument should move us from the common and received opinion. For in that case the giving of the law would have fallen neither on Pentecost nor on any other feast of the Jews, nor would there have been any solemn celebration or remembrance of so great and so glorious a divine work.

units.la: Tum etiam nobis Christianis pulcerrima illa legis latæ, & missi in Pentecoste Spiritus Sancti analogia prorsum perierit.
units.tr: Moreover, for us Christians too, that most beautiful analogy of the giving of the law and of the Holy Spirit sent at Pentecost would be utterly lost.

units.la: Ad locum vero Exod.19. quod attinet, etsi aliquid videtur habere momenti; tamen ad evertendam sententiam communem minimè facit. Neutrum enim expresse ibi dicitur, quòd primo die mensis tertii venerint in desertum Sinai: vel quod tertio die mensis lata lex sit: Textus verò sic habet: Mense tertio egressionis filiorum Israel de terrâ Ægypti, in die hac venerunt in solitudinem Sinai. Moses autem ascendit montem. Et postea ver.10. Vade ad populum, sanctifica eos hodie & cras, lavent q; vestimenta sua; & sint parati in diem tertium, in die enim tertia descendet Dominus coram omni plebe super montem Sinai. Hactenus verba textus. Damus ergo tertio die postquam venerunt in desertum illud, datam legem esse; sed non damus primo die mensis tertii eò eos venisse. Quoniam hoc non dicit Moses: sed tantum: tertio mense venisse, quoto die venerint, non exprimit.
units.tr: As for the passage in Exod. 19, although it seems to have some weight, yet it does not at all serve to overturn the common opinion. For neither of the two things is expressly stated there, that they came into the desert of Sinai on the first day of the third month, or that the law was given on the third day of the month. The text reads thus: In the third month after the going out of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. And Moses went up the mountain. And afterwards, verse 10: Go to the people, sanctify them today and tomorrow, let them wash their garments, and let them be ready for the third day; for on the third day the Lord will come down before all the people upon Mount Sinai. So far the words of the text. We therefore grant that the law was given on the third day after they came into that desert; but we do not grant that they came there on the first day of the third month. For Moses does not say this; he says only that they came in the third month, and does not express on what day of the month they came.

units.la: Qui de die primo accipiunt: illud בחרש in mense, interpretantur in Novilunio: quia חרש & mensem & novilunium significat: Alii verò tertium diem mensis tertii indicari voluntà Mose, cum dicit: Mense tertio egressionis, in die illa; relativum illa referentes ad numerum ternarium mensis, quasi dicat: in mense tertio, & in die eâdem, nempe tertia.
units.tr: Those who take it to be the first day interpret the word בחרש, "in the month," as "at the new moon," since חרש signifies both month and new moon. Others, however, hold that the third day of the third month is indicated by Moses when he says: In the third month of the going out, on that day; referring the relative "that" to the ordinal number of the month, as if he said: in the third month, and on the same day, namely the third.

units.la: Exhac difficultate factum est, ut cum certa sit sententia, legem esse latam quinquagesimo die, in computo tamen quinquagesimi illius diei non omnes conveniant; sed alii alios terminos à quo & ad quem, (ut loquimur) statuendos arbitrentur. Tres sententias insigniores paucis referemus: quartam pro nostrâ subiiciemus.
units.tr: From this difficulty it has come about that, although the opinion that the law was given on the fiftieth day is certain, yet not all agree on the reckoning of that fiftieth day; rather, some think different starting and ending points (as we say) should be fixed. We shall briefly set out three of the more notable opinions and put forward a fourth of our own.

units.la: Quidam numerant à quartâ decimâ lunâ mensis primi, quâ agnum comederunt, usq; ad diem tertium mensis tertii inclusive, sumentes ex primo mense dies septendecim, ex secundo triginta, ex tertio tres: qui in unum collecti conficiunt quinquaginta. Ita Augustinus lib. quaest. in Exod. 2.cap.70. Ex die quo pascha fecerunt, inquit, id est, agnum immolaverunt & ederunt, qui fuit quartus decimus primi mensis, usque ad istum, quo lex datur, dies quinquaginta numerantur; decem & septem scilicet primi mensis, reliqui ab ipso quarto decimo. Deinde omnes triginta secundi mensis, qui faciunt quadraginta septem, & tertius tertii mensis, qui est solemnitate occisi agni quinquagesimus. Haec Augustinus.
units.tr: Some count from the fourteenth day of the first month, on which they ate the lamb, up to the third day of the third month inclusive, taking seventeen days from the first month, thirty from the second, and three from the third; these gathered together make fifty. So Augustine, in Quaestiones in Exodum, book 2, chapter 70: "From the day on which they kept the Passover," he says, "that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb, which was the fourteenth day of the first month, up to that day on which the law was given, fifty days are counted: seventeen of the first month, namely those remaining from the fourteenth; then all thirty of the second month, which make forty-seven; and the third day of the third month, which is the fiftieth, from the solemnity of the slain lamb." Thus Augustine.

units.la: Cæterum, quod pace tanti viri dictum sit, in eo est error, quod à die, quo pascha fecerunt, numerandi initium facit, cum neque die illâ decimâ quartâ: sed decimâ quintâ ex Ægypto Israëlitæ exiverint, neque à decimâ quartâ: sed à decimâ sextâ die juxta legem Levit. 23. (ut est ostensum) quinquaginta dies ad Pentecosten numerare oporteat[?].
units.tr: Yet, with respect to so great a man, I must say that there is an error in this: he makes the counting begin from the day on which they kept the Passover, whereas the Israelites did not leave Egypt on that fourteenth day but on the fifteenth, and the fifty days to Pentecost ought not to be counted from the fourteenth but from the sixteenth day, according to Lev. 23 (as has been shown).

units.la: Rupertus Abbas Tuitiensis ab eâdem quartā decimā lunā cum Augustino numerationem inchoat; non tamen in tertio, ut Augustinus; sed in quarto die mensis tertii, terminat. Existimat enim legem non tertio, sed quarto demum die latam esse, cum nimirum à Mose coràm populo legeretur, & fœdus sanciretur, conjecturā factā ex loco Exod. 24. ubi Moses surrexisse mane, altari sub monte, & statuis duodecim exstructis, mandata Dei, populo proposuisse, ac fœdus inter Deũ populumque pepigisse legitur. Ad computum ergo quinquaginta dierum, sumit ex primo mese dies septendecim, ut Augustinus: Ex secundo nō triginta, ut Augustinus, sed viginti novem pro ratione mensium lunarium, qualibus tunc Hebræos usos esse existimat, quique alterni triginta & viginti novem diebus constant: Ex tertio mese dies quatuor, unde summa quinquaginta dierum exsistit.
units.tr: Rupert, abbot of Tuy, begins the count from the same fourteenth moon as Augustine, but he does not end it on the third day of the third month as Augustine does; he ends it on the fourth day of the third month. For he thinks the law was given not on the third day but only on the fourth, namely when Moses read it aloud before the people and the covenant was ratified. He conjectures this from Exod. 24, where we read that Moses rose early in the morning, set up an altar beneath the mountain and twelve pillars, set before the people the commands of God, and made a covenant between God and the people. So to make up the fifty days he takes seventeen days from the first month, as Augustine does; from the second month not thirty, as Augustine does, but twenty-nine, following the reckoning by lunar months, which he thinks the Hebrews then used, and which alternate between thirty and twenty-nine days; and from the third month four days, so the sum comes to fifty days.

units.la: Verùm & hic duplici errore fallitur. Primùm namque cum Augustino à vero numerandi principio aberrat, ut jam est demonstratum. Deinde Lex non quarto, sed tertio, postquam in desertum Sinai ventum erat, die, non à Mose legente & recitante; sed à Deo ipso tonante & fulgurante: non infra montem; sed in monte promulgata est. Nam quæ latè aliàs legis veteris & novæ miraculorum analogia? quæ comparatio? Accedit & hoc incommodum, quod pro quinquaginta dieb. ipse nobis (si rectè numeremus) quinquaginta & unum substituit. Lunaribus quippe mensibus tunc usos esse Iudæos sumit, quod minimè est certum. Contrarium nos mox ostendemus.
units.tr: But he too is misled by a double error. First, like Augustine, he strays from the true starting point of the count, as has already been shown. Second, the law was not given on the fourth day but on the third day after they had come into the wilderness of Sinai; it was not read and recited by Moses, but proclaimed by God himself thundering and flashing lightning, not below the mountain but on the mountain. For what broad analogy of the miracles of the old and new law is there otherwise? What comparison? There is also this inconvenience: he himself, if we count correctly, substitutes fifty-one days for the fifty. For he assumes that the Jews then used lunar months, which is by no means certain. We shall soon show the opposite.

units.la: Melior itaque & verisimilior Lyrani sup-putatio est, à decimo sexto die mensis primi, seu à secundo azymorum, usque ad sextum diem ter-tii mensis: Sumtis ex Nisan [?] primo mense diebus quindecim; ex Ziph secundo mense viginti novem; ex Sivan tertio mense sex: qui collecti sunt quinquaginta. Sex autem dies Lyra ex tertio mé-se accipit, quia arbitratur, Mosen tertio die in de-sertum venisse, postridie demum populo in ter-tium diem paratus ut esset, præcepisse, & sexto proinde die legem propositam fuisse.
units.tr: A better and more probable reckoning is that of Lyra: from the sixteenth day of the first month, or the second day of unleavened bread, to the sixth day of the third month. Taking fifteen days from the first month, Nisan; twenty-nine from the second month, Ziv; and six from the third month, Sivan, which together make fifty. Lyra takes the six days from the third month because he thinks Moses came into the wilderness on the third day, and only the next day ordered the people to be ready for the third day, so the law was proposed on the sixth day.

units.la: Atqui bene ille quidem ac juxta legem, à sexto decimo primi mensis die numerare incipit: bene etiam tertio, tertii mensis in desertum Mosen venisse censet: bene denique illud, In mense tertio, ut est Exod. 19: In die hac venerunt in desertum; illud, inquam, in die Hac, quod & septuaginta emphaticè verterunt ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ ad præ-cedentem mensis numerum, id est, tertium refert. De primo autem tertii mensis die, sive de ipso Novilunio accipi non potest. Hebræum enim חדש novilunium significat aliquando, cum absolutè sine numero ponitur, ut Psal. 81. Clangite buccinâ בחדש in novilunio. Item 1.Sam.20. Cras est חדש novilunium. At vero cum numerus aliquis, quemadmodum hoc loco apponitur, aliam nisi mensis significationem nusquam habere credo: siquidem non novilunio primo, secundo, tertio: sed mense primo, secundo, tertio dicere Hebræi consuevere.
units.tr: Certainly he begins the count well, and in accordance with the law, from the sixteenth day of the first month; he also rightly thinks Moses came into the wilderness on the third day of the third month; and he rightly takes the words "In the third month, as Exod. 19" as "On this day they came into the wilderness," which the Seventy also rendered emphatically as "on this day" [ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ]. But he refers it to the preceding number of the month, that is, the third. However, it cannot be taken to mean the first day of the third month, or the new moon itself. For the Hebrew word [חדש] sometimes means new moon when it is used absolutely, without a number, as in Psalm 81: "Blow the trumpet at the new moon [בחדש]." Likewise in 1 Sam. 20: "Tomorrow is the new moon [חדש]." But when a number is added, as here, I believe the word has no other meaning than month; for the Hebrews customarily say not "the first, second, third new moon" but "the first, second, third month."

units.la: Cæterum ne hæc quidem sententia errore vacat, eoq; gemino. Primum enim ex textu ostendi non potest, quod sumit Lyranus, Mosen non tertio, sed quarto die, hoc est, postridie quàm venissent in desertum Sinai dixisse populo, ut in die tertium ad audiendam legem parati essent. Nam eodem die, quo in desertum venerunt (quod tertio tertii mensis factum perseveramus) Moses illico montem ad Deum conscendit, mandata ad populum accepit, rediit, exposuit, revocatus statim, eo ipso die ascendit iterum, & ei edixit Jehova, ito ad populum ut sanctifices eos hodie & cras, ut sint in diem tertium parati. Reversus ex templo dixit, Estote parati in diem tertium, quæ omnia historiam recte intuentibus sunt manifesta.
units.tr: But even this opinion is not free from error, and that in two ways. First, it cannot be shown from the text, as Lyra assumes, that Moses did not speak to the people on the third day but on the fourth, that is, the day after they had come into the wilderness of Sinai, telling them to be ready for the law on the third day. For on the very day they came into the wilderness (which we maintain happened on the third day of the third month), Moses at once climbed the mountain to God, received the commands for the people, came back, set them out, and, called back again at once, went up the same day once more, and Jehovah said to him: "Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow, so that they may be ready for the third day. Coming back from the temple, he said: Be ready for the third day." All these things are plain to those who look carefully at the narrative.

units.la: Deinde nec illud congruit, quod sexto decimum die mensis tertii latam legem adfirmat. Nō enim animadvertit, eâ nos ratione à secundo die azymorum ad sextum tertii mensis inclusive dies habituros unum & quinquaginta: ex primo videlicet mense, decem & quinque: Ex secundo triginta (ita enim necessum, ut ostendetur) ex tertio sex diebus computatis.
units.tr: Next, what Lyra affirms, that the law was given on the sixteenth day of the third month, does not agree either. For he does not notice that by that reckoning, from the second day of unleavened bread to the sixth day of the third month inclusive, we would have fifty-one days: from the first month, fifteen; from the second, thirty (for it must be so, as will be shown); and from the third, six days counted.

units.la: Quæ cum ita se habeant, congruentissima videtur sententia, ut legem quinto die mensis tertii in monte Sinai promulgatam esse dicamus. Nam quinto die triduum illud, in quod paratus esse ad audiendum legem jussus erat populus, fuit completum. Tertio enim die Israelitæ in desertum illud venerunt, castra fecerunt, Moses montem conscendit, Dei mandata recepit, descendit; Exsecutus est, & vesperi sanctificare populum copit. Quarto vestimenta eluta fuēre & munda-ta. Quinto demum Deus in montem cum majestate summā inter tonitrua, & fulgura, cernentibus omnibus & trepidantibus descendit, legem tulit.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, the most consistent opinion seems to be that we should say the law was proclaimed on the mountain of Sinai on the fifth day of the third month. For the three-day period, in which the people had been ordered to be ready to hear the law, was completed on the fifth day. On the third day the Israelites came into that wilderness, pitched camp, Moses climbed the mountain, received God's commands, and came down; he carried them out, and in the evening began to sanctify the people. On the fourth day their garments were washed and made clean. Finally, on the fifth day God came down upon the mountain with the greatest majesty, amid thunder and lightning, while all looked on and trembled, and gave the law.

units.la: Neque impossibile videri debet, (ut objicit Bellarminus) omnia ea quæ dicta sunt uno die tertio facta esse: ut in desertum Israelitæ venirent, castra ponerent, Moses bis montem conscenderet, bis descenderet, bis populo conciona-retur. Quid enim absurdi, si dixerimus, eodē die tertio eò venisse maturius, ac ducibus aliis in castrametatione occupatis, Mosen in montem vicinum, non quidem ad verticem usq;: (in quem tandem conscendere est jussus) sed aliquo usque bis adscendisse, bis rediisse, bis jussa Dei ad populum retulisse, non prolixis concionibus, sed præscriptis verbis vesperi eundem sanctificare cœpisse: præsertim cum dies propter vicinum solstitium esset longior.
units.tr: Nor should it seem impossible (as Bellarmine objects) that all the things that have been described were done on one third day: that the Israelites came into the wilderness, pitched their camp, Moses climbed the mountain twice, came down twice, and addressed the people twice. For what is absurd if we say that on that same third day they came there earlier, and while the other leaders were busy with the encampment, Moses climbed a nearby mountain (not indeed to the summit, to which he was finally ordered to climb, but up to some point) twice, came back twice, twice reported God's commands to the people, not in long sermons but in prescribed words, and in the evening began to sanctify them; especially since the day was longer because of the nearby solstice?

units.la: Accedit sententiæ nostræ hæc ratio, quod cō-putus quinquaginta dierum à secundo die azy-morum, usq; ad quintum diem Sivan mensis ter-tii præcisè congruit, ex primo mense, quindecim; ex tertio, quinque; ex secundo triginta diebus cō-putatis, non viginti novem, ut multi volunt. Neque enim Hebræi tempore latę legis menses Lu-nares inæquales habuêre, ut Ruperti & Lyræ fert sententia: sed solaribus æqualibus Ægyptiis an-nis & mensibus à mundi cōditu per annos 3449. usque ad æram Alexandri Magni usi sunt. inde vero ab æra Alexandri usque ad Thalmud congestum annos & menses inæquales usurpare de-mum cœperunt: quos ipsos tamen ad solares A-lexandrinorum & Romanorum beneficio Cy-cli Metonici, reduxerūt. A congesto dehinc Thalmud, circa annum sc. Christi 505. aliam rursus an-ni rationem, usq; in hunc diem sequuntur. Quā de re eruditissimè disputat Clariss. Vir M. Jacobus Christmannus, quem honoris causa nomino, in commentario suo in Alfraganum de Hebreo-rum Calendario.
units.tr: To our opinion this is added: the count of fifty days from the second day of unleavened bread to the fifth day of the month Sivan, the third month, agrees exactly if we count fifteen days from the first month, five from the third, and thirty from the second, not twenty-nine as many want. For the Hebrews at the time the law was given did not have unequal lunar months, as the opinion of Rupert and Lyra holds; they used solar years and months, equal as among the Egyptians, from the creation of the world for 3449 years, down to the era of Alexander the Great. From the era of Alexander, however, down to the compiling of the Talmud, they began to use years and months that were unequal; yet by the help of the Metonic cycle, they brought these back to the solar months of the Alexandrians and Romans. From the compiling of the Talmud onward, about the year of Christ 505, they followed another system of years, down to this day. On this matter the most learned man, the most distinguished M. Jacob Christmann, whom I name out of respect, has argued very learnedly in his commentary on Alfraganus concerning the Hebrew calendar.

units.la: Quæ hactenus de die promulgatæ legis dicta sunt, non est cur plus subtilitatis, quā usus habere existimemus. Etenim absq; his multa scripturæ loca non assequemur: Veteris Ecclesiæ historiam nesciemus: discrimina Iudaicæ & Christianæ Pentecostes non intelligemus. Quare ne de veteri Pentecoste plura adferam, extra omnem dubitationem positum nobis esto, cùm quinquagesimo die, à secundo die azymorum legem à Deo latam constet, ab eodem quoq; tanti beneficii memoriam, in Pentecostes solennitate sancitam fuisse. Nunc ad nostram Pentecosten veniamus.
units.tr: There is no reason to think that more subtlety is needed in what has been said so far about the day on which the law was proclaimed than is useful. For without these points we shall not grasp many passages of Scripture; we shall not know the history of the early Church; we shall not understand the differences between the Jewish and the Christian Pentecost.
