Therefore, so as not to bring forward more about the old Pentecost, let it be placed beyond all doubt that, since it is agreed that God gave the law on the fiftieth day from the second day of unleavened bread, the memory of so great a benefit was also established by him in the solemnity of Pentecost. Now let us come to our Pentecost.

units.la: Nova hæc Pentecoste una est ex anniversariis Ecclesiæ Christianæ solennitatibus; quā quotannis quinquagesimo die à resurrectione servatoris nostri ex mortuis, historia de miraculosa effusione Spiritus sancti super Apostolos, & super omnē carnem toti populo Christiano recognoscenda recolendaque publicè proponitur, idque ingens Dei beneficium communi totius Ecclesiæ voce decantatur, ac celebratur.
units.tr: This new Pentecost is one of the annual solemnities of the Christian Church. On the fiftieth day after the resurrection of our Saviour from the dead, the story of the miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, and upon all flesh, is publicly set forth every year for the whole Christian people to recognise and recall, and this immense benefit of God is sung and celebrated with the common voice of the whole Church.

units.la: Hujus verò solennitatis observatione nequaquam judaizamus, nec pristino servitutis jugo implicamur nos Christiani, ut nonnulli turbatores plaufibiliter tumultuantur ; sed ordine Ecclesiæ utilem tenemus. Longe enim aliter à nobis, aliter à Iudæis festivitas ista celebratur.
units.tr: In observing this solemnity we by no means Judaize, nor are we Christians entangled again in the old yoke of servitude, as some troublemakers noisily clamour for effect; rather, we keep it in the order of the Church, as something useful. For this festival is celebrated by us in a way quite different from the way it is celebrated by the Jews.

units.la: Vetus illa à Deo fancita Iudæis erat pars cultus divini, cerimonia necessaria, typus futurorum bonorum, sanctissime semper observanda: nec sine scelere, sine violatione legis divinæ, sine offensione, sineirâ omnipotentis omitti unquā aut mutari à quoquam hominum poterat : At nova nostra non aliquo Dei mandato præcepta: sed Ecclesiæ libero arbitratu recepta : non necessitate aliquâ cogente; sed consuetudine liberâ suadente in locum veteris substituta, non cultus, non typi causa; sed ordinis, sed honestatis utilitatisque gratiâ observatur, intermittiq; aut mutari ab Ecclesia, si essent probabiles causæ sine peccato liberè posset.
units.tr: That old feast, sanctioned by God, was for the Jews a part of divine worship, a necessary ceremony, a type of good things to come, to be always observed most holily. It could never be omitted or changed by anyone without crime, without violation of the divine law, without offence and anger to the Almighty. Our new feast, however, was not prescribed by any command of God, but was received by the free judgment of the Church; it is not compelled by any necessity, but was introduced by free custom in place of the old one. It is observed not for the sake of worship or of type, but for the sake of order, decency and usefulness; and if there were probable reasons, the Church could freely omit or change it without sin.

units.la: Primam ejus originem sunt, qui ad ipsos Apostolos eam referant, authoritatibus nonnullis sacrarum literarum inducti. Bis enim in Novo Testamento novæ Pentecostes mentio fieri videtur. Semel 1.Cor.16.ubi Paulus Ephesi usq; ad Pentecosten permansurus: iterum Act. 20. ubi idē Paulus festinasse dicitur, ut si fieri posset, die Pentecostes Ierosolymis esset. Verum nos rem istam, ut nō omnino certam in medio relinquimus: tum quia scripturæ illæ à plerisque non absurdè de veteri Pentecoste intelliguntur, cujus solennitatem Iudæi, etiam post Christum exhibitum, usque ad urbis Ierosolymæ eversionem, frequentabant; unde tunc etiam inter Christianos appellatio ejus herebat: tum vero quia historici Ecclesiastici diserte contrarium testantur. Sic enim Socrates hist.Eccl.l. 5. c 21: Neque servator noster neque Apostoli leges nobis de festis praeceperunt, vel servitutis jugum imposuerunt: sed festum, inquit, paschatis, aliaq; festa, libero æquoque eorum judicio, qui in illis diebus beneficia acceperunt recolenda reliquerunt. Neque enim Apostolis propositum fuit, ut de celebrandis festis diebus leges sancirent: sed ut rectæ vivendi rationis & pietatis nobis auctores essent. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Some, moved by certain authorities of Sacred Letters, trace its first origin back to the Apostles themselves. For twice in the New Testament there seems to be mention of a new Pentecost: once in 1 Cor. 16, where Paul is to remain at Ephesus until Pentecost; and again in Acts 20, where the same Paul is said to have hastened "so that, if it were possible, he might be at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost." Yet we leave the matter open, as not wholly certain: partly because those passages are by many not absurdly understood of the old Pentecost, whose solemnity the Jews kept, even after Christ had been revealed, until the overthrow of the city of Jerusalem; whence even then among Christians the name of it clung to it; and partly because the Church historians clearly testify to the contrary. Thus Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 21: "Neither our Saviour nor the Apostles prescribed laws to us about festivals, nor did they impose a yoke of servitude; but the feast of Easter and other feasts they left to be kept in remembrance, by the free judgment of those who received the benefits on those days. For it was not the purpose of the Apostles to enact laws about the celebration of festival days, but to be for us authors of the right rule of living and of piety." Thus he.

units.la: Vt ut sit, libenter cum vetustis scriptoribus agnoscimus perantiquam esse hujus festi in Christiana Ecclesia celebrationem, & originem prope ad ipsa Apostolorum tempora pertinere. Crebra enim ejus apud vetustissimos authores fit mentio. Meminit ejus antiquissimus & disertissimus scriptor Tertullianus, libello de corona militis: meminit Origenes lib. 8. contra Celsum; meminit Irenæus apud Justinum quæst. 115. quem quidem omnino etiam in ea esse sententia video, ut ad Apostolorum tempora originem ejus referri velit. (Si modo is liber est Justini Mart. qui Irenæo aliquanto fuit antiquior:) meminere denique Augustinus, Hieronymus, aliique complures.
units.tr: However that may be, we gladly agree with the ancient writers that the celebration of this festival in the Christian Church is very ancient, and that its origin reaches almost to the very times of the Apostles. For its mention is frequent among the most ancient authors. The most ancient and most eloquent writer Tertullian mentions it in his book On the Crown of the Soldier; Origen mentions it in book 8 against Celsus; Irenaeus mentions it in Justin, question 115, in which I see that he certainly holds the view that its origin is to be referred to the times of the Apostles (if indeed that is the book of Justin Martyr, who was somewhat older than Irenaeus). Finally, Augustine, Jerome, and many others mention it.

units.la: Magnum porro inter veterem illam & hanc nostram Pentecosten hoc etiam discrimen est, quod illam nisi Jerosolymis celebrare nusquam fas erat, quod sacrificia certa, quod epulæ fiebant publicæ, quod non stato celebrabatur tempore; sed de feriâ in feriam, cum secundâ azymorum die migrabat: Nostra è contrario non uni alligata loco ; sed rite ubivis Christianarum gentium: non sacrificiis externis vel sympofiis; sed concionibus sacris, precibus & hymnis de misso Spiritu sancto à nobis peragitur.
units.tr: Moreover, there is also this great difference between that old Pentecost and this new one of ours: the old could be celebrated lawfully nowhere but at Jerusalem; it had fixed sacrifices, and public feasts; it was not celebrated at a fixed time, but moved from day to day, and migrated with the second day of unleavened bread. Ours, on the contrary, is not bound to one place, but is duly kept wherever Christian nations are; it is carried out by us not with external sacrifices or banquets, but with sacred sermons, prayers and hymns concerning the Holy Spirit who was sent.

units.la: Quo loco de consuetudine veterum Christianorum monendum hoc duxi. Cum aliàs plerunque inter precandum ritu geniculationis utere-tur, eos à pascha ad Pentecosten diebus quinquaginta, quemadmodum & singulis Dominicis stātes precari solitos fuisse. Causam ritus ejusmodi discitur[?] Justinus quaest. 115. & qualemcunq; hanc reddit: quod geniculatio in precib. symbolum & nota esset τῆς ἐν τῇ ἁμαρτίας πτώσεως ἡ-μῶν[?], lapsus nostri per peccata: Erecta vero precatio signum esset τῆς ἀναστάσεως, resurrectionis, per quam gratia Christi & à peccatis, & à mortificata in eis morte liberati sumus. Ex Irenæi autem libro de paschate, quem ibidem allegat: In Pente-coste (inquit) genua non inflectimus, quoniam ἐντῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς κυριακῆς[?], h.e. æquivalet diei Dominicæ. Quibus non absimile est, quod Hieronymus contra Luciferianos scriptum reliquit: in more Ecclesiis fuisse, idque ex traditione, ut die Dominico & per omnem Pentecosten nec de genicu-lis adorarent, nec jejunium solverent.
units.tr: On this point I have thought it worth noting the custom of the ancient Christians. Although at other times they commonly used the rite of kneeling in prayer, they were accustomed, from Easter to Pentecost, for those fifty days, as also on each Lord's Day, to pray standing. The reason for this kind of rite is taught by Justin, question 115, and he gives it in some such form: kneeling in prayers was a sign and mark of our fall through sin, but upright prayer was a sign of the resurrection, through which we are freed by the grace of Christ both from sins and from the death that was in them. From the book of Irenaeus On Easter, which he cites in the same place: "At Pentecost (he says) we do not bend the knees, because it is equivalent to the Lord's Day." Not unlike this is what Jerome left written against the Luciferians: that it was the custom in the Churches, and this from tradition, that on the Lord's Day and through the whole of Pentecost they neither adored on their knees nor broke their fast.

units.la: Ineptias verò Pontificiorum, quibus in festo Pentecostes ridiculè ludunt, mittendo columbas candidas è templi fornice, ignem & crustula dejiciendo; pueros verò accurrentes ad crustula aquis largiter perfundendo, ad repræsentandum scilicet Spiritus sancti effusionem, ipsis cum reliquis superstitionibus relinquimus. Quidam nugas illas tali carmine non inelegánter expres-sit.
units.tr: As for the silly trifles of the Papists, with which they foolishly play at the feast of Pentecost, sending white doves down from the vault of the temple, dropping fire and little cakes, and drenching with water the boys who run to the little cakes, to represent, of course, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, we leave them to their superstitions alongside the rest. Someone has expressed those trifles not inelegantly in verse.

units.la: In Pentecoste mites, albaq, columba Funiculis leviter vincta mittuntur ab alto, Lignea postremo calo dependet eodem. Cernis ut idolis ludant doceantq; popellum. Non secum ac puppis tenera assuevere puella, &c.
units.tr: At Pentecost the gentle, white dove, lightly bound with little cords, is sent down from on high; finally a wooden one hangs from the same ceiling. You see how they play with idols and teach the people. Not otherwise than a ship's tender girl has been accustomed, etc.

units.la: Cæterum nostra etiam non, ut vetus, de die in diem quotannis movetur, sed stato semper die Dominico celebratur. Etsi verò ex loco illo Justini antea laudato, ubi dicit, Pentecosten ἐνδιωα-μεῖν τὴν ἡμέραν τῆς κυριακῆς colligere licet, olim in Græcis Ecclesiis non semper in Dominicam incidisse; tamen posteritas non sine causa eam Dominicæ videtur alligasse. Nam dies quinquagesimus à resurrectione Domini in Dominicum semper nobis incidit. Nec dubium est, ipso die Dominico Spiritum sanctum olim cœlo demissum, beatissimos Apostolos divina luce collustrasse. Neq; enim in eorum iverim sententiam, qui die Iovis vel Veneris factum id existimant. Anno quippe passionis & mortis Domini, secundus dies azymorum, à quo numerandam esse Pentecosten supra ostendimus, in feriam primam, quæ nobis Dominica est, incidit, postridie nimirum Sabbathi, in quod Iudæi pascha suum, cum in sextam incideret feriam consuetudine quadam rejecerant. De qua cum eruditi etiam variè sentiant & disputent, hic non est dicendi locus.
units.tr: Moreover, our feast, unlike the old one, is not moved from day to day each year, but is always celebrated on a fixed day, the Lord's Day. Although from that passage of Justin mentioned above, where he says that Pentecost "falls on the Lord's Day," one may gather that in the Greek Churches in former times it did not always fall on a Sunday, nevertheless posterity has not without reason seemed to tie it to the Lord's Day. For the fiftieth day from the resurrection of the Lord always falls on a Sunday for us. Nor is there any doubt that on the Lord's Day itself the Holy Spirit was once sent down from heaven and illumined the most blessed Apostles with divine light. Nor indeed would I go over to the opinion of those who think it happened on a Thursday or a Friday. In the year of the Lord's passion and death, the second day of unleavened bread, from which we have shown Pentecost is to be counted, fell on the first day of the week, which for us is the Lord's Day, namely the day after the Sabbath; the Jews had by some custom put off their Passover when it would have fallen on a Friday. Since learned men also hold and dispute various views on this, this is not the place to discuss it.

units.la: Denique sine etiam multò alio Iudæis, alio nobis festum Pentecostes solenne est. Iudæis præ-ceptum fuit, ut esset vindicationis olim factæ ex miserrima Ægyptiorum servitute, legisq; promulgationis in Sinai solennis recordatio, proq; copiosa messe[?] & maturis frugibus gratiarum a-ctio. Nobis vero nostra Pentecoste recepta est, ut sit memoria Spiritus sancti effusi super Apostolos & omnem carnem, juxta oraculum Ioëlis, quod primum & augustissimum fuit Christi servatoris nostri exaltati in cœlis ad dextram patris.
units.tr: Finally, the feast of Pentecost is solemn for the Jews in one way and for us in quite another. The Jews were commanded to keep it as a solemn remembrance of the deliverance once made from the most wretched servitude in Egypt, and of the promulgation of the law at Sinai, and as an thanksgiving for the abundant harvest and ripe fruits. But for us our Pentecost has been received so that it may be a memorial of the Holy Spirit poured out upon the Apostles and upon all flesh, according to the oracle of Joel; which was the first and most august of the works of Christ our Saviour, exalted in heaven at the right hand of the Father.

units.la: Tametsi enim beneficia Dei ex memoria nunquam deponenda, nec uno tantum quotannis: sed omnibus vitæ nostræ diebus repetenda & recolenda sunt: certa tamen & stata quædam tempora meditationi eorum publicæ, utili bonoque consilio destinantur, quibus nos vel in primis eorum celebrationi solenni vacare decet; nempè quò omnia in Ecclesia ordine fiant: quò populus Christianus ad diligentem meditationem excitetur, & de summis Dei beneficiis solidius e-rudiatur & confirmetur: quò item confessio fidei Christianæ de præcipuis Dei operibus publi-cè contra infideles sonet in Ecclesia, atque hæc ab illis discernatur; quò denique in doctrina de illustrioribus patefactionibus & beneficiis Dei per Christum Ecclesiæ collatis consensus reti-neatur & conservetur.
units.tr: For although the benefits of God must never be dropped from memory, and are to be repeated and recalled not once a year only, but on all the days of our life, nevertheless certain fixed times have been appointed by useful and good counsel for their public meditation, and it is fitting for us to be especially free for their solemn celebration: namely, so that all things in the Church are done in order; so that the Christian people may be stirred to diligent meditation and more solidly instructed and confirmed about the highest benefits of God; so that likewise the confession of the Christian faith concerning the chief works of God may resound publicly in the Church against unbelievers, and be distinguished from them; and finally, so that consent in the doctrine concerning the more illustrious manifestations and benefits of God bestowed on the Church through Christ may be retained and preserved.

units.la: His igitur & non aliis de causis cum nova nobis celebretur Pentecoste, utrumque horum satis jam liquere arbitror, tali observatione neque judaizare Ecclesiam Christianam, neque in Apostoli præceptum aut libertatem suam ullâ ex par-te impingere.
units.tr: For these reasons, and no others, since we celebrate a new Pentecost, I think both of these points are now clear enough: by such observance the Christian Church neither judaizes nor infringes in any way on the command or the liberty of the Apostle.

units.la: De veteri itaque & de nova Pentecoste ha-ctenus: sequitur ut, cum utraque eximiis fulgeat Dei beneficiis: illa quidem promulgatione legis in monte Sinai: nostra vero miraculosa effusione Spiritus sancti, & publicatione Evangelii in universum orbem, hæc ipsa paucis consideremus atque inter se conferamus.
units.tr: So much for the old and the new Pentecost. It follows that, since each shines with remarkable benefits of God, the old through the promulgation of the law on Mount Sinai, and ours through the miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the publication of the Gospel throughout the whole world, we should briefly consider these and compare them with one another.

units.la: Ea enim gratia indubiè Deus utrumque eodem die præstitit beneficium, ut inter se rectius comparari possent. Unde bene etiam anagogen latæ legis & dati Spiritus sancti instituit B. Augu-stinus, camque à Deo potissimum spectatam esse censet. Quin imò D.Paulus posteriori ad Corinthios epistolâ eorundem beneficiorum Dei contentionem non obscurè facit, atque inter se ita confert: ut novum veteri longè anteferat: quò & nos quanta Novi illius beneficii præstantia sit plenius intelligentes, pro eo tanto magis gratos Deo nos exhibere studeamus.
units.tr: For by the same grace God undoubtedly bestowed both benefits on the same day, so that they might be more fittingly compared with each other. Hence Blessed Augustine rightly also set out the anagogical meaning of the law given and of the Holy Spirit given, and holds that God chiefly had this in view. Indeed, in his second letter to the Corinthians, the Apostle Paul clearly sets forth a contrast between these same benefits of God and compares them thus: that the new far surpasses the old. By this, we too, understanding more fully how great the excellence of that New benefit is, should strive all the more to show ourselves grateful to God for it.

units.la: Porrò autem sive in externis symbolis, sive in donis ipsis, sive in donorum fructu effectisque collationem instituamus, ingentem præstantiam novi beneficii, præ veteri illo semper deprehen-demus.
units.tr: Moreover, whether we compare them in their outward signs, in the gifts themselves, or in the fruit and effects of the gifts, we shall always find the enormous superiority of the new benefit over that old one.

units.la: In promulgatione legis olim varia apparuerunt præsentiæ divinæ symbola: sed terribilia & tremenda omnia. Flammis enim latissimis mons totus æstuat; crebris vastisque tremoribus nutat; cœlum atrâ densâque caligine obducitur; perso-nant tubæ; intonant nubes; coruscant fulgetra; populus horrens tremens ad imas vix montis ra-dices hæret; accessu prohibetur, accedenti præ-sentissima mors intentatur. Quæ omnia Dei qui-dem præsentis erant signa; sed inaccessi; sed tre-mendi;sed ignis consumentis.
units.tr: At the promulgation of the law there once appeared various symbols of the divine presence, but all of them were terrifying and dreadful. The whole mountain glowed with widespread flames; it trembled with frequent and violent quakings; the heavens were covered with black and dense darkness; trumpets sounded; clouds thundered; lightnings flashed; the people, trembling and horror-struck, scarcely stood at the lowest foot of the mountain; they were forbidden to approach, and immediate death was threatened to anyone who drew near. All these were indeed signs of the present God, but of a God who was unapproachable, who was dreadful, who was a consuming fire.

units.la: At vero Spiritus sanctus, quando olim in Pentecoste (quæ postrema Judæorum, prima Christianorum vocari jure potest) super Apostolis venit, adhibuit & ipse visibilia symbola præsentiæ suæ, sed minime tremenda. Nam ut Lucas ait, [illegible, ~2 letters] ἀποστόλοις omnibus concorditer eodem loci congregatis, exstitit repente é cœlo sonitus, tanquam ru-entis flatus violenti, qui replevit totam domum, & visa sunt dispertita linguæ instar ignis, seditq; super unumquemque eorum, &c. Miranda quidem hæc & alia fuerunt, sed non terribilia; ventus vehemens: sed non lædens, non terrens; flatus validus; sed non verrens, non noxius; ignis coruscans: sed non urens, non absumens; linguæ dispertitæ: sed nullus dolor, nullus affectus malus. Quæ sane præsentis Spiritus sancti, non homines à Deo ar-centis; sed ultro ad eos accedentis, & cum Deo conjungetis; non percellentis: sed super eos quie-scentis & sedentis signa fuerunt.
units.tr: But when the Holy Spirit came upon the Apostles once at Pentecost (which may rightly be called the last of the Jews and the first of the Christians), he too used visible symbols of his presence, but by no means terrifying ones. For, as Luke says, "when all the Apostles were gathered together in one place with one accord, there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, which filled the whole house; and there appeared to them tongues parting asunder, like as of fire, and it sat upon each one of them," etc. These and other things were indeed wonderful, but not terrifying: a vehement wind, but not harming or frightening; a strong blast, but not sweeping away or hurtful; a flashing fire, but not burning or consuming; divided tongues, but no pain and no evil affection. These were truly signs of the presence of the Holy Spirit, who does not drive men away from God, but rather draws near to them of his own accord and joins them to God; signs not of one who strikes down, but of one who rests and abides upon them.

units.la: Ad dona veniamus. Ea utrobique sunt e-ximia. Magnum etenim beneficium miranda il-la & illustris totius legis divinæ promulgatio: qua Deus se suamque voluntatem magnificen-tissimè patefecit; legem illam, quam ex naturâ ipsâ arripuimus, haurimus, expressimus, ipsis scriptam digitis suis proposuit: vitiositate humana obscuratam planissimè declaravit; peccatis corruptam plenissimè instauravit, ut ad ejus unius, tanquam perfectę obedientiæ, justitiæ & sanctitatis trutinam omnis vita dirigeretur. Cęrimonias & ritus certos, quibus beneficia Messiæ spiritualia adumbrarentur, populus ab aliis gentibus discerneretur, præscripsit; leges denique, quibus ad Messiam usque teneretur politia illa, & Ecclesia conservaretur, sancivit. Hæc, inquam, magna & præclara beneficia fuêre, quibus Deus ex toto genere humano, solius Abrahami posteritatem dignatus fuit.
units.tr: Let us come to the gifts. In both cases they are excellent. The wonderful and illustrious promulgation of the whole divine law was indeed a great benefit, by which God most magnificently revealed himself and his will. He set before us, written with his own fingers, that law which we had seized, drawn in and expressed from nature itself; he made it most plainly clear, though it had been obscured by human wickedness; he restored it most fully, though it had been corrupted by sins, so that the whole of life might be directed by that one law as by the balance of perfect obedience, justice and holiness. He prescribed certain ceremonies and rites by which the spiritual benefits of the Messiah were foreshadowed and by which the people were distinguished from other nations; finally, he enacted laws by which that polity was bound until the Messiah and the Church was preserved. These, I say, were great and splendid benefits, with which God, from the whole human race, deigned to honour the posterity of Abraham alone.

units.la: Verum enim vero longè præclarius his etjam & nobilius beneficium fuit missio Spiritus sancti, præ cujus fulgore vix umbras illa dixeris. Principio multò hic, quàm ibi illustrior fuit Divinitatis totius, seu sacrosanctę Trinitatis patefactio.
units.tr: Yet truly, far more excellent and noble than these even was the benefit of the mission of the Holy Spirit, in whose brightness you could hardly call those things shadows. In the first place, the revelation of the whole Divinity, or of the most holy Trinity, was far more illustrious here than there.

units.la: Pater æternus cœlitus effundit Spiritum sanctum, juxta oraculum Ioëlis: Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem. Et CHRISTI promissionem; Pater mittet paracletum in nomine meo.
units.tr: The eternal Father poured out the Holy Spirit from heaven, according to the oracle of Joel: "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh." And according to the promise of Christ: "The Father will send the Paraclete in my name."

units.la: Filius eundem mittit à patre: quemadmodum dixerat: Ego mittam eum vobis à patre: Et Petrus eventu promissionis veritatem comprobás; Jesus, inquit, dextra Dei evectus, & promissum Spiritum sanctum adeptus à patre effudit hoc quod videtis & auditis.
units.tr: The Son sends the same from the Father, as he had said: "I will send him to you from the Father." And Peter, by the event, confirms the truth of the promise: "Jesus, he says, exalted at the right hand of God, and having received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father, has poured out this which you see and hear."

units.la: Ipse Spiritus sanctus, specie venti, ignis, linguarum adest, extrema symbola sustentans & movens. vens. Non igitur est motus tantum; sed motor: non divina tantum operatio; sed Deus ipse operans: non qualitas; sed revera subsistens, vivus intelligens, super singulos sedet Apostolos, donis eos implet, variarum cognitione linguarum instruit, discussis ignorantiae tenebris nova divinarum rerum luce collustrat, μεγαλεῖα θεοῦ[?] eloqui facit.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit himself is present in the form of wind, fire and tongues, sustaining and moving the outward symbols. Therefore he is not merely a motion but a mover; not merely a divine operation but God himself operating; not a quality but truly a subsisting, living, understanding being. He sits upon each of the Apostles, fills them with gifts, instructs them in the knowledge of various tongues, dispels the darkness of ignorance with a new light of divine things, and makes them speak the mighty works of God.

units.la: Deus igitur est, pari cum æterno Patre & Filio potentia, pari immensitate, pari majestate: quoniam propria Dei habet & operatur.
units.tr: God therefore is, with the eternal Father and the Son, of equal power, equal immensity, equal majesty, since he has and performs the proper works of God.

units.la: Sed enim, ut vetus Pentecostes legis promul-gatione Judæis solennis fuit: ita nova Evangelii divulgatione in universas terrarum oras nobis memorabilis exsistit. Apostoli enim cœlitus Spi-ritu sancto, Doctore omnis veritatis illustrati & confirmati, & induti virtute ex alto, ut Dominus promiserat, mox variis linguis magnalia Dei e-loqui, & doctrinam de gratiâ & remissione pec-catorum, in omnes sub cœlo nationes spargere cœperunt: juxta præceptum Domini; Eritis mi-hi testes & in Jerusalem, & in tota Judæa, Samariaq; & usq; ad ultimas terras. In Pentecoste igitur facta primum est Evangelii in universum orbem publicatio. Cujus ante prædicatio Judææ[?] solùm inclusa, & angustis coarctata terminis fuit.
units.tr: But just as the old Pentecost was solemn for the Jews through the promulgation of the law, so the new one is memorable for us through the spreading of the Gospel to the ends of the earth. For the Apostles, enlightened and confirmed from heaven by the Holy Spirit, the Teacher of all truth, and clothed with power from on high, as the Lord had promised, immediately began to speak the great works of God in various tongues and to spread the doctrine of grace and remission of sins among all the nations under heaven, according to the command of the Lord: "You shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth." Therefore at Pentecost there was first made the publication of the Gospel throughout the whole world. Its earlier preaching had been confined to Judea alone and restricted within narrow limits.

units.la: Atqui hinc obscurum esse non potest, tanto præclarius esse hoc novum beneficium vetere; quanto ipsa Evangelii doctrina legis concionem præcellit, cujus quidem differentiæ rationes A-postolus 2.Cor.3. prolixè exponit.
units.tr: Yet from this it cannot be obscure that this new benefit is as much more excellent than the old as the very doctrine of the Gospel surpasses the preaching of the law, the reasons for which difference the Apostle sets out at length in 2 Cor. 3.

units.la: Lex olim quidem tabulis lapideis inscripta fuit digito Dei: at Evangelium tabulis carneis cordium inscriptum est spiritu Dei viventis. Hoc enim est novum illud fœdus, hæc nova illa lex, quam per Ieremiam promiserat Deus, se inscri-bere velle visceribus nostris, ut cognoscamus i-psum omnes à minimo ad maximum, &c.
units.tr: The law was once indeed written on tables of stone by the finger of God; but the Gospel is written on the fleshy tables of the heart by the Spirit of the living God. For this is that new covenant, this new law, which God promised through Jeremiah, that he would write it upon our inward parts, so that all of us might know him, from the least to the greatest, etc.

units.la: Sed nónne vetus etiam lex nostris inscripta cordibus est, testante Apostolo; gentes ostende-re opus legis in cordibus suis? Rom. 2. Ita sanè est; in natura quippe integra fulgebat & vigebat lex Dei perfectissimè: verum post lapsum Scri-ptura illa tantum non tota deleta est & oblitera-ta: In mentibus horribilis secuta est cæcitas, in cordibus ἀπξία[?], eaque tanta, ut si quæ maximè reliquæ notitiæ æqui & recti etiam supersint, lan-guidè[?] tamen valde, & exiles illæ sint, tantum ad hoc sufficientes, ut omnes coram Dei tribunali simus ἀναπολόγητοι[?]. Sed & aliter lex, aliter Evan-gelii doctrina cordibus inscripta dicitur: legis in-scriptio nuda tantum justitiæ & rectitudinis no-titia est: Evangelii autem vera & salutaris Dei & mediatoris est agnitio, cum fide & obedientia nova conjuncta, quam Spiritus sanctus per Evan-gelium operatur.
units.tr: But is not the old law also written on our hearts, as the Apostle witnesses, when he says that the Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts? Rom. 2. So indeed it is; for in nature, while it was whole, the law of God shone and flourished most perfectly. But after the fall that writing was almost entirely destroyed and erased; in the minds there followed a horrible blindness, and in the hearts a... such that, if any remaining notions of equity and right are still left, they are yet very feeble and slight, sufficient only for this, that we are all without excuse before the tribunal of God. But also the law is said to be written on hearts in one way, and the doctrine of the Gospel in another: the inscription of the law is only a bare knowledge of justice and rectitude; but the Gospel is the true and saving knowledge of God and of the Mediator, joined with new faith and obedience, which the Holy Spirit works through the Gospel.

units.la: Porrò etiam lex est litera occidens; Evan-gelium Spiritus vivificans: illa ministerium mor-tis; hoc vitæ: illa damnationis; hoc justitiæ. Illa enim universum hominum genus maledictione involvit; hoc per Christum ab ea absolvit: illa reos omnes injustitiæ peragit; hoc gratiæ Dei per Christum restituit.
units.tr: Moreover, the law is also the letter that kills; the Gospel the Spirit that gives life; the former the ministry of death, the latter of life; the former of condemnation, the latter of righteousness. For the former binds the whole human race under a curse; the latter through Christ absolves it from that; the former drives all who are guilty of injustice; the latter restores them to the grace of God through Christ.

units.la: Etsi verò lex quoque est doctrina justitiæ & vitæ: non tamen ejus est, quæ in Christo nobis donadonatur : sed justitiæ cujusdam propriæ, quam nemo habet extra Christum; & vitæ cum conditione obedientiæ perfectæ, quæ in solo Christo reperitur. Ea quippe vox legis est: Si ad vitam vis ingredi, serva mandata. Qui servaverit, vivet. Co-tra Evangelii. Resipiscite & credite Evangelio. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit salvus erit.
units.tr: Although the law is also a teaching of righteousness and life, it does not belong to the righteousness that is given to us in Christ, but to a certain proper righteousness, which no one has outside Christ, and to a life on the condition of perfect obedience, which is found in Christ alone. For this is the voice of the law: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. He who keeps them shall live." Against this is the voice of the Gospel: "Repent and believe the Gospel. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved."

units.la: Cum autem legem alibi spiritualem dicit Apostolus, eo non dicit, quasi vivificans, quemadmodum Evangelium, spiritus sit, verum hactenus tantum, quâ & ipsa obedientiam spiritualem requirit, & cum Evangelio conjuncta corda ad conversionem præparat, atque conversis instituendæ vitæ secundum Dei voluntatem norma est & regula. Contrà cum Evangelium quoque occidere & quibusdam odorem mortis ad mortem esse ait[?], culpæ illud & infidelitati homi-num adscribendum, non ipsius Evangelii naturæ est. Per se enim in salutem prædicatur; homines vivificat, fidem accendit, corda convertit. Incredulis vero ut sit occasio damnationis eorum ipsorum contingit vitio.
units.tr: When the Apostle elsewhere calls the law spiritual, he does not mean that it is spirit in the way the Gospel is, giving life; he means only so far as it also requires spiritual obedience, prepares hearts joined with the Gospel for conversion, and is, for those converted, the rule and standard by which a life is to be ordered according to the will of God. On the other hand, when he says that the Gospel too kills, and is to some "the savour of death unto death," this must be ascribed to the fault and unbelief of men, not to the nature of the Gospel itself. For in itself it is preached unto salvation; it gives life to men, kindles faith, and converts hearts. That it becomes an occasion of damnation for unbelievers comes about by their own vice.

units.la: Ad hæc lex quoque temporaria: Evangelium æternum est. Lex enim & prophetæ usque ad Ioannem; & novo inito fœdere, vetus antiquatum & abrogatum merito est. Nam etsi lex regula justitiæ Dei constans & æterna est, quatenus animis naturaliter ingenita, creaturam rationalem ad obedientiam Deo præstandam perpetuò obligat: Abrogata tamen & abolita per Christum est, quatenus damnare nos propter Christi satisfactionem & meritum non potest: nec ad obedientiam interminatione æternæ maledictionis amplius cogit. Nec enim secundum legem amplius nos judicat Deus, nec sub lege sumus, sed sub gratia: & accepimus Spiritum non servitutis & timoris, ut olim: sed libertatis & υἱοθεσίας[?]. Cærimoniæ vero & forensia sublata sunt penitus. Est enim maceries illa diruta, & sole exorto, umbræ evanuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the law is temporary, but the Gospel is eternal. "For the law and the prophets were until John," and with the new covenant made, the old has rightly been made obsolete and abrogated. For although the law, as a rule of God's righteousness, is constant and eternal, in so far as it is naturally implanted in minds and perpetually binds the rational creature to render obedience to God, nevertheless it has been abrogated and abolished through Christ, in so far as it cannot condemn us on account of Christ's satisfaction and merit, nor any longer compel us to obedience by the threat of eternal curse. For God no longer judges us according to the law, nor are we under the law, but under grace; and we have received the Spirit not of bondage and fear, as formerly, but of liberty and adoption. The ceremonies and forensic matters, however, have been wholly taken away. For that wall has been broken down, and when the sun has risen, the shadows have vanished.

units.la: Postremò legis illud ministerium tectum fuit & obscurum vaticiniis & typis variis involutum: Evangelium contra est clarum & retectum. Ibi enim velamen in facie Mosis manebat; hic retectâ facie gloriam Domini in speculo omnes conspicimus, in eandem imaginem de gloriâ in gloriâ transformamur. Quid-ni igitur cum Apostolo concludamus tandem? Si ministerium damnationis gloriosum fuit: quomodo non magis excellat ministerium justitiæ in gloriâ?
units.tr: Lastly, that ministry of the law was covered and obscure, wrapped in various prophecies and types; the Gospel, on the contrary, is clear and uncovered. For there the veil remained upon the face of Moses; here, with the face uncovered, we all behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, and are transformed into the same image from glory to glory. Why then should we not at last conclude with the Apostle: If the ministry of condemnation was glorious, how much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory?

units.la: Breviter dona contulimus: conferamus nunc strictim fructus & effectus. Lex ergo peccata accusabat, ira efficiebat, condenationi[?] omnes adjudicabat. Hinc metus, hinc cōtumacia, hinc pœnæ. Lex jugum erat intolerabile: pædagogia quidem ad Christum, sed cum servitute dura, laboriosa & quasi cogente coniuncta. At vero Spiritus S. adveniens quæ & quanta effecit? Apostolos mirandâ linguarum varietate instruxit, invictâ animi magnitudine, constantia, libertate armavit, muniit. Hinc illi magnalia Dei intrepide loqui, in nomine Christi μετὰ παῤῥησίας[?] docere, fortiter hostibus sese opponere, in afflictionibus suis gaudere, doctrinæ veritatem sanguine suo obsignare. Orem omnium sæculorum admiratione dignissimam! pauci piscatores, rudes, viles, contemti repente omniū linguarū & doctrinarum scientiā perfusi, doctores prodeūt, philosophos oēs, oratores oēs, oēs omniū doctissimos, longissimo post se intervallo relinquūt, orbem peragrāt, ubi que docēt, paucis annis universū nomine & doctrinā Iesu implēt, nullis hostibus cedūt, patiēdo vincunt, moriendo vivunt. Hoc, hoc effecit unus ille Spiritus, hic auctor, hic συνεργος fuit.
units.tr: Briefly we have set out the gifts; let us now run briefly through the fruits and effects. The law, therefore, accused sins, produced wrath, and adjudged all to condemnation. Hence fear, hence stubbornness, hence punishments. The law was an intolerable yoke; it was indeed a schoolmaster leading to Christ, but joined with hard, laborious and, as it were, compelling servitude. But what and how great were the effects when the Holy Spirit came? He instructed the Apostles with a wonderful variety of tongues; he armed and fortified them with invincible greatness of mind, constancy and freedom. Hence they fearlessly spoke the wonderful works of God, taught in the name of Christ "with boldness" [μετὰ παῤῥησίας], bravely set themselves against enemies, rejoiced in their afflictions, and sealed the truth of the doctrine with their blood. O a work most worthy of the admiration of all ages! A few fishermen, rude, base, despised, suddenly bathed in the knowledge of all tongues and teachings, come forth as teachers; they leave all philosophers, all orators, all the most learned of all men, far behind them at the greatest distance; they wander through the world, teach everywhere, within a few years fill the whole world with the name and doctrine of Jesus; they yield to no enemies, they conquer by suffering, and by dying they live. This, this, one and the same Spirit effected; he was the author, he was the fellow-worker [συνεργος].

units.la: Sed an in solis Apostolis efficax fuit? Imo vero etiamnū mentes nostras per Evangeliū vera agnitione Dei & mediatoris illuminat, fidem accendit, corda movet. Hic n. Spiritus ille sapientiæ est, in oēs electos largiter effusus, ut oēs prophetent, omnes cognoscāt Deum, omnes in veritatem ducantur. Hæc est aqua illa munda effusa, hic Spiritus ille pietatis, qui corda nostra purificat, regenerat, sanctificat, per Evangelii verbum & Sacramentorum usum. Hic Spiritus ille gratiæ, & precum est, qui dictat, excitat in nobis preces, per quem clamamus Abba pater. Nam quid precemur nos nescimus: Spiritus est, qui interpellat pro nobis suspiriis inenarrabilibus. Hic paracletus est, hic arrhabo salutis, hic electos consolatur, confirmat & obsignat. Hic consilii & fortitudinis Spiritus nobiscum manet, & non modo dona illa salutis, sed & dona vocationis necessaria in omnibus omnia operatur. Omnia enim efficit unus ille, & idem Spiritus, distribuens privatim illa singulis, sicut vult.
units.tr: But was he effective in the Apostles alone? Indeed, even now he illuminates our minds through the Gospel with true knowledge of God and of the Mediator, kindles faith, and moves hearts. For that Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom, poured out abundantly upon all the elect, so that all may prophesy, all may know God, all may be led into the truth. This is that clean water poured out, this is that Spirit of piety, who purifies, regenerates and sanctifies our hearts, through the word of the Gospel and the use of the sacraments. This is the Spirit of grace and of prayers, who dictates and stirs up prayers in us, by whom we cry "Abba, Father." "For we know not what we should pray for; but the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." He is the Paraclete, he is the pledge of salvation; he comforts, strengthens and seals the elect. This Spirit of counsel and fortitude remains with us, and works in all things, not only those gifts of salvation but also the gifts of calling that are necessary. "For all these things worketh that one and the same Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will."

units.la: Hi Evangelii, hi Spiritus Sancti fructus sunt. Evangelium itaque non nos accusat, ut lex: sed absolabsolvit; non terret, ut lex; sed erigit: non nobis iugum imponit, ut lex; sed detrahit: non Christum in umbris monstrat, ut lex; sed in speculo exhibet.
units.tr: These are the fruits of the Gospel and of the Holy Spirit. The Gospel, therefore, does not accuse us as the law does, but absolves; it does not terrify as the law does, but raises up; it does not impose a yoke upon us as the law does, but removes it; it does not show Christ in shadows as the law does, but sets him forth in a mirror.

units.la: Sed longius oratione provehor, Auditores, quam volui: & temporis me ratio, atque singularis vestra humanitas, ut vela contraham, portumque tandem aliquando respiciam, monet. Quare finem hic dicendi faciam. Ex his autem quae dicta hactenus sunt; liquido dilucet, quanto gloriosior sit, Evangelii promulgatio in Pentecoste, per Spiritum Sanctum in Apostolos effusum, quanto illustrior; quam legis olim latio in monte Sinai fuerit. Ibi enim clare quidem, hic vero clarissime sese Deus patefecit: ibi beneficium magnum quidem; sed hic maximum in Ecclesiam uberrime transfudit.
units.tr: But I have been carried on in my speech longer than I wished, hearers; and the measure of time, together with your singular kindness, warns me to furl my sails and at last look toward the harbour. Therefore I shall make an end of speaking here. From what has been said so far, it is clear how much more glorious the promulgation of the Gospel at Pentecost was, through the Holy Spirit poured out upon the Apostles, and how much more illustrious it was than the giving of the law of old on Mount Sinai. For there God revealed himself clearly, but here most clearly; there he conferred a great benefit, but here he has poured out the greatest benefit most abundantly upon the Church.

units.la: Par proinde est, (ni ingrati esse velimus) ut Domino Deo Servatori nostro, quantas mens nostra capere potest, gratias agamus, quòd Spiritum Sanctum suum largissime, prout promisit, Ecclesiae suae donavit, quòd Evangelium suum ad nos quoque propagavit, atque eo sibi inter nos Ecclesiam colligit; eundemque, ut eadem nobis beneficia diutissime confervet, rogemus & invocemus.
units.tr: It is therefore fitting (unless we wish to be ungrateful) that we give thanks to the Lord God our Saviour, as much as our mind can grasp, that he has most abundantly bestowed his Holy Spirit upon his Church, as he promised, that he has spread his Gospel to us also, and by it gathers his Church among us; and that we ask and invoke him to preserve these same benefits for us for a very long time.

units.la: Quod restat igitur, ad tuam Domine Iesu divinam clementiam, & bonitatem singularem recurrimus: tibi gratias primùm, tibi laudes, tibi honores pro his tantis beneficiis, quorum auctor nobis abitu tuo ad patrem exstitisti, perpetuos deferimus & immortales. Deinde summam tuam rogamus potentiam, ac immensam testamur pietatem, ut in tanta hac omnium rerum cō fusione, Ecclesiam tuam à variis hostibus varie oppugnatam propugnes, contra crudelissimorum nominis tui sanctissimi hostium furores defendas; potentiam ipsorum & superbiam perfringas, ut te omnes unicum, summum, verum æternum Deum & Dominum dominantium agnoscere, revereri & adorare cogantur. Germaniæ[?] nostræ tranquillitatem tueaRis, sartam tectam præstes, hospitia docentium & discentium quieta concedas, pios & salutares principes, recte te agnoscentes & invocantes, Ecclesiarum & scholarum nutricios, excites, serves. In primis Illustriss.[?] principem Dn. FRIDERICUM IV. Electorem Palatinum, Dominum nostrum, & patronum clementissimum. Spiritu sapientiæ, consilii, fortitudinis indies magis magisque regas, in vera pietate, sapientia divina & valetudine[?] prosperâ conserves, ut sub felicissima Celsitud. eius gubernatione & patrocinio, tuis illis[?] donis concessis, quâ diutissime utamur fruamur. Floreat Respub. gaudeat Ecclesia, gratulentur sibi omnes pii, nosq; in hac & futurâ vitâ æternum te laudemus & celebremus.
units.tr: What remains, therefore, is that we have recourse to your divine clemency and singular goodness, Lord Jesus: to you we offer, first, thanks, praises and honours, perpetual and immortal, for these great benefits, of which you became the author to us by your departure to the Father. Then we ask your supreme power and profess your immense piety, that in this great confusion of all things you would defend your Church, assailed in various ways by various enemies, and protect it against the furies of the most cruel enemies of your most holy name; that you would break their power and pride, so that all are compelled to acknowledge, reverence and adore you as the one, highest, true, eternal God and Lord of lords. Guard the tranquillity of our Germany, keep it safe and sound, grant quiet dwellings to teachers and learners; raise up and preserve pious and salutary princes, who rightly acknowledge and invoke you, the nurturers of Churches and schools. Above all, the most illustrious prince, Lord Frederick IV, Elector Palatine, our Lord and most gracious patron: may you rule him more and more each day by the Spirit of wisdom, counsel and fortitude, preserve him in true piety, divine wisdom and prosperous health, so that under his most fortunate government and patronage we may use and enjoy, for a very long time, those gifts of yours that have been granted. May the commonwealth flourish, may the Church rejoice, may all the pious congratulate themselves, and may we praise and celebrate you eternally in this life and in the future.

units.la: Amen, Amen, Domine Iesu, qui cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto, unus Deus vivis & regnas in omnia sæcula. Dixi.
units.tr: Amen, Amen, Lord Jesus, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, one God, world without end. I have spoken.

units.la: ORATIO XII. DE DONO LINGUARUM COLLATO APOSTOLIS in prima Pentecoste.
units.tr: Oration 12: On the Gift of Tongues Bestowed on the Apostles on the First Pentecost.

units.la: Recitata à IOHANNE WELLERO pridie Pentecostes 29. Maij anno 1596.
units.tr: Recited by John Weller on the day before Pentecost, 29 May, in the year 1596.

units.la: VEteris, atque adeo, inde ab ipsis Apostolorum temporibus, consueti Ecclesiæ moris est, ut diebus hisce, folenni festivitate, nec non sin gulari animorum devotione, admirabilis Spiritus Sancti super Apostolos effusionis memoriam repetamus & celebremus. Quæ consuetudo superstitionis, aut alterius cuiusdam ᾧ Διαθήκης[?] nomine à quoquâ sugillari Aristarcho usque adeo non debet; ut potius cuiusvis religione Christiani hominis maximū officium sit, eam sanctâ, religiosâque observatione approbare, approbatam posteris transmittere, sancteque colendam commendare. Maximè verò, nos, qui scholasticum vitæ genus sequimur, doctrinæ cœlesti, sacrosanctisque eius mysteriis rectius aliquanto & accuratius cognoscendis dediti sumus; decetcō-[?]mendatam eam habere, contendereq;, ut, quemadmodum aliis doctrinæ cognitione, morum exemplis, vitæ probitate, præire debemus: maiori item Spiritus S. auxilio, maioribus donis opus habemus: ita etiam præ cæteris maiori quodam atque excellentiori celebrationis genere, beneficiorum eius longe maximorum, memoriam pro sequamur.
units.tr: It is the long-standing custom of the Church, going back to the very times of the Apostles, that in these days we recall and celebrate, with solemn festivity and a special devotion of souls, the memory of the wonderful outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles. This custom should not be censured by anyone as superstition, or as some other thing, as though it were a matter of Aristarchus' rejection; rather, it is the greatest duty of any Christian to approve it by holy and devout observance, to hand it down to posterity once approved, and to commend it to be devoutly kept. Above all, we who follow the scholarly way of life are devoted to learning the heavenly doctrine and its holy mysteries more correctly and more carefully. It is fitting that we hold this custom in regard, and that we strive, just as we ought to go before others in the knowledge of doctrine, in examples of conduct and in integrity of life, so also we need greater help of the Holy Spirit and greater gifts; so too, above all others, we should follow the memory of his by far greatest benefits with a greater and more excellent kind of celebration.

units.la: Cum autem mihi, eam, ut videtis, provinciam suscipienti, non dubium fit, quin & antea probè, sciteque cognita vestris animis hæreat, & per hos etiam festos dies, in plærisque Ecclesiæ cœtibus, copiose iuxta atque luculente explicatum eatur præcipua de Spiritu Sancto doctrina, quis, qualis, & quæ eius beneficia sint: existimavi nihil me vel ab hoc tempore, vel ab his studiis & exercitationibus nostris, alienum facturum, si omissis illis, cæterisque id genus doctrinæ partibus, in præsenti, de linguarum Ecclesiæ collato dono, nonnihil quàm simplicissimè & brevissimè dicerem.
units.tr: Since I, as you see, have undertaken this task, there is no doubt that what has been known well and skilfully before still clings to your minds, and that during these festive days, in most assemblies of the Church, the chief teaching about the Holy Spirit (who he is, what he is like, and what his benefits are) is being explained copiously and clearly. I thought that I would not be acting out of place, either at this time or in these studies and exercises of ours, if, leaving aside those and the other parts of this kind of doctrine, I spoke briefly and as simply as possible, at present, about the gift of tongues bestowed on the Church.

units.la: Cuius quanta sit excellentia, dignitas & maiestas, non existimo, in hac humani generis imbecillitate, quenquam dari posse, qui ingenio suo capere, nedum oratione explicare, atque exornare, satis valeat. Vobis, ut eius aliquam coniecturam æstimationemque facere mentibus vestris queatis; paucis, priusquam ad alia progrediamur, quomodo super Apostolos descenderit Spiritus Sanctus, & quid tum acciderit ex Lucæ Evangelistæ Apostolicâ historiâ commemorabo.
units.tr: I do not think that anyone in this weakness of the human race can be found who is able, by his own wit, to grasp, let alone explain and adorn in speech, how great the excellence, dignity and majesty of this gift is. So that you may be able to form in your minds some conjecture and estimate of it, I will briefly recall, before we proceed to other matters, how the Holy Spirit came down upon the Apostles and what then happened, from the apostolic history of the Evangelist Luke.

units.la: Cum in eo iam esset, ut Dominus Servator ꝑoster[?] peractis in terra omnibus, quæ ad obtinendam asserendamq; generis humani salutem pertinebant, sursum in cœlos recipiebatur; congregatis undecim discipulis suis, etiam atque etiã iniungebat, ut se sursum recepto, Hierosolymis neq; hac, neq; illac declinantes, assiduè exspectarent Patris, de quo sæpè eis locutus esset, promissum: simul etiã recipiebat futurum, ut superveniente in eos spiritu, eiusdē δυνάμεως[?] ac virtutis compotes fierent atque participes. Hi igitur sublato paulò post in cœlum Domino, fidelem dictis obedientiam præstantes, e vestigio in urbem revertuntur; inibi indies precibus ad Deum patrem fusis, promissum præstolantur. Tandem vero in ipsa Pentecostes solemnitate, posteaquã in unum domi cuiusdam conclave, ad unum convenisset omnes, ecce, quid accidit? Derepente ad eos cœlitus deruit Spiritus Sanctus, maximo sonitu, ac velut impetuosissimi venti cuiusdam flatu. Igneam induta formam insidet super unum eorum quemque. Linguæ ipsorum igneæ conspiciuntur ac minutarum quarundam flammularum instar dissectæ atq; diffissæ. Inde extemplo variis, iisque diversissimis loqui linguis cœperunt, ita quidem, ut nulla gens sub sole degeret, cuius illi linguam non, quam optimè, quàm perfectissimè callerent, haud secus ac si vernaculæ eis essent, eas quæ cum primo nutricis lacte imbibissent. Itaque factum, ut, cum ea tèporis solennitate omnium ferè nationum homines in urbe versarentur, visis & auditis Apostolis, suam in quâ quisque nati essent, audientes linguam, mirarentur, obstupe-scerent, & exclamarent, quid hoc rei esse possit? nonne omnes illi, qui loquuntur Galilaei sunt? Quo-modo igitur nos audimus, eos sua quisque lingua, in qua nati sumus, loquentes? Parthi & Medi & Ela-mita, & qui incolimus Mesopotamiam, Judaeam, Cappadociam, Pontum, Asiam, Phrygiam, Pamphy-liam, & Aegyptum & Cyrenaicas partes Lybia, & ad-vena Romani, & Cretes & Arabes, quomodo audi-mus eos nostris linguis rerum divinarum amplitudi-nem eloquentes. Haec, Auditores, perspicua & brevis historiae summa est. Qua sane, si quicquam est aliud, quod nos ad amandum, fovendum & excolendum linguarum donum incitare atque impellere possit, nō video, quid eam ad rem plus roboris & momenti obtinere queat. Ecquid enim auribus vestris accidit, ecquid legistis, vidi-stis, insolentius, inusitatius, admirabilius? Quamquam igitur hoc ita fit, & in eo dignitatis atque excellentiae argumento satis habeatur, quod doni huius amorem ac studium in unoquoque nostrum accendere debeat & possit: eo tamen in praesens toto omisso, aliis haud contemnendis rationibus συνε[?], ostendam, operam in Ecclesia dandam esse, quàm maximam, ut linguarum semel acceptum donum foveatur, conservetur & excolatur. Atque hoc praecipuum orationis nostrae caput erit. Prius tamen, quam illud aggrediar, breviter exponenda quaedam sunt; primum quale fuerit linguarum Apostolis collatum donum: Deinde, quis eius author; tum, quis usus; denique, an etiamnum his nostris temporibus Ecclesiae impertiatur.
units.tr: When the Lord and Saviour was now about to be taken up into heaven, having completed on earth everything that pertained to obtaining and securing the salvation of the human race, he gathered his eleven disciples and again and again charged them that, after he had been taken up, they should not wander this way or that from Jerusalem, but should constantly wait for the promise of the Father, of which he had often spoken to them; at the same time he foretold that, when the Spirit came upon them, they would become partakers and sharers in the same power and virtue. So these men, after the Lord was taken up into heaven shortly afterwards, rendered faithful obedience to his words, and at once returned to the city; there, daily pouring out prayers to God the Father, they awaited the promise. At last, on the very solemnity of Pentecost, after all had come together into one upper room of a certain house, behold, what happened? Suddenly the Holy Spirit came down to them from heaven with a great sound, as though with the blast of a most violent wind. He took the form of fire and settled upon each one of them. Their tongues were seen to be fiery, and divided and split apart like small flames. Immediately they began to speak in various and most diverse tongues, so that there was no nation under the sun whose language they did not know, as well as, and as perfectly as, if it were their native tongue, which they had drunk in with their nurse's milk. And so it came about that, since at that season of the festival men of almost all nations were living in the city, when they saw and heard the Apostles, each hearing the language in which he had been born, they were amazed, astonished and cried out: what can this thing be? Are not all these who speak Galileans? How is it that we hear them, each speaking in his own language in which we were born? Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and we who live in Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt and the Cyrenaic parts of Libya, and the visiting Romans, and Cretans and Arabs: how do we hear them speaking of the greatness of divine things in our own tongues? This, hearers, is the clear and brief sum of the history. Certainly, if there is anything else that can stir and impel us to love, cherish and cultivate the gift of tongues, I do not see what greater strength and weight it could obtain for that purpose. For what has happened to your ears, what have you read or seen more unusual, more unfamiliar, more wonderful? Although this is so, and it is considered enough of a proof of its dignity and excellence that it ought to be able to kindle in each of us love and zeal for this gift, nevertheless, leaving all that aside for the present, I will show, by other reasons not to be despised, that the greatest possible effort must be made in the Church so that the gift of tongues, once received, may be fostered, preserved and cultivated. This will be the chief heading of our oration. Before I take that up, however, certain things must be briefly set out: first, what kind of gift of tongues was bestowed on the Apostles; then, who was its author; next, what its use was; and finally, whether it is still imparted to the Church in our own times.

units.la: Vt ergo qualenam illud Apostolis collatum linguarum donum fuerit, initio intelligamus, nō desunt, qui opinentur, donum illud, veram linguis multis loquendi facultatem non fuisse, sed co[?] miraculo factum, ut Apostolos unâ vernaculâ suâ differentes, omnes, cuicuimodi essent, apud quos sermonem haberent, intelligerent. Verum hanc opinionem rei veritati historiæque minimè consentaneam esse, non difficile est animadvertere. Ubi enim & in qua hominum miraculum parratum[?] & spectatum fuit? Apostolorumne, qui loquebantur, an eorum, qui audiebant? Horum opinor. Illis namque promissus singulariter iam ante paracletus Spiritus Sanctus fuerat: super illos igneâ specie sedebat: in illis linguæ dissectæ & dispertitæ videbantur: de illis rumor in urbem exibat, & ad eos omnis multitudo confluebat. Iam quid agebant illi? ἤρξαντο λαλεῖν ἑτέ-ραις γλώσσαις, inquit Lucas, coeperunt loqui linguis aliis. Hoc quid rei est? an quod illi putant, unâ linguâ & vernacula loqui & à plurimis diversarum linguarum hominibus intelligi? At non unius, sed plurium Evangelistâ mentionem facit; coeperunt, inquiens, loqui linguis, non linguâ. Expressè addit etiam, ἑτέρας[?], aliis. Quo quid significari putemus aliud, quam locutos eos esse linguis & eiusmodi quidem, quæ aliæ, hoc est, diversæ ab ea essent, quam vernaculam habebant; & ut verbo dicam, quas Marcus Evangeliographus non dubitavit novarum appellare nomine? An verò hisce linguis audiri duntaxat coeperunt? an visi duntaxat sunt illis loqui? Immo ipsi, perhibente historia, loqui coeperunt, & cum maximo omnium, qui audiebant intelligebantq;, stupore & admiratione locuti sunt. Quod si ita est, ut autumant illi, scriptum oportuit & sine dubio scriptum legeremus, coepisse eos non linguis, sed lingua, non aliis, sed sua & usitata, non loqui, sed audiri. Sed & donum linguarum tale non fuisse, quo uno, suo idiomate loquentes ab auditoribus eo, quod quisq; tenebat, intelligerentur, ex multis D.Pauli locis & dictis apparet, præsertim eius, q; Corinthiis perscripsit, Epistolæ. Inter alia, cap.12.ponit singulare donum linguarum, seu, ut expressius ille, generum linguarum, & distinguit ab eo, quod est interpretationis earundem. Alii, inquit, dantur per Spiritum facultates edendarum, δυνάμεων[?] alii prophetia, alii discretiones Spiritum, alij genera linguarum, alij interpretatio linguarum. Num omnes prophetæ? doctores? num omnes donum habent sanationum? num omnes linguis loquuntur? num omnes interpretantur. Alibi inquit, Si linguis hominum loquar & Angelorum. Sic: Eo, qui loquitur linguis, maior est, qui prophetat, nisi interpretetur. Item. Lingua cessabunt. Quid multis? Apostolorum libri, Græcè scripti sermone, satis hac re loquuntur. Qui.n. obsecro scriptores illi fuerunt? None ex medio vulgo idiotæ, domi educati, literarum & linguarum externarum, Græcæ præsertim, ignari? Quomodo igitur Græco idiomate, ꝑ[?] didicerat nūq & nuspiā, tot volumina exaraverunt, nisi ex hoc dono? Qua-obrem, Auditores, relictis illis, ita ceseamus, quæ tunc mira acciderunt, in Apostolis accidisse; atque eis linguarum exoticarum tantam notitiam & facultatem contigisse, quanta non solum ad familiarem hominum convictum & societatem obeundam satis esset, sed quanta omnino ad Christi doctrinam ubique Gentium praedicandam & celebrandam magnificè, singulis sufficeret.
units.tr: So, that we may first understand what kind of gift of tongues was bestowed on the Apostles, there are some who think that this gift was not a true ability to speak many languages, but that it was brought about by a miracle, so that the Apostles, though each speaking only his own vernacular, were understood by all, of whatever kind they were, to whom they spoke. But it is not difficult to see that this opinion is not at all consistent with the truth of the matter and with history. For where and in whom was the miracle wrought and witnessed? In the Apostles who spoke, or in those who heard? In the latter, I suppose. For the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, had already been promised in a unique way to the Apostles; over them he sat in the appearance of fire; in them the tongues were seen to be divided and distributed; the rumour went out about them into the city, and the whole multitude flowed together to them. Now what were they doing? "They began to speak in other tongues," says Luke. What is this? Do they think it means that they spoke in one language, their own vernacular, and were understood by very many people of diverse languages? But the Evangelist makes mention not of one language but of several; he says, "they began to speak in tongues," not "in a tongue." He also expressly adds "other," that is, different. What else do we suppose this to mean, than that they spoke in tongues which were other, that is, different from the one they had as their native speech, and, to put it in a word, which the Evangelist Mark did not hesitate to call "new"? Or were they only heard speaking in these tongues? Or were they only seen to speak to them? Nay, as the history testifies, they themselves began to speak, and spoke with the greatest amazement and admiration of all who heard and understood. If it were as they claim, it would have had to be written, and without doubt we would read it written, that they began to speak not in tongues but in a tongue, not in other languages but in their own and customary one, and that they were not spoken but heard. But that the gift of tongues was not such that, speaking in one idiom of their own, they were understood by their hearers in whatever each one held, also appears from many passages and sayings of St Paul, especially from his epistle which he wrote to the Corinthians. Among other things, in chapter 12 he sets out the singular gift of tongues, or, as he says more expressly, the kinds of tongues, and distinguishes it from the gift of interpreting them. "To one," he says, "are given by the Spirit the abilities of working miracles; to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all have the gift of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?" Elsewhere he says, "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels." Likewise: "He who speaks in a tongue is greater than he who prophesies, unless he interprets." Again: "Tongues will cease." Why say more? The books of the Apostles, written in the Greek language, speak enough on this matter. For who, I beg you, were those writers? Were they not uneducated men from the common crowd, raised at home, ignorant of letters and of foreign languages, especially Greek? How then did they write so many volumes in the Greek idiom, which they had never learned from anyone anywhere, unless by this gift? Therefore, hearers, leaving those things aside, let us reckon that these wonderful things happened to the Apostles, and that such a great knowledge and ability in foreign tongues came to them, as would not only be sufficient for them to carry on familiar intercourse and fellowship with men, but would be sufficient for each of them to preach and proclaim the doctrine of Christ magnificently everywhere among the Gentiles.

units.la: Qualè fuerit donû, vidimus: iâ & author quis sit, videamus. Eû esse Spiritû coelestem illû omnium Oratorû ἀρχιδιδάσκαλον, verû & coæternû cum Patre & Filio Deum: ita arbitror esse perspicuû, utin eo asserendo anxiè soliciteq; laborare plane supervacaneû videatur. Pacatis & tranquillis fidelium hominum animis, verbo Dei acquiescere noscentibus, affatim & abûde satis est, quod de eo Evangelistæ & Apostoli diserte testatû reliquerûnt. Lucas expresse mentione Spiritus S. facit, cû ait, repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto & cœperunt loqui linguis aliis, sicut Spiritus eis dabat eloqui. D. Petrus in Apologia suâ idè Ioelis vaticinio demonstrat. Idè D. Paulus testatur 1. Cor. 12. cum alia Ecclesiæ dona, tû hoc etiâ ad Spiritum S. tanquam fontem & authore referens; Deinde quid aliud sibi linguarû differentiarû & ignearû apparitio volebat? Nihil opinor, q; ut ea tanquâ symbolo suam declararet Spiritus S. præsentiam, ostenderetq; se per-missam illâ verèq; ignea vim eius, q; fieri cerneretur, autorem & effectorem esse. Sed & res ipsa satis docet. Quid enim? Subito atq; adeo in ipso temporis articulo omniû, quotquot Sol videt, Gentium linguis loquuntur, homines imperiti, λειβηθρί-ων ἀμαθοσκόποι[?], nulla institutione prævia, nullâque disciplina imbuti. Divinum ergo magisterium in hoc sese omnium manifestissimè exseruit.
units.tr: It is clear enough what kind of gift this was; let us now see who its author is. That the Spirit of heaven, the chief teacher of all the speakers, is true God and co-eternal with the Father and the Son: I think this is so plain that to labour anxiously and laboriously in proving it would seem entirely superfluous. For the minds of believing people, which are calm and quiet and acknowledge the Word of God, it is more than sufficient that the Evangelists and Apostles have left clear testimony about him. Luke expressly mentions the Holy Spirit when he says: "they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Peter, in his own defence, likewise proves it by the prophecy of Joel. Paul too bears witness in 1 Cor. 12, when he refers the other gifts of the Church, and this one as well, to the Holy Spirit as their source and author. Further, what else did the appearance of the different tongues and of the fire mean? Nothing, I suppose, except that the Holy Spirit, by these signs as by a symbol, declared his presence and showed that the power which was seen to work was truly his, and that he was its author and effector. But the thing itself also teaches this plainly. For what happened? Suddenly, and at that very moment, all who were in sight of the sun spoke in the tongues of the Gentiles: men untaught, mere unlearned fishermen, with no prior instruction and steeped in no discipline. The divine teaching therefore showed itself most manifestly in this.

units.la: Nec verò est, quod aliquis hoc loco Dæmoniacos vel arreptitios nobis obiiciat, quos ignotâ aliquid lingua deblaterare forte aliquando contingit. Neque enim loquuntur ipsi, sed malus dæmon per eos ipsorum abutens linguis: miseri interim eorum quæ effutiunt haud quicquam intelligunt, sed tibiarum instar [?] aliunde inflati, sine mente sonos edunt. Itaque cum nostris Apostolis, quid isti tandem commune habent? Hi revera ipsi locuti sunt, & γνῶσις[?] sermonis sui formatores atque effectores extiterunt: illi minimè, verum per ipsos diabolus. Hi quid loquerentur, sciebat, intelligebant, linguas callebant: illi quid & quomodo proferant, neque sciunt, neque intelligunt. Nunc authorem etiam habemus: usum quoque paucis demonstremus miraculi.
units.tr: Nor is there reason for anyone here to object to us the demoniacs or the possessed, who sometimes happen to babble in some unknown tongue. For they do not speak themselves; rather an evil demon, abusing their tongues, speaks through them. Meanwhile those wretched people understand nothing of what they utter, but, like pipes blown from elsewhere, they make sounds without mind. So what in the end do those people have in common with our Apostles? The Apostles truly spoke themselves, and were the formers and effectors of the knowledge of their own speech. The demoniacs by no means; it is the devil who speaks through them. The Apostles knew what they were saying, understood it, and had mastered the languages; the others neither know nor understand what they utter or how. Now we have the author as well; let us briefly show the use of this miracle too.

units.la: Duplex ille potissimum fuit. Unum Apostolus indicat 1. Cor. 14. linguas infidelibus dicens esse signum, nempe, maledictionis & instantis pœnæ, iuxta comminationem Iesaiæ 28. propterea per diversa lingua homines, & per alia labia loquar populo huic, & ita quoque me non audient, dicit Dominus. Nam ut alia signa ædificabant piorum fidem: infidelium verò convincebant obstinationem: ita linguarum exoticarum donum præfratos Iudæos tanto magis redarguebat, quanto illustrius erat propheticarum prædictionum complementum.
units.tr: There was chiefly a twofold use. The Apostle points out the first in 1 Cor. 14, when he calls tongues a sign for unbelievers, namely a sign of curse and of impending punishment, in accordance with the threat of Isaiah 28: "Therefore I will speak to this people by men of other tongues and by other lips, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord." For just as the other signs built up the faith of the godly, but convinced the obstinacy of unbelievers, so the gift of foreign tongues condemned those Jews, already named, all the more, the more illustrious was the fulfilment of the prophetic predictions.

units.la: Alter usus longè fuit augustissimus. Nam linguarum beneficio fieri debuit, ut salutaris Evangelii concio, ex illis Gentis Hebræ angustiis educta, in omnes terras atq; maria propagaretur; omniomnibus populis, gentibus & nationibus annū-ciaretur. Cuius rei, ut specimen atque exemplum habeamus aliquod, non est, quod lōge abeamus. Ex eo est, quod in ipsa Pentecostes solemnitate, Parthi, Medi, Elamitæ, Mesopotamii & cæteri, audiverunt Apostolos suis linguis magnalia Dei memorantes. Quid, Auditores? nos ipsi huic linguarum beneficio debemus, quod in Evangelii cognitionem pervenimus, Christum Dominum & Salvatorem nostrū nominamus & adoramus. Quid enim, amabo, nos Germani de redemtionis salutisque omnis per Christum, Filium Dei præstitę beneficio tenerēmus, nisi fideles Dei ser-vi omnimoda illa linguarum cognitione instru-cti, nostro idiomate doctrinam Christi in hanc etiam mundi plagam disseminassent? Ita verò omnia hæc toti mundo innotuerunt, linguisque intelligi poterant, prædicata & scripta. Hunc si solummodo usum considere-mus & expendamus, quid miseris mortalibus donari potuit præstantius, dignius, utilius? Fateor, linguarum varietatem primitus exquisitis-simæ pœnæ loco inflictam fuisse. Quomodo ergo, inquis, tam ingens fuit donum? Sanè ingens donum hoc, ut illa ingens olim pœna fuit. Tunc enim, una cum esset omnium mortalium lingua, confusionem linguarum induxit Deus in Babel, ut ædificantium Cyclopicum turbaret furorem, atque disiiceret, efficiendo, ut nulli alios intelligere possent. At verò, quando exsistentibus iam multis linguis, illæ pluribus innotescunt, à pluribus intelliguntur, quomodo non peculiare Dei donum fit beneficiumque mortalibus longe utiliffimum? Quantum itaque bonum fit, quantumquead Ecclesiæ ædificationem momenti habeat sermonis communicatio, satis superque, vel illa Babylonicæ ædificationis dissipatio declarat.
units.tr: The second use was by far the most august. For by means of the gift of tongues it was to come about that the preaching of the saving Gospel, led out from the narrow confines of the Hebrew nation, should be spread into all lands and seas, and be announced to all peoples, nations and tribes. To have some specimen and example of this, we need not go far away. It is from this that, at the very festival of Pentecost, Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamians and the rest heard the Apostles recounting the mighty works of God in their own tongues. What of us, hearers? We ourselves owe to this gift of tongues that we have come to the knowledge of the Gospel, and that we name and worship Christ our Lord and Saviour. For, I ask you, what would we Germans have of the benefit of redemption and of all salvation accomplished through Christ the Son of God, unless the faithful servants of God, equipped with that complete knowledge of tongues, had spread the teaching of Christ in our own language even to this quarter of the world? Thus all these things became known to the whole world, and were preached and written in such a way that they could be understood in the languages. If we consider and weigh this use alone, what could be given to wretched mortals that was more excellent, more worthy, more useful? I grant that the variety of tongues was originally inflicted as a most exquisite punishment. How then, you will say, was it so great a gift? Certainly this gift is great, just as that punishment of old was great. For when there was one tongue of all mortals, God brought about the confusion of tongues at Babel, so as to disturb and scatter the Cyclopean fury of the builders, by bringing it about that none could understand the others. But now, when many tongues already exist and these become known to many and are understood by many, how is it not a peculiar gift of God and a benefit by far most useful to mortals? How great a good, then, and how much weight the communication of speech has for the building up of the Church, the very scattering of the Babylonian building sufficiently and more than sufficiently declares.

units.la: Superest, quod quarto quærebatur loco, an etiamnum Ecclesiæ linguarum communicetur donum. Etsi autem nihil videamus, quod illi inusitatæ & admirandæ Apostolorum rationi respondeat, non cernamus Spiritum Sanctum visibiliter hominibus insidentem, nullas igneas & dis-pertitas linguas: haud est tamen, quod quis ideo Ecclesiam, isto linguarum munere orbatam prorsus ac spoliatam arbitretur. Quod enim Ecclesiæ tunc miraculosa ratione: nunc studio atque institutione datur & confertur. Nam quantum ad miraculum attinet, pari id cum cæteris Ecclesiæ concessum fuit ratione & conditione, nempe ut sparsâ & confirmata in homines, quantum satis esset, Evangelii doctrinâ: ipsum pedetentim cessaret & aboleretur. Postquam ergo toti mundo lætissimum de Christo Servatore nuncium innotuit, atque ita constabilitum miraculis fuit, ut de eius veritate, nemo, nisi manifeste impius & pertinax dubitare amplius posset: quemadmodum cætera, ita & hæc miraculosa linguarum collatio cessavit. Interea cum sine earum cognitione haud facile colligi ac doceri Ecclesia queat, non definit Spiritus Sanctus eam institutione studio & exercitatione, publicâ & privatâ, aliquibus Ecclesiæ præstare atque impertiri membris. Hoc est, quod & Apostolus innuit, cum ait, nemo potest Iesum nominare Christum, nisi per Spiritum Sanctum. Et paucis post, per eundem Spiritum datur λόγος σοφίας, λόγος γνώσεως, ἑτέρῳ πίστις[?], ἀγχείσεως[?], πνεῦ-μάτων, γένη γλωσσῶν, ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν. Neque loquitur de donis tantum, quorum illis temporibus in Ecclesia Corinthiacâ usus vigebat; verum in universum de donis, quibus populum suum Deus omnibus temporibus ornaturus & exædificaturus erat. Neque enim ad nos minus, atque ad Corinthios illa pertinet doctrina. Ut nihil de eo dicam, quod hæc dona, maximam partem itâ Ecclesiæ necessaria sunt, ut eis carere non sine maximâ queat iactura. Sed, inquiat aliquis soli igitur, tuâ sententiâ, Ecclesiæ cives hoc munere affecti erunt. At quam multi extra Ecclesiæ pomœria inveniuntur & inventi sunt homines, à fide & religione Christianâ prorsus alieni, qui egregia linguarum cognitione excelluerunt? Utique ita esse diffiteri non possumus. Ergo illi aut Spiritum Sanctum habuerunt, aut donum hoc inter Spiritus Sancti Ecclesiæ collata dona reponendum non erit. Neutrum sequitur. Ratio obscura non est, quoniam, quæ linguarum cognitio impiis atque extra Solomonis porticum versantibus hominibus contingit, non à singulari illa & speciali Spiritus Sancti actione, quæ in solam proprie Ecclesiam fertur, proficiscitur: verum à communi seu generali Dei operatione promanat. Atque hoc pacto non Spiritus Sancti; sed in genere Dei munus ac donum est, quicquid homines extra Ecclesiæ septa boni & præclari tenent. Quæ verò piis, Ecclesiæ membris obtingunt, non solum Dei generalis actionis sunt, sed & Spiritus Sancti specialis. Quemadmodum extra Ecclesiam qualiscunq; Dei cognitio quidem viget: in sola autem Ecclesia Spiritus Sanctus agnoscitur; & operari in sanctis dicitur, quicquid scientiæ & cognitionis eximiæ rerum divinarum & humanarum, prudentiæ, itē m, facundiæ & aliorum donorum, studio & disciplina, divina aspirante gratia, comparatum est. Mundus vero Spiritum Sanctum nec novit, nec accipit, nec operationem eius in se sentit vel percipit ullam.
units.tr: There remains what was asked in the fourth place: whether the gift of tongues is still bestowed on the Church.
