Although we see nothing that corresponds to that unusual and wonderful manner of the Apostles, we do not see the Holy Spirit sitting visibly upon men, nor fiery and divided tongues, yet there is no reason why anyone should therefore think the Church is utterly deprived and stripped of this gift of tongues. For what was given to the Church then in a miraculous manner is now given and conferred by study and instruction. For as far as the miracle is concerned, it was granted to the Church, like the rest, on this condition and under this arrangement: namely, that once the doctrine of the Gospel had been spread and confirmed among men as far as was enough, the miracle itself should gradually cease and be abolished. Therefore, after the most joyful news of Christ the Saviour had become known to the whole world, and had been so firmly established by miracles that no one, except a manifestly impious and obstinate man, could any longer doubt its truth, this miraculous gift of tongues, like the others, ceased. Meanwhile, since the Church cannot easily gather and teach without knowledge of languages, the Holy Spirit does not cease to bestow this upon some members of the Church through instruction, study and exercise, both public and private. This is what the Apostle also hints at when he says: "no one can call Jesus Christ, except by the Holy Spirit." And a little after, through the same Spirit is given "the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, to another faith, ... [gifts of healings, workings of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits], kinds of tongues, interpretation of tongues." Nor does he speak only of the gifts whose use then flourished in the Corinthian Church, but in general of the gifts with which God was to adorn and build up his people in all times. For this teaching pertains to us no less than to the Corinthians. Not to say anything of the fact that these gifts, for the most part, are so necessary to the Church that without them it cannot be without very great loss. But, someone will say, by your opinion, then, only the citizens of the Church will be endowed with this gift. Yet how many men are found, and have been found, outside the boundaries of the Church, wholly alien to the Christian faith and religion, who have excelled by an outstanding knowledge of languages? Certainly we cannot deny that this is so. Therefore either they had the Holy Spirit, or this gift is not to be counted among the gifts of the Holy Spirit bestowed on the Church. Neither follows. The reasoning is not obscure: the knowledge of languages that comes to impious men and to those who dwell outside Solomon's porch does not proceed from that singular and special action of the Holy Spirit, which is properly ascribed to the Church alone, but flows from the common or general operation of God. And in this way whatever good and excellent things men outside the enclosure of the Church possess is a gift and bestowal of God in general, not of the Holy Spirit. But what falls to the pious, the members of the Church, is not only of God's general action but also of the Holy Spirit's special action. Just as outside the Church some knowledge of God does indeed flourish, but in the Church alone the Holy Spirit is acknowledged; and whatever knowledge and cognition of divine and human things, of prudence, eloquence and other gifts is acquired by study and discipline, with divine grace breathing upon it, is said to be worked in the saints. But the world neither knows the Holy Spirit, nor receives him, nor feels or perceives any operation of his in itself.

units.la: Perstrinxi hactenus, quam potui brevissime, Auditores, qualenam fuerit illud Apostolis collatum linguarum donum; quis eius author, quis usus; & etiamnum hodie Ecclesiæ dari à Spiritu Sancto, licet aliter, quam olim est datum oflendi. Nunc quod præcipuè institituti nostri postulat ratio, id vobis persuasum velim, hoc linguarum donum summo studio, summoq; labore ac diligentia in Ecclesia fovendum & excolendum esse. Quis ergo hoc non videt? Nam ut totam illam dignitatis disputationem omittam, quantum ad Dei verbum facilius & rectius intelligendum faciat, imbutum esse variarum linguarum cognitione, præsertim earum quibus illud primitus de scriptum est, locupletissimè quotidiana testatur experientia. Quis enim non animadvertit absq; cis omnes quasi in densissima rerum caligine versari, atque adeo nihil laude dignum, vel potius omnino nihil præstare posse. Sed mussitantes hic quosdam mihi videor audire: Scriptura versa est; quid linguis opus est, quid Hebræa, quid Græca; versa scriptura est. Ita sane, versa est. At cui versiones debemus, nisi huic divino linguarum muneri? unde eas haberemus, nisi docti & eruditi viri linguas novissent, transtulissent. Quanquā, quæ malum confidentia hominum est, versionibus sic acquiescere, adhærere, quasi iis freti, extra omnem erroris aleam versari possimus. Quasi vero non sæpe & magnus dormitet Homerus, itaq; etiam in ipsis illis doctorum hominum translationibus haud abfuerit aliquam erratorum defectuum vel metere segetem. Adhæc semper, opera danda est, ut sententiæ nostræ, quam fieri potest maximè certi simus. At vero neminem unquam translationes, credo, tam facient certum, ac linguæ ipsæ nativæ. Multa legis ex LatinoGer-manica facta, ex Græcis Latina; pro veris habes & certò habes: an non autem multo certius, si eadem Latinè, si Græcè cognoscas? Et quî non majori cum certitudine ex fontibus ipsis aquæ judicium facias, quam ex rivulis? siquidem, ut D.Hieronymus ait, multo purior manat fontis unda, quam fluunt rivuli aquæ. Jam phrasibus & idiotismis, quos in ipsis versionibus sæpenumero retinere necesse est; quid facias? qui sine linguarum noticia tam intelligi non possunt, nedum explicari; quam sine luce ulla colorum discrimina cerni. Quò vero tandem, corruptis & depravatis versionibus recurras, confugias, nisi ad fontes? Licet ergo non infelices eruditissimis hisce temporibus sacræ Scripturæ in medio extent versiones: tamen majoris πληροφορίας[?] ergò, fontes ipsi aspernandi non sunt, ex quibus non solum, ut inquit ille dulcius, sed & tutius aquę hauriun-tur. Cogitate pauca retro, si lubet, majorum no-strorum secula, quibus Monastica ubiq; obtinuit & dominata est barbaries; & videte, quid sit solis versionibus niti ac fidere. Istis temporibus boni illi ventres, fratres inquam, ignaviæ & ignorantię dediti monachi; vulgatæ, quæ dicitur, Latinæ Bibliorum versioni tanquam saxo Polypi, adhærē-[?]scebant, in eā jurabāt: linguarū vero studia susq; deq; habentes, perinde atq; inanes Muscarū bombos æstimabant. Si quis quid melius ex fontibus mōstraret, hæreticū continuō, vulcano confecrādū clamabant. Sed quid factū? Quod non potuit non fieri, cum ideo oīa difficilia, obscura & intricata viderentur, & essent, in eas longè gravissimorum errorum sordes inciderunt, quas videmus, & in quib. expurgandis in hunc usq; diem allaboratur. Jā revocate animos, & ad hanc nostri ævi felicitatē advertite. Excitatę & denuo excultę linguę quantū lucis omnib. doctrinę partib. attulerunt? Quam nunc omnia linguarum beneficio explicata lucida plana? Verū, ut omissis versionib. revertatur, unde digressa est, oratio; sine linguarū noticia, verbum Dei, ut diximus, non solum intelligi, doceri, & explicari, recte nequit, sed nec ꝗ[?] magnum non minus censeri debet propagari, cumq; aliis communicari. Quemadmodū quod unā solum lingua continetur, id in confesso est, intra ejus linguæ peritos homines servari: ita negari non potest, verbum Dei, si dimanare ad alios & plurib. innotescere debeat, transfundendum alias etiam in linguas esse; easq; maxime, quas plures calres calleant atq; intelligant. Quod ut fiat, discedo omninò linguæ sunt, atque iis inprimis scribendum, quæ communiores, omnium latissime patent. Ita olim licet Apostoli omnium linguarum labiis Evangelium prædicarent: eos tamen cernimus, Græco potissimum sermone & stylo, quod vulgatior cæteris esset, cum loquendo, tum scribendo usos fuisse. Ita postea, cum Latina Græcā ad pauciores paulatim redigeret, se ad hanc Apostolici viri, Martyres & Doctores Ecclesiarū eximii contulerūt, eāq; docuerūt & scripserunt. Eadem hodie post vernaculas & domesticas potissimum commendata esse debet, cū velut princeps & regina, per totum fere orbem terrarū dominetur ac regnet. Operæpretium autem fuerit, ut in illis addiscendis, cum proprietatis, tum puritatis diligentem habeamus rationem eāsq; omni studio & cōtentione sectemur. Alioqui n. corrupta & depravata loquendi scribendiq; ratio, quid promereatur? qui legētis animū sibi benevolū attentūq; retinebit? Certè, nemo nō experitur, plerūq; usu venire, ut doctrinā orationis oporteat sustinere fortunā. Cæterū, inquiat aliquis, nō abs re est: sed quo pacto fieri poterit, ut tā multas nos discamus & assequamur studio, q Apostoli olim miraculo? Neq; is ego sum, q à quoq; reqrā[?]. Hoc volo, dico, ex omni isto numero, etiā atq; etiā necessarias occurrere Hebraeā, Græcā, Latinā, & in qua qsq; natus est, vernaculam. At nec has simul omnes possumus. Oēs, ut possint, satagere debent, qui Scholas & Academias persequūtur, inprimis aūt illi, q id agunt, cò aspirāt, ut aliquādo in Ecclesiæ puppi sedentes, clavum teneant, alios doceat, regant, instruant. Et hic satis rigidus es, inquis; ne quidem in hoc hominum ordine, quod vis, obtineas. Rigidus hic non sum. Hi omnino, necesse est, teneant eas, si non perfecte & accurate, certe aliqua ex parte, & quam fieri potest plurimum. Qui earum prorsus rudes & ignari sunt, easq; ne primorib. quidem, quod ajunt, labris delibarunt, eat potius & clavum non in Ecclesie, sed, nescio cujus onerarie, puppi trudant. porro, ut discedamus ab ea linguarum necessitate, quod ad commodiorem verbi Dei & intelligentiam & propagationem requiruntur: non minus etiam ut reliquae liberales & humanitatis propriae disciplina atque artes, Philosophiam puta & Historiam, addisci possint, necessariae sunt. Etenim, qui sunt tandem illi scriptores, qui admirabilium rerum terra coeloq; exsistentium causas aperiunt? nonne Graeci & Latini? Qui de officio, de moribus & virtute disputant? nonne Graeci & Latini? Qui rite definiendi, dividendi, & disputandi, qui etiam ornate copioseq; dicendi praecepta tradunt? nonne Graeci & Latini. Hos autem quomodo, quispiam non Graecus, non Latinus quadantenus, alloqui, legere & audire audit? Et quid, Auditores? Fingite animis vestris eos, quibus docendi in Ecclesia partes commissae sunt, unius saltem linguae Latinae rudes & imperitos esse, quales illi erunt, & quomodo in suo versabuntur officio? Enimvero omnibus idoneis & aptis ad docendum instrumentis, & ipsi destituti erunt, & alios iisdem instruere nequaquam poterunt. Nihil recte secare & proponere, ponere, nihil ornate & copiose, nihil perspicuè explicare valebunt: alios autem quâ ratione docebunt? Atque ita quid sequetur? Classicum ipsa canet Barbaries: literæ, linguę, studia & artes, uno quasi agmine, gruum instar, scholis excedent, avolabunt, aufugient. Deus omen prohibeat. Licet ergo nullus alius linguarum in Ecclesia usus esset: tamen hoc nomine excolendę forent, ut earum adminiculo disciplinę illę non Christiano minus, quam liberali homine dignę doceri ac discì possent; ut barbaries horrida arceretur. Quid vero, quod tres hæ potissimum sunt, Hebræā di-co, Græcam & Latinam, quę semper in Ecclesia, abolitis omnib. aliis conservatę sunt & excultæ. Hebræam cum cęteri omnes mortales, peccato suo dissonas voces haberent, soli Filii Dei in Judæa conservarunt. Huic non ita post longo tempore cum dilatarētur Ecclesię termini, Græca statim adjuncta fuit. Ipsus dein V. T. codex in Græ-cam, & hinc in Latinam translatus est. Præterea quis Ecclesię doctor, non dico magni nominis, sed quis ex multis unus proditus est, quin vel Græ-câ, vel Latinâ docuerit & scripserit. At nec majorum nostrorum ævo cum fœdissimis Barbariei sordib. omnia inquinata & contaminata squale-bant, Latinę & Græcæ Linguæ usus finalem facis-se pausam[?], satis ex scholasticorum, qui vocantur, libris apparet. Nimirum & Deus sapientissimus & Ecclesia unanimi consensu judicarunt, etiam tenuissimam linguarum cognitionem non utile solummodo, sed et maximopere necessariâ esse. Sed ne patientia & humanitate vestra, quam benigne praestare vos adhuc video, abutar, vela con-trahenda erunt. Quamobrem, commilitones & Auditores ornatissimi, cum linguarum, praecipuè, Hebraeę, Graecae & Latinę peritia & ad sacrosan-ctum Dei verbum, & ad reliquam omnem bona-rum artium Cyclopaedian[?] usque adeo necessaria, sit, ut sine[?] ea, illud quidem satis recte, nec intelli-gi nec propagari, haec vero, etiam ne attingi quidem possit: dubitabimus, dubitabimus inquam in illam excolendam omni studio, cura & con-tentione incumbere? Imo agite, tribuamus hoc, Ecclesiae, charissimae[?] matris nostrae, in cujus sinu, gremioque nutrimur & educamur, afflictissimis. Eam ut in errores inducant atq; etiam in pristi-nas barbaricae vastitatis lacunas immergant, ho-stes acerrimi vigilant, sudant, laborant, conten-dunt, omnes artes & machinas conquirunt, o-mnibus literarum & linguarum studiis immo-riuntur: nos, ut eam defendamus & propugne-mus, non operam dabimus? in utramvis securi aurem stertemus[?] ? linguarum studia, optimum ejus armamentarium negligemus, deseremus?
units.tr: I have set out, as briefly as I could, listeners, what that gift of tongues bestowed on the Apostles was; who its author was and what its use was; and I have shown that even today the Holy Spirit gives it to the Church, though not in the way it was once given. Now, what the purpose of our institution especially requires, I want you to be persuaded of this: that this gift of tongues must be cherished and cultivated in the Church with the greatest zeal, effort and diligence. Who does not see this? For, to leave aside the whole question of its dignity, daily experience abundantly testifies that acquaintance with various languages, especially those in which Scripture was first written, makes the Word of God easier and more correctly understood. For who does not notice that without them all men wander as if in the thickest darkness of things, and so can achieve nothing praiseworthy, or rather nothing at all? But here I seem to hear some muttering: "Scripture has been translated; what need is there for languages, for Hebrew or Greek? The Scripture has been translated." Yes indeed, it has been translated. But to whom do we owe the translations, except to this divine gift of languages? Whence would we have them, unless learned and erudite men had known the languages and translated them? Yet, what a foolish confidence men have, to rest and rely on translations as if, trusting in them, we could stand beyond every risk of error! As if Homer did not often nod, so that even in the translations of learned men some lapse or fault could not be found. Moreover, we must always take care that we are as certain as possible of our meaning. But I believe no translations will ever make a man as certain as the native languages themselves. You read many things made from Latin into German, or from Greek into Latin, and you hold them as true and know them to be true; but is it not much more certain if you know them in Latin or in Greek? And how can you not judge the water with greater certainty from the springs themselves than from the streams? For, as St. Jerome says, the water flowing from the spring is much purer than the water of the streams that run from it. Now, what do you do about the phrases and idioms which in the translations themselves must often be retained? They cannot be understood, much less explained, without knowledge of the languages, just as colours cannot be distinguished without any light. And where, finally, when translations are corrupted and depraved, will you run or flee for refuge, except to the sources? Therefore, although in these most learned times translations of Holy Scripture are not unhappily available in our midst, yet for greater full assurance the sources themselves are not to be scorned, from which, as that man puts it, waters are drawn not only more sweetly but also more safely. Think, if you like, for a little while back on the centuries of our forefathers, when monastic ignorance and barbarism held sway and dominated everywhere; and see what it means to rely and depend on translations alone. In those times those good bellies, I mean the brothers, monks given over to idleness and ignorance, clung to the so-called Vulgate Latin version of the Bible as to the rock of the Polyp, and swore by it; but they held the study of languages in no esteem, and thought of it as the empty buzzing of flies. If anyone showed something better from the sources, they at once cried out that he was a heretic and should be burned by fire. But what happened? What could not but happen: since all things seemed and were difficult, obscure and entangled, they fell into the filth of very grave errors, which we see, and from which, to this very day, labour is still being spent on cleansing them. Now recall your minds, and attend to the happiness of our own age. What light have the languages, once revived and again cultivated, brought to all parts of doctrine? How clear and plain are all things now explained by the benefit of languages? But, to leave aside the translations and return to where the discourse has digressed: without knowledge of the languages, the Word of God, as we have said, cannot rightly be not only understood, taught and explained, but also not less must it be considered that it cannot be propagated and communicated to others. Just as what is contained in one language only is admittedly kept among the experts of that language, so it cannot be denied that if the Word of God is to flow out to others and become known to many, it must also be transfused into other languages, and especially into those which more people know and understand. In order that this may happen, I depart altogether from the languages, and it is especially in those that one must write which are most common and extend most widely. Thus, although the Apostles once preached the Gospel with the lips of all tongues, we see that they used especially the Greek language and style, because it was more widespread than the rest, both in speaking and in writing. So afterwards, when Latin gradually reduced Greek to fewer people, the apostolic men, martyrs and eminent teachers of the Churches turned to this, and taught and wrote in it. The same should today be commended above all, after the vernacular and domestic languages, since it, like a prince and queen, rules and reigns over almost the whole earth. It will, moreover, be worthwhile that in learning them we pay careful attention both to propriety and to purity, and pursue them with all zeal and effort. For otherwise, what does a corrupt and depraved manner of speaking and writing deserve? Who will keep the reader's mind well disposed and attentive to himself? Surely everyone has experience that it generally happens that the teaching of a speech must suffer the fortune of its style. "But," someone may say, "this is not beside the point; yet in what way will it be possible for us to learn and attain so many languages with zeal, which the Apostles once did by a miracle?" I am not the kind of man who asks this of anyone. I say this: out of all that number, even and again, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and the vernacular in which each was born are necessary. But neither can we all of these at the same time. All who pursue schools and academies ought to strive, that they may be able to; and especially those who do this and aspire to this, that they may at some time, sitting at the stern of the Church's ship, hold the helm, teach, rule and instruct others. "And you are rather strict," you say; "you cannot even obtain in this class of men what you want." I am not strict here. These men must necessarily hold these languages, if not perfectly and accurately, at least in some part, and as much as possible. Those who are utterly rude and ignorant of them, and have not even tasted them, as they say, with the first lips, let them rather push the helm not of the Church's ship but of some cargo-ship, I know not whose. Further, to turn away from that necessity of languages: they are also necessary for the more convenient understanding and propagation of the Word of God, and not less so, so that the remaining liberal and humane disciplines and arts, Philosophy and History for instance, may be learned. For, who in the end are those writers who explain the causes of the wonderful things existing on earth and in heaven? Are they not the Greeks and Latins? Who discuss duty, morals and virtue? Are they not the Greeks and Latins? Who hand down the precepts of defining, dividing and disputing rightly, and also of speaking ornately and copiously? Are they not the Greeks and Latins? But how can anyone who is neither Greek nor Latin, to some extent, address, read and hear these men? And what, listeners? Imagine in your minds those to whom the parts of teaching in the Church have been entrusted, being unskilled and inexperienced even in the Latin language alone; what sort of men they will be, and how they will conduct themselves in their office? Indeed, they will themselves be lacking all the suitable and apt instruments for teaching, and by no means will they be able to instruct others by the same means. They will be able to cut and set forth nothing rightly, to arrange nothing ornately and copiously, to explain nothing clearly; and by what method will they teach others? And so what will follow? Barbarism itself will sound the trumpet call: letters, languages, studies and arts, like a flock of cranes in one body, will leave the schools, fly away, and flee. May God forbid that omen. Therefore, even if there were no other use of languages in the Church, they would still have to be cultivated on this account, so that with their help those disciplines might be taught and learned, which are worthy of a Christian no less than of a free man; so that horrid barbarism might be kept off. Moreover, there are chiefly these three, I mean Hebrew, Greek and Latin, which have always been preserved and cultivated in the Church, all others having been abolished. Hebrew, when all other mortals had voices discordant because of their sin, the sons of God alone preserved in Judea. Not long after this, when the boundaries of the Church were extended, Greek was immediately added to it. Then the Old Testament itself was translated into Greek, and from there into Latin. Besides, what teacher of the Church, I do not say of great name, but which one of many has been handed down, did not teach and write either in Greek or in Latin? Nor even in the age of our forefathers, when all things were foully soiled and contaminated with the foulest filth of barbarism, does it appear enough from the books of the so-called schoolmen that the use of the Latin and Greek languages had made a final pause. Surely both the most wise God and the Church, by unanimous consent, have judged that even the slightest knowledge of languages is not only useful but also most greatly necessary. But lest I abuse your patience and humanity, which I see you still kindly extend, the sails must be drawn in. Therefore, fellow soldiers and most distinguished listeners, since knowledge of the languages, especially Hebrew, Greek and Latin, is so necessary both for the most sacred Word of God and for the whole encyclopaedia of the other good arts, that without it the one cannot be understood or propagated rightly, and the other cannot even be touched: shall we hesitate, I say, to devote ourselves to cultivating them with all zeal, care and effort? Come, let us ascribe this to the Church, our most beloved mother, in whose bosom and lap we are nourished and brought up. Her most bitter enemies keep watch, sweat, labour, strive; they seek out all arts and machines, they die with study of all letters and languages, in order to lead her into errors and plunge her into the former gaps of barbarous desolation: and we, will we not take pains to defend and protect her? Will we sleep unconcerned on either ear? Will we neglect and desert the study of languages, her best armoury?

units.la: Profecto, cum prius omnia tenebris plusquam Cimmeriis obruta & abdita jacerent, Clemen-tiss.[?] Deus illis discussis hac nostra aetate pristino suo fulgori ac nitori ea quae postliminio resti-tuere dignatus est, literarum & linguarum studia, tanquam ab inferis revocavit, clarissimam Evan-gelii sui facem accendit. Haec Dei maxima bene-ficia flocci pendere, contemnere, quam nefariae & sceleratae ingratitudinis foret? Ejus nota nobis ne inuri queat, sedulo, Ornatiss. studiosi, cavea-mus, mus idque tantò magis, quod ii sumus, quos Deus Sacerdotes & Levitas in Israele esse voluit, quibus doctrinæ sacrorumque mysteriorum cu-stodiam commendavit; quid amplius? quibus eas etiam occasiones opportunitatesque discendi suppeditat, quibus alii si fruerentur, beatos se at-que omnium mortalium felicissimos prædicaret. Valeat igitur apud nos, tristissimus ille & mœ-stissimus Ecclesiæ status, quem prævidemus, & nisi gnavos nos præstiterimus, hisce coràm oculis videbimus: Valeat apud nos ineffabilis Dei cle-mentia, valeat ꝑpria cujusq; salus & conscientia, q; ut tranquillâ & ob nullâ officii neglecti parte ir-requietâ habeamus, alacrib. animis hoc studium ingrediamur, urgeamus; nec dubitemus, qn S. S. fons ille autor & largitor oïs gratiæ & boni in Ec-clesia muneris, laborib. nostris uberrime benedi-ctur: sit, facturusq; ut earū aliqua cedro digna in structi pitia nobis ornamento & honori, Ecclesiæ utilitati atq; emolumento esse possimus & simus.
units.tr: Surely, when all things had previously lain buried and hidden in darkness more profound than the Cimmerian, our most merciful God, having dispelled that darkness in this our age, deigned to restore to their former splendour and brightness those things which had been lost, and He called back, as if from the dead, the studies of letters and languages, and kindled the most brilliant torch of His Gospel. Who would not be sure that to hold these great benefits of God as worth a straw, to despise them, would be the mark of a wicked and criminal ingratitude? Let us, most distinguished students, take care diligently that this brand may never be branded upon us, and all the more so because we are those whom God wished to be priests and Levites in Israel, to whom He entrusted the keeping of doctrine and of the sacred mysteries. What more? He supplies to us the very opportunities and facilities for learning which, if others enjoyed them, they would declare themselves blessed and the most fortunate of all mortals. Let that most sad and mournful state of the Church, which we foresee, and which, unless we show ourselves diligent, we shall see with our own eyes, be far from us. Let the ineffable mercy of God be far from us, and let our own safety and conscience be far from us, so that, having them tranquil and never disturbed by any neglected part of duty, we may enter upon this study with eager minds and press on with it. Nor let us doubt that when that fountain of the Holy Spirit, the author and giver of every grace and good gift in the Church, has blessed our labours most abundantly, He will bring it about that some of these labours, worthy of cedar, may be an ornament and honour to us, and that we may be and become a benefit and advantage to the Church.

units.la: Quod superest; Tibi inclyte & sanctæ Spiritus, sempiterne cum Patre & Filio Deus, gratias totis pectoribus agimus, ꝙ pro incomprehensa tua in Ec-clesiam bonitate ac misericordia, eam cum summis aliis longeq; amplissimis beneficiis, tum etiā hoc admirabili linguarum donoaugere atque orna-re dignatus es: quòd idem etiam superiorib secu-lis neglectum ac barbarico revera cœno demer-sum, dieb. his nostris denuo in lucē ꝑduxisti, ex-poliisti, auxisti. Agnoscimus, sancte Sp. bonitate tuam, ꝯatque utinam, pro eo ac debemus, celebre-mus. Diu quæsumus, conserva nobis hoc inæstimabile bonitatis tuæ munus, daque ut unice gra-tis animis id amplexemur; semper in pretio & delitiis habeamus. Averte à nobis exitiales sævi Draconis & complicum ejus conatus: vastitate Turci barbaricam, Antiochicam Papæ tyrannidem. Defende pios & salutares principes, Ecclesiæ fautores atque nutricios. Nominatim vero Illustriss.[?] principem nostrum atque Electorem, FRIDE-RICUM IV. patronum ac Mecœnatem nostrum clementiss.[?] & illustrissimam Celsitudinis ejus cō-jugem ac sobolem, pientissimam: rege gratia & virtute tua, ut cœlestem veritatem tuam, litterarum, linguarumque illi inservientia studia magis ac magis ament, concordi studio felicique successu propagent. Denique incende in nobis o-mnib. & singulis serium studium seriumque amorem discendi ac promovēdi veritatis doctrinam: carnis nobis adhærescentis fœcem & scoriam in dies exure, ut in omni conversatione nostra quemadmodum tu sanctus es, ipsi quoque sancti simus, & τ̃ δοκίμιον ὑμῶ[?]ν τῆς πίστεως multo pretiosius auro comperiatur nobis laudi esse & gloriæ, cum patefiet Dominus Iesus Christus è cœ-lo: cui tecum & cum æt. Patre gloria & imperium in secula.
units.tr: For the rest: to You, illustrious and holy Spirit, eternal God with the Father and the Son, we give thanks with our whole hearts, that for Your incomprehensible goodness and mercy toward the Church You have deigned to increase and adorn it with this admirable gift of languages, together with other very great and ample benefits; and that You have also brought this gift, which in earlier ages was neglected and truly sunk in barbarian mire, back into the light in these our days, and have refined and enlarged it. We acknowledge Your goodness, Holy Spirit, and would that we might celebrate it as we ought. We beseech You long to preserve for us this inestimable gift of Your goodness, and grant that we may embrace it with single-hearted gratitude and always hold it in esteem and delight. Turn away from us the destructive attempts of the fierce Dragon and of his accomplices: restrain the Turk, who lays waste the barbarian lands, and the Antiochian tyranny of the Pope. Defend the pious and salutary princes, the supporters and nurturers of the Church. In particular, our most illustrious prince and Elector, FREDERICK IV, our most merciful patron and Maecenas, and his most illustrious consort and most pious offspring: rule them by Your grace and virtue, so that they may love more and more Your heavenly truth and the studies of letters and languages which serve it, and may propagate them with united zeal and happy success. Finally, kindle in all of us, and in each one, a earnest zeal and an earnest love for learning and for advancing the doctrine of the truth; burn away day by day the dregs and the dross of the flesh that clings to us, so that in all our conduct, as You are holy, we ourselves also may be holy, and that the proof of our faith, much more precious than gold, may be found to be for praise and glory to us when the Lord Jesus Christ is revealed from heaven, to whom, with You and with the Father, be glory and dominion for ever.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: ORATIO XIII. DE ANIMÆ IMMORTALITATE: EX PLATONIS ET Aristotelis sententia.
units.tr: ORATIO XIII. ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL: FROM THE OPINION OF PLATO AND ARISTOTLE.

units.la: SI ullius rei doctrina atque cognitio magni facienda, si diligenter investiganda, si denique contra hæreticos tum Philosophiæ tum Theologiæ veteres ac recentiores defendenda ac munienda est; certè doctrina de animæ immortalitate talis existimari debet. Hac enim ignorata quis Dei timor? quæ pietas? quæ societas inter mortales consistere potest? Atque hoc ipsum Satan considerans tanquam telis infestissimis per suos satellites pietatem labefactare, luxuriam corroborare, & ad flagitia immanissima furiosas faces præferre sategit[?]. Epicuræos ex Ethnicis aliosque complures suscitavit, qui unà cum corpore mentem interire atque evanescere docebant: Sadducæos in populum sanctum emisit, qui neque angelos neque Dæmonas credebant, & cum animorum immortali essentia corporum quoque ex mortuis resurrectionem atque ἀνάστασιν[?] negabant. Vtinam verò nostra hæc ætas hisce malis releuata esset, veteres casus vtcunque toleraremus. Sed cum horum reliquiæ in magnam orbis partem çeu pestis deterrima effusæ sint, cum passim incé-dium illud conspiciatur & longè lateque graffe-tur,cum denique multi vitæ impuritate nō clam, sed aperté, non voce sed facto ipso animorum post hanc vitam felicitatem tollant, quis quæso tàm alienus à Musarum castris, quis tàm iniquus rerum æstimator tamquevæcors, qui non hanc de immortalitate animæ doctrinam amandam, expendendam, ferioque defendendam esse exi-ftimet? Dignitas ipsa materiæ, utilitas atque ju-cunditas movent, ac quasi vi quadam secreta nos rapiunt ad ejus admirationem. Est enim hæc ex-cellentiffima, quæ universi complexu continen-tur, atque adeò ipsis cœlis præftabilior. Ab hac dicimur & fumus homines, atque bestiis difcer-nimur. Hæc inventrix artium: hæc virtutum o-mnium receptaculum atque sedes, hac denique angelis ipfiqueDeo conformes fumus. Et licet nec oculis cernatur, nec manibus contrectetur, nec ejus effentia fenfib.crassis comprehendi que-at:tamen sicut Cupressi femina minuta quidem sunt adeò, ut oculis quædam percipi vix queant, at in iis tanta arbor tamq; procera inest; ut mul-tas sua proceritate superet;ita mens nostra om-nium maxima,dignissima,excellentissimaque o-pera exercet. Hoc Ariftoteles Vir & ingenio ad-mirabilis, & rerum scientia illustris probè cogno-vit, atque idcirco à tàm præclaro initio suos de a-nima libros exorsus est, in quo tùm dignitatem tum utilitatem apertissimè partim à subjecti ex-cellentia, partim scientiæ certitudine demon-ftrat. Hoc Plato in Phædone gravibus sanè ver-bis afbis asseruit, ac duas hujus doctrinæ utilitates recensuit, ut viam felicitatis ingrediamur vitam secundum virtutem informando, atque iter infelicitatis declinemus à vitiis abhorrendo. Hinc etiam illud, quod præcipuè animadvertendum occurrit perspiciemus, consensum veræ Philosophiæ ac Theologiæ, harmoniamque dulcissimam, cui Philosophiæ imperfectio nihil detrahit. Verum enim vero cum hæc materia sublimis ac præstans ingenii aciem acumenque requirat, orationis flumen desideret, dispositionem omnibus partibus absolutam expetat, cogitabit vestrum forte aliquis, annon insanis? annon majora viribus moves? cur non doctioribus hæc pertractanda relinquis? Magna certè est hujus doctrinæ sublimitas: sed quærendi defatigatio turpis, ubi id quod quæritur, pulcherrimum est. Non Herodotus Thucydiden, nec Cæsarem Ciceronis dicendi ubertas deterruerunt; nec Plato Aristotelem, nec Aristoteles Galenum retraxit atque retardavit à philosophandi studio. Quare, Commilitones, consuetudo hujus collegii laudatissima me impulit, temporisque ratio admonuit, ut hoc argumentum pertractandum suscipererem. Vos eadem benevolentia, qua alios ante me dicentes complexi estis, me quoq; complectimini.
units.tr: If the teaching and knowledge of any subject is to be held in high regard, if it is to be investigated diligently and, finally, if it is to be defended and fortified against heretics, both in philosophy and in theology, both by the ancients and by the moderns, then surely the doctrine of the immortality of the soul ought to be judged of this kind. For if this were unknown, what fear of God would there be? What piety? What society could exist among mortals? Satan, considering this very thing, has laboured, as with most hostile weapons, to undermine piety through his henchmen, to strengthen debauchery, and to hold forth furious torches to the most monstrous crimes. From the heathen he raised up the Epicureans and many others, who taught that the mind perishes and vanishes along with the body. Into the holy people he sent out the Sadducees, who believed neither in angels nor in demons, and who, while denying the immortal essence of souls, also denied the resurrection of bodies from the dead and the ἀνάστασις. Would that our own age were relieved of these evils, so that we might bear the old misfortunes with some patience. But since remnants of these have spread over a great part of the world like a most deadly plague, since that conflagration is seen everywhere and rages far and wide, and since finally many, by the impurity of their lives, take away the happiness of souls after this life, not secretly but openly, not by word but by the very deed itself, who, I ask, is so alien to the camps of the Muses, who is so unfair a judge of things and so foolish, that he does not think this doctrine of the immortality of the soul ought to be loved, weighed and vigorously defended? The very dignity of the matter, its usefulness and its delightfulness move us, and as if by some hidden force they carry us off to admire it. For this is most excellent of all the things that are contained in the embrace of the universe, and indeed it surpasses the heavens themselves. By this we are called and are men, and we are distinguished from the beasts. This is the inventress of the arts; this is the receptacle and seat of all virtues; by this, finally, we are made conformable to the angels and to God Himself. And although it is not seen by the eyes, nor handled by the hands, nor can its essence be grasped by the coarse senses, yet, just as the seed of the cypress is indeed tiny, so that some of them can scarcely be perceived by the eyes, but in them there lies so great and so tall a tree that by its height it surpasses many, so our mind exercises the greatest, most worthy and most excellent of works. Aristotle, a man admirable in genius and illustrious in knowledge of things, clearly knew this well, and therefore he began his books on the soul from so distinguished a beginning, in which he demonstrates its dignity and usefulness most plainly, partly from the excellence of the subject and partly from the certainty of the science. Plato in the Phaedo asserted this in very weighty words, and he listed two uses of this doctrine: that we may enter upon the way of happiness by forming our life according to virtue, and that we may avoid the path of unhappiness by abhorring vices. Hence we shall also see that consensus of true philosophy and theology, and that most sweet harmony, which the imperfection of philosophy does not diminish. But since this lofty and outstanding matter requires the keenness and sharpness of the intellect, desires a flow of speech, and demands a disposition complete in all its parts, perhaps someone among you will think: are you not mad? Are you not attempting things beyond your strength? Why do you not leave these things to be handled by the more learned? Indeed, the sublimity of this doctrine is great, but weariness in inquiry is shameful when that which is sought is most beautiful. Herodotus was not deterred from Thucydides, nor did Caesar's copiousness of speech deter Cicero; neither did Plato draw back Aristotle, nor did Aristotle hold back and delay Galen from the study of philosophizing. Therefore, fellow soldiers, the most praiseworthy custom of this college has impelled me, and the reckoning of the time has admonished me, to undertake the handling of this subject. Embrace me also with that same kindness with which you have embraced the others who spoke before me.

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] ut inquit Socrates in sua apologia, τὸ μὲν τέλος τῆς λέξεως ἐάν, αὐτὸ ἢ τοῦτο σκοπεῖν, εἰ δίκαια λέγω ἢ μή. Δικαστοῦ μὲν αὕτη ἀρετή, ῥήτορος δὲ ἡ ἀληθῆ λέγειν[?]. i.e. Et hoc nunc à vobis contendo, ut dicendi genus praetermittatis, & huc mentem intendatis, intēn-[?] intendatis, an justa, an vero injusta dicam. Hac enim judicis virtus est: Rhetoris ut vera dicendo exprimat. Vt igitur certis finibus oratio nostra inclusa comprehendatur breviter & perspicuè ex Philosophia immortalitatem animæ demonstrabo, ac Aristotelis Platonisq; consensionem declarabo.
units.tr: [illegible, ~20 letters] as Socrates says in his Apology: τὸ μὲν τέλος τῆς λέξεως ἐάν, αὐτὸ ἢ τοῦτο σκοπεῖν, εἰ δίκαια λέγω ἢ μή [the aim of speech is to consider this alone, whether I speak justly or not]. This is the virtue of a judge, but of a rhetorician to speak what is true [ῥήτορος δὲ ἡ ἀληθῆ λέγειν]. That is: And this now I urge upon you, that you set aside the manner of speaking and direct your minds to whether I speak justly or unjustly. For this is the virtue of a judge: a rhetorician expresses by speaking what is true. So that our discourse may be comprehended, enclosed within certain limits, I shall briefly and clearly demonstrate the immortality of the soul from philosophy, and I shall declare the agreement of Aristotle and Plato.

units.la: Deinde argumenta quæ ex scriptis Aristotelis in contrariam partem adferri aut potius detorqueri solent, infirmabo ac in fumum dissipabo. Etsi vero hoc ipsum ex Theologia omnium disciplinarum <bl>ἀρχιτεκτονικὴ</bl> quæ & certitudine principiorum & argumentorum pondere atque gravitate omnes artes superat, effici posset, tamen ut consensus Philosophiæ ac Theologiæ appareat, ut calumniæ retundantur, ut denique in omnium animis Philosophiæ amor excitetur ac confirmetur, ideo Philosophicas rationes adhibebo.
units.tr: Next I shall weaken the arguments which are commonly brought forward, or rather twisted, from the writings of Aristotle on the other side, and I shall scatter them into smoke. Although this very point could be established from theology, the architectonic [ἀρχιτεκτονική] of all disciplines, which surpasses all arts both in the certainty of its principles and in the weight and seriousness of its arguments, nevertheless, in order that the agreement of philosophy and theology may appear, that calumnies may be repelled, and finally that love of philosophy may be aroused and strengthened in the minds of all, I shall therefore employ philosophical reasons.

units.la: Quid enim hoc nostro argumento evidentius, quod nisi cognitum animisque comprehensum haberemus non tam stabilis opinio permaneret, nec confirmaretur diuturnitate temporis, nec una cum ætatibus hominum inveterare potuisset. Etenim videmus cæteras opiniones fictas atque vanas diuturnitate extabuisse. Nam opinionum commenta delet dies, naturæ indicia confirmat.
units.tr: For what is more evident in our argument than this: that unless we had it known and grasped in our minds, the opinion would not remain so stable, nor would it be confirmed by the length of time, nor could it have grown old along with the ages of men. For we see that other opinions, which are fictitious and vain, have wasted away through length of time. For day destroys the inventions of opinions, but confirms the indications of nature.

units.la: Hoc vero recte sentientium animis infixum fuit, Aristotelis Platonisque consensu approbatum, animum, ut loquitur ille, θείας κοινωνον φύσεως ἀξιώσαντον ἀθάνατον esse. Neque nos hoc loco movet aut impedit quod idem Plato verissime elegantissimeque dixit; animum nostrum jam aspicimus, ut multi maris Deum Glaucum intuiti sunt, cujus antiqua natura haud facile perspici potest, eò quod partes corporis sint fracte, σιωπτεχ-φθαι ηοη πάντως λελωβημένη ὑπὸ τῶν κυμάτων. i. e, attritæ & penitus fluctuum sordibus conspurcatæ, aliaque rursus illi inhæreant conchylia lapides alga. Considerandum enim nobis est ὡν ἀπλε-πτη ψυχη, (ut ipsius verbis utar.) καὶ οἷον ἐφιεπη ὁμιλιῶν, ὡς ξυγγρῆς ἐοικε τῷ ἡ θεῳ καὶ ἀθανάτῳ, id est, ad quæ pertingat anima, quibusq; delectetur divina atque immortali essentia cognata, & qualis futura sit, cum soli Deo adhærescet.
units.tr: Indeed this has been fixed in the minds of those who think rightly, and approved by the consensus of Aristotle and Plato, that the soul, as that man says, deemed worthy to be a partaker of the divine nature, is immortal [θείας κοινωνὸν φύσεως ἀξιώσαντον ἀθάνατον]. Nor does it move or hinder us in this place that the same Plato said very truly and elegantly that we now behold our soul, as many have looked upon the sea-god Glaucus, whose ancient nature can hardly be discerned, because its parts are broken off, and it has been wholly mangled by the waves [σιωπτεχ-φθαι ηοη πάντως λελωβημένη ὑπὸ τῶν κυμάτων], that is, worn down and utterly defiled by the filth of the waves, and other shells, stones and seaweed cling to it again. For we must consider the soul, to use his own words, as simple [ὧν ἁπλῆ ψυχή], and as it were pursuing [ἐφιεμένη] those things with which it has intercourse, as being akin to the divine and immortal [ξυγγενὴς ἔοικε τῷ θείῳ καὶ ἀθανάτῳ], that is, with which the soul comes into contact, and in which it delights, being akin to the divine and immortal essence, and what it will be like when it clings to God alone.

units.la: Etenim si Medici non primo intuitu quid herbæ incognitæ in corpore valeant perspiciunt, sed partim odoratu & gustatu investigant, partim ex efficacia atque actionibus inde promanantibus certi reddun-tur, quid mirum si & nos ex operibus mentis insignibus, nisi prorsus de sede mentis deturbati simus perpetuitatem ejus deprehendamus? Nam verissimè Aristoteles observavit experientiaque confirmavit, rem quamlibet ex actionibus cognosci. Actiones enim à forma propria proveniunt, eoque sicut res operatur, sic & ipsa existimari debet. Quomodo verò mens Spirituales essentias, Deum, Angelos ac semetipsam cognosceret, nisi proportione illi responderet? quomodo earum proprietates actionesque intelliget, nisi eadem essentia communicaret, quomodo similes actiones puras & simplices exercebit, si ex elementis crassis corruptioníque obnoxiis conflata est? Sensus nostri & interni & externi ideo duntaxat in sensibilibus objectis versantur, nec capiunt res quantitatis expertes, æque sua natura diversas, versas, quia corporeæ sunt substantiæ ad vitam hanc protegendam & confervandam traditæ atque ingeneratæ. Exteriores sua objecta colorem, sonum, sapores, odores, & qualitates tactiles definita ac descripta habent, quæ si fortiora sunt, labefactant sensus eorumque organa. Interiores licet mirando artificio dispositi & ordinati sint, tamen res simplices nec capiunt nec admittunt. Solus animus spirituales essentias intelligit, eoque spiritualis est, ut & ipsa quæ cognoscit: Solus animus immortales substantias comprehendit & admittit, eoque & ipse immortalis est. Atque hoc ipsum aperte confirmat infinita illa mentis capacitas, quæ cum in hac vita expleri nequeat, alia exspectanda est: Hoc sapientissimi illius vox testatur: [illegible, ~20 letters]; hoc Plato innuit, beatum eum pronuncians, cui in ipsa senectute contingat discere; hoc vigor in senibus, & tota Peripateticorum Schola declarat, ideoque hominem ad cognoscendum & agendum natum esse docet. Nam si intellectus circa omnia versatur, si nihil quod intelligi potest, ab ipso separandum est; si materiæ expertia, materiamque habentia comprehendit, quis illum immortalem neget? Si æternitatem, quæ interminatis seculis nos consequetur, capit, quis eum interire asserat? Hinc colligitur plantarum brutorumque animas ex materia produci, hinc animantes ratione destitutas esse conspicitur. Nam quo pacto assur-gerent ultra res caducas? quo pacto id transcen-derent, ex quo eductæ sunt? Quælibet res suis se adjungit, ac cum iisdem permanet, quibus natutali[?] cognatione juncta est. Mens igitur nostra incredibili celeritate mundum pervagatur, nec contenta hoc universo in cœlum transcendit, cœlos ipsos contemplatur, sidera intuetur, nec in cœlestibus corporibus requiescens ad ipsum Deū pergit, in illo recumbit ac gressum sistit, ulterius non progreditur, alioqui non a Deo, sed a supe-riore creata esset. Quid hoc quæso aliud declarat, quam animæ immortalitatem? quid aliud denotat, quam animas a Deo dari, ad eundem reverti, & æternitate frui? Nihil incorporeum a corporibus, nullum immortale corporeis instrumentis efficitur; Et qualib. adminiculis res quælibet gignitur, talis & ipsa existimanda est. Parentes qui-dem multum sibi juris potestatisq; vendicant in corpus, quod illi cogere, disciplina coercere, educare ac corroborare possint; Animus vero hæc respuit ac excludit. Simplex est, à Deo regitur, nihil concreti mixtiq; in se habet, ad felicitatem reservatur. Hoc Plato animadvertens validissimum inde duxit argumentum: Quod simplex est, & ab elementari hac atq; administra natura non profertur, illud ab elementis exstingui nequit. Corpus propter qualitatū contrarietate atq; lapsum [illegible, ~10 letters] tandem dissolvitur, Anima vero hujus permissionis expers nō deletur. Quis itaq; eā exstinguet? Num Deus? at quorsum condidisset, quod statim erat contrucidaturus? num morte corrumpetur? at hæc teste etiam Platone animam a corpore separat, non interimit.
units.tr: For if physicians do not perceive at first glance what unknown herbs are effective in the body, but partly investigate by smell and taste, and partly are made certain from their efficacy and the actions which proceed from them, what wonder if we too, unless we are utterly driven from the seat of the mind, should perceive its perpetuity from the remarkable works of the mind? For Aristotle observed most truly, and experience confirms, that any thing whatever is known from its actions. For actions proceed from its proper form, and so as a thing operates, so it ought to be judged. But how would the mind know spiritual essences, God, angels, and itself, unless it were proportionate to them? How will it understand their properties and actions, unless the same essence were shared with them? How will it exercise pure and simple actions like these, if it has been compounded from gross elements subject to corruption? Our senses, both inner and outer, are therefore occupied only with sensible objects, nor do they grasp things free of quantity, which are equally diverse in their nature, because they are substances of the body, handed down and implanted for the protection and preservation of this life. The outer senses have their objects defined and described as colour, sound, flavours, odours, and tactile qualities, and if these are too strong, they weaken the senses and their organs. The inner senses, although they are arranged and ordered with wonderful craftsmanship, nevertheless neither grasp nor admit simple things. The mind alone understands spiritual essences, and it is spiritual, so that it is also like the things it knows. The mind alone grasps and admits immortal substances, and therefore it is itself immortal. This very thing is plainly confirmed by that infinite capacity of the mind, which, since it cannot be filled in this life, must be looked for in another. The voice of that most wise man bears witness to this: [illegible, ~20 letters]; Plato hints at this, pronouncing blessed the one to whom it happens to learn even in old age; the vigour of the old and the whole school of the Peripatetics declares this, and therefore teaches that man is born to know and to act. For if the intellect is concerned with all things, if nothing that can be understood is to be separated from it; if it comprehends things free of matter and things having matter, who would deny that it is immortal? If it grasps eternity, which will follow us through endless ages, who would assert that it perishes? From this it is gathered that the souls of plants and beasts are produced from matter; from this it is seen that living things lacking reason are such. For in what way would they rise above perishable things? In what way would they transcend that from which they were drawn out? Every thing joins itself to its own and remains with those to which it is joined by natural kinship. Our mind, therefore, roams through the world with incredible speed, and not content with this universe it rises into heaven, contemplates the heavens themselves, gazes upon the stars, and not resting in the heavenly bodies it proceeds to God Himself, reclines in Him and halts its step, and goes no further; otherwise it would not have been created by God, but by something superior. What, I ask, does this declare other than the immortality of the soul? What does it signify other than that souls are given by God, return to Him, and enjoy eternity? Nothing incorporeal is produced from bodies, and nothing immortal is produced by corporeal instruments; and whatever thing is begotten by whatever aids, such it ought to be judged itself. Parents indeed claim for themselves much right and power over the body, which they can compel, restrain by discipline, educate and strengthen; but the soul rejects and excludes these things. It is simple, it is governed by God, it has nothing compounded or mixed in itself, and it is reserved for happiness. Plato, noticing this, drew from it a very strong argument: what is simple, and is not brought forth from this elementary and servile nature, cannot be extinguished by the elements. The body, on account of the contrariety of its qualities and its [illegible, ~10 letters] fall, is at last dissolved, but the soul, having no share in this permission, is not destroyed. Who then will extinguish it? God? But why would He have created what He was about to slay at once? Will it be corrupted by death? But death, as Plato also testifies, separates the soul from the body; it does not destroy it.

units.la: Ad voluntate jam devenio, ex cujus actionib. animæ essentia sic deprehendere licet, ut nullº dubitationi relinquatur locus. Quod enim in mente est affirmatio & negatio, id in voluntate est fuga & persecutio. Hæc pulcherrima disposi-tio infinitam Dei sapientiam admirandam pote-tiam ostendit, ac in peculiarem finem animas creatas esse demonstrat. Quis enim hujusmodi essentiam tàm concinnis actionibus exornatam interitui objiciet? Voluntas infinita ac insatiabilis est, donec ad Deum perveniat. Hic explet eam, in hac vita non expletur. Neque enim hæc serva est intellectus, sed & per se Domina, licet ille præcedat. Mens illi est velut consultrix ductrixque, non ut regat, & huc illucque torqueat, sed ut dirigat. Libera est ante consultationem, refert omnia ad mentem, cohibet se etiam donec ulterius in-quiratur. Sæpe etiam judicium respuit, ac ad infinitum illud bonum contendit, acstrenua celeri-tate enitur. Sensus nostri omnes ab hisce a-ctionibus prorsus alieni in inferioribus solum-modo versantur. Sic & animantia, appetitu conservationis naturæ artificio ipsis indito reguntur. Ad hunc feruntur, bonum appetunt essentiæ inclinatione ducti atque impulsi, quod ad pro-rogationem hujus vitæ pertinet. Verùm homines quoniam infinitum bonum cognoscunt ac intelligunt, idque sibi utile vident, volunt atque illud appetunt. Itaque naturalis est hic appetitus, & cum naturalis sit, expleri potest teste Aristote-le. Nam nisi facietate placaretur, inanes animis nostris objicerentur larvæ, inanis esset ostensio talis boni, & appetitus nusquam recumberet, sed perpetuis quasi fluctibus jactaretur. Atque hic appetitus tàm insitus est hominum animis, ut etiam ii, qui exstingui omnia arbitrantur, famam tamen captent affectentque. Et certè si nihil animus præsentiret in posterum, & si quibus regionibus vitæ spaciū circumscriptum est, iisdem oēs cogitationes terminaret suas, nec tantis se laboribus frangeret, neque tot curis vigiliisque augeretur, neque toties de vita dimicaret. Nūc insidet quędā in optimo quoq; virtus, quę noctes & dies animū gloriæ stimulis concitat & admonet, non cū vitæ tempore esse dimittendā cōmemorationem nominis, sed cū omni posteritate adæquandam. Quare si vel nulla alia ratio adhiberetur, hęc tamen unica quoslibet convinceret. Sed huc accedunt aliæ, quarū fidem q̄in dubiũ[?] vocat, is merito mentis iudicio privatus existimatur. Etenim si animus noster separatas à corpore actiones habet, liquet illam absque corpore subsistere posse, & tū demum, ut Plato ait, ubi ex hac corporis custodia exierit, germanam suam vividamq; faciem recuperare. Quod ut melius perspiciatur, quis est qui inficietur, intellectum agentem ab omni concretione alienum per se intelligere, semper abstrahere à materia τὰ νοητά, iudicare, ratiocinari, dividere, definire, demonstrare, ordinare, & αὐτὸν καθ' αὑτὸν πεπραγματεύεσθαι ὡς τὰ ὄντα[?]. ut Plato ait. Hæc nō per sensus tàm internos quàm externos, ideoq; neq; bestiæ, quæ communes eosdem nobis cū habent, talia agūt, neq; per corpus, qꝑ[?] brutum est. Restat igitur anima, ut in se hæc omnia efficiat atque moderetur. Hæc phantasmata oblata tanquā radiis collustrat, ac ἀναμνηστικῶς[?] reddit. De voluntate idē existimandū est, quæ nō per corpus fit, sed intra sese nullis instrumentis indiget, nulla admittit nec admittere potest. Cæterum cum intellectus in semetipsum reflectatur atque intelligat cur quæso eū corpori alligaremus? cur in vincula crassa reiiceremus, quibus nec retineri nec commisceri potest, multò minùs quam ferrum cum vitro permiscetur. Hoc Plato considerans παλιγγενεσίαν Philolophicam his verbis describit in Phædone. δεῖ χωρίζειν ὅτι τάχιστα τοῦ σώματος τὴν ψυχήν, καὶ ἐθίζειν αὐτὴν καθ' αὑτὴν παντάχοθεν ἐκ τοῦ σώματος συναγείρεσθαι, καὶ οἷον κεῖν τὸ δυνατόν, καὶ ἐν τῷ νῦν πειρᾶσθαι καὶ ἐν τῷ ἑπειτα[?]. Cuius sententiæ verba sic exprimi possunt. Oportet animum a corpore seiungere, quam celerrime, & ipsum assidua consuetudine assuefacere, ut per se ubiq; ex corpore colligetur & habitet tum in hoc tum in futuro seculo. Atq; hoc ipsum delectationes generosarum mentium declarant, quæ nobis animæ essentiam velut oculis conspiciendam exhibent. Delectationes quò similiores sunt, maioremque cum re quæ amatur, vicinitatem habent, eò sunt diuturniores, maiores, ac suaviores. Quod & Plato significat in Theæteto, Philosophi corpus, ait, in civitate est, Mens autem eius hæc parvi ducens aut potius nihili faciens in cælum fertur, & ut Pindari verbis utar, quæ supra cælos & in cælo sunt, scrutatur, his delectatur, his sese adiungit. Et paulò post no-stram cum Deo similitudinem explicans ait; καὶ πειρᾶσθαι χρὴ, ἐνθένδε ἐκεῖσε φεύγειν ὅτι τάχιστα. φυγὴ δὲ ὁμοίωσις τῷ θεῷ κατὰ δυνατόν, ὁμοίωσις δὲ δίκαιον καὶ ὅσιον μετὰ φρονήσεως. θεῷ γὰρ γνῶσις σοφία γε ἀρε-τὴ ἀλη[?] τὴ ἀληθινὴ, ἡ δὲ ἀγνοία ἀ[?]λαθία καὶ κακία ἐναργὴς, h.e, Quare conandum est inde fugere celerrime. Fuga autem est assimilatio Dei quoad in hominem cadit. Assimilatio illa justitia & sanctitas cum prudentia conjuncta est. Nam Dei cognitio sapientia est & solida expressaque virtus: Ignorantia autem eius insciitia & manifesta vitiositas. Idem Aristoteles docet: τῷ γὰρ οἰκεῖον ἑκάστῳ τῇ φύσει κράτιστον ἢ ἡδύστην ἐστὶ ἑκάστῳ ἢ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ[?], id est, quod proprium est cuiq; eiusq; natura convenientissimum, illud & ei iucun-dissimum est. Licet vero multi reperiantur, qui pluris huius mundi delicias quam res divinas faciunt, qui mentem deprimunt, ac se se proiiciunt in omne libidinis genus: tamen ex sanis & integris judicium fiat: relinquantur sordes. nos generosas mentes complectamur. Illæ semper suis se se adiungunt, delectantur vitæ puritate, meditantur res divinas, iisq; se aggregant, ac eò omni studio contendunt. Hinc etiâ pugna & contentio inter phantasiam & mentem oritur acerrima. Illa deorsum ad corpora trahit, iisque gaudet; hęc ad superiora & præstantissima assurgendo vel se erigendo resistit. Mens proficiscitur ad illa, quæ neque sensu ullo neque phantasia comprehenduntur errantemque tandem & divagantem longissimè per devia phantasiam, cohibet ac coercet. Mens non propendet in huius vitæ delicias, sed præterita recordatur, futura coniectat, & veri falsique rationem inquirit. Phantasia è contrario delicias spectat, & si crassis voluptatibus perfundatur, læta est. Res igitur sempiternæ conformio res sunt menti quàm corporales, illarum naturæ magis cõsors,ac particeps, in his mirifice acqui-scit. Hoc idem & affectus testes locupletissimi ac domestici demonstrant. Quoties mens desolu-tione ac segregatione sui à corpore cogitat, im-perterrita consistit,neq; angitur magnopere. Scit se immortalem esse, & in meliorem conditionem transituram: Scit se tum demum à sordibus cor-poris expurgatum iri; Scit se ex carcere in libertatem, ex tenebris in lucem, ex tristitia in gaudium descensuram. Quod & Socrates in Phædone ait; naturale esse hominibus desiderium sciendi, & sapi-entia, quae cum in hac vita exigua contingat, quas[?] du-bitare ausit[?], quin aliquando haec cupiditas incredibilis & sempiterna satietate expleatur. In hac vita, ut Aristoteles acutissimè demonstravit, mens nostra ad scientiam se habet, quemadmodum oculi noctuarum ad lucem. Quare certissimè hinc evincitur, aliam esse vitā reconditā, ac suo tempore patefa-ciendam. Sensus nostri quoties illi de morte cogi-tant, illico percelluntur, membra pallescunt, sanguis refrigescit, & ad interiora se recipit. Quid ex his efficitur? annō morte manifeste contra mentis naturam esse videmus? Testatur hoc quoq; συνείδησις[?] omnium animis insita, & cruciatus con-scientiae in sceleratis. Quis n. est, aut quis unquam fuit audacia tā ardeti, aut cupiditatibus tā effrenatis, q nō ex ardescēte cōscientia exhorrescat, qui non cohibeatur ac cōtremiscat, simul atq; hæca-culeis pūgit, poenae sentiūtur, metuitur judicium, ac interitus animae, qui tñ fieri nequit, exoptatur: Hunc dolore nec dies lenit ulla, ac mitigat, neq; pharmaca licet præstantissima profligant.
units.tr: I now come to the will, from whose actions the nature of the soul may be grasped in such a way that no room is left for doubt. For what affirmation and negation are in the mind, pursuit and avoidance are in the will. This most beautiful arrangement shows the infinite wisdom of God, which is to be admired, and demonstrates that souls were created for a particular end. For who would hand over to destruction an essence so finely adorned with such harmonious actions? The will is infinite and insatiable until it reaches God. He alone fills it; in this life it is not filled. For the will is not the servant of the intellect, but is mistress in her own right, although the intellect goes before it. The mind is to it like an adviser and guide, not to rule and twist it this way and that, but to direct it. The will is free before deliberation; it refers everything to the mind, and restrains itself even while the matter is further investigated. Often too it rejects judgment and strives towards that infinite good, and strains with swift energy. All our senses, utterly alien to these actions, are occupied only with lower things. So too the animals are governed by the appetite for preserving their nature, which is implanted in them by the artifice of nature. They are carried towards this, and desire the good that pertains to prolonging this life, driven and impelled by an inclination of their being. But men, since they know and understand the infinite good, and see that it is useful to them, will it and desire it. Thus this appetite is natural, and since it is natural, it can be satisfied, as Aristotle testifies. For unless it were appeased by a real satisfaction, empty phantoms would be set before our minds, the display of such a good would be empty, and our appetite would never rest, but would be tossed as if by perpetual waves. And this appetite is so implanted in human minds that even those who think everything perishes nevertheless seek and aspire after fame. And indeed, if the mind foresaw nothing for the future, and if it bounded all its thoughts by the same limits within which the span of life is circumscribed, it would not wear itself out with such great labours, nor be increased by so many cares and sleepless nights, nor so often struggle for its life. Now there dwells in every best person a certain virtue which, night and day, stirs and admonishes the mind with the goads of glory, that the remembrance of one's name is not to be dismissed with the time of life, but is to be made equal to all posterity. Therefore, even if no other reason were brought forward, this one alone would convince anyone. But other reasons are added to it, and whoever calls their trustworthiness into doubt is rightly thought to be deprived of the judgment of the mind. For if our mind has actions separate from the body, it is clear that it can subsist without the body, and then at last, as Plato says, when it has gone out from this custody of the body, it recovers its true and living face. So that this may be seen more clearly, who will deny that the agent intellect, free from all composition, understands by itself, always abstracts intelligible things from matter, judges, reasons, divides, defines, demonstrates, orders, and is occupied with itself by itself as with real things, as Plato says? These acts are not performed through the internal senses any more than the external ones, and therefore not by beasts either, which have the same common senses as we do, nor through the body, which is brutish. It remains, then, that the soul accomplishes and governs all these things within itself. It illumines the phantasms presented to it as if with rays, and renders them recollective. The same must be thought of the will, which is not exercised through the body, but within itself needs no instruments, admits none, and cannot admit any. Moreover, since the intellect is reflected upon itself and understands, why, I ask, should we bind it to the body? Why should we throw it into coarse chains, by which it can neither be held nor mixed, much less than iron is mixed with glass? Plato, considering this, describes philosophical regeneration in these words in the Phaedo: "The soul must be separated from the body as quickly as possible, and must be accustomed to gather itself by itself out of the body on every side, and to dwell by itself, as far as possible, both now and hereafter" [δεῖ χωρίζειν ὅτι τάχιστα τοῦ σώματος τὴν ψυχήν, καὶ ἐθίζειν αὐτὴν καθ' αὑτὴν παντάχοθεν ἐκ τοῦ σώματος συναγείρεσθαι, καὶ οἷον κεῖν τὸ δυνατόν, καὶ ἐν τῷ νῦν πειρᾶσθαι καὶ ἐν τῷ ἑπειτα]. The words of this sentiment can be expressed thus: The soul must be separated from the body as quickly as possible, and must be made accustomed by constant practice to gather itself by itself from the body everywhere, and to dwell both in this and in the future age. And the delights of noble minds themselves declare this, which present the essence of the soul to us as if to be seen with the eyes. The more similar the delights are, and the closer their nearness to the thing that is loved, the more lasting, greater and sweeter they are. Plato also indicates this in the Theaetetus: The body of the philosopher, he says, is in the city, but his mind, holding these things cheap or rather making them nothing, is carried to heaven, and, to use the words of Pindar, it searches out the things that are above the heavens and in the heavens, takes delight in these, and joins itself to them. And a little later, explaining our likeness to God, he says: [καὶ πειρᾶσθαι χρὴ, ἐνθένδε ἐκεῖσε φεύγειν ὅτι τάχιστα. φυγὴ δὲ ὁμοίωσις τῷ θεῷ κατὰ δυνατόν, ὁμοίωσις δὲ δίκαιον καὶ ὅσιον μετὰ φρονήσεως. θεῷ γὰρ γνῶσις σοφία γε ἀρε-τὴ ἀλη[?] τὴ ἀληθινὴ, ἡ δὲ ἀγνοία ἀ[?]λαθία καὶ κακία ἐναργὴς] i.e. Therefore one must strive to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. Flight is assimilation to God as far as it can fall to man. That assimilation is justice and holiness joined with prudence. For knowledge of God is wisdom and true, solid virtue, but ignorance of him is folly and manifest vice. Aristotle teaches the same: [τῷ γὰρ οἰκεῖον ἑκάστῳ τῇ φύσει κράτιστον ἢ ἡδύστην ἐστὶ ἑκάστῳ ἢ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ], that is, what is proper to each thing and most convenient to its nature is also most pleasant to it. Although many are found who value the delights of this world more than divine things, who depress the mind and cast themselves into every kind of lust, yet let judgment be made by the sound and whole: let the dregs be left behind, and let us embrace noble minds. These always join themselves to what is their own, take delight in the purity of life, meditate on divine things, associate themselves with them, and strive towards them with all zeal. Hence also arises the sharpest struggle and contention between imagination and mind. The former drags downward towards bodies and rejoices in them; the latter resists by rising to higher and more excellent things, or by lifting itself up. The mind sets out towards those things which are grasped neither by any sense nor by imagination, and at last restrains and curbs imagination, which wanders and roams far and wide through byways. The mind does not incline towards the delights of this life, but recalls the past, conjectures the future, and inquires into the reason of truth and falsehood. Imagination, on the contrary, looks to delights, and if it is steeped in gross pleasures it is glad. Therefore, since eternal things are more akin to the mind than corporeal ones, and it is more a partner and sharer in their nature, it rests wondrously in them. The feelings too, the most abundant and domestic witnesses, show the same. Whenever the mind thinks of its release and separation from the body, it stands fearless and is not greatly troubled. It knows that it is immortal and will pass into a better condition; it knows that it will then at last be purged of the filth of the body; it knows that it will descend from prison into liberty, from darkness into light, from sadness into joy. Socrates also says this in the Phaedo: It is natural for men to have a desire for knowing, and for wisdom; and since in this life it is attained only in small measure, who would dare to doubt that at some time this incredible and everlasting desire will be satisfied with a satiety? In this life, as Aristotle most acutely demonstrated, our mind stands towards knowledge as the eyes of owls do towards the light. Therefore it is most certainly proved from this that there is another life, hidden away, and to be revealed in its own time. Our senses, whenever they think of death, are at once struck with dread: the limbs grow pale, the blood cools and withdraws into the inner parts. What follows from these things? Do we not see clearly that death is contrary to the nature of the mind? The consciousness implanted in the minds of all bears witness to this as well, and the torments of conscience in the wicked. For who is, or who has ever been, so fiery in audacity or so unbridled in desires, that he does not shudder at a burning conscience, that he is not restrained and does not tremble, as soon as the stings of the scourges are felt, punishment is perceived, judgment is feared, and the destruction of the soul, which nevertheless cannot come about, is desired? No day soothes or mitigates this grief, nor do the most excellent medicines drive it away.

units.la: Præterea si mens unà cum sensibus interiret, nō minus quàm illi in res terrenas intenta esset, summumque bonum sicut & illi in his terrestribus collocaret. Verum si hoc statuatur, longè multumq; superamur à bestiis, quibus terra fundit ex sese pastus varios, varieq; abundantes nihil laborantibus; at nobis vix aut ne vix quidem suppetunt multo labore quærentibus. Quinetiam quid miserius homine; quid tristius mundus aleret? Illias esset malorum. Hinc Socrates in Phædone exclamat de corporis incommoditatibus conquerens; ἕως ἂν τὸ σῶμα ἔχωμεν[?]· ἡ ξυμπεφυρμένη ἡμῖν ψυχὴ μετὰ τῆς τοιαύτης κακῆς[?], ἢ μήποτε κτησόμεθα ἱκανῶς[?], ἢ ὑπὸ[?] ... μυρίας δὲ ἀσχολίας παρέχει τὸ σῶμα,&c. id est, Quamdiu hoc corpore utimur, ac anima tali malo quodammodo obsessa ac permixta est, non consequimur, quod cupimus. Nam innumerabiles molestias corpus parit, ita ut verum omninò sit per corpus nullo modo nobis licere sapere. Bella enim seditiones atque pugnas corpus excitat & corporis cupiditates. Hæ ubi rationis imperiū excusserunt, lasciviunt atque exultant, & in quod cunque nefas, (ut Poetæ verbis utar) descendere non dubitant. Bestiæ hisce curis levatæ nec repugnantibus studiis in contrarias partes abripiuntur, sed quod appetitus suadet consectantur, eoq; feliciores essent, quàm homines.
units.tr: Moreover, if the mind perished together with the senses, it would be no less intent upon earthly things than they are, and it would place the highest good, as they do, in these earthly things. But if this were granted, we would be far surpassed by the beasts, to whom the earth pours forth of its own accord various and abundant foods, without any labour on their part; whereas for us such things scarcely, or hardly at all, are at hand, even for those who seek them with much toil. Indeed, what is more wretched than man, and what more miserable would the world be? It would be full of evils. Hence Socrates in the Phaedo, complaining of the discomforts of the body, exclaims: "As long as we have the body, and our soul is mingled and bound up with such an evil, we never attain what we desire. For the body brings us countless troubles," so that it is altogether true that through the body we can in no way be wise. For the body stirs up wars, seditions and battles, and the body's desires. When these have cast off the rule of reason, they run riot and exult, and do not hesitate to descend into whatever wickedness (to use the words of the poet). Beasts, freed from these cares and not hindered by conflicting pursuits, are not dragged off in opposite directions, but follow what appetite urges; and for this reason they would be happier than men.

units.la: Hæc argumenta omnia licet ex veteri & vera Philosophia deprôta sint, quibus Philosophi saniores tanq; telis ac armis Sophistarū rationes everterūt ac profligarunt: tamen ut manifestius id fiat, paucis locis ex Aristotele & Platone indicabo, q̃ concors quoq; & cŏsentiēs hac de re fuerit horū præclarissimorū virorū sententia. Et ꝑfectò hic mihi ipsum Aristotelē loquentem, deq; iniu- riis conquerentem audire videor. Egóne quod divinum est, quod simplex & ab omni concretio ne alienum est, corruptioni obnoxium dicerem? Egóne simílem bestiis hominem divinissimum animal facerem? Egóne qui artes divagantes ac palantes revocavi, dissipatas in ordinem coëgi, illustravi, explicavi in præcipuo Philosophię dog mate tàm turpiter hæsitarem? Erras profectò qui cunque hæc dicis. Legę ac perpende scripta mea, ne desidia pigritiaque torpescas. Quare auditores repetite mecum ὁμοιότητα sententiarum Aristotelis dulcissimam, quæ licet innumeræ occurrant, tamen brevitatis ergo paucis contenti erimus. Quid verò illustrius ac significantius illo, qui de anima libro 1. occurrit loco contex: 66. ubi expresse notat animum divinum & passionis expertem esse. Cætera, ait, cupiditates destruuntur: at mens nullis machinis nullaq; corruptione exstinguitur. Sic & lib. 2. contex: 22. ait: τὸ δὲ νοῦς ... φανερὸν ... ἀλλ' ἔοικε ψυχῆς γένος ἕτερον εἶναι, καὶ τοῦτο μόνον ... ἀΐδιον ... θνητοῦ hoc est, De mente verò nondum manifestum est, sed hæc videtur aliud animæ genus, & sola separatur tanquam æternum à corruptibili. Quid verò his verbis manifestius dici potest? Sed audiamus illum locū qui lib. 3. cont. 20. extat: Intellectus in actu quo contemplamur, quantum ad operationem, (intellige quatenus per sensus fit) non manet post corpus tamen secundum se ac suum esse immortalis est. Quin & in Metaph. 12. cont. 17. nihil aliud docet, ac intellectum post corpus manere clara voce clamitat. In lib.2.de Generatione animalium cap.5. ab operibus intellectus a corpore separatis, eius immortalitatem probat. Et rursus in physicis de anima lib. 3. cap. 4. & 5. a simplicitate. In Ethic. 10. cap. 7. a coniunctione cum Deo ab actionibus perpetuis & συνεχεστάτοις[?] a felicitate & praemiis, quae post hanc vitam contingent bonis ac ἀϊδίοις[?]. Nam ut ipse loquitur ὁ δὲ νοῦς θεῖός τις ἔοικε ἐγγί-νεσθαι ἀπαθὴς[?] ἢ ἀφθείρεσθαι[?]. Et q d opus est omnium testimoniorum enumeratione, quibus recensendis vix dies sufficiat. Suffragantur etiam atq; nobiscum consentiunt doctissimi Aristotelis inter-pretes ac discipuli, qui praeceptorem suum a tali calunia liberant, Theophrastus, Simplicius, Philoponus atq; alii eruditione praestantes viri. Praetereo hic Graecorum & Latinorum saniorum judicium & laudis praeconium, quo Philosophum iure optimo condecorant.
units.tr: Although all these arguments are drawn from the old and true philosophy, by which the wiser philosophers overthrew and routed the reasonings of the sophists as with weapons and arms, nevertheless, so that this may be made clearer, I shall point out in a few places from Aristotle and Plato how concordant and consistent the opinion of these most distinguished men was on this matter. And indeed I seem to hear Aristotle himself speaking here and complaining of the wrongs done to him. "Would I call that which is divine, which is simple and free from all composition, subject to corruption? Would I make man, the most divine of animals, like the beasts? Would I, who recalled the wandering and straying arts, brought the scattered ones into order, illuminated and explained them, hesitate so shamefully on the chief doctrine of philosophy? You are certainly mistaken, whoever says these things. Read and weigh my writings, lest you grow numb with sloth and laziness." Therefore, hearers, repeat with me the most pleasant agreement of Aristotle's opinions; and although they occur in countless places, we shall be content with a few for the sake of brevity. What is clearer or more significant than that passage which occurs in the first book On the Soul, at chapter 1 (text 66), where he expressly notes that the mind is divine and free from passion? "The other faculties," he says, "are destroyed by desires; but the mind is extinguished by no machinations and no corruption." So also in the second book, at chapter 2 (text 22), he says: "Concerning the mind it is not yet manifest... but it seems to be a different kind of soul, and this alone... is eternal, and is separated from the perishable, as the eternal from the corruptible." What can be said more plainly than these words? But let us hear that passage which stands in the third book, at chapter 4 (text 20): "The intellect in the act by which we contemplate, as regards its operation (that is, insofar as it occurs through the senses), does not remain after the body; yet in itself and in its own being it is immortal." Indeed, in Metaphysics 12, at chapter 7 (text 17), he teaches nothing other than that the intellect remains after the body, and loudly proclaims it. In the second book On the Generation of Animals, chapter 5, he proves its immortality from the works of the intellect, which are separate from the body. And again in the Physics, On the Soul, book 3, chapters 4 and 5, from its simplicity. In the Ethics, book 10, chapter 7, from its union with God, from its perpetual and most continuous actions, and from the happiness and rewards which the good will receive after this life. For, as he himself says: "The intellect seems to be something divine that comes into being, impassible and incorruptible." And why is there need of an enumeration of all the testimonies, which would scarcely be finished in a day? The most learned interpreters and disciples of Aristotle also support us and agree with us, who free their teacher from such a charge: Theophrastus, Simplicius, Philoponus and other men distinguished in learning. I pass over here the judgment and the praises of the wiser Greeks and Latins, with which they rightly honour the philosopher.

units.la: Ad Platonem Deum Philosophorum, ut Cicero ait, iam venio, qui adeo claris expressis ac perspicuis verbis animae immortalitatem asserit, ut saepe non Philosophum, sed Theologum te audire putes. Hinc eius pulcerrimae Philosophiae laudationes, quod sit ἐπανόδος ψυχῆς ἐκ νυκτερινῆς ἡμέρας εἰς ἀληθινὸν τῷ ὄντι[?] αὐγήν[?], hoc est, q;[?] sit egressio animi ex diurnis tenebris in veram Entis lucem. Hinc alia praeclara dicta occurrunt, quibus nos a corporis voluptatibus dehortans ad iustitiae & Sanctitatis studium traducere conatur.
