Quā-vis vero Platonis sententia nunquam sit in dubium devocata, tamen argumenta eius, quibus in Phædone utitur breviter in lucem aspectumque afferam, ubi primum ait: Si omnis motus in contrarium fit, est ergo anima immortalis, alioqui motus finiretur, & omnia morte adobruta ad vitam nunq[?] pervenirent. Deinde à reminiscentia pro-bat, quæ sententia[?] licet ab Aristotelis Philosophia discedat, tñ à nostro instituto aliena dici nequit. Tertio, quod in homine visibile sit & invisibile. Visibile corrumpatur, invisibile codē semper se mo do habeat. Quarto à dignitate & præstantia animæ collata cum corporis partibus. Hinc.n.animam τῷ θείῳ ἢ ἀθανάτῳ ἢ νοητῷ ἢ μονοειδεῖ ἢ ἀδιαλύτῳ[?] similem esse cōtendit. Quin & alias subiicit causas ab honesta sepultura in Ægypto usitata atque observata. Præterea quicquid corrumpitur, id à contrariis dissolvi necesse est. Contrariorum n. pugna atq; contentio omnis corruptionis causa est. Qua ratione vero anima dissolvetur, in qua nulla existit contrarietas: Elementa, ignis, aër, aqua, & terra in animam nihil iuris imperiiq; sibi vendicat, nec mors ea opprimere potest, licet eam separet. Tantum igitur abest, ut aliquid à morte detrimenti accipiat anima, ut potius expurgetur ac libertati restituatur. Denique, lib. 10. de Repub. à pœnis impiorum, quæ in hac vita non infliguntur, & præmiis quibus boni non exornantur, Animæ immortalitatem demonstrat, quo argumento Apostolus quoq; judicii certitudinem declarat. Sic.n. Plato loquitur eo quo dixi loco: ἐπειδὴ καὶ τυγχάνουσί τινα φύσιν οἱ ἀνδραποδώδεις [illegible, ~12 letters] οἱ δὲ ἀπεικέστατοι πᾶν πιέζοντες ὅπως ἂν εἰς τὸν ἐ-[?] πείτω νεντα χρόνον δ' ἀκίνησιν[?]. Ὁ δὲ [illegible, ~3 letters] ἐγὼ τεκμήριον πιστ-[?] μφ[?], ὅτι ἐκ τῆς αἰσθήσεως τοῖς πνευμάτων τῶν ἐνθάδε[?]. αἱ δὲ βέλτιστοι ψυχαὶ μαντευόντων [illegible, ~4 letters] ἕτως ἔχειν[?]. αἱ δὲ μοχθηρότεραι ἢ φασι, κυνλωπέσ δὲ τῶν θείων ἀνδρῶν μαντικὴν [illegible, ~3 letters] ἢ τὰ [illegible, ~2 letters] μή[?], id est: Quoniam autem accidit, ut illi, qui bestiali sunt ingenio semetipsos nihil curent: Ingenui vero omnia sua studia dirigant eo, ut postea immortali gloria vivant. Hinc ego colligo generosissimas mentes praesentione animi cognoscere animae immortalitatem, pessimas autem hoc negligere, sensumque illum extinguere. Sed praestantiores sunt divinationes bonorum quam malorum.
units.tr: Now I come to Plato, the god of philosophers, as Cicero calls him, who asserts the immortality of the soul in such clear, express and perspicuous words that you will often think you are hearing not a philosopher but a theologian. Hence come his most beautiful praises of philosophy, that it is the return of the soul from nocturnal day to the true light of Being, that is, "the egress of the mind from the daytime shadows into the true light of what is." Hence other excellent sayings occur, by which he seeks to call us away from the pleasures of the body and to lead us to the pursuit of righteousness and holiness. Although Plato's opinion has never been called into doubt, I shall briefly bring to light and view the arguments he uses in the Phaedo. There he says, first: "If every motion is toward its contrary, then the soul is immortal; otherwise motion would come to an end, and all things, overwhelmed by death, would never return to life." Second, he proves it from reminiscence; and although this opinion departs from the philosophy of Aristotle, it cannot be called alien to our purpose. Third, because in man there is the visible and the invisible: the visible is corrupted, while the invisible always remains in the same condition. Fourth, from the dignity and excellence of the soul compared with the parts of the body. Hence he contends that the soul is like what is divine, immortal, intelligible, uniform and indissoluble. Indeed he adds other causes too, from the honourable burial customary and observed in Egypt. Moreover, whatever is corrupted must necessarily be dissolved by its contraries; for the strife and contention of contraries is the cause of all corruption. But by what reasoning would the soul be dissolved, in which no contrariety exists? The elements, fire, air, water and earth, claim no right or dominion over the soul, nor can death overcome it, although it separates it. So far, therefore, is the soul from receiving any harm from death, that rather it is purged and restored to liberty. Finally, in the tenth book of the Republic, from the punishments of the impious, which are not inflicted in this life, and from the rewards with which the good are not adorned, he demonstrates the immortality of the soul; by which argument the Apostle also declares the certainty of judgment. For Plato speaks thus in the passage I have mentioned: "Since some people are slavish by nature... and the most vicious... press everything, so that in the time to come... [the text here is corrupt]. And I take as a proof of this... that the spirits of the good souls... prophesy... the worse souls... as they say... the prophetic power of the divine men..." That is: "Since it happens that those who are of a brutish disposition care for nothing of themselves, while the noble direct all their efforts so that afterwards they may live in immortal glory. Hence I gather that the most generous minds know by a presentiment of the soul the immortality of the soul, while the worst neglect this and extinguish that feeling. But the divinations of the good are more excellent than those of the wicked."

units.la: Postquam igitur oratio nostra difficiliores scopulos praetervecta est, superest, ut paucis ad argumenta contraria respondeamus. Veritas explicata est: Falsitas iam minore cum negocio patefiet. Percipite igitur ac considerate, quanta cum iniuria Aristoteles defoedatus ac calumniis dilaceratus sit, percipite quanta astutia ac calliditate rectè eius dicta depravata atque adulterata sint. Non enim desunt hodie etiam, qui Aristotelem cū Epicuro componant, & Aristotelæos appellent Epicuræos. Non desunt qui scribant Aristotelem & providentiam Dei & animæ immortalitatem deridere, mentemque quam non è materiæ potentia existere, sed extrinsecus advenire dicat, in suum universum reverti censere, ut occlusis in domo fenestris lux Solis ad ipsum lucis fontem revertitur. Sed quibus argumentis hasce calumniis comprobent Aristotelemastiges illi, deinceps breviter dispiciamus.
units.tr: Now that our discourse has sailed past the more difficult rocks, what remains is to answer briefly the arguments on the other side. The truth has been laid out; the falsehood will now be exposed with less trouble. Consider, then, and weigh how shamefully Aristotle has been disfigured and torn apart by slanders, and how cunningly and craftily his words have been twisted and corrupted. For there are still today some who pair Aristotle with Epicurus and call the Aristotelians Epicureans. Some write that Aristotle mocks both the providence of God and the immortality of the soul, and that he thinks the mind, which he says does not arise from the power of matter but comes from outside, returns into its universal source, just as light shut out of a house by closed windows returns to the very fountain of light, the sun. But let us briefly examine, next, with what arguments those Aristotle-baiters try to prove these calumnies.

units.la: Praetereo autē hic nō Philosophorum iudicia, sed delirantium somnia, ut Cicero ait, quibus animam vel ignem vel aërem vel crasin & spiritus vitales esse somniarunt. Hos enim & Cic. in I usc: Quæst:acerrimè refutat, & Aristoteles in libris de anima non inelegantèr refellit, ad alia argumen-ta ex Aristotele petita sese oratio convertat.
units.tr: Here I set aside not the judgments of the philosophers but, as Cicero says, the dreams of madmen, who dreamed that the soul is fire, or air, or a mixture, or the vital spirits. Cicero, in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations, refutes these most sharply, and Aristotle in his books On the Soul refutes them not inelegantly. Let my discourse turn to the other arguments drawn from Aristotle.

units.la: Cum enim intellectus teste Philosopho Phantasiæ adminiculo opus suum exsequatur, quo pacto a corruptione liber immunisq; erit? Phantasia perit. Intellectus ergo maneret? hoc fieri non posse videtur. Nam si cum ea copulatus ac devinctus est, si quicquid agit ope beneficioque phantasiæ agit, necesse est, ut eodem naturæ fato pereat. Verum quæ tua, qui sic argumentaris, libido, quæ temeritatis meta? quem ad finem se tua jactabit audacia? Nonne & Plato mentem quandoque corporis instrumentis uti affirmat? num verò idcirco mortalem esse asserit? nequaquam. Sed ut falsitas huius obiectionis, quæ non modo aliena est ab Aristotelica Philosophia sed etiam [illegible, ~6 letters] πτωσῶν[?] cum ea pugnat, appareat, breviter quot intellectiones Philosophus docendi causa constituat videndum est. Primum docet aliam esse simplicium rerum, qua simplices naturæ ac termini percipiuntur; aliam qua simplicia componuntur ac coniunguntur: tertiam qua intellectus semetipsum cognoscit. Atque hæ omnes ad patientem intellectum referuntur. Quarta agentis intellectus est propria, qui ut semper est ἐνέργεια, ita & semper intelligit. Hinc iam clarissimè elucet, ad quam intellectionem phantasiæ adminicula requiratur. Secunda qua simplicia componuntur, non tur,non indiget. Hæc enim per se componit, ac ex potestate propinqua in actum quocunque tē-pore libet,pervenire potest. Nam quemadmodū qui lumen manu tenet, is tenebras quascunque depellere potest: Sic & intellectio hæc, quæ sua potentia simplices iam terminos complectitur, continuò coniungit. Tertia multò minus phantasiæ ope eget. Phantasia enim crassa imaginatione concipit. At mens spiritualis est. Illa tantum in iis versatur, cum quibus proportionem simi-litudinemq; habet. At mens pura est, simplex est, ac omnis compositionis expers. Quarta quæ agentis intellectus est propria, nulla ratione cum phantasia communicat. Relinquitur ergo prima patientis intellectus actio, & hanc dissolvi Aristoteles non diffitetur ea tamen lege, ut essentia intellectus inviolata illæsaque permaneat. Atq; hoc ipsum docet Aristoteles iis ipsis locis, ex quibus hæc cavillatio desumta est. Neque etiam hinc intellectum agentem & patientem diversos esse at-que seiunctos sequitur, sed unus idemque est ali-ter atque aliter ad res percipiendas coparatus & affectus. Impiam etiam atq; à Peripatetica Philosophia alienam esse eam sententiam, quæ Aristotelem intellectum agentem animæ partem esse negare docet conspicitur. Nam si anima, quæ cognoscit, immortalis dicitur, nulla ratione intel-lectus patiens aut excludi aut agens ab eo sepa-rari potest. Si quod simplex est, quod à corpore seiungitur, seiunctasque ab eo actiones habet, a-nima humana appellatur, quomodo intellectus agens animæ humanæ pars negabitur? Verum hic alia emergit difficultas dū Philosophus intellectum patientem φθαρτὸν[?] pronunciat. Sed facilis & expedita est responsio, non intellectum, sed compositionem, qua Phantasiæ devinctus est, perire. Neque etiam ideo intellectus agens totius immortalis dicitur, totiesque collaudatur, quasi patiens excludatur & æternitate spolietur, sed quia ille semper suis partibus defungitur, ac phantasmata oblata collustrat. Hoc ipsum & Plato in Phædone explicans scribit. Animum uti corporis ministerio, non tamen αὐτοκινητικῶς[?] ex illis sensibus & facultatibus componi, sed simplicem esse & perseverare etiam morte accelerante & grassante.
units.tr: For since, as the Philosopher testifies, the intellect carries out its work with the help of the phantasy, how will it be free and exempt from corruption? The phantasy perishes. Would the intellect then remain? This seems impossible. For if it is joined and bound to the phantasy, and whatever it does it does by the aid and benefit of the phantasy, then it must perish by the same fate of nature. But what is your lust, you who argue thus, what is the limit of your rashness? Where will your audacity leap to an end? Does not Plato also affirm that the mind at times uses the instruments of the body? Does he therefore say that it is mortal? By no means. But so that the falsity of this objection, which is not only foreign to Aristotelian philosophy but also (...) fights with it, may appear, we must see briefly how many kinds of intellection the Philosopher lays down for the sake of teaching. First, he teaches that there is one kind by which the simple natures and terms of simple things are grasped; another by which simple things are composed and joined together; a third by which the intellect knows itself. And all these are referred to the passive intellect. The fourth is proper to the agent intellect, which, as it is always actuality, so it always understands. Hence it shines out most clearly to which kind of intellection the aid of the phantasy is required. The second, by which simple things are composed, does not need it. For this composes through itself, and can pass from proximate potency into act at whatever time it pleases; for just as one who holds a lamp in his hand can drive away whatever darkness, so this intellection, which by its own power already grasps simple terms, immediately joins them together. The third needs the help of the phantasy far less. For the phantasy conceives by a gross imagination, but the mind is spiritual. The phantasy is occupied only with those things with which it has proportion and likeness; but the mind is pure, simple, and free of all composition. The fourth, which is proper to the agent intellect, in no way communicates with the phantasy. There remains, therefore, the first action of the passive intellect, and Aristotle does not deny that this is dissolved, on the condition, however, that the essence of the intellect remains unviolated and unharmed. Aristotle teaches this very thing in the same places from which this cavil has been drawn. Nor does it follow from this that the agent and the passive intellect are diverse and separate; rather, it is one and the same, disposed and affected in different ways for perceiving things. It is also seen that the opinion which teaches that Aristotle denies the intellect agent to be a part of the soul is impious and alien to Peripatetic philosophy. For if the soul that knows is called immortal, the passive intellect can in no way be excluded, nor the agent be separated from it. If that which is simple, which is separated from the body and has actions separated from it, is called the human soul, how will the agent intellect be denied to be a part of the human soul? But here another difficulty arises, since the Philosopher pronounces the passive intellect perishable. But the answer is easy and simple: it is not the intellect that perishes, but the composition by which it is bound to the phantasy. Nor is the agent intellect called immortal as a whole, and so often praised, as though the passive were excluded and deprived of eternity; rather, because that one always performs its own functions and illuminates the phantasms presented to it. Plato too, explaining this very thing in the Phaedo, writes: the soul uses the body's service, yet it is not composed, in the manner of self-moving things, of those senses and faculties, but is simple and persists even when death is hastening and raging.

units.la: Præterea nos quibus illustrior cognitio contingit, de hisce facilius iudicare possumus. Quod enim animus sæpe vehementia affectuū abripitur, ad res terrenas pertrahitur, & deniq; multa non nisi per crassa instrumenta percipit, eius immortalitatem interitumque non constituit. Quod & Plato libro 10. de Rep: contendit injustitiam animam in nihilum nō redigere, sed potius hinc immortalitatem sequi propter pœnas nunquam desituras. Hoc quidem Philosophi ex parte viderunt, non tamen penitus fontem scaturiginemq; cognoverunt, plus mali in orbe grassari quàm boni Aristoteles perspexit. Et Homerus duo mali dolia ad sellam Iovis collocata fingit, cum tantum unum vas ex quo promanet bona dicat. Sed hæc imperfecta sunt, & non satis ab illis cognita exploratáque[?].
units.tr: Moreover, we who have a clearer knowledge can judge these matters more easily. For the fact that the mind is often carried away by the violence of the passions, is drawn down to earthly things, and finally perceives many things only through gross instruments, does not establish its immortality or its destruction. Plato too, in book 10 of the Republic, contends that injustice does not reduce the soul to nothing, but rather that immortality follows from it, on account of punishments that will never cease. The philosophers indeed saw this in part, yet they did not fully know the source and fountain; Aristotle perceived that more evil than good rages in the world. And Homer feigns two jars of evil placed at the seat of Jove, while he says that only one vessel from which good flows forth exists. But these things are imperfect and were not sufficiently known and examined by them.

units.la: Ad alias obiectiones me converto. Cum teste Aristotele in physicis de formis corruptibilibus agatur, anima quæ forma est corporis ab interitu vindicari non posse videtur. Aut enim libri de anima conscripti ad physicam non pertinebunt, q;[?] Philosophus expressis verbis negat; aut sibi adversatur atque repugnat. Verùm neutrum cōsequi manifestissimè apparebit, si quid per formas corruptibiles intelligat animadvertamus. Per has profecto non animam denotari satis liquet, quam totiès immortalem pronunciat, & ab interitu liberam solutamque asserit. Quo magis etiam miror, quod ex quibusdam verbis, cæteris quæ repugnant præteritis Aristotelis sententia deformetur. Sed aliter profecto agendum est, ubi contraria sententia & verbis firmata, & argumentis satis corroborata est. Nominat verò Philosophus formas ipsa corpora, quæ qualitatum contrarietate sunt instabilia. De anima intelligi nequit, quæ ex traduce nec educitur, nec rursus resolvitur. Vel si quis acrius urgeat, & hæc minus sufficere putet, tamen Aristoteles[?] nulla pugnantia ascribi potest. Corrumpitur enim anima morte sæviente non in se ac essentiæ ratione, sed forma corporis esse desinit, neque illud amplius informat, non regitac moderatur, non instrumentis eius nititur. Quocirca illud vulgare ex Aristotele desumtum nihil nostræ sententiæ detrahit, aut eius veritatem minuit, ubi omne genitum corruptibile dicitur. Non enim ibi de simplicibus naturis ab omni compositione liberis disserit, sed hoc principium in Platonicos dirigit, qui mundum incepisse docebant, & tamen in perpetuum duraturū statuebant. Verum ex sententia nostri Philosophi anima nō per motum generando proçreatur, nec corporis ad-miniculo perficitur.
units.tr: I turn now to other objections. Since, as Aristotle testifies in the Physics, the discussion concerns corruptible forms, the soul, which is the form of the body, seems unable to be freed from perishing. For either the books written On the Soul will not pertain to physics, which the Philosopher expressly denies, or he contradicts and conflicts with himself. But that neither follows will become very clear if we notice what he means by corruptible forms. Certainly it is quite clear that the soul is not denoted by these, since he pronounces it immortal so often and asserts that it is free and released from perishing. I wonder all the more that Aristotle's opinion is distorted from certain words, while the other passages that contradict it are passed over. But surely one must act otherwise where the contrary opinion is both confirmed by words and sufficiently strengthened by arguments. The Philosopher, however, names as forms the bodies themselves, which are unstable by the contrariety of their qualities. The soul cannot be understood as among these, since it is neither generated from a traducing nor again dissolved. Or if someone presses more sharply and thinks even these insufficient, still no contradiction can be ascribed to Aristotle. For the soul is not corrupted, when death rages, in itself or in the reason of its essence, but ceases to be the form of the body; it no longer informs that body, nor rules and governs it, nor relies on its instruments. Wherefore that common saying taken from Aristotle, that "everything generated is corruptible," takes nothing away from our opinion, nor diminishes its truth, where it is stated. For he does not there discourse on simple natures free from all composition, but he directs this principle against the Platonists, who taught that the world had a beginning, and yet held that it would endure forever. Indeed, in the opinion of our Philosopher, the soul is not begotten by motion in generation, nor is it perfected with the help of the body.

units.la: At dicet quispiam: Si anima movetur, si loco circūscribitur, qui immortalis esse potest? Quod enim motu regitur divisibile est, ratione loci & temporis, quod loco cingitur partem extra partem habet, ac corporea substantia censeri solet. Verum res hic aliter habet. Non.n.omne quod loco cōtinetur divisionem admittit. Sicut nec angeli in cœlo versantes divisionem patiuntur, nec in terra existentes à nobis cōmensurari possunt. Sufficit itaque ut loca definiantur. Et hoc ipsum finitioni Aristotelis non repugnat. Neque etiam necesse est in anima partem moventem & motū dari. Principia namque ista aut non tollunt motum simplicium essentiarum, aut præcipuè corporibus naturalibus competunt, ut locus & divisibilitas.
units.tr: But someone will say: If the soul is moved, if it is circumscribed by place, how can it be immortal? For what is moved by motion is divisible; what is contained by place, by reason of place and time, has part outside part, and is usually regarded as corporeal substance. But here the matter is otherwise. For not everything that is contained by place admits division. Just as angels, dwelling in heaven, suffer no division, nor can those existing on earth be measured by us. It is therefore enough that places be defined; and this itself does not conflict with the definition of Aristotle. Nor is it necessary that a moving part and a moved part be given in the soul. For those principles either do not remove the motion of simple essences, or they belong chiefly to natural bodies, such as place and divisibility.

units.la: Verum ut ad finem oratio mea properet, ultimum restat argumentum, quo ipse Aristoteles de immortalitate animorum dubitationem movet, in Ethicis ad Nicomachum scriptis. Sed age videamus quid isto loco doceat. Statuit homines defunctos versari vel in statu felicitatis vel miseriæ. Deinde eorum felicitatem qui secundū virtutem vixerunt non posse depravari actionibus posterorum malis, & miseriam mortuorum non posse emendari. Aperte enim concludit τοιαῦτα [?] ἡ τηλικαῦτα ὥστε μὴ πτῆσις [?] δαίμονας μὴ δαίμονας ποιεῖν. μήπε ἄλλο [?] τῶν μηδὲν. Hæccine est dubitatio an conclusio manifestissima? Quis quæso tàm omni judicio spoliatus est, qui non videat claris elaris ac perspicuis verbis dubitationem propo-sitam ab Aristotele solvi, quis tàm insignis impu-dentiæ, qui hinc occasionem calumniandi su-mat? Dubitet igitur Plutarchus de sententia Ari-stotelis. Vocet eam in disputationem Galenus, qui in multis seditiones movit Philosophicas: di-gladientur alii, ac Aristotelem Rhetorum more verbis hæc exornasse; suamque sententiam te-xisse dicant. Nobis innocentia eius constat, nobis veritas potior est atque antiquior quàm glo-riolæ inanis aucupium. Quare, Commilitones, si ea quæ dixi sole ipso illustriora sunt, si omnia dixi hausta è fonte naturæ, si tota oratio sibifi-dem ipsis sensibus incorruptis ac integris testibus confirmat, quis est cui sana Philosophia non placeat? quis non addiscat iàm admirabilem tàm jucundam, tamque utilem doctrinam, cuius be-neficio ad disciplinas maximas pervenitur. Quis non Aristotelis Platonisq; scripta legat ac amet, qui viri singulari studio artes excoluerunt, amplificarunt, & venustiores illustrioresque ad nos transmiserunt. Et cum cæterae animantes ad pa-stum abiectæ, solus homo creatus sit, & ad cœli quasi cognationis domiciliique pristini conspe-ctum excitatus, cum species oris ita formata, ut in ea recondití mores effingantur, cum denique oculi quomodo mente affecti simus loquantur, illud diligenter studioseque nobis consideran-dum est, quod Plato in Phædone monet, ἡ ψυ- χὴ ἀθάνατος ἐστι [?] ἐπιμελείας δεῖ [?] πολλῆς [?] ὅπερ τὸ [?] τοῦτο [?]. μόνον ἐν ᾧ καλεῖσθαι τὸ ζῷον, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυ- χῆς, καὶ ὁ κίνδυνος νῦν δὴ καὶ δόξειεν ἂν μάλιστα δει- νὸς εἶναι. νος εἶναι, εἰ τῆς αὐτῆς ἀμελήσειεν[?], h.e. Quoniam im-mortalis est animus, non tantum de illo curam gerendam esse ejus temporis ratione, quod vita nomine defi-nimus, sed universi etiam, quod post hanc vitam reli-quum. Et grave quidem nunc videatur periculum, si quis ipsum animum neglexerit. Expoliamus itaque animam sapientiae studio, expleamus ejus deside-rium rerum divinarum epulis, ut satiati hisce bonis in aeternum cum Deo & sanctis angelis vivamus.
units.tr: But so that my discourse may hasten to its end, there remains one last argument, by which Aristotle himself raises doubt about the immortality of souls, in the books he wrote to Nicomachus on ethics. Yet come, let us see what he teaches in this place. He lays down that the dead remain either in a state of happiness or of misery. Then he holds that the happiness of those who lived according to virtue cannot be corrupted by the evil actions of their descendants, and that the misery of the dead cannot be remedied. For he clearly concludes that such things, or things of such magnitude, do not make men gods from being non-gods... [the Greek is corrupt here and cannot be recovered with certainty]. Is this a doubt or the most manifest conclusion? Who, I ask, is so stripped of all judgment that he does not see that the doubt proposed by Aristotle is solved in clear, plain and perspicuous words? Who is of such remarkable shamelessness that he takes from this an occasion for slander? Let Plutarch therefore doubt the opinion of Aristotle. Let Galen call it into dispute, who has stirred up many philosophical quarrels. Let others wrangle over it, and say that Aristotle, in the manner of the rhetoricians, adorned these matters with words and concealed his own opinion. For us his innocence is established; for us truth is more powerful and more ancient than the empty hunting after vain glory. Wherefore, my fellow soldiers, if what I have said is clearer than the sun itself, if I have said everything drawn from the fountain of nature, if the whole discourse confirms itself with the senses themselves, uncorrupted and whole as witnesses, who is there whom sound philosophy does not please? Who does not learn this now admirable, so pleasant and so useful a doctrine, by whose benefit one arrives at the greatest disciplines? Who does not read and love the writings of Aristotle and Plato, who men of singular zeal cultivated and enlarged the arts, and handed down to us more graceful and more illustrious? And since other living creatures are cast down to pasture, while man alone is created and raised up to the sight of heaven, as it were his kinship and former dwelling, since the form of the countenance is so shaped that hidden manners are portrayed in it, and since finally the eyes speak of how we are affected in mind, we must diligently and eagerly consider what Plato warns in the Phaedo: [Greek: ἡ ψυχὴ ἀθάνατος ἐστι] "Since the soul is immortal, much care must be taken not only of that time which we define by the name of life, but of the whole, which remains after this life. And the danger now seems grave, if anyone should neglect the soul itself," that is, "Since the soul is immortal, not only must care be given to that span of time which we call life, but to the whole that remains after this life. Indeed the peril now may seem grave, if anyone should neglect it." Let us therefore polish the soul with the study of wisdom, and satisfy its desire for divine things with the feasts of heaven, so that, sated with these goods, we may live forever with God and the holy angels.

units.la: Dixi.
units.tr: I have spoken.

units.la: FINIS
units.tr: THE END
